• An early invasive strategy including diagnostic coronary angiography (within 2–72 hours of presentation) followed by revascularization (percutaneous coronary intervention/ coronary artery bypass grafting) is indicated for stabilized patients who are at high risk of coronary events (Based on TIMI, GRACE or HEART score).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient comes with palpitation to ER. His Pulse-180/min and BP-70mm of Hg systolic. ECG shows narrow QRS complex tachycardia with regular heart rate. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. DC Cardioversion

The given clinical scenario of the patient presenting with palpitations and the electrocardiogram (ECG) showing narrow QRS complex tachycardia with regular heart rate suggests a paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. As the patient is hemodynamically unstable (SBP of 70 mmHg), the next step in management is DC (direct current) cardioversion.

PSVT is a narrow QRS complex tachycardia with sudden onset and termination. It mainly presents with dizziness and palpitations. Evaluation of these patients includes monitoring of vitals and ECG.

The ECG below shows PSVT.

Management of PSVT is as follows:

1) When the patient is hemodynamically stable:

• Carotid sinus massage is attempted. It is avoided if carotid bruit is present and if a prior history of stroke is present
• Valsalva maneuver is done when the patient is cooperative
• Intravenous adenosine is useful in most cases. It is usually given in a bolus dose of 6 mg (IV bolus over 2-3 seconds followed by a rapid flush with 20 mL NS followed by a dose of 12 mg if required. However, its usage is contraindicated in patients with prior cardiac transplantation as it can aggravate bronchospasm and atrial fibrillation.
• Intravenous calcium channel blockers such as verapamil or diltiazem and beta-blockers are helpful but can cause hypotension.
• If there is no termination of the PSVT, then the next step is IV ibutilide + AV nodal–blocking agent (or) IV procainamide + AV nodal–blocking agent (or) cardioversion.

2) When the patient is hemodynamically unstable, i.e. when the patient has hypotension (BP<90/60) with unconsciousness or respiratory distress, QRS-synchronous DC cardioversion is done.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with massive abdominal swelling. Paracentesis fluid was sent for lab analysis and results show serum protein to be 3g/dL and ascitic fluid protein to be 1g/dL. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Late Budd Chiari syndrome

The likely diagnosis in the given clinical scenario with serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >1.1g/dL [calculated as serum albumin level - ascitic fluid albumin level, which in this case is 3-1=2g/dL] and ascitic fluid protein <2.5 g/dL is late Budd Chiari syndrome.

Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) can be used to differentiate between ascites due to portal hypertension and non-portal hypertensive ascites. It represents the pressure within the hepatic sinusoids and correlates with the hepatic venous pressure gradient.

It is given by the formula: SAAG = Serum albumin level - Ascitic fluid albumin level

Interpretation of SAAG:

• SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates that the ascites is due to increased pressure in the hepatic sinusoids. It reflects the presence of portal hypertension.
• SAAG <1.1 g/dL indicates that the ascites is not related to portal hypertension. It may be due to infection or malignancy.

In cases with high-SAAG (≥1.1), ascitic protein level analysis further helps in identifying the etiology:

• ≥2.5 g/dL indicates that the hepatic sinusoids are normal and are allowing the passage of protein into the ascites as in early Budd-Chiari syndrome.
• <2.5 g/dL indicates that the hepatic sinusoids have been damaged and scarred and no longer allow passage of protein as in late Budd-Chiari syndrome

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with the complaints of chest pain. Which among the following is the best investigation to diagnose MI within 2-4 hours?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Troponin-T

Measurement of troponin is the best investigation to diagnose MI within 2-4 hours.

Troponin T/I:

• Highly specific for MI
• Troponin I is more important than troponin T.
• Troponins will remain elevated longer than creatine kinase (CK), for up to 14 days.
• This makes troponins a superior marker for diagnosing MI in the recent past (late diagnosis).
• Reinfarction: It is now clear that cardiac troponin (cTn) increases rapidly, even if it is from an abnormal baseline in patients with reinfarction.
• Sometimes cTn concentration is elevated, but stable or decreasing at the time of suspected reinfarction. In this case, the diagnosis of reinfarction requires a 20% or greater increase in the cTn measurement

Creatine kinase (CK):

• Less sensitive and specific than troponins
• When cTn is available, CK-MB should not be used for the initial diagnosis of acute MI

Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH):

• Normally, LDH2>LDH1; but, in MI, LDH1>LDH2. This is called flipping of the LDH ratio.
• Current recommendations suggest that LDH no longer has a role in the diagnosis of MI.

Myoglobin:

• Earliest enzyme to increase after MI.
• Not specific to cardiac muscle and can be elevated to any form of injury to skeletal muscle.

Heart-type fatty acid-binding protein (H-FABP), which mainly exists in cardiomyocytes, has recently emerged as a potential biomarker, which was found to be sensitive for the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction. H-FABP as an early marker and cTnI as a late marker would be the ideal combination to cover the complete diagnostic window for AMI

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with vertigo, diplopia, hoarseness, dysphagia, and left Horner’s syndrome associated with numbness of the left face and right side limbs. Which artery is affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Posterior inferior cerebellar artery

These given features collectively indicate a diagnosis of Wallenberg or lateral medullary syndrome, which is typically caused by a lesion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery.

The patient presents with hoarseness and dysphagia, suggesting the involvement of cranial nerves IX and X, which helps localize the lesion to the medulla. Additionally, the presence of vertigo and diplopia (involving the vestibular nerve), left-sided Horner's syndrome (involving the descending sympathetic tract), numbness on the left side of the face (involving the sensory tract of trigeminal nucleus), and numbness in the right side limbs (involving the lateral spinothalamic tract) further aids in localizing the lesion to the lateral part of the medulla.

The absence of motor symptoms suggests that the pyramidal tracts in the medial aspect of the medulla are not involved, ruling out medial medullary syndrome.

Wallenberg/lateral medullary syndrome affects:

• Descending tract and nucleus of CN V- loss of pain and sensation over the ipsilateral half of the face.
• Inferior cerebellar peduncle – ipsilateral ataxia
• Lateral spinothalamic tract – loss of pain and temperature sensation over the contralateral half of the body.
• CN IX and X - ipsilateral paralysis of palate, vocal cord, diminished gag reflex giving rise to dysphagia, dysarthria.
• Vestibular nucleus - Nystagmus, diplopia, vertigo, nausea
• Descending sympathetic tract – ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome (miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman with Grave's disease was taking antithyroid medication throughout her pregnancy. The baby was born with aplasia cutis congenita. Which drug could have caused this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carbimazole

Carbimazole intake during the first trimester of pregnancy is associated with aplasia cutis congenita.

Carbimazole and methimazole are associated with teratogenic effects such as:

• Aplasia cutis congenita: Congenital absence of scalp hair and skin along with calvarial defects
• Choanal atresia
• Tracheoesophageal fistula
• Fetal goiter

The drug of choice for the treatment of hyperthyroidism during the first trimester of pregnancy is propylthiouracil (PTU). It is because it has lower teratogenic effects than carbimazole or methimazole.

However, propylthiouracil use is limited to the first trimester due to the risk of hepatotoxicity. It is replaced with methimazole (or carbimazole) in the second and third trimesters of the pregnancy.

Radioiodine therapy is contraindicated during pregnancy and lactation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An intubated patient in the ICU had a chest X-ray taken to evaluate for fever spikes over the last 24-48 hours. The radiograph is shown below. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
options: Start antibiotics and send samples for culture
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ultrasound-guided aspiration

The given clinical history of an intubated ICU patient and the X-ray features point toward a diagnosis of pleural effusion. Ultrasound-guided aspiration is the next step in the management of the patient. Antibiotics should be started once the pleural tap has been done and infective etiology is suspected.

Options A and B: ET tube suctioning and chest physiotherapy are done to remove thick secretions out of the upper and lower respiratory tract. It wouldn't help in removing the fluid of a pleural effusion.

Pleural effusion is a common finding in the ICU setting and in intubated patients. Many factors contribute to the impairment of pleural fluid turnover in such cases as prolonged recumbency, ventilator-produced positive pressure, and reduced plasma oncotic pressure.

The diagnosis of pleural effusion may be made by clinical examination (dull note on percussion) or by imaging. A pleural tap for confirmation of diagnosis and to relieve breathing difficulty is now done under ultrasound guidance.

The CXR features of pleural effusion include:

• Obliteration of costophrenic angle on the side of pleural effusion
• Air-fluid interface (meniscus sign)
• Large effusions show: Complete opacification of the lung, mediastinal shift, and tracheal deviation away from the effusion

Differential diagnosis in an intubated patient with opacities on CXR might be pneumonitis secondary to gastric acid or food aspiration. But the X-ray would show patchy infiltration unlike the homogenous density seen in pleural effusion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Components of the MELD (2016) score are all except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Albumin

Albumin is not a component of the MELD (2016) score.

The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) is used as an indicator of short-term survival in patients with end-stage liver disease and to determine organ allocation priorities for liver transplantation. The components of the original MELD model were:

• Serum creatinine
• Serum bilirubin
• INR (international normalized ratio)

In 2016, it was modified to incorporate serum sodium (the MELD-Na score).

The latest MELD 3.0 scoring system has added two additional components:

• Serum albumin
• Female gender

Patients with high scores have poor prognoses without intervention and should therefore be prioritized for transplantation if eligible.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Correct sequence after p wave: A- 'a' wave B- 1st heart sound C- Rapid filling of ventricles D- 't' wave
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ABDC

The correct sequence is ABDC.

A - 'a' wave: The 'a' wave in the JVP waveform corresponds to atrial contraction and occurs just after the P wave on the ECG (which corresponds to atrial depolarization) and just before the first heart sound.

B- 1st heart sound: The closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the beginning of ventricular systole produces the 1st heart sound (S1) as the change in pressure across the AV valves causes them to close. This sound occurs soon after the QRS complex on the ECG waveform representing ventricular depolarization.

The x-descent of the JVP waveform is associated with the ventricular systole. The c-wave occurs due to the bulging of the tricuspid valve into the atrium until the semilunar valves open.

D - 'T' wave: Following ventricular depolarization, the ventricles start to repolarize represented by the 'T' wave on  ECG. The 2nd heart sound (S2) occurs due to the closure of the semilunar valves.

C- Rapid filling of ventricles: Ventricular repolarization triggers the ventricles to enter diastole. During early diastole, there is a phase of rapid filling of the ventricles. This occurs as the atrial pressure exceeds the ventricular pressure, allowing blood to passively flow from the atria to the ventricles.

The 3rd heart sound (S3) may be heard here. This event is associated with the v-wave and the y-descent on the JVP waveform as the ventricle relaxes further.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Dialysis will prevent all except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peripheral neuropathy

Dialysis does not prevent peripheral neuropathy. Complications like seizures, metabolic acidosis, and uremic pericarditis can be prevented by dialysis.

Peripheral neuropathy is postulated to be caused due to middle molecules (50-200kDa). Conventionally used dialysis membranes have pore sizes that prevent larger particles (such as middle molecules) from passing through them.

Suggested methods for the removal of middle molecules include:

• High flux dialysis
• Protein adsorptive membranes
• High-cutoff membranes

Aggressive removal of middle molecules or larger low-molecular-weight proteins (LMWPs) has been a growing concern since it causes massive albumin leakage.

β2-microglobulin (B2M),α1-microglobulin (A1M) and albumin leakage during a dialysis session are useful parameters for assessing middle-molecule removal.

Renal transplantation is the best treatment option available for peripheral neuropathy in diabetes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Following is a graphic representation of a patient admitted to the medicine ward with fever. What could be the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Leptospirosis

The given graphical representation of a biphasic illness (acute and convalescent phases) and relevant investigations at different stages of the disease is consistent with a diagnosis of leptospirosis.

Malaria (Option A) is commonly diagnosed by demonstrating malarial parasites in a peripheral blood smear and not in CSF or urine.

Brucellosis (Option B) follows a characteristic pattern of undulating fever.

The mean incubation period in typhoid (Option D) usually ranges from 10 to 14 days and diagnosed based on examination of blood or stool.

Leptospirosis is a zoonotic disease caused by gram-negative Leptospira bacteria (especially L. interrogans). Direct transmission to humans occurs when broken skin and mucous membranes come into contact with the urine of infected reservoir hosts such as rodents.

Illness is classically biphasic after an incubation period of up to 1 month, though the distinction between the first and second phases is not always clear.

• Acute leptospiremic phase-organism can be cultured from blood (within 1 week of onset of symptoms)
• Resolving immune phase-organism can be cultured from urine (after 1 week)

Most cases are characterized by non-specific symptoms (e.g fever, headache, myalgia and conjunctival suffusion) and resolve spontaneously within a week but a few may progress to a severe form known as Weil's disease which typically presents with a triad of hemorrhage, jaundice, and acute kidney injury.

Diagnosis includes:

• Dark-field microscopy of urine or blood samples
• Serological tests

• Four-fold rise in the level of IgM titers within one month of the onset of symptoms
• Microscopic agglutination test (MAT)

• PCR
• Culture on EMJH or Fletchers media

Treatment:

• Mild disease: Oral doxycycline or azithromycin or ampicillin/ amoxicillin
• Severe disease: IV penicillin

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: High anion gap acidosis with low bicarbonate levels is seen in all the following conditions except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Renal tubular acidosis

Renal tubular acidosis causes normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, not high anion gap acidosis.

Normally, in the serum, the total number of cations is equal to the total number of anions. But, a few of the anionic proteins (e.g., albumin), phosphates, sulfates, and organic anions are not measured and this is called an anion gap. It is the difference between measured cations and measured anions and is estimated as:

Plasma anion gap = [Na+] −([Cl-]+[HCO3-])

The normal anion gap ranges between 6-12 mEq/L.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a patient with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), all the following can be used for treatment except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Streptokinase

Streptokinase is not used in the management of non-ST segment elevation MI (NSTEMI). It is a fibrin non-specific plasminogen activator used as a fibrinolytic agent in the treatment of ST-segment elevation MI (STEMI). Aspirin, clopidogrel, and prasugrel are antiplatelet drugs commonly used in the management of NSTEMI.

Fibrinolytic therapy is not indicated in patients with unstable angina or NSTEMI, unlike in STEMI. This is because STEMI is almost always caused by plaque rupture leading to the formation of an occluding thrombus, whereas, NSTEMI can be caused by a stable non-occluding plaque with some amount of lumen still patent. Fibrinolytic therapy may lead to the rupture of the stable plaque causing more damage.

Acute coronary syndrome is classified into 2 groups:

• ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
• NSTE-ACS

NSTE-ACS further includes:

• NSTEMI (myocyte necrosis present and cardiac troponins elevated)
• Unstable Angina (myocyte necrosis absent and cardiac troponins not elevated)

The treatment of NSTEMI is as follows:

• Admission to a specialized cardiac unit
• Inhaled oxygen
• Bed rest with continuous ECG monitoring
• Monitoring cardiac biomarkers
• Morphine or opioid analgesics
• Nitrates
• Beta-blockers
• Antiplatelet drugs like aspirin, clopidogrel, prasugrel

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In the given acid-base nomogram diagram, areas marked A and D indicate which of the following conditions?
options: Chronic respiratory acidosis, acute metabolic alkalosis
Acute Metabolic alkalosis, acute respiratory acidosis
Acute respiratory acidosis, acute respiratory alkalosis
Acute respiratory acidosis, acute metabolic alkalosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute respiratory acidosis, acute respiratory alkalosis

In the given illustrated acid-base nomogram, the letters A and D indicate acute respiratory acidosis and acute respiratory alkalosis.

An acid-base nomogram, also known as a Davenport diagram, is a graphical representation of acid-base balance to interpret arterial blood gas (ABG) results. It helps determine the primary acid-base disorder and identify compensatory mechanisms.

The y-axis of the acid-base nomogram represents the arterial bicarbonate (HCO3-) levels, and the x-axis represents the arterial pH values. The shaded areas are the range of values of the normal respiratory and metabolic compensations for primary acid-base disturbances.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Iritis is seen in all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rheumatoid arthritis

Iritis is seen in all the above conditions except rheumatoid arthritis.

Iritis or iridocyclitis is also known as anterior uveitis.

Anterior uveitis is seen in:

• Ankylosing spondylitis
• Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis
• Psoriasis
• Reactive arthritis
• Systemic lupus erythematosus
• Leprosy

Posterior uveitis is seen in:

• Vogt-Koyanagi Harada syndrome
• Diseases like toxoplasmosis, cysticercosis, coccidioidomycosis, toxocariasis, histoplasmosis
• Infections- Candida, Pneumocystis carinii, Cryptococcus, Aspergillus, and Cytomegalovirus
• Cat-scratch disease, Whipple’s disease, and brucellosis

Both anterior and posterior uveitis is seen in:

• Sarcoidosis
• Behcet's disease
• Inflammatory bowel disease
• Herpes infections, Syphilis, Lyme disease, TB, onchocerciasis

Intermediate uveitis/pars planitis is seen in multiple sclerosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Resistant hypertension is defined as?
options: BP >160/90 mmHg with three or more anti-hypertensives
BP >140/90 mmHg with three or more anti-hypertensives
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. BP >140/90 mmHg with three or more anti-hypertensives

Resistant hypertension is defined as blood pressure being persistently >140/90 mmHg despite taking three or more antihypertensive agents, including a diuretic.

Resistant hypertension is more common in patients aged >60 years than in younger patients.

Resistant hypertension may be related to pseudohypertension (high office blood pressure and lower home blood pressure measurements), nonadherence to therapy, and secondary causes of hypertension including obesity, excessive alcohol intake, and primary aldosteronism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The laboratory investigations of a 65 year old woman revealed a hemoglobin level of 5.4 g/dl, creatinine level of 6 mg/dl, calcium level of 12 mg/dl, potassium level of 4.4 mmol/L. Her urine output in the last 24 hours was 50 ml. Bone marrow aspiration revealed more than 60% of plasma cells. What would be the next appropriate line of management for this patient?
options: Chemotherapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dexamethasone + fluids

The clinical scenario shows a patient with a bone marrow finding of plasma cells >60% which points to a diagnosis of multiple myeloma.

Anemia (Hb- 5.4 g/dl), hypercalcemia (serum calcium-12 mg/dl) and acute kidney injury (creatinine-6 mg/dl, reduced urine output) are myeloma-defining events suggesting end-organ damage.

The most appropriate next step in managing this patient would be to administer fluids to treat the acute kidney injury and hypercalcemia (hypercalcemia is the most common cause of renal failure in multiple myeloma), and prevent further renal impairment. Therefore, among the given options, dexamethasone and fuids would be the best answer.

Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia and its diagnosis requires bone marrow biopsy finding of ≥ 10% clonal bone marrow plasma cells, a serum/urine M component, and at least one of the myeloma-defining events (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia and bone lesions).

Dialysis (Option A) is indicated in the following conditions:

• Pulmonary edema not responding to diuretics
• Uremic pericarditis, uremic encephalopathy or uremic syndrome
• Metabolic acidosis not responding to treatment
• Hyperkalemia

Lenalidomide + Bortezomib + Dexamethasone (Option B) is the preferred treatment in multiple myeloma and can be initiated after initial management of acute kidney injury.

Chemotherapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation (Option D) in transplant-eligible patients prolongs overall survival in multiple myeloma patients.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The serum electrolyte values of a patient weighing 60kg are given below. Calculate the sodium deficit in the patient. pH: 7.42, Na+: 120 mEq/L, serum K+: 4 mEq/L, serum Cl-: 90 mEq/L.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 720 mEq

The sodium deficit is calculated as (target sodium concentration-current sodium concentration) x 0.6 x Body weight (kg).

Substituting the values, sodium deficit = (140-120) x 0.6 x 60 = 720 mEq.

To calculate the sodium deficit in the patient, we first need to determine the target sodium concentration and compare it to the current sodium concentration.

The target sodium concentration can be calculated using the following formula:
Target Na concentration  = (Lower limit of serum sodium concentration + upper limit of serum sodium concentration) / 2

In this case, we assume the lower limit for the serum sodium concentration is 135 mEq/L, and the upper limit is 145 mEq/L.

Target Na concentration = (135 + 145) / 2= 140 mEq/L

Next, the current sodium deficit can be calculated using the following formula:
Sodium Deficit = (Target sodium concentration-current sodium concentration) x Total Body Water (TBW)

Total Body Water (TBW) = Weight (in kg) × 0.6 (assuming 60% of body weight is water); TBW = 60 × 0.6= 36 liters

Sodium Deficit = (140 - 120) x 36 = 20 x 36 = 720 mEq

Therefore, the sodium deficit in the patient is 720 mEq.

Rapid sodium correction of 4–6 mEq/L should be achieved in the first 6 hours of therapy for patients with acute hyponatremia.

The rate of correction should be comparatively slow in chronic hyponatremia: <6-8 mEq/L in the first 24 h and <6 mEq/L each subsequent 24h, so as to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which among the following is the most life-threatening manifestation of CKD?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyperkalemia

Of the given options, hyperkalemia is the most life-threatening complication of chronic kidney disease (CKD) as it can result in cardiac arrhythmias and sudden death.

CKD is staged based on declining glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and albuminuria. The various clinical manifestations occur due to loss of kidney function and accumulation of various uremic toxins (urea, creatinine, and other products of protein metabolism).

Complications of declining kidney function include:

• Volume overload
• Hyperkalemia
• Metabolic acidosis
• Hyperphosphatemia
• Mineral and bone disorders
• Hypertension
• Anemia
• Dyslipidemia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the factors would suggest a risk for a patient with TIA developing stroke in the future according to ABCD2 scoring?
options: SBP >130 mm Hg and DBP > 80 mm Hg
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diabetes

According to the ABCD2 scoring system, which is commonly used to assess the short-term risk of stroke following a transient ischemic attack (TIA), diabetes would suggest a higher risk factor.

Age more than 60 years, SBP more than 140 or DBP more than 90 mmHg, and duration of TIA of 10-59 minutes or more than 60 minutes are other criteria included in the ABCD2 scoring system.

TIA is defined as episodes of stroke symptoms that last for only a brief period of time (<24 hours). The ABCD2 scoring system is most frequently used to calculate the short-term risk of stroke after TIA.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following are true regarding KF ring?

1. Seen in all patients with neurological involvement
2. Is seen only for Wilson's disease
3. Resolves with desferrioxamine
4. Seen in all patients with hepatic involvement
5. Seen in superior and inferior pole of Descemet's membrane
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 5 only

Among the given options only statements 1 and 5 are true.

Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings are seen in almost all patients of Wilson's disease with neurological involvement. It initially appears as a crescent in the superior pole of Descemet's membrane and gradually extends inferiorly, eventually becoming circumferential in shape.

KF rings occur due to copper deposition in the descemet's membrane. It is golden-brown to greenish-brown in color and can be best seen by slit-lamp examination.

The image below shows a KF ring :

While it is a characteristic sign of Wilson’s disease (statement 2), it can also be seen in:

• Primary biliary cholangitis
• Primary sclerosing cholangitis
• Cholestasis

KF rings are present in almost 95% of patients of Wilson's disease with neurological/psychiatric symptoms compared to around 65% of those with hepatic presentations (statement 4).

They disappear on treatment with copper-chelating agents like d-penicillamine (while desferrioxamine is an iron chelating agent) and reappear with disease progression (statement 3).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is false about mycoplasma pneumonia?
options: Can be cultured in a cell-free medium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Responds well to amoxiclav

Mycoplasma does not respond to amoxicillin-clavulanate (amoxiclav).

Mycoplasma is a bacteria that lacks a cell wall. Since beta-lactam antibiotics (amoxiclav) act on the cell wall of the bacterium, they can not be used in the treatment of mycoplasma infection.

The diagnosis of mycoplasma pneumonia (also known as walking pneumonia/ primary atypical pneumonia) can be established by:

• PCR detection of M. pneumoniae in respiratory secretions
• Serological tests for IgM and IgG antibodies to M.pneumoniae in paired serum samples
• Culture: Mycoplasma can be cultured on PPLO agar, a cell-free medium, and shows a typical fried egg appearance

Chest X-ray usually shows B/L peribronchial and perivascular interstitial infiltrates

Treatment options for mycoplasma pneumonia  include:

•  Macrolides (e.g. azithromycin)
•  Tetracyclines (e.g. doxycycline)
•  Respiratory fluoroquinolones. (e.g. levofloxacin)

Azithromycin is the drug of choice for the management of mycoplasma pneumonia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a treatment option in Guillain Barre syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Steroids

Steroids are not used in the treatment of Guillain Barre syndrome (GBS).

GBS is an acute, fulminant, ascending polyradiculoneuropathy that is autoimmune in nature. GBS is caused when immune response/antibodies against external antigens like infections, vaccines, etc target similar proteins present in the person's nervous tissue. Hence the preferred treatment is to neutralize these autoantibodies using IVIg (I.V. immunoglobulins) or plasmapheresis (Option B and Option C).

GBS manifests as rapidly evolving ascending areflexic motor paralysis with or without sensory disturbance. GBS paralysis can also affect the muscles of respiration, possibly leading to death due to respiratory failure. In such cases, ventilatory support (Option D) is needed.

Note: Steroid therapy is used in Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the drug of choice for hairy cell leukemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cladribine

Cladribine is the drug of choice in hairy cell leukemia.

Cladribine is a purine analogue with potent and curative activity against hairy cell leukemia.

Other treatment options for hairy cell leukemia include deoxycoformycin, interferon-alpha, and splenectomy. Chemotherapy-refractory patients are treated with vemurafenib, a BRAF kinase inhibitor. The addition of rituximab results in more durable remissions.

Cladribine is also used to treat CLL, low-grade lymphomas, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, cutaneous T-cell lymphomas, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia.

The major dose-limiting toxicity of cladribine is myelosuppression.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which part of the internal capsule is affected in hemiplegia due to ischaemic stroke?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Posterior limb

The posterior limb of the internal capsule is affected in hemiplegia due to ischaemic stroke.

Motor fibers (cortico-spinal tract) supplying the extremities are present in the posterior limb, hence a lesion in this region may cause hemiplegia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
You are posted as an intern in casualty. An elderly 60-year-old man is brought to you with complaints of chest pain. He has tested positive for COVID. Which of the following features will prompt you to get this patient admitted to dedicated COVID Health Centre?

A. Respiratory rate of 25/min
B. SpO2 93%
C. Multiple comorbidities
D. Chest pain
E. Age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A, B, C, & E only

A, B, C & E are clinical criteria of admission under COVID-19 ward.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with a history of chest pain with each episode lasting for 20-30 minutes and partial response with sublingual nitrate. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy with ST depression and T wave inversion. He is a known case of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and hypercholesterolemia currently on aspirin, atenolol, metformin, and lovastatin. What is the next best step in management?
options: Increase the dose of beta blocker
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Injection enoxaparin

This patient has features of unstable angina / NSTEMI—recurrent chest pain lasting 20–30 minutes, only partial nitrate relief, and ischemic ECG changes (ST depression and flat T waves) in a high-risk patient (HTN, DM, dyslipidemia). The next best step is anticoagulation with LMWH (enoxaparin) to prevent thrombus propagation.

A. IV GTN infusion – Helps symptom control, but does not address thrombosis.

C. Add clopidogrel – Important, but anticoagulation is prioritized first in acute setting.

D. Increase beta-blocker dose – Useful for rate/ischemia control, but not indicated that its not optimal here.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 51-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to chest tightness that started 30 minutes prior to arrival. He has 2 histories of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Initial ECG Shows ST elevation in leads I and aVL. Cardiac enzymes are elevated. Emergent cardiac catheterization in this patient will most likely show occlusion of which of the following arteries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left circumflex artery

ST elevation in leads I and aVL localizes to the high lateral wall of the left ventricle. High-lateral STEMI is most commonly due to occlusion of the left circumflex (LCX) (or a diagonal branch), and among the given options LCX best fits.

A. Distal LAD – Usually causes anterior/apical changes (V3–V6), not isolated I/aVL.

C. Left main coronary artery – Produces widespread ST changes with severe instability, not isolated high-lateral.

D. Right coronary artery – Inferior MI (II, III, aVF) ± RV involvement

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 55-year-old man comes to the OPD due to recurrent episodes of retrosternal chest pain. The episodes occur during physical activity, usually when he climbs stairs or walks uphill, and resolve after he rests for a few minutes. He is prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin to take as needed when the chest pain occurs. This drug is most likely to relieve this patient's symptoms by causing which of the following hemodynamic changes?
options: Decrease in left ventricular end-diastolic volume
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decrease in left ventricular end-diastolic volume

Sublingual nitroglycerin primarily causes venodilation, which reduces venous return (preload). This leads to a decrease in left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV), lowering myocardial wall stress and reducing oxygen demand, thereby relieving exertional (stable) angina.

A. Decrease in heart rate – Not a primary effect of nitrates; reflex tachycardia may occur.

C. Decrease in peripheral arteriolar resistance – Minor effect; arteriolar dilation is not the main mechanism.

D. Increase in coronary blood flow – Limited in stable angina; symptom relief is mainly from ↓ demand, not ↑ supply.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 58-year-old develops sudden hypotension and a new harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border 3 days after an anterior STEMI. There are pulmonary crackles and elevated JVP. The most appropriate immediate confirmation test in this condition is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urgent echocardiography with Doppler

Sudden hypotension with a new harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border 3 days after an MI strongly suggests a mechanical complication, most classically ventricular septal rupture causing an acute left-to-right shunt with pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock. The fastest and most definitive bedside confirmation is urgent transthoracic echocardiography with color Doppler to demonstrate the septal defect and shunt.

Learning Points

• Post-MI mechanical complications often occur 3 to 5 days after infarction.
• Ventricular septal rupture causes a new harsh holosystolic murmur best heard at the LLSB, shock, and pulmonary edema.
• Best immediate confirmation is urgent echo with color Doppler.
• Papillary muscle rupture causes acute severe MR with a new systolic murmur at the apex and flash pulmonary edema, and echo is also the key test.

Management is urgent stabilization and early surgical or percutaneous intervention.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 60-year-old diabetic female presents with acute myocardial infarction. ECG changes include ST elevation greater than 1 mm in lead aVR. The likely localization of thrombosis is in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Left main or proximal LAD

ST-segment elevation ≥1 mm in lead aVR, especially with widespread ST-segment depression in other leads, is a marker of left main coronary artery (LMCA) or proximal left anterior descending (LAD) artery occlusion, or severe triple-vessel disease. It indicates extensive myocardial ischemia and is associated with a high-risk acute coronary syndrome requiring urgent coronary angiography and revascularization.

Why not the other options?

• A. Right coronary artery: Typically causes inferior wall MI with ST elevation in II, III, aVF.
• B. Distal LAD: Usually causes anterior MI but does not typically produce ST elevation in aVR.
• C. Left circumflex artery: Usually causes lateral or posterior MI with ST elevation in I, aVL, V5–V6, not isolated aVR elevation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presented with an acute onset of chest pain radiating to the left arm and diaphoresis. His ECG and cardiac biomarkers show non-ST elevation myocardial infarction. Which of the following will be used in the treatment of this patient? 1. Atorvastatin 2. Aspirin 3. Clopidogrel 4. Low molecular weight heparin 5. Alteplase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3, 4

NSTEMI is a type of Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) characterized by:

• Partial coronary artery occlusion
• Myocardial necrosis
• No ST elevation on ECG

NSTEMI is managed with anti-ischemic, antiplatelet, anticoagulant, and lipid-lowering therapy.

Standard treatment includes aspirin + clopidogrel (DAPT), high-intensity statin (atorvastatin), and LMWH. High-intensity statins are used for:

• Plaque stabilization
• LDL reduction

However in NSTEMI, fibrinolysis is contraindicated because:

• The artery is not fully occluded
• Thrombolysis increases bleeding risk

Fibrinolytics (alteplase) are not indicated in NSTEMI.

Hence, the correct combination is 1, 2, 3, and 4.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department due to severe central chest pain that started a few hours ago. ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads I, aVL, and V1–V4, along with deep Q wave formation over the next several hours. Cardiac catheterization would most likely reveal which of the following?
options: Atherosclerotic plaque obstructing 50% of the coronary artery lumen, no thrombus
Atherosclerotic plaque obstructing 80% of the coronary artery lumen, no thrombus
Ruptured atherosclerotic plaque with fully obstructive thrombus
Significant coronary artery vasospasm causing flow obstruction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ruptured atherosclerotic plaque with fully obstructive thrombus

This patient has an acute STEMI—evidenced by ST-segment elevation in multiple contiguous leads (I, aVL, V1–V4) and subsequent Q-wave formation, indicating transmural myocardial infarction. The most common underlying mechanism is rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with superimposed, completely occlusive thrombus, leading to abrupt cessation of coronary blood flow.

A. and B. Atherosclerotic plaque obstructing 50% or 80% coronary artery lumen without thrombus – Causes stable angina, not STEMI.

D. Significant coronary artery vasospasm causing flow obstruction – Causes transient ischemia (eg, Prinzmetal angina) without Q waves or persistent ST elevation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 61-year-old woman is hospitalized due to chest pressure and shortness of breath. Two days ago her husband died in a car accident. The patient's medical history is significant for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and gout. Five years ago, she was diagnosed with breast cancer and treated with surgery and chemotherapy. Blood pressure is 165/90 mm Hg and pulse is 95/min and regular. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with T-wave inversions in the anterior leads. Diagnostic coronary angiography shows no evidence of obstructive coronary artery disease. The patient is treated medically and discharged home. Four weeks later, repeat echocardiography demonstrates normal left ventricular wall motion and ejection fraction. Which of the following is the likely cause of this patient's initial presentation?
options: Myocardial hypertrophy and fibrosis due to uncontrolled hypertension
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Catecholamine-induced myocardial stunning

This is classic Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy, triggered by intense emotional stress (sudden death of spouse). A surge of catecholamines causes transient myocardial stunning, leading to chest pain, ECG changes, and reversible LV dysfunction with normal coronaries and complete recovery within weeks.

B. Ischemia-induced transmural myocardial necrosis – Would show obstructive CAD and permanent wall-motion abnormality.

C. Myocardial Hypertrophy and fibrosis due to uncontrolled hypertension – Causes chronic diastolic dysfunction, not acute reversible failure.

D. Toxin-induced myocardial injury – Chemotherapy cardiotoxicity causes persistent, not transient, dysfunction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 64-year-old with inferior STEMI becomes hypotensive. JVP is raised. Lungs are clear. What is the most appropriate immediate management for the likely complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isotonic fluid bolus

This patient has right ventricular infarction (RVI) complicating an inferior wall STEMI, suggested by the triad of:

• Hypotension
• Elevated JVP
• Clear lung fields

Right ventricular dysfunction reduces blood flow to the left ventricle, causing preload-dependent hypotension. Therefore, the immediate treatment is volume expansion with an isotonic fluid bolus to improve right ventricular filling and cardiac output.

Why not the others?

• A. IV nitrates → Reduce preload and can precipitate profound hypotension in RV infarction.
• B. IV furosemide → Decreases preload and worsens hemodynamics.
• D. ACE inhibitor → May further lower blood pressure in the acute setting.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 65-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with an acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. The patient undergoes coronary angiography with stent placement in the left circumflex artery, and he is started on therapy with a beta blocker and antiplatelet agents. On day 3 of hospitalization he experiences chest pain. The pain, described as sharp and radiating to his neck and shoulders, is exacerbated by coughing and swallowing. Temperature is 37.5⁰C (99.5⁰F), blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg, pulse is 90/min and regular, and respirations are 20/min. The lungs are clear on auscultation. There is no peripheral edema. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's chest pain?
options: Pericardial inflammation due to autoimmune reaction to necrotic tissue
Pericardial inflammation due to concomitant viral infection
Pericardial inflammation overlying the necrotic segment of myocardium
Recurrent thrombosis of the culprit coronary vessel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pericardial inflammation overlying the necrotic segment of myocardium

This patient’s day-3 post-STEMI, sharp, pleuritic chest pain radiating to the neck/shoulders and worsened by coughing is classic for early post-MI pericarditis (epistenocardiac pericarditis). It occurs due to direct inflammation of the pericardium overlying the necrotic myocardium, typically within 1–3 days after MI.

A. Pericardial inflammation due to autoimmune reaction to necrotic tissue – This is Dressler syndrome, which occurs weeks to months later.

B. Pericardial inflammation due to concomitant viral infection – Would cause pericarditis independent of recent MI timing.

D. Recurrent coronary thrombosis of culprit coronary vessel – Causes ischemic, pressure-like chest pain, not pleuritic pain.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 77-year-old woman is found dead in her home. On autopsy, hemopericardium secondary to ventricular wall rupture is seen. How long before her death did she probably have a myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3–7 days

Free wall rupture typically occurs during the period when the infarcted myocardium is at its structurally weakest — usually day 3 to day 7 post-MI (occasionally up to \~10 days, rarely beyond 2 weeks).

Why this timing:

• By day 1–3, coagulative necrosis has occurred, but the tissue is still reasonably cohesive.
• Around days 3–7, macrophages actively phagocytose and digest the necrotic myofibers (myomalacia cordis), and neutrophilic/granulation tissue infiltration causes maximal structural weakening — collagen deposition hasn't yet caught up to provide tensile strength.
• This makes the ventricular wall most vulnerable to rupture under intraventricular pressure during this window.
• By >2 weeks, granulation tissue matures into fibrous scar, which is mechanically stronger and resistant to rupture.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A patient with exertional angina has 75% proximal LAD stenosis on CT coronary angiography and remains symptomatic despite optimal medical therapy. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)

Patients with chronic coronary syndrome (stable ischemic heart disease) who have significant coronary artery stenosis (≥70%) and persistent angina despite optimal medical therapy (OMT) should undergo coronary revascularization. In patients with single-vessel proximal left anterior descending (LAD) artery disease, PCI with drug-eluting stent implantation is the preferred revascularization strategy in most cases.

Why not the other options?

• A. Repeat CT coronary angiography: Unnecessary, as the diagnosis is already established and symptoms persist despite treatment.
• C. Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG): Generally preferred for left main disease, triple-vessel disease, complex multivessel CAD (high SYNTAX score), or diabetics with multivessel disease, not isolated proximal LAD disease.
• D. Continue medical therapy alone: Inappropriate because the patient remains symptomatic despite optimal therapy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A pregnant female at 37 weeks of gestation with a history of prosthetic heart valves is currently taking warfarin. She comes for a routine antenatal check-up. What is the appropriate management advice?
options: Switch to low molecular weight heparin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Switch to low molecular weight heparin

Warfarin is contraindicated near term due to risk of fetal intracranial hemorrhage and maternal bleeding during delivery. Warfarin crosses the placenta and can cause: Warfarin embryopathy

Major complications include:

• Nasal hypoplasia
• Stippled epiphyses
• CNS abnormalities
• Fetal bleeding

Because of these risks, warfarin is avoided near delivery.

In pregnant women with prosthetic heart valves, anticoagulation should be switched to low molecular weight heparin in the last weeks.

LMWH does not cross the placenta and provides effective anticoagulation.

Immediate delivery is not indicated solely for anticoagulation management.

| Period | Drug

| ------ | ----

| First trimester | Heparin

| Second trimester | Warfarin may be used in some cases

| Near delivery (after 36 weeks) | Heparin / LMWH

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: Autopsy of a 58-year-old woman shows hemopericardium secondary to ventricular wall rupture is seen. How long before her death did she probably have a myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3–7 days

Ventricular free-wall rupture is a classic mechanical complication of acute myocardial infarction and most commonly occurs 3–7 days after the infarct.

During this period:

• Macrophages remove necrotic myocardial tissue.
• The infarcted wall becomes soft and structurally weak.
• Collagen deposition has not yet provided adequate strength.

Rupture can cause:

• Hemopericardium
• Acute cardiac tamponade
• Sudden death

High-yield timeline

• First 24 hours: Arrhythmias are the most common cause of death.
• 3–7 days: Maximum risk of free-wall rupture, ventricular septal rupture, and papillary muscle rupture.
• 1–2 weeks: Granulation tissue forms and rupture risk falls.
• After several weeks: Dense fibrous scar develops.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: Consider the following statements for diagnosing ventricular aneurysm in a patient with recent myocardial infarction: I. Paradoxical impulse on chest wall II. Persistent ST elevation on ECG III. Unusual bulge from cardiac silhouette on X-ray IV. Presence of pulsus paradoxus Which of the above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, II and III

A left ventricular (LV) aneurysm is a late mechanical complication of a transmural myocardial infarction, usually developing 2 weeks to several months after MI. It results from thinning and outward bulging of the infarcted ventricular wall, leading to a dyskinetic, scarred segment.

Why is C correct?

The following findings are characteristic of a ventricular aneurysm:

• I. Paradoxical precordial impulse: Due to dyskinetic outward bulging of the aneurysm during systole.
• II. Persistent ST-segment elevation on ECG: A classic ECG finding that persists weeks after MI without reinfarction.
• III. Bulge in the cardiac silhouette on chest X-ray: Suggests aneurysmal dilatation of the left ventricle.

IV. Pulsus paradoxus is not a feature of ventricular aneurysm. It is classically seen in:

• Cardiac tamponade
• Constrictive pericarditis (occasionally)
• Severe bronchial asthma/COPD

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: Which of the following clinical feature predict a poor prognosis in a patient with acute myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Presence of left ventricular S3

An S3 gallop in acute myocardial infarction indicates left ventricular failure and increased filling pressures, reflecting significant myocardial dysfunction and is a strong predictor of poor prognosis.

A. Tachycardia – Common stress response; concerning but less specific for prognosis.

B. Bradycardia – Often transient (especially inferior MI) and not independently poor.

D. Raised JVP – Seen in right ventricular infarction; prognosis depends on response to therapy, not universally poor.

questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 35-year-old woman comes to the OPD for a routine physical examination. The patient reports occasional palpitations but has no other chronic medical problems. She has caries of right upper molar tooth and is due to have an extraction next week. She has no significant medical history but had been told that she has "a murmur." The patient's only medication is a daily oral contraceptive. She lives a sedentary lifestyle and reports no dyspnea on routine activity. She developed hives with use of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in the past. Blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg and pulse is 70/min. Physical examination shows no jugular venous distension in the upright position. Normal vesicular breath sounds are heard on chest auscultation. A late systolic murmur heard over the apex prolongs with the Valsalva manoeuvre. Which of the following is recommended for this patient prior to the procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. No antibiotics

This patient has mitral valve prolapse (MVP)—suggested by a late systolic murmur at the apex that increases with Valsalva. Current guidelines recommend infective endocarditis prophylaxis only for high-risk cardiac conditions (eg, prosthetic valves, prior endocarditis, certain congenital heart diseases, cardiac transplant with valvulopathy). MVP without prior endocarditis is not an indication, even before dental extraction.

A. IV ampicillin / D. Oral amoxicillin – Used only when prophylaxis is indicated (not here).

B. IV cefazolin – Alternative for penicillin allergy when prophylaxis is required.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 48-year-old man with a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is undergoing a stress ECG for evaluation of his cardiac function for which a drug has been administered. Pre-test resting ECG reveals a QRS duration of 90 msec (normal: 80-120 msec) and a corrected QTc interval of 400 msec (normal: ≤440 msec). Post-test ECG findings during exercise show a QRS duration of 130 msec with QTc interval of 500msec. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of these ECG findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Quinidine

• Quinidine is a Class IA antiarrhythmic.
• It blocks fast Na⁺ channels → slows phase 0 depolarization → QRS prolongation.
• It also blocks K⁺ channels → prolongs phase 3 repolarization → QT interval prolongation.

Linking to the ECG changes:

• QRS: 90 → 130 ms → due to Na⁺ channel blockade
• QTc: 400 → 500 ms → due to K⁺ channel blockade

Both changes are classic for Class IA drugs, especially quinidine.

Exam takeaway:

• Class IA (Quinidine, Procainamide, Disopyramide) → ↑ QRS + ↑ QT
• Risk: Torsades de pointes due to QT prolongation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 69-year-old man comes to the OPD due to a 6-month history of chest tightness when he walks uphill or climbs stairs. Cardiac examination reveals no murmurs or additional heart sounds. The patient is prescribed a medication that is metabolized to S-nitroso thiols in the vascular smooth muscle cells, and he reports rapid and significant symptom relief. Which of the following components of the cardiovascular system is most susceptible to the medication prescribed to this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Large veins

The drug described is an organic nitrate (eg, nitroglycerin), which is metabolized in vascular smooth muscle to S-nitrosothiols → nitric oxide (NO). NO increases cGMP, causing smooth muscle relaxation. Nitrates act predominantly on large veins, leading to venodilation, reduced preload, decreased myocardial oxygen demand, and rapid relief of exertional angina.

A. Cardiac muscle – Nitrates do not directly increase contractility.

B. Large arteries – Some dilation occurs, but not the primary effect.

D. Small arteries/arterioles – Major targets of drugs like hydralazine, not nitrates.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy presents with fever and migratory pain with swelling involving both knees and ankles for the past 2 weeks. Four weeks earlier, he had an untreated sore throat. Examination reveals a new apical pansystolic murmur. Investigations show: • ESR: 58 mm/hr • CRP: 5.2 mg/dL • ECG: PR interval prolonged • ASO titre: Elevated Which of the following best explains why this child fulfills the diagnostic criteria for acute rheumatic fever?
options: One major + one minor criterion with evidence of streptococcal infection
Two major criteria with evidence of streptococcal infection
One major + two minor criteria with evidence of streptococcal infection
Three minor criteria with evidence of streptococcal infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Two major criteria with evidence of streptococcal infection

Jones Major Criteria

• Carditis (clinical/subclinical)
• Arthritis
• Sydenham chorea
• Erythema marginatum
• Subcutaneous nodules

Jones Minor Criteria

• Fever ≥38°C
• Monoarthralgia
• ESR ≥30 mm/hr or CRP ≥3 mg/dL
• Prolonged PR interval

This child has:

• Carditis (new murmur) → Major
• Migratory polyarthritis → Major
• Fever, raised ESR/CRP, prolonged PR → Minor
• Elevated ASO titre → Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presents with recurrent headaches and a family history of early sudden cardiac deaths. On examination, he has hypertelorism, bifid uvula, and arterial tortuosity. Echocardiography reveals aortic root dilatation. Genetic testing shows a mutation affecting the TGF-β signaling pathway. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Loeys–Dietz syndrome

Loeys–Dietz syndrome is caused by mutations in the TGF-β signaling pathway and is characterized by hypertelorism, bifid uvula/cleft palate, arterial tortuosity, and early aggressive aortic root dilatation, explaining the family history of sudden cardiac death.

A. Marfan syndrome – FBN1 mutation; lacks bifid uvula and arterial tortuosity.

B. Vascular Ehlers–Danlos – COL3A1 mutation; features translucent skin, not craniofacial anomalies.

D. Homocystinuria – Marfanoid habitus with intellectual disability and thrombosis, not TGF-β mutation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 24-year-old man is evaluated due to an episode of syncope. He was jogging when he felt light-headed and passed out, but he did not sustain a head injury. The patient has had 2 similar episodes of light-headedness while jogging. The patient does not use tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drugs. His father died suddenly at age 30. On physical examination, the patient has a harsh systolic murmur. The lungs are clear to auscultation. This patient's symptoms are most likely explained by left ventricular outflow obstruction created by which of the following structures?
options: Aortic valve cusp and interventricular septum
Aortic valve cusp and papillary muscle
Mitral valve leaflet and interventricular septum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mitral valve leaflet and interventricular septum

This young man has classic features of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM)—exertional syncope, family history of sudden cardiac death, and a harsh systolic murmur. In HOCM, asymmetric septal hypertrophy causes systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve leaflet, which moves toward the interventricular septum, creating dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction, especially during exercise.

A. Aortic valve cusp and interventricular septum – Describes subaortic stenosis, not HOCM.

B. Aortic valve cusp and papillary muscle – Not a recognized mechanism of LVOT obstruction.

C. Aortic valve cusps – Seen in aortic stenosis; murmur and mechanism differ.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of syncope. Echocardiography reveals a left atrial myxoma. On examination, she has multiple lentigines over the face and lips and evidence of endocrine hyperactivity. Family history suggests an autosomal dominant disorder. Which of the following genetic mutations is most commonly associated with this patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. PRKAR1A

Carney complex is an autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by:

• Cardiac myxomas
• Spotty skin pigmentation (lentigines)
• Endocrine tumors / hyperactivity

Caused by mutation in:

• PRKAR1A gene
• Encodes regulatory subunit of protein kinase A
• Leads to dysregulated cAMP signaling

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman presents with episodic palpitations and atypical chest discomfort. Cardiac auscultation reveals a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur at the apex, which moves earlier in systole and becomes louder on standing and during Valsalva maneuver, and becomes softer with squatting. Transthoracic echocardiography shows bileaflet mitral valve prolapse with thickened, redundant leaflets and elongated chordae, consistent with myxomatous degeneration. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Barlow syndrome

This patient has classic findings of myxomatous mitral valve prolapse (MVP) with dynamic auscultatory changes.

Clinical findings

• Mid-systolic click + late systolic murmur at apex
•

Murmur:

•

Moves earlier & louder on standing/Valsalva

•

Becomes softer with squatting

This is classic for mitral valve prolapse physiology.

Barlow syndrome = Primary myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve characterized by:

• Thick, redundant leaflets (>5 mm)
• Excess leaflet tissue
• Chordal elongation
• Bileaflet involvement
• Often significant mitral regurgitation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after receiving rapid intravenous infusion of normal saline for dehydration. Shortly after the infusion, her heart rate increases from 72/min to 108/min. Blood pressure remains stable. There is no chest pain or ECG evidence of ischemia. The increase in heart rate in this patient is most likely mediated by which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bainbridge reflex

Rapid IV saline increases venous return, causing right atrial stretch, which stimulates atrial stretch receptors and leads to reflex tachycardia via the Bainbridge reflex. Blood pressure remains stable, and there is no ischemia, fitting this mechanism.

B. J reflex – Triggered by pulmonary congestion; causes bradycardia and hypotension.

C. Baroreceptor reflex – Responds to BP changes; BP here is unchanged.

D. Bezold-Jarisch reflex – Causes bradycardia and hypotension during ischemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents for a preconception visit. She is an elite long-distance swimmer who continues to train regularly. She has no medical history and does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Her blood pressure is 114/66 mm Hg and pulse is 58/min. Physical examination is unremarkable. Compared with an age- and sex-matched sedentary individual, which of the following combinations of cardiovascular changes (Left ventricular ejection fraction; Left ventricular cavity size; Maximum cardiac output) is most likely present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Unchanged; Increased; Increased

Endurance athletes develop physiologic (eccentric) cardiac hypertrophy due to chronic volume overload:

• ↑ Left ventricular cavity size (eccentric dilation)
• Normal ejection fraction at rest
• ↑ Maximum cardiac output due to increased stroke volume

Resting bradycardia is also common due to increased vagal tone.

Why not other options?

A (↓ EF) → Seen in systolic dysfunction, not athletes

B/C (↓ cavity size) → Opposite of endurance adaptation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 33-year-old man presents with fever, chills, cough, and progressive shortness of breath for 1 week. He has a history of intravenous drug use and chronic alcohol consumption. On examination, he is febrile and tachycardic. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Chest imaging reveals multiple bilateral nodular lesions with cavitation, consistent with septic pulmonary emboli. Which of the following is the most appropriate site to auscultate the valve most likely affected in this patient?
options: Left lower sternal border (4th–5th intercostal space)
Cardiac apex (5th intercostal space, midclavicular line)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Left lower sternal border (4th–5th intercostal space)

This patient has right-sided infective endocarditis due to IV drug use, most commonly involving the tricuspid valve.

• Septic emboli travel to lungs → cavitating nodular lesions
• The tricuspid valve is best auscultated at the left lower sternal border (LLSB)

Why not other options?

A. Right 2nd ICS → Aortic valve

B. Left 2nd ICS → Pulmonary valve

D. Apex (5th ICS MCL) → Mitral valve

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old female is hospitalized with progressive exertional dyspnea, lower extremity edema and cough. She also describes frequent nocturnal episodes of breathlessness and recent hoarseness. Auscultation reveals loud first and second heart sounds and a mid-diastolic rumble best heard at the cardiac apex. This patient's hoarseness is most likely caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nerve impingement

This patient has mitral stenosis (mid-diastolic rumble at apex, loud S1, dyspnea, PND). Chronic left atrial enlargement can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness (Ortner syndrome).

A. Laryngeal edema – Seen with allergic reactions or infection, not cardiac causes.

B. Impaired arterial supply – Would cause ischemic injury, not typical in MS.

D. Epithelial sloughing – Seen with chemical or thermal injury, not cardiovascular disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman comes to the office due to exertional dyspnea. The patient has a history of lgA nephropathy; she received hemodialysis for 2 years before undergoing kidney transplantation last month. Chest x-ray reveals cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion. Further evaluation determines that her symptoms are likely due to persistence of the arteriovenous fistula that was used for hemodialysis. Which of the following physiologic changes in 1) cardiac output, 2) systemic vascular resistance and 3) venous return respectively are present in this patient due to the fistula?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increases, decreases, increases

• A persistent AV fistula creates a low-resistance shunt from artery to vein → ↓ systemic vascular resistance (SVR).
• This increases venous return (more blood returns to the heart) → ↑ preload and ↑ cardiac output, which can cause high-output heart failure with cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 43-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe headache, confusion, and visual disturbances for 3 days. He has poorly controlled hypertension. On examination Blood pressure is 224/115 mm Hg and Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilledema. Laboratory evaluation shows mildly elevated serum creatinine. An intravenous antihypertensive agent is started that causes arteriolar vasodilation, improves renal blood flow and Promotes natriuresis. Which of the following drugs is most likely being administered?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fenoldopam

This patient has a hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension) with end-organ damage (papilledema, encephalopathy).

Fenoldopam is a dopamine D1 receptor agonist that:

• Causes arteriolar vasodilation
• Increases renal blood flow
• Promotes natriuresis and diuresis
• Is preferred in hypertensive emergencies, especially with renal involvement

Why not other options?

A. Esmolol → β1-blocker; reduces heart rate, not a primary renal vasodilator

C. Hydralazine → Arteriolar dilator but does not improve renal perfusion significantly

D. Nitroglycerin → Predominantly venodilator; used in ACS, not ideal here

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 44-year-old woman presents with progressive abdominal distension and bilateral pedal edema. She has a history of rheumatic fever in childhood. On examination, the jugular venous pulse shows a prominent a-wave with a slow, prolonged y-descent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tricuspid stenosis

• Prior rheumatic fever → classic cause of right-sided valvular involvement (after mitral).
• Progressive abdominal distension. Bilateral pedal edema→ Suggests systemic venous congestion (right-sided heart failure).

JVP Findings

• Prominent a-wave
• Slow, prolonged y-descent
• In TS, RA contracts against a stenosed tricuspid valve

→ Increased resistance

→ Large, giant a-wave

This is the hallmark of TS.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and dull chest pain. Examination reveals a high-pitched early diastolic murmur at the left sternal border. Chest X-ray shows widening of the mediastinum. CT angiography demonstrates a dilated ascending aorta with aortic regurgitation. Serology is positive for treponemal antibodies. The underlying pathological process responsible for this patient’s condition primarily involves:
options: Immune-complex deposition in the aortic media
Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
Lipid deposition in the intima with foam cell formation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum

Treponemal-positive patient with ascending aortic aneurysm + aortic regurgitation suggests tertiary syphilis. The key pathology is obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, causing ischemia of the aortic media → medial degeneration, scarring (“tree-barking”), aneurysmal dilation, and AR.

A Immune-complex deposition → vasculitides like SLE, not syphilitic aortitis.

C Lipid/foam cells → atherosclerosis (intimal), usually abdominal aorta.

D Caseating granulomas → TB; doesn’t classically cause syphilitic AR/aneurysm.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 46-year-old man develops right leg pain and swelling after a long-haul flight and is diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis. During hospitalization, he suddenly develops right-sided weakness and facial droop. Brain imaging reveals an acute infarction in the left middle cerebral artery territory. Which of the following additional physical examination findings is most likely present in this patient?
options: Early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border
Harsh systolic murmur that increases with standing
Low-pitched diastolic murmur with presystolic accentuation
Fixed splitting of the second heart sound (S2)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fixed splitting of the second heart sound (S2)

This patient likely has a paradoxical embolism, where a thrombus from a deep vein thrombosis travels to the arterial circulation via a right-to-left shunt, most commonly through a patent foramen ovale (PFO) or atrial septal defect (ASD).

• This allows venous emboli to bypass the lungs and enter systemic circulation → ischemic stroke
• ASD classically presents with fixed splitting of S2, due to constant left-to-right shunting that delays pulmonic valve closure regardless of respiration

Why not other options?

A. Early diastolic murmur → Aortic regurgitation

B. Murmur ↑ on standing → Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

C. Presystolic murmur → Mitral stenosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 46-year-old man undergoes right heart catheterization for evaluation of exertional chest pain. During the procedure, pressure tracings are recorded at different locations. At one position, the catheter records phasic pressure changes ranging from 2 mm Hg (minimum) to 25 mm Hg (maximum). After advancing the catheter further, the recorded pressures range from 10 mm Hg (minimum) to 25 mm Hg (maximum). Assuming normal physiology, the first set of pressure readings (2–25 mm Hg) was most likely obtained from which of the following locations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Right ventricle

Each cardiac chamber has characteristic pressure waveforms:

• Right ventricle (RV):

• Systolic: \~15–30 mm Hg
• Diastolic: \~0–5 mm Hg
• Hence, large pressure variation (e.g., 2–25 mm Hg)

• Pulmonary artery (PA):

• Systolic similar to RV (\~25 mm Hg)
• BUT diastolic higher (\~10 mm Hg) → narrower range (10–25 mm Hg)

Thus, the transition from 2–25 → 10–25 mm Hg indicates movement from right ventricle → pulmonary artery.

Why not other options?

A. Left atrium → Low pressures (\~5–10 mm Hg), no large systolic peak

B Left ventricle → Very high systolic (\~120 mm Hg)

C. Pulmonary artery → Diastolic not as low as 2 mm Hg

D. Right atrium → Very low pressures (\~0–5 mm Hg), no high systolic spike

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency department for recurrent vomiting that began 5 hours ago. He describes the vomitus as bloody and containing black specks. He drinks 10-12 beers daily and has not seen a physician in 15 years. He appears pale. Physical examination shows decreased radial pulses, delayed capillary refill, multiple spider angiomata, and a distended abdomen. He is oriented to person but not to place or time. Which of the following is most likely decreased in this patient in response to his hematemesis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Carotid baroreceptor firing activity

He has massive upper GI bleed (hematemesis with shock signs: weak pulses, delayed refill) likely from portal HTN/varices. Acute blood loss → ↓ arterial pressure and stretch → decreased carotid baroreceptor firing, which triggers sympathetic activation (tachycardia, vasoconstriction).

A. Systemic vascular resistance – Increases due to sympathetic vasoconstriction.

B. Fractional tissue O₂ extraction – Increases to maintain VO₂ when delivery falls.

C. Pulmonary vascular resistance – Not the primary compensatory change in hemorrhagic shock.

questions.subject: Medicine

questions.text: A 53-year-old man with hyperlipidemia comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. His home medications include acetaminophen and atorvastatin. Serum studies show elevated total cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations. A drug that activates the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha is added to his existing therapy. This patient is most likely to develop which of the following drug-related adverse effects?
options: Pruritus and flushing of the skin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reddish-brown discoloration of urine

PPAR-α agonists are fibrates (eg, fenofibrate, gemfibrozil). When added to a statin, they increase the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis, which leads to myoglobinuria, causing dark/tea- or reddish-brown urine.

A. Waxing and waning confusion – Seen with hepatic encephalopathy or anticholinergics, not fibrates.

C. Pruritus and flushing of the skin – Classic adverse effect of niacin, not fibrates.

D. Acutely swollen and painful joint – Suggests gout; niacin increases uric acid, fibrates do not.

questions.text: A 54-year-old man presents with diffuse muscle pain, generalized weakness, and marked tenderness a few days after completing treatment for streptococcal pharyngitis. He has a history of hypertension and ischemic heart disease, including a myocardial infarction treated with coronary stenting 6 months ago. His medications include metoprolol, simvastatin, aspirin, clopidogrel, lisinopril, and erythromycin prescribed for his throat infection. On examination, he is afebrile with no rash. Laboratory investigations reveal: • AST: 540 U/L • ALT: 45 U/L • Creatine kinase (CK): 10,100 U/L Which of the following best explains this patient's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Drug interaction

This patient has statin-induced rhabdomyolysis, evidenced by:

• Severe diffuse myalgia and muscle weakness
• Markedly elevated CK (>10,000 U/L)
• AST much higher than ALT, reflecting skeletal muscle injury rather than liver disease

The precipitating factor is the combination of simvastatin and erythromycin.

• Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4, the enzyme responsible for metabolizing simvastatin.
• This markedly increases simvastatin plasma concentrations, predisposing to myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Allergic drug reaction: Usually presents with rash, eosinophilia, fever, or urticaria, not isolated severe CK elevation.
• B. Post-streptococcal autoimmune myositis: Rare and not associated with recent initiation of a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor.
• C. Viral myositis: Typically follows viral illnesses (eg, influenza), not bacterial pharyngitis treated with antibiotics.

High-yield pearl:

• Macrolides (especially erythromycin and clarithromycin), azole antifungals, protease inhibitors, and grapefruit juice inhibit CYP3A4 and significantly increase the risk of simvastatin- and lovastatin-induced rhabdomyolysis.
