questions.text: A 54-year-old man with resistant hypertension is started on an experimental drug that lowers blood pressure without affecting heart rate or cardiac output. It acts by selectively activating potassium channels in vascular smooth muscle, causing membrane hyperpolarization and relaxation. Chronic use leads to fluid retention and hypertrichosis. Which drug is responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Minoxidil

Why: This vignette describes the classic pharmacologic profile of Minoxidil:

Mechanism: Minoxidil is a prodrug converted by hepatic sulfotransferase to minoxidil sulfate, its active form. Minoxidil sulfate opens ATP-sensitive potassium (K⁺-ATP) channels in vascular smooth muscle (predominantly arteriolar). This causes:

• K⁺ efflux → membrane hyperpolarization
• Hyperpolarization closes voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → decreased intracellular Ca²⁺
• Result: smooth muscle relaxation → arteriolar vasodilation → ↓ BP

Key distinguishing features in this vignette:

• Hypertrichosis — a well-known, distinctive side effect of minoxidil (in fact, topical minoxidil is used clinically to treat androgenetic alopecia because of this very effect)
• Fluid/salt retention — occurs due to reflex activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) secondary to vasodilation, requiring co-administration with a diuretic
• Used for resistant/severe hypertension — minoxidil is a potent vasodilator reserved for refractory cases

Why not the others:

• A. Hydralazine — Also an arteriolar vasodilator causing reflex tachycardia and fluid retention, but its mechanism is not via K⁺ channels (more related to NO release/cGMP and interference with IP3-mediated Ca²⁺ release); classically causes a lupus-like syndrome, not hypertrichosis.
• C. Diazoxide — Also a K⁺-ATP channel opener causing vasodilation (used in hypertensive emergencies and as a treatment for hypoglycemia due to insulinoma via inhibition of insulin release), but it is not associated with hypertrichosis; more notably causes hyperglycemia.
• D. Nicorandil — A K⁺-ATP channel opener and nitric oxide donor, used for angina (not primarily hypertension); no hypertrichosis association.

High-yield takeaway:

• K⁺-ATP channel opener + hypertrichosis + fluid retention + used in resistant hypertension = Minoxidil. (Contrast with Diazoxide, which shares the mechanism but is used for hypertensive emergencies/hypoglycemia and lacks the hair growth side effect.)

questions.text: A 55-year-old man comes to the office for follow-up. The patient was diagnosed with hypertension 3 weeks ago, and an ECG performed at that time showed features of left ventricular hypertrophy. He was subsequently referred for echocardiography. The patient feels well and has had no shortness of breath, fatigue, or leg swelling. He has no other medical conditions, takes no medications, and does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg and pulse is 80/min. Physical examination shows normal jugular venous pressure. There are no lung crackles, heart gallops, or lower extremity edema. Echocardiography reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%. Which of the following patterns of chemical mediators is most likely present in this patient?
options: Angiotensin II high, Aldosterone high, ANP high
Angiotensin II low, Aldosterone low, ANP high
Angiotensin II high, Aldosterone low, ANP low
Angiotensin II high, Aldosterone high, ANP low
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Angiotensin II high, Aldosterone high, ANP high

This patient has asymptomatic systolic heart failure (HFrEF) with reduced EF (30%). Reduced cardiac output leads to activation of RAAS, causing ↑ angiotensin II and ↑ aldosterone. At the same time, ventricular stretch from volume/pressure overload stimulates release of ANP, which rises as a compensatory (but insufficient) response.

B. Angiotensin II low, Aldosterone low, ANP high – RAAS would not be suppressed in HFrEF.

C. Angiotensin II high, Aldosterone low, ANP low – Aldosterone typically parallels Ang II.

D. Angiotensin II high, Aldosterone high, ANP low – ANP increases due to ventricular stretch.

questions.text: A 55-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being rescued from a snow-covered mountainous region. On arrival, his core body temperature is 31°C. He is drowsy, with bradycardia and cold, pale extremities. Hemodynamic monitoring shows reduced cardiac output. Which of the following changes in vascular resistance is most likely to be seen in this patient?
options: Increased pulmonary vascular resistance and decreased systemic vascular resistance
Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance and increased systemic vascular resistance
Increased pulmonary vascular resistance and increased systemic vascular resistance
Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance and decreased systemic vascular resistance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased pulmonary vascular resistance and increased systemic vascular resistance

Moderate-to-severe hypothermia (core temperature <32°C) triggers intense sympathetic-mediated peripheral vasoconstriction to conserve heat, resulting in increased systemic vascular resistance (SVR). Hypothermia also causes pulmonary vasoconstriction, leading to increased pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR). These changes contribute to reduced tissue perfusion, increased cardiac workload, and decreased cardiac output.

Why not the other options?

• A. Increased pulmonary vascular resistance and decreased systemic vascular resistance: SVR does not decrease in hypothermia; it increases due to peripheral vasoconstriction.
• B. Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance and increased systemic vascular resistance: Both PVR and SVR increase, not decrease.
• D. Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance and decreased systemic vascular resistance: Vasodilation is not a feature of moderate-to-severe hypothermia.

questions.text: A 55-year-old woman develops proximal muscle pain and elevated CK 3 weeks after starting simvastatin. She requires continued lipid-lowering therapy due to recent ACS. Which statin is the best alternative?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pravastatin

Pravastatin is the best alternative because it is hydrophilic, has minimal CYP450 metabolism, and the lowest risk of statin-associated myopathy. In patients who develop myositis or CK elevation on simvastatin but still need aggressive lipid lowering after ACS, switching to pravastatin is recommended.

A. Atorvastatin – Lipophilic and CYP3A4-metabolized; still higher myopathy risk.

B. Rosuvastatin – Potent but can still cause myopathy; not first choice after intolerance.

D. Lovastatin – Lipophilic and CYP3A4-dependent; similar risk as simvastatin.

questions.text: A 56-year-old asthmatic patient presents with severe headache and vomiting. BP is 220/130 mmHg, and fundus shows papilledema. What is the mechanism of action of the drug of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcium channel blockade

This patient has a hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension) with evidence of acute target-organ damage (severe hypertension, headache, vomiting, and papilledema). In an asthmatic patient, the preferred intravenous antihypertensive is nicardipine, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, because it effectively lowers blood pressure without causing bronchospasm.

• Nicardipine blocks L-type voltage-gated calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle.
• This decreases intracellular calcium, causing arteriolar vasodilation and a rapid reduction in systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure.
• It is particularly useful in hypertensive emergencies and is safe in patients with asthma.

Why not the others?

• A. Stimulation of guanylyl cyclase → Mechanism of sodium nitroprusside via nitric oxide-mediated ↑ cGMP.
• C. K⁺ channel opening → Mechanism of minoxidil and diazoxide.
• D. Increased cAMP → Mechanism of β₂-agonists and some vasodilators, not the drug of choice here.

questions.text: A 58-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with pain in both calves while walking, weak femoral pulses, and erectile dysfunction. He is diagnosed with aortoiliac occlusive disease (Leriche syndrome) secondary to advanced atherosclerosis. Which of the following correctly represents the chronological sequence in the development of the underlying vascular lesion? 1. Endothelial dysfunction 2. Entry and oxidation of LDL with macrophage infiltration 3. Formation of fibrous atherosclerotic plaque 4. Development of fatty streaks
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 → 2 → 4 → 3

The patient's presentation is characteristic of Leriche syndrome, caused by atherosclerotic occlusion of the abdominal aorta or iliac arteries.

The sequence of atherogenesis is:

1. Endothelial dysfunction/injury → increased vascular permeability and leukocyte adhesion.
2. LDL enters the intima and becomes oxidized, attracting monocytes that differentiate into macrophages and form foam cells.
3. Fatty streaks develop due to accumulation of foam cells.
4. Fibrous plaques form following smooth muscle cell migration, collagen deposition, and extracellular matrix production.

questions.text: A 6-year-old child is evaluated for distinctive facial dysmorphism including a flat midface and broad nasal tip, along with hand anomalies. There is a family history suggestive of an autosomal dominant condition. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the TFAP2B gene. Which of the following cardiac abnormalities is most commonly associated with this syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Patent ductus arteriosus

Char syndrome:

• Autosomal dominant
• Gene: TFAP2B
• Triad:
• PDA
• Facial dysmorphism
• Hand anomalies
• Diagnosis is made by syndrome recognition, not murmur description

Char syndrome → TFAP2B mutation → Patent ductus arteriosus

questions.text: A 60-year-old man is admitted with an acute inferior wall myocardial infarction. Shortly after administration of sublingual nitroglycerin, he develops marked bradycardia, hypotension, and lightheadedness. ECG shows no atrioventricular conduction abnormality. On examination, his extremities are warm, and there are no signs of pulmonary congestion. The physician attributes his hemodynamic deterioration to a reflex triggered by reduced left ventricular filling, resulting in enhanced vagal activity. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?
options: Baroreceptor-mediated reflex secondary to elevated arterial pressure
Bainbridge reflex due to increased right atrial filling
Bezold–Jarisch reflex due to ventricular underfilling
Cushing reflex caused by raised intracranial pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bezold–Jarisch reflex due to ventricular underfilling

The Bezold–Jarisch reflex is a cardioinhibitory reflex initiated by stimulation of ventricular mechanoreceptors when the left ventricle is underfilled but contracting vigorously.

It is classically precipitated by:

• Inferior wall myocardial infarction
• Nitrate administration (reduces preload)
• Spinal or epidural anesthesia
• Severe hypovolemia

Physiologic response:

• ↑ Vagal tone → Bradycardia
• Peripheral vasodilation → Hypotension
• Occasionally, transient apnea

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Baroreceptor-mediated reflex secondary to elevated arterial pressure: Activated by increased blood pressure, producing reflex bradycardia; it is not triggered by ventricular underfilling.
• B. Bainbridge reflex due to increased right atrial filling: Caused by increased venous return and right atrial stretch, resulting in tachycardia, not bradycardia.
• D. Cushing reflex caused by raised intracranial pressure: Occurs in raised intracranial pressure and presents with hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration.

questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with complaints of breathlessness on walking a few metres. He adds that he has an uncomfortable awareness of his heartbeat, especially on lying down. Examination reveals widened pulse pressure and pulsating uvula. Which of the following would be the most likely auscultatory finding in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Austin Flint murmur

The patient has classic features of severe aortic regurgitation—exertional dyspnea, palpitations worse on lying down, wide pulse pressure, and pulsating uvula (Müller sign). In chronic severe AR, regurgitant flow impinges on the anterior mitral leaflet, producing a low-pitched mid-diastolic Austin Flint murmur at the apex.

B) Carey Coomb murmur – Mid-diastolic murmur of acute rheumatic fever due to mitral valvulitis.

C) Gallavardin phenomenon – Radiation of aortic stenosis murmur to the apex.

D) Graham Steel murmur – Diastolic murmur of pulmonary regurgitation in pulmonary hypertension.

questions.text: A 60-year-old man undergoes a treadmill exercise stress test. The clinician wants to estimate his age-predicted maximum heart rate for interpretation of the test. What is the approximate maximum heart rate for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 160 beats/min

Age-predicted maximum heart rate (HRmax) is calculated as:

For a 60-year-old,

HRmax = 220-Age

= 220-60 = 160

questions.text: A 60-year-old man with long-standing hypertension presents for routine evaluation. His blood pressure recorded in the clinic is 150/90 mmHg. The physician wants to estimate the mean arterial pressure (MAP) to assess organ perfusion. What is the approximate mean arterial pressure in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 110 mmHg

Mean arterial pressure (MAP) represents the average arterial pressure throughout the cardiac cycle and is an important determinant of organ perfusion. It can be estimated using the formula:

MAP = DBP + 1/3 (SBP − DBP)

For a blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg:

MAP = 90 + 1/3 (150 − 90)

= 90 + 20

= 110 mmHg

Why not the other options?

• A. 100 mmHg – underestimates the calculated MAP.
• C. 120 mmHg – overestimates the MAP.
• D. 130 mmHg – considerably higher than the calculated value.

questions.text: A 60-year-old man with severe acute decompensated heart failure following myocardial infarction is admitted to the ICU. Despite optimal use of diuretics and dobutamine, he continues to have low cardiac output. An intravenous drug is started that increases myocardial contractility and causes vasodilation by increasing intracellular cAMP, independent of β-adrenergic receptors. Which of the following drugs was most likely administered?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Enoximone

Enoximone is a phosphodiesterase-3 (PDE-3) inhibitor

Mechanism:

• Inhibits breakdown of cAMP
• ↑ Intracellular calcium in cardiac myocytes
• → Positive inotropy
• Causes vasodilation (↓ preload & afterload)

Net effect:

• ↑ Cardiac output
• ↓ Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure

Used in short-term management of severe heart failure, especially when β-agonists are insufficient.

questions.text: A 60-year-old man with severe cardiogenic shock is placed on mechanical circulatory support. During a teaching round, the cardiologist explains that if the heart suddenly stops pumping and blood flow throughout the circulation ceases, the pressure in the entire vascular system will eventually equalize to a single value determined by the volume of blood and the compliance of the vessels. Which of the following terms describes this pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mean circulatory filling pressure

Mean circulatory filling pressure (MCFP) is the pressure that exists throughout the entire cardiovascular system when cardiac output is zero and blood flow has ceased, allowing pressures in all vessels to equalize. It is determined by the total blood volume and the compliance (capacitance) of the vasculature, especially the venous system.

MCFP is an important determinant of venous return, as the gradient between MCFP and right atrial pressure drives blood back to the heart.

Why not the other options?

• A. Pulse pressure – the difference between systolic and diastolic arterial pressure.
• B. Critical closing pressure – the pressure below which blood vessels collapse and blood flow stops.
• D. Perfusion pressure – the pressure gradient driving blood flow through an organ (arterial pressure − venous pressure).

questions.subject: Medicine

questions.text: A 60-year-old man, post-MI, had the following lab values. Which of the following must be his treatment plan? LDL - 125mg/dl HDL - 33mg/dl TGL - 270mg/dl
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atorvastatin 80 mg

Post-MI patients are very high–risk ASCVD and require high-intensity statin therapy regardless of baseline LDL. Atorvastatin 80 mg is first-line to aggressively lower LDL and reduce recurrent events. Elevated TG (270 mg/dL) is addressed after statin optimization.

A. Rosuvastatin + fenofibrate – Combination increases myopathy risk; not first-line post-MI.

C. Fenofibrate – Does not reduce post-MI mortality; LDL lowering is priority.

D. Rosuvastatin 10 mg – Moderate-intensity; inadequate for secondary prevention.

questions.text: A 62-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to palpitations and shortness of breath that began an hour ago. Medical history includes hypertension, coronary artery disease, and paroxysmal atrial flutter. Blood pressure is 108/76 mmHg and pulse is rapid. ECG shows atrial flutter with a ventricular rate of approximately 150/ min. The estimated atrial rate based on ECG flutter waves is 300/min. Which of the following is most likely responsible for the rate difference between the atria and the ventricles?
options: Calcium current within the atrioventricular node
Calcium current within the sinoatrial node
Sodium current within an atrioventricular accessory pathway
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Calcium current within the atrioventricular node

In atrial flutter, the atrial rate is \~300/min, but the ventricles typically conduct at \~150/min due to 2:1 AV block. The AV node limits conduction because its action potentials depend on slow L-type calcium channels, which have a long refractory period and decremental conduction. This filters rapid atrial impulses and prevents 1:1 transmission.

B. Calcium current within the SA node – Sets sinus rate, not AV filtering.

C. Sodium current within an AV accessory pathway – Would allow rapid 1:1 conduction (eg, WPW).

D. Sodium current within the atria – Determines atrial depolarization rate, not ventricular response.

questions.subject: Medicine

questions.text: A 63-year-old woman is admitted with progressive dyspnea, fatigue, and lower limb swelling. She has a history of chronic heart failure with multiple prior hospitalizations. On examination, she has elevated JVP, bilateral basal crackles, S3 gallop, and pedal edema. She is started on appropriate therapy, including diuretics. By day 3, her hematocrit increases from 44% to 50%. Arterial blood gas shows PaO₂ = 70 mm Hg, and radioisotope-labeled red blood cell study demonstrates normal total RBC mass. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s polycythemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Relative erythrocytosis

An increase in hematocrit with normal red cell mass indicates relative polycythemia due to decreased plasma volume (hemoconcentration), commonly seen after diuretic therapy in heart failure patients.

• ↑ Hematocrit + normal RBC mass → NOT true polycythemia
• Diuretics → ↓ plasma volume → hemoconcentration
• Mild hypoxia (PaO₂ 70) not sufficient alone to explain increase

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?

A. Polycythemia vera → ↑ RBC mass (not normal)

B. Hypoxic erythrocytosis → requires sustained hypoxia + ↑ RBC mass

C. Renal disease → ↑ EPO → ↑ RBC mass

questions.text: A 64-year-old man presents with acute onset chest discomfort and mild dyspnea following emotional stress. He has a history of long-standing hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg, and pulse is 100/min. ECG shows no evidence of acute ischemia. On cardiac auscultation in the left lateral decubitus position during end-expiration, a low-frequency presystolic sound (S4) is heard best at the apex. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left ventricular hypertrophy

An S4 heart sound (atrial gallop) occurs due to forceful atrial contraction against a stiff, noncompliant ventricle.

• Most commonly seen in left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) due to chronic hypertension
• Indicates diastolic dysfunction (impaired ventricular relaxation)

Why not other options?

A. Papillary muscle dysfunction → Causes mitral regurgitation → holosystolic murmur

C. Increased LV preload → Associated with S3 (volume overload), not S4

D. Aortic regurgitation → Early diastolic decrescendo murmur

questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with exertional dyspnea. On cardiac auscultation, the second heart sound is single during inspiration but becomes split during expiration, with the split widening on expiration. ECG shows a broad QRS complex with features suggestive of a conduction abnormality. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this auscultatory finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left bundle branch block

Reverse (paradoxical) splitting of S2:

• A2 is delayed
• Splitting is heard during expiration
• Split disappears on inspiration

Seen in conditions that delay left ventricular ejection, especially:

• Left bundle branch block (LBBB)
• Aortic stenosis

questions.text: A 65-year-old man with a long history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents to the clinic complaining of dizziness and weakness in his left arm when performing activities like playing table tennis. He has been a chronic smoker for over 40 years. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm, and orthostatic vital signs are normal. A Doppler ultrasound of the left vertebral artery shows retrograde flow instead of normal antegrade flow. Which of the following arteries is most likely stenosed or occluded to cause these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Left subclavian artery

Retrograde flow in the left vertebral artery with exertional left arm symptoms is classic for subclavian steal syndrome. A proximal left subclavian artery stenosis/occlusion (before the vertebral artery origin) causes blood to be “stolen” from the vertebrobasilar circulation, reversing flow in the ipsilateral vertebral artery to supply the arm during exertion.

A. Left internal carotid artery – Would cause anterior circulation TIAs, not vertebral flow reversal.

B. Left vertebral artery – Stenosis would reduce antegrade flow, not cause retrograde steal pattern.

D. Right subclavian artery – Would affect the right vertebral artery, not the left.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes to the OPD for a follow-up appointment. On physical examination, jugular venous pressure is elevated. There is increased intensity of the pulmonic component of S2. Breath sounds are decreased bilaterally with scattered wheezes but no crackles. There is 2+ lower extremity edema. Which of the following hemodynamic parameters is most likely to be increased in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Right ventricular afterload

This patient has cor pulmonale due to COPD with pulmonary hypertension, suggested by loud P2, raised JVP, and peripheral edema. Chronic hypoxic vasoconstriction increases pulmonary vascular resistance, thereby increasing right ventricular afterload.

A. Left ventricular preload – Usually normal or reduced in COPD.

B. Pulmonary arterial compliance – Decreased, not increased, in pulmonary hypertension.

C. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure – Reflects left-sided pressures; typically normal in cor pulmonale.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 67-year-old man presents with progressive shortness of breath and chest tightness. He has a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and long-term smoking. During blood pressure measurement, the cuff is inflated and slowly deflated. At a certain pressure, Korotkoff sounds are heard only during expiration, whereas at a lower pressure, they are heard throughout the respiratory cycle. Which of the following conditions is most likely associated with this physical examination finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pericardial disease

This finding describes pulsus paradoxus, defined as:

• Exaggerated (>10 mm Hg) decrease in systolic blood pressure during inspiration
• Detected by Korotkoff sounds appearing only during expiration at higher pressures

Mechanism:

• Inspiration → ↑ venous return to right heart
• In conditions like cardiac tamponade, the rigid pericardium limits expansion → septum shifts → ↓ LV filling → ↓ systolic BP

Why not other options?

A. Aortic stenosis → Crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur

B. Mitral valve disease → Diastolic murmur or regurgitant murmur

C. Myocardial ischemia → ECG changes, not pulsus paradoxus

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 68-year-old man comes to the OPD due to several weeks of progressive exertional dyspnea and lower extremity edema. Echocardiography shows biventricular dilation and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35%. After initial stabilization, long-term use of which of the following medications will most likely improve survival in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Carvedilol

This patient has chronic systolic heart failure (HFrEF) with dilated cardiomyopathy and reduced EF. Beta-blockers (eg, carvedilol) improve survival by reducing sympathetic overactivation, decreasing arrhythmias, and limiting adverse ventricular remodeling when used long term after stabilization.

A. Furosemide – Improves congestion and symptoms only; no mortality benefit.

B. Amlodipine – Neutral in HFrEF; does not improve survival.

D. Digoxin – Reduces hospitalizations and improves symptoms; no survival benefit.

questions.text: A 71-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to progressive dyspnea and orthopnea for the last week. She has a history of myocardial infarction and systolic heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 15%. The patient is compliant with her medications, which include carvedilol, furosemide, aspirin, lisinopril, and atorvastatin. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg and pulse is 72/min. Examination reveals elevated jugular venous pressure, bibasilar crackles, an S3 heart sound, and bilateral lower extremity pitting edema. The patient is started on dobutamine infusion, which provides significant symptom relief. Echocardiogram shows mild improvement in cardiac contractility. Which of the following is the likely mechanism underlying this patient's clinical improvement?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. G-protein-adenylate cyclase activation

Dobutamine is a β1-adrenergic agonist. It activates Gs protein, stimulating adenylate cyclase → ↑ cAMP → ↑ Ca²⁺ influx in cardiac myocytes, producing positive inotropy and symptomatic relief in severe decompensated systolic HF.

A. Cyclic nucleotide PDE inhibition – Mechanism of milrinone (↑ cAMP by preventing breakdown).

C. Late-phase inward Na⁺ channel inhibition – Ranolazine (antianginal), not inotrope.

D. Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase exchange pump inhibition – Digoxin; different pathway, not dobutamine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 72-year-old man presents with episodic chest pressure and markedly elevated blood pressure. ECG shows nonspecific ST-segment changes. An intravenous antihypertensive drug is administered. Following administration, the patient demonstrates: • Decreased systemic vascular resistance • Decreased heart rate • No significant change in stroke volume Which of the following drugs most likely produced these hemodynamic effects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Labetalol

Labetalol is a combined α1- and β-blocker that produces:

• α1 blockade → ↓ systemic vascular resistance (vasodilation)
• β1 blockade → ↓ heart rate and contractility
• Balanced effect → minimal change in stroke volume

This makes labetalol ideal in hypertensive emergencies, especially when both BP reduction and heart rate control are desired.

Why not other options?

A. Hydralazine → Pure arteriolar vasodilator → ↓ SVR but reflex tachycardia (↑ HR)

C. Metoprolol → β1-selective → ↓ HR but no significant ↓ SVR

D. Nitroprusside → Potent vasodilator → ↓ SVR but reflex ↑ HR

questions.text: A 72-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents with exertional dyspnea and bilateral ankle edema. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 58% with evidence of diastolic dysfunction and left atrial enlargement, consistent with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Which of the following medications has the strongest evidence for reducing heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular death in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dapagliflozin, a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor

SGLT2 inhibitors are the first class of drugs to consistently demonstrate a reduction in both heart failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death across the spectrum of heart failure, including Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF). Current guidelines recommend an SGLT2 inhibitor as foundational therapy for patients with HFpEF, regardless of diabetes status.

• Dapagliflozin (and empagliflozin) significantly reduce:

• Heart failure hospitalizations
• Cardiovascular death (or composite cardiovascular outcomes)

• Benefits occur in patients with or without diabetes.
• Mechanisms include:

• Natriuresis and osmotic diuresis
• Reduced preload and afterload
• Improved myocardial energetics
• Favorable renal effects

Why not the others?

• A. Carvedilol, a beta-blocker → Strong evidence in HFrEF, but no clear mortality benefit in HFpEF.
• B. Sacubitril-valsartan, an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor → May reduce HF hospitalizations in selected HFpEF patients, but benefits are less robust than those seen with SGLT2 inhibitors.
• D. Spironolactone, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist → May decrease hospitalization in some HFpEF patients but has not shown the consistent outcome benefits demonstrated by SGLT2 inhibitors

Quick reference — Drug evidence in HFpEF:

| Drug class | Example | Evidence in HFpEF

| ---------- | ------- | -----------------

| SGLT2 inhibitors | Dapagliflozin, Empagliflozin | Strongest evidence; reduces HF hospitalization + CV death (first-line)

| MRA | Spironolactone | Modest/borderline benefit (TOPCAT); may reduce HF hospitalization

| ARNI | Sacubitril-valsartan | Neutral-to-modest benefit (PARAGON-HF), more so in lower-EF HFpEF

| Diuretics (loop) | Furosemide | Symptomatic relief of congestion; no mortality benefit

| Beta-blockers | Carvedilol, Metoprolol | No proven mortality benefit; used mainly for comorbid indications (e.g., AF, hypertension)

| ACEi/ARB | Lisinopril, Losartan | No consistent mortality benefit; useful for BP/comorbidity control

questions.text: A 74-year-old man comes for a routine health check-up. He has no history of diabetes or renal disease. On repeated blood pressure measurements, his readings are 166/78 mmHg, 170/76 mmHg, and 162/80 mmHg. Peripheral pulses are bounding, and pulse pressure is widened. There is no evidence of aortic regurgitation on echocardiography. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isolated systolic hypertension

Definition of ISH:

• SBP ≥ 140 mmHg
• DBP < 90 mmHg
• Common in the elderly

Due to:

• Decreased arterial compliance
• Aortic stiffening

Leads to:

• Wide pulse pressure
• Increased risk of stroke and cardiovascular events

questions.text: A 74-year-old man comes to the physician for a 6-month history of progressively worsening fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. His pulse is 89/min and blood pressure is 145/60 mmHg. Crackles are heard at the lung bases. Cardiac examination shows a grade 3/6 early diastolic murmur loudest at the left sternal border in the third intercostal space. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Water hammer pulse

This patient has classic features of chronic aortic regurgitation—wide pulse pressure (145/60 mmHg), early diastolic decrescendo murmur best heard at the left sternal border, and symptoms of heart failure. Chronic AR leads to rapid systolic upstroke with rapid diastolic collapse, producing a water hammer (Corrigan) pulse.

A. Pulsus parvus et tardus – Seen in aortic stenosis, not AR.

B. Pulsus paradoxus – Associated with cardiac tamponade or severe asthma.

C. Fixed splitting of S2 – Seen in atrial septal defect.

questions.text: A 76-year-old man is admitted to the hospital due to worsening dyspnea and fatigue. He has a history of chronic atrial fibrillation and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). The patient is started on oral digoxin for rate control. A week later, his serum digoxin level is measured and found to be markedly elevated, despite receiving an appropriate dose. Upon further questioning, it is discovered that the patient was recently started on amiodarone. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the interaction between the drugs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inhibition of P-glycoprotein

Amiodarone inhibits P-glycoprotein (P-gp), a membrane transporter responsible for digoxin efflux in the intestines and renal tubules. Inhibition of P-gp reduces digoxin elimination and increases absorption, leading to elevated serum digoxin levels despite appropriate dosing.

A. Blockade of biliary transport proteins – Not the primary pathway for digoxin clearance.

B. Induction of cytochrome P-450 enzymes – Would decrease drug levels; amiodarone actually inhibits CYPs.

D. Stimulation of Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase – Digoxin inhibits this pump; not a drug–drug interaction mechanism.

questions.text: A male patient with a psychotic disorder is receiving antipsychotic, antidepressant, and antihypertensive medication. He developed tachycardia and chest tightness all of a sudden. He was diagnosed with metabolic acidosis. The ECG revealed a widened QRS complex and a prolonged QT interval. Which of the following drugs is the cause of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amitriptyline

Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA). TCA toxicity classically causes tachycardia, chest tightness, metabolic acidosis, widened QRS complex (Na⁺ channel blockade) and QT prolongation, predisposing to life-threatening arrhythmias.

B. Amlodipine – Causes hypotension, flushing; does not widen QRS or prolong QT.

C. Chlorthalidone – Can cause electrolyte disturbances, not characteristic ECG changes.

D. Enalapril – May cause hyperkalemia or hypotension, not QRS/QT prolongation.

questions.text: A mechanically ventilated patient develops a brief episode of apnea, followed by rapid shallow breathing immediately after receiving a large tidal volume during ventilation. This is accompanied by bradycardia and hypotension. The anesthesiologist suspects activation of pulmonary vagal receptors due to excessive lung inflation. Which of the following physiological reflexes is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. J receptor reflex

The Juxtapulmonary capillary (J) receptor reflex is triggered by stimulation of J receptors (pulmonary C-fiber receptors) located in the alveolar walls close to pulmonary capillaries.

These receptors are activated by:

• Pulmonary congestion
• Pulmonary edema
• Interstitial inflammation
• Pulmonary embolism
• Excessive lung inflation/stretch (can contribute)

Activation produces a characteristic reflex response:

• Initial apnea
• Rapid, shallow breathing (tachypnea)
• Bradycardia
• Hypotension

This reflex is mediated by unmyelinated vagal C fibers.

Why the other options are incorrect?

A. Bezold–Jarisch reflex

• Triggered by stimulation of ventricular mechanoreceptors/chemoreceptors (e.g., inferior MI, severe hypovolemia, spinal anesthesia).
• Produces the triad of:

• Bradycardia
• Hypotension
• Peripheral vasodilation

• Does not characteristically cause apnea followed by rapid shallow breathing.

B. Bainbridge reflex

• Trigger: Increased venous return causing atrial stretch.
• Response: Tachycardia.
• Opposite of the bradycardia seen here.

C. Cushing reflex

• Trigger: Raised intracranial pressure.
• Triad:

• Hypertension
• Bradycardia
• Irregular respiration

• Hypotension is not a feature.

questions.text: A patient has right upper limb BP of 160/85 mmHg and a left upper limb BP of 130/90 mmHg. He also has early diastolic murmur in right 2nd intercostal space. Which of the following is least likely to be associated with these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Supravalvular aortic stenosis

• A significant inter-arm BP difference with an early diastolic murmur (aortic regurgitation) suggests pathology involving the aorta or its branches (eg, flow obstruction or dissection).
• Supravalvular aortic stenosis causes systolic murmur and LV outflow obstruction, not inter-arm BP difference or AR, making it least likely.

B. Coarctation of aorta – Can cause differential upper-limb BP if proximal branches are involved.

C. Takayasu arteritis – Classically causes unequal arm BPs due to large-vessel involvement.

D. Aortic dissection – Commonly presents with inter-arm BP differences and AR murmur.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient on digoxin develops toxicity after starting a new antihypertensive. Which drug is the most likely precipitant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydrochlorothiazide

•

Hypokalemia → ↑ digoxin binding → toxicity

•

Thiazide diuretics cause hypokalemia, which increases digoxin binding to Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, thereby enhancing digoxin toxicity.

•

Starting hydrochlorothiazide commonly precipitates toxicity in patients on digoxin.

A. Spironolactone – Potassium-sparing; may actually reduce hypokalemia-induced toxicity.

C. Losartan – No significant effect on digoxin levels or potassium causing toxicity.

D. Amlodipine – Calcium channel blocker; does not interact with digoxin toxicity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient suddenly stands up after prolonged bed rest and develops transient hypotension. The immediate compensatory response includes increased sympathetic activity and tachycardia. Which receptor primarily senses this initial change?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Carotid sinus baroreceptors

Orthostatic hypotension triggers the baroreceptor reflex, where carotid sinus baroreceptors detect a fall in arterial pressure and initiate rapid sympathetic activation to restore blood pressure.

• Located at carotid sinus (sensitive to stretch/pressure changes)
• Decreased stretch → decreased baroreceptor firing
• Leads to ↑ sympathetic outflow → tachycardia, vasoconstriction
• Rapid, short-term BP regulation mechanism

Differentiation:

• Chemoreceptors: respond to O₂, CO₂, pH changes
• Pulmonary stretch receptors: regulate respiration, not BP

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with suspected cardiac tamponade presents to the AIIMS emergency. You are asked to monitor BP of this patient. All the following precautions should be taken except:
options: Patient should be asked to take deep breaths
The cuff pressure should be increased to 20 mm over systolic pressure
The cuff should slowly deflate until the first Korotkoff sound is heard only during expiration
Pulses paradoxus may not be present
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Patient should be asked to take deep breaths

In suspected cardiac tamponade, blood pressure measurement is done to detect pulsus paradoxus. The patient should breathe normally, not take deep breaths, as deep breathing exaggerates intrathoracic pressure changes and can give false readings.

B. Cuff pressure should be increased to \~20 mmHg over systolic pressue – Correct technique to detect pulsus paradoxus.

C. Cuff should slowly deflate until the first Korotkoff sound is heard only during expiration – Correct method.

D. Pulsus paradoxus may not be present – True; it can be absent in conditions like severe AR or ASD.

questions.text: A previously healthy 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of chest pain on exertion. She takes no medications. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Cardiac stress ECG shows inducible ST-segment depressions in the precordial leads that coincide with the patient's report of chest pain and resolve upon cessation of exercise. Pharmacotherapy with verapamil is initiated. This drug is most likely to have which of the following sets of effects?
options: End diastolic volume (EDV) increase, BP decrease, Contractility decrease, HR decrease
End diastolic volume (EDV) decrease, BP decrease, Contractility decrease, HR decrease
End diastolic volume (EDV) increase, BP no change, Contractility increase, HR decrease
End diastolic volume (EDV) decrease, BP increase, Contractility decrease, HR no change
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. End diastolic volume (EDV) increase, BP decrease, Contractility decrease, HR decrease

Verapamil is a non-dihydropyridine Ca²⁺ channel blocker. It causes negative inotropy (↓ contractility) and negative chronotropy/dromotropy (↓ HR, ↓ AV conduction). It also causes arteriolar vasodilation → ↓ BP. Because HR falls, diastolic filling time increases, so EDV tends to increase.

• EDV decrease – More typical with venodilators (nitrates) or reduced filling.
• Contractility increase – Opposite of verapamil.
• BP no change / BP increase – Not expected with verapamil’s vasodilation.

questions.text: A young athlete was diagnosed to have harsh ejection systolic murmur at the Erb’s point. Which of the following maneuvers would most likely increase the intensity of the murmur?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Valsalva maneuver

A harsh ejection systolic murmur at Erb’s point in a young athlete suggests hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM). The murmur increases when preload decreases, as this worsens LV outflow tract obstruction—this occurs during the Valsalva maneuver.

A. Isometric hand grip – Increases afterload; decreases HOCM murmur.

C. Squatting – Increases preload and afterload; reduces murmur intensity.

D. Leaning forward – Enhances aortic murmurs, not HOCM.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following are normal age-related changes seen in the human heart, except:
options: Dilatation of the aorta with rightward shift
Increase in left ventricular cavity size
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increase in left ventricular cavity size

With normal aging, the heart shows concentric LV remodeling with increased wall thickness and a reduced LV cavity size, along with left atrial enlargement due to diastolic dysfunction. The aorta dilates and elongates, often shifting rightward.

A. Increased left atrial cavity size – Normal due to age-related diastolic dysfunction.

B. Decreased left ventricular cavity size – Typical concentric remodeling of aging.

C. Dilatation of the aorta with rightward shift – Common age-related vascular change.

questions.text: An 11-year-old child diagnosed with acute rheumatic fever with carditis and having no residual valvular pathology comes to your clinic. How many years of prophylaxis should be given to this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 10 years

Secondary prophylaxis should be given until 21 years of age (i.e., for 10 years in this child).

• ARF without carditis → 5 years or until 21 years of age (whichever is longer)
• ARF with carditis (no residual disease) → 10 years or until 21 years of age (whichever is longer)
• ARF with residual valvular disease →10 years or until 40 years of age (whichever is longer)

questions.text: An 55 year old man presents with dyspnea and swelling of his feet. On examination, rales are heard and he is found to have an enlarged heart on chest x-ray. Which of the following is the best drug will delay the progression in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Captopril

This patient has chronic heart failure (dyspnea, edema, cardiomegaly). ACE inhibitors such as captopril delay disease progression and improve survival by reducing afterload and preload and attenuating pathologic ventricular remodeling.

A. Furosemide – Improves symptoms (diuresis) but does not improve survival.

B. Carvedilol –SHOULD NOT be given in decompensated heart failure (presence of rales in this question indicates that)- I hope you haven't marked this!!

C. Digoxin – Improves symptoms and reduces hospitalization, not mortality.

questions.text: An 82-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. He has had no chest pain or dyspnea but he has constipation of recent onset. He was hospitalized 2 weeks ago for atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and was discharged home with oral medications after appropriate management. Medical history is also significant for hypertension and severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease requiring home supplemental oxygen. ECG shows new-onset second-degree atrioventricular block. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause of his current condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diltiazem

Diltiazem is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that slows AV nodal conduction. In an elderly patient recently treated for AF with RVR, it can precipitate second-degree AV block, especially with underlying conduction system disease. Constipation is also a known side effect.

A. Amlodipine – Dihydropyridine CCB; causes vasodilation, does not cause AV block.

C. Hydrochlorothiazide – Diuretic; causes electrolyte issues, not AV nodal block.

D. Esmolol – Short-acting IV β-blocker; unlikely to cause delayed AV block after discharge.

questions.subject: Medicine

questions.text: An infant with restrictive cardiomyopathy and neutropenia is found to have a mutation affecting mitochondrial inner membrane integrity. Which gene mutation explains both findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tafazzin

Tafazzin mutation causes Barth syndrome, an X-linked disorder due to defective cardiolipin remodeling in the mitochondrial inner membrane, leading to restrictive/dilated cardiomyopathy, neutropenia, skeletal myopathy, and growth delay.

A. Dystrophin – Causes Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy; no neutropenia or mitochondrial defect.

C. LMNA – Associated with dilated cardiomyopathy and laminopathies, not neutropenia.

D. MYH7 – Sarcomeric protein mutation causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy only.

questions.text: Below (proximal) the carotid sinus, carotid artery clamping is likely to result in:
options: Increase in the discharge of carotid sinus afferent nerves
Decreased heart rate and blood pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase in vasomotor centre activity

Clamping the carotid artery below (proximal to) the carotid sinus reduces the pressure transmitted to the carotid sinus baroreceptors. This leads to decreased baroreceptor firing, which in turn causes disinhibition of the vasomotor center (RVLM) → increased sympathetic outflow.

B. Increase in discharge of carotid sinus afferent nerve – Happens when pressure at the sinus increases, not decreases.

C. Decreased heart rate and blood pressure – Opposite occurs; HR and BP increase due to sympathetic activation.

D. Baroreceptor adaptation – Refers to long-term resetting, not an acute clamping effect.

questions.text: Calculate the cardiac index for the following reading: HR = 110 bpm Body surface area = 2 m2 EDV = 130 ml ESV= 50 ml
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 4.4 L/min/m2

Stroke volume = EDV − ESV = 130 − 50 = 80 mL (0.08 L)

Cardiac output = HR × SV = 110 × 0.08 = 8.8 L/min

Cardiac index = CO / BSA = 8.8 / 2 = 4.4 L/min/m²

questions.text: In a His bundle electrogram, the AH interval most accurately represents conduction through which of the following?
options: Internodal atrial pathways up to the AV node
Transitional cells between atrial myocardium and AV node
His–Purkinje system proximal to the bundle bifurcation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Compact atrioventricular nodal tissue

Why this is correct (exam logic):

•

AH interval = time from atrial depolarization (A) to His bundle activation (H)

•

This time delay occurs within the AV node, specifically compact AV nodal tissue

•

AV node has:

•

Slow Ca²⁺-mediated conduction

• Few gap junctions → physiological delay

Why other options are wrong (traps)

A. Internodal atrial pathways up to the AV node → Part of atrial conduction, not AH interval

B. Transitional cells between atrial myocardium and AV node → Minor contribution; not the primary determinant of AH delay

D. His–Purkinje system proximal to the bundle bifurcation → Reflected by HV interval, not AH

questions.text: In the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, 2 points are given for all of the following except:
options: Prior stroke or transient ischemic attack
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diabetes mellitus

In the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, 2 points are assigned for age ≥75 years and for prior stroke/TIA/systemic thromboembolism, as these carry the highest stroke risk in atrial fibrillation.

A. Age ≥75 years – Scores 2 points.

B. Prior stroke/TIA – Scores 2 points due to strong recurrence risk.

C. Systemic thromboembolism – Included with stroke/TIA as 2 points.

D. Diabetes mellitus – Scores 1 point, not 2.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: In what phase of the cardiac cycle do expect to see peak left ventricular pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ventricular ejection

Peak left ventricular pressure occurs during ventricular ejection, when the left ventricle contracts forcefully after the aortic valve opens, generating the maximum systolic pressure needed to eject blood into the aorta.

A. Isovolumetric relaxation – Pressure is falling after aortic valve closure.

B. Rapid filling – Diastolic phase with low ventricular pressure.

C. Isovolumetric contraction – Pressure is rising but has not yet reached peak; valves are still closed.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: On the ECG of a normal cardiac cycle, the ventricular myocardium is absolutely unresponsive to any stimulus from the start of the QRS complex until early into the T-wave. At what point during ventricular repolarization does the relative refractory period begin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. At one-third of repolarization

The ventricular effective (absolute) refractory period extends from the beginning of the QRS complex through much of the T wave, during which ventricular myocytes cannot be re-excited regardless of stimulus strength. This refractory period is crucial in preventing tetanic contraction of the heart.

The relative refractory period (RRP) begins when approximately one-third of ventricular repolarization has occurred, corresponding to the latter part of the action potential.

• During the early phase of repolarization, many sodium channels remain inactivated.
• Once about one-third of repolarization is complete, some sodium channels recover from inactivation.
• A stronger-than-normal stimulus can now trigger an action potential, marking the start of the relative refractory period.

| Period | Excitability

| ------ | ------------

| Absolute refractory period | No stimulus can evoke a response

| Relative refractory period | Only a stronger-than-normal stimulus can evoke a response

| Supernormal period | Even weaker stimuli may trigger excitation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following antiarrhythmics will increase both the action potential and the effective refractory period?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Procainamide

Why:

• Procainamide is a Class IA antiarrhythmic, and Class IA drugs have a signature electrophysiologic profile: they prolong both the action potential duration (APD) and the effective refractory period (ERP).
• This happens via moderate sodium channel blockade combined with additional potassium channel blockade, which slows repolarization and widens the AP.

Class IA "big three":

• Quinidine, Procainamide, Disopyramide — all share this AP/ERP-prolonging signature, along with QT prolongation risk (torsades) as the clinical downside.

Why the others don't fit:

| Option | Class | Effect on AP duration | Effect on ERP

| ------ | ----- | --------------------- | -------------

| C. Procainamide | IA | ↑ Increased | ↑ Increased

| B. Lignocaine | IB | ↓ Decreased | ↓/unchanged — shortens AP, used in ischemic/depolarized tissue

| A. Propafenone | IC | Minimal/no change | Minimal/no change on normal tissue ERP

| D. Encainide | IC | Minimal/no change | Minimal/no change

questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following are true about subclinical myocarditis? 1. Palpitations 2. Elevated BNP 3. Regional wall motion abnormalities in ECHO 4. Elevated troponin 5. Low LVEF in ECHO
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3, 4, 5

Subclinical myocarditis often lacks prominent symptoms but shows objective evidence of myocardial injury or dysfunction. Patients may have elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin), raised BNP due to myocardial stress, regional wall-motion abnormalities, and even reduced LVEF on echocardiography despite minimal symptoms.

1. Palpitations – Not a usual feature of myocarditis; thik of arrythmias when palpitations mentioned.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following drug-mechanism pairs is incorrectly matched?
options: Omapatrilat — Dual ACE and vasopeptidase inhibitor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Levosimendan — Myofilament calcium channel blocker

Levosimendan is a calcium sensitizer, not a calcium channel blocker. It binds troponin C, increasing myocardial contractility without significantly increasing intracellular calcium, thereby improving cardiac output with relatively less increase in oxygen demand.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following electrolyte abnormality is an independent predictor of adverse outcome in a patient with CHF?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hyponatremia

In chronic heart failure, hyponatremia is an independent predictor of adverse outcomes and mortality. It reflects severe neurohormonal activation (↑ ADH, RAAS) and advanced disease rather than a simple electrolyte imbalance.

A) Hypernatremia – Uncommon in CHF and not a standard prognostic marker.

C) Hypokalemia – Increases arrhythmia risk but is usually drug-related, not independent.

D) Hyperkalemia – Seen with renal failure/RAAS blockade; prognostic impact is secondary.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for the bradycardia seen in Cushing reflex?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Baroreceptor activation

In Cushing reflex, raised intracranial pressure causes cerebral ischemia, leading to sympathetic activation and severe hypertension. The resulting increase in arterial pressure stimulates baroreceptors, which trigger a reflex parasympathetic response, producing bradycardia.

A) Heart failure – Not the mechanism of reflex bradycardia here.

C) Cardiac conduction defect – Not involved in Cushing reflex.

D) Increased RVLM activity – Causes hypertension, not bradycardia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following statements are true of the baroreceptor reflex pathway? 1. Rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM) is inhibited by CVLM. 2. Caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM) releases GABA. 3. Nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) releases GABA. 4. Stretch receptors are stimulated by increased blood pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 4

In the baroreceptor reflex, increased blood pressure stretches carotid sinus and aortic arch receptors, increasing afferent firing to the NTS. NTS activates the CVLM, which releases GABA to inhibit the RVLM, reducing sympathetic outflow and lowering BP.

1. CVLM inhibits the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM): True – CVLM inhibits RVLM.

2. Caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM) releases GABA: True – CVLM is GABAergic.

3. Nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) releases GABA: False – NTS is primarily glutamatergic, not GABAergic.

4. Stretch receptors are stimulated by increased blood pressure: True – Stretch receptors respond to increased BP.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: While studying regional blood flow physiology, a student notes that an organ receiving a very high proportion of cardiac output relative to its metabolic demand will show a low arteriovenous oxygen difference. Which organ best fits this description, and why?
options: Heart muscle — high oxygen extraction due to near-maximal resting extraction reserve
Kidney — high flow primarily serves filtration, not metabolic/oxygen demand
Skin — high flow driven by thermoregulation, with high oxygen extraction
Brain — constant high flow with minimal oxygen extraction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kidney — high flow primarily serves filtration, not metabolic/oxygen demand

The kidneys receive approximately 20–25% of cardiac output, far exceeding their metabolic requirements. As a result, they extract relatively little oxygen from the blood, producing one of the lowest arteriovenous (A–V) oxygen differences among major organs.

• Renal blood flow is maintained primarily to support glomerular filtration and solute handling, not to meet high metabolic demand.
• Because oxygen extraction is low, renal venous blood retains a relatively high oxygen content.
• Therefore, the A–V oxygen difference is small.

Why not the others?

• A. Heart muscle — high oxygen extraction due to near-maximal resting extraction reserve → Extracts \~70–80% of delivered oxygen at rest; has one of the highest A–V O₂ differences.
• C. Skin — high flow driven by thermoregulation, with high oxygen extraction → Blood flow varies for thermoregulation; oxygen extraction is not characteristically high.
• D. Brain— constant high flow with minimal oxygen extraction → High blood flow but also substantial oxygen utilization; A–V difference is greater than that of the kidney.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: You diagnose a patient with amyloidosis-induced restrictive cardiomyopathy. Consider the following statements regarding this condition and identify the correct option:
options: It is associated with diastolic dysfunction
Clinical features may resemble constrictive pericarditis
ECG often shows low-voltage QRS complexes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All of the above

Amyloidosis causes restrictive cardiomyopathy characterized by severe diastolic dysfunction with relatively preserved systolic function early on. Clinically, it can mimic constrictive pericarditis. Despite increased ventricular wall thickness on echo, the ECG often shows low-voltage QRS complexes due to amyloid infiltration. LVEF is typically normal in early stages, declining late.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of sudden-onset palpitations, dizziness, and mild chest discomfort. ECG during one such episode confirms paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT). Which of the following is the drug of choice for prophylaxis of PSVT?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oral Verapamil

PSVT is a sudden-onset tachycardia originating above the ventricles.

Most common mechanism: Re-entry circuits involving the AV node

Types include:

| Type | Mechanism

| ---- | ---------

| AVNRT | AV node re-entry

| AVRT | Accessory pathway (WPW)

| Atrial tachycardia | Ectopic atrial focus

PSVT is commonly due to AV nodal re-entry, so prophylaxis targets AV nodal conduction.

Oral verapamil blocks L-type calcium channels in the AV node, preventing re-entry circuits.

IV adenosine and IV beta blockers are used for acute termination, not long-term prevention.

It is important to differentiate acute termination vs prophylaxis.

| Situation | Treatment

| --------- | ---------

| Acute attack | IV Adenosine

| Prevention | Oral Verapamil / Beta blockers

| AF Rate Control | Beta blockers / Verapamil

Adenosine has no oral role due to its very short half-life.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 46-year-old male with a history of depression has been treated with fluoxetine for the past six months. He presented to the emergency department with altered consciousness and an ECG showing QT prolongation, with a QTc of 447ms. Recently, he was prescribed an additional medication for chronic pain management. Which of the following drugs was most likely added to his regimen that could have contributed to his current condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methadone

Methadone is well known to cause QT interval prolongation by blocking cardiac potassium channels. Methadone is an opioid analgesic used for:

• Chronic pain
• Opioid dependence therapy

However it can: Block delayed rectifier potassium channels (IKr)

Result:

• Delayed ventricular repolarization
• QT prolongation

Concomitant use with fluoxetine (CYP inhibitor) increases methadone levels, enhancing QT prolongation risk.

Dangerous Consequence: Torsades de Pointes-

Torsades de pointes is:

• Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
• Associated with prolonged QT interval

Symptoms:

• Syncope
• Palpitations
• Sudden cardiac death

This predisposes to torsades de pointes and altered consciousness.

Morphine and tramadol have minimal QT effects, and piperidine is not implicated.

Common Drugs That Prolong QT

| Drug Class | Examples

| ---------- | --------

| Antiarrhythmics | Quinidine, Sotalol

| Antibiotics | Macrolides, Fluoroquinolones

| Antipsychotics | Haloperidol

| Antidepressants | SSRIs, TCAs

| Opioids | Methadone

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of palpitations, shortness of breath, and dizziness. The child has no significant past medical history. On examination, the heart rate is 220 beats per minute, blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, and the child appears anxious but is otherwise stable. An ECG confirms the diagnosis of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT). What is the initial recommended dose of adenosine for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 0.1 mg/kg

Typical characteristics:

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Sudden onset | Re-entry circuit

| Narrow QRS | Supraventricular origin

| HR 180–250 bpm | Typical in PSVT

Most common mechanism: AV nodal re-entry tachycardia (AVNRT).

Initial management depends on hemodynamic stability.

Stable patient

1️⃣ Vagal maneuvers

2️⃣ IV Adenosine

Unstable patient- Synchronized cardioversion

This child is stable, so adenosine is appropriate.

In pediatric PSVT, IV adenosine is the first-line drug for acute termination in hemodynamically stable patients.

The initial recommended dose is 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 6 mg) given as a rapid IV bolus.

If ineffective, a second dose of 0.2 mg/kg may be administered.

Maximum single dose usually: 12 mg

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Half-life | <10 seconds

| Route | Rapid IV bolus

| Use | PSVT termination

| ECG effect | Transient AV block

Higher doses are not used initially due to risk of adverse effects.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy presents with complaints of palpitations. His ECG reveals a narrow complex tachycardia, and he is hemodynamically stable. The physician initiates amiodarone therapy for rhythm control. Amiodarone exerts its primary antiarrhythmic effect by acting on which phase of the cardiac action potential?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phase 3 – Repolarization

| Class | Target | Example

| ----- | ------ | -------

| Class I | Na⁺ channels | Lidocaine

| Class II | β-blockers | Propranolol

| Class III | K⁺ channels | Amiodarone

| Class IV | Ca²⁺ channels | Verapamil

Amiodarone is a Class III antiarrhythmic that primarily blocks potassium channels.

This action prolongs phase 3 repolarization, increasing action potential duration and refractory period.

Blocking potassium channels results in:

• Increased refractory period
• Reduced re-entry circuits
• Stabilization of cardiac rhythm

This makes amiodarone effective for:

• Atrial fibrillation
• Ventricular tachycardia
• Ventricular fibrillation

The effect helps terminate and prevent re-entry tachyarrhythmias.

Sodium (phase 0), calcium (phase 2), and phase 4 effects are secondary, not primary.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient came with complaints of palpitations and dyspnea for 4 hours. On ECG, he was found to have atrial fibrillation with no other cardiovascular symptoms. What is the next best step in management?
options: Look for left atrial thrombus with carotid doppler
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ventricular rate control

ECG shows Atrial Fibrillation (AF).

AF is characterized by:

• Irregularly irregular rhythm
• Absent P waves
• Fibrillatory baseline

This is acute atrial fibrillation (<48 hours) without hemodynamic instability or severe symptoms.

Initial management is ventricular rate control using AV nodal blockers.

Drugs Used for Rate Control

| Drug | Mechanism

| ---- | ---------

| Beta blockers | Slow AV node conduction

| Non-DHP calcium blockers | AV node blockade

| Digoxin | ↑ vagal tone → slows AV node

Emergent cardioversion is reserved for instability, and anticoagulation/thrombus evaluation is considered later.

Thus, rate control is the next best step.

| Situation | Management

| --------- | ----------

| Unstable AF | DC cardioversion

| Stable AF | Rate control

| Long-term | Anticoagulation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient on antidepressants presented to you with hypotension. An ECG was done, which showed wide QRS complexes and right axis deviation. How will you manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IV NaHCO3

The combination of:

• Antidepressant use
• Wide QRS complex
• Hypotension

strongly suggests: Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) toxicity

The drug of choice for TCA toxicity is: IV Sodium Bicarbonate

Mechanism:

1️⃣ Alkalinizes blood

2️⃣ Reduces TCA binding to sodium channels

3️⃣ Increases sodium concentration

Result:

• Narrowing of QRS complex
• Improved cardiac conduction

Antidepressant overdose (classically tricyclic antidepressants) causes sodium channel blockade, leading to wide QRS complexes and hypotension.

IV sodium bicarbonate reverses Na⁺ channel blockade and corrects acidosis.

This narrows QRS and improves hemodynamics.

Antiarrhythmics, beta blockers, and phenytoin are contraindicated or ineffective in TCA toxicity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient was brought to the emergency room after consuming 8 digoxin tablets. On examination, he was found to be unstable, with a heart rate of 56 beats per minute. An ECG revealed a third-degree heart block. What is the next step in this patient's care?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Digoxin Immune Fab

| Finding | Significance

| ------- | ------------

| Digoxin ingestion | Possible overdose

| Bradycardia | Increased vagal tone

| Complete heart block | Classic toxicity complication

This patient has acute digoxin toxicity with life-threatening bradyarrhythmia (complete heart block) and hemodynamic instability.

The definitive treatment is Digoxin Immune Fab, which binds free digoxin and rapidly reverses toxicity. Treatment: Digoxin Immune Fab

The antidote for digoxin toxicity is: Digoxin Immune Fab (Digoxin-specific antibody fragments)

Mechanism:

• Antibody binds free digoxin
• Forms inactive complexes
• Complexes are excreted in urine

Result: Rapid reversal of toxicity.

DC cardioversion is contraindicated as it can precipitate malignant arrhythmias in digoxin toxicity.

Antiarrhythmics like lidocaine or phenytoin are adjuncts, not definitive therapy in unstable patients.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a previous history of myocardial infarction and ventricular arrhythmia is on treatment for the same since a few months. He developed fatigue, dyspnea, and weight gain. He had also developed pulmonary fibrosis. Which of the following drugs is responsible for the above-mentioned side effects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amiodarone

For ventricular arrhythmias after MI, one of the most commonly used drugs is: Amiodarone

Amiodarone belongs to:

• Class III antiarrhythmic drugs

Amiodarone is used for ventricular arrhythmias post-MI and has a characteristic adverse-effect profile.

It causes pulmonary fibrosis, along with fatigue, dyspnea, weight gain, and thyroid dysfunction.

Amiodarone pulmonary toxicity (APT) exhibiting a pulmonary interstitial fibrosis pattern. Computed tomography (CT) scans obtained at the level of both lower lobes revealed intralobular and interlobular septal thickenings in the peripheral regions of both lower lobes (arrowheads), and interlobular septal thickenings in the central and middle regions of the right lower lobe (arrows).

These toxicities are due to its iodine content and tissue accumulation with long half-life. Beta blockers, aspirin, and spironolactone do not cause pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young male presented with palpitations and hence ECG was taken. ECG demonstrated narrow complex tachycardia and his BP was 70/40 mm of Hg. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Synchronized DC Cardioversion

The patient has narrow complex tachycardia with hemodynamic instability (BP 70/40 mmHg). Unstable tachyarrhythmias require immediate synchronized DC cardioversion regardless of QRS width.

| Feature | Cardioversion | Defibrillation

| ------- | ------------- | --------------

| Synchronization | Yes | No

| Used for | SVT, AF, VT with pulse | VF, pulseless VT

| Energy | Lower | Higher

Adenosine and vagal maneuvers are reserved for stable SVT.

Amiodarone is not first-line in acute unstable narrow complex tachycardia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An athlete who was planning for some kind of physical activity sport comes for a routine health checkup. All routine investigations turned out to be normal with non-significant ECG findings except he had a PR interval of 0.21 seconds. Which of the following is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. First degree heart block

A PR interval >0.20 seconds indicates delayed AV nodal conduction.

This is diagnostic of first-degree heart block, often seen in athletes due to increased vagal tone.

It is usually asymptomatic and benign with no dropped beats.

Second- and third-degree blocks show intermittent or complete AV dissociation, not isolated PR prolongation.

| AV Block | ECG Finding

| -------- | -----------

| First degree | Prolonged PR interval

| Second degree (Mobitz I) | Progressive PR prolongation

| Second degree (Mobitz II) | Sudden dropped QRS

| Third degree | AV dissociation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly man with diabetic nephropathy presented to the emergency department with palpitations and chest discomfort. The ECG revealed large T-waves. Laboratory tests revealed elevated potassium levels. Which of the following drugs can cause intracellular movement of potassium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Epinephrine

| Finding | Significance

| ------- | ------------

| Diabetic nephropathy | Kidney cannot excrete potassium

| Peaked T waves | Classic ECG sign of hyperkalemia

Hyperkalemia presents with tall, peaked T waves on ECG.

Epinephrine (β₂-agonist action) drives potassium into cells by stimulating Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Treatment strategies include:

| Mechanism | Example

| --------- | -------

| Stabilize cardiac membrane | Calcium gluconate

| Shift K⁺ into cells | Insulin, β-agonists (epinephrine)

| Remove K⁺ from body | Dialysis, diuretics

Epinephrine stimulates: β₂-adrenergic receptors

This activates: Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump

Result:

• Potassium moves from blood into cells

Thus, serum potassium decreases.

This causes a rapid transient reduction in serum potassium.

Glucagon, atropine, and lactic acid do not shift potassium intracellularly.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Takotsubo cardiomyopathy: 1. There is acute right ventricular dysfunction characterized by dilation of the right ventricular apex. 2. It can be precipitated by acute emotional stress and is frequently associated with an underlying neuro-psychiatric disorder. 3. Symptoms and ECG findings often mimic acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction. 4. Ventriculography shows normal left ventricle and apical ballooning of the right ventricle. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 and 3

• 1. Acute right ventricular dysfunction with apical dilation: Incorrect

• Takotsubo cardiomyopathy primarily involves transient left ventricular dysfunction, classically with apical ballooning.
• Right ventricular involvement can occur, but it is not the defining feature.

• 2. Precipitated by acute emotional stress: Correct

• Also called stress cardiomyopathy, it is commonly triggered by intense emotional or physical stress.
• It is frequently associated with psychiatric or neurological disorders.

• 3. Mimics acute STEMI: Correct

• Patients may present with acute chest pain, ST-segment elevation, and elevated cardiac biomarkers, closely mimicking acute myocardial infarction.
• Coronary angiography typically shows no obstructive coronary artery disease.

• 4. Ventriculography shows normal LV and apical ballooning of RV: Incorrect

• The characteristic finding is LV apical ballooning, not right ventricular apical ballooning.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Osborn waves in ECG show prolonged repolarization with a distinctive convex elevation of the J point. These waves are associated with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Systemic hypothermia

Osborn (J) waves are positive deflections at the J point on ECG and are classically associated with systemic hypothermia (typically when core temperature is <32°C). They result from delayed ventricular repolarization and become more prominent as body temperature decreases.

Why not the other options?

• B. Acute pericarditis: Causes diffuse concave ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression, not Osborn waves.
• C. Acute myocarditis: May show nonspecific ST-T changes, arrhythmias, or conduction defects, but not characteristic Osborn waves.
• D. Brugada syndrome: Shows coved ST-segment elevation in V1–V3 with RBBB-like pattern, distinct from Osborn waves.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The SA node is situated at the junction of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. SVC and RA

The sinoatrial (SA) node, the heart’s primary pacemaker, is located subepicardially at the junction of the superior vena cava (SVC) and the right atrium (RA), near the upper end of the crista terminalis.

Key points:

• Location: Junction of the SVC and right atrium.
• Function: Initiates the normal cardiac impulse at a rate of 60–100 beats/min, producing normal sinus rhythm.
• Blood supply:

• Right coronary artery (RCA) in approximately 60% of individuals.
• Left circumflex artery (LCX) in approximately 40%.

• The impulse spreads through the atria to the AV node, then to the Bundle of His, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is an inhibitor of ATP binding cassette efflux pumps?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Verapamil

ATP-binding cassette (ABC) efflux pumps like P-glycoprotein reduce intracellular drug concentration.

Verapamil is a well-known P-glycoprotein (ABC transporter) inhibitor, increasing intracellular drug levels. Function:

• Pumps drugs and toxins out of cells
• Protects tissues from toxic accumulation

Verapamil is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.

Besides blocking L-type calcium channels, it also: Inhibits P-glycoprotein (ABC efflux pump)

Effects:

• Increases intracellular drug concentrations
• Can reverse multidrug resistance in cancer cells

Cancer cells often overexpress P-glycoprotein, which pumps chemotherapy drugs out of the cell.

This causes: Multidrug resistance (MDR)

Verapamil inhibits this pump and can increase chemotherapy effectiveness.

This property is used to overcome multidrug resistance in certain settings.

Main clinical effects:

| Effect | Mechanism

| ------ | ---------

| ↓ Heart rate | AV node calcium channel blockade

| ↓ Contractility | Reduced Ca²⁺ entry

| Vasodilation | Smooth muscle relaxation

Clinical uses:

• Supraventricular tachycardia
• Atrial fibrillation rate control
• Hypertension
• Angina

Tacrolimus, nifedipine, and diltiazem are substrates rather than potent inhibitors.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs, when given with erythromycin, can cause QT prolongation and Torsades de pointes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Astemizole

Astemizole is a second-generation antihistamine metabolized by CYP3A4.

Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4, leading to elevated astemizole levels.

Astemizole is a second-generation antihistamine.

It can block: Delayed rectifier potassium channels (IKr)

This causes:

• Delayed repolarization
• QT interval prolongation

Because of this risk, astemizole has been withdrawn in many countries.

This causes QT prolongation and predisposes to torsades de pointes.

Cetirizine, loratadine, and promethazine have minimal QT risk with erythromycin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of NAME syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ebstein’s anomaly

NAME syndrome includes Nevi, Atrial myxoma, Myxoid neurofibroma, and Ephelides. Atrial myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults.
