Location: Left atrium (most common)

Usually attached to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis. Key features:

• Pedunculated gelatinous tumor

• May prolapse into the mitral valve orifice

• Causes ball-valve obstruction

Atrial myxoma produces a characteristic sound called: Tumor plop

Occurs during early diastole when the tumor moves into the mitral valve opening.

NAME syndrome is related to Carney complex, a genetic disorder.

Features of Carney complex include:

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| Cardiac myxoma | Most important

| Skin pigmentation | Lentigines

| Endocrine tumors | e.g., pheochromocytoma

| Myxoid tumors | Skin/soft tissue

Cardiac involvement is classically atrial myxoma, not valvular congenital defects.

Ebstein’s anomaly is unrelated to NAME syndrome.

Pheochromocytoma may be seen in related myxoma syndromes but Ebstein’s anomaly is not a component.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a typical feature of stable angina?
options: Pain commonly radiates to the trapezius
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pain commonly radiates to the trapezius

• Stable angina presents as retrosternal pressure or heaviness precipitated by exertion or emotional stress and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin.
• Pain classically radiates to the left shoulder, left arm, jaw, neck, or back.
• Radiation to the trapezius ridge is characteristic of acute pericarditis, not angina.
• Typical episodes are brief (2–5 minutes) and often show a gradual crescendo–decrescendo pattern.
• Levine's sign (clenched fist over the chest) is a classic clinical sign of ischemic chest pain.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements are true about PR interval? 1. It denotes atrial depolarization. 2. Normal duration is 0.12–0.20 second. 3. Prolongation denotes impaired AV nodal conduction. 4. A short PR interval occurs in WPW syndrome. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

The PR interval is the time from the beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the QRS complex. It represents the time taken for the electrical impulse to travel from the atria through the AV node, bundle of His, and Purkinje system to the ventricles.

• Statement 1. It denotes atrial depolarization: Incorrect.

• The P wave denotes atrial depolarization.
• The PR interval represents AV conduction time, not atrial depolarization alone.

• Statement 2. Normal duration is 0.12–0.20 second: Correct. Normal PR interval = 0.12–0.20 seconds (3–5 small squares).
• Statement 3. Prolongation denotes impaired AV nodal conduction: Correct. PR interval >0.20 seconds indicates delayed AV nodal conduction, classically seen in first-degree AV block.
• Statement 4. A short PR interval occurs in WPW syndrome: Correct. A short PR interval (<0.12 seconds) is seen in Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome due to conduction through an accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent), bypassing the AV node.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is the appropriate scoring system used to assess the risk of stroke in patients of non-valvular chronic atrial fibrillation on oral anticoagulation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CHA₂DS₂-VASc

The CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is the standard risk stratification tool used to estimate the risk of ischemic stroke in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation (AF) and to guide the need for oral anticoagulation.

CHA₂DS₂-VASc Score

| Risk Factor | Points

| ----------- | ------

| C – Congestive heart failure/LV dysfunction | 1

| H – Hypertension | 1

| A₂ – Age ≥75 years | 2

| D – Diabetes mellitus | 1

| S₂ – Prior Stroke/TIA/Systemic embolism | 2

| V – Vascular disease (MI, PAD, aortic plaque) | 1

| A – Age 65–74 years | 1

| Sc – Sex category (Female) | 1

Interpretation:

• 0 (men) or 1 (women due to sex alone): Low risk; anticoagulation usually not indicated.
• ≥1 (men) or ≥2 (women): Consider oral anticoagulation.
• ≥2 (men) or ≥3 (women): Oral anticoagulation is recommended unless contraindicated.

Why not the other options?

• A. HAS-BLED: Assesses bleeding risk in patients receiving anticoagulation, not stroke risk.
• B. AMT-4: Abbreviated Mental Test for cognitive assessment.
• C. CURB-65: Severity score for community-acquired pneumonia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following responses to intravenous adenosine is correctly matched?
options: Ventricular tachycardia — Termination and complete recovery
Atrial flutter — Termination and complete recovery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atrio-ventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia — Termination

Adenosine is an ultra-short-acting antiarrhythmic drug that transiently blocks conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node by activating A1 adenosine receptors, causing hyperpolarization and slowing AV nodal conduction. It is the drug of choice for terminating AV node-dependent supraventricular tachycardias, particularly AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT.

AVNRT depends on re-entry through the AV node. By producing a transient AV nodal block, adenosine interrupts the re-entry circuit, leading to termination of the arrhythmia.

Why not the other options?

• A. Atrial fibrillation — Termination: Incorrect. Adenosine does not terminate atrial fibrillation; it may transiently slow the ventricular rate by blocking AV nodal conduction.
• C. Ventricular tachycardia — Termination and complete recovery: Incorrect. Adenosine is not effective for most ventricular tachycardias (except rare idiopathic outflow tract VT).
• D. Atrial flutter — Termination and complete recovery: Incorrect. Adenosine may produce transient AV block, helping reveal flutter waves, but does not terminate atrial flutter.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: 18-year-old female presented with high fever and pain in knee and ankle joints. On examination, the patient had a pan-systolic murmur at the apex. Rheumatoid factor is negative. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute Rheumatic Fever

Acute rheumatic fever presents with migratory polyarthritis of large joints and carditis following streptococcal infection.

A pan-systolic murmur at the apex indicates mitral regurgitation due to rheumatic carditis.

Diagnosis of ARF is based on Modified Jones Criteria.

Major Criteria

| Major feature

| -------------

| Carditis

| Migratory polyarthritis

| Chorea

| Erythema marginatum

| Subcutaneous nodules

Minor Criteria

| Minor feature

| -------------

| Fever

| Arthralgia

| Elevated ESR / CRP

| Prolonged PR interval

Evidence of recent streptococcal infection is also required.

Rheumatoid factor is negative, supporting a non-RA etiology.

Septic arthritis is usually monoarticular, and ankylosing spondylitis involves axial joints.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with acute heart failure with pulmonary edema, severe breathlessness and bilateral basal crepitations. Which drug should be administered immediately?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Furosemide

• IV furosemide is the immediate drug of choice in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
• It has a dual benefit: within 5–10 minutes it causes venodilation → ↓ preload → ↓ pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, giving symptomatic relief even before diuresis begins; subsequently it inhibits the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ (NKCC2) cotransporter in the thick ascending limb → brisk diuresis → ↓ volume overload.
• Given IV because gut wall edema impairs oral absorption.

Other options:

• A. Digoxin: Is a positive inotrope with slow onset; useful only in HF with rapid AF — not for acute pulmonary edema rescue.
• C. Mannitol: Is an osmotic diuretic that first expands intravascular volume → will worsen pulmonary edema. Contraindicated here.
• D. Acetazolamide: Is a weak diuretic causing metabolic acidosis; upharsed in altitude sickness/glaucoma, not acute LVF.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An 11-year-old child who weighs 26 kg with a history of streptococcal pharyngitis presents to you with fever and arthralgia. There is no evidence of carditis. How often is benzathine penicillin recommended for prophylaxis of rheumatic heart disease?
options: 600000 IU Once in 3 weeks for next 5 years
600000 IU Once in 3 weeks for next 10 years
1200000 IU Once in 3 weeks for next 10 years
1200000 IU Once in 3 weeks for life
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 600000 IU Once in 3 weeks for next 10 years

This child has acute rheumatic fever without carditis and no established valvular disease. Benzathine penicillin G is used because it:

• Provides long-acting antibiotic coverage
• Prevents recurrent streptococcal infection

Administration: Intramuscular injection every 3 weeks

For secondary prophylaxis in ARF without carditis, benzathine penicillin is given for 5 years or until age 21 (whichever is longer). In this case, since the child is 11 years old, we will give prophylaxis for the next 10 years since (21-11 years) is longer than 5 years.

| Category | Duration from the last attack

| -------- | -----------------------------

| Rheumatic fever without carditis | 5 years or until 21 years of age (whichever is longer)

| Rheumatic fever with carditis but no residual heart disease | 10 years or until 21 years of age (whichever is longer)

| Rheumatic fever with carditis + residual heart disease | 10 years or until 40 years of age (whichever is longer)

In children weighing <30 kg, the recommended dose is 600,000 IU IM every 3 weeks.

Hence, 600000 IU once in 3 weeks for the next 10 years is correct.

The "Whichever is Longer" Rule — A Common Trap

Students often memorize "no carditis = 5 years" and stop there. But the full rule is:

5 years OR until age 21 — whichever gives MORE time

So you must always calculate both and pick the larger number:

| Child's Age | 5 years from now | Until age 21 | Choose

| ----------- | ---------------- | ------------ | ------

| 11 years | Age 16 | Age 21 = 10 more years | 10 years ✅

| 17 years | Age 22 = 5 more years | Age 21 = 4 years | 5 years ✅

| 18 years | Age 23 = 5 more years | Age 21 = 3 years | 5 years ✅

Why Not Option C (1.2 million IU)?

Add this explicitly since 20.9% chose it:

• 1,200,000 IU is for children ≥30 kg.
• This child weighs 26 kg < 30 kg → dose is 600,000 IU.

The weight cutoff is a second trap layered onto the duration trap — both must be applied correctly to reach B.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Aschoff Nodules are a pathognomonic cardiac finding in which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rheumatic carditis

Aschoff nodules (Aschoff bodies) are the characteristic histopathological lesions of acute rheumatic fever, particularly rheumatic carditis. They represent areas of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by inflammatory cells, including characteristic Anitschkow cells (“caterpillar cells”).

Why not the other options?

• B. Infective endocarditis: Shows vegetations containing microorganisms, fibrin, and inflammatory cells, not Aschoff bodies.
• C. Rheumatoid arthritis: May produce rheumatoid nodules, characterized by central fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by palisading histiocytes.
• D. Takayasu arteritis: Causes granulomatous inflammation of large arteries with intimal thickening and fibrosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Infiltration of the small-intestine mucosa with ‘foamy’ macrophages, which stain positive with Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) reagent, is a characteristic feature of which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Whipple’s disease

Whipple’s disease is caused by Tropheryma whipplei, a gram-positive actinomycete. The organism accumulates within macrophages in the lamina propria of the small intestine, producing characteristic foamy macrophages that stain strongly PAS-positive.

Why not the other options?

• A. Radiation enteropathy: Causes mucosal atrophy, ulceration, fibrosis, vascular injury, and telangiectasia after radiation exposure.
• B. Coeliac disease: Shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes; PAS-positive foamy macrophages are absent.
• C. Tropical sprue: Causes villous atrophy and malabsorption, but does not show PAS-positive macrophages.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Jones criteria for the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever has several major and minor criteria. Which of the following are included in the major or minor criteria of Jones criteria? 1. Carditis 2. Erythema nodosum 3. Polyarthralgia 4. Short PR interval 5. Sydenham chorea
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, and 5

The diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever is based on the Jones criteria, which include major and minor manifestations along with evidence of a preceding Group A streptococcal infection.

Jones Criteria (Acute Rheumatic Fever)

Major Criteria

• Carditis
• Polyarthritis
• Chorea
• Erythema marginatum
• Subcutaneous nodules

Minor Criteria

Clinical:

• Arthralgia
• Fever

Laboratory:

• Elevated ESR / CRP
• First-degree atrioventricular (AV) block

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Thickened ventricular wall with normal diastolic function is a feature of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Athlete’s heart

Athlete’s heart is a physiological adaptation to intensive exercise, characterized by mild symmetrical left ventricular wall thickening with preserved systolic and normal diastolic function. It is a benign and reversible condition that must be differentiated from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: Causes pathological ventricular hypertrophy with impaired diastolic relaxation (diastolic dysfunction) and may produce LV outflow tract obstruction.
• B. Restrictive cardiomyopathy: Characterized by severe diastolic dysfunction due to a stiff ventricle; wall thickness is usually normal or increased only in infiltrative diseases.
• C. Endomyocardial fibrosis: A type of restrictive cardiomyopathy causing marked diastolic dysfunction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: True about Rheumatic heart disease are: 1. Caused by group A beta hemolytic streptococci 2. Aschoff bodies are seen 3. Shows only myocarditis 4. Shows only aortic rupture
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2

Rheumatic heart disease follows Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infection.

Aschoff bodies are the characteristic histopathological lesion.

It causes pancarditis (endocarditis, myocarditis, pericarditis), not isolated myocarditis.

| Layer | Pathology

| ----- | ---------

| Endocardium | Valvulitis

| Myocardium | Aschoff bodies

| Pericardium | Fibrinous pericarditis

There is no aortic rupture in rheumatic heart disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which among the following according to the latest guidelines is NOT an indication to IE prophylaxis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atrial Septal Defect

According to AHA / ESC guidelines, antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended only for high-risk cardiac conditions.

It is not recommended for most congenital heart diseases, including isolated ASD.

This change was made to:

• Reduce unnecessary antibiotic use
• Prevent antibiotic resistance

Infective endocarditis prophylaxis is indicated in high-risk cardiac conditions only.

These include prior IE, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, and cardiac transplant with valvulopathy.

An atrial septal defect (isolated, unrepaired) is a low-risk lesion and does not require prophylaxis.

Hence, ASD is not an indication for IE prophylaxis. Prophylaxis is mainly recommended before: Dental procedures involving gingival manipulation

Typical drug:

• Amoxicillin 2 g orally (adults)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are major criteria under the Jones Criteria for Acute Rheumatic Fever? 1. Chorea 2. Erythema marginatum 3. Subcutaneous nodules 4. Polyarthralgia Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The five major Jones criteria are:

1. Carditis
2. Polyarthritis
3. Chorea (Sydenham's chorea)
4. Erythema marginatum
5. Subcutaneous nodules

So Chorea, Erythema marginatum, and Subcutaneous nodules are all major criteria.

Why option with Polyarthralgia is wrong: This is the key trap in the question — polyarthralgia is a minor criterion, not major. The major criterion is polyarthritis (objective joint inflammation), while polyarthralgia (joint pain without objective inflammation) only counts as minor — and importantly, if polyarthritis is already used as a major criterion, polyarthralgia cannot also be counted as a minor criterion in the same patient (to avoid double-counting the same joint symptom).

Minor criteria (for reference, high-yield alongside majors):

• Fever
• Polyarthralgia (only if polyarthritis isn't used as major)
• Elevated ESR/CRP
• Prolonged PR interval on ECG (only if carditis isn't used as major)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is correct regarding acute rheumatic fever?
options: Acute cases can present with aortic valve rupture.
Happens 2 weeks after Group B streptococcus infection.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aschoff bodies are seen.

Acute rheumatic fever is a post-infectious, immune-mediated disease that occurs 2–3 weeks after pharyngeal infection with Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus. It is characterized pathologically by pancarditis involving the endocardium, myocardium, and pericardium, and the presence of Aschoff bodies in the myocardium is a hallmark feature.

Key concepts:

• Aschoff bodies are granulomatous lesions with Anitschkow cells (caterpillar nuclei) and are pathognomonic of acute rheumatic fever
• Pancarditis is typical, with endocarditis leading to valvular involvement (commonly mitral valve)
• It follows Group A streptococcal pharyngitis, not Group B
• Valve damage is due to inflammation and scarring, not acute rupture

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following would most likely lead to a decrease in the intensity of the murmur in a patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Squatting

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is characterized by:

• Asymmetric septal hypertrophy
• Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction

This obstruction changes depending on ventricular volume. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, murmur intensity depends on the degree of LV outflow tract obstruction. Squatting causes:

• Increased venous return (preload)
• Increased LV volume

This widens the LV outflow tract.

Result: Reduced obstruction → decreased murmur

The murmur intensity depends on left ventricular volume.

| LV Volume | LVOT Obstruction | Murmur

| --------- | ---------------- | ------

| Low volume | More obstruction | Louder murmur

| High volume | Less obstruction | Softer murmur

Squatting increases venous return and afterload, enlarging LV cavity size and reducing septal–mitral apposition.

This decreases LVOT obstruction, thereby reducing murmur intensity.

Valsalva and diuretics worsen obstruction, while digoxin increases contractility.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct for subcutaneous nodules in Rheumatic fever?
options: They are present over flexor aspect of forearm
The usual size of these nodules is 3–5 cm
They typically appear more than 3 weeks after onset of other clinical manifestations
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. They typically appear more than 3 weeks after onset of other clinical manifestations

Subcutaneous nodules are one of the major Jones criteria for the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever (ARF). They are a late manifestation, typically appearing more than 3 weeks after the onset of other clinical features such as arthritis or carditis, and are strongly associated with severe rheumatic carditis.

Subcutaneous nodules:

• Appear weeks after the onset of rheumatic fever (usually >3 weeks). ⭐
• Often coexist with carditis.
• Tend to resolve spontaneously over weeks.

Why not the other options?

• A. They are present over flexor aspect of forearm: Incorrect. They occur over extensor surfaces and bony prominences, such as the elbows, knees, ankles, spine, and occiput.
• B. They are painful tender nodules: Incorrect. They are painless, firm, and non-tender.
• C. The usual size of these nodules is 3–5 cm: Incorrect. They are usually small (0.5–2 cm) in diameter.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old female with a history of chest pain and upper respiratory tract infection, seven days ago, presents with shortness of breath. She has BP of 100/60 mm Hg and a pulse rate of 110/min. Chest x-ray reviews an enlarged heart, which appears like a water bottle. Which of the following is incorrect?
options: Loud S1 is a common finding
Echo will show diastolic RA/RV collapse
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Loud S1 is a common finding

The water-bottle shaped heart on chest X-ray strongly suggests:

Pericardial Effusion → Cardiac Tamponade

Supporting clues:

| Finding | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Tachycardia | Compensatory response

| Hypotension | Reduced cardiac output

| Dyspnea | Reduced ventricular filling

In cardiac tamponade, muffled heart sounds are a key finding, not a loud S1.

The definitive treatment is: Pericardiocentesis

A needle is inserted into the pericardial space to remove fluid and relieve pressure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 54-year-old female presented with shortness of breath. On examination, she had bibasal crackles and S3. Echocardiogram revealed poor cardiac contractility with an EF of 33%. Which of the following drugs can reduce mortality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bisoprolol

This patient has HFrEF with reduced ejection fraction (33%).

Bisoprolol, a β₁-selective blocker, has proven mortality benefit in chronic systolic heart failure.

It reduces sympathetic overactivity and adverse ventricular remodeling.

Propranolol, pindolol, and labetalol do not show survival benefit in HFrEF.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 64-year-old male with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with fatigue and exertional dyspnea. He is compliant with his medications. An echocardiogram reveals normal systolic function and grade 2 diastolic dysfunction, left ventricular hypertrophy, left atrial enlargement, and a preserved ejection fraction (EF 60%). His BNP is elevated at 980 pg/mL. He has had two hospital admissions for heart failure in the past year. He is currently euvolemic and is on optimal doses of beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Perform coronary angiography to rule out ischemic cardiomyopathy
Initiate loop diuretics and SGLT2 inhibitors
Start digoxin to enhance myocardial contractility
Initiate Ivabradine to reduce heart rate and improve diastolic filling
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Initiate loop diuretics and SGLT2 inhibitors

This patient has HFpEF (preserved EF, diastolic dysfunction, LVH, LA enlargement, elevated BNP). Management focuses on symptom control and reducing hospitalizations, not increasing contractility. Unlike HFrEF, HFpEF has limited mortality-reducing therapies. However two important treatments help:

1️⃣ Diuretics

Purpose:

• Reduce pulmonary congestion
• Control volume overload

Loop diuretics commonly used:

• Furosemide
• Torsemide

SGLT2 inhibitors improve outcomes and reduce HF admissions in HFpEF, while loop diuretics relieve congestion. They improve:

• Diuresis
• Cardiac metabolism
• Renal protection

| Feature | HFrEF | HFpEF

| ------- | ----- | -----

| EF | ↓ (<40%) | Normal (>50%)

| Problem | Weak contraction | Stiff ventricle

| Therapy | ACEi, BB, ARNI, MRA | Diuretics, SGLT2i

Digoxin and ivabradine have no proven outcome benefit in HFpEF, and ranolazine is for angina, not HF control.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with symptoms of exertional and nocturnal dyspnea, cardiomegaly observed on imaging, pedal edema, a gallop rhythm on cardiac auscultation, and rales in both lungs. Based on this clinical presentation, which suggests congestive heart failure (CHF), which of the following drugs would be most appropriate to prevent the progression of the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Captopril

This presentation is classic congestive heart failure with volume overload and cardiomegaly. The symptoms indicate congestive heart failure with reduced cardiac output.

Classic clues:

| Finding | Mechanism

| ------- | ---------

| Dyspnea | Pulmonary congestion

| S3 gallop | Rapid ventricular filling

| Pedal edema | Systemic venous congestion

| Cardiomegaly | Ventricular remodeling

Heart failure triggers several compensatory mechanisms:

1️⃣ Sympathetic activation

2️⃣ Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)

3️⃣ ADH secretion

While initially helpful, these mechanisms cause:

• Vasoconstriction
• Fluid retention
• Ventricular remodeling

Which worsens heart failure.

ACE inhibitors (captopril) prevent disease progression by reducing afterload, inhibiting RAAS, and limiting ventricular remodeling.

They provide mortality benefit and slow HF progression.

| Effect | Benefit

| ------ | -------

| ↓ Afterload | Improves cardiac output

| ↓ Aldosterone | Reduces fluid retention

| ↓ Ventricular remodeling | Slows CHF progression

Diuretics and digoxin improve symptoms, while beta blockers are added later once the patient is stabilized. ACE inhibitors are first-line therapy in CHF.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young patient presented with PND, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. However, the patient succumbed to her illness. On autopsy, the lungs showed hemosiderin-laden macrophages. In all of the following it can occur, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right heart failure

• Hemosiderin-laden macrophages (“heart failure cells”) result from chronic pulmonary congestion with RBC extravasation and breakdown.
• They are seen in left-sided heart failure, pulmonary venous obstruction, and volume overload states causing raised pulmonary capillary pressure.

These macrophages appear brown due to iron deposition. They indicate chronic pulmonary venous hypertension.

Analyzing Each Option

| Option | Causes Pulmonary Venous HTN? | Heart Failure Cells?

| ------ | ---------------------------- | --------------------

| A — Right heart failure | ❌ RHF → systemic venous congestion, NOT pulmonary | EXCEPT ✅

| B — Protein-losing enteropathy | ❌ No mechanism for pulmonary venous HTN | EXCEPT ✅

| C — Pulmonary venous obstruction | ✅ Directly raises pulmonary venous pressure | Yes ✅

| D — Volume overload | ✅ → Biventricular failure → pulmonary congestion | Yes ✅

The Controversy

This is genuinely controversial because both A and B are mechanistically correct "excepts."

Why A (Right heart failure) is the standard expected answer:

• Classic teaching: RHF causes systemic congestion (hepatomegaly, pedal edema, JVD), NOT pulmonary venous hypertension
• Therefore heart failure cells should NOT occur in isolated RHF
• Most Indian textbooks (Harsh Mohan, Robbins) frame it this way

Why B (Protein-losing enteropathy) could also be argued:

• PLE has absolutely no mechanism for pulmonary venous HTN
• It causes hypoalbuminemia → generalized edema, but not specifically pulmonary venous congestion
• Some argue B is a "cleaner" except than A

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: High output cardiac failure is caused by which of the following diseases? 1. Beri-beri 2. Severe anaemia 3. Thyrotoxicosis Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

High-output cardiac failure occurs when the heart pumps an abnormally high cardiac output, but this is still insufficient to meet the body’s markedly increased metabolic demands or reduced systemic vascular resistance.

Causes of high-output heart failure include:

• Beri-beri (Thiamine deficiency): Causes peripheral vasodilation, reduced systemic vascular resistance, and increased cardiac output.
• Severe anaemia: Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity leads to compensatory increase in cardiac output to maintain tissue oxygen delivery.
• Thyrotoxicosis: Increases metabolic rate, heart rate, and myocardial contractility, resulting in increased cardiac output.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a symptom of cardiac failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Non-pulsatile elevation of JVP

Heart failure causes venous congestion and reduced cardiac output, producing a combination of:

• Pulmonary symptoms (left heart failure)
• Systemic venous congestion (right heart failure)

Typical symptoms include:

| System | Symptoms

| ------ | --------

| Pulmonary | Dyspnea, orthopnea, PND

| Systemic venous | Pedal edema, hepatomegaly

| General | Fatigue

Framingham Criteria for Congestive Heart Failure, a classic exam favorite used to clinically diagnose CHF. Diagnosis requires:

Either

• 2 Major criteria

OR

• 1 Major + 2 Minor criteria

Diagnostic Criteria

| Major Criteria | Explanation

| -------------- | -----------

| Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND) | Sudden breathlessness during sleep

| Neck vein distension (elevated JVP) | Reflects increased right atrial pressure

| Pulmonary rales (crepitations) | Due to pulmonary edema

| Cardiomegaly | Seen on chest X-ray

| Acute pulmonary edema | Severe LV failure

| S3 gallop | Rapid ventricular filling in HF

| Increased central venous pressure (>16 cm H₂O) | Venous congestion

| Hepatojugular reflux | JVP rises with liver compression

| Weight loss >4.5 kg in 5 days with treatment | Response to diuresis

| Minor Criteria | Explanation

| -------------- | -----------

| Bilateral ankle edema | Venous congestion

| Night cough | Pulmonary congestion

| Dyspnea on exertion | Reduced cardiac output

| Hepatomegaly | Congestive hepatomegaly

| Pleural effusion | Fluid accumulation

| Vital capacity reduced by 1/3 | Lung restriction

| Tachycardia (>120/min) | Sympathetic activation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is a famous large prospective study that helped establish risk factors for coronary heart disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Framingham study

The Framingham Heart Study (FHS) is the landmark prospective cohort study that identified the major modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors for coronary heart disease (CHD) and laid the foundation for modern cardiovascular prevention.

• A. Adelaide study ✗

• Not a landmark study for CHD risk factors.

• B. Birmingham study ✗

• Not associated with establishing CHD risk factors.

• C. Framingham study ✓

• Began in 1948 in Framingham, Massachusetts, USA.
• Followed thousands of participants over decades to identify risk factors for cardiovascular disease.

• D. Pittsburg study ✗

• Not the classic prospective study for CHD risk factors.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old female presented with dyspnea and chest pain. Which of the following proves that she has aortic stenosis rather than aortic regurgitation?
options: Increase in myocardial oxygen consumption is seen with increased pressure work than volume
Aortic stenosis causes reduced pressure at the aortic valve
Workload has nothing to do with myocardial oxygen consumption
Increased pressure - Increase in preload more than afterload
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase in myocardial oxygen consumption is seen with increased pressure work than volume

Valvular diseases affect the heart in two major ways:

| Type | Example | Cardiac Work

| ---- | ------- | ------------

| Pressure overload | Aortic stenosis | Pressure work

| Volume overload | Aortic regurgitation | Volume work

Pressure overload requires more myocardial oxygen consumption (MVO₂).

Thus, this helps differentiate AS from AR.

Aortic stenosis causes a pressure overload, requiring the left ventricle to generate high systolic pressures.

Myocardial oxygen consumption correlates more with pressure work than volume work, favoring a diagnosis of aortic stenosis.

In contrast, aortic regurgitation produces volume overload with relatively lower pressure work.

Thus, increased oxygen demand due to pressure overload distinguishes aortic stenosis.

B) Aortic stenosis causes reduced pressure at the aortic valve

Incorrect.

In AS: LV pressure increases, creating a pressure gradient across the valve.

C) Workload has nothing to do with oxygen consumption

Myocardial oxygen consumption is directly related to cardiac workload.

D) Increased pressure → increase in preload more than afterload

Pressure overload mainly increases afterload, not preload.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient with a history of head trauma presents with blood pressure of 180/100 mmHg, bradycardia, and elevated intracranial pressure. Which reflex best explains this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cushing's reflex

Cushing reflex (Cushing triad) is a physiological response to markedly increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Rising ICP reduces cerebral perfusion pressure, triggering sympathetic activation to increase systemic blood pressure and maintain cerebral blood flow. The resulting hypertension activates baroreceptors, producing reflex bradycardia, while brainstem compression leads to irregular respirations.

Why not the other options?

• A. Bainbridge reflex: Reflex tachycardia in response to increased venous return and right atrial stretch.
• C. Bezold–Jarisch reflex: Causes hypotension, bradycardia, and vasodilation due to ventricular mechanoreceptor activation, commonly during inferior wall MI or spinal anesthesia.
• D. Baroreflex: Regulates short-term blood pressure but does not explain the characteristic triad associated with raised ICP.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: During analysis of an aortic pressure tracing, a small notch is observed on the descending limb of the pressure curve immediately after ventricular ejection. Which event is responsible for this dicrotic notch?
options: Rapid filling of the left ventricle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Closure of the aortic valve

• The dicrotic notch (incisura) on the aortic pressure tracing occurs immediately following closure of the aortic valve.
• At the end of ventricular systole, left ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure. This produces a brief tendency for blood to flow backward toward the left ventricle, causing the aortic valve to close. The combination of transient retrograde flow and elastic recoil of the aorta produces the characteristic dicrotic notch.

The dicrotic notch therefore marks:

• End of ventricular ejection → Aortic valve closure → Beginning of isovolumetric relaxation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: During inspiration, the systolic blood pressure decreases due to:
options: Increased venous return to the right heart transiently reduces LV filling
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased venous return to the right heart transiently reduces LV filling

During inspiration, intrathoracic pressure becomes more negative.

This has two major cardiovascular consequences:

1️⃣ Increased venous return to the right heart

Negative intrathoracic pressure pulls more blood from systemic veins into the right atrium and right ventricle.

2️⃣ Interventricular septal shift

Because the RV fills more, the RV expands and pushes the interventricular septum toward the LV.

This causes:

• Reduced LV filling
• Reduced LV stroke volume
• Transient fall in systolic BP

Hence systolic BP normally falls by about 5 mmHg during inspiration.

Mechanism Flow- Inspiration → ↓ Intrathoracic pressure → ↑ Venous return to RV → RV dilation → Septum shifts left → ↓ LV filling → ↓ Stroke volume → ↓ Systolic BP

Interventricular Dependence- Both ventricles share the pericardial space. When RV filling increases suddenly:

• RV expands
• LV chamber size decreases temporarily
• LV stroke volume falls

This phenomenon is called ventricular interdependence.

A) Decreased pulmonary compliance- Pulmonary compliance affects lung mechanics, not the primary mechanism of inspiratory BP drop.

B) Increased peripheral vascular resistance- Peripheral resistance does not increase during inspiration and is unrelated to the transient BP fall.

C) Increased left ventricular filling-This is the opposite of what happens.

Inspiration → LV filling decreases due to septal shift.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following explains the difference in biphasic blood flow between the right and left coronaries?
options: Low pressure developed during right ventricular systole
High pressure developed during right ventricular systole
Reversal of flow during end of atrial systole
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Low pressure developed during right ventricular systole

Coronary blood flow differs between the left and right coronary arteries because of differences in the pressure generated by the ventricles during systole. The right ventricle develops much lower systolic pressure than the left ventricle, resulting in less compression of the intramyocardial coronary vessels. Consequently, right coronary artery blood flow occurs during both systole and diastole (biphasic flow), whereas left coronary artery flow occurs predominantly during diastole.

• Low right ventricular systolic pressure causes minimal compression of right coronary vessels, allowing continued systolic perfusion.

Why not the other options?

• B. High pressure developed during right ventricular systole: Incorrect. The right ventricle generates much lower systolic pressure than the left.
• C. Thick right ventricular wall: Incorrect. The right ventricular wall is thinner, not thicker.
• D. Reversal of flow during end of atrial systole: Incorrect. Not responsible for the biphasic flow pattern.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following features are characteristic of the Bezold–Jarisch reflex? 1. Hypotension 2. Bradycardia 3. Hypopnea 4. Tachycardia Which among the options are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3

The Bezold–Jarisch reflex is triggered by ventricular mechanoreceptor stimulation, often during inferior wall ischemia. Classic triad-

• Bradycardia

• Hypotension

• Hypopnea (reduced respiration)

It causes increased vagal tone leading to bradycardia and hypotension.

There is also hypopnea due to reflex inhibition of respiration.

The Bezold–Jarisch reflex increases vagal tone, which causes: Bradycardia

Tachycardia is not a feature of this reflex.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect about baroreceptors?
options: Located in the thick muscle layer
Afferent fibers pass via the glossopharyngeal nerve branch
Sensitive to changes in arterial pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Located in the thick muscle layer

Arterial baroreceptors are stretch receptors sensitive to changes in arterial pressure.

They are located in the adventitia of the carotid sinus and aortic arch, not in the thick muscle layer, thick muscle layer = tunica media, baroreceptors are located in the adventitia and elastic wall regions

Baroreceptors are mechanoreceptors that detect stretch in arterial walls.

| Location | Nerve Supply

| -------- | ------------

| Carotid sinus | Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

| Aortic arch | Vagus nerve (CN X)

Pathway:

1️⃣ Increased BP stretches arterial wall

2️⃣ Baroreceptors increase firing

3️⃣ Signals sent to medulla (nucleus tractus solitarius)

4️⃣ Sympathetic activity decreases

5️⃣ Parasympathetic activity increases

Result: Decreased heart rate and blood pressure

Afferent impulses from the carotid sinus travel via the glossopharyngeal nerve (Hering’s nerve).

Thus, location in the thick muscle layer is incorrect.

| Reflex | Receptor Location | Stimulus | Afferent Nerve | Response

| ------ | ----------------- | -------- | -------------- | --------

| Baroreceptor reflex | Carotid sinus, Aortic arch | ↑ Blood pressure | CN IX (carotid), CN X (aortic) | ↓ HR, ↓ BP

| Bainbridge reflex | Right atrium | ↑ Venous return / atrial stretch | Vagus | ↑ Heart rate

| Bezold–Jarisch reflex | LV wall receptors | Ventricular stretch/ischemia | Vagal C fibers | Bradycardia, hypotension

| Cushing reflex | Brainstem | ↑ Intracranial pressure | CNS | Hypertension + bradycardia

| Chemoreceptor reflex | Carotid bodies | Hypoxia, hypercapnia | CN IX, X | ↑ respiration, ↑ BP

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient who was being treated for hypertriglyceridemia developed flushing, gout, hyperglycemia, and raised liver enzymes. Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nicotinamide

Niacin (nicotinic acid) causes flushing, hyperuricemia (gout), hyperglycemia, and hepatotoxicity. Correct answer is C because nicotinic acid (niacin) used for hypertriglyceridemia causes flushing (prostaglandin mediated), hyperuricemia leading to gout, hyperglycemia, and hepatotoxicity with raised liver enzymes.

Statins mainly cause myopathy and mild liver enzyme elevation. Fibrates cause myopathy and gallstones. Ezetimibe mainly reduces cholesterol absorption and is usually well tolerated.

| Drug | Key Side Effect

| ---- | ---------------

| Niacin | ⭐ Flushing + gout + hyperglycemia

| Statins | Myopathy

| Fibrates | Gallstones

| Ezetimibe | Minimal systemic side effects

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A diabetic, hypertensive, and post-MI patient on atorvastatin, metoprolol, and aspirin has lipid profile results of total cholesterol: 238 mg/dL, triglycerides: 125 mg/dL, HDL: 50 mg/dL, and LDL: 160 mg/dL. Which additional medications should be considered to optimize lipid management in this patient? 1. Bemepedoic acid 2. Ezetimibe 3. Gemfibrozil 4. Evolocumab
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 4

This is a very high–risk ASCVD patient (diabetes, hypertension, post-MI) with persistently elevated LDL despite statin therapy. Target LDL according to major guidelines: <55 mg/dL

But his LDL is: 160 mg/dL

So intensification of lipid therapy is required.

Ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, and PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab) are appropriate add-on agents to further lower LDL.

| Drug | Target

| ---- | ------

| Statins | HMG-CoA reductase

| Bempedoic acid | ATP citrate lyase

| Ezetimibe | Intestinal cholesterol absorption

| PCSK9 inhibitors (Evolocumab) | LDL receptor degradation

Triglycerides are normal, so gemfibrozil is not indicated.

Thus, the correct combination is 1, 2, and 4.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient being treated for hypertriglyceridemia developed flushing, gout, hyperglycemia, and raised liver enzymes. Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nicotinamide

Niacin (Vitamin B3) is a lipid-lowering drug that:

• Reduces triglycerides
• Increases HDL
• Decreases LDL moderately

Mechanism: Inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue

This reduces release of free fatty acids to the liver, decreasing VLDL synthesis.

Nicotinamide (niacin) is used to treat hypertriglyceridemia and is known for flushing due to prostaglandin release.

It can cause hyperuricemia leading to gout, hyperglycemia, and elevated liver enzymes.

Niacin has several very characteristic side effects, often tested in exams.

| Side Effect | Mechanism

| ----------- | ---------

| Flushing | Prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation

| Hyperglycemia | Reduced insulin sensitivity

| Hyperuricemia → gout | Reduced uric acid excretion

| Hepatotoxicity | Liver metabolism

These adverse effects are characteristic and dose-related.

Statins, fibrates, and ezetimibe do not produce this combination of side effects.

A) Atorvastatin

Statins mainly cause:

• Myopathy
• Elevated liver enzymes

But flushing and gout are not typical.

B) Fenofibrate

Fibrates cause:

• Gallstones
• Myopathy (with statins)

But not flushing.

D) Ezetimibe

Mechanism: Inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption (NPC1L1).

Side effects are minimal.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient receiving cholesterol-lowering therapy develops facial flushing and erythema. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Niacin

Niacin (vitamin B3) is an antihyperlipidemic drug that commonly causes facial flushing, warmth, and erythema due to prostaglandin (PGD₂ and PGE₂)-mediated vasodilation of cutaneous blood vessels. This adverse effect can be minimized by taking aspirin 30 minutes before niacin or by using extended-release formulations.

• Niacin mechanism: Inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue → ↓ VLDL synthesis → ↓ LDL; also markedly increases HDL (most effective drug for raising HDL).
• Characteristic adverse effect: Flushing due to prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation.
• Other adverse effects: Hyperuricemia (may precipitate gout), hyperglycemia, hepatotoxicity, and pruritus.
• Prevention of flushing: Aspirin or NSAIDs before niacin therapy.
• Lipid effects: ↓ LDL, ↓ Triglycerides, ↑ HDL (greatest HDL increase among lipid-lowering drugs).

Why not the other options?

• A. Atorvastatin: Common adverse effects include myalgia, myopathy, elevated liver enzymes, and rarely rhabdomyolysis; flushing is not characteristic.
• B. Ezetimibe: Inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption; generally well tolerated with occasional gastrointestinal symptoms.
• C. Gemfibrozil: Fibrate associated with myopathy (especially with statins), gallstones, and elevated liver enzymes, not facial flushing.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a PCSK-9 inhibitor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Evolocumab

PCSK9 (Proprotein Convertase Subtilisin/Kexin Type 9) is a liver enzyme that regulates LDL receptor degradation.

Normally:

1️⃣ LDL receptors bind LDL cholesterol

2️⃣ LDL is taken into hepatocytes

3️⃣ LDL receptors are recycled back to the cell surface

But when PCSK9 binds LDL receptors, it causes: Receptor degradation

This results in higher LDL levels in blood.

Evolocumab is a PCSK-9 inhibitor that increases LDL receptor recycling on hepatocytes. This leads to marked reduction in LDL-cholesterol, especially in high-risk ASCVD patients.

| Drug | Type

| ---- | ----

| Evolocumab | Monoclonal antibody

| Alirocumab | Monoclonal antibody

Indications include:

• Familial hypercholesterolemia
• Very high-risk ASCVD
• Patients not controlled with statins + ezetimibe

Ezetimibe inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption, evinacumab targets ANGPTL3, and everolimus is an mTOR inhibitor.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is an inhibitor of the intestinal mucosal transporter NPC1L1, responsible for the absorption of dietary and biliary cholesterol?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ezetimibe

Ezetimibe is a cholesterol absorption inhibitor that selectively blocks the Niemann–Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) transporter on the brush border of enterocytes in the small intestine. This reduces the absorption of dietary and biliary cholesterol, leading to decreased hepatic cholesterol stores and increased LDL receptor expression, thereby lowering LDL cholesterol.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Atorvastatin: An HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin) that decreases hepatic cholesterol synthesis, not intestinal absorption.
• B. Fenofibrate: A PPAR-α agonist that primarily lowers triglycerides by increasing lipoprotein lipase activity.
• C. Metformin: An oral antidiabetic drug that reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves insulin sensitivity; it has no effect on NPC1L1.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding bempedoic acid:
options: It is a non-competitive Inhibitor ATP citrate lyase
It inhibits the de novo synthesis of cholesterol in hepatocytes
It can be used concomitantly with statins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is a non-competitive Inhibitor ATP citrate lyase

Bempedoic acid works upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in the cholesterol synthesis pathway.

This enzyme: ATP-Citrate Lyase (ACL)

converts citrate → acetyl-CoA, which is required for cholesterol synthesis.

Bempedoic acid inhibits ATP citrate lyase, a key enzyme upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in hepatic cholesterol synthesis. Bempedoic acid blocks cholesterol synthesis earlier than statins, Less muscle toxicity compared to statins

It is a dicarboxylic acid that reduces de novo cholesterol synthesis in hepatocytes.

Statin + Bempedoic acid → synergistic LDL reduction

It can be safely used in combination with statins for additive LDL reduction.

adverse effects:

• Hyperuricemia

• Gout

• Tendon rupture (rare)

The inhibition of ATP citrate lyase is not non-competitive, making option A false.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: ‘Tumour Plop’ is a characteristic auscultatory finding seen in which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atrial myxoma

A tumor plop is a characteristic low-pitched diastolic sound produced when an atrial myxoma moves through the atrioventricular valve during ventricular filling. It is classically associated with left atrial myxoma, where the tumor intermittently obstructs the mitral valve.

Why not the other options?

• B. Arrhythmogenic ventricular cardiomyopathy: Characterized by ventricular arrhythmias and right ventricular structural abnormalities; tumor plop is not a feature.
• C. Constrictive pericarditis: Classically produces a pericardial knock, an early diastolic sound due to abrupt cessation of ventricular filling.
• D. Dilated cardiomyopathy: May produce S3 gallop due to volume overload and ventricular dilation, but not a tumor plop.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 27-year-old primigravida at 20 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with rheumatic mitral stenosis. Echocardiography shows a mitral valve area of 1.2 cm². She experiences mild exertional dyspnea (NYHA Class II) but has no pulmonary edema, atrial fibrillation, or features of heart failure. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Continue medical management with regular antenatal follow-up
Elective mitral valve replacement during pregnancy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Continue medical management with regular antenatal follow-up

Pregnancy increases:

• Blood volume by 40–50%
• Cardiac output by 30–50%
• Heart rate

These physiological changes can worsen mitral stenosis by increasing left atrial pressure and the risk of pulmonary congestion.

However, this patient is:

• NYHA Class II
• Hemodynamically stable
• Has no heart failure or pulmonary edema

Therefore, conservative (medical) management with close maternal and fetal surveillance is appropriate.

Management includes:

• Regular antenatal and cardiology follow-up
• Activity modification
• Salt restriction if needed
• Beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol) if symptomatic tachycardia develops
• Diuretics if pulmonary congestion occurs
• Anticoagulation only if atrial fibrillation or another indication is present

Why not the other options?

• A. Immediate percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy (PBMV): Reserved for severe symptomatic mitral stenosis (NYHA III/IV) or patients with pulmonary edema or refractory symptoms despite optimal medical therapy. It is not indicated in a stable NYHA II patient.
• C. Elective mitral valve replacement during pregnancy: Open-heart surgery during pregnancy carries significant maternal and fetal risks and is reserved for patients in whom PBMV is not feasible and who have life-threatening disease.
• D. Termination of pregnancy: Not indicated. Most women with NYHA Class I–II mitral stenosis can continue pregnancy with appropriate multidisciplinary care.

High-yield pearl

Management of mitral stenosis in pregnancy

| Clinical status | Recommended management

| --------------- | ----------------------

| NYHA I–II, stable | Medical management + close antenatal follow-up

| NYHA III–IV or pulmonary edema despite medical therapy | Percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy (preferably in the 2nd trimester)

| Severe disease not amenable to PBMV | Cardiac surgery only if life-saving

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old male is suspected of having hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM). Which of the following statements are likely to be true on his examination? 1. Maneuvers that decrease LV preload will cause the murmur to intensify. 2. Maneuvers that decrease LV afterload will cause decrease in intensity of murmur. 3. Murmur of HOCM becomes softer with passive leg raising. 4. Murmur of HOCM becomes louder with squatting. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 3

In hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM), the dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction increases when the left ventricular cavity becomes smaller (↓ preload or ↓ afterload). Therefore, maneuvers that reduce LV volume increase the murmur, while those that increase LV volume decrease the murmur.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Maneuvers that decrease LV preload will cause the murmur to intensify ✔️: True. Maneuvers that decrease preload (e.g., Valsalva, standing) reduce LV cavity size and increase murmur intensity.
• 2. Maneuvers that decrease LV afterload will cause decrease in intensity of murmur ❌: False. Decreasing afterload (e.g., amyl nitrite) increases, not decreases, the murmur.
• 3. Murmur of HOCM becomes softer with passive leg raising ✔️: True. Passive leg raising increases venous return (preload), enlarges the LV cavity, and softens the murmur.
• 4. Murmur of HOCM becomes louder with squatting ❌: False. Squatting increases preload and afterload, thereby reducing LVOT obstruction and softening the murmur.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and intermittent palpitations. She has a history of recurrent sore throats during childhood. On cardiac auscultation, there is a loud first heart sound (S1) followed by a high-pitched sound shortly after the second heart sound (S2), preceding a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumbling murmur heard best at the cardiac apex. The additional heart sound described is most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mitral stenosis

An opening snap (OS) is a high-frequency early diastolic sound produced by the abrupt opening of a stenotic but still mobile mitral valve. It is a classic auscultatory finding in rheumatic mitral stenosis.

• The sequence is: S2 → Opening Snap → Mid-diastolic rumbling murmur.
• A shorter A2–OS interval indicates more severe mitral stenosis because elevated left atrial pressure forces the valve open earlier.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Aortic stenosis: Produces an ejection click (if valve is mobile) and an ejection systolic murmur, not an opening snap.
• C. Mitral regurgitation: Causes a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla; no opening snap.
• D. Aortic regurgitation: Causes an early diastolic decrescendo murmur and may have an Austin Flint murmur, but not an opening snap.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old male patient presented to the hospital with palpitations. Physical examination showed a diastolic murmur in the left 3rd intercostal space. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aortic regurgitation

A diastolic murmur best heard at the left 3rd intercostal space (Erb’s point) is classic for aortic regurgitation.

It is an early diastolic, high-pitched decrescendo murmur due to backflow from aorta to LV. In AR:

• The aortic valve does not close properly
• Blood flows backward from aorta → left ventricle during diastole

This causes:

• Volume overload of the LV
• Increased stroke volume

Aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation are systolic murmurs.

Aortic regurgitation produces high pulse pressure, causing several classic signs:

| Sign | Description

| ---- | -----------

| Water hammer pulse | Bounding pulse

| Corrigan pulse | Rapid rise and fall pulse

| De Musset sign | Head nodding

| Quincke sign | Capillary pulsation

These occur due to large stroke volume and rapid diastolic runoff.

Tricuspid regurgitation is holosystolic and best heard at the left lower sternal border.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old man with dyspnoea on exertion has been found to have a single second heart sound and a loud diamond-shaped, rough quality systolic murmur best heard at the right 2nd intercostal space, radiating to the right carotid artery. Which one of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aortic stenosis

Key clinical features of aortic stenosis:

• Murmur: Harsh, crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur (diamond-shaped)
• Best heard: Right 2nd intercostal space.
• Radiation: Carotid arteries.
• S2: Soft or single in severe disease.
• Symptoms (classic triad):

• Angina
• Syncope (especially on exertion)
• Dyspnoea/heart failure

• Pulse: Slow-rising, low-volume pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus).

Why not the other options?

• A. Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA): Continuous “machinery” murmur in the left infraclavicular area.
• B. Ventricular septal defect (VSD): Harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.
• D. Pulmonary stenosis: Ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, radiating to the left shoulder/back.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient came with a history of dyspnea, fatigue, and palpitations for 6 months. He gave a history of acute rheumatic fever in childhood. On examination, JVP was elevated, irregularly irregular pulse, hepatomegaly, and pedal edema were present. There was a left parasternal heave. On auscultation, opening snap with MDM murmur was present. All are true in this case except:
options: Presystolic accentuation of MDM is a hallmark of this condition
Increased risk of stroke is present
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Presystolic accentuation of MDM is a hallmark of this condition

Key clues:

• History of rheumatic fever
• Opening snap
• Mid-diastolic murmur

This indicates Rheumatic Mitral Stenosis (MS).

This patient has rheumatic mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation and secondary right heart failure.

In AF, atrial contraction is absent, so there is no presystolic accentuation of the mid-diastolic murmur.

RHF features and absent ‘a’ wave in JVP are expected due to AF.

Mitral stenosis with AF carries a high risk of thromboembolism and stroke.

| Feature | Mitral Stenosis (MS) | Mitral Regurgitation (MR) | Aortic Stenosis (AS) | Aortic Regurgitation (AR)

| ------- | -------------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------- | -------------------------

| Timing | Diastolic | Systolic | Systolic | Diastolic

| Murmur type | Mid-diastolic rumble | Holosystolic | Ejection systolic | Early diastolic

| Best heard | Apex | Apex | Right 2nd ICS | Left sternal border

| Radiation | None | Axilla | Carotids | Down left sternal border

| Special sound | Opening snap | None | Ejection click | None

| Characteristic sign | Presystolic accentuation | Pansystolic murmur | Pulsus parvus et tardus | Water hammer pulse

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient has a cardiac murmur that is best heard at the right second intercostal space. It increases with expiration. Also, the murmur reduces in intensity during sustained handgrip but increases in intensity on inhalation of amyl nitrite. The likely lesion is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aortic stenosis

Aortic stenosis (AS) produces an ejection systolic murmur best heard at the right second intercostal space, often radiating to the carotids. The murmur becomes louder during expiration (left-sided murmur), decreases with sustained handgrip (↑ afterload reduces the transvalvular gradient), and increases with amyl nitrite (↓ afterload increases the pressure gradient across the stenotic valve).

Why not the other options?

• A. Ventricular septal defect: Murmur is best heard at the left lower sternal border and increases with handgrip.
• C. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy: Murmur is best heard at the left sternal border and decreases with handgrip, but amyl nitrite also increases the murmur; the location here favors AS.
• D. Mitral regurgitation: Holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla and increases with handgrip.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young athlete was diagnosed to have HOCM and has a harsh ejection systolic murmur. Which of the following maneuvers would most likely increase the intensity of the murmur?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Valsalva maneuver

HOCM is characterized by:

• Asymmetric septal hypertrophy
• Dynamic obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT)

This obstruction varies depending on ventricular volume.

Correct answer is B because Valsalva maneuver decreases venous return and left ventricular preload, which worsens left ventricular outflow tract obstruction in HOCM and increases murmur intensity.

Isometric handgrip and squatting increase preload/afterload and reduce obstruction, decreasing murmur intensity. Leaning forward is classically used to accentuate aortic regurgitation murmur.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In which of the following cases does paradoxical splitting occur? 1. Severe aortic stenosis 2. Right bundle branch block 3. Right ventricular pacing 4. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Paradoxical (reversed) splitting of the second heart sound (S2) occurs due to delayed closure of the aortic valve (A2). As a result, P2 occurs before A2, the split is heard during expiration, and narrows or disappears during inspiration.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Severe aortic stenosis ✔️ – Delays left ventricular ejection → delayed A2.
• 2. Right bundle branch block ❌ – Delays P2, causing wide physiological splitting, not paradoxical splitting.
• 3. Right ventricular pacing ✔️ – Produces an LBBB-like activation pattern, delaying LV contraction and A2.
• 4. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy ✔️ – Prolonged LV ejection delays A2.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Malar telangiectasia is classically associated with diseases such as scleroderma. Such an association of malar telangiectasia can also be seen with which of the following cardiac lesions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic mitral stenosis

Malar telangiectasia (malar flush) is a characteristic facial finding seen in chronic severe mitral stenosis due to long-standing pulmonary hypertension, reduced cardiac output, and peripheral vasodilatation. Although telangiectasia is classically associated with connective tissue disorders such as systemic sclerosis, a similar malar flush is a well-recognized clinical sign of advanced mitral stenosis.

• Chronic mitral stenosis causes:

• Low cardiac output
• Pulmonary hypertension
• Peripheral vasodilatation

• This produces the characteristic pinkish-purple malar flush (“mitral facies”) over the cheeks.

Why not the other options?

• B. Aortic regurgitation: Characterized by bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, Corrigan pulse, Quincke’s sign, etc., not malar flush.
• C. Constrictive pericarditis: Presents with raised JVP, Kussmaul sign, and pericardial knock, not malar telangiectasia.
• D. Dilated cardiomyopathy: Causes features of heart failure without the characteristic mitral facies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Reverse splitting of second heart sound is most commonly seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. LBBB

Paradoxical (reverse) splitting of the second heart sound (S2) occurs when aortic valve closure (A2) is delayed, causing P2 to occur before A2. The split is heard during expiration and narrows or disappears during inspiration, which is the opposite of normal physiological splitting.

• Most common cause: Left bundle branch block (LBBB) due to delayed left ventricular depolarization and prolonged left ventricular ejection.
• Other causes:

• Severe aortic stenosis
• Left ventricular pacing
• Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM)

Differentiate from other options:

• A. ASD: Fixed wide splitting of S2.
• B. Severe MR: Produces a pansystolic murmur; paradoxical splitting is not a typical finding.
• D. Pulmonary hypertension: Loud P2; splitting may become narrow but is not paradoxical.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The murmur of mitral regurgitation is best heard at:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cardiac apex

Mitral regurgitation (MR) produces a high-pitched, blowing pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur that is best heard at the cardiac apex with the diaphragm of the stethoscope. The murmur typically radiates to the left axilla because the regurgitant jet is directed toward the left atrium.

• The mitral valve is best auscultated at the cardiac apex (left 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line).
• MR produces a pansystolic murmur that begins with S1, extends throughout systole, and ends at S2.
• Radiation to the left axilla is a classic finding.

Why not the other options?

• A. Tricuspid area: Best for tricuspid regurgitation, whose murmur increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign).
• B. Aortic area: Best for aortic stenosis and aortic sclerosis murmurs.
• D. Pulmonary area: Best for pulmonary valve lesions and the pulmonary component of the second heart sound (P2).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The murmur of Mitral Stenosis corresponds to which of the following component of the ECG?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. P wave

Mitral stenosis produces a diastolic murmur.

The murmur occurs when: Blood flows from Left Atrium → Left Ventricle during diastole through a narrow mitral valve.

However, the loudest part of the murmur occurs just before ventricular systole, during atrial contraction.

This is called: Presystolic accentuation

Atrial contraction corresponds to the P wave of ECG.

Remember the sequence:

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following conditions can produce a third heart sound (S₃) on auscultation? 1. Young age 2. Pregnancy 3. Left ventricular failure 4. Mitral stenosis Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The third heart sound (S₃) is a low-pitched early diastolic sound heard just after S₂ during the rapid passive filling phase of the ventricle. It is produced by sudden deceleration of blood entering a compliant or volume-overloaded ventricle.

• Statement 1. Young age: Correct. An S₃ is physiological in children, adolescents, and young adults (usually up to 40 years of age) due to a compliant ventricle.
• Statement 2. Pregnancy: Correct. Pregnancy is a high-output, volume-overload state and may be associated with a physiological S₃.
• Statement 3. Left ventricular failure: Correct. In left ventricular failure, S₃ is pathological and reflects volume overload and ventricular dilatation. It is often referred to as a ventricular gallop.
• Statement 4. Mitral stenosis: Incorrect. Mitral stenosis is associated with an opening snap (OS) after S₂, not an S₃.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following heart sounds are best heard with the bell of the stethoscope? I. Opening snap II. Systolic click III. Third heart sound IV. Mid diastolic murmur Select the correct answer using the code below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. III and IV

The bell of the stethoscope is designed to detect low-frequency sounds, whereas the diaphragm is better for high-frequency sounds.

Sounds Best Heard with the Bell

III. Third Heart Sound (S3)

• Low-pitched early diastolic sound
• Heard best at the apex with the bell
• Associated with:

• Heart failure
• Dilated cardiomyopathy
• Normal in children and young adults

IV. Mid-Diastolic Murmur

• Low-frequency murmur
• Examples:

• Mitral Stenosis
• Tricuspid stenosis

• Heard best with the bell placed lightly over the apex (mitral stenosis)

Sounds Best Heard with the Diaphragm

I. Opening Snap

• High-frequency sound
• Due to abrupt opening of a stenotic mitral valve
• Best heard with the diaphragm

II. Systolic Click

• High-pitched sound
• Seen in Mitral Valve Prolapse
• Best heard with the diaphragm

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the Opening Snap (OS) in a patient of mitral stenosis?
options: OS is best heard with the bell of stethoscope
Intensity of OS becomes louder when the valve is calcified
OS moves closer to the second sound (S2) as the stenosis becomes more severe
OS is best heard at the second left intercostal space
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. OS moves closer to the second sound (S2) as the stenosis becomes more severe

The opening snap (OS) is a high-pitched early diastolic sound produced by the sudden tensing of a stenotic but still mobile mitral valve as it opens after the aortic component of the second heart sound (A2). It is a characteristic auscultatory finding in rheumatic mitral stenosis.

Why is C correct?

• Severe mitral stenosis → Higher left atrial pressure → Earlier mitral valve opening → Shorter A2–OS interval.
• Therefore, the opening snap moves closer to S2 as stenosis becomes more severe.

Why not the other options?

• A. OS is best heard with the bell of stethoscope: Incorrect. The opening snap is a high-pitched sound and is best heard with the diaphragm.
• B. Intensity of OS becomes louder when the valve is calcified: Incorrect. A heavily calcified and immobile valve produces a soft or absent opening snap.
• D. OS is best heard at the second left intercostal space: Incorrect. It is best heard just medial to the apex or at the left lower sternal border, not at the pulmonary area.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is correct with regard to Carey Coombs murmur?
options: Soft systolic murmur due to mitral regurgitation
Soft mid-diastolic murmur due to mitral valvulitis
Harsh early diastolic murmur due to aortic regurgitation
Blowing late systolic murmur due to aortic stenosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Soft mid-diastolic murmur due to mitral valvulitis

The Carey Coombs murmur is a soft, short mid-diastolic murmur heard at the cardiac apex during the acute phase of rheumatic fever. It is caused by active inflammation (valvulitis) of the mitral valve, resulting in turbulent blood flow across the inflamed but non-stenotic mitral valve.

The murmur is:

• Mid-diastolic
• Soft and low-pitched
• Best heard at the apex with the bell of the stethoscope
• Caused by rheumatic mitral valvulitis, not true mitral stenosis

Why not the other options?

• A. Soft systolic murmur due to mitral regurgitation: Acute rheumatic fever may produce a pansystolic murmur due to mitral regurgitation, but this is not the Carey Coombs murmur.
• C. Harsh early diastolic murmur due to aortic regurgitation: Describes the murmur of aortic regurgitation, unrelated to Carey Coombs murmur.
• D. Blowing late systolic murmur due to aortic stenosis: Incorrect. Aortic stenosis produces an ejection systolic murmur, not a late systolic murmur.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presented with serial blood pressure recordings of above 140/90 mmHg. Which one of the following signs is not a clue for an underlying cause of hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitiligo

Vitiligo is not a typical clinical clue for secondary hypertension.

• A. Radio-femoral delay — Clue for secondary hypertension

• Suggests coarctation of the aorta, a secondary cause of hypertension.
• Femoral pulses are delayed and weaker compared with radial pulses.

• B. Enlarged kidneys — Clue

• May suggest polycystic kidney disease, an important renal cause of secondary hypertension.

• C. Bull neck and buffalo hump — Clue

• Characteristic of Cushing syndrome, which can cause secondary hypertension through excess cortisol.

• D. Vitiligo — Not a typical clue

• Vitiligo is associated with autoimmune disorders but is not a characteristic clinical clue to a specific secondary cause of hypertension.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 38-year-old male presents to the outpatient clinic with complaints of excessive stress and difficulty maintaining a work-life balance. On examination, his blood pressure is 150/100 mm Hg. His fasting blood glucose is 150 mg/dL and he is slightly overweight. He has no significant past medical history and is not on any medications. Physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: Advise rest and no pharmacological treatment is required
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Start telmisartan

This patient has Stage 2 hypertension (150/100 mm Hg) with metabolic risk factors (diabetes, overweight).

Guidelines recommend immediate pharmacologic therapy plus lifestyle modification for BP ≥140/90 mm Hg.

Telmisartan (ARB) is appropriate as it provides BP control and metabolic/renal protection, especially in diabetics.

Lifestyle measures alone are insufficient, and tirzepatide or steroids are not indicated for BP control.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 52-year-old male diabetic presents with recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia. On examination, Pulse: 84 beats/minute, BP: 160/100 mm Hg, Chest and CVS examination unremarkable. Which of the following antihypertensive should be avoided in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Propranolol

In patients with diabetes mellitus and recurrent hypoglycemia, non-selective β-blockers, particularly propranolol, should be avoided because they mask the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia (tachycardia, tremors, palpitations, anxiety) and delay recovery by inhibiting glycogenolysis. In contrast, ACE inhibitors and ARBs (e.g., Telmisartan) are the preferred antihypertensive agents in diabetic patients due to their reno- and cardioprotective effects.

• A. Propranolol: Non-selective β-blocker that masks hypoglycemic symptoms and may prolong hypoglycemia.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Telmisartan: An ARB and a first-line antihypertensive in diabetes, especially in patients with albuminuria or diabetic kidney disease. It does not mask hypoglycemia.
• C. Torsemide: A loop diuretic used for edema and hypertension; although it may cause electrolyte disturbances, it is not contraindicated because of hypoglycemia.
• D. Amlodipine: A calcium channel blocker with no effect on hypoglycemia awareness.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 58-year-old male presents to a PHC for a routine check-up. His blood pressure readings on two separate occasions are 148/90 mmHg and 152/96 mmHg. He is asymptomatic and has no known comorbidities. What is the most appropriate next step in management according to current hypertension guidelines?
options: Initiate treatment only if BP exceeds 160/100 mmHg
Start Amlodipine 5 mg once daily and advise lifestyle modification
Refer to a higher center for further evaluation
Start the patient on IV anti-hypertensive drugs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Start Amlodipine 5 mg once daily and advise lifestyle modification

Two readings ≥140/90 mmHg confirm Stage 2 hypertension on office measurements. Current practice recommends initiating pharmacotherapy along with lifestyle modification, even in asymptomatic patients.

A long-acting calcium channel blocker (Amlodipine) is an appropriate first-line agent.

IV drugs and referral are unnecessary in stable, uncomplicated hypertension.

A) Initiate treatment only if BP >160/100

This was older guideline practice.

Current recommendations treat ≥140/90.

C) Refer to higher center

Not needed because:

• Patient is stable
• No complications

Primary care can manage.

D) Start IV antihypertensives

Used only in: Hypertensive emergencies

Examples:

• Stroke
• Aortic dissection
• Pulmonary edema

This patient is asymptomatic.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 58-year-old male with chronic kidney disease presents for routine follow-up. His blood pressure is 140/100 mm Hg. Urine analysis reveals significant proteinuria. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive agent for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Telmisartan

In chronic kidney disease with proteinuria, BP control should also reduce intraglomerular pressure.

ARBs (telmisartan) reduce efferent arteriolar resistance, lowering proteinuria and slowing CKD progression. Telmisartan is an Angiotensin II Receptor Blocker (ARB).

It blocks: AT₁ receptors

This prevents the effects of angiotensin II.

Effects include:

• Vasodilation
• Reduced aldosterone release
• Reduced intraglomerular pressure

Beta blockers and thiazides do not provide renoprotective effects in proteinuric CKD.

Spironolactone increases hyperkalemia risk in CKD and is not first-line.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a blood pressure of 230/110 mmHg, severe headache, blurred vision, and signs of end-organ damage. Which is the drug of choice for immediate blood pressure reduction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sodium nitroprusside

Hypertensive emergency is defined as severe hypertension (usually ≥180/120 mmHg) associated with acute target-organ damage (e.g., hypertensive encephalopathy, stroke, acute heart failure, aortic dissection, acute kidney injury). It requires immediate but controlled reduction of blood pressure using intravenous antihypertensive agents. Sodium nitroprusside is a rapid-acting arterial and venous vasodilator that is classically used for rapid BP reduction in hypertensive emergencies because of its immediate onset and short duration of action.

Why not the other options?

• A. Hydrochlorothiazide: Oral thiazide diuretic used for chronic hypertension, not emergencies.
• B. Amlodipine: Oral calcium channel blocker with a slow onset of action; unsuitable for acute BP reduction.
• D. Losartan: Oral angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) used for long-term hypertension management, not hypertensive emergencies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with a history of long-standing hypertension is brought to the emergency department with sudden-onset severe headache, vomiting, blurred vision, and altered mental status. His blood pressure is 240/135 mmHg, and fundus examination reveals papilledema, consistent with a hypertensive emergency. A non-contrast CT head excludes intracranial hemorrhage. Which of the following is the appropriate initial dose?
options: Labetalol 20 mg IV administered slowly over 2 minutes
Labetalol 4 mg IV infusion over 60 minutes
Labetalol 200 mg orally as the initial treatment
questions.explanation:
