Correct answer: A. Labetalol 20 mg IV administered slowly over 2 minutes

A hypertensive emergency is defined as markedly elevated blood pressure accompanied by acute target-organ damage, such as:

• Hypertensive encephalopathy
• Papilledema
• Intracranial hemorrhage
• Acute ischemic stroke (selected cases)
• Acute pulmonary edema
• Aortic dissection
• Acute kidney injury

These patients require rapid but carefully controlled reduction in blood pressure using intravenous antihypertensive agents.

Labetalol is commonly used because it blocks both:

• α₁-receptors → vasodilation
• β₁/β₂-receptors → decreases heart rate and cardiac output

The recommended initial regimen is:

• 20 mg IV over approximately 2 minutes
• If needed, repeat with 20–80 mg IV every 10 minutes or begin a continuous infusion (0.5–2 mg/min) until the target blood pressure is achieved.

The goal is not to normalize blood pressure immediately. Instead:

• Reduce the mean arterial pressure (MAP) by no more than 20–25% within the first hour, then gradually lower it over the next 24–48 hours (except in specific conditions such as aortic dissection).

Why not the other options?

• B. Labetalol 4 mg IV infusion over 60 minutes: Incorrect. This is far below the recommended therapeutic starting dose and is not a standard regimen.
• C. Labetalol 200 mg orally as the initial treatment: Incorrect. Oral therapy is inappropriate in hypertensive emergencies because rapid, titratable blood pressure control is required.
• D. Labetalol 1 mg IV bolus: Incorrect. This dose is subtherapeutic and is not recommended in current treatment protocols.

High-yield pearl

Hypertensive urgency vs emergency

| Feature | Hypertensive urgency | Hypertensive emergency

| ------- | -------------------- | ----------------------

| Blood pressure | Very high | Very high

| Target-organ damage | Absent | Present

| Treatment | Oral antihypertensives | IV antihypertensives

| Preferred IV drugs | — | Labetalol, Nicardipine, Clevidipine, Nitroprusside (selected cases)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with a known history of diabetes mellitus presents with a BP of 150/90 and dizziness. What is the best way to manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diet, Exercise, Lifestyle modification + Amlodipine

A BP of 150/90 mmHg in a patient with diabetes mellitus requires pharmacologic treatment along with lifestyle modification. Combination of HTN + diabetes increases risk of:

• Coronary artery disease
• Stroke
• Diabetic nephropathy
• Retinopathy

Thus aggressive BP control is required.

Diabetics have a lower BP target, so drug therapy is indicated at ≥140/90 mmHg.

Amlodipine is an effective first-line agent with good tolerability and metabolic neutrality. Amlodipine blocks: L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle

Effects:

• Arterial vasodilation
• ↓ Peripheral resistance
• ↓ Blood pressure

| Drug Class | Example

| ---------- | -------

| Calcium channel blockers | Amlodipine

| ACE inhibitors | Enalapril

| ARBs | Losartan

| Thiazide diuretics | Hydrochlorothiazide

Lifestyle measures alone are insufficient, and beta blockers or prazosin are not preferred first-line options.

A) Metoprolol

Beta blockers are not first-line in uncomplicated hypertension, especially in diabetics. They may:

• Mask hypoglycemia
• Worsen insulin resistance.

B) Lifestyle modification alone

Not adequate because: BP >140/90 with diabetes requires drug therapy.

C) Prazosin

Alpha-1 blocker, Used mainly in:

• Resistant hypertension
• Benign prostatic hyperplasia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 71-year-old male presents with headache, dizziness, nausea with palpitations. The patient is already on treatment for diabetes and hypertension. The blood pressure reading is 220/140 mmHg. Which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. This is a case of hypertensive emergency which can be managed by intravenous sodium nitroprusside. 2. An immediate normalization of the blood pressure should be the target. 3. Secondary causes of hypertension, like renovascular disease are uncommon in patients with hypertensive emergency. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 only

• 1. Hypertensive emergency managed by IV sodium nitroprusside: Correct

• A BP of 220/140 mmHg with acute symptoms is concerning for a hypertensive emergency, provided there is acute target-organ damage.
• IV sodium nitroprusside is a rapidly acting IV antihypertensive that can be used in hypertensive emergencies.

• 2. Immediate normalization of BP: Incorrect

• BP should not be normalized immediately, as this can cause cerebral, coronary, or renal hypoperfusion.
• Generally, reduce MAP by no more than \~25% during the first hour, then gradually toward approximately 160/110 mmHg over the next 2–6 hours, depending on the clinical situation.

• 3. Secondary causes of hypertension\, like renovascular disease are uncommon in hypertensive emergency: Incorrect

• Secondary hypertension should be considered, particularly in severe/resistant or abruptly worsening hypertension.
• Causes include renovascular disease, renal parenchymal disease, pheochromocytoma, primary aldosteronism, and Cushing syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A hypertensive patient is taking three antihypertensive drugs including diuretics but the blood pressure is not controlled. He also has hypokalemia. Which of the following drug should be used to manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spironolactone

Resistant hypertension on three drugs including a diuretic suggests aldosterone-mediated volume excess.

Associated hypokalemia further supports hyperaldosteronism.

Hypokalemia strongly suggests: Excess aldosterone

Aldosterone causes:

• Na⁺ retention → hypertension
• K⁺ loss → hypokalemia

This condition is known as:

Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome)

Spironolactone, an aldosterone antagonist, is the drug of choice in resistant hypertension.

It controls BP and corrects hypokalemia, unlike loop diuretics or potassium supplements alone.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A person was taking an antihypertensive drug and continued taking it despite developing constipation, dry mouth, and dizziness. He was taking it regularly but forgot to take it during a trip abroad and has now developed a hypertensive emergency. Which antihypertensive was he likely taking?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Clonidine

Clonidine is a centrally acting α₂-agonist that commonly causes dry mouth, constipation, and sedation. It acts on the brainstem (medulla) to:

• Decrease sympathetic outflow
• Reduce norepinephrine release

Result:

• ↓ Heart rate
• ↓ Peripheral vascular resistance
• ↓ Blood pressure

Abrupt withdrawal leads to rebound sympathetic overactivity, causing severe hypertension or hypertensive emergency.

This withdrawal phenomenon is characteristic of clonidine. This is why clonidine must be tapered slowly, not stopped abruptly.

Calcium channel blockers and RAAS inhibitors do not cause rebound hypertension on sudden cessation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Cilnidipine does not cause reflex tachycardia because it blocks:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. N-type calcium channels

Cilnidipine blocks:

• L-type calcium channels → vasodilation
• N-type calcium channels → ↓ sympathetic neurotransmitter release

Why less reflex tachycardia?

N-type blockade reduces norepinephrine release from sympathetic nerve terminals.

Thus:

• Vasodilation occurs
• Reflex sympathetic activation is suppressed

High-yield comparison:

| Drug | Special feature

| ---- | ---------------

| Amlodipine | L-type blocker

| Cilnidipine | L + N type blocker

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In case of hypertensive emergency in a child, blood pressure should be reduced by up to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 10% in the first hour

Hypertensive emergency in children is defined as severe hypertension with evidence of acute target-organ damage (e.g., hypertensive encephalopathy, seizures, heart failure, acute kidney injury). Blood pressure should be lowered gradually, as rapid reduction can compromise cerebral, renal, and coronary perfusion due to impaired autoregulation.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. 10% over the first 8 hours: The initial reduction should begin within the first hour, not be delayed over 8 hours.
• B. 15% over the first 8 hours: Reduction should be more controlled initially, with the first target achieved within 1 hour.
• D. 15% in the first hour: A 15% reduction in the first hour may be excessive and increases the risk of cerebral and renal hypoperfusion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Most important mechanism for rapid development of tolerance to organic nitrates:
options: Inhibition of mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase due to depletion of intracellular sulfhydryl groups by reactive nitrogen species
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inhibition of mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase due to depletion of intracellular sulfhydryl groups by reactive nitrogen species

Organic nitrates require: Mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase (mtALDH) for conversion to nitric oxide.

Mechanism of tolerance:

• Reactive oxygen/nitrogen species:

• Deplete intracellular sulfhydryl (-SH) groups
• Inactivate mtALDH
• Reduce NO generation

High-yield pathway:

Prevention:

• Nitrate-free interval

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statement regarding use of ACE inhibitors in hypertension is true?
options: They decrease blood pressure by decreasing peripheral vascular resistance
They decrease blood pressure by decreasing cardiac output
They increase blood pressure by increasing peripheral vascular resistance
They increase blood pressure by increasing cardiac output
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. They decrease blood pressure by decreasing peripheral vascular resistance

The Renin–Angiotensin–Aldosterone System (RAAS) regulates blood pressure.

Sequence:

1️⃣ Kidney releases renin

2️⃣ Renin converts angiotensinogen → angiotensin I

3️⃣ ACE converts angiotensin I → angiotensin II

Angiotensin II causes:

• Vasoconstriction
• Aldosterone secretion
• Sodium retention

ACE inhibitors lower blood pressure primarily by reducing angiotensin II–mediated vasoconstriction. ACE inhibitors also increase: Bradykinin levels

Because ACE normally breaks down bradykinin.

This leads to:

• Vasodilation
• Side effects like dry cough

This leads to a decrease in peripheral vascular resistance (afterload).

Cardiac output is usually preserved, not reduced.

Hence, BP reduction occurs due to vasodilation, not changes in cardiac output.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 33-year-old patient presented with chest pain, shortness of breath, and edema. On examination, his pulse was irregularly irregular, his JVP was elevated and showed a prominent ‘Y’ descent. On auscultation, he had a high-pitched diastolic sound. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Constrictive Pericarditis

Constrictive pericarditis presents with elevated JVP and a prominent ‘Y’ descent due to rapid early diastolic filling.

The high-pitched early diastolic sound (pericardial knock) is characteristic.

Systemic congestion with edema and dyspnea reflects impaired ventricular filling.

Cardiac tamponade has an absent Y descent, and valvular lesions do not produce a pericardial knock.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 56-year-old male, chronic heavy smoker, presented with breathlessness. On examination, pulse 96/min, BP 112/70 mm Hg and a pansystolic murmur showing Carvallo’s sign with murmur getting louder on deep inspiration. Which one of the following statements is true regarding examination of JVP in him?
options: C wave is attenuated and V wave is accentuated
V wave and C wave merge
V wave and C wave merge and Y descent is blunted
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. V wave and C wave merge

The patient has tricuspid regurgitation (TR), suggested by a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign). In TR, regurgitation of blood into the right atrium during systole produces giant C-V (CV) waves due to fusion of the C and V waves in the JVP.

Why not the other options?

• A. V wave is attenuated: Incorrect. V wave is markedly prominent in TR.
• B. C wave is attenuated and V wave is accentuated: Incorrect. The C and V waves fuse, forming a giant CV wave.
• D. V wave and C wave merge and Y descent is blunted: Incorrect. Y descent is brisk (prominent) in TR due to rapid right atrial emptying; a blunted Y descent is seen in cardiac tamponade.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A hypertensive patient presents with an irregularly irregular pulse and a loud P2 on auscultation. Upon examination of the Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP), which finding is most likely to be observed in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Absent a wave

An irregularly irregular pulse indicates atrial fibrillation.

| Wave | Cause

| ---- | -----

| a wave | Atrial contraction

| c wave | Tricuspid valve bulging

| v wave | Venous filling of atrium

| x descent | Atrial relaxation

| y descent | Ventricular filling

In AF, atrial contraction is absent, leading to loss of the ‘a’ wave in JVP.

A loud P2 suggests associated pulmonary hypertension.

Cannon waves occur with AV dissociation, not atrial fibrillation.

B) Cannon a wave

Occurs when atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve.

Seen in:

• Complete heart block
• AV dissociation

C) Rapid x descent

Seen in conditions like cardiac tamponade.

D) Rapid y descent

Seen in constrictive pericarditis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to you with an irregularly irregular pulse of 120/minute and a pulse deficit of 20. Which of the following would be the JVP finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Absent a wave

Pulse deficit = difference between:

• Apical heart rate
• Peripheral pulse rate

In AF:

• Some ventricular contractions are too weak to produce a peripheral pulse

Thus, pulse deficit occurs. An irregularly irregular pulse with pulse deficit indicates atrial fibrillation.

In AF, organized atrial contraction is absent, leading to loss of the ‘a’ wave in JVP.

Cannon ‘’ waves occur with AV dissociation, not AF.

Thus, the characteristic JVP finding is an absent ‘a’ wave.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with peripheral edema has the following findings on clinical examination: • A soft systolic murmur at the lower left sternal border with raised JVP showing prominent C-V wave. • The murmur increases in intensity on deep inspiration. The most likely valvular abnormality is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tricuspid regurgitation

Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) presents with a pansystolic murmur best heard at the lower left sternal border, prominent C-V waves in the JVP, and a murmur that increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign) due to increased venous return to the right heart. Peripheral edema and raised JVP are features of right-sided heart failure.

Why not the other options?

• A. Ventricular septal defect: Harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border but no prominent C-V waves or inspiratory accentuation.
• B. Mitral regurgitation: Pansystolic murmur best heard at the apex, radiating to the axilla; does not increase with inspiration.
• D. Mitral valve prolapse: Characterized by a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur, best heard at the apex.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Kussmaul’s sign is a clinical feature of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Constrictive pericarditis

Kussmaul’s sign is a paradoxical rise (or failure to fall) in jugular venous pressure (JVP) during inspiration due to impaired right ventricular filling. It is a classic finding in constrictive pericarditis, where the rigid pericardium restricts ventricular expansion.

Why not the other options?

• B. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy: Characterized by a systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva; Kussmaul’s sign is not a feature.
• C. Anteroseptal myocardial infarction: May cause LV failure or arrhythmias but does not typically produce Kussmaul’s sign.
• D. Dilated cardiomyopathy: Causes elevated JVP in heart failure, but Kussmaul’s sign is not characteristic.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The height of the Jugular Venous Pulse is determined by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right atrial pressure

The Jugular Venous Pulse (JVP) is a clinical indicator of right atrial pressure (RAP) because the internal jugular vein is in direct communication with the superior vena cava and right atrium, with no intervening valves.

Key points:

• Height of JVP = Right atrial pressure (Central Venous Pressure).
• Normal JVP is ≤3–4 cm above the sternal angle (approximately 6–8 cm H₂O above the right atrium).
• Raised JVP indicates elevated right atrial pressure, seen in:

• Right heart failure
• Constrictive pericarditis
• Cardiac tamponade
• Tricuspid regurgitation
• Superior vena cava obstruction (venous distension without pulsations)

• JVP reflects right-sided cardiac hemodynamics and does not directly indicate left atrial or left ventricular pressure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are typical physical findings in pericardial effusion? 1. Raised JVP 2. Hypotension 3. Oliguria 4. Water hammer pulse Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Pericardial effusion is the accumulation of fluid within the pericardial sac. When the accumulation is large or rapid, it can cause cardiac tamponade, leading to impaired ventricular filling, reduced cardiac output, and hemodynamic compromise.

• Statement 1. Raised JVP: Correct. Raised JVP occurs due to impaired right atrial filling and elevated systemic venous pressure.
• Statement 2. Hypotension: Correct. Hypotension results from reduced ventricular filling and decreased cardiac output. It is one of Beck’s triad in cardiac tamponade.
• Statement 3. Oliguria: Correct. Oliguria develops due to reduced renal perfusion secondary to low cardiac output.
• Statement 4. Water hammer pulse: Incorrect. Water hammer pulse (collapsing pulse) is seen in aortic regurgitation, PDA, and other high stroke volume states—not in pericardial effusion or cardiac tamponade.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following types of pulse is generated in accordance with the Frank-Starling law?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pulsus alternans

The Frank–Starling law states: The force of ventricular contraction increases with increasing ventricular filling (preload).

In simple terms: More end-diastolic volume → stronger contraction → greater stroke volume. This mechanism allows the heart to adjust cardiac output automatically.

Pulsus alternans shows alternating strong and weak beats due to beat-to-beat variation in stroke volume. It reflects impaired myocardial contractility where ventricular filling influences force of contraction via the Frank–Starling mechanism.

Seen classically in left ventricular systolic dysfunction.

A) Pulsus bisferiens

Pulse with two systolic peaks.

Seen in:

• Aortic regurgitation
• Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

B) Pulsus paradoxus

Fall in systolic BP >10 mmHg during inspiration.

Seen in:

• Cardiac tamponade
• Severe asthma
• Constrictive pericarditis

Respiratory phenomenon, not Frank-Starling related.

Not related to Frank-Starling mechanism.

D) Pulsus parvus

Weak, small pulse.

Seen in:

• Severe aortic stenosis

Due to reduced stroke volume, not alternating contractility.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of these conditions will cause a large ‘a’ wave and P WAVE in JVP and ECG respectively?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tricuspid stenosis

The ‘a’ wave in JVP corresponds to right atrial contraction against the tricuspid valve.

In tricuspid stenosis, right atrial contraction faces increased resistance, producing a prominent ‘a’ wave. It occurs just before ventricular systole.

Sequence: ECG: P wave → Atrial contraction → JVP ‘a’ wave

Mitral valve lesions affect left-sided pressures and do not enlarge the JVP ‘a’ wave.

Aortic valve lesions primarily alter arterial pulse, not JVP waveform.

Clinical Causes of Giant ‘a’ Wave-

| Condition | Mechanism

| --------- | ---------

| Tricuspid stenosis | RA contracts against stenotic valve

| Pulmonary hypertension | RV pressure overload

| Pulmonary stenosis | Increased resistance

| Right ventricular hypertrophy | Reduced RV compliance

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: 60-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to difficulty climbing stairs and dyspnea on exertion over the last 6 weeks. Blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg and pulse is 78/min. Skin examination shows scattered ecchymoses. Laboratory results show mild hyperglycemia and elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol. Serum cortisol level is at the upper limit of normal and is not suppressed following administration of low-dose dexamethasone. Serum ACTH level is elevated. Chest x-ray reveals a right lower lobe lung mass. Which of the following changes are most likely to occur after administration of high-dose dexamethasone in this patient?
options: Could be any of the above
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. No change in cortisol

Ectopic ACTH syndrome occurs when a non-pituitary tumor (commonly small cell lung carcinoma) secretes ACTH, causing ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome.

Key diagnostic principle (dexamethasone suppression test):

• Pituitary Cushing disease: Cortisol suppresses with high-dose dexamethasone.
• Ectopic ACTH production: Cortisol does NOT suppress with either low- or high-dose dexamethasone because ACTH secretion from the tumor is not regulated by normal hypothalamic–pituitary feedback.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 20-year-old patient presented with salt craving, skin pigmentation, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Addison's disease

| Finding | What it indicates

| ------- | -----------------

| Salt craving | Aldosterone deficiency

| Hyperpigmentation | ↑ ACTH → primary cause

| Hyponatremia | ↓ aldosterone

| Hyperkalemia | ↓ aldosterone

| Metabolic acidosis | ↓ H⁺ excretion

Primary adrenal insufficiency causes deficiency of both cortisol and aldosterone, leading to salt wasting, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis. Elevated ACTH produces characteristic skin hyperpigmentation and salt craving reflects mineralocorticoid loss. This constellation is classic for Addison’s disease. Cushing and Conn syndromes cause hypertension and hypokalemia, not salt loss.

| Condition | Na⁺ | K⁺ | BP | Pigmentation

| --------- | --- | --- | --- | ------------

| Addison’s | ↓ | ↑ | ↓ | ⭐ Present

| Cushing | ↑ | ↓ | ↑ | Absent

| Conn syndrome | ↑ | ↓ | ↑ | Absent

| Pheochromocytoma | Normal | Normal | ↑ (episodic) | Absent

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 21-year-old patient presented with weakness and fatigue. His BP was 80/60 mm Hg and his reports showed a serum Na+ of 127 mEq/L and serum K+ of 5.2 mEq/L. On examination, the patient had hyperpigmentation in the knuckles, arms, and legs. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Primary adrenal insufficiency

Hypotension with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and diffuse hyperpigmentation is classic for primary adrenal insufficiency. Loss of aldosterone causes salt wasting and hyperkalemia, while cortisol deficiency raises ACTH, leading to pigmentation. This electrolyte pattern excludes SIADH, which has no hyperkalemia. Conn syndrome causes hypertension and hypokalemia, the opposite profile.

| Condition | Na⁺ | K⁺ | BP | Pigmentation

| --------- | --- | --- | --- | ------------

| Addison’s | ↓ | ↑ | ↓ | ⭐ Present

| Conn’s syndrome | ↑ | ↓ | ↑ | Absent

| SIADH | ↓ | Normal | Normal | Absent

| B12 deficiency | Normal | Normal | Normal | May have pigmentation but no electrolyte changes

• Hyperpigmentation = primary adrenal failure ⭐
• Hyponatremia + hyperkalemia = aldosterone deficiency
• Hypotension = cortisol deficiency
• Most common cause = autoimmune

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old man with congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) presents with bilateral testicular enlargement and infertility. Ultrasound shows bilateral testicular masses near the mediastinum testis, consistent with testicular adrenal rest tumors (TART). What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High-dose glucocorticoid therapy

In congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency, chronic elevation of ACTH stimulates ectopic adrenal tissue in the testes, leading to testicular adrenal rest tumors (TART). These tumors commonly occur near the mediastinum testis and can cause testicular enlargement, infertility, and obstruction of seminiferous tubules.

First-line treatment: High-dose glucocorticoid therapy

Why not other options:

• A. Bilateral orchiectomy:

• TART are benign and ACTH-dependent.
• Usually regress with glucocorticoids, so surgery is unnecessary.

• B. Radiotherapy:

• Tumors are not malignant and are hormone-driven, so radiation is not useful.

• D. Chemotherapy:

• Used for malignancy; TART is benign adrenal rest tissue.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient presents with hypertension and hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. CT scan shows a mass of 1.5 cm over the kidney with elevated ARR. What is the next best step for the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adrenalectomy

• Hypertension with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis and elevated aldosterone–renin ratio indicates primary hyperaldosteronism. A unilateral adrenal mass consistent with an aldosterone-producing adenoma is treated definitively with adrenalectomy. Surgery corrects hypertension and hypokalemia.
• Lifelong spironolactone is reserved for bilateral adrenal hyperplasia or non-surgical candidates.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue, anorexia, and weight loss over the past 3 months. She has a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus and reports that her insulin requirements have decreased recently. On examination, there is diffuse hyperpigmentation, especially over the palmar creases. Laboratory evaluation shows that serum cortisol levels do not increase after administration of exogenous ACTH. Which of the following patterns of electrolyte abnormalities is most likely in this patient?
options: Normal sodium, decreased potassium, decreased chloride, increased bicarbonate
Decreased sodium, increased potassium, increased chloride, decreased bicarbonate
Decreased sodium, decreased potassium, decreased chloride, increased bicarbonate
Normal sodium, increased potassium, normal chloride, normal bicarbonate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decreased sodium, increased potassium, increased chloride, decreased bicarbonate

This patient has primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), suggested by:

• Hyperpigmentation → ↑ ACTH (POMC → MSH)
• No response to ACTH stimulation → adrenal gland failure
• Associated autoimmune condition (type 1 DM)

Pathophysiology:

• ↓ Aldosterone

• ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption → hyponatremia
• ↓ K⁺ excretion → hyperkalemia
• ↓ H⁺ excretion → metabolic acidosis (↓ bicarbonate)

• ↑ Chloride to maintain electroneutrality → hyperchloremia

Why not other options?

A. Patterns with hypokalemia → suggest hyperaldosteronism

C. Metabolic alkalosis (↑ bicarbonate) → seen in vomiting/diuretics

D. Normal electrolytes → not consistent with adrenal failure

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 31-year-old woman comes to the AIIMS OPD due to a 6.8-kg weight gain over the last few months. The patient also has experienced weakness and cannot lift weights that she was able to lift before the onset of her symptoms. On examination, blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg and pulse is 88/min and regular. Neurologic examination shows proximal muscle weakness. Dark terminal hair is present on the lower abdomen. Fasting laboratory results are as follows: Sodium-142 mEq/L Potassium-3.6 mEq/L Chloride-98 mEq/L Bicarbonate-28 mEq/L Calcium-9.2 mg/dL TSH-2.2 mlU/L (N-0.5 to 5.0 mIU/L) Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluating this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test

This patient has features suggestive of Cushing syndrome (weight gain, hypertension, proximal muscle weakness, hirsutism).

Diagnostic Algorithm:

1.  Screen for hypercortisolism

→ Overnight low-dose DST / 24-hr urinary cortisol / late-night salivary cortisol

2.  If positive → measure ACTH

• Low ACTH → adrenal tumor
• High ACTH → pituitary (Cushing disease) or ectopic ACTH

3. Then imaging (pituitary MRI, adrenal CT, etc.)

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• A. Early-morning cortisol level: Not useful because cortisol normally peaks in the morning.
• C. Serum ACTH level: Done after confirming hypercortisolism, to determine the source.
• D. Cosyntropin test: Used to diagnose Addison diseases, not Cushing syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 31-year-old woman presents with progressive weight gain despite strict calorie restriction and regular exercise over the past 6 months. She also reports difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a seated position, irregular menstrual cycles, insomnia, and increasing anxiety. On examination, her blood pressure is 160/100 mmHg. She has proximal muscle weakness, coarse terminal hair over the lower abdomen, and central adiposity. Laboratory investigations reveal: • Fasting glucose: 130 mg/dL • Sodium: 142 mEq/L • Potassium: 3.6 mEq/L • Bicarbonate: 28 mEq/L • TSH: 2.2 mIU/L (normal) Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation to evaluate the suspected endocrine disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test

This patient has several features highly suggestive of Cushing syndrome:

• Progressive central weight gain
• Proximal muscle weakness
• Hypertension
• Hyperglycemia
• Menstrual irregularities
• Hirsutism
• Psychiatric symptoms (anxiety, insomnia)

The first step in evaluation is to confirm hypercortisolism before determining its cause.

Recommended screening tests (any one):

• Overnight 1-mg low-dose dexamethasone suppression test ✅
• 24-hour urinary free cortisol
• Late-night salivary cortisol

In normal individuals, dexamethasone suppresses ACTH secretion, resulting in low morning cortisol. Failure of suppression suggests Cushing syndrome.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Early morning cortisol: Cortisol follows a diurnal rhythm and has significant overlap between normal individuals and patients with Cushing syndrome; it is not a reliable screening test.
• C. Plasma ACTH level: Measured only after hypercortisolism has been confirmed to distinguish ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome.
• D. Serum testosterone: May explain hirsutism but does not account for the constellation of findings suggestive of cortisol excess.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 34-year-old patient presents with lethargy and tiredness. On examination, he has hyperpigmentation around the lips. His BP is 90/60 mm Hg and heart rate is 110/min. Labs revealed a Na⁺ of 125 mEq/L and a K⁺ of 5.5 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone

| Finding | Meaning

| ------- | -------

| Hyperpigmentation | ↑ ACTH → primary cause

| Hypotension | cortisol deficiency

| Hyponatremia | aldosterone deficiency

| Hyperkalemia | aldosterone deficiency

Findings suggest primary adrenal insufficiency with cortisol and aldosterone deficiency causing hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hyperpigmentation. Treatment requires glucocorticoid plus mineralocorticoid replacement.

GLUCOCORTICOID:

Hydrocortisone → 15–25 mg/day (divided doses)

• 10 mg morning + 5 mg afternoon (± 5 mg evening)

MINERALOCORTICOID:

Fludrocortisone → 0.05–0.2 mg/day (usually 0.1 mg once daily)

GOALS:

• Maintain BP, electrolytes (Na↑, K↓)

• Avoid hypotension & hyperkalemia

STRESS DOSE (VERY IMPORTANT):

• Increase hydrocortisone 2–3× during illness/surgery

ACUTE CRISIS:

• IV Hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus → then 200 mg/day

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman is being evaluated for endocrine disorders. It is noted that some hormones are stored in secretory granules before release, while others are synthesized on demand and not stored. Which of the following hormones is not stored before secretion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cortisol

• Hormones differ in their storage and release mechanisms based on their chemical nature.
• Peptide and protein hormones (e.g., insulin, growth hormone):

• Synthesized in advance
• Stored in secretory granules
• Released by exocytosis on demand

• Thyroid hormones (T3/T4):

• Unique among amines
• Stored extracellularly in the colloid (thyroglobulin) of the thyroid gland
• Released after proteolysis

• Steroid hormones (e.g., cortisol):

• NOT stored
• Synthesized on demand from cholesterol
• Rapidly diffuse out of cells after synthesis

Why not other options:

• A. Insulin: Stored in pancreatic β-cell granules
• B. Thyroxine (T4): Stored in colloid (thyroglobulin-bound form)
• C. Growth hormone: Stored in anterior pituitary granules

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents to the clinic with fatigue, hair loss, and constipation. She has a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus, well controlled on insulin, and celiac disease, which she manages with a gluten-free diet. On physical examination, she has dry skin but no other obvious abnormalities. On laboratory evaluation, her thyroid function test is abnormal. What is the most likely underlying syndrome?
options: Immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked disease
Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, M-protein, and skin changes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2 (APS-2)

Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 2 (APS-2) is an adult-onset autoimmune disorder characterized by the coexistence of autoimmune adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) with autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes mellitus. It typically occurs in young to middle-aged women and may be associated with other autoimmune conditions such as celiac disease, vitiligo, and pernicious anemia.

Why not other options:

• A. APS-1

• Childhood onset
• Triad: mucocutaneous candidiasis + hypoparathyroidism + Addison disease
• Patient is adult (35 years) with none of these features.

• C. IPEX syndrome

• X-linked FOXP3 mutation
• Occurs in male infants with severe autoimmune enteropathy.
• Patient is an adult female.

• D. POEMS syndrome

• Plasma cell disorder.
• Features: polyneuropathy, organomegaly, monoclonal protein, skin changes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 37-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to a two-month history of abdominal pain, salt craving, and weight loss. She also has dizziness on standing. Her mother and sister have hypothyroidism. Blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg supine and 80/50 mm Hg standing. Laboratory results are as follows. Which of the following changes are expected in this patient?
options: Serum Na Low, Serum K low, urine Na low, urine K high
Serum Na Low, Serum K high, urine Na high, urine K low
Serum Na Low, Serum K low, urine Na normal, urine K high
Serum Na normal, Serum K low, urine Na low, urine K high
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serum Na Low, Serum K high, urine Na high, urine K low

This patient has primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) due to adrenal cortex destruction, leading to aldosterone deficiency.

Effect of low aldosterone on kidney:

• ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption in distal nephron → ↑ urinary sodium loss → hyponatremia
• ↓ K⁺ excretion → hyperkalemia
• Therefore, urine Na⁺ increases and urine K⁺ decreases.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 38-year-old female patient presents with buffalo hump, moon facies, and abdominal striae. She is a known case of SLE on steroids. Which of the following is the next best investigation that should be done in her?
options: Low-dose dexamethasone followed by high-dose dexamethasone suppression test
ACTH levels followed by the high-dose dexamethasone suppression test
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Serum Cortisol with ACTH levels

In this patient: Exogenous glucocorticoids mimic cortisol.

Therefore:

| Level | Effect

| ----- | ------

| Hypothalamus | ↓ CRH

| Pituitary | ↓ ACTH

| Adrenal cortex | Atrophy

| Cortisol production | ↓ endogenous cortisol

Thus, the HPA axis becomes suppressed.

Correct answer is A because the patient has features of Cushing syndrome in the setting of chronic steroid use, so the first step is to confirm endogenous vs exogenous hypercortisolism by measuring serum cortisol and ACTH.

Exogenous steroid use suppresses ACTH and endogenous cortisol production.

| Type | Cause

| ---- | -----

| Exogenous (most common) | Steroid therapy

| ACTH-dependent | Pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease)

| | Ectopic ACTH (small cell lung carcinoma)

| ACTH-independent | Adrenal adenoma

| | Adrenal carcinoma

Because the HPA axis is suppressed, sudden steroid withdrawal can cause:

Acute adrenal crisis

Symptoms:

• hypotension
• hypoglycemia
• shock

Thus, steroids must be tapered gradually.

Dexamethasone suppression tests are used only after confirming endogenous Cushing syndrome, not in suspected iatrogenic cases.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of fatigue, weight loss, salt craving, and dizziness upon standing. She has no significant medical history and takes no medications. Her mother was recently diagnosed with hypothyroidism. On examination, her blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg supine and 80/50 mm Hg standing. Laboratory results reveal the following: Sodium 129 meq/l Potassium 5.9 meq/l Chloride 100 meq/l Bicarbonate 21 meq/l Creatinine 1.4 mg/dl BUN 38mg/dl Which of the following in circulating hormone levels are expected in this patient?
options: Cortisol low, Aldosterone low, ADH high, Norepinephrine high
Cortisol normal, Aldosterone low, ADH normal, Norepinephrine normal
Cortisol low, Aldosterone low, ADH normal, Norepinephrine normal
Cortisol high, Aldosterone low, ADH high, Norepinephrine high
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cortisol low, Aldosterone low, ADH high, Norepinephrine high

This patient has features of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease).

• Fatigue, weight loss, salt craving
• Orthostatic hypotension
• Hyponatremia (Na⁺ 129 mEq/L)
• Hyperkalemia (K⁺ 5.9 mEq/L)
• Family history of autoimmune disease → suggests autoimmune adrenal destruction

Hormonal pattern in primary adrenal insufficiency:

• ↓ Cortisol → adrenal cortex failure
• ↓ Aldosterone → Na⁺ loss, K⁺ retention, hypotension
• ↑ ADH → due to hypovolemia and cortisol deficiency
• ↑ Norepinephrine → compensatory sympathetic activation to maintain blood pressure

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight loss, dizziness on standing, and hyperpigmentation of the skin. Blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg. Laboratory tests show hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. She is diagnosed with primary adrenal insufficiency. Which of the following findings is not expected in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased protein breakdown

Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) results from deficiency of both cortisol and aldosterone. Aldosterone deficiency causes renal sodium loss, volume depletion, hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia, while increased ACTH production leads to hyperpigmentation.

Why is D correct?

• Increased protein breakdown is a feature of cortisol excess (Cushing syndrome), not cortisol deficiency.
• In Addison disease, the absence of cortisol reduces its normal catabolic effects on protein metabolism.

Why not the other options?

• A. Low blood pressure – expected due to volume depletion and reduced vascular responsiveness.
• B. Decreased extracellular fluid volume – occurs because of aldosterone deficiency and sodium loss.
• C. Decreased sodium–potassium ratio – results from hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presented with weight gain, proximal muscle weakness, purple striae, and easy bruising. What is the likely underlying condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypercortisolism

Correct answer is A because weight gain, proximal muscle weakness, purple striae, and easy bruising are classic features of Cushing syndrome due to excess cortisol.

Hypercortisolism causes protein catabolism, skin thinning, and central fat redistribution.

| Mechanism | Clinical Effect

| --------- | ---------------

| ↑ Protein breakdown | Muscle weakness

| ↓ Collagen synthesis | Thin skin → easy bruising

| Fat redistribution | Central obesity

| Skin thinning | Purple striae

Causes of Hypercortisolism

| Type | Cause

| ---- | -----

| Exogenous | Steroid therapy (most common)

| ACTH-dependent | Pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease)

| | Ectopic ACTH (small cell lung cancer)

| ACTH-independent | Adrenal adenoma/carcinoma

Thyroid, parathyroid, or aldosterone excess do not produce this characteristic constellation of findings.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old lady, who is a known case of rheumatoid arthritis, presents with obesity, moon facies, abdominal striae and hypertension. Overnight dexamethasone suppression test shows serum cortisol >50 nmol/L and serum ACTH <1.1 pmol/L. Adrenal imaging and brain CT/MRI are unremarkable. The likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Exogenous glucocorticoid use

ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome with normal adrenal imaging in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis strongly suggests exogenous glucocorticoid use. Chronic steroid therapy suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, resulting in very low ACTH levels and Cushingoid features such as central obesity, moon facies, abdominal striae, and hypertension. Since the cortisol is coming from an external source, adrenal glands are often normal or atrophic on imaging.

Why not the other options?

• A. Cushing’s disease: Caused by a pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma → ACTH is elevated or inappropriately normal, and pituitary MRI may show an adenoma.
• B. Ectopic ACTH-secreting tumour: Causes markedly elevated ACTH with severe hypercortisolism; ACTH is not suppressed.
• D. Adrenal adenoma: Produces ACTH-independent hypercortisolism with low ACTH, but adrenal imaging would reveal an adrenal mass, which is absent here.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with persistent hypertension, progressive weight gain, and proximal muscle weakness. Laboratory evaluation reveals elevated serum cortisol levels with suppressed plasma ACTH. Which of the following is the next best investigation in the workup of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CT scan of the abdomen

Interpretation:

• High cortisol + suppressed ACTH → ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome
• This usually indicates an adrenal source (e.g., adrenal adenoma, adrenal carcinoma, or adrenal hyperplasia).

Next step → Imaging of the adrenal glands, typically with a CT scan of the abdomen, to identify an adrenal tumor.

Diagnostic approach (high-yield):

1. Confirm hypercortisolism (e.g., low-dose dexamethasone suppression test).
2. Measure ACTH.
3. If ACTH low → adrenal cause → CT abdomen.
4. If ACTH high/normal → ACTH-dependent → MRI pituitary or tests for ectopic ACTH.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 54-year-old man with a history of chronic duodenal ulcer disease presents with new-onset muscle weakness and pedal edema. On examination, his blood pressure is elevated. Laboratory investigations reveal hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. He reports taking a drug Carbenoxolone for ulcer healing. Which of the following best explains the adverse effects produced by this drug?
options: Increased aldosterone secretion from adrenal cortex
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inhibition of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2

Carbenoxolone can cause apparent mineralocorticoid excess by inhibiting the enzyme 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11β-HSD2) in the kidney.

Mechanism:

• Normally, 11β-HSD2 converts cortisol → cortisone in renal tubular cells.
• Cortisone cannot activate mineralocorticoid receptors, protecting them from cortisol.
• Inhibition of 11β-HSD2 → cortisol accumulates and stimulates mineralocorticoid receptors.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old female with a prolonged history of systemic lupus erythematosus, treated with multiple medications is being evaluated on autopsy. Records from the patient's most recent office visit show an elevated blood pressure and examination findings of facial plethora, truncal obesity, and skin ecchymoses. The patient's adrenal glands is most likely to reveal which of the following findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bilateral cortical atrophy

Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid therapy (commonly used to treat autoimmune diseases like SLE) causes iatrogenic Cushing syndrome.

Mechanism:

• Exogenous steroids suppress hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH via negative feedback.
• ↓ ACTH leads to reduced stimulation of the adrenal cortex.
• Over time, this causes bilateral adrenal cortical atrophy, particularly of the zona fasciculata and zona reticularis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient was brought to the emergency department in an unconscious state. The patient is dehydrated and the blood pressure of the patient is 90/60 mm Hg. Laboratory investigations revealed the serum potassium level of 6.0 mEq/L, sodium level of 129 mEq/L, and blood glucose level of 40 mg/dL. The patient has a history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) for which he was prescribed medication by a local physician; however, the patient abruptly discontinued the medication a few weeks ago. Based on the clinical presentation and laboratory findings, which of the following drugs should be administered as a life-saving measure to treat this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydrocortisone

Correct answer is A because abrupt withdrawal of chronic steroids in an RA patient can precipitate acute adrenal crisis with hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia.

Cortisol deficiency-

| Effect | Result

| ------ | ------

| ↓ gluconeogenesis | Hypoglycemia

| ↓ vascular tone | Hypotension

| ↓ stress response | Shock

This reflects cortisol and aldosterone deficiency causing shock and electrolyte imbalance.

Immediate life-saving treatment is IV hydrocortisone with fluids, which corrects both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency.

Hydrocortisone provides:

Glucocorticoid effect (cortisol replacement)

Mineralocorticoid effect (aldosterone-like action)

➡ Corrects:

• hypotension
• hypoglycemia
• electrolyte imbalance

Immediate steps:

1️⃣ IV Hydrocortisone

2️⃣ IV fluids (normal saline + dextrose)

3️⃣ Correct electrolytes

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with hypertensive episodes, with an MRI abdomen showing a suprarenal mass, is planned for surgery. A 24-hour urine shows elevated metanephrine levels. What drug will be given preoperatively and also intraoperatively?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phenoxybenzamine

Phenoxybenzamine is a nonselective irreversible α-blocker used preoperatively in pheochromocytoma to prevent catecholamine-induced hypertensive crises.

Phenoxybenzamine = irreversible α-blocker

Blocks α₁ and α₂ receptors

Causes vasodilation

Preoperative

• Classically Phenoxybenzamine (α-blocker) → given days before surgery

Intraoperative BP control

• Need short-acting, titratable drug
• Nicardipine (IV CCB) is preferred:

• Rapid onset
• Easily adjustable
• Controls hypertensive surges during tumor manipulation

Question asks: “preoperative AND intraoperative”

• Among options, Phenoxybenzamine seems most appropriate due to its traditional use-case in pheochromocytoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with pheochromocytoma is scheduled for surgical removal. Which of the following is the correct preoperative pharmacological management?
options: Start phenoxybenzamine first, followed by propranolol if needed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Start phenoxybenzamine first, followed by propranolol if needed

Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla that can cause severe hypertension during surgery. Preoperative α-adrenergic blockade is mandatory before β-blockade to prevent unopposed α-adrenergic stimulation, which can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. The standard regimen is to start phenoxybenzamine (irreversible non-selective α-blocker) 7–14 days before surgery, followed by a β-blocker (e.g., propranolol) only after adequate α-blockade if tachycardia persists.

Why not the other options?

• A. Start propranolol alone before surgery: Contraindicated. β-blockade first causes unopposed α-adrenergic vasoconstriction, leading to severe hypertension.
• C. Start propranolol first, then phenoxybenzamine: Incorrect for the same reason; β-blockers should never precede α-blockade.
• D. No preoperative medication is required: Incorrect. Preoperative adrenergic blockade is essential to reduce the risk of intraoperative hypertensive crises.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman previously treated for Cushing disease underwent bilateral adrenalectomy 2 years ago. She now presents with progressive hyperpigmentation, headaches, and new-onset visual field defects. MRI shows an enlarging pituitary mass with markedly elevated ACTH levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nelson syndrome

Nelson Syndrome

This is a classic post-bilateral adrenalectomy complication.

Step 1 — Original disease:

Cushing disease = ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma → bilateral adrenal hyperplasia → excess cortisol

Step 2 — Treatment:

Bilateral adrenalectomy removes both adrenal glands → cortisol drops to zero

Step 3 — Loss of negative feedback:

Cortisol normally suppresses the pituitary via negative feedback. With no adrenals, there is no cortisol → no feedback inhibition on the pre-existing pituitary tumor

Step 4 — Tumor goes unchecked:

The pituitary adenoma grows aggressively and secretes massive amounts of ACTH (and MSH, since ACTH is cleaved from POMC alongside α-MSH)

The Classic Triad of Nelson Syndrome

| Feature | Mechanism

| ------- | ---------

| Hyperpigmentation | Excess ACTH → excess α-MSH → melanocyte stimulation

| Headaches + visual field defects | Enlarging pituitary mass compressing the optic chiasm (bitemporal hemianopia)

| Markedly elevated ACTH | Uninhibited tumor secretion

Why Not the Others?

• Sheehan syndrome — pituitary infarction post-partum hemorrhage → low ACTH/hormones, no mass
• Conn's syndrome — primary hyperaldosteronism (adrenal adenoma), no pituitary involvement
• Addison's disease — primary adrenal insufficiency → high ACTH but no pituitary mass, no prior adrenalectomy context

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young patient presents with persistently elevated blood pressure. Investigations reveal hypokalemia associated with metabolic alkalosis. Kidney function tests are normal, and there is no history of any drug intake. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Conn syndrome

The combination of persistent hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis is the classic biochemical profile of primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome). Autonomous aldosterone secretion causes increased sodium and water reabsorption, resulting in hypertension, while simultaneously increasing potassium and hydrogen ion excretion, leading to hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Renin levels are typically suppressed due to negative feedback.

• Screening test: Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) ↑ (↑ aldosterone, ↓ renin)
• Most common causes: Aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma (Conn syndrome) and bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
• Treatment:

• Unilateral adenoma → Laparoscopic adrenalectomy
• Bilateral hyperplasia → Spironolactone or eplerenone

• Differentiate from secondary hyperaldosteronism:

• Primary: ↑ Aldosterone, ↓ Renin
• Secondary (e.g., renal artery stenosis): ↑ Aldosterone, ↑ Renin

Why not the other options?

• A. Carcinoid syndrome: Presents with flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm, and elevated urinary 5-HIAA; hypertension with hypokalemic alkalosis is not a feature.
• B. Pheochromocytoma: Causes episodic hypertension with headache, palpitations, and sweating due to catecholamine excess; serum potassium is usually normal.
• D. Cushing syndrome: May produce hypertension and hypokalemia because of cortisol’s mineralocorticoid activity, but is accompanied by features such as central obesity, moon facies, purple striae, proximal muscle weakness, and glucose intolerance.

Exam Pearls:

• Classic triad: Hypertension + Hypokalemia + Metabolic alkalosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All are true in conn syndrome except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High plasma renin

Conn syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) is caused by excess aldosterone secretion, usually from an adrenal adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia.

Excess aldosterone → increased Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺/H⁺ excretion in the distal nephron.

Characteristic features

• High aldosterone levels
• Suppressed plasma renin activity (due to negative feedback from volume expansion)
• Hypokalemia
• Metabolic alkalosis (due to increased H⁺ loss)
• Diastolic hypertension without edema (because of aldosterone escape mechanism)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Cortisone is administered into a 20 yr old woman for treatment of autoimmune disorder. Which of the following is most likely to occur ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increase insulin secretion

Administration of exogenous glucocorticoids (e.g., cortisone) increases blood glucose levels by stimulating hepatic gluconeogenesis, decreasing peripheral glucose uptake, and promoting protein and fat catabolism. The resulting hyperglycemia stimulates pancreatic β-cells to increase insulin secretion.

Why not other options:

A. Increase cortisol secretion

• Exogenous cortisone suppresses the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis.
• Negative feedback → ↓ CRH and ↓ ACTH → ↓ endogenous cortisol production.

C. Increase ACTH secretion

• Glucocorticoids exert negative feedback on the pituitary.
• Therefore, ACTH decreases, not increases.

D. Increase muscle mass

• Glucocorticoids cause protein catabolism.
• Leads to muscle wasting, not increased muscle mass.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Cushing syndrome is not a feature of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medulloblastoma

Cushing syndrome results from excess glucocorticoids (cortisol) and may occur due to ACTH-dependent or ACTH-independent causes.

ACTH-dependent causes:

• Pituitary adenoma → called Cushing disease
• Ectopic ACTH production, commonly from small cell (oat cell) carcinoma of the lung

ACTH-independent causes:

• Adrenal tumors (e.g., adrenal carcinoma or adenoma) that produce excess cortisol.

Medulloblastoma is a malignant cerebellar tumor of childhood and does not produce ACTH or cortisol, so it is not associated with Cushing syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Increase in which of the following hormone is responsible for Hyperpigmentation in Addison's disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ACTH

In Addison disease, low cortisol removes negative feedback on the pituitary, causing marked elevation of ACTH. ACTH is derived from POMC, which also produces MSH, stimulating melanocytes and causing diffuse hyperpigmentation.

| Component | Derived From | Function

| --------- | ------------ | --------

| ACTH | POMC | Stimulates adrenal cortex

| MSH | POMC | Stimulates melanocytes

| Cortisol | Adrenal cortex | Negative feedback

| | |

Aldosterone and ADH do not affect skin pigmentation. Cortisol is decreased, not increased, in primary adrenal insufficiency.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Liquorice misuse, by inhibiting 11 beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 enzyme, can cause a ‘condition which resembles the clinical features of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mineralocorticoid excess

Liquorice (glycyrrhizin) inhibits 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11β-HSD2) in the renal collecting ducts. Normally, 11β-HSD2 converts cortisol → cortisone, preventing cortisol from activating the mineralocorticoid receptor.

When inhibited:

• ↑ Cortisol action on mineralocorticoid receptors → sodium retention + potassium/H⁺ loss → hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis.
• This produces apparent mineralocorticoid excess (AME).

Why not other options?

• A. Gonadotropin excess: Not the mechanism of liquorice toxicity.
• B. Thyrotropin excess: Not involved.
• C. Mineralocorticoid excess — Correct: Mimics hyperaldosteronism, despite low/normal aldosterone levels.
• D. Parathyroid hormone excess: Not involved.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Under which one of the following conditions, the HPA axis suppression is likely to result in crisis due to adrenal insufficiency following withdrawal of glucocorticoids?
options: If glucocorticoids have been given by intravenous route for five days
If glucocorticoids have been administered orally for one week
If glucocorticoids have been prescribed repeatedly for short courses within the previous year
If the dose is less than equivalent of 5 mg prednisolone per day
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. If glucocorticoids have been prescribed repeatedly for short courses within the previous year

Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) axis suppression occurs when exogenous glucocorticoids suppress endogenous CRH → ACTH → cortisol production. Abrupt withdrawal in patients with significant suppression can precipitate adrenal insufficiency or adrenal crisis, especially during physiological stress.

Repeated short courses of glucocorticoids within the previous year can cumulatively suppress the HPA axis. Even if each course is brief, repeated exposure may impair adrenal responsiveness, increasing the risk of adrenal crisis after withdrawal.

Factors Increasing Risk of HPA Axis Suppression

• Long duration of glucocorticoid therapy (>3–4 weeks)
• High-dose glucocorticoid therapy
• Evening/night-time dosing
• Repeated courses of systemic steroids
• Recent glucocorticoid exposure within the previous year

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect

• A. IV glucocorticoids for 5 days → Usually insufficient to cause significant HPA suppression.
• B. Oral glucocorticoids for 1 week → Generally do not cause clinically significant adrenal suppression.
• D. <5 mg prednisolone/day → Considered a physiologic or low dose with minimal risk of HPA axis suppression.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis of a middle-aged patient presented with episodic headache, palpitations and increased 24-hour urinary levels of metanephrines?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pheochromocytoma

Symptoms suggest: Intermittent sympathetic overactivity

Classic triad:

• Headache
• Palpitations
• Sweating

Lab clue:

• ↑ Metanephrines (very specific)

Diagnosis: Pheochromocytoma

Episodic headache, palpitations, and elevated urinary metanephrines are classic for pheochromocytoma. Excess catecholamine secretion produces paroxysmal sympathetic surges and hypertension. Urinary metanephrines are sensitive markers of catecholamine excess.

The other tumors do not produce this characteristic biochemical pattern.

Neuroblastoma

• Occurs in children
• Not typical in adults

Carcinoid tumor

• Causes flushing and diarrhea
• Due to serotonin secretion, not catecholamines

Brain tumor

• May cause headache
• Does not explain palpitations or elevated metanephrines

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which dosing strategy most appropriately mimics physiologic cortisol secretion?
options: 30 mg hydrocortisone once daily at bedtime
20 mg/day in divided doses, with the larger portion given in the morning
5 mg/day hydrocortisone, titrated upward only during illness
40 mg/day in three equal doses spaced evenly across 24 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 20 mg/day in divided doses, with the larger portion given in the morning

Glucocorticoid replacement therapy should mimic the normal circadian rhythm of cortisol secretion, in which cortisol levels are highest in the early morning and gradually decline throughout the day. Therefore, physiologic replacement is best achieved by administering hydrocortisone in divided doses, with the largest dose given in the morning.

• Typical replacement dose: 15–25 mg hydrocortisone/day.
• Given in 2–3 divided doses:

• Largest dose in the morning (e.g., 10–15 mg)
• Smaller dose in the afternoon (e.g., 5 mg)

• Closely reproduces normal endogenous cortisol secretion.

Why not the others?

• A. 30 mg at bedtime → Opposes physiologic rhythm and may cause insomnia, Cushingoid effects, and HPA suppression.
• C. 5 mg/day hydrocortisone, titrated upward only during illness → Inadequate replacement for most patients with adrenal insufficiency.
• D. 40 mg/day in three equal doses spaced evenly throughout 24 hours → Does not mimic normal circadian cortisol secretion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are correct regarding Cortisol? 1. Levels are highest in the morning on waking. 2. Cortisol falls dramatically during an illness. 3. More than 95% circulating cortisol is protein bound. 4. It is the major glucocorticoid in humans and can also activate mineralocorticoid receptors. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3 and 4

• 1. Levels are highest in the morning on waking✅: Cortisol exhibits a diurnal rhythm, peaking in the early morning (6–8 AM) and reaching its lowest level around midnight.
• 2. Cortisol falls dramatically during an illness❌: Cortisol increases during illness, trauma, surgery, and other stress states as part of the stress response.
• 3. More than 95% circulating cortisol is protein bound✅: Most cortisol is bound to CBG (transcortin) and albumin; only the free fraction is biologically active.
• 4. It is the major glucocorticoid in humans and can also activate mineralocorticoid receptors✅: Cortisol is the major glucocorticoid and can bind mineralocorticoid receptors, although in the kidney it is normally inactivated by 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11β-HSD2).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is considered the initial recommended test for diagnosing pheochromocytoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 24 hr urinary total metanephrines

Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of chromaffin cells.

Most arise from: Adrenal medulla

Extra-adrenal tumors are called: Paragangliomas

Correct answer is A because the preferred initial screening test for pheochromocytoma is measurement of metanephrines, which reflect continuous catecholamine metabolism and have high sensitivity.

24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines are recommended for initial biochemical diagnosis.

Imaging (MRI/MIBG) is done only after biochemical confirmation. Plasma catecholamines fluctuate and are less reliable for screening.

Pheochromocytoma can occur in several genetic syndromes.

| Syndrome | Gene

| -------- | ----

| MEN 2A / MEN 2B | RET mutation

| Von Hippel–Lindau disease | VHL gene

| Neurofibromatosis type 1 | NF1 gene

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a stimulus for catecholamine synthesis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyperglycemia

Catecholamines are stress hormones produced by the adrenal medulla.

Correct answer is C because catecholamine synthesis is stimulated by sympathetic activation such as stress, exercise, nicotine (smoking), and postural change like standing.

Hyperglycemia suppresses sympathetic drive, whereas hypoglycemia is a strong stimulus for catecholamine release.

Catecholamine secretion increases during sympathetic activation or stress.

Common physiological stimuli:

| Stimulus | Mechanism

| -------- | ---------

| Exercise | Increased sympathetic activity

| Smoking | Nicotine stimulates sympathetic ganglia

| Standing posture | Orthostatic sympathetic activation

| Hypoglycemia | Counter-regulatory response

These conditions increase epinephrine and norepinephrine release.

When blood glucose is high:

• Insulin secretion increases
• Sympathetic activation decreases
• No need for counter-regulatory hormones

Therefore: Catecholamine synthesis is not stimulated by hyperglycemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not seen in Conn's syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypernatremia

Conn’s syndrome = Primary hyperaldosteronism

Cause: Excess aldosterone secretion from adrenal cortex independent of RAAS regulation.

Correct answer is B because Conn’s syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) causes sodium retention with volume expansion, but serum sodium is usually near normal due to escape mechanisms. Even though sodium is retained: The body activates escape mechanisms:

Aldosterone Escape

• Pressure natriuresis
• ANP release
• Increased GFR

These prevent significant sodium accumulation in plasma.

Therefore:

| Sodium effect

| -------------

| Total body sodium ↑

| Serum sodium ≈ normal

Hence hypernatremia is uncommon.

It classically presents with hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis from increased potassium and hydrogen ion loss.

Thus, hypernatremia is not a typical finding.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct statement about a patient with a retroperitoneal mass, episodic hypertension, palpitations, and increased urinary VMA levels?
options: It can be associated with MEN 2A
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It can be associated with MEN 2A

| Syndrome | Components

| -------- | ----------

| MEN 2A ⭐ | Medullary thyroid carcinoma + pheochromocytoma + parathyroid hyperplasia

| MEN 2B | Medullary thyroid carcinoma + pheochromocytoma + mucosal neuromas

The presentation suggests pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting tumor classically causing episodic hypertension and elevated urinary VMA. Pheochromocytoma is associated with MEN 2A due to RET mutation along with medullary thyroid carcinoma and hyperparathyroidism.

Most tumors are benign, unilateral, and occur in adults. Bilateral tumors are mainly seen in familial syndromes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not correct regarding primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease)?
options: Orthostatic hypertension is a common clinical feature
Skin hyperpigmentation is seen due to elevated ACTH levels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Orthostatic hypertension is a common clinical feature

Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) occurs due to destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex, leading to a deficiency of cortisol and aldosterone.

Because of volume depletion and low blood pressure, patients commonly develop orthostatic hypotension, not orthostatic hypertension.

Typical findings in Addison's disease:

• Hypotension / orthostatic hypotension
• Hyperkalemia
• Hyponatremia
• Hyperpigmentation of skin and mucosa
• Possible mild increase in serum creatinine due to dehydration

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is a cause of Secondary Hyperaldosteronism?
options: Inadequate renal perfusion due to renal artery stenosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inadequate renal perfusion due to renal artery stenosis

Secondary hyperaldosteronism results from increased activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) due to reduced renal perfusion or decreased effective circulating blood volume. Unlike primary hyperaldosteronism, aldosterone secretion is renin-dependent, so both plasma renin and aldosterone levels are elevated.

• D. Inadequate renal perfusion due to renal artery stenosis: Reduced renal blood flow stimulates renin release, activating the RAAS, which leads to secondary hyperaldosteronism.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma (Conn syndrome): Causes primary hyperaldosteronism with ↑ aldosterone and ↓ renin.
• B. Idiopathic bilateral adrenal hyperplasia: Another cause of primary hyperaldosteronism.
• C. 11-Deoxycorticosterone-secreting adrenal tumour: Causes mineralocorticoid excess independent of aldosterone, with suppressed renin and aldosterone.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: With regard to the treatment of phaeochromocytoma, beta-blocker should never be given before alpha-blocker because it may cause:
options: Paradoxical rise in blood pressure due to unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction
Paradoxical fall in blood pressure due to unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction
Paradoxical rise in blood pressure due to unopposed alpha-mediated vasodilation
Paradoxical fall in blood pressure due to unopposed alpha-mediated vasodilation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Paradoxical rise in blood pressure due to unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction

In pheochromocytoma, excessive catecholamines cause intense α₁-mediated vasoconstriction. If a β-blocker is administered before adequate α-blockade, β₂-mediated vasodilation is blocked while α₁-mediated vasoconstriction remains unopposed. This can produce a severe paradoxical rise in blood pressure, potentially precipitating a hypertensive crisis.

Why not the other options?

• B. Paradoxical fall in BP due to unopposed α-mediated vasoconstriction: Incorrect. α₁-mediated vasoconstriction raises blood pressure.
• C. Rise in BP due to unopposed α-mediated vasodilation: Incorrect. α₁ receptors cause vasoconstriction, not vasodilation.
• D. Fall in BP due to unopposed α-mediated vasodilation: Incorrect for the same reason.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 53-year-old man comes to the physician complaining of increased urinary frequency for the past 4 weeks. He has no burning with urination, urgency, or difficulty initiating urination. He wakes up several times at night to urinate. His mouth feels dry all the time and he drinks fluids almost every hour to alleviate his thirst. The patient's medications include hydrochlorothiazide and amlodipine for hypertension. His sister was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus at a young age. His blood pressure is 120/76 mm Hg, pulse is 85/min, and respirations are 15/min. His body mass index is 32 kg/m². Laboratory results are as follows: Blood glucose-93 mg/dL Serum sodium-150 mEg/L Serum potassium-4.1 mEq/L Bicarbonate-24 mEq/L Blood urea nitrogen-21 mg/dL Serum creatinine-1.1 mg/dL Serum uric acid-10.1 mg/dL (N- 3.5-7.2 mg/dL) Serum osmolality-314 mOsm/kg (N- 275 to 295 mOsm/kg) Urine osmolality-124 mOsm/kg (N-500 - 800 mOsm/kg) Which of the following is most consistent with this patient's findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Central Diabetes insipidus

Central diabetes insipidus is caused by deficient secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) from the posterior pituitary, leading to impaired water reabsorption in the collecting ducts.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 64-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department due to confusion and lethargy. The patient was asymptomatic when her husband left for work in the morning, but when he arrived home, he found her in bed weak and disoriented. The patient's medical conditions include type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension, for which she takes multiple medications. Laboratory testing shows an elevated serum C-peptide level. If her current condition is due to an antidiabetic drug, which of the following is the most likely culprit agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glyburide

Sulfonylureas (e.g., glyburide) treat type 2 diabetes by stimulating pancreatic β-cells to release insulin through closure of ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels. This leads to:

• Increased endogenous insulin secretion
• Elevated C-peptide levels (because insulin is produced by the pancreas)

Excess insulin release can cause severe hypoglycemia, especially in elderly patients or with long-acting sulfonylureas like glyburide.

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. Acarbose: Does not increase insulin secretion → hypoglycemia uncommon.
• B. Canagliflozin: Lowers glucose by urinary glucose excretion, not insulin release.
• D. Long-acting insulin: Exogenous insulin lacks C-peptide, so C-peptide would be low.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 10-year-old diabetic child in DKA has blood glucose 450 mg/dL, pH 7.18, and bicarbonate 8 mEq/L. Why should early insulin infusion (within the first hour) be specifically avoided in paediatric DKA?
options: Insulin causes hyperkalaemia worsening the acidosis
Early insulin causes rapid intracellular glucose shift reducing serum osmolality causing cerebral oedema and death
Insulin activates RAAS worsening sodium retention
Early insulin inhibits lipolysis paradoxically worsening ketosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Early insulin causes rapid intracellular glucose shift reducing serum osmolality causing cerebral oedema and death

The child has moderate diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). In paediatric DKA, the most feared complication is cerebral oedema, which is the leading cause of mortality. Starting insulin before adequate fluid resuscitation causes a rapid fall in blood glucose and serum osmolality, leading to movement of water into brain cells and cerebral swelling. Therefore, initial management is isotonic saline (10–20 mL/kg over the first hour) to restore intravascular volume. Continuous IV insulin (0.05–0.1 U/kg/hour) is started only after at least 1 hour of fluid therapy, and without an initial insulin bolus, to minimize the risk of cerebral oedema.

High-Yield

• Paediatric DKA: Fluids first, insulin later (after ≥1 hour).
• Most common cause of death: Cerebral oedema.
• Never give an insulin bolus in paediatric DKA.
• Begin potassium replacement once urine output is established and serum potassium is not elevated.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department due to confusion, abdominal pain, and vomiting for the past two days. Her parents report that she has been excessively thirsty and urinating frequently over the last few weeks. On examination, her vital signs are as follows: temperature 37.2°C (99°F), pulse 110/min, blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 28/min. Laboratory investigations reveal the following: • Glucose 320 mg/dL • Sodium 132 meq/l • Potassium 5.2 meq/l • Bicarbonate 12 meq/l • Arterial pH 7.25 • Urinalysis: Positive for urine and ketones Which of the following factors most likely contributed to the development of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Islet leukocytic infiltration

Type 1 diabetes mellitus results from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells by T-lymphocytes, leading to absolute insulin deficiency. The characteristic pathological finding is lymphocytic infiltration of the pancreatic islets (insulitis).

Loss of insulin causes:

• Decreased glucose uptake
• Increased lipolysis and ketone body production
• High anion gap metabolic acidosis, producing diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).

Clinical features of DKA include:

• Polyuria and polydipsia
• Dehydration and hypotension
• Abdominal pain and vomiting
• Tachypnea (Kussmaul breathing)
• Altered mental status

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with fatigue, abdominal pain, and confusion. Laboratory results reveal the following: Glucose (serum) 720 mg/dL Sodium 132 meq/l Potassium 5.2meq/l Bicarbonate 10meq/l Arterial pH 7.25 Creatinine 1.5mg/dl Blood urea nitrogen 35mg/dl Urinalysis: Positive for urine and ketones Which of the following electrolyte findings would most likely be seen in this patient?
options: Extracellular potassium concentration increase, Intracellular potassium concentration decrease
Extracellular potassium concentration increase, Intracellular potassium concentration increase
Extracellular potassium concentration decrease, Intracellular potassium concentration increase
Extracellular potassium concentration decrease, Intracellular potassium concentration decrease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Extracellular potassium concentration increase, Intracellular potassium concentration decrease

In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), total body potassium is depleted, but serum (extracellular) potassium is often elevated.

Mechanism:

• Insulin deficiency prevents potassium from entering cells.
• Metabolic acidosis causes H⁺ to move into cells and K⁺ to shift out.
• This leads to increased extracellular potassium despite decreased intracellular potassium and total body potassium depletion due to osmotic diuresis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman is brought to the ED during an acute panic attack. She is breathing rapidly and deeply, and reports tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips. Examination shows flexion of the wrist and MCP joints with extension of the interphalangeal joints. Total serum calcium is 9.2 mg/dL (normal); serum albumin is normal. All of the following statements about this patient's calcium physiology are true except:
options: Her hyperventilation produces a respiratory alkalosis, lowering blood H⁺ concentration
The rise in pH allows albumin to bind more calcium, reducing the ionized calcium fraction despite an unchanged total calcium
The fall in ionized calcium leads to decreased PTH secretion, which worsens her symptoms
Ionized calcium — not total calcium or albumin concentration — is the primary regulator of PTH secretion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The fall in ionized calcium leads to decreased PTH secretion, which worsens her symptoms

Why C is false (the exception): A falling ionized calcium is sensed by the parathyroid CaSR and increases PTH secretion — an appropriate homeostatic response, not a paradoxical suppression. PTH goes up, not down.

Quick clinical anchors:
