• A. Her hyperventilation produces a respiratory alkalosis, lowering blood H⁺ concentration: ↓ PaCO₂ → ↓ H⁺ → alkalemia.
• B. The rise in pH allows albumin to bind more calcium, reducing the ionized calcium fraction despite an unchanged total calcium: Ca²⁺ and H⁺ compete for the same anionic sites on albumin; fewer protons = more calcium bound = less free calcium. Total calcium is normal, which is why measuring total calcium here is misleading.
• D. Ionized calcium — not total calcium or albumin concentration — is the primary regulator of PTH secretion: Albumin changes shift total calcium without touching ionized calcium, so PTH is unaffected; pH changes shift the ionized fraction, so PTH responds.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to a 4-month history of amenorrhea. She has also had a whitish nipple discharge from both breasts. The patient has taken several pregnancy tests at home that have been negative. She has also had increased fatigue, depressed mood, and weight gain over this time. The patient has had no headaches or vision changes. On physical examination, there is thinning of the outer third of the eyebrows. The thyroid is enlarged and nontender to palpation. The skin appears dry. Her thyroxine (T4) levels are low, TSH is elevated, and antithyroid peroxidase antibodies are positive. Prolactin levels are 30 ng/ml. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism causing this patient's elevated prolactin level?
options: Activation of lactotrophs by antithyroid peroxidase antibodies
Binding of dopamine receptors by antithyroid peroxidase antibodies
Inhibition of dopamine release by TSH
Stimulation of lactotrophs by thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stimulation of lactotrophs by thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH)

Primary hypothyroidism (e.g., autoimmune thyroiditis), low T4 leads to increased hypothalamic thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) to stimulate the pituitary.

TRH has two actions on the anterior pituitary:

• ↑ TSH secretion
• ↑ Prolactin secretion by stimulating lactotrophs

This results in mild hyperprolactinemia, which can cause:

• Amenorrhea
• Galactorrhea

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 29-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to hair loss. The patient has fatigue and decreased libido, and her menstrual cycles have not returned since her delivery 8 months ago. The thyroid is nontender. Laboratory results show decreased serum TSH and free thyroxine (T4) levels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Secondary hypothyroidism

Secondary hypothyroidism occurs due to pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction, resulting in decreased TSH secretion and low thyroid hormone levels (T4). Failure of menstrual cycles to return after delivery, along with fatigue and low libido, suggests postpartum pituitary dysfunction (e.g., Sheehan syndrome) causing secondary hypothyroidism. Key diagnostic pattern:

• Low TSH
• Low T4

This contrasts with primary hypothyroidism, where TSH is elevated.

Why not other options:

• A. Chronic autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto)

• Primary hypothyroidism → ↑ TSH, ↓ T4
• Patient has ↓ TSH and ↓ T4, so not primary.

• B. Graves disease:

• Causes hyperthyroidism → ↓ TSH, ↑ T4
• Patient has low T4, not high.

• C. Postpartum thyroiditis:

• Usually, transient hyperthyroid phase → hypothyroid phase
• Hypothyroid phase shows ↑ TSH, ↓ T4.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 29-year-old woman with a pituitary microadenoma has been receiving cabergoline 1 mg per week. She presents at 12 weeks of gestation. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Advise termination of pregnancy as cabergoline was continued during the first trimester
Follow up with serum prolactin levels monthly
Perform MRI of the sella to look for tumor enlargement
Reassure the patient and evaluate further only if symptoms such as headache or visual disturbance develop
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Reassure the patient and evaluate further only if symptoms such as headache or visual disturbance develop

Prolactin-secreting pituitary microadenomas (microprolactinomas) are commonly treated with dopamine agonists such as cabergoline or bromocriptine, which suppress prolactin secretion and shrink the tumor.

Management during pregnancy:

• Once pregnancy is confirmed, dopamine agonists are usually discontinued in patients with microadenomas.
• The risk of tumor enlargement during pregnancy is very low (\~2–3%) for microadenomas.
• Routine MRI or prolactin monitoring is not recommended, because prolactin levels naturally rise during pregnancy and do not correlate with tumor size.

Recommended approach

• Reassure the patient
• Clinical monitoring only
• Investigate further only if symptoms of tumor expansion appear, such as:

• Headache
• Visual field defects

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 29-year-old woman with a prolactin-secreting pituitary microadenoma is started on bromocriptine. Which of the following conditions, if also present in this patient, would make bromocriptine an inappropriate choice of therapy?
options: An acute psychotic episode with delusions and hallucinations
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome following antipsychotic use
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. An acute psychotic episode with delusions and hallucinations

Bromocriptine is a dopamine D₂ receptor agonist used to treat hyperprolactinemia and prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas (prolactinomas). By stimulating dopamine receptors on lactotrophs, it suppresses prolactin secretion and reduces tumor size.

• Dopamine agonists increase central dopaminergic activity.
• In patients with acute psychosis, enhanced dopamine signaling can worsen delusions, hallucinations, and other psychotic symptoms.
• Therefore, bromocriptine is relatively contraindicated in active psychotic disorders.

Why not the others?

• A. Persistent hyperprolactinemia → This is a primary indication for bromocriptine.
• B. Comorbid Type 2 diabetes mellitus → Bromocriptine has approved uses in type 2 diabetes and is not contraindicated.
• D. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) following antipsychotic use → Dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine may actually be used in the treatment of NMS by restoring dopaminergic activity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of irregular menses, milky discharge from her nipples, fatigue, and weight gain. Menses occur at irregular 25-40-day intervals and last 1-2 days with minimal flow. 5 months ago, she was started on clozapine for treatment of schizophrenia. She has hypothyroidism but has not been taking levothyroxine over the past 6 months. Visual field examination show no abnormalities. Her serum thyroid-stimulating hormone is 17.0 U/mL and serum prolactin is 85 ng/mL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the nipple discharge in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypothyroidism

Untreated primary hypothyroidism can cause hyperprolactinemia and galactorrhea due to increased thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) from the hypothalamus.

• In primary hypothyroidism, decreased thyroid hormone leads to increased TRH secretion.
• TRH stimulates both TSH and prolactin release from the anterior pituitary.
• Elevated prolactin suppresses GnRH, resulting in menstrual irregularities, oligomenorrhea, and galactorrhea.

Why other options are incorrect:

B. Prolactinoma: Usually causes very high prolactin (>200 ng/mL) and often visual field defects. This patient has moderate elevation (85 ng/mL) and normal visual fields.

C. Ectopic prolactin production: Extremely rare cause of hyperprolactinemia.

D. Adverse effect of medication: Antipsychotics can increase prolactin, but clozapine has minimal prolactin-elevating effect.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old man with adult-onset growth hormone deficiency complains of fatigue, increased fat mass, and reduced exercise capacity. He has poor adherence to daily subcutaneous injections prescribed previously. His endocrinologist switches him to a preparation that allows once-weekly administration by prolonging systemic exposure through reversible binding to circulating proteins. Which of the following drugs is most likely prescribed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Somapacitan

Somapacitan is a long-acting growth hormone (GH) analog used for adult growth hormone deficiency. It is designed for once-weekly subcutaneous administration because it reversibly binds to circulating albumin, which prolongs its systemic half-life and maintains sustained GH activity.

Why not the others (brief):

• Somatrem: Recombinant GH requiring daily injections.
• Mecasermin: Recombinant IGF-1, used mainly in severe primary IGF-1 deficiency, not GH replacement.
• Pegvisomant: Growth hormone receptor antagonist used to treat acromegaly, not GH deficiency.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman reports irregular menstruation and 4.5 kg weight gain over 6 months. BP is 152/86 mmHg, BMI is 31 kg/m². Physical exam shows abdominal and supraclavicular fat accumulation, hyperpigmentation in skin creases, and wide abdominal striae. Which of the following sets of laboratory findings are most likely to be seen in this patient?
options: Normal 24-hour urinary cortisol, Normal ACTH, ↑ DHEAS
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ↑ 24-hour urinary cortisol, ↑ ACTH, ↑ DHEAS

This patient has classic features of ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, including central obesity, hypertension, wide violaceous striae, menstrual irregularities, and skin hyperpigmentation. Hyperpigmentation strongly suggests elevated ACTH levels, which stimulate melanocortin receptors through increased production of POMC-derived peptides.

Why A?

• ↑ 24-hour urinary cortisol → Confirms cortisol excess.
• ↑ ACTH → Indicates ACTH-dependent disease (e.g., Cushing disease or ectopic ACTH production).
• ↑ DHEAS → ACTH stimulates the adrenal zona reticularis, increasing adrenal androgen production.

| Cause | Cortisol | ACTH | DHEAS

| ----- | -------- | ---- | -----

| Pituitary ACTH adenoma (Cushing disease) | ↑ | ↑ | ↑

| Ectopic ACTH syndrome | ↑↑ | ↑↑ | ↑

| Adrenal adenoma/carcinoma | ↑ | ↓ | Normal/↓

| Exogenous glucocorticoids | ↓ endogenous cortisol | ↓ | ↓

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to moderate pain in her lower back, hips, and knees for the past several weeks. She has no associated morning stiffness. The patient has end-stage renal disease due to diabetic nephropathy and has been on Hemodialysis for the past 2 years. Her other medical problems include type 1 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 20 years ago and sarcoidosis diagnosed 8 years ago. Physical examination shows no obvious bone or joint deformity, and she has full range of motion in all joints. Laboratory results are as follows: Sodium-136 mEq/L Potassium-3.9 mEq/L Bicarbonate-23 mEq/L Creatinine-3.1 mg/dL Calcium-7.9 mg/dL (N-8.5 to 10.5 mg/dl) Phosphorus-6.1 mg/dL (N-2.8 to 4.5 mg/dL) Albumin-4.1 g/dL (N-3.4 to 5.4 g/dL) Which of the following is the most likely histopathological abnormality underlying this patient's current symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. PTH hyperplasia

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) leads to secondary hyperparathyroidism due to disturbances in calcium-phosphate metabolism.

Mechanism:

• ↓ Renal phosphate excretion → Hyperphosphatemia
• ↓ Renal 1α-hydroxylase activity → ↓ calcitriol (active vitamin D)
• ↓ Intestinal calcium absorption → Hypocalcemia

These changes chronically stimulate the parathyroid glands, causing diffuse parathyroid hyperplasia and increased parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 4-month-old baby presented with a history of constipation, lethargy, and poor activities. Clinical examination reveals jaundice, hypotonia and there was no palpable goiter. Laboratory investigations revealed a low T4 and elevated TSH levels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thyroid dysgenesis

Congenital Hypothyroidism — Cause Localization Framework

| Feature | Thyroid Dysgenesis | Dyshormonogenesis | Central Hypothyroidism | Iodine Deficiency

| ------- | ------------------ | ----------------- | ---------------------- | -----------------

| T4 | ↓ | ↓ | ↓ | ↓

| TSH | ↑↑ | ↑↑ | ↓ / Normal | ↑↑

| Goiter | Absent | Present | Absent | Present

| Inheritance | Sporadic (mostly) | AR | Varies | Environmental

| Frequency | Most common (85%) | \~10–15% | Rare | Region-dependent

Key Exam Pearls

Thyroid Dysgenesis subtypes (all goiter-absent):

• Athyreosis (complete agenesis) — most severe
• Ectopic thyroid — most common subtype of dysgenesis; sublingual thyroid is the classic location
• Hypoplasia — partial tissue, partial function

Dyshormonogenesis — why the goiter?

• TSH chronically elevated → stimulates residual thyroid tissue → compensatory hypertrophy → goiter. Enzyme defects involved include TPO, thyroglobulin, pendrin (Pendred syndrome = deafness + goiter).

Central hypothyroidism trap:

• Low T4 + inappropriately low/normal TSH — the pituitary is the problem, not the thyroid. This is the classic distractor.

Newborn Screening Logic:

• Primary hypothyroidism detected by high TSH on heel-prick screening
• Central hypothyroidism can be missed on TSH-only screens → some programs now include T4 measurement to catch this

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 40-year-old male presents with increased thirst and increased frequency and volume of urination. His random blood sugar was 205 mg/dl, what appropriate investigations should be done? i) HbA1c ii) Urine ACR iii) Echocardiography iv) Fundoscopy v) ECG vi) Serum protein electrophoresis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. i, ii, iv, v

In a patient with suspected or newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus, evaluation should include confirmation of glycemic status and screening for early diabetic complications.

Appropriate initial investigations include:

• HbA1c → assesses long-term glycemic control (average glucose over \~3 months).
• Urine albumin–creatinine ratio (ACR) → screens for diabetic nephropathy (microalbuminuria).
• Fundoscopy → detects diabetic retinopathy.
• ECG → evaluates cardiovascular disease, which is common in diabetics.

Tests like echocardiography and serum protein electrophoresis are not routine initial investigations for newly diagnosed diabetes unless specific clinical indications are present.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 42-year-old man is found to have persistent mild hypercalcemia during a routine health check-up. He is asymptomatic and has no history of renal stones or fractures. Laboratory investigations reveal low urinary calcium excretion, and a positive family history of similar biochemical findings in multiple first-degree relatives. Genetic analysis confirms a mutation in the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) gene. Which of the following laboratory and genetic findings is most consistent with this diagnosis?
options: Low PTH level with CaSR inactivating mutation
Normal PTH level with CaSR activating mutation
High PTH level with CaSR activating mutation
High PTH level with CaSR inactivating mutation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. High PTH level with CaSR inactivating mutation

Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia (FHH) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by an inactivating mutation of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR).

The CaSR is expressed in:

• Parathyroid glands (regulates PTH secretion)
• Kidneys (regulates urinary calcium excretion)

Pathophysiology

Normally:

• High serum calcium activates the CaSR.
• This suppresses PTH secretion and increases urinary calcium excretion.

In FHH:

• The CaSR is inactivated, so the parathyroid gland perceives serum calcium as being "low."
• Consequently:

• PTH secretion is not adequately suppressed (normal or mildly elevated).
• Kidneys increase calcium reabsorption, resulting in hypocalciuria despite hypercalcemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit due to severe sepsis caused by a ruptured abdominal abscess. She has been receiving high-dose intravenous corticosteroids for hypotension management over the past three days. On examination, she is alert but appears critically ill. Laboratory results are as follows: • TSH: 1.2 µU/mL (normal range: 0.4–4.0 µU/mL) • Free T4: 1.1 ng/dL (normal range: 0.8–1.8 ng/dL) • Free T3: 0.6 pg/mL (normal range: 2.0–4.4 pg/mL) Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Euthyroid sick syndrome

Euthyroid sick syndrome (non-thyroidal illness syndrome) occurs in severe systemic illness such as sepsis, trauma, or critical illness. Thyroid gland function is normal, but peripheral thyroid hormone metabolism is altered. Typical laboratory pattern:

• ↓ Free T3 (most common finding)
• Normal or ↓ T4
• Normal or slightly ↓ TSH

Mechanism:

• Severe illness and stress hormones (e.g., cytokines, glucocorticoids)
• ↓ peripheral conversion of T4 → T3 due to reduced 5′-deiodinase activity

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 50-year-old man comes to the OPD following transsphenoidal resection of a growth hormone secreting pituitary adenoma. Three months ago, the patient was diagnosed with acromegaly. MRI of the pituitary showed a 14 mm sellar mass pressing on the optic chiasm and extending into the right cavernous sinus. The surgeon was able to only partially resect the pituitary mass because of the extension into the right cavernous sinus. Medical therapy for acromegaly with octreotide is planned. Which of the following changes are likely to occur following octreotide treatment in this patient?
options: GH low, IGF-1 low, adenoma size low
GH low, IGF-1 low, adenoma size unchanged
GH low, IGF-1 unchanged, adenoma size low
GH unchanged, IGF-1 low, adenoma size unchanged
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GH low, IGF-1 low, adenoma size low

Octreotide, a somatostatin analogue, is used for medical treatment of acromegaly, especially when pituitary adenoma cannot be completely resected.

Mechanism and effects:

• Inhibits growth hormone (GH) secretion from pituitary somatotroph cells
• Leads to decreased hepatic production of IGF-1
• Has an antiproliferative effect on the pituitary adenoma, often causing tumor shrinkage

Result after treatment:

• ↓ GH
• ↓ IGF-1
• ↓ Adenoma size

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 52-year-old female with diabetes mellitus has experienced a decrease in her HbA1c levels from 7.6 to 6.7 after starting a new oral medication. Laboratory tests show that she has high levels of GIP and GLP-1 and low levels of glucagon. Which of the following oral drugs was most likely administered to this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alogliptin

DPP-4 inhibitors improve glycemic control by increasing endogenous incretin hormones (GLP-1 and GIP). These hormones enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion and suppress glucagon release, leading to a reduction in blood glucose and HbA1c.

Alogliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor that prevents the degradation of GLP-1 and GIP, resulting in elevated levels of these incretins and decreased glucagon secretion. This mechanism explains the laboratory findings of high GLP-1/GIP levels with low glucagon.

Why not other options:

A. Voglibose: α-glucosidase inhibitor; delays carbohydrate absorption. Does not increase GLP-1 or GIP.

C. Pramlintide: Amylin analogue; suppresses glucagon but does not raise GLP-1/GIP and is injectable, not oral.

D. Liraglutide: GLP-1 receptor agonist; mimics GLP-1 but does not increase endogenous GLP-1 or GIP levels and is injectable.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 52-year-old man with long-standing diabetes presents with fatigue and decreased urine output. Blood investigations are advised including serum urea estimation to assess renal function. Which of the following methods is most commonly used in clinical laboratories for estimation of serum urea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urease–GLDH method

• Serum urea estimation in clinical laboratories is most commonly performed using the Urease–GLDH (glutamate dehydrogenase) enzymatic method, which is highly specific, sensitive, and widely automated.
• Principle of Urease–GLDH method:

• Urease hydrolyzes urea → ammonia (NH₃) + CO₂
• Ammonia reacts with α-ketoglutarate in the presence of GLDH, converting NADH → NAD⁺
• The decrease in NADH absorbance (at 340 nm) is proportional to serum urea concentration

Why not other options:

A. Jaffe reaction:

• Used for serum creatinine, not urea
• Based on reaction with picric acid

C. Biuret method: Used for total protein estimation

D. Diazotization method: Used for bilirubin estimation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 53-year-old woman presents for a routine health check-up. She has no active complaints. Her medical history is unremarkable except for mild osteoarthritis. Her family history is significant for diabetes mellitus in her father and breast cancer in her mother. On examination, her blood pressure is elevated. Laboratory evaluation reveals fasting plasma glucose levels ≥140 mg/dL on multiple occasions. Which of the following is the most likely cause of death in this patient if her condition remains uncontrolled?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute myocardial infarction

Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus are at markedly increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, which is the leading cause of mortality.

Pathophysiology:

• Chronic hyperglycemia → endothelial dysfunction
• ↑ advanced glycation end-products (AGEs)
• ↑ oxidative stress and inflammation
• Accelerated atherosclerosis of coronary arteries

This results in a significantly increased risk of:

• Myocardial infarction (most common cause of death)
• Stroke
• Peripheral arterial disease

Why not other options?

A. Breast cancer → unrelated to diabetes mortality risk

B. HHS → acute complication, less common cause of death overall

D. Renal failure → major morbidity but less common cause of death than CVD

Stroke → common but second to MI

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 56-year-old obese woman with type 2 diabetes has osteoporosis and prefers an oral agent that promotes weight loss. Which is the most appropriate choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Semaglutide

Oral semaglutide is the only oral GLP-1 receptor agonist. It promotes weight loss, improves glycemic control, and avoids injections. Pioglitazone increases fracture risk, canagliflozin has been associated with fractures in some studies, and liraglutide requires subcutaneous administration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the OPD for evaluation of short stature. Her parents have noticed that she bears little resemblance to her 2 older siblings. Other findings include low-set ears, a high arched palate, a webbed neck, and cubitus valgus. Chromosomal analysis reveals a 45, XO karyotype. The patient is started on a medication to improve growth and normalize her height. Which of the following intracellular pathways is stimulated by the medication used in this patient?
options: Binding of activated receptors to DNA to modify transcription.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. JAK-STAT pathway

Turner syndrome (45,XO) commonly presents with short stature, webbed neck, low-set ears, high-arched palate, and cubitus valgus. Treatment for short stature is recombinant growth hormone (GH).

Growth hormone acts via the JAK–STAT signaling pathway:

• GH binds to cytokine receptor–type GH receptors
• Activates Janus kinase (JAK)
• JAK phosphorylates STAT proteins
• STATs enter the nucleus and regulate gene transcription, promoting growth (mainly via IGF-1).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive increase in the size of hands and feet, coarsening of facial features, deepening of voice, and tingling sensations in both hands suggestive of carpal tunnel syndrome. On evaluation, his serum IGF-1 level is elevated. Which of the following findings is not expected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypoglycemic attacks

Acromegaly results from excess growth hormone (GH), usually due to a pituitary somatotroph adenoma, leading to elevated IGF-1 levels. GH has anti-insulin effects, causing insulin resistance and hyperglycemia, so hypoglycemic attacks are not expected.

Common associated findings in acromegaly:

• Galactorrhea → due to co-secretion of prolactin or pituitary stalk compression
• Bitemporal hemianopia → compression of the optic chiasm by pituitary macroadenoma
• Colonic polyps and increased colorectal cancer risk
• Carpal tunnel syndrome from soft-tissue overgrowth

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman is diagnosed with type Il diabetes mellitus. She has a history of chronic kidney disease. Which of the following statement is correct about the management of this patient?
options: Metformin is contraindicated in all stages of CKD
Pioglitazone is avoided as it is exclusively metabolized by kidneys
Glipizide can be used in renal disease
Linagliptin can be used only after dose reduction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glipizide can be used in renal disease

In patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus with chronic kidney disease (CKD), the choice of antidiabetic drugs depends on their renal clearance and risk of hypoglycemia.

• Glipizide is a short-acting sulfonylurea that is primarily metabolized in the liver and produces inactive metabolites, making it safer in patients with renal impairment compared with other sulfonylureas (e.g., glyburide). Therefore, it can be used in CKD.

Key related facts:

• Metformin is not contraindicated in all CKD stages; it is avoided mainly when eGFR <30 mL/min due to risk of lactic acidosis.
• Pioglitazone is metabolized in the liver, not kidneys, so renal metabolism is not the reason for avoiding it.
• Linagliptin is excreted via the bile and does not require dose adjustment in CKD.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 67-year-old man presents with fatigue and weight gain over 6 months. He has a history of hypertension. Examination reveals a firm, irregularly enlarged thyroid gland. Laboratory findings: • ↑ TSH • ↓ Free T4 • ↑ LDL cholesterol and total cholesterol • Mild hypertriglyceridemia Which of the following best explains the mechanism of hypercholesterolemia in this patient?
options: Activation of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor alpha (PPAR-α)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decreased hepatic LDL receptor expression

In hypothyroidism, reduced thyroid hormone levels lead to decreased expression of hepatic LDL receptors, which are responsible for clearing LDL cholesterol from circulation.

• ↓ LDL uptake by the liver
• ↑ circulating LDL cholesterol → hypercholesterolemia

Thyroid hormones normally:

• Upregulate LDL receptor gene expression
• Enhance cholesterol clearance

Thus, deficiency leads to impaired LDL clearance, not overproduction.

Why not other options?

• A. PPAR-α activation → seen with fibrates → ↓ triglycerides
• C. ↑ Lipoprotein lipase → enhances triglyceride clearance
• D. ↑ HMG-CoA reductase → increases synthesis, but main issue here

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 68-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to a burning sensation in her chest and throat for the past 2 weeks. Associated symptoms include trouble swallowing. Medical history is significant for osteoporosis, and she has no known drug allergies. It is determined that the patient's current symptoms are caused by one of her medications, which is discontinued. Her symptoms subsequently resolve. The medication responsible for this patient's presentation is also associated with which of the following side effects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Osteonecrosis of the jaw

This patient likely developed pill-induced esophagitis due to an oral bisphosphonate (commonly used for osteoporosis).

Mechanism:

Bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate) inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, increasing bone mineral density. However, they can irritate the esophageal mucosa, causing burning chest pain, dysphagia, and esophagitis if taken improperly.

Important adverse effects of bisphosphonates:

• Esophagitis and esophageal ulceration
• Osteonecrosis of the jaw (especially after dental procedures)
• Atypical femoral fractures with long-term use

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy is brought for evaluation of behavioral changes over the past year, including hyperactivity, impulsivity, and poor academic performance. On examination, he has a diffusely enlarged, non-tender thyroid gland. Laboratory findings show: • TSH: elevated • T4: elevated • T3: elevated Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Resistance to thyroid hormone

This patient has thyroid hormone resistance (Refetoff syndrome), characterized by:

• Elevated T3 and T4 with inappropriately normal or elevated TSH
• Due to mutation in thyroid hormone receptor (TRβ) → reduced tissue responsiveness

Pathophysiology:

• Peripheral tissues are resistant → reduced negative feedback
• Pituitary continues to secrete TSH → thyroid enlargement (goiter)
• Mixed clinical picture:

• Some tissues → hyperthyroid features (e.g., hyperactivity)
• Others → relatively hypothyroid

Why not other options?

• A. Hashimoto thyroiditis → ↑ TSH, ↓ T4
• B. TBG excess → ↑ total T4 but normal TSH
• C. Dyshormonogenesis → hypothyroidism pattern

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 70-year-old man with a long-standing medical history is on multiple medications. He has developed excessive bilateral breast tissue enlargement. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Goserelin

Gynecomastia (benign enlargement of male breast tissue) occurs due to an imbalance between estrogen and androgen activity, often caused by medications that reduce androgen levels or increase estrogenic effects.

Goserelin is a GnRH agonist used in conditions such as prostate cancer. With continuous administration, it suppresses LH and FSH secretion, leading to decreased testosterone production. The resulting relative increase in estrogen effect can cause gynecomastia and breast tenderness.

Why not other options:

• Tamoxifen – a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that is actually used to treat gynecomastia.
• Terbinafine – antifungal; gynecomastia is not a typical adverse effect.
• Procainamide-Anti-arrythmic-Not associated with gynecomastia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A full-term newborn is noted on routine screening to have elevated TSH and low thyroxine (T4) levels. The infant appears clinically well. Imaging reveals a small ectopic thyroid gland located near the base of the tongue. Early initiation of thyroid hormone replacement therapy is most important to prevent which of the following complications?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Impaired neurocognitive development

This newborn has congenital hypothyroidism, most commonly due to thyroid dysgenesis (ectopic or absent thyroid gland).

Thyroid hormone is essential for:

• Neuronal migration
• Myelination
• Synapse formation

Deficiency during early life leads to:

• Irreversible intellectual disability (cretinism)
• Developmental delay
• Growth retardation

Early treatment with levothyroxine (within the first 2 weeks of life) prevents these complications and allows normal neurodevelopment.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient suffering from hyperthyroidism is administered a drug that acts by inhibiting the release of thyroid hormone. Identify the drug.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Potassium iodide

Potassium iodide inhibits the release of preformed thyroid hormones (T₃ and T₄) from the thyroid gland through the Wolff–Chaikoff effect. This rapid antithyroid action makes it useful in the short-term management of hyperthyroidism and thyroid storm.

• High doses of iodide:

• Inhibit thyroid hormone release
• Decrease thyroid gland vascularity and size
• Reduce iodide organification (transiently)

• Acts within hours to days, much faster than thionamides.

Why not the others?

• A. Propylthiouracil (PTU) → Inhibits thyroid peroxidase and peripheral T₄ → T₃ conversion; does not primarily inhibit hormone release.
• B. Radioactive iodine → Destroys thyroid tissue by β-radiation.
• C. Thiocyanate → Inhibits iodide uptake into the thyroid gland.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with type 2 diabetes on metformin and an add-on drug presents with mild elevation of liver transaminases on routine monitoring. The drug is stopped and liver enzymes normalize. Which add-on drug was most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vildagliptin

Vildagliptin, a DPP-4 inhibitor used as add-on therapy with metformin in type 2 diabetes, is associated with reversible elevation of liver transaminases (hepatotoxicity). Therefore, periodic monitoring of liver function tests (LFTs) is recommended, and the drug should be discontinued if significant enzyme elevation occurs, after which levels usually normalize.

Why not others (brief):

• Sitagliptin: DPP-4 inhibitor but minimal hepatic toxicity; no routine LFT monitoring needed.
• Empagliflozin: SGLT2 inhibitor; main effects glycosuria, weight loss, genital infections, not hepatotoxicity.
• Repaglinide: Meglitinide causing hypoglycemia and weight gain, not typical transaminase elevation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A woman presents with signs of hyperthyroidism. Which feature is not typically associated with her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reduced protein breakdown

Hyperthyroidism increases the basal metabolic rate and produces a hypercatabolic state.

Key physiologic effects include:

• Increased protein breakdown (proteolysis) → muscle wasting and weakness
• Increased heart rate and stroke volume → high cardiac output
• Decreased peripheral vascular resistance due to vasodilation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: An obese man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and malaise. Arterial blood gas analysis shows a pH of 7.20. Urinalysis is positive for glucose and ketone bodies, but his serum glucose is 130 mg/dL. Which of the following antidiabetic drugs is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Canagliflozin

This patient has euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (euglycemic DKA):

• Metabolic acidosis
• Ketonuria/ketonemia
• Typical DKA symptoms
• Blood glucose that is normal or only mildly elevated, usually <250 mg/dL

Canagliflozin is an SGLT2 inhibitor. It reduces glucose reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule, causing glycosuria and lowering the measured blood glucose. Despite this, insulin deficiency and increased glucagon activity may promote lipolysis and ketogenesis, leading to ketoacidosis.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Metformin – Can cause lactic acidosis, especially in severe renal failure or hypoxia, but does not typically cause ketonuria with euglycemia.
• B. Vildagliptin – A DPP-4 inhibitor; it is not characteristically associated with diabetic ketoacidosis.
• C. Pioglitazone – A thiazolidinedione associated with weight gain, edema, and worsening heart failure, not euglycemic DKA.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Drugs used only for control of post-prandial hyperglycemia includes: 1. Voglibose 2. Repaglinide 3. Ertugliflozin 4. Lispro 5. Miglitol 6. Acarbose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. All except 3

Drugs used primarily to control postprandial (post-meal) hyperglycemia are those that either delay carbohydrate absorption or provide a rapid, short-lived increase in insulin action/secretion around meals. These include α-glucosidase inhibitors (acarbose, miglitol, voglibose), meglitinides (repaglinide), and rapid-acting insulin analogs (lispro).

Why not Ertugliflozin?

• Ertugliflozin is an SGLT2 inhibitor that lowers glucose by increasing urinary glucose excretion.
• It reduces both fasting and postprandial glucose levels and is not used exclusively for postprandial control.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Regarding thyroid storm, which statement is false?
options: Symptoms can include diarrhea, vomiting, jaundice, and confusion
High-dose propranolol can reduce T4 to T3 conversion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mortality is 10% despite treatment

Thyroid storm is a life-threatening exacerbation of thyrotoxicosis characterized by severe hypermetabolic state and multisystem involvement.

• High fever, tachycardia, agitation, confusion
• Gastrointestinal symptoms: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice
• Can be precipitated by stressors such as infection, trauma, or surgery (including non-thyroid surgery).
• Management principles:

• β-blockers (high-dose propranolol) to control adrenergic symptoms and reduce peripheral conversion of T4 → T3
• Antithyroid drugs (PTU or methimazole)
• Iodine and glucocorticoids

Mortality remains high (\~20–30% even with treatment), therefore the statement “mortality is 10% despite treatment” is false.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: SIADH is not observed in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Primary pulmonary emphysema

Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone secretion (SIADH) is characterized by excess ADH release, leading to water retention, dilutional hyponatremia, decreased serum osmolality, and concentrated urine.

Common causes of SIADH include:

• Malignancies: especially small cell (oat cell) carcinoma of lung producing ectopic ADH
• Neurological disorders: e.g., multiple sclerosis, head injury, meningitis
• Certain metabolic disorders: e.g., acute intermittent porphyria
• Drugs and pulmonary diseases (pneumonia, tuberculosis)

Primary pulmonary emphysema is not typically associated with SIADH, making it the incorrect option.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Two days after vaginal delivery of a healthy newborn at term, a 32-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, is unable to breastfeed. Her labor was complicated by antepartum hemorrhage and she received two units of packed red blood cells. Her pulse is 99/min and blood pressure is 90/55 mm Hg. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following sets of serum findings?
options: ACTH low, Aldosterone low, Cortisol low
ACTH low, Aldosterone high, Cortisol low
ACTH high, Aldosterone normal, Cortisol low
ACTH low, Aldosterone normal, Cortisol low
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ACTH low, Aldosterone high, Cortisol low

Severe postpartum hemorrhage can cause ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary, leading to Sheehan syndrome. This results in hypopituitarism, commonly presenting with failure to lactate due to prolactin deficiency, hypotension, and fatigue after delivery.

Hormonal pattern in Sheehan syndrome:

• ↓ ACTH → leads to ↓ cortisol (secondary adrenal insufficiency)
• Aldosterone remains increased because it is mainly regulated by the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, not by ACTH.

Typical findings:

• ↓ ACTH
• ↓ Cortisol
• ↑ Aldosterone

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following hormone–receptor interactions acts via the IP₃–DAG second messenger system?
options: Angiotensin II on vascular smooth muscle and vasopressin acting via V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
Angiotensin II on vascular smooth muscle and vasopressin acting via V2 receptors on epithelial cells
Angiotensin II acting on epithelial cells and vasopressin acting via V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
Angiotensin II acting on epithelial cells and vasopressin acting via V2 receptors on epithelial cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Angiotensin II on vascular smooth muscle and vasopressin acting via V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle

Hormones that act through Gq protein–coupled receptors activate phospholipase C (PLC), which generates the second messengers IP₃ (inositol triphosphate) and DAG (diacylglycerol).

• IP₃ → releases Ca²⁺ from the endoplasmic reticulum
• DAG → activates protein kinase C

Key hormones using the IP₃–DAG pathway:

• Angiotensin II (AT₁ receptors) on vascular smooth muscle → vasoconstriction
• Vasopressin (ADH) acting on V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle → vasoconstriction

Important contrast:

• V2 receptors of vasopressin act via Gs → cAMP, causing water reabsorption in renal collecting ducts.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following laboratory findings is characteristic of pseudohypoparathyroidism?
options: Low urinary cyclic AMP (cAMP) level after parathyroid hormone (PTH) administration
Normal urinary cyclic AMP (cAMP) level after PTH administration
Elevated urinary cyclic AMP (cAMP) level after PTH administration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Low urinary cyclic AMP (cAMP) level after parathyroid hormone (PTH) administration

Pseudohypoparathyroidism is a disorder characterized by end-organ resistance to parathyroid hormone (PTH) despite normal or elevated PTH levels.

• Caused by a defect in the Gsα protein signaling pathway.
• The kidney does not respond to PTH, so the cAMP second messenger is not generated properly.

Typical laboratory findings

• Low serum calcium
• High serum phosphate
• Elevated PTH levels
• Low urinary cyclic AMP (cAMP) after administration of exogenous PTH

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following pairs of drugs and its indications is matched incorrectly?
options: Octreotide – Treatment of diarrhea associated with vasoactive intestinal peptide tumors.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bromocriptine – Treatment of precocious puberty

Bromocriptine is a dopamine (D2) agonist that inhibits prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary. It is primarily used in the treatment of hyperprolactinemia, prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas (prolactinomas), acromegaly, and Parkinson disease. It is not used for precocious puberty, making this pair incorrect.

Correct drug–indication pairs:

• Octreotide → used for secretory diarrhea in VIPoma and also in acromegaly.
• Desmopressin → used for central diabetes insipidus and nocturnal enuresis.
• Leuprolide → a GnRH agonist used in infertility (controlled ovarian stimulation), prostate cancer, endometriosis, and precocious puberty.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presented with abdominal pain and vomiting. Lab values are given below. What is the next best step of management? Lab Values: • RBS = 450 mg/dL • pH = 7.0 • HCO₃ = 4 • Na = 145 • K = 4.8 mEq/L
options: 10 ml/kg NS over 20 min (10% deficit correction) followed by insulin infusion with 20 mmol/L KCl with bicarbonate
20 ml/kg 1/2 NS over 20 min (7% deficit correction) followed by insulin infusion and KCl 40 meq/L
20 ml/kg NS over 20 min with (10% deficit correction) followed by insulin infusion and KCl 40 meq/L
20 ml/kg RL over 20 min with (10% deficit correction) followed by insulin infusion and KCl 40 meq/L
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 20 ml/kg NS over 20 min with (10% deficit correction) followed by insulin infusion and KCl 40 meq/L

Correct answer is C according to ISPAD guidelines, as the labs show severe diabetic ketoacidosis (glucose 450, pH 7.0, HCO₃ 4). First step is rapid isotonic fluid resuscitation with 20 ml/kg normal saline to restore perfusion.

After initial fluids, insulin infusion is started, 0.1 units/kg/hour with potassium replacement because total body potassium is depleted despite normal serum K.

Effects:

• Stops ketogenesis
• Reduces glucose
• Stops lipolysis

Bicarbonate is not routinely given unless pH < 6.9. Half-normal saline and RL are not preferred for initial resuscitation in pediatric DKA.

RL not preferred initially.

Reasons:

• Lactate → metabolized to bicarbonate
• May interfere with ketone monitoring
• NS is standard guideline recommendation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient with heart failure and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c of 7.8%) present with progressive dyspnea. Which is the preferred antidiabetic drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dapagliflozin

Correct answer is A because SGLT2 inhibitors like dapagliflozin improve heart failure outcomes by reducing preload, afterload, and hospitalization risk, independent of glucose control.

They are preferred in type 2 diabetes with coexisting heart failure.

Renal Action

• Block SGLT2 in proximal tubule
• ↑ glucose excretion
• ↑ sodium excretion

| Effect | Benefit in HF

| ------ | -------------

| Osmotic diuresis | ↓ preload

| Natriuresis | ↓ volume overload

| ↓ BP | ↓ afterload

| Improved cardiac metabolism | better efficiency

Sulfonylureas and DPP-4 inhibitors do not provide heart failure benefit. Metformin is useful but does not confer the same HF-specific outcome advantage.

Type 2 DM + Heart Failure

Preferred drugs:

| Class | Examples

| ----- | --------

| SGLT2 inhibitors | Dapagliflozin, Empagliflozin

Avoid / caution:

| Drug | Reason

| ---- | ------

| Sulfonylureas | hypoglycemia

| TZDs (pioglitazone) | worsen edema

| Some DPP-4 inhibitors | HF risk

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old male presented with polyuria, polydipsia and polyphagia for the last 3 months. His fasting plasma glucose is 106 mg/dL and random blood glucose is 220 mg/dL. Which one of the following statements is correct regarding his diagnosis?
options: He has definitive diagnosis of diabetes mellitus
He does not have diabetes mellitus
Diagnosis of diabetes mellitus is indeterminate as HbA1c value is not provided
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. He has definitive diagnosis of diabetes mellitus

Diabetes mellitus can be diagnosed by plasma glucose criteria or HbA1c. In a patient with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia), a random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL is sufficient to establish the diagnosis.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. He has impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) ✗: IGT is diagnosed by a 2-hour plasma glucose of 140–199 mg/dL during a 75-g OGTT, not by random glucose.
• C. He does not have diabetes mellitus ✗: Incorrect because the random plasma glucose criterion is fulfilled.
• D. Diagnosis is indeterminate as HbA1c is not provided ✗: HbA1c is not essential when diagnostic plasma glucose criteria are already met.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 52-year-old male has uncontrolled diabetes. Which one of the following tests will help in early detection of nephropathy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urine albumin

Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and end-stage renal disease (ESRD). The earliest clinically detectable marker of diabetic nephropathy is moderately increased albuminuria (microalbuminuria), which reflects early glomerular damage before a decline in glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

Urine albumin estimation, preferably the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) in a spot urine sample, is the screening test of choice for early detection.

• Urine albumin (UACR) detects microalbuminuria (30–300 mg/day), the earliest manifestation of diabetic nephropathy. ⭐
• Early detection allows timely intervention with ACE inhibitors/ARBs, strict glycemic control, and blood pressure control to slow disease progression.

Why not the other options?

• A. Blood urea level: Rises only in advanced renal dysfunction and is not useful for early detection.
• B. Serum creatinine level: Often remains normal until approximately 50% of renal function is lost; therefore, it is an insensitive marker of early nephropathy.
• C. Ultrasonography: Useful for assessing kidney size and structural abnormalities but cannot detect early diabetic nephropathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a history of diabetes mellitus presents with heart failure characterized by a reduced ejection fraction and low urine output. Which of the following anti-diabetic medications has been recently approved for the treatment of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and may also improve diuresis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Empagliflozin

Correct answer is A because empagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor) is approved for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and improves outcomes independent of diabetes control.

Empagliflozin blocks SGLT2 in proximal tubule

⬇

↓ Glucose reabsorption

⬇

↑ Glucose excretion

⬇

Osmotic diuresis

⬇

↓ Plasma volume

⬇

↓ Preload & afterload

⬇

Improves heart failure

It promotes osmotic diuresis and natriuresis, helping relieve congestion and improve cardiac function.

DPP-4 inhibitors, thiazolidinediones, and insulin do not provide this heart failure benefit.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with diabetes mellitus develops painful vesicular lesions involving a unilateral dermatome in the axillary region (herpes zoster) after starting antidiabetic therapy. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sitagliptin

DPP-4 (dipeptidyl peptidase-4) is identical to CD26, a surface glycoprotein on T lymphocytes that functions as a T-cell costimulatory molecule. Inhibiting DPP-4 with sitagliptin therefore has an immunomodulatory effect, blunting T-cell activation — and because varicella-zoster reactivation is controlled by cell-mediated (T-cell) immunity, gliptins are associated with an increased risk of infections, including herpes zoster, nasopharyngitis and upper respiratory tract infections.

Other gliptin adverse effects: acute pancreatitis, bullous pemphigoid, severe arthralgia, and (with saxagliptin/alogliptin) hospitalization for heart failure.

Other options:

• A. Metformin → GI upset, B₁₂ deficiency, lactic acidosis. No immune effect.
• C. Pioglitazone → fluid retention, CHF, weight gain, fractures, bladder cancer.
• D. Glibenclamide → hypoglycemia, weight gain.

Management: Antiviral — acyclovir/valacyclovir/famciclovir, started within 72 h.

Pearl: DPP-4 = CD26 = T-cell marker → gliptins ↑ infection risk.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with diabetes mellitus on glibenclamide is started on gemfibrozil. Later, he develops recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia. What is the mechanism of drug interaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gemfibrozil causes inhibition of CYP2C9

Sulfonylureas (glibenclamide, glipizide, glimepiride) are metabolized principally by CYP2C9. Gemfibrozil — and more potently its glucuronide metabolite — is a strong inhibitor of CYP2C8 and also inhibits CYP2C9 and OATP1B1 transport. Inhibition reduces the hepatic clearance of glibenclamide, raising its plasma concentration and prolonging half-life. The result is exaggerated insulin secretion → recurrent hypoglycemia.

Other options:

• A. Enzyme induction: Would do the opposite — increased metabolism → loss of glycemic control, not hypoglycemia. Inducers = rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine.
• B. Increased renal excretion of glibenclamide: Would lower drug levels → hyperglycemia; also glibenclamide is largely hepatically cleared.
• D. Reduced GI absorption: Again lowers bioavailability → hyperglycemia.

Pearl:

• Inhibitor → ↑ effect of substrate.
• Inducer → ↓ effect.
• Gemfibrozil + repaglinide is the classic dangerous CYP2C8 pair (contraindicated).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All of the following are criteria for diagnosis of DKA except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. S. Potassium < 3.5 mEq/L

Correct answer is D because diagnostic criteria for DKA include hyperglycemia (>250 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.3), and increased anion gap metabolic acidosis.

Insulin deficiency

⬇

↑ lipolysis

⬇

↑ free fatty acids

⬇

Liver → ketone bodies

⬇

Metabolic acidosis (high anion gap)

Serum potassium is often normal or elevated initially due to extracellular shift despite total body potassium depletion.

Hypokalemia is a complication during treatment, not a diagnostic criterion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All of the following are ligand-gated ionotropic receptors except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. H2 receptor

Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels that act rapidly by directly opening ion channels.

Ionotropic receptors among the options:

• Nicotinic receptor → ligand-gated Na⁺/K⁺ channel
• 5HT3 receptor → ligand-gated cation channel
• GABA-A receptor → ligand-gated Cl⁻ channel

H2 receptor:

• Histamine H2 receptor is a Gs-coupled GPCR
• Activates adenylate cyclase → ↑ cAMP
• Not an ion channel

High-yield ionotropic receptors:

| Glutamate | Ligand-gated ion channels: NMDA, AMPA

| --------- | -------------------------------------

| GABA | Ligand-gated: GABA A, GABA C (B-GPCR)

| Acetylcholine | Nicotinic → Ligand-gated

| Norepinephrine, 5HT, Dopamine, Ach-M | GPCR (except 5HT3 which is ligand-gated)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following pancreatic hormones: 1. Insulin 2. Islet amyloid polypeptide (Amylin) 3. Glucagon 4. Somatostatin Which of the above is/are secreted by beta cells of the pancreatic islets?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 2

The β-cells of the pancreatic islets secrete insulin and islet amyloid polypeptide (amylin), which work together to regulate postprandial glucose levels. Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, while amylin slows gastric emptying, suppresses glucagon secretion, and promotes satiety.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Insulin✅: Secreted by β-cells; lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis.
• 2. Islet amyloid polypeptide (Amylin)✅: Co-secreted with insulin by β-cells; delays gastric emptying and suppresses postprandial glucagon release.

Incorrect options:

• 3. Glucagon❌: Secreted by α-cells, not β-cells.
• 4. Somatostatin❌: Secreted by δ-cells, where it inhibits the release of both insulin and glucagon.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP): 1. GLP-1 is an incretin hormone. 2. GIP is an incretin hormone. 3. GLP-1 is released from gastrointestinal ‘L-cells’. 4. GIP is released from gastrointestinal ‘M-cells’. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 3

1. GLP-1 is an incretin hormone: Correct

• GLP-1 enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion after meals.
• It also suppresses glucagon secretion and slows gastric emptying.

2. GIP is an incretin hormone: Correct

• GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide) stimulates glucose-dependent insulin secretion.

3. GLP-1 is released from L-cells: Correct

• L-cells are mainly present in the distal ileum and colon and secrete GLP-1.

4. GIP is released from M-cells: Incorrect

• GIP is secreted by K-cells, mainly in the duodenum and jejunum.
• M-cells are associated with specialized epithelial cells over lymphoid follicles, not GIP secretion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements: Statement I: Waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio are more powerful predictors of subsequent risk of type 2 diabetes than Body Mass Index (BMI). Statement II: Central obesity is an important determinant of insulin resistance, the underlying abnormality in most cases of type 2 diabetes. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II is the correct explanation of Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II is not the correct explanation of Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II is the correct explanation of Statement I

Central (abdominal/visceral) obesity is a stronger predictor of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) than overall obesity measured by Body Mass Index (BMI). Measures such as waist circumference (WC) and waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) better reflect visceral fat, which is closely associated with insulin resistance, the key pathogenic mechanism in T2DM.

• Statement I: Waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio are more powerful predictors of subsequent risk of type 2 diabetes than Body Mass Index (BMI): ✓

• Waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio are better predictors of future T2DM risk than BMI because they assess abdominal fat distribution rather than total body weight.

• Statement II: Central obesity is an important determinant of insulin resistance, the underlying abnormality in most cases of type 2 diabetes: ✓

• Central obesity promotes insulin resistance through increased release of free fatty acids, inflammatory cytokines, and adipokines from visceral adipose tissue.

• Statement II correctly explains Statement I because visceral fat is metabolically more active and strongly linked to insulin resistance.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: IGF-1 and IGF-2 (Insulin-like Growth Factors) are structurally most similar to which of the following molecules?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Proinsulin

Stepwise synthesis

| Stage | Structure

| ----- | ---------

| Preproinsulin | signal peptide + A + B + C

| Proinsulin | A chain + B chain + C peptide

| Insulin | A chain + B chain only

During processing:

• C-peptide is removed
• A and B chains remain linked by disulfide bonds

Correct answer is B because IGF-1 and IGF-2 retain structural similarity to proinsulin, including homologous A and B chains connected by a C-peptide–like domain.

Unlike insulin, IGFs are not cleaved to remove the connecting peptide, so their tertiary structure resembles intact proinsulin.

C-peptide alone and preproinsulin do not share the same functional folded structure as IGFs.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, what is the feature of stage 3 beta cell destruction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Autoimmune +ve dysglycemic symptomatic

| Feature | Stage 1 | Stage 2 | Stage 3 ⭐

| ------- | ------- | ------- | ---------

| Autoantibodies | Present | Present | Present

| Blood glucose | Normal | Abnormal (dysglycemia) | High (diabetes)

| Symptoms | Absent | Absent | Present

| β-cell destruction | Early | Moderate | Severe (>80–90%)

| Clinical diagnosis | No | No | Yes (T1DM)

Autoantibodies in Type 1 DM

| Antibody | Target

| -------- | ------

| Anti-GAD | Glutamic acid decarboxylase

| Anti-insulin | Insulin

| Anti-IA2 | Tyrosine phosphatase

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, which of the following cell types exhibit decreased glucose uptake as a result of insulin deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Skeletal Muscle

Correct answer is B because skeletal muscle requires insulin-dependent GLUT-4 transporters for glucose uptake, so insulin deficiency markedly reduces glucose entry into these cells.

RBCs and brain use insulin-independent transporters (GLUT-1/GLUT-3). Liver uptake via GLUT-2 is also insulin independent.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Insulin independent absorption occurs in all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adipose

Correct answer is A because adipose tissue requires insulin-dependent GLUT-4 transporters for glucose uptake.

RBCs and brain use insulin-independent transporters (GLUT-1/GLUT-3). Pancreatic cells primarily use GLUT-2, which is also insulin independent.

Thus adipose tissue is the exception.

A) Adipose → Insulin dependent

• Uses GLUT4
• Needs insulin for glucose uptake

Without insulin: Glucose cannot enter adipose cells efficiently

B) RBC → Insulin independent

• Uses GLUT1
• Always takes up glucose

Reason:  RBC depends entirely on glycolysis

C) Pancreas → Insulin independent

• Uses GLUT2
• Functions as a glucose sensor

D) Brain → Insulin independent

• Uses GLUT3
• High affinity transporter

Ensures: Constant glucose supply to brain

In Diabetes Mellitus

• Adipose & muscle cannot take up glucose
• Leads to:

• hyperglycemia
• lipolysis
• ketone formation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Insulin Resistance Syndrome (Syndrome X) is associated with which of the following? 1. Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus 2. Hyperinsulinaemia 3. Dyslipidaemia 4. Hypercalcaemia Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Insulin Resistance Syndrome (Syndrome X), also known as Metabolic Syndrome, is a cluster of metabolic abnormalities caused by insulin resistance. It significantly increases the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), cardiovascular disease, and stroke.

• Statement 1. Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Correct. Type 2 diabetes mellitus is strongly associated with insulin resistance and may develop when pancreatic β-cells fail to compensate.
• Statement 2. Hyperinsulinaemia: Correct. Hyperinsulinaemia is an early feature due to compensatory increased insulin secretion by pancreatic β-cells.
• Statement 3. Dyslipidaemia: Correct. Atherogenic dyslipidaemia is characteristic and includes:

• ↑ Triglycerides
• ↓ HDL cholesterol
• Small dense LDL particles

• Statement 4. Hypercalcaemia: Incorrect. Hypercalcaemia is not a feature of insulin resistance syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: When blood glucose levels are increased to 2–3 times their normal value and then maintained at that level for a consistent period, which of the following statements best describes the pattern of insulin secretion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1st it rises then remains elevated

| Phase | Timing | Source | Pattern

| ----- | ------ | ------ | -------

| Phase 1 | Minutes | Stored insulin | Rapid spike

| Phase 2 | Hours | Newly synthesized insulin | Sustained plateau

Sustained hyperglycemia produces biphasic insulin secretion: an initial rapid first phase from release of preformed insulin, followed by a prolonged second phase due to new insulin synthesis. When glucose remains high, secretion does not fall back to baseline but stays elevated. This classic two-phase response is a hallmark of normal β-cell physiology.

Loss of first phase is an early feature of type 2 diabetes.

| Condition | Phase 1 | Phase 2

| --------- | ------- | -------

| Normal | Present | Present

| Type 2 DM |  Lost early | Reduced

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which is not considered in the diagnosis of Metabolic syndrome:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hip Circumference

The criteria for diagnosing metabolic syndrome usually include a combination of factors such as central obesity (usually measured by waist circumference), elevated blood pressure, elevated fasting glucose, high triglycerides, and low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol.

Metabolic syndrome: NCEP-ATP III

1. Central obesity:

>102 cm (India-90cm) in men

>88 cm (India-80cm) in women

2. Elevated triglycerides: >150 mg/dL

3. HDL

< 40 mg/dL in men

< 50 mg/dL in women.

4. Blood pressure: >130/85 mm Hg

5. Fasting glucose: >100 mg/dL

Metabolic syndrome increases risk of:

• Type 2 diabetes
• Cardiovascular disease
• Stroke

Management Focus on:

Lifestyle

• weight reduction
• exercise
• diet control

Pharmacological

• statins (lipids)
• antihypertensives
• metformin (insulin resistance)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following antidiabetic drugs may cause weight gain? 1. Glimepiride 2. Pioglitazone 3. NPH insulin 4. Sitagliptin Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Weight gain is a known adverse effect of insulin, sulfonylureas, and thiazolidinediones. Glimepiride (sulfonylurea) increases insulin secretion, pioglitazone (TZD) causes fluid retention and increased adiposity, and NPH insulin promotes anabolic effects, all leading to weight gain. Sitagliptin (DPP-4 inhibitor) is weight neutral.

Why not the other option?

• Sitagliptin: Does not cause significant weight gain; it is generally weight neutral.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are long-acting insulin analogues? 1. Lispro 2. Glargine 3. Detemir 4. Degludec Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

1. Lispro: Incorrect

• Lispro is a rapid-acting insulin analogue.
• Onset: \~15 minutes; duration: \~3–5 hours.

2. Glargine: Correct

• Glargine is a long-acting basal insulin analogue.
• Provides relatively peakless insulin action for about 24 hours.

3. Detemir: Correct

• Detemir is a long-acting basal insulin analogue.
• Its prolonged action is due to albumin binding.

4. Degludec: Correct

• Degludec is an ultra-long-acting insulin analogue with a duration of action >42 hours.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs used in the management of diabetes is associated with unexplained diarrhea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metformin

Correct answer is D because metformin commonly causes gastrointestinal adverse effects including diarrhea due to increased intestinal glucose utilization and altered gut motility.

| Mechanism | Effect

| --------- | ------

| ↑ intestinal motility | faster transit

| ↓ glucose absorption | osmotic effect

| ↑ bile salt malabsorption | irritation

| Altered gut microbiota | fermentation changes

This side effect is dose related and often improves with gradual dose escalation or extended-release formulations.

Metformin is a biguanide that primarily acts on the liver. Key actions:

1️⃣ ↓ Hepatic gluconeogenesis

2️⃣ ↑ Peripheral insulin sensitivity

3️⃣ ↓ Intestinal glucose absorption

Pioglitazone causes edema/weight gain. Sitagliptin is generally well tolerated. Glimepiride mainly causes hypoglycemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs used in the management of type 2 diabetes is associated with an increased risk of urinary tract infections?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dapagliflozin

SGLT2 (Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2) sits in the proximal convoluted tubule and reabsorbs \~90% of filtered glucose back into blood.

Dapagliflozin blocks SGLT2

↓

Glucose is NOT reabsorbed → spills into urine (glucosuria)

↓

Glucose-rich urine = perfect growth medium for bacteria/fungi

↓

UTIs + genital mycotic infections (especially Candida)

Adverse Effect Profile of SGLT2 Inhibitors

| Side Effect | Mechanism

| ----------- | ---------

| UTI / genital thrush | Glucosuria → microbial growth

| Fournier's gangrene | Rare but life-threatening perineal necrotizing fasciitis

| DKA (euglycemic) | Even with normal glucose — reduced insulin secretion + ketogenesis

| Hypotension/dehydration | Osmotic diuresis from glucosuria

| Polyuria, polydipsia | Osmotic effect

| Fournier's gangrene | Rare genital/perineal necrosis

| AKI | Volume depletion

| Bone fractures | Canagliflozin specifically

| LDL rise | Mild

Why Not the Others?

| Drug | Class | Infection risk?

| ---- | ----- | ---------------

| Pioglitazone | Thiazolidinedione | Bladder cancer, fluid retention — not UTI

| Sitagliptin | DPP-4 inhibitor | Nasopharyngitis, pancreatitis — not UTI

| Metformin | Biguanide | GI side effects, lactic acidosis — not UTI

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following findings are seen in Diabetic Retinopathy on fundus examination? 1. Microaneurysm 2. Dot and blot hemorrhage 3. Retinal thickening 4. Neovascularization Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the most common microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus and a leading cause of preventable blindness. Fundus examination reveals characteristic retinal vascular changes, beginning with microaneurysms and progressing to hemorrhages, exudates, and neovascularization in advanced disease.

Why is B correct?

• 1. Microaneurysm✅: Earliest clinically detectable sign of diabetic retinopathy.
• 2. Dot and blot hemorrhage✅: Characteristic of non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR).
• 4. Neovascularization✅: Hallmark of proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR).

Incorrect statement:

• 3. Retinal thickening❌: Indicates diabetic macular edema (DME) rather than being a characteristic feature used to classify diabetic retinopathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following glucose lowering agent can be given as an injectable drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Semaglutide

Semaglutide is a Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity. It is administered as a subcutaneous injection once weekly, where it improves glycemic control by enhancing glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppressing glucagon release, delaying gastric emptying, and promoting satiety.

Why is D correct?

• D. Semaglutide: A GLP-1 receptor agonist available as a once-weekly subcutaneous injection (an oral formulation is also available, but the injectable form is the classic exam answer). It also provides cardiovascular and weight-loss benefits.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Pioglitazone: An oral thiazolidinedione (TZD) that improves insulin sensitivity.
• B. Metformin: An oral biguanide and the first-line drug for type 2 diabetes.
• C. Sitagliptin: An oral DPP-4 inhibitor that increases endogenous incretin levels.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following insulins has a cloudy preparation and requires resuspension prior to injection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lente

Cloudy insulin preparations contain insulin crystals or protamine, which settle on standing and therefore must be gently resuspended (rolled between the palms) before injection to ensure uniform dosing.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• A. Lente ✓

• An intermediate-acting insulin containing zinc-insulin crystals.
• It is a cloudy suspension and requires resuspension before administration.

• B. Glargine ✗

• A long-acting insulin analogue.
• It is a clear solution and should not be mixed or resuspended.

• C. Detemir ✗

• A long-acting insulin analogue.
• It is a clear solution and does not require mixing.

• D. Degludec ✗

• An ultra-long-acting insulin analogue.
• It is also a clear solution.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following may be seen during clinical examination in a patient of Diabetes mellitus? 1. Necrobiosis lipoidica 2. Charcot neuroarthropathy 3. Exudative maculopathy 4. Acanthosis nigricans Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

All four findings can be associated with diabetes mellitus.

• 1. Necrobiosis lipoidica: Correct.

• Strongly associated with diabetes, particularly type 1 DM.
• Presents as yellow-brown, atrophic plaques with prominent telangiectasia, usually on the shins.

• 2. Charcot neuroarthropathy: Correct.

• Occurs due to diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
• Repeated unrecognized trauma causes joint destruction, classically affecting the midfoot.
• The foot may become warm, swollen, and deformed.

• 3. Exudative maculopathy: Correct.

• A manifestation of diabetic retinopathy, particularly diabetic macular edema.
• Retinal leakage produces hard exudates, which may form a circinate pattern around the macula.

• 4. Acanthosis nigricans: Correct.

• Associated with insulin resistance, particularly in type 2 DM.
• Presents as hyperpigmented, velvety thickening of the skin, commonly in the neck and axillae.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following receptors acts via a Gs-coupled GPCR pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Beta-1 adrenergic receptor

G-protein associations:

• Gs → ↑ cAMP
• Gi → ↓ cAMP
• Gq → ↑ IP3/DAG and ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺

Option analysis:

• A. Alpha-1 adrenergic receptor → Gq
• B. Beta-1 adrenergic receptor → Gs
• C. M1 muscarinic receptor → Gq
• D. M2 muscarinic receptor → Gi

Gs-alpha subunit:

• FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH,
• CRH, hCG, ADH-V2, MSH, PTH, Calcitonin, H2, Glucagon, GHRH
• All B receptors

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct with regard to glucose homeostasis? 1. Insulin level rises postprandially. 2. Major portion of postprandial glucose is used by skeletal muscle. 3. Brain uses glucose in an insulin-dependent manner. 4. Glucagon is secreted during exercise. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Glucose homeostasis is maintained by the coordinated actions of insulin and counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, and growth hormone). Insulin predominates in the fed state, promoting glucose uptake and storage, while glucagon predominates during fasting and exercise, maintaining blood glucose by stimulating hepatic glucose production.

Why is B correct?

• 1. Insulin level rises postprandially✅: Increased blood glucose after a meal stimulates pancreatic β-cells to release insulin.
• 2. Major portion of postprandial glucose is used by skeletal muscle✅: Skeletal muscle is the largest site of insulin-mediated glucose uptake and glycogen storage after meals.
• 4. Glucagon is secreted during exercise✅: Exercise stimulates glucagon secretion, increasing hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis to maintain blood glucose.

Incorrect statement:

• 3. Brain uses glucose in an insulin-dependent manner❌: The brain utilizes glucose via insulin-independent GLUT1 and GLUT3 transporters.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following antidiabetic drugs is recommended for weight loss in obese patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Liraglutide

Liraglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, promotes weight loss by increasing satiety, delaying gastric emptying, and reducing appetite. It is recommended for obese patients with type 2 diabetes, particularly those who would benefit from both glycemic control and weight reduction.

Why not the other options?

• A. Glimepiride: Sulfonylurea; causes weight gain due to increased insulin secretion.
• C. Sitagliptin: DPP-4 inhibitor; generally weight neutral.
• D. Insulin: Commonly associated with weight gain.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following insulin preparations has the longest effective duration of action?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Degludec

Insulin degludec is an ultra-long-acting basal insulin with the longest duration of action among currently available insulin preparations. This provides a flat, peakless insulin profile with less day-to-day variability and a lower risk of nocturnal hypoglycemia.

Evaluation of the options:

• A. Detemir: False.

• Long-acting insulin with a duration of 18–24 hours.
• May require twice-daily dosing in some patients.

• B. Glargine: False.

• Long-acting insulin with a duration of approximately 24 hours (up to \~36 hours for some formulations).
• Usually given once daily.

• C. NPH: False.

• Intermediate-acting insulin with a duration of 12–18 hours.
• Has a pronounced peak, increasing the risk of hypoglycemia.

| Insulin | Type | Onset | Peak | Duration

| ------- | ---- | ----- | ---- | --------

| NPH | Intermediate | 1–2 h | 4–12 h | 12–18 h

| Detemir | Long-acting | 1–2 h | Minimal | 18–24 h

| Glargine | Long-acting | 1–2 h | Peakless | \~24 hours

| Degludec | Ultra-long-acting | \~1 h | Peakless | >42 hours

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is true regarding asymmetrical motor diabetic neuropathy?
options: Weakness and wasting of proximal muscles of lower limbs
Hyper-exaggerated reflexes in the affected limb
Glucocorticoids are the treatment of choice
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Weakness and wasting of proximal muscles of lower limbs

Asymmetrical motor diabetic neuropathy, also called diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy (diabetic amyotrophy), typically presents with acute/subacute, unilateral thigh or hip pain followed by proximal weakness and wasting. It may later become bilateral.

Why not the other options?

• B. Painless wasting of muscles: Incorrect. Classically, there is severe unilateral proximal thigh/hip pain followed by muscle weakness and wasting.
• C. Hyper-exaggerated reflexes: Incorrect. Peripheral neuropathy causes reduced or absent reflexes, particularly the knee jerk.
• D. Glucocorticoids are the treatment of choice: Incorrect. Treatment is mainly glycemic optimization, analgesia, physiotherapy, and supportive care. The benefit of immunotherapy such as steroids remains uncertain.

| Feature | Diabetic Amyotrophy | Distal Symmetric Polyneuropathy (classic DM neuropathy)
