| ------- | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------

| Distribution | Proximal, asymmetric | Distal, symmetric ("stocking-glove")

| Onset | Acute/subacute | Chronic, insidious

| Pain | Prominent | Variable (often painless or mild)

| Mechanism | Microvasculitis/ischemic | Metabolic (chronic hyperglycemia)

| Correlation with glycemic control | Poor correlation | Strong correlation

| Association | Weight loss, may occur early in DM | Long-standing diabetes

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following levels of hypoglycaemia corresponds to a blood glucose level of 50 mg/dL leading to cognitive impairment and need for corrective treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Level 2

• Level 2 hypoglycemia is defined as a blood glucose level <54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L), regardless of symptoms. It is considered clinically significant and generally requires prompt corrective treatment.
• A blood glucose of 50 mg/dL therefore falls under Level 2 hypoglycemia.

Why not other options?

• Level 0: No longer part of the standard ADA classification.
• Level 1: Glucose <70 but ≥54 mg/dL.
• Level 3: Severe hypoglycemia characterized by altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance, irrespective of glucose level.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is true regarding the use of SGLT2 inhibitors in management of diabetes mellitus?
options: They are used in type 1, type 2 and pancreatogenic forms of diabetes mellitus
They cause increase in blood pressure by 3–6 mm Hg and hence avoided in hypertensive patients
Their glucose-lowering effect is dependent on insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity
Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis may occur during treatment if there is a concurrent illness
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis may occur during treatment if there is a concurrent illness

SGLT2 inhibitors lower blood glucose by blocking renal glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule, independent of insulin. A rare but important adverse effect is euglycemic DKA, especially during acute illness, surgery, fasting, dehydration, or reduced insulin doses.

Why others are wrong?

• A. They are used in type 1, type 2 and pancreatogenic forms of diabetes mellitus: Not routinely used in type 1 DM (↑ risk of DKA).
• B. They cause increase in blood pressure by 3–6 mm Hg and hence avoided in hypertensive patients: They decrease blood pressure by \~3–6 mm Hg.
• C. Their glucose-lowering effect is dependent on insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity: Their action is independent of insulin secretion and sensitivity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which receptor helps in improvement of insulin resistance in Type-2 Diabetes Mellitus with regular exercise and physical activity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. GLUT4

Exercise increases translocation of GLUT4 to skeletal muscle cell membranes independent of insulin.

During exercise:

Muscle contraction

⬇

Activation of intracellular pathways (AMPK etc.)

⬇

GLUT4 translocation to cell membrane

⬇

↑ Glucose uptake into muscle

⬇

↓ Blood glucose

⬇

Improved insulin sensitivity

This enhances glucose uptake and improves insulin sensitivity in type 2 diabetes.

| Transporter | Tissue | Insulin Dependence

| ----------- | ------ | ------------------

| GLUT1 | RBC, brain | No

| GLUT2 | Liver, pancreas | No

| GLUT3 | Brain | No

| GLUT4 ⭐ | Muscle, adipose | Yes

GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive glucose transporter in muscle and adipose tissue. Other GLUT isoforms are not exercise-responsive.

| Feature | Insulin Action | Exercise Action

| ------- | -------------- | ---------------

| GLUT4 activation | Yes | Yes

| Requires insulin | Yes | ❌ No

| Effect on glucose | ↓ glucose | ↓ glucose

| Role in T2DM | Impaired | Improves

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 27-year-old lady underwent thyroidectomy for thyroid carcinoma. Postoperatively she developed muscle cramps, perioral and peripheral paresthesia, and carpopedal spasm. Which one of the following interventions is appropriate?
options: Nerve conduction velocity in both upper and lower limbs and administer methylcobalamin
EMG of both lower limbs and administer oral prednisolone
Measure serum ionized calcium and administer intravenous calcium gluconate
Measure serum bicarbonate and administer intravenous bicarbonate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Measure serum ionized calcium and administer intravenous calcium gluconate

Hypocalcemia due to postoperative hypoparathyroidism is a common complication of thyroidectomy. It typically presents within 24–72 hours with perioral numbness, paresthesias, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm, tetany, and positive Chvostek/Trousseau signs. Diagnosis is confirmed by serum ionized calcium, and symptomatic hypocalcemia requires immediate intravenous calcium gluconate.

Why not the other options?

• A. Nerve conduction velocity in both upper and lower limbs and administer methylcobalamin: Nerve conduction studies and methylcobalamin are indicated for peripheral neuropathy, not acute postoperative tetany.
• B. EMG of both lower limbs and administer oral prednisolone: EMG and prednisolone have no role in hypocalcemia after thyroidectomy.
• D. Measure serum bicarbonate and administer intravenous bicarbonate: Bicarbonate is used for metabolic acidosis, not for neuromuscular symptoms caused by hypocalcemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents with recurrent renal calculi, proximal muscle weakness, and low mood. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated serum PTH with normal serum calcium. Primary hyperparathyroidism is suspected. Which of the following is the investigation of choice for preoperative localization of the abnormal gland?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tc-99m sestamibi scan

• Recurrent renal stones + proximal weakness + depression → classic hyperparathyroid symptom cluster
• ↑ PTH with normal Ca → early / normocalcemic primary hyperparathyroidism

Why Tc-99m Sestamibi is IOC

• Mechanism: Radiotracer (Tc-99m sestamibi) is taken up by mitochondria-rich parathyroid adenoma cells
• Shows persistent uptake in abnormal parathyroid tissue (vs thyroid washout)
• High sensitivity for detecting single adenoma (most common cause)

Step 4: Why not other options?

• A) Neck ultrasound

• Operator dependent
• Misses ectopic glands

• B) MRI neck

• Used only if sestamibi inconclusive

• D) CT neck

• 4D-CT used in difficult/recurrent cases, not first-line

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old lady presents with complaints of fatigue, muscle weakness along with bilateral multiple renal calculi which were picked up on a routine ultrasound. Further workup revealed serum calcium levels of 11.4 mg%. What is the next best investigation required to arrive at a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sestamibi scan

The patient has features suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism:

• Hypercalcemia (11.4 mg/dL)
• Recurrent/multiple renal calculi (“stones”)
• Muscle weakness and fatigue

The diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism is first established biochemically by demonstrating elevated or inappropriately normal serum PTH in the presence of hypercalcemia. Once the biochemical diagnosis is made, the best imaging modality for preoperative localization of a parathyroid adenoma is a Tc-99m Sestamibi scan.

Why not the other options?

• A. MRI neck: Not routinely used as the first imaging modality; reserved for difficult or recurrent cases.
• C. CECT head and neck: Not the standard initial investigation for parathyroid adenoma localization.
• D. NCCT head and neck: Does not adequately localize parathyroid lesions.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with history of “bones, stones and abdominal groans” due to generalized aches and pains and renal calculus colic. Which is the most discriminatory blood investigation?
options: Thyroid function tests (Free T3, Free T4, TSH)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Parathyroid hormone assay

The classic presentation of “Bones, Stones, Abdominal Groans, and Psychic Overtones” is suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism, most commonly caused by a parathyroid adenoma. The most discriminatory investigation is a serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) assay, which confirms PTH-dependent hypercalcemia.

• A. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) assay:

• Investigation of choice to confirm primary hyperparathyroidism.
• Shows elevated or inappropriately normal PTH despite hypercalcemia.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Thyroid function tests (Free T3, Free T4, TSH): Evaluate thyroid disorders and do not diagnose hyperparathyroidism.
• C. Cortisol levels: Used in adrenal disorders such as Cushing syndrome or adrenal insufficiency.
• D. Insulin and C-peptide levels: Used in the evaluation of hypoglycemia and insulinoma, not hypercalcemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with malignancy develops humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy. Arrange the following steps in the appropriate sequence of management. 1. IV saline hydration to promote calciuresis 2. Bisphosphonate therapy 3. Loop diuretics after hydration 4. Find the source of exogenous ca
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 4, 1, 3, 2

Hypercalcemia of malignancy is a medical emergency. Initial management focuses on eliminating factors that worsen hypercalcemia, restoring intravascular volume, promoting renal calcium excretion, and inhibiting bone resorption.

The correct sequence of management is:

1. Stop external calcium intake and discontinue drugs that aggravate hypercalcemia (e.g., thiazides, vitamin D supplements, lithium).
2. IV normal saline hydration to correct dehydration and enhance urinary calcium excretion.
3. Loop diuretics (only after adequate hydration and if clinically indicated) to further increase calciuresis.
4. IV bisphosphonates (e.g., zoledronic acid, pamidronate) to inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and provide sustained calcium reduction.

Why not the other options?

• Hydration must precede loop diuretics to avoid worsening volume depletion.
• Bisphosphonates are not immediate-acting and should be administered after initial stabilization with hydration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to Vitamin D deficiency: 1. Vitamin D deficiency is common in northern latitudes. 2. Vitamin D deficiency is more likely to develop in people with dark skin. 3. Exposure to UV light is advisable in patients with Vitamin D deficiency. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Vitamin D deficiency is common worldwide and results from inadequate sunlight exposure, reduced cutaneous synthesis, poor dietary intake, malabsorption, or impaired metabolism. Individuals living in higher (northern) latitudes, those with dark skin, and people with limited sun exposure are at increased risk. Management includes vitamin D supplementation along with adequate exposure to sunlight (UVB radiation).

Why is D correct?

• 1. Vitamin D deficiency is common in northern latitudes✅: Reduced UVB exposure limits cutaneous vitamin D synthesis.
• 2. Vitamin D deficiency is more likely in people with dark skin✅: Increased melanin reduces UVB-mediated vitamin D production.
• 3. Exposure to UV light is advisable in patients with Vitamin D deficiency✅: Regular sunlight (UVB) exposure enhances endogenous vitamin D synthesis and complements supplementation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Deficiency of which of the following mineral(s) can lead to hypocalcemia by impairing the ability of the parathyroid gland to secrete parathyroid hormone? 1. Phosphate 2. Magnesium 3. Sodium 4. Potassium Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 only

To recognize severe magnesium deficiency as an important cause of hypocalcemia due to impaired PTH secretion and peripheral PTH resistance.

1. Phosphate: Incorrect

• Phosphate excess can cause hypocalcemia by binding calcium, but phosphate deficiency does not impair PTH secretion.

2. Magnesium: Correct

• Severe hypomagnesemia impairs PTH secretion and causes resistance to PTH, resulting in hypocalcemia.

3. Sodium: Incorrect

• Sodium deficiency does not directly impair PTH secretion.

4. Potassium: Incorrect

• Potassium deficiency does not cause hypocalcemia by impairing PTH secretion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: PTH increases Calcium in blood. This is due to:
options: Rapid release of calcium by osteocytes
Rapid release of calcium by osteoclasts
Rapid release of calcium from bones and increased calcium reabsorption in kidneys
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rapid release of calcium from bones and increased calcium reabsorption in kidneys

Parathyroid hormone (PTH) primarily acts to increase the concentration of calcium in the blood. It achieves this through several mechanisms:

1. Stimulation of osteoclasts to resorb bone, leading to the release of calcium from the bones.
2. Increased absorption of calcium in the intestines.
3. Stimulation of the kidneys to reabsorb more calcium, reducing its excretion in the urine.

a) Rapid release by osteocytes

PTH mainly works via osteoblast → osteoclast activation

b) Rapid release by osteoclasts

Does not include kidney contribution

d) Increase calcium reabsorption in kidneys

Kidney alone cannot significantly raise Ca without bone contribution

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which among the following drugs decreases the serum parathyroid hormone levels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcitriol

Correct answer is B because calcitriol (active vitamin D) increases intestinal calcium absorption and raises serum calcium, which suppresses parathyroid hormone via negative feedback.

Key regulators of PTH:

| Factor | Effect on PTH

| ------ | -------------

| Low Ca²⁺ | ↑ PTH

| High Ca²⁺ | ↓ PTH

| Calcitriol | ↓ PTH

| Phosphate | ↑ PTH

Calcitriol acts on:

| Organ | Effect

| ----- | ------

| Intestine | ↑ Ca absorption

| Kidney | ↑ Ca reabsorption

| Bone | ↑ remodeling

Risedronate reduces bone resorption but does not directly suppress PTH. Lithium can increase PTH and cause hyperparathyroidism. Diuretics have variable effects and are not primary PTH suppressors.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are causes of hypocalcemia in a child? I. Hypomagnesemia II. Hypophosphatemia III. Metabolic acidosis IV. Pseudohypoparathyroidism Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I and IV

Hypocalcemia is defined as a low serum ionized calcium or total serum calcium (after correction for albumin). It commonly presents with neuromuscular irritability, including tetany, seizures, muscle cramps, laryngospasm, and prolonged QT interval on ECG.

Among the important causes in children are hypomagnesemia and pseudohypoparathyroidism.

Why is D correct?

• I. Hypomagnesemia ✔

• Correct.
• Magnesium deficiency impairs parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion and causes PTH resistance, leading to hypocalcemia.
• Hypocalcemia due to hypomagnesemia will not correct until magnesium is replaced.

• II. Hypophosphatemia ✘

• Incorrect.
• Hypophosphatemia is usually associated with increased calcium levels or normal calcium.
• Hyperphosphatemia, not hypophosphatemia, commonly causes hypocalcemia.

• III. Metabolic acidosis ✘

• Incorrect.
• Acidosis reduces calcium binding to albumin, thereby increasing ionized (physiologically active) calcium.
• Alkalosis, not acidosis, precipitates symptomatic hypocalcemia by decreasing ionized calcium.

• IV. Pseudohypoparathyroidism ✔

• Correct.
• It is caused by end-organ resistance to PTH, resulting in:

• Hypocalcemia
• Hyperphosphatemia
• Elevated PTH levels

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not typically associated with Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1)?
options: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus association is high
Association with mucocutaneous candidiasis is high
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus association is high

Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome (APS). APS refers to a group of autoimmune disorders affecting multiple endocrine glands simultaneously. It results from immune-mediated destruction of endocrine tissues.

Three major types exist:

| Syndrome | Typical Features

| -------- | ----------------

| APS-1 | Hypoparathyroidism + Candidiasis + Adrenal insufficiency

| APS-2 | Addison disease + Type 1 DM + Autoimmune thyroid disease

APS-1 (Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1) Also called: APECED (Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy-Candidiasis-Ectodermal Dystrophy)

Cause:

• Mutation in AIRE gene
• Located on chromosome 21

The AIRE protein allows the immune system to develop tolerance to self-antigens.

Mutation leads to failure of central immune tolerance → autoimmunity.

| Feature | APS-1 | APS-2

| ------- | ----- | -----

| Gene | AIRE mutation | Polygenic

| Age | Childhood | Adulthood

| Hypoparathyroidism | Common | Rare

| Candidiasis | Classic feature | Absent

| Type 1 DM | Rare | Common

| Thyroid disease | Rare | Common

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for management of severe hypercalcemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intravenous infusion of normal saline

Severe hypercalcemia (serum calcium >14 mg/dL or symptomatic hypercalcemia) is a medical emergency. The initial treatment is aggressive intravenous hydration with isotonic normal saline, which corrects volume depletion and enhances renal calcium excretion (calciuresis). Definitive therapies are added after adequate hydration.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Intravenous pamidronate: A bisphosphonate that inhibits bone resorption, but its effect begins only after 24–48 hours. It is given after adequate hydration.
• B. Oral phosphate supplementation: Not used routinely because of the risk of metastatic calcification and other adverse effects.
• D. Hemodialysis: Reserved for refractory severe hypercalcemia, especially in patients with renal failure, heart failure, or inability to tolerate aggressive hydration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 14-year-old developed rapid growth and had long legs and large hands, and coarse facial features. Which of the following tests are used to make a confirmatory diagnosis?
options: No supression of GH after glucose administration
No supression of IGF1 after glucose tolerance test
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. No supression of GH after glucose administration

The confirmatory test for suspected gigantism/acromegaly is failure of GH suppression after oral glucose load. Normally, hyperglycemia suppresses GH to very low levels; persistent elevation confirms autonomous GH secretion.

| Test | Role | Why

| ---- | ---- | ---

| IGF-1 | Screening | Stable, reflects GH

| OGTT (GH suppression test) ⭐ | Confirmatory | Tests feedback control

| Random GH | Not useful | Fluctuates

Random GH levels fluctuate and are unreliable, while IGF-1 is a screening marker, not confirmatory. IGF-1 is not used for suppression testing.

| Feature | Gigantism | Acromegaly

| ------- | --------- | ----------

| Age | Children | Adults

| Epiphysis | Open | Closed

| Growth | Height ↑ | No height ↑

| Features | Long limbs | Coarse features

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old male presents with complaints of excessive thirst and frequent urination throughout the day. He mentions having to wake up multiple times at night to urinate. On further questioning, he reports a history of head injury one month ago. His fasting blood glucose is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Desmopressin

Polyuria + polydipsia can be:

| Condition | Key clue

| --------- | --------

| Diabetes mellitus | ↑ glucose

| Diabetes insipidus | Normal glucose

| Psychogenic polydipsia | psychiatric

Here: Glucose normal + head injury → think DI

Head injury followed by polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia, and normal glucose suggests central diabetes insipidus due to ADH deficiency. The treatment of choice is desmopressin, an ADH analogue that restores water reabsorption in the collecting ducts. Normal ADH function-

ADH (vasopressin) released from posterior pituitary

⬇

Acts on V2 receptors in kidney (collecting duct)

⬇

Insertion of aquaporin channels

⬇

Water reabsorption

⬇

Concentrated urine

Tolvaptan is used in SIADH, not DI. Insulin is irrelevant, and thiazides are mainly used in nephrogenic DI.

| Feature | Central DI | Nephrogenic DI

| ------- | ---------- | --------------

| ADH level | ↓ | Normal/↑

| Cause | Head injury, tumor | renal resistance

| Treatment | ⭐ Desmopressin | Thiazides, NSAIDs

| Response to ADH | Yes | No

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman delivers a stillborn infant. She is distressed and requests medical management to suppress lactation. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic agent for suppression of lactation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bromocriptine

Bromocriptine, a dopamine (D2) agonist, suppresses lactation by inhibiting prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary. It may be used for lactation suppression after stillbirth, neonatal death, or when breastfeeding is contraindicated, provided there are no contraindications to therapy.

Why not the other options?

• B. Calcitonin: Regulates calcium metabolism; has no role in lactation suppression.
• C. Oxytocin: Promotes milk ejection (let-down reflex) and uterine contraction; it does not suppress milk production.
• D. Misoprostol: A prostaglandin E₁ analogue used for medical abortion, cervical ripening, and postpartum hemorrhage, not lactation suppression.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman, having lost her newborn, is producing breast milk, which risks developing into a breast abscess due to milk stasis and incomplete emptying. Which drug can prevent this complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cabergoline

Dopamine (from hypothalamus) tonically inhibits prolactin secretion from anterior pituitary.

So: ↑ Dopamine → ↓ Prolactin → ↓ Milk production

Why Cabergoline Works

Cabergoline = D2 receptor agonist → mimics dopamine → suppresses prolactin → stops lactation → prevents milk stasis → prevents breast abscess

Why the Others Fail

| Drug | Class | Effect on Prolactin

| ---- | ----- | -------------------

| Mifepristone | Progesterone/glucocorticoid antagonist | No effect on prolactin

| Cabergoline ✓ | D2 agonist | ↓ Prolactin → suppresses lactation

| Chlorpromazine | D2 antagonist (antipsychotic) | ↑ Prolactin → causes galactorrhea

| Metoclopramide | D2 antagonist (antiemetic) | ↑ Prolactin → causes galactorrhea

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with increased urine output. On evaluation, his urinary output was around 4 L/day; urinary osmolality was 200 mosmol/L. Which of the following are various differential diagnosis? I. Psychogenic polydipsia II. Solute diuresis III. Central diabetes insipidus IV. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, III and IV

Polyuria is defined as a urine output >3 L/day in adults. The first step in evaluating polyuria is to measure the urine osmolality.

This patient has:

• Urine output = 4 L/day (polyuria)
• Urine osmolality = 200 mOsm/kg (dilute urine)

A low urine osmolality (<300 mOsm/kg) indicates water diuresis, and the major differential diagnoses are:

• Psychogenic (primary) polydipsia
• Central diabetes insipidus (CDI)
• Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (NDI)

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Solute diuresis

• Solute diuresis (e.g., uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, mannitol therapy, urea diuresis) produces high urine osmolality (>300 mOsm/kg) due to increased urinary solute excretion.
• Therefore, it is not consistent with a urine osmolality of 200 mOsm/kg.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old male patient presents to the OPD with abdominal striae. He denies any history of long-term drug use. On examination, he has centripetal obesity, buffalo hump and hypertension. After diagnosis by dexamethasone suppression test, which of the following is the next appropriate investigation?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of adrenal gland
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plasma ACTH levels

After confirming endogenous Cushing syndrome with a screening test (e.g., overnight dexamethasone suppression test), the next step is to measure plasma ACTH levels to determine whether the hypercortisolism is ACTH-dependent or ACTH-independent. This guides the subsequent imaging investigation.

• Plasma ACTH is the first investigation after biochemical confirmation of Cushing syndrome.
• Interpretation:

• Low ACTH → ACTH-independent (adrenal adenoma/carcinoma) → CT/MRI adrenal
• Normal or high ACTH → ACTH-dependent (pituitary adenoma or ectopic ACTH secretion) → Pituitary MRI ± Inferior petrosal sinus sampling (IPSS)

Why not the other options?

• A. MRI of brain: Done only after ACTH is elevated or inappropriately normal, suggesting a pituitary source (Cushing disease).
• C. CECT of adrenal gland: Indicated only if ACTH is suppressed, suggesting an adrenal cause.
• D. Non-contrast CT of adrenal gland: Also performed after low ACTH confirms ACTH-independent disease, not immediately after diagnosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with large, sweaty hands, macroglossia, and prominent frontal bossing. The patient also reports increasing shoe size and difficulty wearing rings that previously fit. Considering the clinical features, which of the following tests is the most appropriate initial investigation?
options: GH levels after 2 hours of administration of 75g glucose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Age-matched IGF-1 levels

The features suggest acromegaly, and the best initial screening test is age-adjusted IGF-1 because it reflects integrated GH secretion and is persistently elevated.

Random GH fluctuates due to pulsatile release, making it unreliable. Failure of GH suppression after oral glucose is confirmatory, not the first step. GHRH levels are not used for routine screening.

GH after glucose (OGTT suppression test)

This is a confirmatory test, not initial.

In normal: Glucose-> GH suppressed

In acromegaly: GH remains high

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A female patient with infertility presents with galactorrhea. Evaluation reveals a 7mm prolactinoma. She is worried about her conception chances. What is the appropriate drug in this situation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bromocriptine

Both BROMOCRIPTINE AND CABERGOLINE are dopamine agonists that suppress prolactin. The distinction is subtle but exam-favourite:

| Feature | Cabergoline | Bromocriptine

| ------- | ----------- | -------------

| Dosing | Once or twice weekly | Twice daily

| Efficacy | Superior — better prolactin normalization + tumor shrinkage | Less effective

| Tolerability | Better (fewer GI side effects) | More nausea/vomiting

| Preferred for prolactinoma | Yes — first line | Second line generally

| Preferred in pregnancy | No | Yes

Bromocriptine has been the gold standard for prolactinoma + fertility for decades:

• First dopamine agonist proven to restore ovulation and achieve successful pregnancies
• Decades of reproductive safety data — known to be safe to continue through conception and into early pregnancy
• Can be continued without stopping when pregnancy is confirmed (unlike cabergoline which is typically stopped)
• Specifically studied and approved for infertility due to hyperprolactinemia

This is a 7mm = Microprolactinoma

| Size | Classification | Concern in pregnancy

| ---- | -------------- | --------------------

| <10mm | Microprolactinoma | Low risk of growth in pregnancy

| >10mm | Macroprolactinoma | Higher risk of expansion → monitor closely

For microprolactinoma: dopamine agonist can often be stopped once pregnant as tumor unlikely to enlarge significantly.

Why Not C or D?

• Octreotide — somatostatin analogue; used for acromegaly/GH-secreting tumors, not prolactinoma
• Pegvisomant — GH receptor antagonist; used for acromegaly refractory to other treatment

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A middle-aged male patient presents with chin protrusion, excessive sweating, hormone receptor antagonist used to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pegvisomant

There are three main drug classes used in acromegaly, and examiners often test their differences:

1. Somatostatin analogues → decrease GH secretion
2. Dopamine agonists → decrease GH (mild effect)
3. GH receptor antagonists → block GH action

Pegvisomant belongs to the third category

The features describe acromegaly, and pegvisomant is a GH receptor antagonist that blocks peripheral GH action and lowers IGF-1. It is used when surgery or somatostatin analogs are inadequate.

Octreotide suppresses GH release but is not a receptor antagonist. Cabergoline is a dopamine agonist, and olcegepant is unrelated to GH.

A. Octreotide

• Somatostatin analogue
• ↓ GH secretion from pituitary
• Not a receptor antagonist

C. Cabergoline

• Dopamine agonist
• Mildly suppresses GH
• Mainly used in prolactinoma

D. Olcegepant

• CGRP antagonist
• Used in migraine
• No role here

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient came to the medical OPD with complaints of polyuria. He has a history of undergoing total hypophysectomy. His Na+ levels are found to be 155 mEq/L, urine osmolality was 200 mOsm/L. What is the definitive management?
options: DDAVP for 2 weeks and then discontinue
Upsetting of receptors so no treatment is required
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. DDAVP supplementation for lifelong

Total hypophysectomy causes central diabetes insipidus due to permanent ADH deficiency.

ADH normally acts on kidney collecting ducts

⬇

Inserts aquaporin channels

⬇

Water reabsorption

⬇

Concentrated urine

| Parameter | Finding | Meaning

| --------- | ------- | -------

| Serum Na⁺ | 155 | Water loss (hypernatremia)

| Urine osmolality | 200 | Dilute urine

| History | Hypophysectomy | Central cause

Hypernatremia with low urine osmolality confirms inability to concentrate urine. Definitive therapy is lifelong desmopressin (DDAVP) replacement to restore water reabsorption.

Temporary therapy or thiazides are used in nephrogenic DI, not central DI.

| Feature | Central DI | Nephrogenic DI

| ------- | ---------- | --------------

| ADH | ↓ | Normal

| Cause | Pituitary damage | Kidney resistance

| Treatment | ⭐ Desmopressin | Thiazides

| Response to ADH | Yes | No

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A pituitary tumor that overproduced growth hormone was surgically removed from a patient. The resection was discovered to be insufficient. What is the patient's first-line treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Octreotide

Persistent acromegaly after incomplete surgery is treated first-line with somatostatin analogues.

Surgery (first-line)

⬇

If incomplete or residual tumor

⬇

Medical therapy (first-line drug = somatostatin analogue)

⬇

Radiotherapy (if needed)

Therefore, after incomplete surgery → Octreotide

Octreotide suppresses GH secretion from pituitary adenoma and lowers IGF-1 levels. It is the preferred medical therapy when surgery is inadequate. GnRH analogues like leuprolide/goserelin/nafarelin have no role in GH-secreting tumors.

| Situation | Best Drug

| --------- | ---------

| Residual acromegaly after surgery | ⭐ Octreotide

| Refractory to somatostatin analogues | Pegvisomant

| Mild disease | Cabergoline

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A pregnant female presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea. MRI shows pituitary adenoma. What is the best management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bromocriptine

In pregnancy, the drug of choice for prolactinoma is: Bromocriptine

Because:

• Safe in pregnancy
• Extensive clinical experience
• Effectively lowers prolactin

Hypothalamus releases dopamine

⬇

Dopamine acts on pituitary (D2 receptors)

⬇

↓ Prolactin secretion

Bromocriptine is the preferred dopamine agonist in prolactinoma during pregnancy because of its long safety record for fetal exposure. It suppresses prolactin and reduces tumor size while preserving fertility.

Surgery is reserved for drug-resistant or compressive tumors.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Functioning pituitary adenoma most commonly arises from which one of the following cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lactotroph

Pituitary adenomas are benign tumors arising from the adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary). Functioning pituitary adenomas secrete excess pituitary hormones, and the most common functioning pituitary adenoma is a prolactinoma, which arises from lactotroph cells.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Somatotroph: ✗

• Secretes Growth Hormone (GH).
• Causes gigantism (children) or acromegaly (adults).
• Second most common functioning pituitary adenoma.

• C. Corticotroph: ✗

• Secretes ACTH.
• Causes Cushing disease.

• D. Thyrotroph: ✗

• Secretes TSH.
• Rare; causes secondary hyperthyroidism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a patient with a prolactinoma, the mechanism by which prolactin causes amenorrhea is through which of the following actions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decreasing GnRH

• ↑ Prolactin (from prolactinoma)
• Suppresses GnRH pulse generation from hypothalamic arcuate nucleus
• ↓ LH + ↓ FSH from anterior pituitary
• ↓ Ovarian follicle development + ↓ estrogen
• No LH surge → no ovulation → amenorrhea

Why GnRH is the Primary Target

Prolactin acts at the hypothalamus, not directly on the pituitary or ovary. It disrupts the pulsatile secretion of GnRH — and pulsatility is everything:

| GnRH Pattern | Effect

| ------------ | ------

| Normal pulsatile | LH + FSH released normally

| Suppressed (hyperprolactinemia) | ↓ LH + FSH → anovulation

| Continuous/non-pulsatile | Also suppresses LH/FSH (used therapeutically in GnRH agonists)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Many GPCR receptors act via an increase in cAMP. The steps involved in this mechanism are given below. Which of the following is the correct sequence of events in the cAMP signal transduction pathway? 1. Activation of adenylate cyclase 2. Activation of PKA 3. Conversion of ATP to cAMP 4. Phosphorylation of target proteins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, 2 and 4

Correct answer is B because GPCR activation first stimulates adenylate cyclase (1), which converts ATP to cAMP (3).

cAMP then activates protein kinase A (PKA) (2).

Activated PKA phosphorylates downstream target proteins (4), producing the cellular response.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following growth hormone analogue that is not used for treatment of GH deficiency but is used in the treatment of HIV-associated lipodystrophy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tesamorelin

Tesamorelin is a GHRH analogue used to reduce visceral adiposity in HIV-associated lipodystrophy by stimulating endogenous GH release. It is not used for routine treatment of GH deficiency.

| Drug | Type | Main Use

| ---- | ---- | --------

| Somatropin | Recombinant GH | ⭐ GH deficiency

| Sermorelin | GHRH analogue | GH deficiency (stimulates GH)

| Pegvisomant | GH receptor antagonist | Acromegaly

| Tesamorelin ⭐ | GHRH analogue | HIV lipodystrophy

Somatropin is recombinant GH for deficiency states, while pegvisomant is a GH receptor antagonist used in acromegaly. Sermorelin is used diagnostically or for GH deficiency, not lipodystrophy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is/are growth hormone receptor antagonist(s) indicated in the treatment of Acromegaly? 1. Octreotide 2. Lanreotide 3. Pasireotide 4. Pegvisomant Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4 only

• 1. Octreotide: Incorrect. Somatostatin receptor agonist; suppresses GH secretion.
• 2. Lanreotide: Incorrect. Somatostatin receptor agonist; suppresses GH secretion.
• 3. Pasireotide: Incorrect. A somatostatin receptor ligand, particularly active at SSTR5, that suppresses GH secretion.
• 4. Pegvisomant: Correct. A growth hormone receptor antagonist that blocks GH action and decreases IGF-1 production.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following conditions can cause euvolaemic hyponatraemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypothyroidism

Euvolemic hyponatremia is characterized by low serum sodium with normal extracellular fluid volume, without clinical evidence of edema or dehydration. It is most commonly caused by syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), but hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency are important endocrine causes that must always be excluded.

• Hypothyroidism can cause euvolemic hyponatremia by:

• Decreasing cardiac output and GFR
• Increasing ADH secretion
• Reducing free water clearance

• The resulting water retention dilutes serum sodium without causing significant edema.

Why not the other options?

• A. Adrenocortical failure: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) usually causes hypovolemic hyponatremia due to aldosterone deficiency causing sodium loss. (Secondary adrenal insufficiency may present with euvolemic hyponatremia.)
• C. Nephrotic syndrome: Causes hypervolemic hyponatremia due to edema and water retention.
• D. Burns: Cause hypovolemic hyponatremia because of fluid and sodium losses.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is correct regarding arginine vasopressin antagonist Tolvaptan?
options: It is useful in hypovolemic hyponatremia
It should be used for at least 1 year
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It is an oral drug

Tolvaptan is a selective vasopressin V₂ receptor antagonist that promotes free water excretion (aquaresis) without significant sodium loss. It is administered orally and is primarily used in the treatment of euvolemic and hypervolemic hyponatremia, particularly in patients with SIADH, heart failure, and cirrhosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. It is useful in hypovolemic hyponatremia: Incorrect. Tolvaptan is contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatremia because it can worsen volume depletion.
• B. It antagonises the V₁ receptor: Incorrect. Tolvaptan selectively blocks V₂ receptors in the renal collecting ducts. (Conivaptan blocks both V₁a and V₂ receptors.)
• C. It should be used for at least 1 year: Incorrect. Therapy is generally short-term for hyponatremia due to the risk of hepatotoxicity. In SIADH, treatment duration depends on the underlying cause. In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), it may be used long-term under close monitoring, but this is not a general recommendation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 27-year-old female patient presents with weight loss, anxiety, tachycardia, and restlessness. The resting pulse was 110 beats per minute. Which of the following tests should be done next to evaluate her condition further?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. TSH

TSH is the best initial screening test for suspected hyperthyroidism because it is the most sensitive indicator of thyroid function.

| Test | Role | When Used

| ---- | ---- | ---------

| TSH ⭐ | Initial screening | First test

| Free T4 | Confirm severity | After TSH

| Total T3 | Sometimes used | Less preferred

| Thyroid scan | Etiology | Later step

In thyrotoxicosis, TSH is characteristically suppressed due to negative feedback from elevated thyroid hormones. Free T4 or T3 are measured only after an abnormal TSH to confirm and classify severity. Thyroid scan is reserved for etiologic evaluation, not first-line screening.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old female presented to emergency with fever, agitation and delirium. She was on regular medication of Carbimazole 40 mg daily, but missed her doses for the last 2 days. Which of the following scoring systems would you like to do to assess severity of disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Burch-Wartofsky score

The patient has fever, agitation, delirium, and recent discontinuation of carbimazole, suggesting thyroid storm, a life-threatening complication of severe thyrotoxicosis. The Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale (BWPS) is the most widely used clinical scoring system to assess the likelihood and severity of thyroid storm.

Why is B correct?

• The Burch-Wartofsky score assigns points based on:

• Temperature
• Central nervous system manifestations (agitation, delirium, seizures, coma)
• Tachycardia
• Heart failure
• Atrial fibrillation
• Gastrointestinal/hepatic dysfunction
• Precipitating event (e.g., stopping antithyroid drugs, infection, surgery)

Interpretation:

• <25 → Thyroid storm unlikely
• 25–44 → Impending thyroid storm
• ≥45 → Highly suggestive of thyroid storm

Why not the other options?

• A. DAS 28 score: Measures disease activity in rheumatoid arthritis.
• C. Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS): Assesses disability in multiple sclerosis.
• D. Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score: Evaluates organ dysfunction in sepsis and critically ill patients, not thyroid storm.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A middle aged patient presenting with change in her voice, anemia, recent hair loss and cold intolerance has been diagnosed with Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Which of the following antibody is commonly seen in such patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anti thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibody

Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland leading to hypothyroidism.

It is characterized by high titers of anti–thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies.

Anti-TPO antibodies mediate thyroid follicular cell damage via immune mechanisms.

Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) function:

• Oxidation of iodide
• Iodination of tyrosine
• Coupling → T3 & T4 formation

Anti-TPO antibodies:

• Attack TPO enzyme
• Impair hormone synthesis
• Cause gland destruction

➡ Hallmark of Hashimoto thyroiditis

TSIg and anti–TSH receptor antibodies are associated with Graves’ disease, not Hashimoto thyroiditis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A middle-aged woman presents with weight gain, cold intolerance, and painless enlargement of the thyroid gland. Which of the following antibodies is not likely to be present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. TSH receptor autoantibody

Recognize the antibody profile of Hashimoto thyroiditis, the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions. Patients typically present with weight gain, cold intolerance, and a painless diffuse goiter. The disease is characterized by anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin (anti-Tg) antibodies, while TSH receptor–stimulating autoantibodies are characteristic of Graves disease, not Hashimoto thyroiditis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Anti-TPO antibody: Most sensitive marker for Hashimoto thyroiditis; present in >90% of cases.
• B. Anti-thyroglobulin (Anti-Tg) antibody: Present in many patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis, though less sensitive than anti-TPO.
• C. TSH receptor blocking antibody: May be present in a subset of Hashimoto patients and contributes to hypothyroidism by inhibiting TSH action.
• D. TSH receptor autoantibody (stimulating antibody/TSI): Characteristic of Graves disease, causing hyperthyroidism by stimulating the TSH receptor; not expected in Hashimoto thyroiditis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman at 8 weeks of gestation is diagnosed with hyperthyroidism. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment option?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Propylthiouracil

Propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester because methimazole/carbimazole are teratogenic and linked to embryopathy.

| Trimester | Drug of Choice | Reason

| --------- | -------------- | ------

| 1st trimester | ⭐ PTU | Less teratogenic

| 2nd & 3rd trimester | Methimazole | Less hepatotoxic

PTU also reduces peripheral T4→T3 conversion, helping rapid control of thyrotoxicosis. After the first trimester, therapy is often switched to methimazole due to PTU hepatotoxicity risk.

| Drug | Mechanism

| ---- | ---------

| PTU | ↓ T3/T4 synthesis + ↓ T4 → T3 conversion

| Methimazole | ↓ T3/T4 synthesis only

Methimazole causes teratogenic effects:

| Defect | Description

| ------ | -----------

| Aplasia cutis | Absence of scalp skin

| Choanal atresia | Nasal blockage

| Esophageal atresia | Feeding difficulty

Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young woman presents with weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance, and tremors. She has exophthalmos on examination. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Graves' disease

Graves’ disease is an autoimmune hyperthyroid state characterized by weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance, and tremors due to excess thyroid hormone.

Autoantibodies (TSH receptor antibodies)

⬇

Stimulate TSH receptors

⬇

↑ T3 and T4 production

⬇

Hyperthyroidism

Exophthalmos is a hallmark feature caused by autoimmune orbital fibroblast activation and glycosaminoglycan deposition.

• Most common cause of hyperthyroidism = Graves’ disease
• Pathognomonic sign = exophthalmos ⭐
• Caused by TSH receptor antibodies
• TSH ↓, T3/T4 ↑

This eye involvement is specific for Graves among thyrotoxic states. The other options do not produce thyrotoxicosis with ophthalmopathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following pharmacological agents: 1. Liothyronine 2. Levothyroxine 3. Carbimazole 4. Sodium ipodate Which of the above may be included in the treatment of myxoedema coma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 2

Myxedema coma is a life-threatening form of severe hypothyroidism. Treatment includes intravenous levothyroxine (T4), with or without liothyronine (T3), along with IV hydrocortisone (until adrenal insufficiency is excluded), supportive care, and correction of precipitating factors.

Why not the other options?

• 3. Carbimazole: Antithyroid drug used for hyperthyroidism; contraindicated in myxedema coma.
• 4. Sodium ipodate: Used historically in thyrotoxic crisis to inhibit T4→T3 conversion; has no role in myxedema coma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following pharmacological agents: 1. Propranolol 2. Sodium ipodate 3. Propylthiouracil 4. Liothyronine Which of the above can be used for the treatment of thyrotoxic crisis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 3

Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis) is a medical emergency requiring rapid reduction of thyroid hormone synthesis, release, and peripheral effects. Treatment includes:

• Propranolol – Controls adrenergic symptoms and reduces peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
• Propylthiouracil (PTU) – Inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis and peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
• Sodium ipodate (an iodinated contrast agent) – Inhibits peripheral T4→T3 conversion and reduces thyroid hormone release (historically used).

Why not the other option?

• 4. Liothyronine (T3): It is thyroid hormone used to treat hypothyroidism/myxedema coma, and would worsen thyrotoxicosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding ‘Factitious Thyrotoxicosis’: 1. Induced when patients consume excessive amounts of levothyroxine. 2. The exogenous levothyroxine suppresses secretion of pituitary TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone). 3. Serum thyroglobulin level is elevated. 4. T₄ : T₃ ratio is high. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Factitious thyrotoxicosis results from exogenous thyroid hormone ingestion and is characterized by suppressed TSH, low thyroglobulin, and a high T₄:T₃ ratio. Low radioactive iodine uptake also supports the diagnosis.

1. Excessive levothyroxine intake: Correct

• Factitious thyrotoxicosis results from exogenous thyroid hormone ingestion, usually levothyroxine.

2. Suppressed TSH: Correct

• Exogenous T₄ causes negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis → ↓ TRH and markedly ↓ TSH.

3. Serum thyroglobulin is elevated: Incorrect

• Thyroglobulin is typically low, because endogenous thyroid hormone synthesis is suppressed.
• This helps differentiate factitious thyrotoxicosis from subacute thyroiditis, where thyroglobulin is usually elevated.

4. High T₄:T₃ ratio: Correct

• Exogenous levothyroxine is predominantly T₄, and therefore produces a high T₄:T₃ ratio.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the transporter of iodine from follicular cells to follicular cavity within the thyroid gland:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pendrin

| Transporter | Location | Function

| ----------- | -------- | --------

| NIS (Na⁺/I⁻ symporter) | Basolateral membrane | Blood → cell

| Pendrin | Apical membrane | Cell → colloid

| TPO (enzyme) | Colloid | Organification

Pendrin transports iodide from thyroid follicular cells across the apical membrane into the follicular lumen for organification. The Na⁺/I⁻ symporter works on the basolateral membrane to bring iodide into the cell from blood. Defective pendrin impairs iodide efflux into colloid. This apical transport step is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In the management of a thyroid storm, a critical and life-threatening condition due to an excess of thyroid hormone, a variety of medications are used to control the symptoms and the overactive thyroid. Which of the following drugs is NOT typically used in the treatment of thyroid storm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aspirin

Thyroid storm = extreme thyrotoxicosis → life-threatening emergency

Management aims to:

• Block hormone synthesis
• Block hormone release
• Control symptoms
• Reduce peripheral effects

Aspirin is avoided in thyroid storm because salicylates displace T3/T4 from thyroid-binding globulin, increasing free hormone levels and worsening thyrotoxicosis.

Beta-blocker (Propranolol)

⬇

Antithyroid drug (PTU / Methimazole)

⬇

Iodine (Lugol’s iodine)

⬇

Steroids

⬇

Supportive care (fluids, cooling, paracetamol)

Propranolol controls adrenergic symptoms and reduces peripheral T4→T3 conversion, while Lugol’s iodine blocks hormone release.

| Drug | Role in Thyroid Storm

| ---- | ---------------------

| Propranolol ⭐ | Controls tachycardia + ↓ T4→T3

| PTU | ↓ synthesis + ↓ T4→T3

| Methimazole | ↓ synthesis

| Lugol’s iodine ⭐ | ↓ hormone release

| Steroids | ↓ T4→T3 + adrenal support

| Paracetamol (Acetaminophen) | Fever control

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Iodine has complex effects on thyroid function. Very high concentrations of iodine inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis and release. This effect is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wolff-Chaikoff effect

The Wolff–Chaikoff effect is the transient inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis and release following exposure to large amounts of iodine. It occurs due to inhibition of iodine organification within the thyroid gland and is the basis for using potassium iodide in thyroid storm and before thyroid surgery.

Why not the other options?

• B. Jod-Basedow effect: Iodine-induced hyperthyroidism, seen in patients with autonomous thyroid tissue (e.g., multinodular goiter).
• C. Reverse Wolff–Chaikoff effect: Refers to the escape phenomenon, where the thyroid resumes normal hormone synthesis after a few days despite continued iodine exposure.
• D. Reverse Jod-Basedow effect: Not a recognized physiological phenomenon.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Low serum thyroglobulin levels are seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thyrotoxicosis factitia

Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is a protein produced exclusively by thyroid follicular cells and serves as a marker of endogenous thyroid hormone production. It is useful in differentiating the causes of thyrotoxicosis.

A. Thyrotoxicosis factitia ✓

• Caused by exogenous ingestion of thyroid hormone.
• Since the thyroid gland is suppressed and not actively producing hormone, serum thyroglobulin is low.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Subacute thyroiditis ✗: Destruction of thyroid follicles releases stored thyroglobulin, resulting in high serum thyroglobulin.
• C. Graves’ disease ✗: Increased thyroid hormone synthesis and secretion cause elevated thyroglobulin.
• D. Toxic multinodular goitre ✗: Autonomous thyroid nodules produce excess hormone, leading to increased thyroglobulin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following diseases is characterized by destructive lymphoid infiltration of the thyroid gland leading to fibrosis and enlargement of the thyroid gland with an increased risk of developing thyroid lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis

Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas and is an autoimmune thyroid disorder characterized by destructive lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland, leading to progressive fibrosis and thyroid enlargement (goiter). Patients with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis have a significantly increased risk of developing primary thyroid lymphoma, particularly Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (DLBCL) and MALT lymphoma.

• D. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis:

• Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid by T-lymphocyte-mediated inflammation.
• Associated with anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies.
• Increases the risk of primary thyroid lymphoma.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. de Quervain’s thyroiditis: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, usually post-viral, presents with a painful, tender thyroid and transient thyrotoxicosis.
• B. Multinodular goitre: Non-inflammatory enlargement of the thyroid with multiple nodules; not associated with thyroid lymphoma.
• C. Riedel’s thyroiditis: Rare fibrosing thyroiditis causing a hard, “woody” thyroid, but not associated with lymphoid infiltration or increased lymphoma risk.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is false in patients with thyroid eye disease?
options: It can lead to vision loss
Response to vision symptoms is adjuvant to thyrotoxicosis response
10% of euthyroid patients can have eye involvement.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Response to vision symptoms is adjuvant to thyrotoxicosis response

Thyroid Eye Disease (TED) — Why B is FALSE

TED has an independent disease course from thyroid hormone status. Treating hyperthyroidism does not automatically treat the eye disease — they run on separate tracks.

Mechanism of TED

TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb)

↓

Target orbital fibroblasts (which express TSH receptors)

↓

Fibroblasts → differentiate into adipocytes + myofibroblasts

↓

Glycosaminoglycan (GAG) deposition (hyaluronic acid) → osmotic swelling

↓

Extraocular muscle enlargement + orbital fat expansion

↓

Proptosis, lid retraction, diplopia, optic nerve compression

High-Yield Exam Points

• Radioactive iodine (RAI) can actually worsen TED — important clinical caveat
• Treatment of TED = IV glucocorticoids (active phase) ± orbital decompression
• TED is most common cause of unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults

Why Each Option is True (and B is the odd one out)

| Option | True/False | Reasoning

| ------ | ---------- | ---------

| A Vision loss | TRUE | Optic nerve compression → compressive optic neuropathy

| B Eye response = adjuvant to thyrotoxicosis response | FALSE | TED activity is independent — eyes can worsen even when euthyroid

| C NOSPECS classification | TRUE | Standard grading: No signs, Only signs, Soft tissue, Proptosis, EOM, Corneal, Sight loss

| D 10% euthyroid patients | TRUE | TED occurs in hyper, hypo, and even euthyroid patients

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following drugs is not a secondary cause of weight gain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thyroxine

• A. Sulphonylureas: Can cause weight gain by increasing insulin secretion.
• B. Glucocorticoids: Cause weight gain through increased appetite, insulin resistance, and fat redistribution.
• C. Thyroxine: Correct. Thyroxine is generally associated with weight loss, not weight gain, when given appropriately. Excess thyroid hormone increases basal metabolic rate.
• D. β-blockers: Can cause modest weight gain, partly by reducing energy expenditure and physical activity tolerance.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: With regard to management of hypothyroidism, consider the following statements: 1. Treatment is with levothyroxine replacement. 2. It is taken as a single daily dose. 3. Average dose is 1.6 μg/kg/day. 4. Full dose per weight should be started in those with coronary artery disease. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Hypothyroidism is treated with lifelong levothyroxine (T4) replacement, which restores normal thyroid hormone levels and normalizes TSH. Levothyroxine is administered as a single daily oral dose, preferably on an empty stomach, and the dose is adjusted according to TSH levels, age, body weight, and associated comorbidities.

Why is A correct?

• 1. Treatment is with levothyroxine replacement: Levothyroxine (T4) is the treatment of choice for hypothyroidism.
• 2. It is taken as a single daily dose: Owing to its long half-life (\~7 days), levothyroxine is administered once daily.
• 3. Average dose is 1.6 μg/kg/day: The full replacement dose in healthy adults is approximately 1.6 μg/kg/day.

Incorrect statement:

• 4. Full dose per weight should be started in those with coronary artery disease: Patients with coronary artery disease or elderly patients should be started on a low dose (12.5–25 μg/day) and titrated gradually to avoid precipitating angina, arrhythmias, or myocardial infarction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: With regards to treatment of thyrotoxicosis of Graves’ disease, consider the following statements: 1. Propylthiouracil is suitable in breastfeeding patients. 2. Large goitre is an indication for thyroidectomy. 3. Radioiodine is recommended for management in pregnancy. 4. Agranulocytosis is a complication associated with carbimazole. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

Graves’ disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism, resulting from TSH receptor-stimulating autoantibodies. Treatment options include antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine (RAI), and thyroidectomy, with the choice depending on the patient’s age, pregnancy status, goiter size, and comorbidities.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Propylthiouracil is suitable in breastfeeding patients✅: PTU (and low-dose methimazole/carbimazole) can be used during breastfeeding, as only small amounts are secreted into breast milk.
• 2. Large goitre is an indication for thyroidectomy✅: Surgery is preferred in patients with large goiters, compressive symptoms, suspected malignancy, or those unsuitable for RAI.
• 4. Agranulocytosis is a complication associated with carbimazole✅: A rare but serious adverse effect of carbimazole and methimazole; patients should stop the drug and seek medical attention if they develop fever or sore throat.

Incorrect statement:

• 3. Radioiodine is recommended for management in pregnancy❌: Radioiodine is absolutely contraindicated during pregnancy and lactation, as it crosses the placenta and destroys the fetal thyroid gland.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 19-year-old woman with no comorbidities presented with numbness and paraesthesia of the fingers along with the characteristic finding as shown in the image below. She has no other illnesses and she says these episodes occur when she is under excess stress or during cold climates. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary Raynaud's phenomenon

The image along with the history of no previous illness is most likely of primary Raynaud's phenomenon.

Raynaud's phenomenon:

* Episodic digital ischemia due to the vasospasm of digital arteries.

* Cold exposure or emotional stress can trigger it.

* The blanching/ischemic phase of the phenomenon with pallor/cyanosis is often accompanied by numbness and paraesthesia.

* Capillaries and venules dilate and cyanosis results from the deoxygenated blood that is present in these vessels.

* Color changes are usually well-demarcated and are confined to the fingers or toes.

* In the rewarming phase, digital vasospasm resolves and blood flows into the dilated arterioles and capillaries increase dramatically causing reactive hyperemia which imparts bright red color to the digits.

* Some may experience only pallor cyanosis while others experience both pallor and cyanosis.

Types of Raynaud's:
1.Primary/idiopathic

2. Secondary associated with other diseases like:

* Collagen vascular diseases: scleroderma, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, dermatomyositis, polymyositis

* Arterial occlusive diseases: atherosclerosis of the extremities, thromboangiitis
obliterans, acute arterial occlusion

* Neurologic disorders: intervertebral disk disease, syringomyelia

* Blood dyscrasias: cold agglutinins, cryoglobulinemia, cryofibrinogenemia,

* Trauma: vibration injury, electric shock, cold injury, typing, piano playing

* Drugs and toxins: ergot derivatives, methysergide, β-adrenergic receptor
blockers

Management:

* Reassurance, warm clothing, and avoiding cold exposures.
exposure.

* Reduce or abstain from smoking and reduce stress levels.

* Drug treatments such as CCB's(nifedipine, amlodipine), alpha 1 blockers ( prazosin) are used only for advanced cases.

* In secondary Raynauds's Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors like sildenafil, tadalafil may improve symptoms.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 25 year old male developed progressive loss of vision in both the eyes who has been on low dose oral steroid therapy for last 10 years.What is the most likely reason for his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cataract

A common side effect of long-term steroid intake is cataracts.

The most common type of cataract seen in steroid-induced is posterior subcapsular cataract.

Drugs causing cataracts:

Drugs
Type of cataract

Corticosteroids
Discoid, posterior subcapsular

Anticholinesterases
Anterior subcapsular

Chlorpromazine
Yellow-brown anterior capsular granules/stellate/anterior polar

Busulfan
Posterior subcapsular

Chloroquine
White, flaky, posterior subcapsular

Amiodarone
Anterior subcapsular

Pearl PF1393: Diseases and Their Associated Cataracts

Disease

Type of cataract

Myotonic dystrophy

Christmas tree cataract

Wilson’s disease

Copper deposition (Chalcosis)

Penetrating trauma

Sunflower cataract

Diabetes mellitus

Snowflake/ Snowstorm cataract

Down's syndrome

Stellate/ Snowflake/ Snowstorm cataract

Hypoparathyroidism (Hypocalcemia)

Hypovitaminosis D

Congenital lamellar (zonular) cataract

Atopic dermatitis

Shield cataract (anterior subcapsular)

Posterior subcapsular cataract

Congenital rubella

Nuclear cataract

Galactosemia

Oil drop cataract

(Reversible cataract)

Complicated cataract

(Iridocyclitis, high myopia)

Posterior subcapsular cataract

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old male was brought to the emergency room with a history of RTA. GCS progressively declines over hours and axial T2 MRI below shows multiple small hypointense lesions at corticomedullary junction and basal ganglia, what is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diffuse axonal injury

Axial T2 -weighted MR image at the equivalent level demonstrates numerous foci of haemorrhage not seen on CT, manifesting as multiple hypointense punctate foci within the subcortical and deep white matter of both hemispheres and within the corpus callosum. It is suggestive of diffuse axonal injury.

Diffuse axonal injury (white matter shearing) is the result of shearing forces, typically from rotational acceleration.

Diffuse axonal injury is characterised by multiple focal lesions with a characteristic distribution:

* Typically located at the grey-white matter junction, in the corpus callosum and in more severe cases in the brainstem.

* CT may be normal.

* MRI is the modality of choice for assessing suspected diffuse axonal injury even in patients with entirely normal CT of the brain.

* MRI, particularly using SWI (Susceptibility Weighted Imaging) or GRE (Gradient Echo) sequences, reveals small susceptibility artefacts. These are typically seen at the grey-white matter junction, corpus callosum, or brainstem.

Pearl PF1100: Diffuse Axonal Injury

Features of diffuse axonal injury

Mechanism
Primarily a non-impact rotational acceleration-decceleration injury (this leads to deformation of the axons by stretching them)

Pathology

Changes in permeability of the axolemma

Axonal swelling

Intracellular calcium accumulation

Proteolysis

Collapse of the cytoskeleton

Histology

'Retraction balls or globes' - bulbous and clubbed axons. Seen earliest at 12-18 hours.

Immuno-histochemistry

Beta-amyloid precursor protein - considered to be the most reliable indicator of axon damage. Seen earliest at 2-3 hours.

Retraction balls:

* The force generated by violent shaking or rotational injury (as in a passenger ejected from the moving vehicle) can produce stretching of axons in cerebral white matter.

* Microscopic examination does not show any axonal injuries up to 12 hrs after injury

* After 12 hrs the axons first appear dilated then club shaped and finally appear as round balls known as retraction balls which indicates transected axons.

* The number of retraction balls begins to decrease after 2-3 weeks after injury and cluster of microglial cells appear followed by astrocytosis and demyelination.

Image shows scattered axonal retraction balls stained with Congo Red (arrows):

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy has presented with multiple episodes of hematemesis. On admission his vitals are stable and splenomegaly is noted. The mother tells that at birth the boy had developed jaundice and an exchange transfusion procedure had been performed through the umbilicus after birth. The most likely cause of hematemesis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Portal vein thrombosis

The most likely cause of hemetemesis in this patient is Portal vein thrombosis.

Hemetemesis along with splenomegaly is suggestive of portal hypertension.

The mother says that he has gone an exchange transfusion via umbilical catheterization and after birth. As catheter acts as a foreign body it might have caused thrombosis of the portal vein leading to portal hypertension.

The umbilical vein drains into portal vein with around 50% of the blood entering  the hepatic circulation while the other 50% bypasses the liver to enter the inferior vena cava.

The fetal circulation :

Other options:

B) Sinusoidal fibrosis refers to the deposition of fibrous tissue within the liver sinusoids. While this condition can contribute to liver dysfunction, it is less likely to be the primary cause of hematemesis in this case.

C) Hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (previously known as veno-occlusive disease) is a condition characterized by the blockage of small hepatic veins, resulting in congestion within the liver. It can cause liver dysfunction but is not typically associated with hematemesis.

D) Budd-Chiari syndrome is a condition characterized by the obstruction of the hepatic veins, leading to impaired blood flow out of the liver. It can cause liver dysfunction and portal hypertension, but it is less likely to present with splenomegaly and hematemesis in a young child.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with sudden onset of a headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating. He had several such episodes in the past. During these episodes, his BP is found to be high. A 24-hour urinary metanephrine is elevated. What is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pheochromocytoma

The most likely etiology is pheochromocytoma. Patients commonly present with a classical triad of palpitation, headache and profuse sweating. The presence of this triad in association with hypertension and elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrine makes pheochromocytoma a likely diagnosis.

Pheochromocytoma is one of the important endocrine causes of secondary hypertension.

Secondary causes of hypertension are:

* Renal causes- Renal artery stenosis, renal cysts, fibromuscular dysplasia

* Adrenal causes- Primary aldosteronism, Cushing's syndrome, pheochromocytoma

* Other endocrine causes- Hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, acromegaly

* Coarctation of aorta

* Obstructive sleep apnea

* Preeclampsia/eclampsia

* Prolonged use of oral contraceptive pills, adrenal steroids, nasal decongestants can also cause hypertension

* Monogenic hypertension- these conditions are due to the mutation of a single gene. Eg. Liddle's syndrome

Pearl PF0131: Clinical features of Pheochromocytoma (By frequency of occurrence)

* Clinical triad:

* Headaches – M/C symptom

* Profuse sweating

* Palpitations and tachycardia

* Hypertension, sustained or paroxysmal – M/C Sign

* Anxiety and panic attacks

* Weight loss

* Polyuria and polydipsia

* Constipation

* Orthostatic hypotension

* Dilated cardiomyopathy

* Erythrocytosis

* Elevated blood sugar

* Hypercalcemia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents to the OPD with palpitation and weight loss. On examination, both of her legs had the following lesion given below. On applying pressure, the indentation does not persist on release. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. What is the probable etiological cause for the oedema?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myxedema

A bilateral presentation of non-pitting oedema in the lower limbs along with features of palpitation and weight loss in the given scenario point towards a diagnosis of pretibial myxedema. And most probably it is due to the underlying thyroid disease.

Pretibial myxedema/Thyroid dermopathy  (localized edematous and thickened pretibial plaque formation) in seen secondary to Grave's disease.

Other options:

Option C: While chronic lymphangitis and acute lymphatic filariasis can also cause non-pitting oedema, they usually have a unilateral/localized presentation and the given clinical history is not relevant to this condition.

Option B and D: Nephrotic syndrome and heart failure cause bilateral pitting oedema. Also, the clinical scenario given above does not fit either of them.

Causes of generalized oedema include:

* Heart failure

* Chronic renal failure

* Nephrotic syndrome

* Liver cirrhosis

Causes of localized oedema:

* Thrombophlebitis

* Chronic lymphangitis

* Resection of regional lymph nodes

* Filariasis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 37-year-old male who is a chronic alcoholic abstained from alcohol. 3 days later, he was brought to the emergency with complaints of disorientation, tremors, hallucinations, and hypertension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Delirium tremens

The clinical features are suggestive of delirium tremens.

Delirium tremens occurs after 2-4 days of abstinence in a heavy or chronic drinker. It usually resolves spontaneously in 7 days but may cause the death of the patient due to cardiovascular collapse or infections or self-injury.

The characteristic clinical features include:

* Clouding of consciousness with disorientation in time and place.

* Distractibility and lack of attention.

* Visual, auditory, and/or tactile hallucinations.

* Autonomic disturbance with tachycardia, fever, hypertension, sweating and pupillary dilatation.

* Psychomotor agitation and ataxia

* Insomnia

* Dehydration with electrolyte imbalance.

Delirium tremens is treated using benzodiazepines starting with a higher dosage which is gradually tapered as withdrawal symptoms disappear. In cases of chronic alcohol use, vitamin deficiency (especially thiamine) may be co-existing and hence bolus doses of thiamine are given to prevent/treat Wernicke encephalopathy.

Other options:

* Alcoholic hallucinosis is characterised by the presence of hallucinations (usually auditory) during partial or complete abstinence. However, the other symptoms given in the question are not seen, and the patient present with clear consciousness.

* Korsakoff ’s psychosis: It is seen n patients with chronic alcohol use usually followed by Wernicke’s encephalopathy, together referred to as Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Patients with korsakoff's psychosis present with memory disturbances, which is not seen in the given case.

* Marchiafava-Bignami disease is a rare disorder seen in chronic alcoholics, associated with epilepsy, ataxia, dysarthria, hallucinations, spastic limb paralysis, and deterioration of personality and intellectual functioning.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 46-year-old chronic alcoholic male presents to the OPD with fever, headache, shortness of breath, chest pain, and productive cough for the last two days. On examination, there was bronchial breathing on the right side, increased vocal fremitus, increased vocal resonance, and a dull note on percussion. The patient's plain radiograph is shown below. Which is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Klebsiella pneumoniae

The given clinical scenario is highly suggestive of lobar pneumonia. The above chest x-ray shows a bulging fissure sign. The likely causative organism is Klebsiella pneumoniae.

Klebsiella pneumonia is associated mostly with alcoholics and shows upper lobe involvement, cavitation, and pneumatocele (also seen in S. aureus). The patient presents with red currant-jelly sputum.

A bulging fissure sign is classically seen in Klebsiella pneumonia. It represents expansive lobar consolidation causing fissural bulging or displacement by copious amounts of inflammatory exudate within the affected parenchyma. Classically, it is associated with right upper lobe consolidation due to Klebsiella pneumonia.

Other diseases that manifest a bulging fissure include any space-occupying process in the lung, such as pulmonary hemorrhage, lung abscess, and tumor.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 47-year-old woman was brought to the casualty in an unconscious state after having suddenly collapsed. As there was no pulse, cardiopulmonary resuscitation was started and the monitor showed the following rhythm. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 mg epinephrine IV

The patient has an organized, apparently normal ECG without a pulse - i.e the patient has pulseless electrical activity (PEA). A pulseless electrical activity involves a heterogeneous group of cardiac rhythms all without a pulse.

The immediate treatment for this is giving chest compressions and 1 mg epinephrine at the earliest until more definitive therapy to the cause can be instituted.

It is essential to rule out the reversible causes of cardiac arrest because the treatment for each of them is different and PEA is likely to persist until the cause is treated.
