* 5 H’s:

* Hypovolemia

* Hypoxia

* Hydrogen ion (acidosis)

* Hypokalemia or hyperkalemia

* Hypothermia

* 5 T’s:

* Tension pneumothorax

* Tamponade (cardiac)

* Toxins

* Thrombosis (pulmonary)

* Thrombosis (coronary)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old lady with hypertension is brought with shortness of breath and dyspnea on exertion for the past week. Physical examination reveals the presence of elevated jugular venous pressure and crepitations in the lungs along with palpable liver 3 cm below the costal margin. The image of her legs is given below what is the finding called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pitting pedal edema

The clinical scenario is likely of congestive cardiac failure and the physical finding is pitting pedal edema.

In congestive cardiac failure due to the increased peripheral venous pressure excess fluid transudates and causes the above finding of peripheral edema.

* Peripheral edema is usually symmetric and dependent in HF and occurs predominantly in the ankles and the pretibial region in ambulatory patients.

* In bedridden patients-edema may be found in the sacral area (presacral edema) and the scrotum.

* Long-standing edema may be associated with indurated and pigmented skin.

Pearl PF1527: Edema: Key Points

Edema: Key Points

Edema is the result of the movement of fluid from the vasculature into the interstitial spaces; the fluid may be protein-poor (transudate) or protein-rich (exudate).

Causes:

* Increased hydrostatic pressure (e.g., heart failure)

* Decreased colloid osmotic pressure caused by reduced plasma albumin, either due to decreased synthesis (e.g., liver disease, protein malnutrition) or to increased loss (e.g., nephrotic syndrome)

* Increased vascular permeability (e.g., inflammation), which is usually localized but may occur throughout the body in severe systemic inflammatory states such as sepsis

* Lymphatic obstruction (e.g., infection or neoplasia)

* Sodium and water retention (e.g., renal failure)

Pearl PF1528: Summary of Pathogenesis of Major Findings in Congestive Heart Failure

Summary of Pathogenesis of Major Findings in Congestive Heart Failure

Abnormality

Cause

Weakness, exercise intolerance, fatigue

Left ventricle output inadequate to perfuse muscles; especially, failure of output to rise with exercise

Ankle, sacral edema

Increased peripheral venous pressure →increased fluid transudation.

Hepatomegaly

Increased peripheral venous pressure →increased resistance to portal flow.

Pulmonary congestion

Increased pulmonary venous pressure →pulmonary venous distention and transudation of fluid into air spaces

Dyspnea on exertion

Failure of left ventricular output to rise during exercise → increased pulmonary venous pressure

Paroxysmal dyspnea, pulmonary edema

Probably a sudden failure of left heart output to keep up with the right heart output →acute rise in pulmonary venous and capillary pressure →transudation of fluid into air spaces.

Orthopnea

Normal pooling of blood in lungs in supine position added to the already congested pulmonary vascular system; increased venous return not put out by the left ventricle. (Relieved by sitting up, raising the head of the bed, lying on extra pillows.)

Cardiac dilation

Greater ventricular end-diastolic volume.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of chest pain which is seen only on exertion or exercise and lasts 2-5 minutes. He was assessed and was diagnosed with a case of stable angina however his BP was consistently elevated. What is the most appropriate antihypertensive for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atenolol

The antihypertensive drug of choice in stable angina is beta-blockers which is atenolol here.

Atenolol is a cardioselective beta-blocker that works by decreasing cardiac contractility and heart rate which decreases cardiac output and blood pressure.

Beta-blockers are also used in congestive cardiac failure which has been shown to decrease their mortality rates.

Stable angina:

* Stable angina is caused by an imbalance in coronary perfusion (due to chronic stenosing coronary atherosclerosis) relative to myocardial demand.

* Squeezing, central, substernal discomfort

* Crescendo-decrescendo in nature

* Typically lasts 2 to 5 min

* Can radiate to either shoulder & to both arms (especially the ulnar surfaces of the forearm & hand)

* It also can arise in or radiate to the back, interscapular region, the root of the neck, jaw, teeth, and epigastrium.

Other types of angina

* Prinzmetal variant angina is an uncommon form of episodic myocardial ischemia; it is caused by coronary artery spasm.

* Unstable or crescendo angina refers to a pattern of increasingly frequent, prolonged (>20 min), or severe angina or chest discomfort that is described as frank pain, precipitated by progressively lower levels of physical activity or even occurring at rest.

Pearl PF0731: Anti-anginal drugs

Anti-anginal drugs can be divided into the following categories:

* Nitrates - Dilates veins > arteries. Reduces preload.

* Calcium channel blockers - Blocks L-type calcium channels

* Dihydropyridines - Amlodipine, nifedipine

* Non-dihydropyridines - Verapamil, Diltiazem

* Beta-blockers - Decreases heart rate, contractility and oxygen demand

* Other drugs

* Ranolazine - Late Na+ channel blocker

* Ivabradine - Inhibit funny currents in SA node

* Nicorandil - K+-ATP channel agonist

* Trimetazidine - pFOX inhibitor

* Fasudil - Rho-kinase inhibitor

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman presented with deformity of the hand as shown below. There is decreased motion in the small joints and loss of wrinkle lines on the facial skin. Her chest radiograph showed prominent bilateral lower lobe infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scleroderma

In the above clinical scenario of a woman presenting with decreased motion of small joints, loss of wrinkles on face, chest x-ray showing bilateral lower lobe infiltrates, and image showing sclerodactyly are suggestive of scleroderma.

Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by progressive fibrosis caused by excessive deposition of extracellular matrix in various tissues and organs. The key features of SSc include vascular injury, inflammation, and the presence of disease-specific autoantibodies.

SSc is classified into two types based on the extent of skin involvement.

* Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis / CREST syndrome

* Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis

In limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc) or CREST syndrome, fibrosis affects the acral areas of the body - mainly the face and the skin distal to the elbows and knees. The progression of skin fibrosis is slow, but microvascular changes, such as Raynaud’s phenomenon, often appear years before skin involvement. LcSSc generally has a favorable prognosis, with a 10-year survival rate exceeding 90%.

CREST syndrome consists of the following:

* Calcinosis cutis

* Raynaud’s phenomenon

* Esophageal dysmotility

* Sclerodactyly

* Telangiectasia

The images shows features of Raynaud's phenomenon and calcinosis cutis:

The antibodies tested in systemic sclerosis include:

* Antinuclear antibody (ANA) - positive in most cases of systemic sclerosis. The absence of this antibody suggests considering an alternate diagnosis.

* Antitopoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibody - usually positive with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

* Anti-RNA polymerase I and III antibodies - usually positive with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

* Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) - usually positive in limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

The common pulmonary manifestations of scleroderma include interstitial lung disease(ILD), and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) leading to cor pulmonale.

Management is based on disease-modifying and organ-specific drugs. For

* Raynaud’s phenomenon and digital ulcers: Warm socks and gloves are recommended. Calcium channel blockers, sildenafil, fluoxetine and losartan can be added if symptoms persist. Prostacyclin and bosentan can be used for healing of digital ulcers.

* GI complications: Esophageal dysmotility can be treated with domperidone or metoclopramide. Bacterial overgrowth has to be treated with antibiotics.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 53-year-old patient was brought to the emergency room with altered sensorium and rapid shallow breathing. His abdomen is distended with palpable hepatomegaly and splenomegaly and sclerae are icteric. The other examination findings are given below. Laboratory tests show that the AST: ALT ratio is 3:1. What is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alcoholic liver disease

In the above clinical scenario of a patient presenting with altered consciousness, jaundice (scleral icterus), and signs of liver cirrhosis (distended abdomen, hepatomegaly), spider naevi, Terry nails, and the characteristic AST>ALT is suggestive of alcoholic liver disease.

In alcoholic liver disease, the AST:ALT ratio is typically >2:1. A ratio of >3:1 is strongly supportive and seen in significant alcohol-related liver injury.

The ratio is due to the deficiency of pyridoxal 5’-phosphate seen in alcoholics. It is a cofactor needed for ALT activity.

* Aspartate transaminase (AST) - 10-40 IU/L

* Alanine transaminase (ALT) - 10-40 IU/L

The AST:ALT ratio can be interpreted as follows:

AST:ALT
Condition

<1
Chronic viral hepatitis, Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease

>1
Cirrhosis

>2:1

Suggestive of alcoholic liver disease

Alcohol intake is associated with the deficiency of pyridoxal phosphate, which in turn leads to decreased levels of ALT enzyme. So, AST>ALT.

>3:1
Highly suggestive of alcoholic liver disease

Other options:

Option B: In acute viral hepatitis, the aminotransferases are often elevated > 500 IU (400-4000 IU/L) due to extensive cell injury.

Option C: In autoimmune hepatitis, aminotransferase levels are elevated and fluctuate in the range of 100-1000 IU/L. Autoimmune hepatitis may present as acute or chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis. Commonly associated symptoms include fatigue, anorexia, pruritis, arthralgias, upper abdominal discomfort, and skin rashes including acne among others.

Option D: Acute acetaminophen poisoning (paracetamol tablets ingestion).In acute acetaminophen poisoning, the aminotransferases are elevated > 1000 IU and may exceed 10,000 IU/L due to acute hepatocellular injury.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old patient presented with chronic projectile vomiting and weight loss. What is the expected metabolic abnormality to be seen here?
options: Hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hyponatremia
Hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypernatremia
Hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypercalcemia
Hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic acidosis with hyponatremia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hyponatremia

The expected metabolic abnormality to be seen in this patient is hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hyponatremia.

The persistent vomiting results in these abnormalities along with paradoxical aciduria.

* Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-).

* Kidneys try to compensate for alkalosis by secreting Na+ and HCO3- causing hyponatremia. However, loss of sodium stimulates the secretion of aldosterone through the RAAS pathway.

* The aldosterone causes active reabsorption of sodium in exchange for K+ and H+ ions.

* Loss of potassium ions leads to the development of hypokalemia.

* Loss of H+ ions in urine lowers the urinary pH resulting in aciduria. It is called paradoxical aciduria since the body initially loses H+ ions due to the loss of HCl, and instead of compensating for that loss, the body is losing more H+ ions through urine.

Pearl PF0290: Causes of Acid-Base Disorders

Metabolic acidosis

Metabolic alkalosis

Respiratory acidosis

Respiratory alkalosis

Chronic renal failure

questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presents with weakness in right arm for 6 hours duration. The weakness gradually became lesser and resolves. She is a known case of diabetes and hypertension and is obese.Which of the following is the probable diagnosis of this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Transient ischaemic attack

The clinical scenario with weakness of arms lasting for less than 24 hours is most likely a Transient ischaemic attack.

Transient Ischaemic attack:

* episodes of stroke symptoms that last only<24 h(most TIAs last <1 h).

* arise from the emboli to the brain or insitu thrombosis of an intracranial vessel.

* in TIA the occluded blood vessel reopens and thus the neurologic function is restored.

* risk factors include hypertension ,atrial fibrillation ,diabetes ,smoking,hyperlipidemia.

* if imaging(CT/MRI) shows brain infarction then it is a stroke, regardless of the duration of symptoms.

* can progress to stroke and the risk of future stroke is calculated using the ABCD2 score.

* combination of aspirin and clopidogrel is given to decrease the risk of stroke following TIA.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old male patient presented with chest pain, exertional dyspnea and syncope. He was diagnosed as a case of Aortic stenosis and his Chest Xray was taken which is shown below.What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Post stenotic dilatation of aorta

The most likely diagnosis is post stenotic dilatation of aorta.

Post-stenotic dilatation is seen in patients with AS and/or aortic regurgitation, patients with a haemodynamically normal bicuspid aortic valve and following aortic valve replacement.

The aetiology is unknown  and it may involve an abnormality in the process of extracellular matrix remodelling in the aortic wall including inadequate synthesis, degradation and transport of extracellular matrix proteins.It can be attributed to haemodynamic factors caused by a stenotic valve( aortic stenosis commonly),involving high velocity and turbulent flow downstream of the stenosis, or due to intrinsic pathology of the aortic wall.

Aortic stenosis is narrowing of the aortic valve. It may be caused due to the calcification of normal aortic valve, calcification of congenital bicuspid valve and rheumatic heart disease.

Three cardinal clinical features of aortic stenosis are:

* Exertional dyspnea: This occurs due to the left ventricular(LV) diastolic dysfunction. Raised end-diastolic LV volume and reduced LV compliance lead to increased LV pressure, leading to elevation of pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. This causes exertional dyspnea.

* Angina pectoris: It occurs due to the combination of the increased O2 needs of hypertrophied myocardium and reduction of O2 delivery

* Syncope: It occurs due to the combination of decreased cardiac output and systemic arterial dilation which lead to reduction of cerebral perfusion.

questions.text: A 68-year-old male came to the physician with complaints of chronic back pain and easy fatigability and past history of multiple urinary tract infections in the last 3 months. His ESR is elevated and X-ray of his skull is shown below. Which of the following investigations is useful for diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serum electrophoresis

Chronic back pain , elevated ESR and typical “punched out” lesions on Xray is consistent with the suspected diagnosis of Multiple Myeloma in this case. The investigation helpful in diagnosis in the above options is serum electrophoresis.

Multiple myeloma involves a malignant proliferation of plasma cells, resulting in excessive production of abnormal immunoglobulins, causing a spike called the M band in Serum Electrophoresis.

The given image demonstrates a sharp peak ("church spire” or M band) in the gamma globulin region. This is characteristically seen in a patient with multiple myeloma.

Certain common diseases and their electrophoretic pattern:

Condition

Smooth increase in gamma globulins

Multiple myeloma
Gamma globulin part is increased (M BAND)

Reduced albumin and compensatory increase in globulin

Gamma globulin reduced

α1 antitrypsin deficiency
α1 band is thin and even lost sometimes

Multiple myelomas:

* Malignant neoplasm of plasma cells characterized by:

* Presence of monoclonal immunoglobulin or light chains in the serum and urine

* Bone destruction (lytic lesions)

* Disease of older adults, with a peak age of incidence of 65 to 70 years

* Signs and symptoms

* Hypercalcemia

* Pathologic fractures/lytic bone lesions

* Renal failure

* Anemia

* Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray

* Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin

* Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

* Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20%plasma cells (normal is < 5%)

* Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation (High level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation.)

* Plasma cell tumors are positive for CD138

Note:

* Recurrent bacterial infections causing pneumonia and urinary tract infections due to reduced immunity because of hypogammaglobulinemia and abnormalities in T-cell functions.

* Normocytic normochromic anemia is seen as a result of the replacement of bone marrow by tumor cells and reduced renal function.

* Chronic inflammation, increased plasma cells and anemia result in increased ESR in multiple myeloma patients.

* Bone pain caused by the proliferation of tumor cells and increased osteoclast activity. There is also suppression of osteoblast activity to form new bone. This results in hypercalcemia.

* Bone alkaline phosphatase is a marker of bone growth and is not increased in this patient due to suppressed osteoblast activity.

questions.text: A patient has approximately 20 episodes of loose stools per day and a reduced urine output. Which of the following laboratory values will be seen in this patient? BUN:Cr -BUN (Blood Urea Nitrogen) and Creatinine ratio Urine Na- Urine sodium FENa- Fractional Excretion of Sodium
options: BUN:Cr >40:1, Urine Na <40, FENa <1%, Urine Osmolality >500
BUN:Cr >20:1, Urine Na <20, FENa <1%, Urine Osmolality >500
BUN:Cr >20:1, Urine Na <20, FENa <1%, Urine Osmolality >250
BUN:Cr >40:1, Urine Na <20, FENa <1%, Urine Osmolality >250
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. BUN:Cr >20:1, Urine Na <20, FENa <1%, Urine Osmolality >500

This patient is having prerenal azotemia due to dehydration from loose stools. The laboratory values consistent with the diagnosis of prerenal azotemia include BUN:Cr >20:1, urine Na <20, FENa <1%, and urine Osmolality >500.

AKI (acute kidney injury) is defined as a decline in kidney function within 7 days, resulting in the accumulation of nitrogenous waste and other toxic metabolites usually excreted in the urine. It includes a variety of conditions that share some common features such as elevated creatinine levels and reduced urine output. It is broadly divided into three categories:

Intrinsic causes can further be divided into acute tubular necrosis, acute glomerulonephritis, and acute interstitial nephritis. Ischemia and nephrotoxins are the main causes of acute tubular necrosis. Nephrotoxins can be exogenous, such as vancomycin, cisplatin, and iodinated contrast agents used for CT imaging. Endogenous toxins include myoglobin, uric acid, and haemoglobin. Crush injuries, heat stroke, and myopathies can result in rhabdomyolysis, releasing large amounts of myoglobin. The urine/plasma creatinine ratio is usually ≤ 40. In acute tubular necrosis, urinary sodium is >20 mEq/L.

Prerenal azotemia arises due to a reduced renal plasma flow. Common causes include hypovolemia, liver failure, and congestive heart failure. The urine/plasma creatinine ratio is ≥ 40, and urinary sodium is usually < 20mEq/L/L.

Bladder outlet obstruction, urethral obstruction, and benign prostatic hyperplasia lead to postrenal azotemia. Urinary sodium can be variable.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with symptoms of fatigue and a blood smear showed macrocytic anemia. Her methyl malonate levels were normal , however, homocystinuria was seen. Serum B12 values are normal. What is the appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Folate therapy

The most appropriate management in this patient with normal B12 stores is folate therapy.

The patient described presented with megaloblastic anemia. The most common causes include vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency. This patient has been empirically treated with folate supplements.

The metabolisms of folate and vitamin B12 are interlinked. Administering folate for patients with peripheral neuropathy and macrocytic anemia can improve the blood picture but aggravate the neurological symptoms due to unmasking of vitamin B12 deficiency.

Conversion of methyl tetrahydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate requires vitamin B12. Accumulation of methyl tetrahydrofolate due to vitamin B12 deficiency is called the folate trap. Supplementation of only folic acid thus depletes the stores of vitamin B12. Thus, for all patients being treated with folate, vitamin B12 supplementation is advised.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient who is a tour guide on Mount Everest presented with blisters on her hand as shown in the figure below. She has severe pain and on examination is erythematous and tender. Which of the following is not used in the management of this patient?
options: Apply heat to the area and cast it as soon as possible
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Apply heat to the area and cast it as soon as possible

The diagnosis in this patient is frostbite. Management does not involve the application of heat to the area and casts it as it is contraindicated in frostbite.

In frostbite, tissue damage results from severe environmental cold exposure or from direct contact with a very cold object. Tissue injury results from both freezing and vascular stasis. Frostbite typically involves the extremities or the exposed regions of the face. Clinical features include decreased sensation (especially for pain, and temperature sensations) in the acral tips and extremities. The affected area appears mottled,waxy or violaceous. Patients may have a wood-like sensation in the affected area.

Treatment:

* Initial treatment is by rapid rewarming, or thawing, where the affected area is placed in a water bath for 30 to 60 minutes at 37–40°C (99–104°F). Rewarming by exercise, rubbing, or friction is not advised.

* Analgesics such as ibuprofen are often required during rewarming.

* Antithrombotics, thrombolytics, and vasodilators such as prostacyclin can be given to improve circulation after rewarming.

* Frost bites are associated with an increased risk of infections and tetanus. Therefore, the injured area should be cleaned with soap or antiseptic, and sterile dressings should be applied. Tetanus prophylaxis must be given, but, empirical antibiotics are not recommended.

* The patient must be monitored for the development of compartment syndrome.

* Elective late amputation after imaging may be required in severe cases.

questions.text: A patient with breast carcinoma presents with swelling of ankle for the past 3 months. Urine examination shows heavy proteinuria and haematuria. Renal biopsy is likely to reveal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Membranous glomerulonephritis

A kidney biopsy in a patient with features of nephrotic syndrome secondary to carcinomas would most probably reveal membranous glomerulonephritis.

Membranous glomerulonephritis:

* Primary/idiopathic membranous glomerulonephritis

* Secondary membranous glomerulonephritis

* Infection: Hepatitis B and C, syphilis, malaria, schistosomiasis, leprosy, filariasis

* Cancer: Breast, colon, lung, stomach, kidney, esophagus, neuroblastoma

* Drugs: Gold, mercury, penicillamine, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents, probenecid

* Autoimmune diseases: Systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, primary biliary cirrhosis, dermatitis herpetiformis, bullous pemphigoid, myasthenia gravis, Sjogren’s syndrome, Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

* Other systemic diseases: Fanconi’s syndrome, sickle cell anemia, diabetes, Crohn’s disease, sarcoidosis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, Weber-Christian disease, angiofollicular lymph node hyperplasia.

* It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in the elderly.

* Most common nephropathy associated with malignancy.

* The highest incidence of renal vein thrombosis.

* Light microscopy shows uniform thickening of the basement membrane along with peripheral capillary loops.

* Immunofluorescence shows diffuse granular deposits of IgG and C3.

* Pathological findings:

* Light microscopy: Uniform thickening of the basement membrane along the peripheral capillary loops

* Immunofluorescence: Diffuse granular deposits of IgG and c3.

* Electron microscopy: Dense subepithelial deposits.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with inflammatory bowel disease presents with the following lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyoderma gangrenosum

The given image along with the history of Inflammatory bowel disease is most likely pyoderma gangrenosum.

Pyoderma gangrenosum:

* dermatological extraintestinal manifestation of IBD (inflammatory bowel disease).

* begins as a pustule and progresses to an ulcer with necrotic tissue and exudates.

* may occur years before the onset of bowel symptoms and is usually associated with severe disease.

* Lesions are commonly found on the dorsal surface of the feet and legs but may occur on the arms, chest, and even the face.

* very difficult to treat and often requires IV antibiotics and IV glucocorticoids.

* Other drugs used in its management include dapsone, IV cyclosporine, and infliximab.

Note:

Other dermatological manifestations associated with IBD include erythema nodosum, Sweet syndrome (neutrophilic dermatosis), perianal skin tags, psoriasis, and metastatic Crohn's disease (cutaneous granulomas).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A postoperative cardiac surgical patient developed sudden hypotension, raised central venous pressure, pulsus paradoxus at the 4th post operative hour. The most probable diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cardiac tamponade

The case is that of Cardiac tamponade as the patient has sudden Low BP and pulsus paradoxus.

Cardiac tamponade:

Accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space raises the intra pericardial pressure, hence poor ventricular filling and fall in cardiac output.

It is characterized by:

* Hypotension.

* Pulsus paradoxus.

* Increased pulse rate.

* Prominent X descent.

* Muffled heart sound.

* Ewart’s sign (bronchial breathing at left angle of scapula).

* Beck’s triad: Falling BP, Raised JVP, Small quiet heart.

Investigation:

* X-ray chest - Big globular heart.

* ECG - Low voltage, Electrical alternans.

* ECHO - Echo free zone around the heart.

* Cath - Diastolic collapse of right atrium and right ventricle.

Treatment: Drainage of fluid

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young male patient presents with a history of high-grade fever for the last 5 days. When his hands were examined, the following lesions were seen which were painless and a new regurgitant murmur is heard. Echocardiogram shows the presence of a mass on the mitral valve. Which of the following abdomen finding will be present here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Splenomegaly

In the above clinical scenario of a patient presenting with high-grade fever, new-onset murmur, and faint, red, painless macules on palms and soles (called as Janeway lesions), the most probable diagnosis for this patient would be infective endocarditis (IE). The most common abdominal finding is splenomegaly..

Infective endocarditis is characterized by the presence of large, friable, irregular vegetations on heart valves. Patients with infective endocarditis can have cardiac or non-cardiac manifestations.

Cardiac manifestations of IE:

* Presence of new regurgitant murmurs

* Congestive heart failure due to valve dysfunction

* Perivalvular abscesses and intracardiac fistulae- This is caused due to the extension of infection beyond the valves and into the adjacent myocardial tissue

* Conduction system defects- due to the damage of the interventricular septum by the abscess.

* Embolization of coronary arteries

Noncardiac manifestations of IE are:

* Arterial emboli- causing pain of ischemia of the organs

* Roth's spots- retinal hemorrhages with a pale center

* Janeway lesions- In contrast to Osler's nodes, these are faint, red, painless macules on palms and soles. They occur as a result of septic embolization and are commonly associated with staphylococcal IE.

* Glomerulonephritis

* Positivity for rheumatoid factor

* Petechiae on the oral and conjunctival mucosa

* Splinter subungual hemorrhages-painless, dark red lines in the nailbed.

* Mycotic aneurysms

* Splenomegaly

* Osler’s nodes (shown in the image below) are tender, red nodules that typically appear on the pads of the fingers and toes. Occurs due to immune complex deposition and vasculitis.

Image given below shows Roth spots.

Pearl PF0379: Modified Duke's criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis

Diagnosis of Infective endocarditis is by Duke's Criteria, which requires either:

* Clinical criteria

* Pathologic criteria

If clinical criteria are used, definitive endocarditis is defined by the presence of 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor criteria.

Presence of single pathological criteria is definitive of infective endocarditis.

Clinical Criteria

Major Criteria

1. Positive blood culture

Typical microorganism for IE from 2 separate blood cultures.

(or)

Persistently positive blood culture of an organism consistent with IE from:

• Blood cultures drawn >12 h apart.
• All of 3 or a majority of ≥4 separate blood cultures, with first and last drawn at least 1 h apart.

(or)

Single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetti or phase I IgG antibody titer of >1:800.

2. Evidence of endocardial involvement

Echocardiographic identification of oscillating intracardiac mass on valve or implant or in the path of regurgitant jets

(or)

New Valvular regurgitation

Minor Criteria

1. Predisposing heart lesion or intravenous drug use

2. Fever ≥38.0°C (≥100.4°F)

3. Vascular lesions: Major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival hemorrhages, Janeway lesions.

4. Immunological evidence: Glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor.

5. Microbiologic evidence: Positive blood culture but not meeting the major criterion, or serologic evidence of active infection with an organism consistent with infective endocarditis.

Pathological Criteria

1. Microorganisms demonstrated by culture or histologic examination, in vegetation, embolus from vegetation, or intracardiac abscess

(or)

2. Histologic confirmation of active endocarditis in vegetation or intracardiac abscess

Note: The diagnosis of endocarditis is rejected if an alternative diagnosis is established, if symptoms resolve and do not recur with ≤4 days of antibiotic therapy, or if surgery or autopsy after ≤4 days of antimicrobial therapy yields no histologic evidence of endocarditis.

questions.text: An 8-year-old girl presents with abrupt onset of fever, oliguria, nausea, smoky urine, and puffy eyes. The parents say that she had lesions on her face similar to the ones shown in the image below, 2 weeks ago which are now resolving. Which of the following findings will be present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. RBCs in urine

This patient's clinical features with h/o honey-crusted lesions on the face (impetigo) are suggestive of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Patients will present with haematuria and urine microscopy will reveal red blood cells.

The PSGN patient presents with hematuria, red cell casts in the urine, azotemia, oliguria, hypertension, mild to moderate proteinuria, and edema (features of the nephritic syndrome). It usually appears 1 to 4 weeks after a streptococcal infection of the pharynx or skin (impetigo). It occurs most frequently in children 6 to 10 years of age. In adults, it is less benign. Poststreptococcal GN is caused by immune complexes containing streptococcal antigens and specific antibodies, which are formed in situ.

The histologic picture shows enlarged hypercellular glomeruli. The hypercellularity is caused by infiltration by leukocytes and proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells. The proliferation and leukocyte infiltration are typically global and diffuse.

Some glomerular diseases may progress from one pattern to another or may present with considerable overlap between them, as a nephritic–nephrotic syndrome; features of nephrotic syndrome can concurrently occur with any form of nephritic syndrome but are most commonly seen with diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (seen in systemic lupus erythromytosus) and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.

Pearl PF1531: Skin and soft tissue lesions caused by Streptococcus

Streptococcus causes a variety of skin and soft tissue infections. These include:

a. Impetigo- Infection of superficial layers of the skin. It presents as superficial vesicles which break down and are then encrusted by honey-colored scab. It usually occurs in children.

The given image shows impetigo:

b. Erysipelas- Infection of the superficial epidermis. It presents as an erythematous raised lesion with sharply demarcated edges that differentiate it from the surrounding skin.

The given image shows erysipelas- note the clear demarcation at the nasolabial folds seen in facial erysipelas.

c. Cellulitis- Infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue. It presents with erythema and edema. It can be differentiated from erysipelas by - i. Erysipelas is a raised lesion whereas cellulitis is not, ii. Cellulitis is poorly demarcated from the surrounding skin whereas erysipelas is clearly demarcated.

The given image shows cellulitis:

d. Necrotizing fasciitis- Infection involving the fascial planes. It presents with dark areas of necrosis, erythema, and edema.

The given image shows necrotizing fasciitis with areas of erythema and necrosis:

d. Myositis and myonecrosis- Infection of the muscle.

The given image shows necrotizing myositis:

questions.text: Prophylactic cranial radiation is given for which of the following cancers?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lung cancer

Prophylactic cranial irradiation is given in lung cancer, more specifically small cell carcinoma of lung.

Prophylactic cranial irradiation(PCI) is given to  either LD-SCLC(limited disease small cell lung carcinoma) or ED-SCLC(end stage small cell lung carcinoma) who have responded
well to initial therapy.

In LD-SCLC patients complete remission is seen while in ED-SCLC the occurence of symptomatic brain metastases is decreased and prolonged disease free interval compared to when no PCI.

Small-cell carcinoma of the lung is the most aggressive type of lung cancer.

This tumor originates from neuroendocrine progenitor cells (Kulchitsky cells), which are present in the lining bronchial epithelium.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The device seen in the following image is____?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cardiac pacemaker

The device shown in the figure is a cardiac pacemaker.

A cardiac pacemaker is an electronic device kept under the skin that senses intrinsic heart rhythms and provides electrical stimulation when indicated.

In adults, permanent pacemakers are most commonly implanted with access to the heart by way of the subclavian–superior vena cava venous system.

The three types of cardiac pacemaking are

*

Single-chamber pacemaker–one pacing lead is implanted in the right atrium or ventricle.

*

Dual-chamber pacemaker-two pacing leads are implanted (one in the right ventricle and one in the right atrium) which is the most common type of cardiac pacemaking.

*

Biventricular pacing (cardiac resynchronization therapy [CRT])- in addition to single-or dual-chamber right heart pacing leads, a lead is advanced to the coronary sinus for left ventricular epicardial pacing.

The most common indications for cardiac pacemaking: SA Node dysfunction, Carotid sinus hypersensitivity, and vasovagal syncope.

In SA Node dysfunction some of the indications are :

* symptomatic bradycardia or sinus pause

* due to essential long-term drug
therapy.

* symptomatic chronotropic incompetence

* atrial fibrillation with bradycardia and pauses >5

* syncope of unknown origin

Complications:

1. Acute

* infection

* hematoma

* pneumothorax

* cardiac perforation

* diaphragmatic/phrenic nerve stimulation

* lead dislodgment

2. Chronic

* infection

* erosion

* lead failure

Rotation of the pacemaker pulse generator in its subcutaneous pocket is referred to as “twiddler’s syndrome” can wrap the leads around the generator and produce dislodgment with failure of the pacemaker.

Enhancements in battery technology and component design have produced a pacing system small enough to be implanted in the heart without the need for a transvenous lead.

questions.text: The flow-volume curve of a patient after spirometry is given below. The most likely diagnosis in this patient is______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. COPD

The flow-volume curve above shows an obstructive type of disease which is COPD(chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) in the options.

Diseases like COPD, Asthma, emphysema, endobronchial neoplasm present with obstructive flow patterns. Although all airflow is diminished, expiratory prolongation predominates, and MEF < MIF.  The increased total lung capacity, vital capacity, and residual volume will shift the flow volume loop to left.

Other options:

Myasthenia gravis, asbestosis presents with ventilatory restriction due to reduced respiratory muscle strength. The flow-volume curve shows decreased Total lung capacity, Vital capacity, Residual volume. Hence, the loop shifts towards the right. This is seen in restrictive lung disease.

In Vocal cord paralysis there is variable extrathoracic upper airway obstruction therefore the inspiratory curve is flattened.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Visual field testing of a patient revealed the following type of loss. Where is the likely site of lesion in optic pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Occipital lobe

The image shows homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. The likely site of the lesion is occipital lobe.

Homonymous hemianopia (HH) involves loss of vision on the same side of the visual field in both eyes. HH is characteristically seen in lesions involving the visual pathway posterior to the optic chiasma.

HH may be either complete or incomplete.

* A complete HH is characterised by loss of entire hemifield on the same side in both eyes.

* An incomplete HH is characterised by partial loss of visual field on the same side in both eyes. Incomplete HH is further classified as congruous or incongruous, depending on whether the extent of partial loss of visual field in both the eyes is same or different, respectively.

Lesions involving occipital lobe usually shows macular sparing because macular representation is seperate and quite large as compared to peripheral vision. Moreover, macular area in occipital lobe is supplied both by posterior and middle cerebral artery. In case of vascular lesions (eg stroke) affecting occipital lobe, it is less likely to involve both these arteries.

Pearl PF0246: Lesions in the optic pathway

Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above.

* The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other.

* A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye.

* Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia.

* A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness).

* Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

questions.text: Which clinical examination is being done in the picture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fluid thrill

The clinical examination elicited is Fluid thrill.

The fluid thrill is elicited to clinically diagnose ascites.

It is not a reliable sign and is only felt when there is a large amount of fluid under tension.

Method: The patient is placed supine and his abdomen is exposed after consent. Place one hand of the examiner flat over the lumbar region while an assistant's hand is kept firmly on the midline of the abdomen with the side of his hand kept longitudinally. This is done to dampen any impulse that can be transmitted via the fat of the abdominal wall. Now the examiner flicks or taps the opposite side of the abdomen where his palm is not resting and a fluid thrill or wave is felt on the resting hand.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common delayed symptom of head and neck radiation therapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Xerostomia

The most common delayed symptom of head and neck radiation therapy is xerostomia.

Complications of Radiotherapy

* Xerostomia- most common

* Mucositis

* Temporary or permanent dysgeusia (altered taste perception)

* Osteoradionecrosis is related to tooth caries and results from decreased production of saliva and damage to the microvasculature of the mandible and maxilla.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following pneumoconiosis is associated with an increased incidence of tuberculosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Silicosis

Silicosis is associated with an increased incidence of tuberculosis.

Silica causes pulmonary alveolar macrophage dysfunction and hence, patients with silicosis have a higher risk of developing lung infections from organisms like M. Tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria and fungi.

Radiographic imaging of silicotuberculosis shows cavitation.

In silicotuberculosis: it is still unclear whether silico-tuberculotics are really tubercular or purely silicosis, because

* Sputum is rarely AFB+ve

* Children and women of silicotuberculosis patients do not develop tuberculosis

* The post-mortem on silicotuberculosis fail to prove the existence of tuberculosis disease

* Radiological evidence of both the condition is similar

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old child was brought to the OPD following a sting on his toe. On examination, he had tachycardia, hypertension, tongue fasciculations, hypersalivation, and dilated pupils. Local examination of the wound showed mild erythema. He remembers the animal having a curved tail upwards. Which of the following has most likely bitten him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Scorpion

The clinical stem with the description of the animal is suggestive of a scorpion bite.

Most scorpion stings cause pain at the site of the bite. Systemic toxicity occurs in <10% of stings but is more commonly seen in infants and children. The venom is a clear, colorless toxalbumen and is generally classified as either hemolytic or neurotoxic.

The venom is a potent autonomic stimulator resulting in the release of massive amounts of catecholamines from the adrenals. It also has a direct effect on the myocardium.

It can present as neurotoxicity with restlessness or seizure-like activity, abnormal oculomotor function, loss of pharyngeal muscle control leading to respiratory compromise. Tongue fasciculations and hypersalivation are also common. Cardiovascular toxicity from systemic envenomation includes tachycardia, hypertension, pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic shock.

If the scorpion has hemolytic venom, the reaction is mainly local, with edema, pain, and reddening. This usually lasts for one to two hours.

Treatment:

* Pain- Paracetamol, NSAIDs, or opioids

* Sedation for agitation, oculomotor abnormalities, uncoordinated neuromuscular activity, muscle spasms- Benzodiazepines

* Hypertension and pulmonary edema -Prazosin counteract the adrenergic surge that can lead to these effects

* Cardiogenic shock- Antivenom, prazosin, nitroglycerin, dobutamine

* Cholinergic effects- Atropine

* Supportive care wound care

Note: Massive amounts of catecholamines are also released by a species of spider called the Black Widow spider which is fatal if bitten.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old man presented with high-grade fever, and purpuric rash as shown in the image below. CSF sample showed gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following is the most likely aetiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neisseria meningitidis

The above image shows a purpuric rash seen in meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitidis, which are gram-negative diplococci.

The organism enters the body through the nasopharynx by attaching to the epithelial cells with the help of pili. From nasopharynx, they enter the bloodstream producing bacteremia, and the symptoms may resemble upper respiratory tract infection.

Fulminant meningococcemia is the severe form, where the patient presents with high-grade fever and hemorrhagic rash. There is thrombosis of several small blood vessels in various organs with perivascular infiltration and petechial haemorrhages.

Some patients with fulminant meningococcemia may also develop disseminated intravascular coagulation, and circulatory collapse, a condition known as Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old female present with unsteady gait, forgetfulness, and labile moods. One physical exam, the neurologist notices that her iris appear multicolored with concentric rings around the periphery as below.The most likely diagnosis is______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wilson's disease

The image above shows fine, pigmented and granular deposits in the cornea. This finding along with the clinical scenario is characteristically seen in Wilson’s disease.

Wilson's disease:

* Autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutation of the ATP7B gene, resulting in impaired copper excretion into bile and a failure to incorporate copper into ceruloplasmin.

* Located on chromosome 13

* This disorder is marked by the accumulation of toxic levels of copper in principally the liver, brain, and eye.

* In the liver, copper binds to a α2-globulin (apoceruloplasmin) to form ceruloplasmin. Circulating ceruloplasmin is eventually degraded within lysosomes, after which the released copper is excreted into bile. This degradation/excretion pathway is the primary route for copper elimination.

* Deficiency in the ATP7B protein causes a decrease in copper transport into bile, impairs its incorporation into ceruloplasmin, and inhibits ceruloplasmin secretion into the blood. These changes cause copper accumulation in the liver and a decrease in circulating ceruloplasmin. The accumulated copper causes toxic liver injury.

* Toxic injury to the brain primarily affects the basal ganglia, particularly the putamen, which shows atrophy and even cavitation.

* Kayser-Fleischer rings, are dark rings that appear to encircle the iris of the eye. They are due to copper deposition in part of the cornea (Descemet's membrane).

Diagnosis of Wilson disease is based on:

* decrease in serum ceruloplasmin

* an increase in hepatic copper content (the most sensitive and accurate test).

* increased urinary excretion of copper (the most specific screening test).

* neurologic involvement presents as movement disorders (tremor, poor coordination, chorea or choreoathetosis) or rigid dystonia (spastic dystonia, mask-like facies, rigidity and gait disturbances.

* psychiatric symptoms such as depression, phobias, compulsive behavior, and labile mood.

* hemolytic anemia may occur due to the toxicity of copper to red cell membranes.

* Histology

* Excess copper deposition can often be demonstrated by special stains (rhodamine stain for copper, orcein stain for copper-associated protein).

* Fatty change (steatosis)

* Hepatocyte ballooning with prominent Mallory-Denk bodies.

Note:Sunflower cataracts are another ocular manifestation of Wilson disease and occur when copper deposits accumulate in the lens.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old female with a history of recurrent headaches presented for further evaluation. On further workup, hemoglobin and total WBC count were normal while an elevated platelet count was seen. Bone marrow aspiration showed increased megakaryocytes and a JAK2 mutation. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Essential thrombocytosis

The likely diagnosis in this patient is essential thrombocytosis also known as essential thrombocythemia.

Essential thrombocytosis is a clonal stem cell disorder characterized by elevated platelet count with no evidence of prolonged platelet survival.

It is estimated that a significant number of patients with essential thrombocytosis are diagnosed incidentally when the patient obtains a complete blood count for an unrelated reason.

Symptoms such as headaches, dizziness, and, visual changes can be seen in the minority of symptomatic patients. Complications such as thrombosis, bleeding (likely due to qualitative and quantitative alterations in the platelets), and first-trimester pregnancy loss are seen in patients with significant thrombocytosis.

Thrombocytosis also leads to certain microvascular manifestations such as :

* Headaches

* Lightheadedness or syncope

* Atypical chest pain

* Acral paresthesia

* Livedo reticularis

* Erythromelalgia (transient burning sensation of hands and feet)

* Transient visual disturbances such as amaurosis fugax, scintillating scotomata, etc

Bone marrow biopsy reveals prominent large to giant megakaryocytes with abundant cytoplasm and lobulated nucleoli. A vast majority of patients demonstrate JAK2, CALR, or the MPL mutation.

Other options:

Option A: Patients with polycythemia vera present with elevated hemoglobin levels.

Option C: Although primary myelofibrosis is associated with JAK 2 mutation, bone marrow aspiration yields a dry tap due to fibrosed bone marrow.

Option D: Chronic myeloid leukemia is characterized by the presence of a Philadelphia chromosome resulting from reciprocal translocation t(9;22) forming the BCR-ABL fusion gene. They have hypercellular marrow due to a massively increased number of maturing granulocytic precursors

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presented with the finding shown in the given image. What is this physical finding called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Clubbing

The given image shows digital clubbing.

Clubbing is a selective bulbous enlargement of the distal segments of the fingers and toes due to the proliferation of connective tissue, particularly on the dorsal surface.

Clubbing can occur secondary to:

* Pulmonary disease: Lung cancer, bronchiectasis, asbestosis, sarcoidosis, lung abscess, cystic fibrosis, tuberculosis, and mesothelioma

* Cardiac disease: Cyanotic congenital heart disease, other causes of right-to-left shunting, and bacterial endocarditis.

* Gastrointestinal disease: Ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease, primary biliary cirrhosis, cirrhosis of the liver.

* Skin disease: Palmoplantar keratoderma, and Fischer-Volavsek syndrome.

* Malignancies: Thyroid cancer, thymus cancer, Hodgkin disease, and disseminated chronic myeloid leukemia.

Note: It is interesting to note that, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) per se does not cause clubbing. But, if clubbing is present in a patient with COPD underlying lung cancer and bronchiectasis must be ruled out.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with headache, vomiting, amenorrhea, galactorrhea, loss of libido, acromegaly, and infertility. On examination, she has bitemporal hemianopia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mammosomatotrope adenoma

The symptoms of headache, vomiting, galactorrhea, infertility, decreased libido, acromegaly is suggestive of excess prolactin and growth hormone along with features of raised intra-cranial tension. The most likely diagnosis is a mammosomatotrope adenoma of the pituitary.

Prolactinomas are the most frequent type of hyperfunctioning pituitary adenomas. They are usually found in adults. They may be functioning or non-functioning. Based on the size, they can be called microadenomas if <1 cm in diameter and macroadenomas if ≥1 cm in diameter.

The symptoms include

* Headache and vomiting

* Bitemporal hemianopia suggestive of a local mass effect

* Increased intracranial pressure due to a pituitary tumour

* In females- amenorrhea, galactorrhea, loss of libido, and infertility

* In males- impotence, loss of libido, and gynecomastia

The diagnosis of prolactinoma is most likely to be associated with a prolactin level >200 μg/L.

Treatment is only required in symptomatic cases as microadenomas rarely progress to macroadenomas. Dopamine and dopamine agonists are used and they act as inhibitory signals to prolactin secretion in the pituitary. Cabergoline is a long-acting dopamine receptor agonist with high D2 receptor affinity and is the preferred drug for the treatment of hyperprolactinemia

Excessive GH secreted before puberty results in gigantism. Acromegaly occurs when excessive GH is secreted after puberty (after fusion of long bone epiphysis).

Increased secretion of growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor- 1 (IGF-1) results in acral bone overgrowth. Patients present with frontal bossing, increased hand and foot size, mandibular enlargement with prognathism, and widened space between the lower incisor teeth. Soft tissue swelling results in increased heel pad thickness, increased shoe size, ring tightening, characteristic coarse facial features, and a large fleshy nose. Other manifestations seen in GH excess are cardiomyopathy, left ventricular hypertrophy, obstructive sleep apnea, diabetes mellitus, etc.

Serum IGF-1 levels and GH suppression test with oral glucose are useful in the diagnosis. The levels of GH do not reduce in response to the oral glucose load. GH-secreting adenomas are managed with surgery. Transsphenoidal resection is the preferred surgery.

Other options:

Option A: Corticotroph adenoma secrete ACTH. They present with features of Cushing's disease.

Option B: Gonadotroph adenoma secrete FSH and LH. They can present with  polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), infertility, menstrual irregularities, ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) in women, and testicular hypertrophy and sexual dysfunction in men.

Option D: Gliomas are neoplasms that originates from glial cells. They present with headaches, nausea, vomiting, seizures, and in more advanced cases weakness or altered mental status.

Pearl PF1847: MEN 1 Syndrome Features

Chromosome 11q13 / MEN1 gene

Also known as Wermer’s syndrome

Characteristic tumors seen in:

* Parathyroid adenoma – 90 % - Most common overall

* Entero pancreatic tumors - Most common functioning tumor is gastrinoma (most common site is duodenum)

* Pituitary adenoma – Most common is prolactinoma

* Mnemonic – Par Pan Pit – in decreasing order of frequency

Associated tumors are:

* Angiofibroma

* Collagenomas

* Adrenal cortical tumors

* Lipoma

* Neuroendocrine tumors - gastric, thymic, lungs

* Meningioma

* Pheochromocytoma

* Carcinoid tumors, usually of the foregut

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45 -year-old presented with severe pain in the right leg below the knee. He had a history of restricted ambulation and prolonged bed rest due to his severe back pain. He has no other comorbidities or history of smoking. On examination of his right calf, discoloration and significantly increased girth are noted and are shown below. What is the most probable clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Deep vein thrombosis

Deep vein thrombosis due to immobilization and venous stasis is the most likely cause.

Deep Vein Thrombosis:

DVT most commonly occurs in the calf veins and less often in the proximal veins of the thigh and pelvis. Deep vein thrombosis is caused due to 3 broad categories of risk factors (Virchow's triad):

* Hemodynamic changes (stasis or turbulence)

* Hypercoagulability

* Endothelial injury/dysfunction

Causes

* Postoperative thrombosis: (Most common cause)

* Following childbirth

* Trauma- to leg, ankle, thigh, pelvis

* Muscular violence

* Immobility – Bed-ridden patients, individuals on long-duration air or bus travel (Traveller’s thrombosis).

* Debilitating illness, obesity, immobility, bed rest, pregnancy, puerperium, oral contraceptives, estrogens.

Sites

* Pelvic veins—common

* Leg veins—common in femoral and popliteal veins (Common on the left side).

Features of DVT

* Fever-commonest

* Tense, tender, warm, pale/bluish, shiny swelling calf

* Positive Homan’s, Mose’s, or Neuhof’s signs

* Inverted champagne bottle sign

* Commonly it is asymptomatic

* Features of pulmonary embolism

Treatment

* Rest, the elevation of the limb, bandaging the entire limb with

* crepe bandage.

* Anticoagulants: Heparin/low molecular weight

* heparin, warfarin, phenindione.

* Palma operation

* May-Husni operation

Pearl PF1167: Prophylaxis for DVT

Mechanical prophylaxis

Early ambulation

Acts by activating the calf pump mechanism

Pneumatic compression stocking

Prevents stasis by periodically compressing the calves

Pharmacological prophylaxis

Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) - Enoxaparin

Fondaparinux

Prevent thrombus formation by inhibiting factor Xa

Apixaban

Rivaroxaban

Oral factor Xa inhibitors

Unfractionated heparin (UFH)

Prevents action of factors VIII - XII and production of thrombin/fibrin.

Used in renal insufficiency

Warfarin

Inhibits hepatic production of factors II, VII, IX and X

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old female patient presents to you with complaints of dryness in the mouth and eyes. Serum testing reveals positive anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies. The test shown in the image below was positive with a score of 5 mm in 5 minutes without anesthesia. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sjogren syndrome

The test shown above is Schirmer's test and the likely diagnosis is Sjögren's syndrome.

Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune disorder that involves lymphocytic infiltration of the exocrine glands. This manifests as xerostomia (dry mouth) and keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes). It is associated with autoantibodies anti-Ro/SS-A and anti-La/SS-B.

Keratoconjunctivitis sicca can be diagnosed by Schirmer's test. This test measures the quantity of tears produced. Two marked strips of paper are placed between the globe and the lower eyelid and the patient is instructed to close their eyes for 5 minutes. The tears produced spread along the paper by capillary action. The distance is measured. A score of more than 10 mm is considered to be normal while that of less than 5 mm is considered deficient.

A number of other systems can be involved as well. For example, atrophic gastritis, esophageal mucosal atrophy, and vaginal dryness. Extraglandular or systemic manifestations can also be present. These manifest as fatigue, arthritis, Raynaud's phenomenon, and myalgia.

Diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome requires the following:

* Eye and/or mouth dryness

* Eye tests disclose keratoconjunctivitis sicca

* Mouth evaluation reveals dry oral mucosa and/or

* Presence of anti-Ro or anti-La autoantibodies

A labial (lip) biopsy is a must to confirm the diagnosis and determine the prognosis.

Treatment of Sjögren's syndrome is directed at treating the symptoms and complications. Artificial tears can be used for dry eyes and propionic acid gel for vaginal dryness. Pilocarpine can help increase oral secretions and hydroxychloroquine can be used to treat arthritis.

Pearl PF1555: Extraglandular manifestations of Sjögren’s syndrome

The extraglandular manifestations of Sjögren’s syndrome are as follows:

* Non-specific

* Arthralgia or arthritis - It is the most common extraglandular manifestation. It is usually non-erosive and leads to Jacoud’s arthropathy

* Raynaud’s phenomenon

* Accumulation of peri-epithelial lymphocytes

* Interstitial lung disease - Most common type is non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)

* Renal tubular acidosis - Distal (type 1) RTA

* Primary biliary cirrhosis

* Immune complex-mediated

* Small vessel vasculitis - Presents as cutaneous palpable purpura

* Glomerulonephritis with cryoglobulinemia

* Peripheral neuropathy

* Lymphoma

* Extranodal marginal zone B cell lymphoma of mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue (MALToma).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old male presents with chest pain and breathlessness which increases on lying down and is relieved on sitting upright. On examination, heart sounds are muffled. His chest X-ray is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pericardial effusion

The given clinical features and X-ray appearance of the money bag heart is suggestive of pericardial effusion.

Plain PA chest X-ray shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette. There is effacement of the normal cardiac borders, development of a ‘flask’ or ‘water bottle’ cardiac configuration, and bilateral hilar overlay which are features of pericardial effusion. It is also known as money bag or leather bottle-shaped heart.

Pericardial effusions occur when excess fluid collects in the pericardial space (a normal pericardial sac contains approximately 30-50 mL of fluid).

Investigation of choice: Echocardiography.

Signs on plain radiograph include:

* Globular enlargement of the cardiac shadow giving a water bottle configuration.

* Lateral CXR may show a vertical opaque line (pericardial fluid) separating a vertical lucent line directly behind the sternum (paracardial fat) anteriorly from a similar lucent vertical lucent line (epicardial fat) posteriorly; this is known as the Oreo cookie sign.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 49-year-old man presents with flu-like symptoms and a palmoplantar rash as seen below. On examination, he has epitrochlear lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Secondary syphilis

This clinical scenario of maculopapular rash with flu-like symptoms and epitrochlear lymphadenopathy points to secondary syphilis.

* Secondary syphilis occurs within 6 weeks to 8 weeks of onset of primary chancre.

* It is characterized by the following:

* Onset of systemic manifestations includes symptoms such as malaise, headache, loss of appetite, sore throat

* Generalized symmetric, asymptomatic maculopapular rash on the palms and soles of the feet

* Generalized adenopathy in 50% cases

* Condyloma lata are the classic findings; these are highly contagious exophytic broad excrescences that ulcerate. These are commonly seen on the vulva, perianal area and upper thighs.

Pearl PF1554: Stages of syphilis

* Primary Syphilis:

Chancre- Painless, indurated, usually single

Lymphadenopathy- Painless, unilateral or bilateral, shotty and rubbery inguinal nodes

Dory flop sign- As the chancre is too hard to fold, it will flip over once the prepuce is retracted back.

The chancre self heals in 1-4 months.

Secondary Syphilis:

A & B: Generalized rash(non-itchy, no vesicles, and palm and sole involvement).

This is the most common lesion.

C & D: Condyloma lata.

E: Moth-eaten alopecia (Non-scarring)

F: Mucous patches(Flat erosions on the tongue which can coalesce and form snail track ulcers).These are the most infectious lesions.

G: Pigmentary plaques

H: Psoriasiform syphilitic lesions

Generalized diffuse non-tender lymphadenopathy

Tertiary Syphilis:

Gummatous syphilis(deep punched-out ulcers, with gum-like secretions on the floor)

Pseudo-chancre redux is a gumma occurring at the site of a previously healed ulcer

CVS-Aortitis and aneurysm of the ascending aorta

CNS-General paresis of the insane and tabes dorsalis

Latent Syphilis-Period between secondary and tertiary syphilis, when the patient is asymptomatic clinically, and only serological evidence of infection is present.

* Early latent- Within 1 year of infection

* Late latent- After 1 year of infection

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 54-year-old woman presents to you with complaints of swollen fingers, heartburn, and occasional joint pains. On examination, the skin over her hands is shiny, taut, and thickened with non-pitting edema.There is associated interstitial lung disease and presence of ANA antibodies, topoisomerase I antibodies and Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis here ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis

The clinical scenario with ANA antibodies,topoisomerase I antibodies and Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies is diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

Systemic sclerosis is an autoimmune disorder of connective tissue resulting in fibrosis of the skin, internal organs, and vasculature. It is characterized by Raynaud’s phenomenon, ischemia of the digits, sclerodactyly, and cardiac, lung, gut, and renal disease. The peak age of onset is between the fourth and fifth decades of life.

It is divided into:

* Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (30% of cases) - poor prognosis

* Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (70% of cases)

The antibodies tested in systemic sclerosis include:

* Antinuclear antibody (ANA) - positive in most cases of systemic sclerosis. The absence of this antibody suggests considering an alternate diagnosis.

* Antitopoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibody - usually positive with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

* Anti-RNA polymerase I and III antibodies - usually positive with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

* Anti centromere antibody (ACA) - usually positive in limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old male patient presented to the hospital with palpitations. On examination, a diastolic murmur is heard in the left third intercostal space and pistol shot sound is heard over the femoral arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aortic regurgitation

The presence of a diastolic murmur along with the pistol shot sound over the femoral is most likely to be due to aortic regurgitation.

Due to aortic regurgitation, there is a backflow of the blood from the aorta to the ventricle, during the diastole. This increases the end-diastolic (EDV) volume in the left ventricle and at the same time decreases the diastolic blood pressure (DBP).

Increased EDV leads to an increase in stroke volume and systolic blood pressure (SBP). The patient develops wide pulse pressure due to increased SBP and decreased DBP. The clinical manifestations in AR is mainly due to the wide pulse pressure.

As the regurgitation worsens, the ventricle undergo dilatation and eccentric hypertrophy to eject the additional amount of regurgitant blood. Eventually, these adaptive measures fail and left ventricular failure develops.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 56-year-old female with a history of myocardial infarction 2 years back now came with complaints of a cough and breathlessness on walking for a short distance. On examination, there was dullness to percussion and reduced breath sounds on the right side. Chest X-ray showed moderate pleural effusion. Thoracocentesis was performed under ultrasound guidance and the lab investigations are given below. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis in this patient? Pleural fluid findings: * Appearance: turbid * pH: 7.1 * Protein: 3.2 g/dL * Lactate dehydrogenase: 80 U/L (normal serum LDH - 50-150 U/L) * Pleural fluid protein/serum protein ratio : 0.34 * Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH : 0.3 * Glucose: 54 mg/dL * WBC count: 4000 cells/μL with > 50% lymphocytes * Adenosine deaminase: 30 U/L * AFB smear microscopy: negative * Gram staining and microscopy: no organisms, no pus cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Congestive heart failure

This patient's clinical presentation and laboratory findings are suggestive of congestive heart failure in which the effusion is transudative in nature.

In this patient,

* Pleural fluid protein/serum protein ratio : 0.34 (<0.5)

* Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH : 0.3 (<0.6)

* Pleural fluid LDH is < 2/3rd the upper limit of normal serum LDH (normal serum LDH - 50-150 U/L)

In this patient, according to Light's criteria, the pleural effusion is transudative.

Examples of transudative pleural effusions are effusions due to congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, and nephrosis. Exudative pleural effusions are caused by malignancies, bacterial infections, rheumatoid pleuritis, and pulmonary embolism

Other options:

Option A: In parapneumonic pleural effusion too, the effusion is exudative with pH < 7.2 and glucose < 60 mg/dL. However, the WBC count is usually >10,000 cells/μL with a predominance of neutrophils. Appearance is generally cloudy.

Option B: Pleural effusion associated with malignant pleural effusion is exudative in nature.

Option D: Although tubercular pleural effusion is also exudative with a predominance of lymphocytes, adenosine deaminase levels < 40 U/L as in this patient rules out tubercular effusion.

* GI: Esophageal perforation, pancreatic disease, intraabdominal abscess etc.,

* Collagen vascular disease: SLE, rheumatoid pleuritis, Wegener's, Churg Strauss syndrome etc.,

* Drug-induced pleural disease: nitrofurantoin, dantrolene, bromocriptine, amiodarone etc.,

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman who recently received a kidney transplant 2 months ago develops a high fever and severe dyspnea with a dry hacking cough. Chest x-ray reveals bilateral interstitial infiltrates that are diffuse and urine examination shows 'owl-eye' appearance of cells. Which of the following agents is most likely responsible for her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cytomegalovirus

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is an important cause of morbidity and mortality after allogeneic transplant. Interstitial pneumonia (IP) is the most common manifestation of CMV, in transplant recipients.

The predominant pathogen to infect the renal transplant recipients in the period around 1 to 4 months following the transplantation is cytomegalovirus (CMV).The most common CMV presentation in kidney transplant patients is fever (most common), leukopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, myalgia, and arthralgia.

CMV infection in immunocompromised hosts:

The infection is contained by host immune response where virus remains latent in leukocytes. Then reactivates when host becomes immunocompromised, and may cause:

* Retinitis (especially in AIDS patients)

* Pneumonia (especially in transplant patients)

* Esophagitis

Diagnosis:

* Giant cells with “owl’s eye” intranuclear inclusionbodies found in tissues/urine

* Serology (negative monospot test as compared to EBV mononucleosis)

* Detection in buffy coat culture (CMV infects WBCs)

Other options:

* Option a: Adenovirus is associated with conjunctivitis and acute respiratory disease in military recruits, among other diseases.

* Option c: Although influenza can cause pneumonia, there is no mention of season, and CMV is still the most common cause in transplant patients.

* Option d: Respiratory syncytial virus is usually seen in children (especially premature infants).
