questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old man presented with chronic pain in his hand, knees, and hips,aggravated on climbing stairs, while pain in his hands increases when he writes or types. He also complains of stiffness in his joints in the morning, which lasts for around half an hour. On examination of the hands, Herbeden's and Bouchard's nodes are visible. X-ray of the knee showed narrowed joint space with osteophytes. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Osteoarthritis

The clinical vignette points to a diagnosis of osteoarthritis (OA).

Osteoarthritis is the most common cause of chronic knee pain in persons aged over 45 years. The early phases typically present with episodic joint pain following overactive use of the diseased joint. As the disease progresses, the pain becomes continuous and may be associated with stiffness of the affected joint. Morning stiffness if present, is usually brief for around 30 minutes. Clinical signs include:

* Tenderness of the joint

* Bony swelling

* Decreased and painful range of movement

* Crepitus when the joint is moved

* Weakness and wasting of muscles acting on the joint

* Signs of inflammation

* Deformity and instability in severe cases

The joints involved in osteoarthritis are:

* Distal and proximal interphalangeal joints (DIP, PIP)

* First carpometacarpal joint (base of the thumb)

* Hip

* Knee

* First metatarsal phalangeal joint (MTP)

* Cervical and lumbosacral spine

The wrist, elbow, and ankle joints are usually spared.Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes are nodules in osteoarthritis that are palpable in the distal interphalangeal joint and proximal interphalangeal joints respectively.

The characteristic features of OA seen on plain radiographs are:

* Marginal osteophyte formation

* Localized joint space narrowing

* Sclerosis of the underlying bone

* Subchondral bone cysts

* Loose bodies and chondrocalcinosis

The image below is an X-ray of osteorthritis showing the presence of osteophytes, narrowing of the joint space (arrow), and subchondral bone sclerosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 72-year-old retired pilot presents to a neurologist, accompanied by his wife, with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus ,ataxia, and visual disturbances. FLAIR MRI scans is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Variant CJD

The clinical scenario of rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, ataxia and visual disturbances along with the FLAIR MRI which shows hockey stick sign, is diagnostic of variant CJD.

The hockey stick sign refers to the hyper-intense signal involving the pulvinar and dorsomedial thalamic nuclei bilaterally on FLAIR or DWI. This sign is commonly indicative of variant (infectious acquired) CJD. Whereas MRI in sporadic CJD reveals abnormalities in the cortical grey matter called cortical ribboning.

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is a spongiform encephalopathy that is characterized by rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, akinetic mutism, cerebellar/visual disturbances. It is fatal and death usually within a year or less from the onset.

The proteins that make up the prions (PrP) are present even normally in the cells. This normal form, PrPc, is in a predominantly α-helical configuration and is sensitive to proteases. However, the prions (infectious form) are in an abnormal β-pleated configuration and are called PrPSc. This pathological form is not degradable by proteases and converts the normal form- PrPc to the abnormal form- PrPSc. This abnormal protein gets deposited as plaques and degeneration of surrounding neuronal and glial tissue occurs characterized by intracellular vacuoles, leading to a characteristic spongiform encephalopathy. There is no associated inflammatory response to these agents.

Four types of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease have been described:

* Sporadic (sCJD): Most common;

* Variant (vCJD): Bovine spongiform encephalopathy (mad cow disease), Kuru;

* Familial (fCJD): These individuals carry a PrPc mutation and include Gerstmann-Sträussler- Scheinker syndrome and fatal familial insomnia;

* Iatrogenic (iCJD): Maybe seen occurring after corneal transplantation, liver transplantation, use of contaminated neurosurgical instruments, use of cadaver-derived hormones, or stereotactic depth electrodes.

Clinically, CJD presents with predominantly CNS manifestations with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus (startle myoclonus is common), ataxia, akinetic mutism, visual disturbances, and pyramidal/extrapyramidal dysfunction. Insomnia, apathy, and other behavioral abnormalities may be seen.

CSF is predominantly normal but may show a positive assay for 14-3-3 protein. MRI on FLAIR sequencing and diffusion-weighted imaging will show increased intensity in the basal ganglia region and a characteristic 'cortical ribboning', in sporadic CJD. Diagnosis of CJD can be established on brain biopsy either by measuring PrPSc or by demonstrating the characteristic neuropathological features of spongiform encephalopathy. EEG may show periodic triphasic or multiphasic sharp-wave complexes seen as spikes or spike-wave pattern.

Management is mainly supportive as the disease is usually fatal within a year of onset of symptoms.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A adult patient presents with pulsatile swelling in the neck below the angle of jaw which produces an outward expansile impulse. The consultant in suspicion of a condition did a MRI angiography which is shown below.Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carotid body tumour

The clinical scenario of pulsatile swelling along with the MRI angiography which shows splaying of internal and external carotid arteries called as Lyre’s sign, is diagnostic of carotid body tumour.

Carotid body tumour:

* It arises from the chemoreceptor cells in the carotid body, hence called chemodectoma.

* Mostly presents after 40 years.

* It is a very slow-growing tumour.

Features:

* Painless swelling which is pulsatile.

* Bruit can be heard with a stethoscope.

* It moves from side to side but not vertically.

* It may extend into the parapharyngeal space and present in the oropharynx.

* Some tumours are functional and secrete catecholamines.

Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI with gadolinium are diagnostic and also show the extent of the tumour. MRI angiography shows splaying of internal and external carotid arteries (Lyre’s sign). Serum catecholamines and urinary meta-nephrines and vanillyl mandelic acid (VMA) should be estimated.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) or biopsy should not be done because of the vascularity of tumour.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A girl presents with prolonged menstrual bleeding and her investigations showed- normal platelet count, PT, and aPTT while bleeding time was increased. On further analysis, a deficiency of GpIIb-IIIa was found. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glanzman thrombasthenia

The clinical vignette is suggestive of Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

* Autosomal recessive platelet surface receptor disorder of GPIIb/IIIa (ITG αIIbβ3), either qualitative or quantitative - Faulty platelet aggregation and diminished clot retraction.

* Acquired GT is seen with platelet transfusions, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, multiple myeloma, myelodysplastic syndrome, hairy cell leukemia, and acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

* Normal platelet morphology and normal platelet count, prolonged bleeding time, absent or decreased clot retraction, and normal platelet aggregation in the presence of ristocetin.

* Platelet aggregation is absent in the presence of epinephrine, collagen, arachidonic acid, ADP.

* Under flow cytometric analysis, CD41 and CD61 levels are markedly decreased or absent

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with frequent urination, nocturia, and enuresis. 24-hour urine volume was measured and recorded to be 7 liters. The urine osmolarity was 260 mOsm/L. ADH assay was performed and the recorded values were reported as 0.8 pg/ml. An MRI of the brain was performed and T1 weighted indicated the absence of the bright spot. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pituitary DI

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of pituitary diabetes insipidus.

Approach to the question:

* A 24-hour urine volume greater than 3 liters is suggestive of polyuria.

* Urine osmolarity < 300 mOsm/ L is suggestive of DI or primary polydipsia.

* ADH assay < 1pg/mL = Primary polydipsia or central DI.

* Finally, the absence of a pituitary bright spot in the MRI brain is suggestive of central diabetes insipidus.

In nephrogenic DI, the ADH levels will be greater than 1pg/mL.

In the case of primary polydipsia, a pituitary bright spot will be observed.

In solute loss (mannitol or hypertonic saline infusion), urine osmolality is greater than 300 mOsm/L.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient was asked to copy the face of a clock and his drawing is shown below. What is the correct term to be used here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemispatial neglect

Hemispatial neglect is the inability to report, respond, or orient to stimuli in one-half of the space despite having no motor or sensory deficits.

A patient with neglect is asked to draw a clock, their drawing might show only the numbers 12 to 6, or all 12 numbers might be on one half of the clock face with the other half distorted or blank, like the image shown in the image below.

Neglect patients may also ignore the contralesional side of their body; for instance, they might only shave, or apply makeup to, the non-neglected side. These patients may frequently collide with objects or structures such as door frames on the side being neglected.

Other options:

Option A: Confabulation is a phenomenon in which the patient fills in memory gaps with inaccurate information. Further investigating the statement made by the patients may reflect past experiences or bizarre, fantastic stories.  This fabrication of false information is not done on purpose.

Option C: Apraxia: Inability to perform a movement or task when asked despite having the desire and physical capability to carry it out.

Types of apraxia:

* Kinetic: Inability to execute the fine acquired motor movement, the lesion is in the precentral cortex.

* Ideomotor: Fails to perform on command. The lesion is in the parietal lobe.

* Constructional: liability to reproduce simple geometric figures by drawing. The lesion is in the pathway between the occipital or parietal area.

* Ideational: Loss of ability to formulate an ideational plan for the execution of the complex act. The lesion is in the dominant parietal lobe.

Option D: Astrexis/Flapping tremor is a type of negative myoclonus characterized by irregular lapses of the posture of various body parts. Mostly associated with hepatic encephalopathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A person with dyspnoea has a slight limitation in physical activity and doing ordinary activity causes symptoms but he is asymptomatic at rest. To which class does he belong, based on the New York Heart Association Functional Classification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Class II

Based on the slight limitation of physical activity and ordinary activities causing symptoms he comes under Class II in NYHA classification.

NYHA classification of heart failure:

NYHA class
Description

I

• No limitation of physical activity
• Ordinary physical activity does not cause symptoms

II

• Slight limitation of physical activity
• Comfortable at rest, but ordinary physical activity causes symptoms

III

• Marked limitation of physical activity
• Comfortable at rest, but less than ordinary physical activity causes symptoms

IV

• Unable to carry out any physical activity without symptoms or symptoms at rest

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A veterinary surgeon presents with complaints of fever, muscle pain, joint pain, fatigue, and weight loss for the past few weeks. On further inquiry, he says that his fever persists for weeks before it resolves only to be followed by a relapse. You obtain his blood sample and inoculate it on the medium given below to isolate the suspected organism. Which of the following is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Brucella

This clinical vignette is suggestive of Brucellosis caused by organisms belonging to the Brucella species. The culture medium depicted in the given image is the Castenada biphasic medium.

Brucella are small, non-motile, aerobic, capnophilic coccobacilli. The most important species that are pathologic to humans are B.melitensis, B. suis, and B.abortus.

Brucellosis is a zoonosis. It is transmitted to humans from contact with or consumption of contaminated products from goats, sheep, cattle, buffaloes, pigs, and other animals.

Once the infection is transmitted, these bacteria resist intracellular digestion and proliferate within the reticuloendothelial system for a long time. This is the reason why brucellosis often becomes chronic and is resistant to simple antimicrobial therapy. The host immune response is mainly cell-mediated involving activated macrophages, helper T-cells, and mediators such as TNF alpha, TNF gamma, IL-1, and IL-12.

Clinically, patients may present with an acute infection comprised of undulant fever, as in this patient, characterized by a rising and falling fever. They may also have arthralgia, muscular pain, sweating, loss of weight, and appetite. CNS symptoms such as fatigue, irritability, and depression might also occur. Chronic infection tends to be episodic with non-specific symptoms.

Laboratory diagnosis of brucellosis is important and includes several methods such as-

* Polymerase chain reaction is a sensitive and reliable method of detection.

* Culture of Brucella species can be done from specimen including blood, bone marrow aspirate, lymph node aspirate, CSF, and urine. Preferred method and medium of culture includes the Castaneda method. It is a biphasic medium. The solid component is the agar slant and the liquid is the broth. The medium is inoculated with the specimen and incubated for four days in an upright position. Serial subcultures can be obtained by slanting the broth over the agar periodically to inoculate new colonies.

* Serological methods include standard agglutination test (SAT), complement fixation test, Coomb’s antiglobulin test, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Cut-offs for significant titers are variable depending on the endemicity. Endemic areas or history of laboratory exposure require agglutinin titers of 1:320–1:640 or higher and in nonendemic areas, a titer of more than or equal to 1:160 is considered diagnostic.

* Tests for animals and animal products include tests such as the milk ring tests and Rose Bengal card tests.

* Milk ring test- A sample of milk is mixed well with hematoxylin stained brucella antigen and incubated. If the sample contains antibodies to brucella antigens, agglutination occurs with the agglutinate rising to the top as a blue ring. If the sample does not contain antibodies to brucella antigens, the whole of the sample is uniformly stained blue.

Treatment includes antimicrobial therapy with at least two agents for six weeks duration. The preferred combination is IM streptomycin 0.75-1g per day for two to three weeks along with doxycycline 100mg BD for six weeks.

Prevention of Brucellosis is important by screening and abiding by safety standards in farms and dairy industries, and also by pasteurization of milk and milk products.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An HIV-positive patient presents with the following finding. What is the diagnosis & WHO clinical stage of HIV?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oral candidiasis & WHO Stage 3

Oral candidiasis (Thrush) is categorized as WHO clinical stage 3.

Oral Candidiasis (Thrush), and oral hairy leukoplakia, are oral lesions characterized in WHO clinical Stage 3. They generally occur in patients with CD4+ T cell counts of <300/μL.

Differentiating oral candidiasis and oral hairy leukoplakia:

* Oral Candidiasis (Thrush) appears as a white, cheesy exudate, on an erythematous mucosa in the posterior oropharynx. The diagnosis is made by direct examination of pseudohyphal elements.

* Oral hairy leukoplakia presents as white, frondlike lesions, generally along the lateral borders of the tongue and sometimes on the adjacent buccal mucosa(image below). Despite its name, oral hairy leukoplakia is not considered premalignant. Lesions are associated with immunosupression and Ebstein-Barr virus (EBV).

Pearl PF1360: Clinical stages of HIV in children/ infants

Stage 1

* Asymptomatic

* Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy

Stage 2

* Unexplained persistent hepatosplenomegaly

* Papular pruritic eruptions

* Extensive wart virus infection

* Extensive molluscum contagiosum

* Recurrent oral ulcerations

* Unexplained persistent parotid enlargement

* Linear gingival erythema

* Herpes zoster

* Recurrent or chronic upper respiratory infections (otitis media, otorrhoea, sinusitis, tonsilitis)

* Fungal nail infections

Stage 3

* Unexplained moderate malnutrition not adequately responding to standard therapy

* Unexplained persistent diarrhea (14 days or more)

* Unexplained persistent fever (above 37.6 °C intermittent or constant, for longer than one month)

* Persistent oral candidiasis (after first 6-8 weeks of life)

* Oral hairy leukoplakia

* Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis/periodontitis

* Lymph node TB

* Pulmonary TB

* Severe recurrent bacterial pneumonia

* Symptomatic lymphoid interstitial pneumonitis

* Chronic HIV-associated lung disease including bronchiectasis

* Unexplained anemia (<8 g/dL), neutropenia (<0.5 x 109/L) or chronic thrombocytopenia (<50 × 109/L)

Stage 4

* Unexplained severe wasting, stunting or malnutrition not responding to standard therapy

* Pneumocystis pneumonia

* Recurrent severe bacterial infections (e.g., empyema, pyomyositis, bone or joint infection, meningitis, but excluding pneumonia)

* Chronic Herpes Simplex infection; (oro-labial or cutaneous of more than one month's duration or visceral at any site)

* Extrapulmonary TB and disseminated non-tuberculosis mycobacterial infection

* Kaposi Sarcoma

* Oesophageal candidiasis (or candidiasis of trachea, bronchi or lungs)

* Central nervous system toxoplasmosis (after one month of life)

* HIV encephalopathy

* Cytomegalovirus infection; retinitis or CMV infection affecting another organ, with onset at age over 1 month)

* Extrapulmonary cryptococcosis (including meningitis)

* Disseminated endemic mycosis (extrapulmonary histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis)

* Chronic cryptosporidiosis and isosporiasis

* Cerebral or B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma

* Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy

* Symptomatic HIV-associated nephropathy or HIV-associated cardiomyopathy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ventricular tachycardia

The above ECG shows ventricular tachycardia.

The features in the above ECG suggesting the diagnosis are as follows:

* Wide QRS complex with abnormal morphology (marked with red arrows)

* Absence of the P waves

* Rate >100/min- in the given ECG, it is ~180 beats/min (1500/no. of small boxes between two R waves)

Ventricular fibrillation would have no discreet QRS complexes. The given ECG shows ventricular fibrillation:

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the tachycardia depicted in the given ECG.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atrial flutter

The given ECG is suggestive of atrial flutter.

The given ECG shows narrow QRS complexes, hence it is supraventricular tachycardia. The RR intervals are regular and the normal P waves are replaced by sawtooth-shaped waves (red arrows), known as flutter waves. Hence, it is most likely to be atrial flutter.

In atrial flutter, the ventricular rate is determined by the AV conduction ratio. The commonest AV ratio is 2:1. As the atrial rate is around 300 bpm, AV conduction ratio of 2:1 results in a ventricular rate of ~150 bpm.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a diabetic patient, which of these is a macrovascular complication that occurs in the later stage of the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coronary artery disease

The macrovascular complication of diabetes given in the options is coronary heart disease, all others are microvascular complications.

Complications of Diabetes Mellitus

Microvascular
Macrovascular

• Eye disease
• Retinopathy (Non-proliferative/ proliferative)
• Macular edema
• Neuropathy
• Sensory and motor (mono and polyneuropathy)
• Nephropathy

• Coronary heart disease
• Peripheral arterial disease
• Cerebrovascular disease

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which disease is being represented in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cushing's syndrome

The given picture describes Cushing's.

Cushing's syndrome is characterized by clinical features that result from chronic exposure to excess glucocorticoids that can be due to

* Prolonged exogenous administration of glucocorticoids (Iatrogenic: Most common cause of Cushing's syndrome)

* Excess endogenous cortisol secretion

* Ectopic ACTH production

Important clinical features:

* Moon facies

* Purple skin striae

* Abnormal masculinization (acne, bruising, enlargement of the clitoris in girls)

* Pubertal developmental delay and amenorrhea in girls

* Proximal muscle weakness

* Osteoporosis

* Hypertension

* Hyperpigmentation

* Hypokalemic alkalosis

* Hyperglycemia

* Sepsis

The high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is done only after a diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome is established in a patient.

The high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is used in patients with confirmed Cushing syndrome. It helps to differentiate between Cushing's disease (i.e a pituitary cause) and ectopic ACTH production.

The basis for this test is that in subjects with Cushing's disease, a higher dose of dexamethasone (usually 8 mg) is required to suppress ACTH secretion and drop cortisol levels in serum, urine, and saliva.

Standard 2-day (high dose) dexamethasone suppression test:

* Serum cortisol level and/or 24-hour urinary free cortisol is measured as a baseline, and then dexamethasone 2 mg orally is taken every 6 hours for 48 hours; urine for free cortisol is collected during the test and serum cortisol is checked 6 hours after the last dose. The suppression of cortisol secretion to >50 % of the baseline is considered positive and indicative of Cushing's disease

The following four investigations are used to establish an initial diagnosis of endogenous Cushing's syndrome as per the clinical guidelines of the endocrine society.

* 24-hour urinary free cortisol (increased 3x above normal)

* Midnight salivary cortisol ( >5nmol/L)

* Overnight dexamethasone suppression (plasma cortisol >50 nmol/L at 8-9 AM after 1 mg dexamethasone at 11 PM)

* Standard 2-day (low dose) dexamethasone suppression test (plasma cortisol > 50 nmol/L after 0.5 mg dexamethasone 6th hourly for 48 hours).

Pearl PF0309: Causes of Cushing's Syndrome

Iatrogenic (Most common cause)

* Exogenous administration of glucocorticoids

Endogenous Causes

* ACTH Dependent – (90 % of endogenous causes)

* Cushing’s disease – ACTH-producing pituitary adenoma

* Ectopic ACTH syndrome – Due to ACTH secretion by

* Bronchial or pancreatic carcinoid tumors

* Small-cell lung cancer

* Medullary thyroid carcinoma

* Pheochromocytoma

* ACTH Independent – (10% )

* Adrenocortical adenoma

* Adrenocortical carcinoma

Rare causes

* Macronodular adrenal hyperplasia

* Primary pigmented nodular adrenal disease

* McCune – Albright syndrome

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which is the best confirmatory method to ensure that the central line is in the jugular vein?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chest Xray

A chest X-ray is the best method to confirm the position of the central line in the jugular vein.

The position of the catheter is confirmed by radiological confirmation with an X-ray. Comparison of the blood’s color or PaO2 with an arterial sample can also be done, however, they can be misleading or inconclusive, and more than one confirmation method should be used. In cases where transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is used, the guidewire can be seen in the right atrium, confirming venous entry.

Central line catheterization:

Indications:

* monitoring central venous pressure (CVP)

* administration of fluid to treat hypovolemia and shock

* infusion of caustic drugs and total parenteral nutrition

* gaining venous access in patients with poor peripheral veins.

Contraindications:

* tumors or clots

* tricuspid valve vegetations that could be dislodged or embolized during cannulation

* site-related complications-subclavian vein cannulation is relatively contraindicated in patients who are receiving anticoagulants(due to the inability to provide direct compression in the event of an accidental arterial puncture), avoid central venous cannulation on the side of a previous carotid endarterectomy due to the possibility of unintentional carotid artery puncture.

Sites:

* the subclavian vein is associated with a greater risk of pneumothorax, but a reduced risk of other complications during prolonged cannulations

* right internal jugular vein provides a combination of accessibility and safety

* left-sided internal jugular vein catheterization has an increased risk of pleural effusion and chylothorax

* the external jugular veins can also be used as entry sites, but due to the acute angle at which they join the great veins of the chest, are associated with a slightly increased likelihood of failure to gain access.

* femoral veins can also be cannulated, but are associated with an increased risk of line-related sepsis.

Risks:

* site infection, bloodstream infection, air or thrombus embolism

* arrhythmias (indicating that the catheter tip is in the right atrium or ventricle), hematoma, pneumothorax, hemothorax, hydrothorax, chylothorax

* cardiac perforation, cardiac tamponade, trauma to nearby nerves and arteries

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: _______ excreted in the urine are used as a screening test for pheochromocytoma.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Urinary metanephrines and VMA

Urinary metanephrines and VMA excreted in the urine are screening tests for pheochromocytoma.

Vanillyl Mandelic Acid is the end product of the catabolism of catecholamines, whereas metanephrines are the byproducts in the catabolism of catecholamines and are excreted in the urine in patients with pheochromocytoma.

* VMA is the urinary product of both epinephrine and norepinephrine.

* In pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma, there is an excessive synthesis of catecholamines which causes the enhanced synthesis of VMA and its excretion in the urine.

* It is a good screening test for pheochromocytoma and is also used to diagnose and follow up neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroma.

Option B: Albumin is excreted in Nephrotic syndrome.

Option C: 5-HIAA (5-hydroxy indole acetic acid) is excreted in Carcinoid syndrome.

Option D: Glucose is excreted in Diabetes Mellitus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 20-year-old male presented with a 1-week history of yellow skin and sclerae but is otherwise asymptomatic. He gives a history of viral infection for 10 days which resolved 2 days back. There is a history of a similar episode of icterus 2 years back for a period of 2 weeks. On further questioning, he adds that he used to have long basketball practice hours 2 years back and he used to be physically drained during that period. The current serum bilirubin is 2.4 mg/dL, unconjugated bilirubin 2.1mg/dl, conjugated bilirubin is 0.3mg/dl. Serum AST and ALT levels are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gilbert syndrome

Gilbert syndrome is the most likely diagnosis in this patient.

This patient's mild jaundice and its presence seen only during a period of stress PLUS increase in unconjugated bilirubin and normal AST, ALT levels strongly point towards a diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome.

Gilbert syndrome is a benign, familial disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern characterized by mild intermittent jaundice usually seen during stress, illnesses, or any other precipitating factors. There is no hemolysis or underlying liver disease. The condition is recognized to arise from a mutation in the promoter region of the UGT1A1 gene, which results in mildly decreased UDP-Glucoronyltransferase production. UDP-Glucoronyltransferase is required for the conjugation of bilirubin.

Precipitating factors in Gilbert syndrome:

* Dehydration

* Fasting

* Menstrual periods

* Illness

* Vigorous exercise.

Other options:

* Crigler-Najjar syndrome is of two types with type 1 having absent/trace UDP-Glucoronyltransferase production and type 2 having <10% of the normal enzyme activity. Hence, type 1 is far more severe and leads to kernicterus and neurological damage in babies. Type 2 may also lead to kernicterus occasionally. Unconjugated bilirubin is elevated. Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in a 25-year-old male is less likely to be due to Criggler Najar type 1 syndrome. It is because patients usually die in infancy or early childhood despite the best treatment.

* Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a benign autosomal recessive disease that is characterized by chronic conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and conspicuous brown-black melanin-like pigment deposition in the liver. The disease is caused due to mutation in multidrug resistance protein 2 (MRP-2) in hepatocytes, which is required for the transport of non-bile salt organic anions at the canalicular membranes. Liver biopsy shows characteristic deposition of black-colored pigment.

* Rotor syndrome: similar to Dubin-Johnson syndrome but with a milder presentation. Increased conjugated bilirubin levels. Liver biopsy does not show black colored liver

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presented with excessive fatiguability towards the end of the day that improved with rest. He also gives history of ptosis, difficult in speech and swallowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myasthenia gravis

In the above clinical scenario of a patient with fatiguability that worsen with repetitive movements but resolve after rest, ptosis, dysarthria, and dysphagia. is very characteristic of myasthenia gravis.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. Females are more commonly affected than males and the disease tends to occur in middle age. It is due to the autoantibody-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the post-synaptic membrane. This consequentially leads to a decreased transmission at the neuromuscular junction. Failure of transmission results in muscle weakness.

Clinical features of myasthenia gravis:

* Muscle weakness and fatiguability increase with repeated use or during late in the day and may improve following rest or sleep. Limb weakness is proximal and asymmetrical

* Cranial muscles particularly the lids and extraocular muscles are involved early in the course - diplopia, ptosis

* Facial weakness - snarling expression on smiling

* Weakness in chewing

* Speech with nasal timbre due to the weakness of palate and tongue

* Difficulty in swallowing

* Deep tendon reflexes are intact

* Myasthenic crisis - acute exacerbation of muscle weakness especially intercostal and diaphragmatic muscles resulting in ventilatory failure. It is most commonly due to infection and anticholinesterase medication overuse.

Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma and other autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Grave's disease, neuromyelitis optics, systemic lupus erythematosus, etc.

Diagnosis:

* Ice-pack test - application of ice pack over the eyes improves ptosis (decreases activity of acetylcholinesterase, this increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and increase transmission)

* Antibodies associated with myasthenia gravis: Anti-AChR antibodies, Anti-MuSK antibodies, Anti-LRP4 antibodies

* Repetitive nerve stimulation test shows a decremental response.

* Edrophonium chloride or Tensilon test - improvement of symptoms occurs on injecting edrophonium. Edrophonium is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. This increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and improves transmission.

Treatment:

* Anticholinesterase drugs - Pyridostigmine.

* Thymectomy.

* Immunosuppression therapy with glucocorticoids, azathioprine, tacrolimus, rituximab, etc.

* Plasmapheresis and intravenous immunoglobulin.

Other options:

Option B: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is an autoimmune disorder affecting the presynaptic membrane at the neuromuscular junction. It is due to the autoantibodies against the P/Q-type calcium channels at the motor nerve terminal which results in the impaired release of Ach from the presynaptic nerve terminal.

Patients present with proximal muscle weakness of the lower limbs, ptosis, and diplopia. However, symptoms might improve after brief exercise. Deep tendon reflexes are absent or reduced. They also experience autonomic dysfunction and present with dry mouth and impotence. It is most commonly associated with small cell lung cancer.

Repetitive nerve stimulation test shows an incremental response at higher rates. Treatment involves plasmapheresis, immunotherapy, and drugs such as 3,4-Diaminopyridine (3,4-DAP) and pyridostigmine.

Option C: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is X-linked muscular dystrophy due to mutations in the dystrophin gene. It most commonly affects boys in their childhood.

Patients initially present with proximal muscle weakness predominantly of the lower limbs. Calf muscle hypertrophy is a cardinal feature. Other features include mental retardation, cardiac failure, and myoglobinuria. Elevated serum creatinine kinase levels and genetic testing are diagnostic of DMD.

Option D: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease that most commonly presents with arthralgia with early morning stiffness. It predominantly occurs in middle-aged women. Other important features of SLE include malar rash, discoid rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, pleuritis, pericarditis, and  lupus nephritis. Anti nuclear antibodies, Anti-dsDNA antibodies, anti-smith antibodies are positive in SLE.

Pearl PF1621: Auto antibodies in a few disorders

Auto-antibodies in myasthenia gravis:

i) Anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies

ii) Anti-muscle-specific kinase (MuSK) antibodies

iii) Anti-low density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4 (LRP4) antibodies

Anti-C1q antibodies are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and membrane proliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN).

Anti-Smith antibodies (Anti-Sm) are associated with SLE.

Anti-lysosome associated membrane protein-2 (LAMP-2) antibodies are associated with certain types of vasculitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old female patient presents with cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, and on examination slow ankle jerk with a TSH level of 15 IU/L and low T3, and T4. Of the following, the next best step in the management of this patient is to:
options: Order a thyroid radionuclide uptake and scan
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Begin treatment with levothyroxine (LT4)

The likely diagnosis in this patient is hypothyroidism. Thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine should be started immediately after diagnosis.

Laboratory investigations in a patient with hypothyroidism would show low levels of total and free T3, T4, and rT3, with high TSH levels and normal combined protein levels.

Normally, the thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) is released by the hypothalamus. It stimulates the pituitary gland to release the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which in turn stimulates the thyroid gland to produce T3 and T4 hormones. Elevated TSH with a low level of free T4 is suggestive of primary hypothyroidism.

In the case of secondary hypothyroidism, TSH levels may be low, normal, or even slightly increased. The latter is due to the secretion of immunoactive but bio-inactive forms of TSH. The diagnosis is confirmed by the detection of a low unbound T4 level.

Patients with hypothyroidism often present with tiredness, weakness, dry skin, hair loss, difficulty concentrating, poor memory, constipation, cold intolerance, and weight gain with poor appetite. On examination, they may have cool peripheral extremities, puffy faces, hyporeflexia, bradycardia, and peripheral edema.

The best outcomes occur when levothyroxine therapy is started immediately after diagnosis. The clinical effects of levothyroxine replacement are slow to appear.

If there is no residual function, the daily replacement dose of levothyroxine is usually 1.6 μg/kg body weight (typically 100–150 μg), ideally taken at least 30 minutes before breakfast.

TSH responses are gradual and should be determined 2 months following the initiation of treatment or change in dose. Once the full replacement is achieved and TSH levels are stable, TSH measurement is recommended at annual intervals.

In patients who have developed hypothyroidism following treatment of Graves' disease, lower doses are needed for replacement. This is because there is often underlying autonomous function, necessitating lower replacement doses (typically 75–125 μg/d).

Pearl PF1342: Causes of hypothyroidism:

Primary (Low T3, T4 > Raised TSH levels)
Secondary (Low TSH levels > Low T3, T4)
Tertiary ( Low TRH > Low TSH > Low T3,T4 )

Hashimoto’s thyroiditis

RAI therapy for Grave’s disease

Post thyroidectomy

Excessive iodine intake - Wolff Chiakoff effect

Subacute thyrioditis

Medications: Antithyroid drugs, lithium

Iodine deficiency, dyshormonogenesis

Pituitary tumour

Pituitary resection or ablation

Hypothalamic insufficiency

Resistance to thyroid hormone

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic is brought to the hospital due to fever and abdominal pain. He was diagnosed to have a cirrhotic liver 2 years back. The ascitic fluid shows a neutrophil count of 360 cell/ microliter. Which of the following is the drug of choice in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cefotaxime

This patient’s clinical features are suggestive of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). The drug of choice in this patient is cefotaxime.

SBP is characterized by spontaneous infection of the ascitic fluid without an intraabdominal source. It is commonly seen in adults in association with liver cirrhosis. The pathogens involved are Escherichia coli, streptococci, enterococci, and pneumococci.

In a patient with ascites, SBP presents with fever and acute abdominal pain. On examination, tachycardia, tachypnea, and signs of peritonitis are seen. Hepatic encephalopathy and gastrointestinal bleeding may also occur.

Diagnosis is by paracentesis and an ascitic fluid neutrophil count of >250/mm3 is suggestive of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Ascitic fluid culture may reveal pathogenic organisms.

The first line of empirical treatment is with IV cefotaxime 2g for 5 days. After 48 hours of antibiotic therapy, repeat paracentesis is done to confirm the reduction in absolute neutrophil count by 25%. Albumin infusion can be given as it decreases the risk of renal failure and improves patient survival. Early diagnosis and treatment improve the prognosis.

For prophylaxis, oral once daily, ciprofloxacin or norfloxacin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (double strength) is given. IV ceftriaxone may be used in hospitalised patients. Prophylaxis can help to reduce the risk of recurrent SBP, as well as the risk of other complications, such as hepatorenal syndrome and mortality. Prophylaxis for SBP should be considered in the following patients:

* Patients who have survived an episode of SBP

* Patients with low-protein ascites (total ascitic protein less than 1 g/dL) and impaired kidney function (serum creatinine 1.2 g/dL or higher)

* Patients with decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class C)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents to you with features of anemia, fever, and recurrent nosebleeds. On examination there is hepatosplenomegaly, Lab investigations revealed: Hb = 6 g/dL, TLC count = 40,000/ cu.mm with 10% blasts and platelet count = 12,000/cu.mm. On further investigation, t(8;21) was detected in the blasts. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML)

The given clinical picture suggests leukemia.

For the diagnosis of acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML), the blast cell count should be ≥20% either in the peripheral blood or bone marrow, as per WHO criteria.

However, there are three important exceptions. For cases with lower blast count (<20%), a diagnosis of AML can be made if there is the presence of any one of the following three cytogenetic abnormalities:

* t(15;17)

* t(8;21)

* Inversion 16 or t(16;16)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 54-year-old man was brought to the casualty with fever, headache, focal seizures. EEG shows focal temporal lobe spikes. CSF sample analysis shows 50 cells with 90% Lymphocytes and 10% Neutrophils. What would be the drug of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acyclovir

The given clinical scenario and investigations are suggestive of Encephalitis for which the drug of choice is intravenous acyclovir. The treatment is effective only if it is started early.

The clinical hallmark of encephalitis is the acute onset of fever and focal neurologic signs and with hemorrhagic necrosis especially the temporal lobe if there is HSV encephalitis. The most sensitive investigation is HSV DNA demonstration in CSF by PCR.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old construction factory worker presents with dyspnoea. He has been working in this industry for the past 25 years. Which is the most specific malignancy that we can expect in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Malignant mesothelioma

Construction factory workers show an increased risk of exposure to asbestos. The most specific malignancy in a patient with asbestosis is malignant mesothelioma.

Malignant mesothelioma is a rare malignant tumour of the pleura, associated with heavy asbestos exposure. The lifetime risk of developing mesothelioma in heavily exposed individuals is as high as 7% to 10%.

Asbestosis is a diffuse interstitial fibrosing disease of the lung. Characteristic findings include:

* Irregular or linear opacities - Pleural plaques that are usually first noted in the lower lung fields are the chest radiographic hallmark of asbestosis.

* An indistinct heart border or a “ground-glass” appearance in the lung fields may be seen.

* Pulmonary function testing in asbestosis reveals a restrictive pattern with a decrease in both lung volumes and diffusing capacity along with mild airflow obstruction (due to peribronchiolar fibrosis).

* Lung cancer is the most common asbestos-related cancer.

* Mesothelioma (pleural and peritoneal) is the most specific asbestos-related cancer.

Adenocarcinoma of lung is still the most common malignancy seen in patients with asbestosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old male patient comes to your clinic with 8-month history of shortness of breath and non-productive cough. He has smoked half a pack of cigarettes for the past 30 years. On physical examination, clubbing is seen and fine crackles are heard on both sides during inspiration. You perform pulmonary function tests and it shows an FVC of 78% and FEV1/FVC ratio of 92%. You request a CT scan of the chest. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pulmonary fibrosis

Pulmonary fibrosis is the most likely diagnosis in this patient, given his symptoms, such as shortness of breath, persistent nonproductive cough,clubbing, bilateral inspiratory crackles, pulmonary function tests, and imaging findings.

The image shows the presence of honeycombing (black arrows), traction bronchiectasis (white arrow), and a reticular pattern (black dotted arrows). The lesions are typically located along subpleural regions.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is the most common cause of interstitial lung disease (ILD) of unknown cause. This entity has a higher predominance in males(usually the sixth and seventh decades).Typical pathological finding in IPF is Usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP).

Investigations:

* PFTs: Demonstrate a restrictive pattern.

* High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT):

* Subpleural reticular opacities

* Architectural distortion

* Traction bronchiectasis

* Honeycomb appearance

Note: The incidence in men is higher than in women.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with a history of COPD presents with sudden onset increased shortness of breath. His ABG analysis reveals pH - 7.24, pCO2 - 60 mm Hg, pO2- 52 mmHg, and HCO3 - 27 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV)

This given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute exacerbation of COPD with ABG showing respiratory acidosis. The next step for this patient would be to start non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV).

Initial management of acute exacerbation of COPD includes:

* Bronchodilators: Inhaled beta-agonists and muscarinic antagonists.

* Antibiotics

* Supplemental oxygen

* Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV)

If initial NIPPV fails, then, invasive PPV may be provided. However, during the invasive PPV, the tidal volume is reduced to prevent damage to the alveolar structures. This decrease in minute ventilation causes progressive hypercapnia, which is however permitted to a certain extent for the benefit of the patient (commonly known as permissive hypercapnia).

The severity of COPD assessed by Global Initiative for Lung Disease (GOLD) is classified as:

Severity

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 68-year-old male presents with chronic back pain, easy fatigability, and a history of multiple urinary tract infections over the past 3 months. His ESR is elevated, and a skull X-ray is shown below. Which of the following investigations would be useful for diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serum electrophoresis

The clinical scenario is indicative of multiple myeloma, and a useful diagnostic test would be serum electrophoresis.

Multiple myeloma involves a malignant proliferation of plasma cells, resulting in excessive production of abnormal immunoglobulins, causing a spike called the M band in Serum Electrophoresis.

The given image demonstrates a sharp peak ("church spire” or M band) in the gamma globulin region. This is characteristically seen in a patient with multiple myeloma.

Certain common diseases and their electrophoretic pattern:

Condition
Electrophoretic pattern

Chronic infections
Smooth increase in gamma globulins

Multiple myeloma
Gamma globulin part is increased (M BAND)

Liver cirrhosis
Reduced albumin and compensatory increase in globulin

Primary immune deficiency
Gamma globulin reduced

α1 antitrypsin deficiency
α1 band is thin and even lost sometimes

Multiple myelomas:

* Malignant neoplasm of plasma cells characterized by:

* Presence of monoclonal immunoglobulin or light chains in the serum and urine

* Bone destruction (lytic lesions)

* Disease of older adults, with a peak age of incidence of 65 to 70 years

* Signs and symptoms

* Hypercalcemia

* Pathologic fractures/lytic bone lesions

* Renal failure

* Anemia

* Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray

* Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin

* Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

* Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20%plasma cells (normal is < 5%)

* Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation (High level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation.)

* Plasma cell tumors are positive for CD138

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 72-year-old man presented with weight loss, decreased appetite, and iron deficiency anemia. Chest X-ray was done and given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lung metastasis

The X-ray depicts multiple large, well-circumscribed, round pulmonary metastases that look similar to cannonballs. Hence it is known as cannonball metastasis that is seen in lung metastasis.

The most common primaries to result in pulmonary metastases in adults include:

* Breast carcinoma

* Colorectal carcinoma

* Renal cell carcinoma

* Uterine leiomyosarcoma

* Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A child presents with Hb 6.3 with a history of repeated blood transfusions. Investigations show MCV- 70 fl and the peripheral smear showed a hypochromic microcytic picture. Which of the following investigations should be done next in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hb electrophoresis

The given clinical scenario of repeated transfusions, low Hb, low MCV, and a hypochromic microcytic picture in the smear is suggestive of thalassemia and Hb electrophoresis should be done in this for diagnosis.

Hb Electrophoresis is used for newborn screening. High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is the investigation of choice but is not as definitive as globin gene sequencing.

Each individual carries 2 beta-chain genes and 4 alpha-chain genes.

Haemoglobin levels:

* Normal hemoglobin pattern- HbA=95%, HbA2=3.5%, HbF =1.5%

* Beta-thalassemia trait- HbA=90%, HbA2=5%, HbF=5%

* Beta-thalassemia intermedia- HbA=45%, HbA2=5%, HbF=50%

Clinical features in thalassemia:

* Anaemia

* Jaundice and pigment gallstones

* Skeletal deformities including facial deformities, changes in body habitus, osteopenia/osteoporosis

* Iron overload

* Growth impairment

* Hepatosplenomegaly

* Endocrine abnormalities including hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus

* Heart failure and arrhythmias

Laboratory studies:

* Peripheral smear is likely to show microcytic hypochromic anaemia with target cells, teardrop cells, and some coarse basophilic stippling in certain cases. These findings are non-specific.

* High RBC count

* Low reticulocyte count

* ↑ LDH
↑ Indirect bilirubin
↓ Haptoglobin
Coombs test negative

* High transferrin saturation, normal serum iron levels, elevated ferritin levels

Other options:

Option A: Measurement of serum iron is necessary to monitor for iron overload in case of repeated blood transfusion. But in this case, the first step is to confirm the diagnosis by doing Hb electrophoresis.

Option B: Direct Coomb's test is used to test for AIHA- Autoimmune hemolytic anaemia. Given the history, AIHA seems unlikely and it usually occurs in adults and is unusual in a child.

Option C: Osmotic fragility test is a test done in the case of hereditary spherocytosis. It presents with splenomegaly, anemia, and hyperbilirubinemia. The MCV is decreased and MCHC is increased due to dehydration. It is unlikely to have a history of chronic blood transfusion.

Pearl PF0864: Thalassemia syndromes

Normally each individual carries 4 functional alpha chain genes and 2 functional beta chain genes. Alpha and beta-thalassemia are inherited disorders in which there is reduced production of alpha-globin or beta-globin chains, respectively.

* Alpha thalassemia: Gene deletion is the most common cause of reduced α-chain synthesis.

* Beta +- thalassemia: The most common cause is splicing mutation.

* Beta 0- thalassemia: Chain terminator mutations are the most common cause.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A man was working in a field and he suddenly collapsed on a hot summer afternoon. On examination, there were no physical signs of dehydration but radial pulse was present. His serum electrolytes level was normal. The doctor found that the body temperature was 106 degrees Fahrenheit. Which of the following should be given as first aid in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cover with cool damp sheets

The given clinical vignette in a patient with no signs of dehydration and body temperature of 106oF is highly suggestive of heatstroke. The first step among the following options is to cover the patient with a cool damp sheet to reduce body temperature.

The following are the first aid measures to be done for heatstroke:

* Move the person to a cool environment.

* Remove any restricting clothes to dissipate the heat.

* Try cooling the patient by blowing air using a fan, spraying water using a hose or sponge, using cool damp sheets or blankets, immersing the patient in a tub of water or shower, ice bath, etc.

* Place ice packs on the groin, neck, back, and armpits where the blood vessels are seen close to the skin, which reduces temperature fast.

* If the patient is not breathing or with no pulse then CPR has to be initiated.

Heatstroke/ thermic fever/ heat hyperpyrexia is due to the failure of the heat regulation center of the hypothalamus. It is caused by failure of cutaneous circulation and sweating. The predisposing factors include high temperature, increased humidity, minor infections, old age, lack of acclimatization, alcoholism.

Heatstroke can be:

* Exertion-induced heat stroke is seen in people with prolonged exposure to or physical exertion in high temperatures, usually without adequate training.

* Sedentary heatstroke is a disease of elderly or infirm people whose cardiovascular systems are unable to adapt to the stress of a hot environment and release sufficient heat such that body temperature rises.

All the signs of shock are present. Patients usually present with a sudden collapse accompanied by loss of consciousness. Typical vital sign abnormalities include tachypnea, tachycardias, hypotension, and a widened pulse pressure. Other specific signs include rapid Kussmaul type of breathing, the absence of sweating with dry, hot skin, delirium, coma, convulsions, rhabdomyolysis, multiorgan failure.

Although there is no single specific diagnostic test, clinical features of exposure to heat stress, CNS dysfunction, and core temperature >104.9-degree Fahrenheit (> 40.5 degrees Celsius) help establish the preliminary diagnosis. The body temperature must be measured rectally.

Treatment includes rapidly cooling the body with ice water till the rectal temperature falls below 1020F.

Autopsy findings include the presence of edema and reduction of Purkinje's cells in the cerebellum.

There is no role of antipyretics in the control of environmentally induced hyperthermia. They also exacerbate the complications (acute kidney injury, hepatic failure, DIC).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient came to casualty complaining of a severe headache. On examination, there was no focal neurological defect. However, neck rigidity was present. The casualty medical officer ordered an emergency CT which revealed the following finding. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH).

The most common cause of SAH is trauma. The most common spontaneous cause of SAH is the rupture of berry aneurysms.

It clinically presents as a thunderclap headache with neck rigidity, transient loss of consciousness and no focal neurological deficit. Non-contrast CT shows blood in the basal cistern.

Although sudden headache in the absence of focal neurological symptoms is the hallmark of aneurysmal rupture, focal neurological deficits may occur.

Pearl PF0339: Intracranial Hemorrhage (ICH)

Extradural hemorrhage (EDH):

* Source: Arterial bleed

* MC- Middle meningeal artery

* Cause- Trauma

* Clinical features: Lucid interval is characteristic

* CT – Lentiform opacity

* Treatment: A large or rapidly evolving EDH requires surgical evacuation

Subdural hemorrhage (SDH)

* Source: Venous bleed

* Bridging dural veins

* Causes: Trauma, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, alcohol abuse, shaken baby syndrome

* Clinical features

* Acute SDH: may be associated with lucid interval

* Chronic SDH: drowsiness, headache

* CT- crescentic opacity

* Treatment: May resolve spontaneously or require surgical drainage

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)

* Source: Arterial bleed

* Causes:

* MC – Trauma

* 2nd MC – Rupture of berry aneurysm

* MC sites: Terminal ICA, MCA bifurcation, top of basilar artery

* Clinical features: Thunderclap headache with neck stiffness +/- FND

* Investigations:

* Non-contrast CT brain,

* CSF xanthochromia (peaks in 2 days and subsides in 2 weeks)

* Treatment:

* Clipping/coiling of berry aneurysm,

* Triple H therapy – hypertension, hypervolemia, and hemodilution to prevent vasospasm

Intraparenchymal hemorrhage- (MC type of ICH)

* Source- Arterial bleed

* Causes:

* MC – hypertension

* Trauma, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, bleeding disorders, neoplasms, vascular malformations

* MC sites:

* Putamen (basal ganglia)

* Thalamus

* Cerebellum

* Pons

* Treatment:

* Correction of any identified coagulopathy by infusing prothrombin complex concentrates, FFP or fresh platelets as required

* Surgical evacuation for cerebellar hematoms >3 cm in size

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient comes with a blood pressure of 160/100 mmHg and left-sided facial paralysis and weakness for 8 hours. Her CT is shown below. What would be your next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Observation and monitoring

This patient with sudden onset hemiparesis and a normal CT could have a transient ischemic attack or an ischemic stroke. The next step for this patient would be observation and monitoring.

Non-contrast CT(NCCT) is the imaging modality of choice in patients with acute stroke. CT may appear normal for the first few hours and the infarct may not appear until 24-48 hours. Diffusion-weighted MRI(DWMRI) is more sensitive to detecting early brain infarction.

Initial treatment of acute ischemic stroke includes maintaining the patient's airway, breathing, and circulation. Complications such as hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia, or fever should be treated if present.

Thrombolysis with alteplase is the first-line therapy for acute ischemic stroke and should be initiated within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. Since this patient arrived 8 hours later which is outside of window period, the appropriate management would be observation and monitoring. Endovascular mechanical thrombectomy is done in patients who do not respond to thrombolytic therapy or in whom thrombolysis is contraindicated. Oral aspirin is recommended for the acute treatment of ischemic stroke.

Labetalol, nicardipine, and clevidipine are the first-line anti-hypertensive agents used in the acute phase of stroke. If the patient is to receive thrombolytic therapy, maintain BP ≤185/110mmHg. If not, BP should not be treated acutely unless it is more than 220/120 mmHg. BP should be lowered cautiously by only 15% in the first 24 hours in order to preserve perfusion to the ischemic penumbra.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with severe pain and swelling in his knee joint since 10 days. He also complains of pain and discomfort during urination. He says that he had diarrhoea one month ago and he has been unwell since then. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reactive arthritis

The given scenario describes acute arthritis following an infection which is also associated with urethritis and generalized malaise. These features are suggestive of reactive arthritis.

Reactive arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthritis that occurs as a consequnece of a recent enteric or urogenital infection. It is associated with HLA B27. It is also associated with extra-articular manifestations:

* Urogenital- urethritis, prostitis, cervicitis

* Ocular- conjuctivitis, anterior uveitis

* Mucocutaneous- oral ulcers, keratoderma blennorrhagica, circinate balanitis

It presents as a triad of arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis in some patients.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient was admitted to the ICU 48 hours after the fracture of the femur. The saturation of oxygen in the rebreathing unit was 100% but his SpO2 remained at 60%. The patient is in a state of confusion. Chest radiograph showed lung fields to be clear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fat embolism

The most likely diagnosis of the above clinical scenario is a fat embolism. The presence of respiratory insufficiency and altered mental status following a long bone fracture (fracture of the femur) favors the diagnosis.

Fat embolism syndrome results from the presence of numerous fat emboli within the microcirculation. It most commonly occurs after the fracture of the long bone or pelvis. They present with non-specific symptoms like tachypnea, tachycardia, and fever that manifest within 24- 48 hours after the injury. Damage to the microvasculature of various organs leads to :

* Mild hypoxia to rapidly progressing respiratory failure.

* Depression of the central nervous system.

* Petechial rashes

* Hemorrhagic lesions of the retina.

Pearl PF1166: Gurd's criteria for diagnosing fat embolism syndrome

Major criteria

* Axillary or subconjunctival petechiae

* Hypoxemia with PaO2 <60 mmHg, FIO2 < 0.4

* CNS depression disproportionate to the hypoxemia

* Pulmonary edema

Minor criteria

* Tachycardia (HR >110 beats per minute)

* Pyrexia (temp >38.50C)

* Emboli visible in retina

* Fat globules in urine

* Fat globules in sputum

* Unexplanied drop in hematocrit or platelet count

* Increased ESR

At least one major criterion and four minor criteria are required to make a diagnosis of fat embolism syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A resident is evaluating a patient, who presented with acute onset of chest pain and dyspnea, for pulmonary embolism. Which of the following imaging test should be performed to confirm this diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT pulmonary angiography

CT pulmonary angiography should be performed as it is the principal imaging test for the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism (PE).

Option A: Most patients with acute PE have normal echocardiograms. However, echocardiography is a very useful diagnostic tool for detecting conditions that may mimic PE, such as acute myocardial infarction, pericardial tamponade, and aortic dissection.

Option C: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan is now considered a second-line test for diagnosing PE. It is mainly used when CT findings are inconclusive or the patient cannot receive intravenous contrast.

Option D: MR pulmonary angiography may detect large proximal PE but is not reliable for smaller segmental and subsegmental PE. It is used when neither CT angiography nor ventilation-perfusion scan can be done.

The images below demonstrate a pulmonary embolus (marked by arrows). The image of the gross specimen shows saddle thromboembolism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young male child was brought for psychiatric evaluation for intellectual disability. On examination, his IQ was 45. He has a long face, large ear, large testis and a cardiac murmur. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fragile X syndrome

The given clinical vignette along with the family history is suggestive of fragile X syndrome.

* Fragile X syndrome is the second most common genetic cause of mental retardation (Down syndrome being the most common).

* It is caused by a trinucleotide mutation in the familial mental retardation-1 (FMR1) gene.

* When the cells were cultured in a folate-deficient medium, the cytogenetic alteration was discovered as a break in the staining in the long arm of the X chromosome. As it appeared that the chromosome was “broken” at this locale, it was named as a fragile site.

* In fragile X syndrome, the affected males are mentally retarded, with an IQ in the range of 20 to 60.

* The characteristic phenotypic features includes:

* Long face with a large mandible

* Large everted ears

* Large testicles (macro-orchidism)

* In some cases, hyperextensible joints, a high arched palate, and mitral valve prolapse may also be noted.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly obese man was brought to casualty with complaints of severe chest pain for the last two hours. He has also had profuse sweating, pain in the left arm, nausea, and one episode of vomiting. On examination, his pulse rate is 58 per minute and blood pressure is 90/60 mm of Hg. ECG was done and it shows the following finding. Cardiac biomarker showed elevated troponin levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inferior wall MI

The given presentation of chest pain, and elevated biomarkers depict that the patient has a myocardial infarction. In the ECG, there is elevation of ST-segments in leads II, III, aVF, with reciprocal change in lead aVL. This depicts inferior wall MI. It mainly occurs due to blockage of the posterior descending branch of the right coronary artery.
