questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly woman presented with symptoms of confusion, thirst, and abdominal pain. On examination, she had pallor and thoracic spine tenderness. Her lab investigations showed the following findings. An X-ray of her skull is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? * Hb - 6.9g/dL * WBC 4000/cm3 with normal differential count * Serum calcium 13mg/dL * Creatinine 2.3mg/dL * Total protein 9g/dL * Albumin 2.4g/dL * Urinalysis: positive for Bence-Jones proteins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Multiple myeloma

The given clinical features along with hypercalcemia, elevated creatinine suggestive of renal failure, anemia, osteolytic bone lesions (CRAB features), hypoalbuminemia with elevated total proteins and Bence Jones proteinuria make multiple myeloma the most likely diagnosis.

Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia with the proliferation of plasma cells derived from a single clone. It is associated with an increased osteoclast activity with suppression of osteoblast activity, causing punched-out lytic lesions in the bone and hypercalcemia.

Signs and symptoms

* Bone pain is the most common symptom

* Pathologic fractures

* Recurrent bacterial infections

* Renal failure

* Normocytic normochromic anemia, elevated ESR, Hypercalcemia, normal ALP (ALP is a marker of bone growth and hence is not increased in multiple myeloma)

* Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray

* Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin

* Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

* Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20% plasma cells (normal is < 5%)

* Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation (High level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation)

Revised International Myeloma Working Group criteria for the diagnosis of multiple myeloma:

Presence of ≥10% clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow or confirmation of a plasmacytoma in bone or extramedullary tissue by biopsy

Plus

Any one or more of the following myeloma-defining events:

*  Evidence of end-organ damage specific to plasma cell proliferative disorder (CRAB features)

* HyperCalcemia: Serum calcium level >1 mg/dL higher than the upper limit of normal or >11 mg/dL

* Renal insufficiency: Creatinine clearance <40 mL/min or serum creatinine >2 mg/dL

* Anemia: Haemoglobin level of >20 g/L (2gm/dl) below the lowest limit of normal, or Hb <10 g/dL

* Bone lesions: At least one osteolytic lesion identified on X-ray, CT or PET-CT.

* Any one or more of the following biomarkers of malignancy:

* Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥60%

* Serum involved/uninvolved free light-chain ratio of 100 or greater

* >1 focal lesion on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) that is at least 5 mm or greater in size.

Note:

* The presence of at least one of these markers is considered sufficient for a diagnosis of multiple myeloma, regardless of the presence or absence of symptoms or CRAB features.

* Each of these markers has been shown to be associated with an approximately 80% or higher risk of developing myeloma-related organ damage within two years.

Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) is usually due to a solitary parathyroid adenoma and is not associated with anemia and hypoalbuminemia. It is characterized by hypercalcemia and low serum phosphorus in presence of elevated PTH levels. 24-hour urine calcium should be checked which will be normal or elevated in PHPT but will be decreased in familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia. Prior neck irradiation is the only known risk factor. The clinical features are known as the "bones, stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans" which include:

* Renal: renal stones (most common clinical manifestation), nephrocalcinosis, UTI, renal insufficiency

* Musculoskeletal: Osteitis fibrosa cystica, osteopenia causing osteoporosis, proximal myopathy

* Gastrointestinal: constipation due to hypercalcemia, peptic ulcer disease, and rarely pancreatitis

* Neuropsychiatric: decreased concentration, fatigue, and depression

First-line treatment includes bisphosphonates and calcitonin is usually used as a bridge until sustained action of bisphosphonates is seen. Surgery is the definitive management for PHPT and Sestamibi scan is the most accurate and reliable investigation for imaging parathyroid glands prior to surgery. Elevated ALP  levels are seen in concomitant bone diseases, and such patients may develop postoperative hypocalcemia due to hungry bone syndrome.

Milk alkali syndrome occurs on ingestion of large amounts of calcium and vitamin D supplements. It results in hypercalcemia, alkalosis, and renal impairment leading to nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis.

Pearl PF0580: WHO Classification of Plasma Cell Neoplasms

Plasma cell neoplasms and variants

Plasma cell myeloma

• Non secretory: No secretion of Ig, No M component.

• Smoldering: M protein in serum ≥ 30 g/L and/or ≥10% clonal plasma cells in bone marrow, and no related organ or tissue impairment.

• Plasma-cell leukemia: >20% plasma cells in the peripheral blood or Absolute plasma cell count of >2 X 109/L.

Plasmacytoma

• Solitary plasmacytoma: Localized tumour of monoclonal plasma cells with no clinical features of plasma cell myeloma.

• Extramedullary(extraosseous) plasmacytoma: Localized plasma cell neoplasms that arise in tissues other than bone.

Monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition diseases

• Primary amyloidosis: Tumor secreting light chains that are deposited as beta-pleated sheet structure (amyloid light chain).

• Systemic light and heavy chain diseases: Secrete abnormal light or heavy chain or both, which do not form beta pleated sheet, stain Congo Red or contain amyloid P component.

Plasma cell neoplasms with associated paraneoplastic syndrome

POEMS syndrome- Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, Monoclonal gammopathy, Skin changes.

TEMPI syndrome

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An intern observed that a patient was unresponsive, and an ECG which was performed urgently showed an arrhythmia as below. DC shock was delivered but the arrhythmia persisted and the patient is still unresponsive. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Start CPR

The patient is in cardiac arrest and the rhythm shown is ventricular fibrillation. Since one defibrillation is given and the patient is still unresponsive, CPR has to be given for 2 minutes after which the rhythm will be assessed again.

The management of ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia is the same. Chest compressions are to be started following defibrillation.

Defibrillation involves delivering an electrical current between two pads placed on the chest so as to interrupt the disorganized cardiac activity and restore an organized cardiac rhythm. The energy that must be applied is

* Monophasic defibrillator: 360 J

* Biphasic defibrillator: 120-200 J

It is of utmost necessity to defibrillate at the earliest because the chances of survival decrease by 7-10% every minute without defibrillation.

Pearl PF1316: Adult Basic Life Support (BLS) Algorithm (Updated as per 2020 guidelines)

Pearl PF1606: High quality CPR for adults

* Push hard: 5-6cm depth

* Push fast: 100-120/min frequency

* Allow for complete chest recoil

* Minimize interruptions in compressions <10 seconds

* Avoid excessive ventilation

* Rotate compressor every 2 min or earlier if fatigued

* If no advanced airway, 30:2 compression-ventilation ratio

Attempt to improve CPR quality if :

* Quantitative waveform capnography - PETCO2 <10mmHg,

* Intra-arterial pressure - If relaxation phase (diastolic) pressure <20mmHg

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Following gastrectomy, the patient is most likely to have which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin B12 deficiency

After gastrectomy, the patient is likely to have vitamin B12 deficiency.

Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum. Vitamin B12 binds to intrinsic factor, a protein secreted by the parietal cells of the stomach, and the complex is absorbed across the ileal mucosa. Hence after gastrectomy IF-B12 complex is not formed and there is impaired absorption of vitamin B12.

Folic acid is absorbed mainly in Jejunum.

Gastric ulcer does not occur following gastrectomy.

Constipation is not common after gastrectomy.

Pearl PF1304: Major Sites of Absorption of Hematopoietic Factors

* Duodenum + upper jejunum: Iron

* Jejunum: Folate

* Terminal Ileum: Vitamin B12

Mnemonic - Dude Is Just Feeling Ill Bro

Pearl PF0380: Causes of Megaloblastic Anemia

Vitamin B12 Deficiency causes:

* Decreased Intake

* Inadequate diet

* Vegetarianism

* Impaired Absorption

* Intrinsic factor deficiency

* Pernicious anemia

* Gastrectomy

* Malabsorption states

* Diffuse intestinal disease (e.g., lymphoma, systemic sclerosis)

* Ileal resection

* Ileitis

* Competitive parasitic uptake

* Fish tapeworm infestation

* Bacterial overgrowth in blind loops and diverticula of bowel

Folic Acid Deficiency causes:

* Decreased Intake

* Inadequate diet

* Alcoholism

* Infancy

* Impaired Absorption

* Malabsorption states

* Intrinsic intestinal disease

* Anticonvulsants

* Oral contraceptives

* Increased Loss

* Hemodialysis

* Increased Requirement

* Pregnancy, infancy

* Disseminated cancer

* Markedly increased hematopoiesis

* Impaired Utilization

* Folic acid antagonists

* Unresponsive to vitamin B12 or folic acid therapy

* Metabolic inhibitors of DNA synthesis and/or folate metabolism

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the rhythm in the following ECG rhythm strip.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Normal sinus rhythm

The above ECG strip shows normal sinus rhythm.

The features in this ECG that suggest this diagnosis are as follows:

* The QRS complexes are narrow (<120 ms or 3 small squares) which implies that the impulse is supraventricular and is conducted via the normal conduction pathway.

* Each QRS complex is preceded by a P wave. This means that all the atrial depolarizations that arise in the sinus node are conducted to the ventricles.

* The PR interval is constant for all the impulses and is normal(<200 ms) in duration.

* The RR interval is constant which implies a regular rhythm.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: If all Extraocular muscles are paralysed ,where would you suspect the lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Midbrain and Pons

If all Extraocular muscles are paralysed , the lesion can be suspected in Midbrain and Pons.

All the extraocular muscles (including inferior oblique) are innervated by the oculomotor (III) nerve except:

* Lateral rectus which is supplied by abducens (VI) nerve

* Superior oblique which is supplied by trochlear (IV) nerve

The nuclei of Cranial Nerve 3, 4 arises from Midbrain and Cranial Nerve 6 from Pons.

There are seven extraocular muscles present in the eye. They are:

* Levator palpebrae superioris - Which elevates the upper eyelids

* Four recti muscles - Superior, inferior, medial, and lateral recti

* Two obliques - Superior and inferior oblique

The muscles originate from the back of the orbit in a common tendinous ring called the annulus of Zinn and are inserted into the sclera.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Tall and tented T waves, wide QRS, and absent P wave are features of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyperkalemia

Hyperkalemia produces a sequence of changes usually beginning with narrowing and peaking (tenting) of the T waves. Further elevation of extracellular K+ leads to:

* AV conduction disturbances.

* Diminution in P-wave amplitude.

* Widening of the QRS interval.

The ECG changes that can be seen in hyperkalemia depend on the extent of hyperkalemia.

S. No.
Serum potassium level
ECG change

1
5.5 - 6.5 mEq/L
tall, peaked T waves with 'tented' or 'pinched' shape

2
6.5 - 7.5 mEq/L
loss of P waves

3
7.0 - 8.0 mEq/L
widened QRS complex

4
> 8.0 mEq/L
sine wave

Severe hyperkalemia eventually causes cardiac arrest with a slow sinusoidal type of mechanism("sine-wave" pattern) followed by asystole.

The most common cause of hyperkalemia is kidney failure. Drugs that cause hyperkalemia include angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, potassium-sparing diuretics.

Treatment of hyperkalemia involves the following

* Administer intravenous calcium gluconate which raises the threshold and reduces excitability. It is cardioprotective

* Administer regular insulin with dextrose. The insulin will reduce the serum potassium concentration by causing an intracellular shift. The dextrose will counteract the hypoglycemic effects of insulin.

* Remove potassium with calcium-based resins, diuretics, or hemodialysis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Treatment of Grade I Meningioma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Surgical excision

Treatment of Grade I Meningioma is Simple surgical excision.

Meningioma:

Meningiomas are predominantly benign tumors of adults, usually attached to the dura, that arise from the meningothelial cells of the arachnoid. Meningiomas may be found along any of the external surfaces of the brain as well as within the ventricular system, where they arise from the stromal arachnoid cells of the choroid plexus.

Meningiomas are usually rounded masses with well-defined dural bases that compress the underlying brain but are easily separated from it. The surface of the mass is usually encapsulated by thin, fibrous tissue and may have a bosselated or polypoid appearance.

They may also grow en plaque, in which the tumor spreads in a sheetlike fashion along the surface of the dura.

WHO grading of meningiomas:

* Grade I - Most meningiomas fall under this category. For example - Syncytial, fibroblastic, transitional, psammomatous, secretory, microcytic.

* Simple surgical excision is the treatment.

* Grade II - They are also called atypical meningiomas. These have a higher rate of recurrence and more aggressive growth. For example- Clear cell and chordoid type of meningiomas.

* These may require radiotherapy in addition to surgery.

* Grade III - These are called anaplastic (malignant) meningiomas and are highly aggressive tumors - Papillary and rhabdoid meningiomas are examples. Surgical excision of the tumor and the tissue it has invaded is the mainstay.

* Radiotherapy is an additional treatment. The recurrence rate is high even after tumor excision.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the diagnosis if the axis is on the mark "?" from the diagram shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right axis deviation

The image shows the cardiac axis greater than +100 degrees and thus it shows right axis deviation.

The cardiac axis represents the mean QRS axis (direction of mean depolarization vector).

The normal adult QRS axis is directed downward and to the left, which is between -30 degrees and +100 degrees.

The position of lead aVF is at +90 degrees (shown in the image below). If the cardiac axis is also at +90 degrees, it would be in the same direction as lead aVF and hence aVF would show maximum R wave amplitude.

If the mean axis is:

* More negative than –30 degrees- left axis deviation

* More positive than +100 degrees- right axis deviation

* Lies between -90 to +180 degrees- extreme axis deviation

The image below shows the position of lead aVF with respect to the normal cardiac axis and the axis deviations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most commonly seen pattern in chest CT of patients affected with COVID-19?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ground glass opacity

Ground glass opacity (GGO) is the most commonly seen pattern in chest CT of patients with COVID-19.

Some of the typical features seen in the CT scans of COVID-19 patients include:

* Ground glass opacities

* Consolidation

* Air bronchograms

* Interlobular septal thickenings

* Visible intralobular lines (crazy-paving pattern)

* Reversed halo sign

The image given below shows an axial CT scan with multiple patchy areas of pure ground-glass opacities bilaterally. GGO are hazy areas with slightly increased density in lungs without obscuration of underlying bronchial and vascular margins.

The image given below shows a CT scan with bilateral GGO in the lower lobe (red frames) and air bronchogram (white arrow) in the left subpleural area. Air bronchograms appear like air-filled bronchi within a highly attenuated parenchymal background. These are dilated bronchi filled with mucus plugs and do not truly contain air.

The image given below shows a CT scan with multiple consolidation areas and interlobular septal thickening (arrows) in both the lungs. The pulmonary interstitial structures such as interlobular septa and intralobular lines can thicken and manifest as small linear opacities.

The image given below shows a CT scan with crazy-paving pattern (black circled areas). It is defined as the presence of GGOs with superimposed interlobular septal thickening giving the appearance of irregular paving stones.

The image given below shows a CT scan with multiple lesions with reversed halo sign(arrows). The reversed halo sign or atoll sign is the presence of a ring-like area of consolidation with a superimposed rounded GGO.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drug is not used for a patient diagnosed with sarcoidosis with multi organ involvement?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fludrocortisone

The drug that is not used in the treatment of multisystemic sarcoidosis is Fludrocortisone.

The first-line drug for sarcoidosis is prednisolone.

Management of sarcoidosis:

* Asymptomatic patients- monitored for disease progression

* Localized/ limited cutaneous and ocular lesions- treated using topical steroids

* Multisystem involvement:

* Systemic steroids

* Other drugs like hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and infliximab are considered when the steroids are ineffective or not tolerated

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 26-year-old male with a history of respiratory tract infection 4 weeks ago is unable to stand or walk for the past 2 weeks and the weakness is progressive, ascending, and symmetrical in nature. The lower limbs were involved before and gradually the upper limbs were also affected. On examination you note areflexia. Pain and proprioception are preserved. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Guillain-Barré syndrome

The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS).

GBS is an acute, fulminant polyradiculoneuropathy that is autoimmune in nature. GBS is caused when immune response/antibodies against external antigens like infections, vaccines, etc target similar proteins present in the person's nervous tissue.

Clinical features are rapidly evolving areflexic motor paralysis with or without sensory disturbance. Respiration is compromised when it involves respiratory muscles. In such cases, ventilatory support is needed.

High-dose intravenous immune globulin (IVIg) or plasmapheresis are equally effective for typical GBS. IVIg is the initial therapy chosen because of its ease of administration and good safety record.

Other options:

Option B: Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular disorder due to autoimmune damage to the acetylcholine receptors. It is characterized by weakness and muscle fatiguability. Weakness increases with usage. Ocular features like ptosis and diplopia can be seen. Proximal limb weakness is also present.

Option C: Polymyositis is one of the inflammatory myopathies characterized by symmetric and proximal muscle weakness. This weakness usually worsens over several weeks to months. It is more common in women. Most patients improve with immunotherapies, but they require lifelong treatment.

Option D: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease characterized by multiple episodes of neurological deficits due to patchy white matter lesions that involve various sites of the brain. It is caused by an autoimmune response directed against components of the myelin sheath. The demyelinated plaques are the hallmark of MS

Pearl PF1047: Mechanism of Immunopathogenesis of Guillain-Barre Syndrome

The following sequence of events, takes into consideration, the development of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) associated with Campylobacter jejuni infection.

* B cells recognize glycoconjugates on jejuni (Cj) that cross-react with ganglioside present on Schwann cell surface and subjacent peripheral nerve myelin.

* Most of the B cells are activated via a partially T cell–dependent route and secrete primarily IgG autoantibodies. Some B cells, activated via a T cell–independent mechanism, secrete primarily IgM

* The activated B cells escape from Peyer’s patches into regional lymph nodes.

* Activated T cells also function to assist in the opening of the blood-nerve barrier, facilitating penetration of pathogenic autoantibodies.

* The earliest changes in myelin consist of edema between myelin lamellae and vesicular disruption of the outermost myelin layers.

* These effects are associated with activation of the C5b-C9 membrane attack complex and mediated by calcium entry; it is possible that the macrophage cytokine tumor necrosis factor (TNF) also participates in myelin damage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 29-year-old male patient presents to the OPD with a 10-year history of coarse facial features and progressive enlargement of the hands and feet. Laboratory evaluation revealed elevated IGF-1 and non-suppressible growth hormone levels after the 75 g glucose challenge test. A diagnosis of acromegaly is made. Which of the following drugs is preferred for the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lanreotide depot formulation

Lanreotide depot formulation is useful in the management of acromegaly.

Acromegaly commonly occurs due to growth hormone-secreting somatotrophic adenoma. Increased secretion of growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor- 1 (IGF-1) results in acral bone overgrowth. Patients present with frontal bossing, increased hand, and foot size, mandibular enlargement with prognathism, and widened space between the lower incisor teeth. Soft tissue swelling results in increased heel pad thickness, ring tightening, characteristic coarse facial features, and a large fleshy nose.

The cardiovascular system has a significant impact on GH excess characterized by cardiomyopathy with arrhythmias, left ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, and hypertension.

Other manifestations seen in growth hormone excess are obstructive sleep apnea and diabetes mellitus.

Serum IGF-1 levels and GH suppression test with oral glucose are useful in the diagnosis. The levels of GH do not reduce in response to the oral glucose load.

GH-secreting adenomas are managed with surgery. Transsphenoidal surgical treatment is the preferred surgery. The preferred medical treatments include long-acting injectable somatostatin receptor ligand (SRL) depot formulations of octreotide and lanreotide as well as oral octreotide capsules. Another drug that is useful in acromegaly is pegvisomant. It is a growth hormone receptor antagonist and therefore, antagonizes the actions of GH.

Other options:

Option B: Terlipressin is a vasopressin analogue that acts selectively on V1 receptors and is used in the management of bleeding oesophageal varices and hepatorenal syndrome.

Option C: Ketoconazole is used in the management of Cushing's disease. Ketoconazole inhibits several P450 enzymes and effectively lowers cortisol levels in most patients with Cushing’s disease.

Option D: Leuprolide is a long-acting GnRH agonist. It is used as a palliation of carcinoma prostate, uterine fibroids, endometriosis, and precocious puberty. Side effects include hot flashes, decreased bone mineral density, vaginal dryness, and erectile dysfunction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presented with complaints of bone pain and abdominal cramps. Her family says she has a history of abnormal behavior. The consultant doctor arrived at a provisional diagnosis based on the clinical features. Which of the following would be the best investigation to arrive at a definitive diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sestamibi scan

The given clinical features are suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism. Parathyroid adenoma is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism and the Tc99m sestamibi scan is used for diagnosis of parathyroid adenoma.

Clinical features of hyperparathyroidism:

* Bones:

* Pathological fractures

* Subperiosteal bone resorption - 2nd and 3rd digits, most common in radial aspect

* Salt and pepper skull

* Osteitis fibrosa cystica or VonReckling Hausen’s disease

* Stones

* Multiple and recurrent renal stones - most common

* Nephrocalcinosis

* Abdominal groans - colicky due to pancreatitis

* Psychiatric overtones - raised PTH causing CNS depression and psychiatric symptoms

* Band keratopathy

* Features of hypercalcemia -

* Vomiting

* Confusion

* ECG changes: increased PR interval, shortened QT interval

Nuclear medicine scanning with radiolabeled Sestamibi is a widely used technique. Sestamibi accumulates in parathyroid adenomas. This radionuclide is concentrated in the thyroid and parathyroid tissue but usually washes out of normal thyroid tissue in under an hour. It persists in abnormal parathyroid tissue. It is now regarded as the most accurate and reliable method for imaging the parathyroid glands.

Other options:

Option A: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is not commonly used to image the parathyroid glands

Option B: Ultrasonography of the neck is a safe and widely used technique for the localization of abnormal parathyroid glands.

Option D: Multiphase CT imaging has become widely utilized to localize the disease. It gives both anatomical as well as functional information about the parathyroid glands. The disadvantage is the higher radiation dose when compared to others.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient with a history of smoking a pack of cigarettes for the past 15 years presents with hemoptysis. Chest X-ray shows a 3cm upper lobe mass near the apex of the lung, What is the next best step for the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT guided biopsy

In this patient who is a chronic smoker, presenting with hemoptysis and a 3cm mass in the apex of the lung, there is a high concern for bronchogenic carcinoma. Among the given options CT guided biopsy is the best next step in evaluating the mass.

Focal pulmonary lesions that are >3cm in diameter are called lung masses and are presumed to be bronchogenic carcinoma. Nodules that have a high probability of being malignant, should undergo biopsy, and CT-guided biopsy is commonly preferred.

To summarize :

* Investigation of choice - Plain CT  > PET

* Gold standard investigation - CT guided Biopsy.

Other options:

Option A: As this patient requires a biopsy of the mass, just a bronchoscopy without a biopsy would not be sufficient for evaluation.

Options C and D: Sputum cytology may help diagnose lung cancer but has lower specificity and sensitivity than CT guided biopsy. Sputum cytology and sputum AFB would rather be preferred for infective conditions.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 49-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of watery diarrhea, dehydration, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria. Which of the following neuroendocrine tumors can be responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. VIPoma

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of VIPoma.

Vasoactive intestinal peptide-secreting tumors (VIPomas) are neuroendocrine tumors that secrete excessive amounts of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). The condition is known as Verner–Morrison syndrome or WDHA syndrome.

WDHA stands for:

* WD - Watery Diarrhea

* H – Hypokalemia

* A – Achlorhydria

Diagnosis can be made by the demonstration of an elevated plasma VIP level and the history of large-volume diarrhea.

Treatment includes correction of dehydration, hypokalemia, and electrolyte losses with fluid and electrolyte replacement. Long-acting somatostatin analogs such as octreotide and lanreotide are the drug of choice.

Pearl PF0939: Pancreatic Endocrine Neoplasms

Endocrine neoplasm

Syndrome

Glucagonoma

Mild diabetes mellitus, a characteristic skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema), and anemia

Insulinoma

Clinically significant hypoglycemia

Gastrinoma

Peptic ulceration often unresponsive to therapy and in unusual locations such as the jejunum

Somatostatinoma

Diabetes mellitus, cholelithiasis, steatorrhea, and hypochlorhydria

VIPoma

Watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria, or WDHA syndrome

Pancreatic polypeptide-secreting endocrine tumors

Present as mass lesions as even high plasma levels of this hormone fail to cause symptoms

* Islet hyperplasia (previously known as nesidioblastosis) is seen in maternal diabetes, Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome , and rare mutations in the β-cell K+-channel protein or sulfonylurea receptor.

* In maternal diabetes, the fetal islets respond to hyperglycemia by increasing their size and number. In the postnatal period, these hyperactive islets may be responsible for serious episodes of hypoglycemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presented with recurrent respiratory infections with thickened sputum. Chest X-ray showed bronchial wall thickening. He has been suffering from steatorrhea since birth. Which of the following is the first differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystic fibrosis

The given clinical history suggests a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis. The gross image shows pus-filled bronchial air spaces and dilated bronchi extending into the periphery, typical of bronchiectasis. Therefore, the genetic defect and the associated complication are defective ATP-gated chloride channels and bronchiectasis respectively.

Cystic fibrosis (CF)/mucoviscidosis is an autosomal recessive disorder with a mutation in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator (CFTR) gene on chromosome 7q.

Following is the diagrammatic representation of the 6 categories of mutations seen in CFTR protein.

Systemic manifestations of CF:

Respiratory system:
1. Recurrent sino-pulmonary infections with pathogens including Staphylococcus aureus, Hemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas aeroginosa, and Burkholderia cepacia.
2. Chronic cough with thick foul smelling/ sometimes bloody sputum
3. Lung manifestations like bronchiectasis, atelectasis, infiltrates, and hyperinflation.
4. Nasal polyps.
5. Clubbing.

Gastrointestinal system:
1. Intestinal abnormalities including meconium ileus, steatorrhea, and rectal prolapse.
2. Pancreatic insufficiency and pancreatitis.
3. Liver cirrhosis and prolonged neonatal jaundice.
4. Failure to thrive due to severe malnutrition.

Others:
1. Salt-loss syndromes.
2. Congenital absence of vas deferens leading to obstructive azoospermia.

Diagnostic tests:
1. Immunoreactive trypsinogen for newborn screening of cystic fibrosis.
2. Sweat chloride test: Increased chloride concentration >60 mEq/L is diagnostic.
3. Genetic testing for CFTR gene mutations is the gold standard and should be done for all cases.
4. Nasal transepithelial potential difference can be estimated in equivocal cases.

Diagnostic criteria:
Presence of

* Clinical symptoms affecting at least one organ system (respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary) or

* Positive newborn screening or

* A sibling with cystic fibrosis.

Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by

* Two positive sweat chloride test results obtained on separate days or

* Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or

* An abnormal measurement of nasal potential difference.

Management:

* Mucus accummulation: Chest physiotherapy, aerosolized dornase alpha (recombinant DNase), N-acetyl cysteine, albuterol, corticosteroids, and hypertonic saline.

* Respiratory infections: Antibiotics (oral for Staphylococcus and aerosolized for Pseudomonas).

* Pancreatic insufficiency: Pancreative enzyme supplements.

* Malabsorption: Nutritional supplementation along with fat-soluble vitamins (K, E, D, and A) and minerals.

Correction of the defect can be via:

* Lumacaftor, an FDA approved drug that corrects the misfolding and reverts the Phe508del mutation defect

* Ivacaftor potentiates CFTR channel opening and stimulates ion transport

End-stage pulmonary failure requires lung transplantation.

Other options:

Option A: Respiratory distress syndrome is also known as hyaline membrane disease. It occurs due to the decreased production and secretion of the lung surfactant. It is seen mainly in preterm babies. The radiograph will show the presence of low lung volumes, a diffuse reticular granularity of the parenchyma (ground-glass appearance), and air bronchograms.

Option C: Alpha-1 antitrypsin (α1AT) is a plasma glycoprotein synthesized predominantly by hepatocytes. α1AT deficiency is an autosomal-recessive disorder of protein misfolding. The liver is affected due to the accumulation of the misfolded protein within hepatocytes and presents as chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma. Deficiency of α1AT protein results in excessive degradation of alveoli by neutrophil elastase, causing panacinar emphysema.

Option D: Malabsorption syndromes such as celiac disease, and tropical sprue present with diarrhea, steatorrhea, nutritional deficiencies, and weight loss. Histopathological examination of a duodenal biopsy would reveal villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intracellular lymphocytes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presented with difficulty in activities like climbing stairs, getting up from a chair, and combing hair. Violaceous erythema of the upper eyelids was noted. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dermatomyositis

The presence of upper eyelid lilac erythema is suggestive of heliotrope rash. This along with the clinical presentation suggestive of proximal myopathy points toward a diagnosis of dermatomyositis. Dermatomyositis has a predilection for proximal > distal muscle involvement.

Classic cutaneous signs in dermatomyositis:

* Heliotrope rash/ eyelid erythema- violaceous erythema of the upper eyelids. Pathognomonic of dermatomyositis.

* V sign- confluent macular erythema over the lower anterior neck and upper anterior chest

* Shawl sign- confluent macular erythema over the upper back and lateral aspect of arms

* Gottron’s papules- erythematous papules and plaques over the extensor surface of the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints. Pathognomonic of dermatomyositis.

* Gottron's sign- erythematous rash over the extensor surfaces of joints such as the knuckles, elbows, knees, and ankles

* Mechanic’s hands- rough, hyperkeratotic lines on the lateral and palmer areas of the fingers

* Scalp erythema and hair loss

* Facial rash- confluent erythema in the malar distribution involving the cheeks, nasal bridge, and nasolabial folds

* Nail fold changes

* Flagellate erythema- linear erythema on the upper back with pruritus

* Poikiloderma- mottled pattern of hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules with telangiectasias

* Cutaneous calcinosis- accumulation of calcium deposits in the skin

Facial rash in dermatomyositis-

Eyelid erythema/ heliotrope rash in dermatomyositis-

V- sign in dermatomyositis-

Shawl sign in dermatomyositis-

Flagellate erythema in dermatomyositis-

Gottron papules in dermatomyositis-

Poikilodermatous changes in dermatomyositis-

Option A: Inclusion body myositis involves both proximal and distal muscles with a predilection for finger/wrist flexors/knee extensors. It is characterized by asymmetric weakness of wrist and finger flexors in arms and quadriceps in legs. Dysphagia is also commonly seen. It is common in adults >50 years of age. Creatinine kinase levels are normal or slightly elevated. Antibodies against 5' nucleotidase are seen in the blood.

Option C: Polymyositis is one of the inflammatory myopathies characterized by symmetric and proximal muscle weakness. This weakness usually worsens over several weeks to months. It is more common in women. Most patients improve with immunotherapies, but they require lifelong treatment. Elevated levels of creatinine kinase (CK) and muscle biopsy showing non-specific inflammatory cells in perimysium locations are seen.

Option D: Thickened and indurated skin, called scleroderma, is the distinguishing hallmark of systemic sclerosis. Systemic sclerosis is an autoimmune disease of unknown etiology, complex pathogenesis, and variable clinical presentations. The skin manifestation is described salt-and-pepper appearance. Other features include Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, vasculopathic ulcers over the bony prominences, severe flexion contractures, and expressionless facies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old male presented with unexplained fever and prolonged respiratory distress despite appropriate treatment. A diagnosis of cryptic tuberculosis was made. Which of the following is the correct statement related to this condition?
options: Negative skin tuberculin test and negative chest X-ray
Positive skin tuberculin test and positive chest X-ray
Positive skin tuberculin test and negative chest X-ray
Negative skin tuberculin test and positive chest X-ray
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Negative skin tuberculin test and negative chest X-ray

The true statement about cryptic tuberculosis is a negative skin tuberculin test and a negative chest X-ray.

Cryptic disseminated TB refers to patients who have disseminated TB with less “typical” chest radiographic abnormalities, including normal and non-miliary patterns. It has an insidious onset that mainly affects the middle-aged and elderly. There are no localizing signs, absence of choroidal tubercles, normal chest x-rays, and negative tuberculin skin test.

It was found that the presence of underlying diseases such as HIV infection, chronic renal disease, diabetes, immunosuppression, and endocrine disorders alter the typical presentation, which often delays or leads to a missed diagnosis of cryptic tuberculosis.

Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic granulomatous systemic disease. The underlying pathophysiology is type IV hypersensitivity reaction. It can present as pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB. Symptoms include fever, night sweats, weight loss, cough, and hemoptysis. Histopathological examination reveals caseating tubercles with multinucleated giant cells and epitheloid cells.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old patient with a history of smoking presents with high-grade fever, cough, confusion, and diarrhea. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates in bilateral lower lung fields. On sputum gram stain, no organisms were detected. Laboratory results reveal Na: 126mEq/L, AST:62, ALT:56, RBS:112 mg/dl, serum bilirubin of 0.8mg%, and a positive HIV test. Which of the following organisms is responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Legionella

The given clinical scenario of the patient in the setting of an HIV infection, hyponatremia, and negative sputum gram stain is suggestive of legionnaire's disease. Legionnaire’s disease is caused by Legionella pneumophila.

They are found in lakes, streams, and other water bodies. Infection is mostly spread by inhalation of the bacteria from aerosols produced by contaminated air conditioners, humidifiers, nebulizers, etc.

It is mostly asymptomatic under the age of 40 years. Some risk factors for increasing the severity of the infection are smoking, older age and immunosuppression (as seen in this patient). It may present as a severe, rapidly progressive disease with high fever, chills, hypoxia, diarrhea, and delirium. On chest x-ray, patchy, often multilobar consolidation is seen. Pleural effusion may also occur. Initial lab findings include leukocytosis or leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, elevated liver enzymes, and renal dysfunction.

A milder form of a clinical syndrome known as Pontiac fever, which is usually self-limiting and only has mild symptoms of fever, myalgia, and headache.

Microscopy of the sputum samples shows numerous leucocytes without any organism. Gram staining of the sterile sites like pleural fluid and lung tissues show faint gram-negative bacilli. They require a counterstain of basic fuschin as safranin stains the bacteria very poorly. They are a group of fastidious, aerobic gram-negative bacteria. They can be grown on a buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar.

Diagnosis is established with the help of direct fluorescent antibody tests and BCYE culture specimens. Urine antigen tests and molecular assays may also be used.

The below image shows the Direct Fluorescent Antibody Test.

As L. pneumophila is an intracellular pathogen, antibiotics that reach high intracellular concentrations must be used.

Macrolides and quinolones are the antibiotics of choice and are effective as monotherapy. Alternatively, agents like doxycycline may also be used. B-lactams, monobactams, and aminoglycosides are not considered to be effective. The total duration of therapy is 10-14 days for immunocompetent hosts and up to 3 weeks for immunosuppressed patients.

Other options:

The clinical scenario in the setting of hyponatremia and elevated liver enzymes, in the absence of sputum gram stain points more towards legionella as the underlying pathogen rather than Streptococcus, Pneumocystis, or Klebsiella.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A chronic smoker presented with bilateral pitting pedal edema, and abdominal distension. On examination, he had ascites and auscultation revealed an S3. Which of the following defects can be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tricuspid regurgitation

The clinical features of bilateral pedal edema, abdominal distention, S3 heart sound are suggestive of right ventricular (RV) failure. The history of chronic smoking suggests that the patient is suffering from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)which results in cor pulmonale. Tricuspid regurgitation may be the underlying valvular defect in this patient.

The main pathophysiology behind cor pulmonale is pulmonary hypertension and increased right ventricular (RV) afterload which is sufficient to cause RV dilation with or without hypertrophy. This alters both the structure and function of the RV. In parenchymal lung diseases, primary pulmonary vascular disorders, or chronic hypoxia, the pulmonary vessels undergo vascular remodeling, vasoconstriction, and destruction leading to increased pulmonary artery pressures and increased RV afterload.

Anatomically, the right ventricle is thin-walled, compliant, and can handle volume overload better than pressure overload. Sustained pressure overload eventually leads to RV dysfunction and failure.

Dyspnea is the most common symptom. Other symptoms include pedal edema, abdominal distension due to ascites, the murmur of tricuspid regurgitation, an S3 gallop, and a palpable RV heave along the left sternal border. The jugular venous pressures (JVP) are elevated with prominent v waves indicative of tricuspid regurgitation. Other features include hepatomegaly, pulsatile liver, tenderness in the right upper quadrant, and pitting pedal edema.

The ECG in severe pulmonary hypertension shows P-pulmonale, right axis deviation, and RV hypertrophy. Spirometry and lung volumes show obstructive and/or restrictive defects seen in parenchymal lung diseases. Echo can be used to measure RV wall thickness and chamber dimensions, while doppler ECHO can be used to assess pulmonary artery pressures. Cardiac catheterization confirms the diagnosis of pulmonary hypertension and can exclude elevated left-sided pressures as a cause of heart failure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with a fever for 11 days with neck rigidity. A lumbar puncture was done and it showed lymphocytes predominantly, sugar- 50mg, and protein- 3000mg/dl. Gram-staining was negative. Chest X-ray of the patient shows upper lobe involvement with hilar lymph node enlargement. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tuberculous meningitis

The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and CSF findings is tuberculous meningitis.

Tuberculous meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis is caused by the formation of tubercles in the brain parenchyma. This happens during the hematogenous spread of the bacilli during primary infection. Another possibility is that a subependymal tubercle has burst into the subarachnoid space.

Tuberculous meningitis presents as a subacute infection and has a longer course than bacterial meningitis. Ocular nerve palsy is a common association as there is marked meningeal involvement at the base of the brain. The patient can also develop hydrocephalus.

The CSF sample shows pellicle or cobweb-like clots. Acid-fast bacilli can be best isolated from these. There is usually lymphocytic leukocytosis, low glucose concentration, and elevated proteins. CSF culture remains the gold standard for diagnosis.

The clinical triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity is common to all types of meningitis. Nuchal rigidity is the resistance of the neck to passive flexion and is pathognomonic of meningeal irritation. Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are other features of meningeal irritation. Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) is a complication that presents as papilledema, disorientation, or dilated poorly reactive pupils.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with complaints of sudden onset headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating. The patient has had multiple similar episodes in the past. During these episodes, the patient's blood pressure is elevated. A 24-hour urinary metanephrine is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pheochromocytoma

The most likely diagnosis in this patient is pheochromocytoma.

Pheochromocytoma is a rare tumor of the sympathetic system arising from the adrenal medulla. Patients commonly present with a classical triad of palpitation, headache, and profuse sweating. Patients also present with hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias. These symptoms are due to an excess of catecholamines secreted by the tumor.

Other options:

Option A: Addison's disease is a primary adrenal insufficiency in which the adrenal is unable to secrete adequate amounts of cortisol (glucocorticoid), and aldosterone (mineralocorticoid). The features are fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, low blood pressure, postural hypotension, hypoglycemia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, salt craving, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia.

Option B: Renal artery stenosis is a relatively common finding in older patients with chronic essential hypertension. However, it is clinically significant (i.e. renovascular hypertension) only if the stenosis is greater than 75% in both renal arteries or 50% stenosis with post-stenotic dilatation. Main causes include atherosclerosis (most common), usually seen in patients > 45 years and fibromuscular dysplasia, seen in women < 50 years.

Option D: Hyperthyroidism presents with clinical features that include heat intolerance and sweating, tachycardia, and palpitations, weight loss with increased appetite, diarrhea, and oligomenorrhea. Clinical findings include exophthalmos, tremors, and myopathy.

Pearl PF1539: Pheochromocytoma

Features:

* When pheochromocytoma is associated with the MEN syndrome it is rarely malignant.

* Phaeochromocytomas are greyish-pink on the cut surface and are usually highly vascularised.

* Zellbalen cells and nuclei with salt and pepper chromatin are seen.

Factors indicating more chances of malignancy:

* An increased PASS (phaeochromocytoma of the adrenal gland scale score)

* High number of Ki-67-positive cells

* Vascular invasion or a breached capsule

Diagnosis:

* Urinary catecholamine and VMA level assay are most sensitive screening test.

* MRI is the IOC.

* Biopsy and CT Contrast scan are contraindicated in order to avoid Hypertensive crisis.

Treatment:

* Adrenalectomy is preferred TOC.

* Size<5 cm -  Laparoscopic adrenalectomy

* Preop Alpha blockers should be given

* Mitotane should be started as adjuvant or palliative treatment

Pearl PF0131: Clinical features of Pheochromocytoma (By frequency of occurrence)

* Clinical triad:

* Headaches – M/C symptom

* Profuse sweating

* Palpitations and tachycardia

* Hypertension, sustained or paroxysmal – M/C Sign

* Anxiety and panic attacks

* Weight loss

* Polyuria and polydipsia

* Constipation

* Orthostatic hypotension

* Dilated cardiomyopathy

* Erythrocytosis

* Elevated blood sugar

* Hypercalcemia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with dyspnea and distended neck veins that increase on inspiration. There is no murmur. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Constrictive pericarditis

The patient presenting with dyspnea and Kussmauls signs as evidenced by the distended neck veins that increase on inspiration, likely has underlying constrictive pericarditis.

Constrictive pericarditis: It is a condition where a thickened, fibrotic, and often calcified pericardium restricts the diastolic filling of the heart.

In developing countries, infectious etiologies like tuberculosis or viral infections are the most common cause of this condition. Cardiac surgery and radiation therapy are also common causes. Other causes include connective tissue disease, uremia, neoplasm, or idiopathic.

Clinically the patients may present with dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, ascites. On examination neck veins may be distended and will show a positive Kussmauls sign. On auscultation, heart sound smay be distant and a pericardial knock at the cardiac apex may be heard. This occurs due to the abrubt cessation of ventricular filling.

JVP findings - There is a rapid 'x' and 'y' descent. The rapid 'y' descent is more prominent and reflects rapid early ventricular diastolic filling. This occurs due to the constricting pericardium, increasing the atrial pressures.

Diagnosis: Diagnosis is difficult and is confirmed by multiple investigations

* Hallmark findings of pericardial constriction are pericardial thickening, calcification, and abnormal ventricular diastolic function.

* The X-ray can be normal or there may be non-specific cardiac enlargement, calcification, and roughened cardiac outline.

* CT and MRI are more sensitive investigations.

Constrictive pericarditis will have prominent y descent, prominent x descent, and Kussmaul's sign. Normally, the venous pressure should fall by at least 3 mmHg with inspiration. Kussmaul’s sign is defined by either a rise or a lack of fall of the JVP with inspiration.

Other options:

Option B: Aortic regurgitation would present with a diastolic murmur.

Option C: Tricuspid stenosis may also present similarly with congestive hepatomegaly, and venous distention, however, in this patient the absence of a murmur makes the diagnosis unlikely. Tricuspid stenosis will have prolonged y wave on JVP.

Option D: Pulmonary arterial hypertension would present with a prominent jugular "a" wave, palpable left parasternal lift, and loud S2 which are not seen in this patient.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman presents with a history of headaches for the past 9 months that worsen in a recumbent position and improves as the day progresses. She also gives a history of taking oral contraceptives. Fundal examination shows papilledema. There are no focal neurological deficits. What is the probable cause of her headaches?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pseudotumor cerebri

This female patient with recurring headaches, that have a positional and diurnal variation, takes oral contraceptive pills and raised intracranial pressures (as evidenced by papilledema) likely has pseudotumor cerebri (idiopathic intracranial hypertension)

Risk factors include:

* Female sex

* Obesity

* Nalidixic acid

* Tetracycline

* Vitamin A

* Oral contraceptives

* Use of or withdrawal from corticosteroids

Evaluation requires brain imaging, with MRI being the most common initial study. Elevated CSF opening pressure on lumbar puncture is the hallmark of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) even in the absence of fundal changes.

The initial treatment is with acetazolamide. Topiramate may also be used. Weight loss and stopping the medications that are causing IIH must also be done.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young male patient presents with ptosis and muscle weakness which reportedly worsens in the evening and improves in the morning. This is relieved by neostigmine. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myasthenia gravis

From the given clinical picture, myasthenia gravis is the most likely diagnosis. This patient has symptoms of ptosis, progressive weakness, and excessive fatiguability which improves with rest.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. It is due to the autoantibody-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the post-synaptic membrane. This consequentially leads to a decreased transmission at the neuromuscular junction. Failure of transmission results in muscle weakness.

Females are more commonly affected than males and the disease tends to occur in middle age.

Clinical features of myasthenia gravis:

* Muscle weakness and fatiguability increase with repeated use or late in the day and may improve following rest or sleep. Limb weakness is proximal and asymmetrical

* Cranial muscles particularly the lids and extraocular muscles are involved early in the course - diplopia, ptosis

* Facial weakness - snarling expression on smiling

* Weakness in chewing

* Speech with nasal timbre due to the weakness of the palate and tongue

* Difficulty in swallowing

* Deep tendon reflexes are intact

* Myasthenic crisis - acute exacerbation of muscle weakness especially intercostal and diaphragmatic muscles resulting in ventilatory failure. It is most commonly due to infection and anticholinesterase medication overuse.

Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma and other autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Grave's disease, neuromyelitis optics, systemic lupus erythematosus, etc.

Diagnosis:

* Ice-pack test - application of ice pack over the eyes improves ptosis (decreases activity of acetylcholinesterase, this increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and increases transmission)

* Antibodies associated with myasthenia gravis: Anti-AChR antibodies, Anti-MuSK antibodies, Anti-LRP4 antibodies

* Repetitive nerve stimulation test shows a decremental response.

* Edrophonium chloride or Tensilon test - improvement of symptoms occurs on injecting edrophonium. Edrophonium is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. This increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and improves transmission.

Treatment:

* Anticholinesterase drugs - Pyridostigmine.

* Thymectomy.

* Immunosuppression therapy with glucocorticoids, azathioprine, tacrolimus, rituximab, etc.

* Plasmapheresis and intravenous immunoglobulin.

Other options:

Option B: Huntington's disease (HD) also known as Huntington chorea is associated with CAG repeats and anticipation. It has an adult-onset and is associated with the degeneration of striatal neurons. Features such as chorea and dementia are commonly seen in these patients. The characteristic features of HD include involuntary movements, dementia, and behavioral changes.

Option C: ALS is the most common progressive motor neuron disease. The pathologic hallmark of ALS includes the involvement of lower motor neurons of the ventral/ anterior horn of the spinal cord, cranial nerves innervating the bulbar muscles, and the afferent corticospinal upper motor neurons in layer five of the motor cortex. Progressive upper motor neuron (UMN) palsy (exaggerated reflexes, extensor plantar), lower motor neuron (LMN) palsy (muscle weakness, atrophy, fasciculations), and pseudobulbar palsy (dysarthria, tongue spasticity), with normal bladder, bowel and sensory function are suggestive of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

Option D: The classical presentation of ptosis with progressively declining ocular movement is characteristic of chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO). CPEO may occur in isolation, in association with Kearns-Sayre syndrome (mitochondrial myopathy associated with mitochondrial DNA deletions), or oculopharyngeal dystrophy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young patient presents with a severe headache. He has never experienced a headache of this severity before. He has hypertension and nuchal rigidity on examination. Which of the following could be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

The clinical manifestations of neck stiffness and severe headache (like never before) suggests a diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is the bleeding into the subarachnoid space, which is the area between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater surrounding the brain. The diagnosis is suspected when a hyperattenuating material is seen filling the subarachnoid space. Most commonly this is apparent around the circle of Willis, on account of the majority of berry aneurysms occurring in this region, or in the Sylvian fissure.

Young males with a history of spontaneous sudden onset severe headaches with seizures should raise suspicion for subarachnoid hemorrhage (aneurysmal). The most common cause of SAH is head trauma and the second common cause is the rupture of a saccular aneurysm.

Symptoms include:

* Severe headache (thunderclap headache)

* Rapid onset vomiting

* Confusion or a lowered level of consciousness

* Seizures

* Neck stiffness or neck pain

Other options:

Cluster headache is a rare form of primary headache. It is characterized by deep excruciating pain that is usually retroorbital, and unilateral. It usually lasts for short duration of 8-10 weeks a year followed by a pain-free interval. It is associated with lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, and ptosis. In acute cases, oxygen therapy is useful. Subcutaneous and nasal sumatriptan can be used.

The classic clinical triad of fever, headache, and neck rigidity is suggestive of meningitis. Other common complaints are nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. Nuchal rigidity (“stiff neck”) is the pathognomonic sign of meningitis. Hip and knee flexion on passive flexion of the neck is called Brudzinsky's sign.

Encephalitis presents similar to meningitis with fever, altered mental status, and focal or diffuse neurological symptoms.

Pearl PF1866: Intracranial haemorrhage

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly male on bed rest for many months presented with breathlessness and chest pain. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CT pulmonary angiogram

This clinical scenario is suggestive of acute pulmonary embolism (PE) most likely due to deep vein thrombosis(DVT). This patient's immobility puts him at an increased risk of DVT. Pulmonary angiogram is the principal imaging test for diagnosis.

Clinically, patients present with sudden onset of dyspnea, syncope, chest pain, and hypotension. Associated clinical features are tachycardia, and tachypnea.

Investigations:

CT of the chest with intravenous contrast(CT pulmonary angiogram) is the principal imaging test for the diagnosis of PE. It also helps to visualize the chambers of the heart. It can also help in identifying alternative diagnoses like emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary mass, etc.

Lung scanning is the second-line diagnostic test for PE, used in patients who cannot tolerate intravenous contrast. Perfusion scan defect indicates absent or decreased blood flow.

ECG changes in acute PE are characterized by the classic S1Q3T3 changes, due to right ventricular strain and ischemia:

* A prominent S wave in lead I

* Q wave in lead III

* An inverted T wave in lead III

It is an insensitive sign but specific.

Echocardiography- It is a non-reliable diagnostic imaging tool. Most patients with PE have a normal echocardiogram, therefore, it is not a reliable test. However, it can be used to detect other conditions that commonly mimic PE like acute myocardial infarction, pericardial tamponade, and aortic dissection. McConnell's sign is one of the indirect findings on echo. It is hypokinesis of the right ventricular free wall with the hyperkinetic or normal motion of the right ventricular apex.

Treatment includes anticoagulation: parenteral unfractionated heparin, low molecular weight heparin, or fondaparinux with bridging to warfarin or parenteral therapy switched to a direct thrombin inhibitor such as dabigatran or oral anticoagulants(anti-Xa agents) such as rivaroxaban or apixaban followed by maintenance therapy.

Pulmonary embolism rule out criteria (PERC):

Pearl PF1032: Chest X Ray signs in pulmonary embolism

Westermark's sign- Area of focal oligemia

Chest radiograph reveals an engorged pulmonary trunk with an abrupt cutoff of pulmonary vascularity in the distal portions bilaterally, indicative of the "Westermark sign" (arrows).

Palla's sign- enlarged right descending pulmonary artery

Remember- A normal or nearly normal chest x-ray often occurs in PE.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An HIV-positive man presents with a high-grade fever. Examination reveals a positive Kernig's sign. CSF shows reduced glucose, increased protein, and increased leukocytes. A diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis is made. What is the appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Liposomal amphotericin B+ flucytosine

The appropriate management in this patient of cryptococcal meningitis is liposomal amphotericin B (LAMB)+ flucytosine

Cryptococcus is the leading infectious cause of meningitis in patients with AIDS. It generally occurs in untreated patients, with CD4+ T cell counts <100/μL. Most patients present with a picture of subacute meningoencephalitis. The CSF profile may show modest elevations in WBC or protein levels and a decrease in glucose. The CSF opening pressure is usually elevated (yeast colonies obstruct the free flow of CSF causing increased CSF pressure).

The diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis is made by the identification of Cryptococcus neoformans yeast cells in CSF with India ink stain or by the detection of cryptococcal antigen using latex agglutination (CrAg).

Prophylaxis: Oral fluconazole when CD4+ T cell count is <100/μL.

Treatment:

* Induction - Liposomal amphotericin B with flucytosine for at least 2 weeks, continuing with amphotericin alone ideally until the CSF culture turns negative.

* Maintenance - Oral fluconazole until the CD4+ T cell count has increased to >200 cells/μL for 6 months in response to cART.

Other Options:

Option A: Vancomycin would be appropriate for bacterial meningitis caused by organisms like Streptococcus pneumoniae or methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

Option B: High dose fluconazole with flucytosine is used in cryptococcal meningitis, but they are not the first-line therapy for the induction phase. Fluconazole with flucytosine is typically used in the consolidation phase after initial treatment with amphotericin B, or in resource-limited settings where amphotericin B is not available.

Option C: Voriconazole while effective against many fungi, is not the drug of choice for cryptococcal meningitis. It's primarily indicated for invasive aspergillosis and other specific fungal infections.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Bell's palsy involves_______
options: Ipsilateral upper and lower halves of the face.
Contralateral upper and lower halves of the face.
Ipsilateral lower half of the face.
Contralateral lower half of the face.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ipsilateral upper and lower halves of the face.

Bell's palsy involves the ipsilateral upper and lower halves of the face.

Bell's palsy is a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve and involves the ipsilateral side of the upper and lower halves of the face. Bell's palsy is an idiopathic, peripheral facial paralysis, or paresis of acute onset.

If the patient attempts to close the eye, the eyeball would turn up and out - this is known as the Bell's phenomenon. Decreased tearing, hyperacusis, taste disturbances, otalgia, weakness of the facial muscles, poor eyelid closure, etc can be seen. When the patient smiles, the face becomes distorted and lateralizes to the side opposite the palsy. Flattening of the forehead and nasolabial fold on the side affected by palsy.

Treatment of Bell's palsy involves prednisone 60-80 mg daily during the first 5 days and then tapered over the next 5 days. The use of artificial tears and covering the eye at night prevents corneal drying.

The image below shows that the right half of this patient's face is weak and the right facial nerve is affected.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Elective splenectomy is preferred in which of the following conditions? G6PD deficiency- Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hereditary spherocytosis

Elective splenectomy is done in case of hereditary spherocytosis.

Hereditary spherocytosis is a type of hereditary hemolytic anemia that is passed down in an autosomal dominant pattern. Mutations of the red blood cell surface proteins spectrin and ankyrin can result in unstable cell membranes, leading to hemolysis.

This disorder can present at a young age with severe jaundice and fatigue. The unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia predisposes the patient to develop gallstones.

Laboratory findings include normocytic anemia with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The peripheral smear will show large spherical red blood cells without central pallor. The diagnosis can be confirmed by the acid glycerol lysis test and the eosin-5′-maleimide (EMA)–binding test.

There is no specific treatment available besides splenectomy. However, due to the possible adverse effects, it is only indicated in severe cases and after the child attains puberty in moderate cases. It should be followed up with the appropriate antibiotic and vaccine prophylaxis.

Other options:

Option (A): Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is a type of inherited hemolytic anemia. It is associated with exacerbations after consuming anti-malarial drugs and in periods of oxidative stress. The peripheral smear shows characteristic "bite cells". In G6PD deficiency, uncontrolled oxidative stress causes hemoglobin to denature and form Heinz bodies. G6PD deficiency is largely preventable by avoiding exposure to triggering factors.

Option (B): Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is a hemolytic disorder that also presents with pancytopenia and a tendency to form venous thrombi. It occurs due to defective GPI anchors on the red blood cell surface which are normally used to anchor CD 59 (cell-protective proteins) to the surface. These patients can present with episodes of dark brown urine in the morning, anemia, pancytopenia, and recurrent abdominal pain due to thrombosis of abdominal veins.

Bone marrow transplantation is done for the treatment. Recently humanized monoclonal antibody eculizumab is used.

Option (D): Hairy cell leukemia is a distinctive B cell neoplasm, that predominantly affects middle-aged males. Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase is the cytochemical stain characteristically shown by leukemic hairy cells. Patients commonly present with massive splenomegaly due to infiltration of the leukemic cells. Pancytopenia due to marrow involvement can also be seen. These tumors respond well to chemotherapy and BRAF (B-type Raf proto-oncogene) inhibitors, and they have an excellent prognosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Ground-glass appearance on HRCT is seen in which of the following condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Silicosis

Silicosis on HRCT shows a ground-glass appearance.

Silicosis is due to the inhalation of crystalline silicon dioxide (silica) seen in individuals employed in sandblasting or rock mining. Macrophages phagocytose inhaled silica particles, thereby activating and releasing inflammatory mediators (IL-1, IL-8) that cause fibroblast recruitment.

Microscopy reveals coalescent nodules of whorled collagen fibers surrounded by a peripheral zone of silica-laden macrophages. HRCT shows a “crazy paving” pattern due to interlobular septal thickening on the background of ground-glass opacity.

Given below is a HRCT image of silicosis:

Option A: Asbestosis - X-ray shows peripheral reticular opacities predominantly in the lower zones. It predominantly affects the lower lobes of the lung, in contrast to other forms of pneumoconiosis, which affect the upper lobes.

Option C: Anthracosis/coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a pulmonary condition seen in coal miners. The inhaled carbon pigment is engulfed by alveolar or interstitial macrophages, which accumulate in the connective tissue. Initially, it causes simple coal workers pneumoconiosis with little or no pulmonary dysfunction. With continued exposure, lung tissue undergoes progressive massive fibrosis which is called complicated coal workers pneumoconiosis. The upper lobes of the lungs are commonly involved.

Simple coal workers' pneumoconiosis appears as small round nodular opacities with an occasional appearance of reticular or reticulonodular opacities. Compared to silicosis, the nodules in CWP tend to have less well-defined margins and a more granular appearance.

Option D: Cotton dust causes byssinosis and can induce occupational asthma. It is characterized clinically as occasional (early-stage) and then regular (late-stage) chest tightness toward the end of the first day of the workweek-Monday chest tightness.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In the sagittal section of the brain given below the colored area represents the paracentral lobule. Which of the following structures are affected in a lesion to this area?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perineum and leg

The area marked in the picture is the paracentral lobule. The structures affected in a lesion to this area are the perineum and leg.

The paracentral lobule is supplied by the A2 segment of the anterior cerebral artery. Lesions in the paracentral lobule lead to :

* Weakness and loss of sensation in the contralateral lower limb (paraplegia).

* Urinary incontinence

* Fecal incontinence

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The most common cause of Cushing's disease in a 60-year-old male is ______ ACTH - Adrenocorticotropic hormone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pitutary microadenoma

The most common cause of Cushing's disease in a 60-year-old male is pituitary microadenoma.

Cortisol production is increased by adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) released from the pituitary gland in the brain. Hypercortisolemia (cortisol overproduction) causes Cushing syndrome, most often when a pituitary adenoma (a benign tumor) produces an excess of ACTH, resulting in Cushing's disease. The increased ACTH causes increased cortisol production, about three times more than the normal level.

The illustration given below shows the clinical features of Cushing syndrome.

Administration of large doses of dexamethasone can be used to differentiate between ACTH-dependent and ACTH-independent Cushing’s syndrome.

The illustration given below shows the diagnostic algorithm to determine the cause of Cushing syndrome.

In normal physiologic states, the ACTH levels are higher in the early morning as compared to the rest of the day. However, they are not as high as those in Cushing's disease.

Pearl PF0133: Causes of Cushing's Syndrome

Endogenous Causes

* Ectopic ACTH syndrome – Due to ACTH secretion by

* Bronchial or pancreatic carcinoid tumors

* Small-cell lung cancer

* Medullary thyroid carcinoma

* Pheochromocytoma

* ACTH Independent – (10% )

* Adrenocortical adenoma

* Adrenocortical carcinoma

Rare causes

* Macronodular adrenal hyperplasia

* Primary pigmented nodular adrenal disease

* McCune – Albright syndrome

Pearl PF0134: Screening/Confirmatory Test for Diagnosing Cushing's Syndrome

* 24-h urinary free cortisol excretion increased above normal (3x)

* Dexamethasone overnight test

* Plasma cortisol >50 nmol/L at 8–9 a.m. after 1 mg dexamethasone at 11 p.m.

* Midnight plasma cortisol >130 nmol/L

* Midnight salivary cortisol >5 nmol/L

* Low dose Dexamethasone test – Best initial test

* Plasma cortisol >50 nmol/L after 0.5 mg dexamethasone q6h for 2 days

If a number of these tests are positive then a diagnosis of Cushing’s syndrome is confirmed.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs reduce mortality in a patient with heart failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Metoprolol

Metoprolol is a beta-blocker that is found to reduce mortality in a patient with heart failure.

Beta-blockers have been shown to prolong survival, prevent arrhythmia, and improve symptoms of heart failure and left ventricular ejection fraction, especially in patients with chronic heart failure.

The drugs which reduce mortality in patients with heart failure are :

* ACE inhibitors

* Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs)

* Angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI)

* Beta-blockers

* Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists

* Spironolactone

* Eplerenone

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a cause of exudative pleural effusion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rheumatoid arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis is a cause of exudative pleural effusion.

Pleural effusion refers to the pathological accumulation of fluid in the pleural space due to:

* excess fluid formation from the interstitial spaces of the lung, parietal pleura, or peritoneal cavity

* decreased fluid removal by the lymphatics

Light’s criteria can be used to differentiate between transudative and exudative pleural effusions. Exudative effusions will meet at least one of the following criteria:

* Pleural fluid protein/serum protein >0.5

* Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH >0.6

* Pleural fluid LDH is more than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum.
