Beta-blockers, calcium antagonists (not dihydropyridines), digoxin, opioids, organophosphorus insecticides, centrally acting alpha agonists, e.g. clonidine

Seizures
Tricyclic antidepressants, theophylline, antihistamines, anticonvulsants, non-steroidal drugs, phenol, phenothiazines, isoniazid, cocaine, carbon monoxide, organophosphorus insecticides, strychnine

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a unilateral throbbing headache in the temporal region and light sensitivity associated with photophobia, nausea and vomiting. She reports that each episode lasts for a maximum of 24 hours, which was relieved by giving triptans. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Migraine

The clinical picture of throbbing unilateral headache, light sensitivity associated with photophobia, nausea and vomiting and responsiveness to triptans indicates a diagnosis of migraine.

Migraine is the second most common cause of headaches, after tension headaches. It is characterized by unilateral and throbbing headaches of moderate to severe intensity. Other features of migraine include deep-seated pain and sensitivity to environmental and sensory stimuli. The headache can be triggered by glares, bright lights, sounds, hunger, stress, physical exertion, hormonal fluctuations during menses, lack of or excess sleep, or alcohol.

Management of migraine includes nonpharmacologic management and pharmacologic measures. Triggers unique to the patient should be avoided. Lifestyle modifications to avoid excessive caffeine and alcohol, and to maintain a healthy sleep cycle are necessary.

Pharmacological treatment can be divided into abortive treatment of acute attacks and prophylaxis to prevent acute attacks. Acute attacks can be treated with acetaminophen, aspirin NSAIDs, antiemetics and triptans. Triptans (Sumatriptan, Zolmitriptan) are used in moderate to severe migraine or when simple analgesics have not been effective. Prophylaxis with beta-blockers like propranolol, valproate, and topiramate.

Migraine is associated with the release of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) within the trigeminal nucleus. Hence, newer therapies using CGRP antagonists and monoclonal antibodies to CGRP and its receptor are effective in treating and preventing migraine. They are considered to be as effective as triptans and are better tolerated.

Other options:

Option A: Anxiety primarily involves psychological symptoms like excessive worry, restlessness, and rapid heartbeat, while migraines are neurological and present with severe headaches, nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound. Anxiety can sometimes trigger migraines, but they are distinct conditions with different underlying causes.

Option B: Hypertension is a chronic condition characterized by persistently high blood pressure, often without immediate symptoms, while migraines are episodic and involve severe headaches with nausea and sensory sensitivity. Unlike migraines, hypertension can lead to long-term complications like heart disease and stroke.

Option D: Tension headache is a common type of headache characterized by a dull, bilateral, pressing or tightening pain, often described as a "band around the head." It is typically triggered by stress, poor posture, or muscle tension and does not involve nausea or sensitivity to light and sound.

Pearl PF1050: Simplified diagnostic criteria for migraine

Repeated attacks of headache lasting 4-72 h in patients with a normal physical examination, no other reasonable cause for the headache, and

At Least 2 of the following features

* Unilateral pain

* Throbbing pain

* Aggravation by movement

* Moderate or severe intensity

Plus at Least 1 of the following features

* Nausea/vomiting

* Photophobia and phonophobia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with fatigue and chronic diarrhea for 4 months. Endoscopy reveals several ulcers in the gastric antrum and the descending duodenum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of gastrinoma Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Zollinger Ellison Syndrome (ZES)/Gastrinoma is a neuroendocrinal tumour characterized by hypersecretion of gastrin resulting in gastrointestinal tract ulcers. It occurs more commonly in a sporadic pattern but can be associated with MEN-1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia-1) syndromes in the familial pattern. Gastrinoma is most commonly located in the gastrinoma triangle (Passaro's triangle) bounded by the lines connecting the:

* cystic duct

* the junction between the second and third parts of the duodenum

* the junction between the neck and body of the pancreas

The most common presentations of gastrinoma are epigastric pain, diarrhoea, and peptic ulcers. The ulcers occur at typical locations (proximal duodenum) and atypical locations (distal duodenum, jejunum). Duodenal ulcers are the most common. Gastrinoma if associated with marked gastric acid production and recurrent peptic ulcer is called Zollinger Ellison syndrome.

Diagnosis:

The gastric pH <2, basal acid output >15 mEq/hr and serum gastrin concentration more than 1000 pg/ml (normal is <100 pg/ml) confirm the diagnosis of gastrinoma. When the diagnosis is in doubt (like gastrin levels 100-1000 pg/ml), then a secretin test is performed. A secretin test is considered positive when serum gastrin levels are more than 200 pg/ml on secretin administration and confirms the diagnosis of gastrinoma.

For localization of the tumour for surgical management, CT or MRI scans should be done first. If the tumour is not localized on these scans, then somatostatin receptor scintigraphy or endoscopic ultrasound is done for better localization.

Treatment of ZES :

High-dose Proton Pump Inhibitor followed by surgery.

Surgeries that can be done are:

* Distal Pancreatectomy– if lesion in body or tail of the pancreas

* Enucleation– if lesion in the head of the pancreas

* Full-thickness excision– if lesion in duodenum

* MEN associated– surgery done only if size>2.5cm

Other options:

Option A: VIPoma is characterized by watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome). It is caused by the release of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) from the tumor.

Option C: Glucagonomas, α-cell tumors are associated with increased serum levels of glucagon. The patient presents with mild diabetes mellitus, a characteristic skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema), and anemia. They occur most frequently in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women and are characterized by extremely high plasma glucagon levels.

Option D: Insulinomas, β-cell tumors are the most common pancreatic endocrine neoplasms. These are usually benign and often cause symptomatic hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemic symptoms appear when blood glucose levels fall below 50 mg/dL. The symptoms usually develop after fasting or exertion and improve after glucose intake.

Pearl PF2047: Clinical features of gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome)

Most common symptom: Abdominal pain.

Gastrin hypersecretion stimulates gastric acid secretion, leading to peptic ulcers that occur at atypical sites like the duodenum and jejunum and are refractory and multiple.

Diarrhea is due to

* Acid-induced injury to the small intestine mucosa

* Inability of the intestinal tract to absorb large volumes of fluids secreted by the stomach

* Inactivation of pancreatic lipase by low pH

* Precipitation of bile salts.

The unique characteristic of acid-induced diarrhea is that it is controlled by nasogastric aspiration of gastric secretions.

Pearl PF1838: Diagnostic tests in Zollinger Ellison Syndrome

To confirm the diagnosis of ZES,

* Gastric pH <2.5 and

* Serum gastrin >1000pg/ml (normal <100pg/ml)

Provocative tests can be done like the secretin stimulation test when the diagnosis is in doubt. An increase in serum gastrin >200pg/ml following an IV bolus of secretin (2U/kg) is diagnostic.

Other tests:

* BAO >15mEq/h (or >5mEq/h if they have had a procedure for peptic ulcer)

* BAO: MAO ratio is increased (>0.6)

(BAO=Basal acid output; MAO=Maximal acid output)

For localization

* Initial investigation - CT or MRI

* Best investigation - Endoscopic ultrasound

* If the tumor is not localized - Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with progressive increase in shortness of breath. On examination, left parasternal heave is noted. On auscultation, a systolic murmur is heard. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pulmonary stenosis

The patient presents with worsening shortness of breath, and examination reveals a left parasternal heave and a systolic murmur on auscultation, pointing to the diagnosis of pulmonary stenosis.

Pulmonary stenosis is a congenital heart defect where there is a narrowing of the pulmonary valve or the area just below the valve, obstructing blood flow from the right ventricle to the lungs. This leads to increased pressure in the right ventricle, causing it to work harder to pump blood. The condition may range from mild to severe and can result in symptoms like shortness of breath, fatigue, and cyanosis in severe cases.

On physical examination, a left parasternal heave is often noted due to right ventricular hypertrophy, and auscultation typically reveals a systolic ejection murmur heard best at the upper left sternal border. If left untreated, severe pulmonary stenosis can lead to right heart failure and other complications. Treatment may involve balloon valvuloplasty or surgery, depending on the severity of the obstruction.

Other options:

Option A: Pulmonary regurgitation is the backward flow of blood into the right ventricle due to insufficient closure of the pulmonary valve. It often presents with a diastolic murmur heard at the left upper sternal border and can lead to right heart enlargement if severe.

Option C: Pulmonary artery hypertension is a condition characterized by elevated blood pressure in the pulmonary arteries, leading to strain on the right side of the heart. Symptoms may include shortness of breath, fatigue, and chest pain, and it can result from various causes like lung diseases or heart conditions.

Option D: Pulmonary embolism is a blockage in one of the pulmonary arteries, usually caused by a blood clot that travels to the lungs from the legs (deep vein thrombosis). It can lead to symptoms like sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, and potentially life-threatening complications if untreated.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a history of infection two weeks ago developed progressively ascending, bilaterally symmetric flaccid weakness in the lower limbs, which later involved the upper limbs. Examination reveals absent spinal cord reflexes. Based on the given findings, what could be the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy

The given clinical scenario of a patient with a history of infection two weeks ago who develops progressively ascending, bilaterally symmetric flaccid weakness in the lower limbs, later affecting the upper limbs and on examination absent spinal cord reflexes are seen. These findings suggest a likely diagnosis of Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (AIDP).

AIDP is the most common type of Guillain-Barre syndrome(GBS). GBS is usually associated with a history of upper respiratory infection (URI) or acute gastroenteritis (AGE) 1-3 weeks prior. The causative organisms may be Campylobacter jejuni, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

It presents with ascending motor paralysis, primarily affecting the lower limbs before progressing to the upper limbs. Sensory deficits may or may not be present, while deep tendon reflexes are absent. In severe cases, transient bladder dysfunction can occur. Autonomic manifestations include loss of vasomotor control, postural hypotension, and cardiac dysrhythmias.

Histological examination shows inflammation of peripheral nerves, manifested as perivenular and endoneurial infiltration by lymphocytes, macrophages, and a few plasma cells. On electron microscopy, an early effect on myelin sheaths is seen. There is segmental demyelination induced by the actions of activated macrophages.

There are several types of Guillain–Barre syndrome:

* Demyelinating:

* Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) - most common.

* Axonal:

* Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN).

* Acute motor-sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN).

* Regional GBS syndromes: Miller–Fisher syndrome (MFS).

Diagnosis is made upon clinical presentation. CSF findings of elevated protein without pleocytosis help to rule out other similar conditions. Treatment includes initiating intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIg) or plasmapheresis. IVIg is the initial therapy preferred, as it has a better safety record. In severe cases, patients may require ventilatory support.

Other options:

Option B: Multiple sclerosis is characterized by chronic inflammation and demyelination that causes multiple neurological symptoms such as optic neuritis, muscle spasticity, and facial weakness. The presence of oligoclonal bands on protein electrophoresis is diagnostic.

Option C: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) differs from Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) as it involves both upper and lower motor neuron degeneration, whereas GBS is a purely lower motor neuron disorder. Additionally, ALS progresses gradually without sensory loss, while GBS has an acute onset and may involve sensory symptoms.

Option D: Transverse myelitis differs from Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) as it involves spinal cord inflammation, leading to a sensory level, bowel/bladder dysfunction, and often spasticity, whereas GBS primarily affects the peripheral nerves with ascending flaccid paralysis. Additionally, MRI shows spinal cord lesions in transverse myelitis, while GBS is diagnosed through nerve conduction studies and CSF analysis.

Pearl PF1047: Mechanism of Immunopathogenesis of Guillain-Barre Syndrome

The following sequence of events, takes into consideration, the development of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) associated with Campylobacter jejuni infection.

* B cells recognize glycoconjugates on jejuni (Cj) that cross-react with ganglioside present on Schwann cell surface and subjacent peripheral nerve myelin.

* Most of the B cells are activated via a partially T cell–dependent route and secrete primarily IgG autoantibodies. Some B cells, activated via a T cell–independent mechanism, secrete primarily IgM

* The activated B cells escape from Peyer’s patches into regional lymph nodes.

* Activated T cells also function to assist in the opening of the blood-nerve barrier, facilitating penetration of pathogenic autoantibodies.

* The earliest changes in myelin consist of edema between myelin lamellae and vesicular disruption of the outermost myelin layers.

* These effects are associated with activation of the C5b-C9 membrane attack complex and mediated by calcium entry; it is possible that the macrophage cytokine tumor necrosis factor (TNF) also participates in myelin damage.

* AMAN-Acute motor axonal neuropathy

* AMSAN-Acute motor sensory axonal neuropathy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a history of pneumonia develops pleural effusion. What is the expected finding in the pleural fluid analysis for parapneumonic effusion?
options: Pleural protein ratio less than 0.5 of serum protein
Pleural LDH less than 2/3rd of serum LDH
Pleural LDH less than 0.6 of serum LDH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pleural pH less than 7.2

In the above clinical scenario of a patient with a history of pneumonia who develops a pleural effusion, the expected finding in the pleural fluid analysis for parapneumonic effusion is pleural pH less than 7.2.

Pleural effusion refers to the pathological accumulation of fluid in the pleural space due to:

* excess fluid formation from the interstitial spaces of the lung, parietal pleura or peritoneal cavity

* decreased fluid removal by the lymphatics

Pleural effusion may present with:

* dyspnea

* pleuritic pain

* dry cough

* associated symptoms like fever, weight loss, oedema, and ascites depending on the aetiology.

On examination, there may be:

* tachypnea, in a large effusion

* dullness to percussion

* decreased/absent breath sounds at the base(s)

* other signs present vary with the underlying aetiology.

The aetiology of pleural effusion can be:

* Exudative: Due to a disruption in pleural fluid formation and drainage because of local factors.

* Transudative: Due to a disruption in pleural fluid formation and drainage due to systemic factors.

Light’s criteria can be used to differentiate between transudative and exudative pleural effusions. Exudative effusions will meet at least one of the following criteria:

* Pleural fluid protein/serum protein >0.5.

* Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH >0.6.

* Pleural fluid LDH is more than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum and pleural pH less than 7.2.

Recommended tests for all diagnostic thoracocentesis include:

* Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and protein

* Microscopy and culture

* Cytology and differential count

* Glucose, pH, triglycerides, amylase, hematocrit, AFB culture, and PCR can be done if a particular aetiology is suspected.

If the difference between the protein levels in the serum and the pleural fluid is > 3.1 g/dL, it is likely to be transudative pleural effusion. If the glucose levels are less than 60mg/dL, then the effusion is likely due to exudative causes like malignancy, bacterial infections (parapneumonic effusion), and rheumatoid pleuritis.

If the pleural fluid cytology, culture, glucose, and staining do not yield any result, perform spiral CT to rule out pulmonary embolism and assess the markers of tuberculosis.

Pearl PF0570: Types of pleural effusion

Transudative Pleural effusion

* Congestive heart failure

* Cirrhosis

* Nephrotic syndrome

* Peritoneal dialysis

* Superior vena cava obstruction

* Myxedema

* Urinothorax

Exudative Pleural effusion

* Neoplastic disease: metastatic disease and mesothelioma

* Infectious disease

* Pulmonary embolization

* GI: Esophageal perforation, pancreatic disease, intraabdominal abscess etc.,

* Collagen vascular disease: SLE, rheumatoid pleuritis, Wegener's, Churg Strauss syndrome etc.,

* Post coronary bypass surgery

* Asbestos exposure

* Sarcoidosis

* Drug-induced pleural disease: nitrofurantoin, dantrolene, bromocriptine, amiodarone etc.,

* Radiation therapy

* Hemothorax

* Chylothorax

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with diabetes mellitus has a fasting blood sugar of 180 mg/dL and HbA1c of 8.5%. The treatment was started on Tab metformin 500mg, and his blood sugar has come down to 140 mg/dL, but his HbA1c remains above 7.3%. What is the next step in management?"
options: Continue metformin at the same dose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increase Tab Metformin to 1000mg

The next step in management is increasing the dose of metformin to 1000mg.

Increasing the dose of metformin is the first step in improving the glycemic control of patients with type 2 diabetes whose HbA1c levels are > 6.5% while receiving a dose of less than 2000 mg daily which is the maximum tolerable dose by which we can benefit from increasing dose, confirming that the efficacy of metformin is dependent upon dosage.

According to American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes , Metformin is the preferred first line therapeutic agent for type 2 Diabetes unless contraindicated or not tolerated by the patient. Other hypoglycemic agents are added considering patient preferences, hypoglycemia risk and other comorbidities.

Antidiabetic Drugs that pose a risk of leading to hypoglycemia (insulin secretagogue):

* Sulfonylureas

* Meglitinides: Nateglinide, Repaglinide

The following drugs are not directly responsible for stimulating insulin secretion and hence do not cause hypoglycemia:

* Metformin

* Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor

* Pioglitazone

* DPP-4 inhibitor: Sitagliptin

Note:

While alpha-glucosidase inhibitors themselves do not cause hypoglycemia, the risk of hypoglycemia is increased when they are taken along with insulin or insulin secretagogues.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with liver cirrhosis presents with breathing difficulty due to massive ascites. Which is an incorrect statement about this case?
options: Serum albumin ascites gradient of > 1.1 g/dL
Serum albumin ascites gradient of <1.1 g/dL
Ascitic protein level <2.5 g/dL suggests damage to hepatic sinusoids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serum albumin ascites gradient of <1.1 g/dL

The incorrect statement in the given clinical scenario of a patient with liver cirrhosis presenting with breathing difficulty due to massive ascites is a Serum albumin ascites gradient of <1.1.

SAAG >1.1 g/dl and ascitic protein <2.5 g/dl are seen in ascites due to cirrhosis.

Serum ascites albumin gradient (SAAG):

* Calculated by subtracting the ascitic albumin concentration from the serum albumin level.

* Reflects the pressure within the hepatic sinusoids

* SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates that the ascites are due to increased pressure in the hepatic sinusoids. It reflects the presence of portal hypertension.

* SAAG <1.1 g/dL indicates that the ascites are not related to portal hypertension. It may be due to infection or malignancy.

Ascitic protein level:

* ≥2.5 g/dL indicates that the hepatic sinusoids are normal and are allowing the passage of protein into the ascites. eg. cardiac ascites

* <2.5 g/dL (Option C)  indicates that the hepatic sinusoids have been damaged and scarred and no longer allow passage of protein. Eg. cirrhosis

Other Options:

Option A: Serum albumin ascites gradient of > 1.1 g/dL is a correct statement as liver cirrhosis presents with SAAG >1.1 g/dl and ascitic protein <2.5 g/dl.

Option D: Secondary hyperaldosteronism is due to aldosterone released in response to the activation of the renin-angiotensin system, and usually seen in cirrhosis, heart failure, and nephrosisand can lead to massive ascites and similar finding as cirrhosis.

Pearl PF1584: Serum Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young female presents with vomiting episodes for the past few days. Interpret the ABG report of pH: 7.53, pCO2 48 mm Hg and HCO3: 33 meq/L.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metabolic alkalosis

This ABG pattern is consistent with metabolic alkalosis secondary to prolonged vomiting, leading to the loss of hydrogen ions (H⁺) and chloride (Cl⁻) from gastric secretions.

The primary disturbance is metabolic alkalosis (high HCO₃⁻ and elevated pH). This is likely caused by excessive vomiting, which leads to loss of gastric acid (HCl), increasing bicarbonate levels.

Interpretation of the ABG:

Step 1: The pH of 7.53 is above the normal limits (7.35–7.45) and thus implies the presence of alkalosis.

Step 2: Plasma HCO3- is 33 mEq/L and is higher than the normal limits (22–28 mEq/L). This implies that the alkalosis is due to an increase in the plasma HCO3- and is thus metabolic in origin. The only cause of metabolic alkalosis from the given options is vomiting.

The compensatory response is respiratory, where the body retains CO₂ (hypoventilation) to counteract the alkalosis. This explains the elevated pCO₂ 48 mmHg [normal limits (35 - 45 mmHg)]. However, compensation is incomplete, as the pH remains alkalotic.

On the contrary, normal plasma HCO3- with a decrease in pCO2 levels would point to a respiratory cause of alkalosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young lady presents with recent-onset palpitations and dizziness. Her ECG shows absent P waves and an irregularly irregular RR interval. Her pulse rate is 140 bpm and BP is 80/60 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Synchronized cardioversion

In the given clinical scenario, the patient presenting with recent-onset palpitations and dizziness with ECG showing irregularly irregular rhythm with absent p waves, is suggestive of atrial fibrillation. Since the patient is hemodynamically compromised (hypotension), synchronized cardioversion is the most appropriate management.

Urgent electrical cardioversion is indicated if a patient with AF has shock or severe hypotension, pulmonary edema or ongoing myocardial infarction. Although there is a risk of potential thromboembolism if the patient has not been put on anticoagulation before, the need for rate control outweighs this risk. In these patients, heart rate control is achieved using IV β-blockers or calcium channel blockers like verapamil (Option B) or diltiazem. Additionally, they are also given subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin as soon as possible.

In hemodynamically stable patients with AF of >48 hours duration or unknown duration, there is a high risk of formation of a thrombus in the left atrium. If the patients are cardioverted at this stage, this thrombus can embolize into the systemic circulation, leading to end organ damage, such as stroke. Therefore, for these patients, any of the following two management strategies can be followed:

* Give anticoagulation for 3 weeks → cardioversion (pharmacological or electrical) → continue anticoagulation for 4 more weeks

* Start anticoagulation and do transesophageal echocardiography → if thrombus is absent, do cardioversion (pharmacological or electrical) → continue anticoagulation for 4 more weeks. If a thrombus is present, then cardioversion is delayed by 3 weeks.

Direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are preferred over warfarin for anticoagulation. However, warfarin is the preferred drug if the patient has a mechanical prosthetic valve, advanced CKD or moderate-severe mitral stenosis.

Apart from anticoagulation, the most important aspect of the treatment of chronic AF is rate control. The drugs used for this are β blockers (such as metoprolol) and calcium channel blockers (such as diltiazem and verapamil). Reversion to sinus rhythm can be done electrically or using medications. Pharmacological cardioversion can be done using ibutilide, dofetilide and amiodarone (class III antiarryhthmics- Option A) or flecainide and propafenone (class Ic drugs).

Atrial fibrillation rhythm is irregularly irregular. P waves are absent, these irregular waves are known as fibrillation waves, characteristic of atrial fibrillation.

Other options:

Option C: Adenosine is the first-line drug for Supraventricular tachycardia. It blocks conduction across the AV node and terminates the SVT. It is given as a 6-18 mg bolus

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young male presents with left-sided facial weakness. On examination, the patient is able to wrinkle his forehead and is able to close the right eye partially, and his mouth deviates towards the right side when smiling. Based on these findings, which of the following statements best describes the type and location of the lesion?
options: Supranuclear facial palsy on the left side
Infranuclear facial palsy on the right side
Supranuclear facial palsy on the right side
Infranuclear facial palsy on the left side
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Supranuclear facial palsy on the right side

The given clinical scenario of a young male presenting with weakness of the lower half of the left side of his face and presence of wrinkling on the forehead and normal eyelid closure indicates an upper motor neuron lesion (UMN). The most appropriate diagnosis is supranuclear facial palsy on the right side.

In facial palsy, the angle of the mouth deviates towards the normal side. In this patient, since the mouth deviates towards the right, the left facial nerve is affected.

In an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion, wrinkling on the forehead and eyelid closure remains intact. In this lesion, the contralateral side of the face is affected. The first-order neurons from the right cerebral hemisphere cross over (right to left) at the cortical level and relay in the left facial nerve nucleus in the pons. From here the second-order neurons (left facial nerve) descend and supply the left side of the face.

Hence, right UMN lesion causes paralysis of the lower half of the face on the left side and can cause drooping on the left side.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An obese patient presented with pain in the right hypochondrium. He has a history of unhealthy food consumption. On examination, the liver was palpable below the costal margin. On USG, grade 2 fatty liver was diagnosed. What will be the initial management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reduce weight and lifestyle changes

In this clinical scenario, an obese patient presents with right hypochondrial pain and a history of poor dietary habits. Examination reveals a palpable liver, and ultrasound confirms Grade 2 fatty liver, suggesting Non-Alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH). The initial management involves weight reduction and lifestyle modifications, including a healthier diet and regular physical activity.

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is associated with diabetes and obesity. The fatty change may also be caused by the effect of toxins (including certain medications), protein malnutrition, dyslipidemia, and anoxia. Bleomycin, Methotrexate, Doxycycline, and L-asparaginase are other drugs causing hepatic steatosis.

Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is characterised by hepatic steatosis which is complicated by histologically evident hepatocyte death and inflammation. Currently, biopsy is the best investigation to establish the diagnosis.

The current approach to NAFLD management focuses on treatment to avoid or decrease the risk factors for NASH (like obesity, insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, and dyslipidemia) and lifestyle changes as initial management.

Alpha-tocopherol or vitamin E is the first-line treatment considered for non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). In many studies, vitamin E was well-tolerated and showed modest improvements in AST levels, radiographic features of hepatic steatosis, and/or histologic features of NASH.

* Vitamin E should only be considered as the first-line pharmacotherapy for non-diabetic NASH patients.

* Dose: 800 IU/day.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Chvostek's sign is seen in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypocalcemia

The Chvostek's sign is seen in hypocalcemia.

Chvostek's sign is a clinical indicator of hypocalcemia, seen in conditions like hypoparathyroidism and vitamin D deficiency. It is elicited by gently tapping the facial nerve just anterior to the ear, which triggers involuntary twitching of the facial muscles, particularly around the mouth and eye.

While a positive Chvostek's sign suggests neuromuscular excitability due to low calcium levels, it is not always specific, as mild twitching can also occur in healthy individuals. This sign is often assessed alongside Trousseau's sign to confirm hypocalcemia. Trousseau’s sign indicates hypocalcemia and is demonstrated by inflating a blood pressure cuff above the systolic level for 180 seconds. This causes an involuntary carpal spasm, resulting in contraction of the hand and fingers. It signifies increased neuromuscular excitability due to low calcium levels.

Symptoms and signs of hypocalcemia include:

* laryngeal spasms

* mild digital circumoral numbness

* cardiac arrhythmias

* paresthesia

* Chvostek's sign and Trousseau's sign, as shown in the images below.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Graham Steell murmur is heard in _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pulmonary regurgitation

Graham Steell murmur is the early to mid-diastolic murmur heard in pulmonary regurgitation.

Graham Steell murmur is a high-pitched murmur heard best at the left second intercostal space and is often louder with inspiration. This murmur occurs due to pulmonary regurgitation, which in this case, is secondary to pulmonary hypertension. It can also be seen in patients with COPD due to the development of cor pulmonale leading to pulmonic hypertension.

Other options:

Option A: Pulmonary stenosis is a narrowing of the pulmonary valve or artery, obstructing blood flow from the right ventricle to the lungs. It is associated with a harsh systolic ejection murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border, often with a systolic thrill.

Option C: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a condition where the heart muscle thickens, often affecting the interventricular septum. It is associated with a systolic ejection murmur that increases with the Valsalva manoeuvre and decreases with squatting.

Option D: A ventricular septal defect (VSD) is a congenital heart defect where there is an abnormal opening in the septum between the left and right ventricles. It is typically associated with a holosystolic murmur heard at the left lower sternal border.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The INR ratio recommended for the administration of warfarin in patients with mechanical heart valves is ______________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2.5 – 3.5

The INR ratio recommended for the administration of warfarin in patients with mechanical heart valves is around 2.5-3.5.

Prothrombin time is sensitive to the reduction in levels of prothrombin, factor VII, and factor X. The test is performed by adding thromboplastin, which is a reagent containing tissue factor, phospholipid and calcium to citrated plasma and determining the time to clot formation.

Due to the variable sensitivity of thromboplastin, the International normalized ratio (INR) was developed to standardize the reporting of prothrombin time. In INR, the patient’s prothrombin time is divided by mean normal prothrombin time and this ratio is multiplied by the International Sensitivity Index (ISI) of the particular thromboplastin reagent.

Warfarin therapy should be monitored with INR every 3–4 weeks. The target INR is 2.0–3.0. In patients with mechanical heart valves, the target INR is 2.5–3.5.

Other options:

Option A: The INR range of 1.0-1.5 means the state of body is in hypercoaguable state and itis too low for beneficial effects, hence it is not recommended.

Option B: In most of the patients on regular warfarin therapy,  the  target INR is around 2.0-3.0, but it is not recommended in patients with mechanical heart valve.

Option D: INR >3.5 (3.5- 4.5)can result in increased adverse effects like bleeding and is not recommended for any condition.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The patient came to the ER with pain on the left side of the chest radiating to the left arm and shoulder following exercise. The pain subsided after some time. What is the next step in management? ECG-Electro cardio graphy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. ECG

The given clinical scenario of a patient coming to the ER with pain on the left side of the chest radiating to the left arm and shoulder can be suggestive of ACS (Acute Coronary Syndrome), and the next best step in management is doing an ECG.

Acute coronary syndromes (ACS) includes:

* Unstable angina(UA)

* Non-ST elevation myocardial infarction(NSTEMI)

* ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)

The diagnosis of ACS can be based on the ECG findings-:

STEMI-  Features of MI on ECG:

* ST-segment elevation: Zone of injury

* T wave inversions

* Deep Q waves: late sign to develop

* New left bundle branch block (LBBB)

NSTEMI- Features of NSTEMI on ECG (Troponins are elevated)

*  ST-segment depression

* Deep T-wave inversions

Unstable Angina - Features of Unstable Angina on ECG (Troponins are not elevated)

* Hyperacute T-wave

* T-wave flattening

* Inverted T-waves

* ST depression

The following protocol must be followed in the management of patients with acute coronary syndrome:

* Stabilization of airway, breathing, and circulation

* Administration of O2

* Treatment of sustained ventricular arrhythmia rapidly according to ACLS protocols

* Give aspirin 325 mg

* History and examination, assess cardiac biomarkers

* Give three sublingual nitroglycerin tablets each 5 min apart. Add IV nitroglycerin for the persistence of symptoms.

* Treat left heart failure if present with an after-load reducing agent or loop diuretic

* Give beta-blockers

* Give morphine for the persistence of anxiety and discomfort related to MI

* In patients with STEMI - Reperfusion with PCI or fibrinolysis (if PCI is unavailable within 120 min) followed by antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy. In patients with NSTEMI - antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy are indicated.

Pearl PF1415: Localisation of MI based on ST elevations in different leads

Extensive anterior - I, aVL, V1-V6

Lateral - I, aVL

Inferior - II, III, aVF

Anteroseptal - V1-V4

Anterolateral - I, aVL, V3-V6

Posterior - ST depression and tall R in V1-V4

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The patient came to the ER with pain on the left side of the chest radiating to the left arm and shoulder for the last 40 minutes. ECG shows ST depression in precordial leads. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Low dose aspirin + clopidogrel

The given clinical scenario of a patient coming to the ER with pain on the left side of the chest radiating to the left arm and shoulder for the last 40 minutes. ECG showing ST depression in precordial leads is suggestive of NSTEMI(Non-ST elevation Myocardial infarction) and the next best step in management is low-dose aspirin with clopidogrel.

Acute coronary syndrome is classified into 2 groups:

* ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI).

* NSTE-ACS.

NSTE-ACS further includes:

* NSTEMI (myocyte necrosis present and cardiac troponins elevated).

* Unstable Angina (myocyte necrosis absent and cardiac troponins not elevated).

The diagnosis of NSTE-ACS is based on the following:

Severe chest discomfort with at least one of 3 features:

* Occurring at rest or minimal exertion and lasting for more than 10 minutes

* Recent onset

* Crescendo pattern

ECG showing:

* ST segment depression

* T wave inversion

Elevated cardiac troponins in case of NSTEMI.

Management of NSTE-ACS:

To provide relief of pain and discomfort, initial treatment includes bed rest, nitrates, beta-blockers, and inhaled oxygen (only if arterial O2 saturation <90%).

Antithrombotic therapy consisting of antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs:

* Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT): Aspirin (162-325 mg) AND one ADP receptor inhibitor (Ticagrelor, clopidogrel or prasugrel).

* Anticoagulation: Enoxaparin, unfractionated heparin, fondaparinux or bivalirudin.

* An early invasive strategy including diagnostic coronary angiography (within 2–72 hours of presentation) followed by revascularization. (percutaneous coronary intervention/ coronary artery bypass grafting) is indicated for stabilized patients who are at high risk of coronary events (Based on TIMI, GRACE or HEART score).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The patient is admitted with low urine output, and lab reports show BUN: 140 mg/dL, serum creatinine: 8.0 mg/dL, and 2+ protein on urine dipstick. Which of the following is most useful for distinguishing acute kidney injury (AKI) from chronic kidney disease (CKD)? BUN-Blood urea nitrogen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Creatinine clearance

In a patient admitted with low urine output, BUN of 140 mg/dL, serum creatinine of 8.0 mg/dL, and 2+ protein on urine dipstick, the most useful criterion for differentiating acute kidney injury (AKI) from chronic kidney disease (CKD) is creatinine clearance.

Acute kidney injury (AKI) is defined as an increase in serum creatinine by 1.5 times of baseline value over 7 days.

Acute kidney injury is defined as an abrupt (within hours) decrease in kidney function, which encompasses both injury (structural damage) and impairment (loss of function). It is characterized by abrupt deterioration in kidney function, manifested by an increase in serum creatinine level with or without reduced urine output.

AKI is defined as any of the following:

* Increase in serum creatinine to ≥1.5 times baseline (50% higher), which is known or presumed to have occurred within the prior 7 days.

* Increase in serum creatinine by ≥0.3 mg/dL from baseline within 48 hours.

* Urine volume of <0.5 ml/kg/h for 6 hours.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The patient presents with headache, vomiting and nuchal rigidity. Guarded LP was done and shows turbid CSF. Microscopy shows 90% PMN cells with sugar of 40 mg/dL and protein of 200 mg/dl. Which is correct about the management of this case? LP-Lumbar puncture CSF-Cerebro spinal fluid PMN-Polymorpho nuclear cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin

The given clinical scenario of a patient presenting with headache, vomiting, and nuchal rigidity and a guarded lumbar puncture revealing turbid CSF with 90% PMN cells, a sugar level of 40 mg/dL, and protein of 200 mg/dL is suggestive of bacterial meningitis and the appropriate management includes treatment with ceftriaxone plus vancomycin.

The most common cause of meningitis in adults over 20 years of age is Streptococcus pneumoniae.

The classic clinical triad of meningitis includes fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity. Other common symptoms include decreased consciousness, nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and seizures. Cutaneous signs such as petechiae, purpura, or an erythematous macular rash may be present.

Brudzinski's sign and Kernig's sign can indicate meningeal irritation.

* Brudzinski's sign is positive when there is involuntary flexion of the hips and knees in response to passive neck flexion.

* Kernig's sign is positive when there is resistance and pain in extending the knee with the hip flexed at 90 degrees (given below)

When bacterial meningitis is suspected, blood cultures should be obtained, and empirical antimicrobial therapy should be initiated without delay. The diagnosis is confirmed by examining cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). CSF analysis shows increased polymorphonuclear leukocytes, decreased glucose concentration, increased protein concentration, and increased opening pressure. CSF bacterial cultures and Gram stain are used to identify the causative organism.

Prompt initiation of empirical antimicrobial therapy is crucial in suspected cases of bacterial meningitis. Commonly used antibiotics include third- or fourth-generation cephalosporins (such as ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, or cefepime) that cover Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae and Vancomycin if there is a high suspicion of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection. Ampicillin with metronidazole is added when Listeria monocytogenes is suspected, particularly in neonates, pregnant women, individuals over 50 years, and immunocompromised individuals.

Other Options:

Option A: Amphotericine B plus flucystosine for at least 2 weeks is used as Induction agent for Cryptococcus with CNS involvement in HIV patient.

Option B: Acyclovir is used as a drug of choice for treating Viral meningitis  especially caused by HSV and is not useful in managing bacterial meningitis.

Option D: Tubercular meningitis can be treated with Rifamapicin plus isoniazid. But they are not indicated in bacterial meningitis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is correct about first-degree heart block?
options: Normal PR and prolonged RR interval
Prolonged PR and normal RR interval
Short PR and normal RR interval
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prolonged PR and normal RR interval

The correct statement about the first-degree heart block is the ECG shows prolonged PR and normal RR interval.

First-degree heart block is characterized by a fixed, prolonged PR interval without any dropped beats. It indicates a delay in conduction through the AV node, but all atrial impulses still reach the ventricles. It is most often asymptomatic. Canon waves are observed in JVP. It carries a very good prognosis and no treatment is needed.

A heart block is caused by an interruption of impulse conduction within the conducting system of the heart. It may be sinoatrial, atrioventricular, or intraventricular. Atrioventricular blocks are further divided into type I, type II and type III blocks. The type II blocks are subdivided into Mobitz type I and Mobitz type II blocks.

First Degree Heart Block: It occurs due to slowing of conduction through the AV junction. It is characterized by prolonged PR > 0.2s and equal RR intervals.

Second Degree Heart Block: It occurs due to the intermittent failure of electrical impulse conduction from the atrium to the ventricle. It is characterized by a missed QRS. It is of two types:

* Mobitz type 1/ Wenckebach occurs due to the decremental conduction of electrical impulses in the AV node. It is characterized by a progressive PR elongation leading to an eventual drop in the QRS complex. This may be seen in young athletes.

* Mobitz type 2 occurs in the distal or infra-His conduction system and is often associated with intraventricular conduction delays.  It is characterized by an intermittent failure of conduction of the p wave without any change in the preceding impulses. On ECG there is a fixed PR interval and missed QRS.

Third Degree Heart Block/Complete Heart Block

It occurs when none of the impulses from the atria are conducted to the ventricles. It is characterized by

* Escape rhythm

* RR equal, PP equal

* P waves > QRS waves

* No relationship between P & QRS.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding intrinsic acute kidney injury? Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. BUN:Creatinine < 20:1

The correct statement regarding intrinsic acute kidney injury is BUN: Creatinine < 20:1

AKI (acute kidney injury) is defined as a decline in kidney function within 7 days, resulting in the accumulation of nitrogenous waste and other toxic metabolites usually excreted in the urine. It includes a variety of conditions that share some common features such as elevated creatinine levels and reduced urine output. It is broadly divided into three categories:

* Prerenal azotemia

* Intrinsic parenchymal disease

* Postrenal obstruction

Intrinsic causes can further be divided into acute tubular necrosis, acute glomerulonephritis, and acute interstitial nephritis. Ischemia and nephrotoxins are the main causes of acute tubular necrosis. Nephrotoxins can be exogeneous such as vancomycin, cisplatin, and iodinated contrast agents used for CT imaging. Endogenous toxins include myoglobin, uric acid, and haemoglobin. Crush injuries, heat stroke, and myopathies can result in rhabdomyolysis releasing large amounts of myoglobin. The urine/plasma creatinine ratio is usually ≤ 40.

In acute tubular necrosis, urinary sodium is >20 mEq/L.

Prerenal azotemia arises due to a reduced renal plasma flow. Common causes include hypovolemia, liver failure, and congestive heart failure. The urine/plasma creatinine ratio is ≥ 40 and urinary sodium is usually <20mEq/L.

Bladder outlet obstruction, urethral obstruction, and benign prostatic hyperplasia lead to postrenal azotemia. Urinary sodium can be variable.

The factors that can help differentiate prerenal and renal causes of AKI are as follows:

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with brown-colored urine, flank pain, and fatigue for the last 3 days. He has 2+ proteinuria with 20 red cells/HPF and dysmorphic red blood cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

A child presenting with acute onset (3 days) flank pain, cola-colored urine, and mild to moderate proteinuria is suggestive of a nephritic syndrome picture. The only disease which causes this out of the given options is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).

PSGN is primarily caused by group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infections in children aged 5 to 12 years. It is caused by immune complexes containing streptococcal antigens (M protein of cell wall) and specific antibodies. PSGN typically manifests as an acute nephritic syndrome, appearing either 1 to 2 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis or 3 to 6 weeks after streptococcal pyoderma. The severity of kidney involvement can vary, ranging from asymptomatic microscopic hematuria with normal renal function to gross hematuria with acute renal failure. Edema, hypertension, and oliguria may be present depending on the extent of renal involvement.

Laboratory findings commonly include a significant decrease in serum C3 levels during the acute phase, with values returning to normal within 6 to 8 weeks. To confirm the diagnosis, evidence of a preceding streptococcal infection is necessary. The antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer often increases following pharyngitis, while the anti-deoxyribonuclease B level is a reliable indicator of cutaneous streptococcal infection.

Light microscopic examination reveals enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with diffuse mesangial and endothelial proliferation, as well as leukocyte infiltration. Immunofluorescence analysis demonstrates granular deposits of IgG and complement C3 along the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and in the mesangium. Electron microscopy primarily shows subepithelial humps, with subendothelial deposits observed in early stages of the disease.

Managing the acute effects of renal insufficiency (sodium restriction and diuretics) and hypertension is the mainstay. Antibiotic therapy with a 10-day course of penicillin is recommended to limit the spread of nephritogenic pathogens. But antibiotics do not alter the natural course of PSGN. Complete resolution of the hematuria and proteinuria in the majority of children occurs within 3–6 weeks of the onset of nephritis but 3–10% of children may have persistent microscopic hematuria, non-nephrotic proteinuria, or hypertension.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 20-year-old IV drug user presents with fever. On examination, his temperature is 38.5°C, and fundoscopic examination reveals spots over the fundus. Laboratory investigations show a leukocyte count of 20,000/cu mm, and blood cultures have been sent. Infective endocarditis is suspected. How many minor Duke's criteria are fulfilled in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

This patient, who is an intravenous drug user, with a fever of 38.5°C and spots on the fundus, indicating immunologic phenomena has 3 minor Duke's criteria.

Infective endocarditis is associated with bacterial or fungal infection of the valvular or endocardial surface of the heart. The definitive diagnosis can only be established by histological and microbiological examinations of the vegetation.

However, a diagnostic schema called, modified Duke criteria, is usually used for diagnosis. The criteria are based on clinical, laboratory, and echocardiographic findings commonly encountered in patients with endocarditis, as described below.

The diagnosis is made based on the presence of

* Two major criteria, or

* One major and three minor criteria, or

* Five minor criteria.

Note: There has been a recent update in the modified Duke's criteria, which is given in the pearl below.

Pearl PF1994: Modified Duke's criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis

Diagnosis of Infective endocarditis is by Duke's Criteria, which requires either:

* Pathologic criteria

* Clinical criteria

If clinical criteria are used, definitive endocarditis is defined by the presence of 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor criteria.

The presence of single pathological criteria is definitive of infective endocarditis.

Note: The diagnosis of endocarditis is rejected if an alternative diagnosis is established either when:

* Symptoms resolve and do not recur with <4 days of antibiotic therapy OR

* If surgery or autopsy yields no pathologic or macroscopic evidence of endocarditis in <4 days of antimicrobial therapy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presents with the following lesions that started 2 days after he developed a fever. On examination, there are generalized vesicular eruptions over the trunk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chicken pox

The above image showing multiple vesicular lesions on the trunk is suggestive of chickenpox or varicella caused by the varicella-zoster virus.

Chickenpox

Chickenpox or varicella is caused by the varicella-zoster virus. Most infections occur before the age of 5 but can occur in older children and adults. The lesions develop in 3-5 crops and are polymorphic (present at different stages in each site). In 2–4 days, a dry crust forms leaving a shallow pink depression which, in the absence of secondary infection, heals without scarring. It is non-contagious after the lesions have crusted.

Characteristics of the rash of chickenpox:

* Superficial

* Pleomorphic

* Centripetal

* Unilocular

* Symmetrical

* Spares palms and soles, affects flexor surfaces and axilla

* Rapid evolution

* Dewdrop on Rose-petal appearance (shown in the image below)

Complications of VZV occur with disseminated varicella or with reactivation of infection. This more commonly occurs in immunocompromised patients. Complications include:

* Bacterial infections of the skin and soft tissues

* Pneumonia

* Hepatitis

* Acute cerebellar ataxia

* Encephalitis

* Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy

* Sepsis

* Shingles/Herpes Zoster: vesicular lesions are confined to the unilateral segment of the sensory nerve (dermatome). In children, the rash is mild, with complete resolution within 1-2 weeks. Unlike in adults, postherpetic neuralgia is unusual in children.

Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) is a human herpesvirus that causes varicella (chickenpox) as a primary infection and then remains in a latent form in the dorsal root ganglia for a variable period after which it can reactivate to cause herpes zoster (shingles).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old female presents with daytime sleepiness, impaired concentration, and impaired memory. On examination, her BMI is 43 kg/m2, blood pressure is 170/100 mm of Hg. Her awake arterial blood gas analysis shows bicarbonate - 33 mEq/L, PaCO2 - 53 mmHg, PaO2 - 70 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome

The most probable diagnosis of this patient with awake high pCO2, low pO2, and BMI of 41 is obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS)/ Pickwickian syndrome is characterised by alveolar hypoventilation during wakefulness in obese people (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2), not explained by other causes of hypoventilation.

Patients with OHS are obese and have a history of daytime hypersomnolence, loud snoring, choking during sleep fatigue, impaired concentration and memory, a small oropharynx, and a thick neck.

OHS may be associated with the following findings:

* Elevated serum bicarbonate (>27 mEq/L)

* Hypercapnia (PaCO2 >45 mmHg)

* Hypoxemia (PaO2 <70 mmHg)

* Polycythemia

Other options:

Option A: Central sleep apnea is characterized by a lack of respiratory effort during sleep, leading to recurrent pauses in breathing. It's less likely in this case due to the hypercapnia (elevated PaCO2) seen.

Option B: Narcolepsy involves excessive daytime sleepiness, sudden loss of muscle tone (cataplexy), sleep paralysis, and hallucinations during sleep onset. It doesn't typically cause elevated PaCO2.

Option D: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) involves repeated episodes of partial or complete upper airway obstruction during sleep. While obesity is a risk factor for OSA, the arterial blood gas analysis findings are more consistent with OHS.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 37-year-old female complains of recurrent episodes of discomfort, pain, and a sensation of pressure behind her left eye. She has intermittent proptosis, that is reducible. Her symptoms and signs are accentuated when she bends forward. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Orbital varices

This patient presenting with intermittent, reducible proptosis and associated features is most consistent with a diagnosis of orbital varices.

Orbital varices:

* They are venous malformations of the orbit caused by vascular dysgenesis.

* Patients usually present with non-pulsatile, intermittent, and reducible proptosis.

* On activities such as forward bending or lowering of the head, turning the head forcefully, hyperextension of the neck, and coughing, the varices fill up, causing proptosis, and then, they regress on shifting to a non-dependent position.

Treatment:

* Small lesions generally do not require treatment

* Surgical excision is technically difficult and often incomplete because the lesions are friable and bleed easily; Specialized techniques such as embolization and carbon dioxide laser surgery may be helpful.

Other options:

Option A,D: Orbital hemangioma or orbital dermoid cysts will cause consistent symptoms and may not necessarily intensify with movements.

Option C: The patient's young age and the recurrent nature of the symptoms make metastasis less probable.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 38 year old male patient presented with complaints of paranasal sinus pain and bloody nasal discharge for the past few days. He also has a previous history of hemoptysis and hematuria. Imaging revealed multiple, bilateral, nodular cavitary infiltrates. Which of the following antibodies would be positive in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. c-ANCA

The clinical features of this patient suggest granulomatosis with polyangitis which is positive for anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) in 90% of patients. Granulomatosis polyangitis has a very high specificity for anti-proteinase 3 ANCA.

Granulomatosis polyangitis is an autoimmune small vessel vasculitis syndrome characterized by granulomatous vasculitits of the upper and lower respiratory tracts with glomerulonephritis. Incidence is equal in bot males and females and the mean age of onset is 40 years.

Histopathologic hallmarks are necrotising vasculitis of small arteries and veins with granuloma formation.

Upper respiratory tract features : Paranasal sinus pain & discharge and purulent/ bloody nasal discharge. Patient may or may not develop mucosal ulceration leading to septal perforation and saddle nose deformity.

Lower respiratory tract features : Cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, chest comfort, endobronchial disease leading to atelectasis. Lung involvement appears as multiple, bilateral, nodular cavitary infiltrates. Lung biopsy will reveal necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis.

Renal involvement : Renal involvement progresses from focal segemental glomerulitis to rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis. But granulomas are rare in renal biopsy. Mild glomerulitis with proteinuria, hematuria and red blood cell casts.

May also involve the eyes, skin, heart and brain.

Laboratory findings : Elevated C-reactive protein and/or erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Positive antiproteinase 3 ANCA.

Treatment : 2 phases, induction and maintainence phases. Glucocorticoids + immunosuppressive agent
Severe disease : Induced by rituximab or cyclophosphamide.
Remission maintainence : Rituximab/ azathioprine/ methotrexate/ mycophenolate mofetil.
Limited only to sinonasal tissues : Trimethoprim-Sulfomethoxazolemmay be tried.

Other options :

* Option B & C. ANA and Anti-histone antibodies are more specific to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

* Option D. Anti-Jo 1 antibodies are specific to inflammatory myopathies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old female patient presents with complaints of dryness in the mouth and eyes. She also has dysphagia. On examination, dental caries and enlarged cervical lymph nodes are noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sjogren syndrome

The patient's clinical features of dry eyes, dry mouth and dysphagia along with cervical lymphadenopathy and dental caries are suggestive of Sjögren's syndrome.

Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune disorder that involves lymphocytic infiltration of the exocrine glands. This manifests as xerostomia (dry mouth) and keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes). It is associated with autoantibodies anti-Ro/SS-A and anti-La/SS-B.

Keratoconjunctivitis sicca can be diagnosed by Schirmer's test. This test measures the quantity of tears produced. Two marked strips of paper are placed between the globe and the lower eyelid and the patient is instructed to close their eyes for 5 minutes. The tears produced spread along the paper by capillary action. The distance is measured. A score of more than 10 mm is considered to be normal while that of less than 5 mm is considered deficient.

A number of other systems can be involved as well. For example, atrophic gastritis, esophageal mucosal atrophy, and vaginal dryness. Extraglandular or systemic manifestations can also be present. These manifest as fatigue, arthritis, Raynaud's phenomenon, and myalgia.

Diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome requires the following:

* Eye and/or mouth dryness

* Eye tests disclose keratoconjunctivitis sicca

* Mouth evaluation reveals dry oral mucosa and/or

* Presence of anti-Ro or anti-La autoantibodies

A labial (lip) biopsy is a must to confirm the diagnosis and determine the prognosis.

Treatment of Sjögren's syndrome is directed at treating the symptoms and complications. Artificial tears can be used for dry eyes and propionic acid gel for vaginal dryness. Pilocarpine can help increase oral secretions and hydroxychloroquine can be used to treat arthritis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old male presents with complaints of sudden, involuntary, and uncontrollable dance-like movements. He also complains of facing difficulty with his memory. His wife says he has gotten very emotional recently. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Huntington's chorea

The clinical presentation of sudden, involuntary, and uncontrollable dance-like movements, along with cognitive and emotional symptoms, is characteristic of Huntington's disease (HD), also known as Huntington's chorea.

Huntington's disease (HD) is a degenerative disease of the caudate and putamen (“striate neurons”) caused by an autosomal dominant inheritance of a trinucleotide repeat (CAG) in the Huntington gene (chromosome 4), which results in motor, behavioral, oculomotor, and cognitive dysfunction. HD is characterized by rapid, nonpatterned, semi-purposeful, involuntary choreiform movements of limb, face, or trunk. A phenomenon referred to as anticipation is seen particularly in males, with subsequent generations having larger numbers of repeats and earlier ages of disease onset.

Tetrabenazine and deutetrabenazine are inhibitors of VMAT2 and cause presynaptic depletion of catecholamines. Deutetrabenazine is a newer form of tetrabenazine approved for the treatment of chorea associated with Huntington's disease. Deutetrabenazine takes advantage of the stronger bonds that deuterium forms with carbon (deuterated tetrabenazine). They have a longer half-life than the corresponding products of tetrabenazine metabolism.

Tetrabenazine is extensively metabolized by CYP2D6. It may cause hypotension and depression with suicidal tendencies. It can also cause Parkinsonism. Deutetrabenazine has adverse effects similar to those of tetrabenazine.

Other Options:

* Parkinson's disease is characterized by tremors, bradykinesia (slow movement), and rigidity. It does not typically cause the dance-like choreiform movements seen in HD.

* Friedreich ataxia is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the nervous system, causing progressive ataxia (loss of coordination). It does not typically present with choreiform movements.

* Alzheimer's disease primarily affects memory and cognitive function, but it does not cause dance-like choreiform movements.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old male patient presents with difficulty in breathing and dizziness. He has been undergoing treatment for lung cancer. On examination, breath sounds were reduced over the left inferior-scapular region. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pleural effusion

The clinical scenario of dyspnea, dizziness, and reduced breath sounds over the left inferior-scapular region in a patient with lung cancer is suggestive of pleural effusion.

Pleural effusion refers to the pathological accumulation of fluid in the pleural space due to

* Excess fluid formation from the interstitial spaces of the lung, parietal pleura, or peritoneal cavity.

* Decreased fluid removal by the lymphatics.

Pleural effusion may present with dyspnea, pleuritic pain, dry cough, and associated symptoms like fever, weight loss, edema, and ascites depending on the etiology. On examination, there may be tachypnea, dullness on percussion and decreased/absent breath sounds at the base(s).

The etiology of pleural effusion can be of two types:

* Exudative: disruption in pleural fluid formation and drainage because of local factors. Examples include malignancy, infections, and pulmonary embolism.

* Transudative: disruption in pleural fluid formation and drainage due to systemic factors. Examples include congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome.

Light’s criteria can be used to differentiate between transudative and exudative pleural effusions. Exudative effusions will meet at least one of the following criteria:

* Pleural fluid protein/serum protein >0.5

* Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH >0.6

* Pleural fluid LDH is more than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum.

Recommended tests for all diagnostic thoracocentesis include:

* Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and protein

* Microscopy and culture

* Cytology and differential count

* Glucose, pH, triglycerides, amylase, haematocrit, AFB culture and PCR can be done if a particular etiology is suspected.

Other options:

*

Constrictive pericarditis: Symptoms may include swelling in the legs, fatigue, and discomfort, but it's not directly associated with reduced breath sounds or localized findings on lung examination.

*

Cardiac tamponade is characterized by the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space leading to impairment of diastolic relaxation of the cardiac chambers. This leads to a decline in cardiac output. The characteristic signs of cardiac tamponade are Beck's triad, which consists of hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and elevated jugular venous pressure.

*

Pneumothorax: It can cause sudden, sharp chest pain and difficulty breathing, but it often presents with hyper-resonant percussion (tapping on the chest) and decreased breath sounds on the affected side.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old bedridden patient develops acute onset dyspnea and chest pain. A CT pulmonary angiography was done. Which screening test will be useful to determine the etiology of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. D-dimer measurement

In a bedridden patient presenting with sudden onset dyspnea and chest pain, there is a concern for possible pulmonary embolism (PE). Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) can be suspected in this patient because of his bedridden status. The screening test used for DVT is the D-dimer measurement.

DVT of the leg is complicated by the immediate risk of pulmonary embolus and sudden death. Patients are at risk of developing a post-thrombotic limb and venous ulceration.

Virchow's Triad: three factors important in the development of venous thrombosis.

* Endothelial injury (vascular Injury)

* Hypercoagulability of blood

* Stasia or turbulence of blood flow

The most important predisposing factor is hospital admissions for the treatment of a medical or surgical condition

Diagnosis:

D-dimer measurement: If normal, no indication for further investigation but if raised, a duplex ultrasound examination of the deep veins should be performed.

Duplex ultrasound is the investigation of choice for diagnosis of DVT (Filling defects in flow and lack of compressibility indicate the presence of a thrombosis)

Ascending venography shows thrombus as a filling defect, which is now rarely required

Treatment

* Rest, elevation of the limb, and bandaging the entire limb with a crepe bandage.

* Anticoagulants: Heparin/low molecular weight heparin, warfarin, phenindione.

* Palma operation

* May-Husni operation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old male with an acute ischemic stroke is undergoing thrombolysis with IV alteplase. He currently weighs 80 kg. What is the appropriate dose of alteplase to be given to this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 8 mg

The dose of alteplase for Intravenous thrombolysis is 0.9 mg/kg. This patient weighs 80 kg, therefore the required dose would be 0.9 x 80 = 72 mg. 10% of this is given as a bolus followed by the remainder of the total dose over 1 hour. So the required initial dose is 7.2mg ∼ 8mg

This should be immediately administered to patients with ischemic stroke who arrive in the window period within 4.5 hours of symptom onset.

Administration of rtPA:

* IV access with two peripheral IV lines (avoid arterial or central line placement)

* Review eligibility for rtPA

*

Give 0.9 mg/kg IV (maximum 90 mg), with 10% as an initial bolus. The rest of the is given as an infusion over 1 hour.

*

Frequent cuff blood pressure monitoring

*

No other antithrombotic treatment for 24 h

* If there is a decline in neurologic status or uncontrolled blood pressure, stop the infusion, give cryoprecipitate, and reimage brain emergently

* Avoid urethral catheterization for ≥2 h

Indications for thrombolysis in stroke

* Clinical diagnosis of stroke

* Onset of symptoms to time of drug administration <3 hours/4.5 hours

* Age ≥ 18 years

* CT scan showing no haemorrhage or edema of >1/3rd of the MCA territory

Contraindications of thrombolysis in stroke

* Sustained BP >185/110 mmHg despite treatment

* Bleeding diathesis

* Recent head injury or Intracerebral hemorrhage

* Major surgery in preceding 14 days

* Minor stroke symptoms

* Gastrointestinal bleeding in preceding 21 days

* Recent myocardial infarction

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient presented with acute onset left-sided hemiparesis. The symptoms started 3 hours ago. On examination, blood pressure is 200/100 mm of hg. CT head is shown below. Which of the following should not be done in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immediate thrombolysis

The clinical scenario of the patient with acute onset left-sided hemiparesis and CT head findings showing hyperdensity on the right side suggest an intra-parenchymal hemorrhage. Given the presence of a hemorrhagic stroke on CT scan, thrombolysis should not be done.

Thrombolysis refers to the dissolution of the intravascular clots to prevent ischemic damage and improve blood flow.

Contraindications for thrombolysis :

* Sustained blood pressure >185/110 mmHg despite treatment

* Bleeding diathesis

* Recent head injury or intracerebral hemorrhage

* Major surgery in the preceding 14 days

* Gastrointestinal bleeding in the preceding 21 days

* Recent myocardial infarction

Indications for thrombolysis:

* Clinical diagnosis of an acute ischemic stroke

* The onset of symptoms to time of drug administration <4.5 hours

* CT scan showing no hemorrhage or edema of >1/3 of MCA territory

* Age of the patient >18 years

Treatment of Intracranial hemorrhage:

Non-surgical:

* Clotting factor administration, if the patient was on blood thinners;

* Blood pressure control to reduce the risk of more bleeding; and

* Measuring and controlling ICP and edema (pressure on brain tissue due to clot) using osmotic therapy such as mannitol and hypertonic saline.

Surgical:

* Stereotactic clot aspiration

* Craniotomy, followed by clot removal

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presented with back pain for the past 3 months. On examination, he has pallor, and gamma globulins are elevated. Liver function tests are normal. X-ray spine shows multiple lytic lesions. Which of the following cells are involved in the pathogenesis of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Plasma cells

The given clinical scenario of a patient with backache for the past 3 months and multiple lytic lesions is suggestive of multiple myeloma, a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia with the proliferation of plasma cells derived from a single clone.

Bone pain is the most common symptom of multiple myeloma. Tumor cells release osteoclast activating factors (OAFs), which increase osteoclast activity and accelerated bone destruction. Furthermore, there is suppression of osteoblast activity to form new bone. Lysis of the bone leads to hypercalcemia. Patients with multiple myeloma also have an increased susceptibility to infections because of diffuse hypogammaglobulinemia (decreased production and increased destruction) of normal antibodies.

Other important features of multiple myeloma include:

* Renal failure

* Normocytic and normochromic anemia

* Hyperviscosity syndromes

* Elevated ESR

* Normal alkaline phosphatase due to suppression of osteoblast activity.

* Monoclonal protein in serum protein electrophoresis

* Urinalysis shows free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence-Jones proteins)

Diagnostic Criteria for Multiple Myeloma include:

Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥10% (or) biopsy-proven bony or extramedullary plasmacytoma

plus

Any one or more of the following myeloma-defining events:

* Evidence of end-organ damage attributable to the underlying plasma cell proliferative disorder, specifically: (CRAB features)

* Hypercalcemia: Serum calcium level >1 mg/dL higher than the upper limit of normal or >11 mg/dL

* Renal insufficiency: Serum creatinine >2 mg/dL

* Anemia: Hemoglobin level of >2 g/dL below the lowest limit of normal, or Hb <10 g/dL

* Bone lesions: One or more osteolytic lesions on radiography, computed tomography (CT), or positron emission tomography (PET).

* Any one or more of the following biomarkers of malignancy:

* Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥ 60%

* Serum involved / uninvolved free light-chain ratio of 100 or greater.

* >1 focal lesion on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents to the OPD with bilateral swelling of lower limbs. On examination, there is elevated JVP, hepatomegaly, and ascites. What is your provisional diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cardiac failure

The given clinical scenario of elevated JVP, hepatomegaly and edema is suggestive of cardiac failure.

Heart failure is a complex clinical syndrome that occurs because the ventricle is unable to fill with or eject blood. The etiology of heart failure includes:

* Hypertension (most common cause)

* Diabetes mellitus

* Coronary artery disease

* Cardiomyopathies

* Chronic kidney disease

* High output states, such as beriberi, thyrotoxicosis, severe anemia

Signs and symptoms of heart failure are:

Right heart failure
Left heart failure

Due to congestion in the systemic circulation
Due to congestion in the lungs.

Symptoms and signs:

• Raised JVP
• Congestive hepatomegaly
• Positive hepatojugular reflux
• Ascites
• Bilateral pitting edema
• Weight gain- due to edema
• Fatigue- due to ↓pumping of blood to lungs leading to ↓oxygenation of the blood

Symptoms and signs:

• Dyspnea on exertion
• Orthopnea
• Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (characteristic of LVF)
• Pulmonary rales
• Increased PCWP
• Fatigue- due to ↓cardiac output

questions.text: A female patient with celiac disease is recommended a gluten-free diet. Which among the following can she consume?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rice

Rice can be consumed on a gluten-free diet.

The primary management of celiac disease is avoiding gluten in the diet.
