questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old female was brought to the emergency department by her husband after a suspected suicide attempt by drug overdose. She is experiencing seizures and difficulty breathing. On examination, she has a fever, a heart rate of 186 beats per minute, and a blood pressure of 70/50 mmHg. Additionally, she has a dry mouth and dilated pupils. Her arterial blood gas (ABG) shows a pH of 7.1, bicarbonate at 14 mmol/L, and pCO2 at 30 mm Hg. The ECG findings are also provided. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tricyclic antidepressant overdose

The given clinical scenario of a patient having seizures, metabolic acidosis, tachycardia, hypotension, and pupillary dilatation and an ECG finding showing a wide QRS complex and prolonged QT interval, is suggestive of tricyclic antidepressant toxicity.

ECG of a patient with tricyclic antidepressant overdose shows three major findings: sinus tachycardia (from anticholinergic and adrenergic effects), prolongation of the QRS complex (from slowed ventricular conduction), and prolongation of the QT interval (from delayed repolarization).

Tricyclic antidepressant overdose:

Clinical features: Seizures, respiratory depression, drowsiness, delirium, Sinus tachycardia, hypotension, prolonged PR/QRS/QT interval, arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia, fibrillation). Anticholinergic symmptoms like dilated pupils, dry mouth, urinary retention, hyperthermia

Treatment: Oxygen supplementation and IV fluids. Activated charcoal if the patient is brought within two hours of ingestion (unless ileus present), IV sodium bicarbonate (attenuates the TCA-induced cardiotoxicity and metabolic acidosis)

Note: Dialysis is not very helpful in the management of TCA overdose.

ECG of a patient with tricyclic antidepressant overdose shows three major findings, sinus tachycardia (from anticholinergic and adrenergic effects), prolongation of the QRS complex (from slowed ventricular conduction), and prolongation of the QT interval (from delayed repolarization) as given below,

Other options:

Option B: Atropine is an anticholinergic drug. It acts through reversible, competitive inhibition of the postsynaptic muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. It is indicated in the treatment of organophosphate/muscarinic poisoning, in bradycardia, and to reduce salivary secretions. The adverse effects of atropine are due to the antimuscarinic effects, including xerostomia, blurring of vision, photophobia, tachycardia, flushing, warm, dry skin, constipation, urinary retention, anhidrosis, delirium, and coma. Intoxication with atropine results in all the above symptoms along with convulsions, and circulatory collapse due to respiratory failure. Death may occur secondary to respiratory paralysis.

Option C: Lithium Toxicity is associated with symptoms like nausea, vomiting, ataxia, coarse tremors, dysarthria, seizure, and hyperreflexia. There is no specific antidote, and treatment is mainly supportive. In severe toxicity, dialysis is the most effective treatment. It is associated with Ebstein anomaly.

Option D: The most common cardiac manifestations of digitalis toxicity include atrioventricular junctional rhythm, premature ventricular depolarizations, ventricular bigeminy, ventricular tachycardia, and second-degree AV blockade. After cardiovascular system, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea i.e., GIT effects are more pronounced. Altered color perception can also be seen in case of digoxin toxicity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old female presents with headache, fever, and nuchal rigidity. Lumbar puncture was done, and CSF analysis shows abundant lymphocytes with normal glucose and elevated proteins. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Viral meningitis

The given clinical picture of headache, fever, and nuchal rigidity, and CSF examination findings of abundant lymphocytes with normal sugar and elevated proteins are suggestive of viral meningitis.

The CSF findings in viral meningitis are usually pleocytosis, normal or mildly elevated protein (20-80 mg/dL), normal glucose levels, and slightly elevated opening pressure. The total CSF cell count usually ranges from 25 to 500 cells/microliter, predominantly lymphocytes.

The classic clinical triad of fever, headache, and neck rigidity is suggestive of meningitis. Other common complaints are nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. Nuchal rigidity (“stiff neck”) is the pathognomonic sign of meningitis. Hip and knee flexion on passive flexion of the neck is called Brudzinsky's sign. Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) is a complication that presents as papilledema, disorientation, or dilated, poorly reactive pupils.

Other options:

Option A: In bacterial meningitis, classic CSF abnormalities include polymorphonuclear (PMN) leukocytosis (>100 cells/μL in 90% of cases), decreased glucose concentration (<40 mg/dL), elevated protein concentration (>45 mg/dL in 90%), and increased opening pressure (>180 mmH₂O in 90%). Additionally, CSF bacterial cultures are positive in >70% of patients, and Gram stain identifies organisms in >60% of cases.

Option B: The characteristic CSF abnormalities in fungal meningitis are a mononuclear or lymphocytic pleocytosis, an increased protein concentration, and a decreased glucose concentration.

Option C: The classic CSF abnormalities in tuberculous meningitis are elevated opening pressure, lymphocytic pleocytosis (10–500 cells/μL), elevated protein concentration in the range of 100–500 mg/dl, and decreased glucose concentration in the range of 20–40 mg/dL.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old female with a complaint of fatigue and dysphagia presents to the hospital with the peripheral blood smear given in the image. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Plummer Vinson Syndrome

The above clinical scenario of a 30-year-old female with dysphagia and fatigue, and microcytic hypochromic anemia on PBS is consistent with the diagnosis of Plummer-Vinson Syndrome.

Plummer-Vinson syndrome is also known as Paterson-Brown-Kelly syndrome, and it predisposes to hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma and consists of four features with a higher incidence in women:

* Dysphagia

* Iron-deficiency anaemia

* Weight loss

* Esophageal webs.

Treatment includes correcting iron-deficiency anemia, which may improve dysphagia and pain. Oesophageal bougies can be used during upper endoscopy to dilate the post-cricoid webs and allow normal swallowing and passage of food.

The image below shows the endoscopic appearance of the post-cricoid esophageal web.

Other options:

Option A: B12 deficiency presents as megaloblastic anemia with neurological features, not as microcytic RBC with dysphagia. It is more common in pure vegetarian patients.

Option B: Hemolytic Anemia typically presents with jaundice, raised LDH, reduced haptoglobin with schistocytes in PBS.

Option D: Iron deficiency anemia presents with microcytic hypochromic RBC, but it does not present with dysphagia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient presents with hypertension and hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. CT scan shows a mass of 1.5 cm over the kidney with elevated ARR. What is the next best step for the management of this patient? ARR - aldosterone renin ratio.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adrenalectomy

The patient has hypertension, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, elevated ARR, unilateral adrenal mass (1.5 cm) strongly points to aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma, which is managed surgically with an adrenalectomy.

Primary hyperaldosteronism is characterized by hypersecretion of aldosterone with suppressed plasma renin levels (due to the negative feedback). The most frequent causes are unilateral adrenal adenoma and bilateral adrenal hyperplasia.

Clinical features include

* Hypertension (most common)

* Hypokalemia

* Metabolic alkalosis

* Polyuria (due to ANP)

* Polydipsia (due to polyuria)

* Muscle weakness

CT or MRI is used to detect the tumour. In a patient with bilateral micronodular hyperplasia, there could be a unilateral non-functioning tumour. Selective adrenal vein sampling can be done to differentiate between unilateral and bilateral disease.

Conservative management with 3-6 months of MRI surveillance is done in non-functional adrenal tumours of < 4cm. Medical management is done in patients with bilateral disease, the commonly implemented therapeutic approach is treatment with spironolactone and antihypertensive medication.

Surgical management is done in unilateral and asymmetrical bilateral disease by unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy. A subtotal resection can be considered in the case of a typical single Conn’s adenoma. However, it is not superior to unilateral adrenalectomy.

Other options:

Option A: Spironolactone on a lifelong basis is indicated in bilateral adrenal hyperplasia or in unilateral adrenal adenoma if surgery is contraindicated. Spironolactone is a competitive inhibitor of the mineralocorticoid receptor in the late distal tubule and collecting duct of the kidneys. It causes a decrease in sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal tubule. As a result, spironolactone promotes sodium diuresis but maintains body potassium levels.

Option C: ACTH stimulation test is used to diagnose adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease), not primary hyperaldosteronism. ACTH stimulation test or cosyntropin test involves the administration of an exogenous, synthetic peptide that has an activity similar to ACTH on the adrenal glands. Serum cortisol levels are measured prior to, and after the administration of the synthetic peptide. Cortisol levels lower than the cut-off value indicate a failure of the adrenal glands to increase the production of cortisol in response to synthetic ACTH, thus confirming the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency.

Option D: Dexamethasone suppression test used for Cushing’s syndrome. The high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is used in patients with confirmed Cushing syndrome. It helps to differentiate between Cushing's disease (i.e. a pituitary cause) and ectopic ACTH production.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old female patient presents with progressive limb weakness for the past 1 year. On examination, muscle fasciculations and hypertonia are noted, and the sensory system is intact. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis

The above clinical scenario of a 38-year-old female with progressive limb weakness for the past 1 year, and signs of both UMN lesion (hypertonia LMN lesion (fasciculations) with intact sensory system is the hallmark of ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis).

The pathologic hallmark of ALS is the death of the affected lower motor neurons (LMN) consisting of the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord and their homologs in the brainstem, upper motor neurons (UMN) consisting of the corticospinal tract and corticobulbar tract originating in the motor cortex. The hereditary forms of ALS have mutations in the genes encoding for superoxide dismutase (SOD 1) present on chromosome 21. Clinically, the patient presents with :

* LMN findings: fasciculations, muscle cramps, asymmetric distal weakness, atrophy, and bulbar palsy.

* UMN findings: spasticity, increased reflexes, flexor spasms, and pseudobulbar palsy.

* Pseudobulbar effect: degeneration of corticobulbar projections manifested as inappropriate laughing, crying, or yawning, which is often mood incongruent or may be triggered by stimuli that would not have elicited such a response.

Interestingly, even during the late stages, sensory, bowel, and bladder, ocular motility, and cognitive functions are preserved.

Other options:

Option A: Becker muscular dystrophy leads to abnormal dystrophin formation, whereas the dystrophin gene mutation in DMD leads to dystrophin deficiency, usually present in childhood with proximal muscle weakness and LMN signs, not UMN signs.

Option B: Multifocal motor neuropathy mimics LMN lesions, but it never produces UMN signs, often presenting with nerve conduction blocks.

Option C: Spinal muscular atrophy is a degenerative disorder that mainly affects the spine and produces purely LMN symptoms.

* Inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (GBS and CIDP)

With asymmetric Weakness

* Compressive mononeuropathy, plexopathy, or radiculopathy

* Polyradiculopathy or plexopathy due to diabetes mellitus

* Cryptogenic or idiopathic sensory polyneuropathy (CSPN)

* Meningeal carcinomatosis or lymphomatosis

* Hereditary plexopathy (HNPP, HNA)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with persistent hypercalcemia for the past 1.5 years. His parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels are within the normal range. What is the most likely underlying cause? PTH - parathormone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sarcoidosis

The given clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of sarcoidosis.

In sarcoidosis, granulomas increase vitamin D activation, causing chronic hypercalcemia while PTH remains normal. Hypercalcemia may be seen, due to increased synthesis of calcitriol – 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D, by alveolar macrophages. More commonly, there may be hypercalciuria, which can lead to nephrocalcinosis.

Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease that most commonly presents as cough, dyspnea, dry eyes, and usually has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Lesions of the eyes and skin are also very common in these patients. It is seen more in middle-aged women than in men.

Sarcoidosis results from an increase in CD4+ T-cells (increased CD4+:CD8+ ratio). As a result, cytokines like IL-2, TNF, IL-8, and IFN-gamma will increase.

It presents with granulomas in multiple organs. They are classically described as non-caseating granulomas composed of epithelioid macrophages with giant cells. There is no central necrosis as there would be in tubercular granulomas. Naked granulomas are non-caseating granulomas minimally surrounded by lymphocytes. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) levels are elevated in this condition as sarcoid granulomas secrete it.

Star-shaped inclusions called asteroid bodies and laminated calcium and protein-containing bodies called Schaumann bodies are also found in the giant cells of most of these granulomas. These are not pathognomonic to sarcoidosis and can also be found in other granulomatous diseases like tuberculosis.

Other options:

Option A: Malignancy usually causes acute, severe hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH, not chronic hypercalcemia with normal PTH.

Option C: Parathyroid hyperplasia is a cause of primary hyperparathyroidism, so PTH would be elevated, not normal. It typically involves all four parathyroid glands.

Option D: CKD typically causes hypocalcemia due to phosphate retention and impaired vitamin D activation, not hypercalcemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 38 year old male presents to the OPD with complaints of excessive stress and difficulty maintaining a work life balance .On examination BP is 150/100 and FBS is 150 mg/dl. He has no significant history and is not on any medications. Physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?
options: Advise rest only, no pharmacological treatment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Start Telmisartan

The above clinical scenario of a 38-year-old male, with  BP: 150/100 and FBS is 150 mg/dl, is consistent with the diagnosis of Stage 2 Hypertension according to the AHA 2017 guidelines. The next step would then be to start Anti-Hypertensive medications like Telmisartan (Angiotensin Receptor Blocker) considering the sugar levels..

Drugs used in Hypertension: The first-line drug classes include

* Diuretics (Chlorthalidone, Indapamide): Side effects - Hypokalemia, impaired glucose, impaired lipid, increased uric acid.

* Calcium Channel Blockers (Amlodipine): Side effects - Hypotension

* ACE inhibitors (Lisinopril): Side effects: Dry cough, angioedema

* ARBs (Losartan): Generally well tolerated, with rare hyperkalemia

Diuretics are preferred for their long half-life and proven cardiovascular benefit. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are particularly useful in patients with diabetes and chronic kidney disease because of their nephroprotective properties. ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be used together, as combination therapy raises the risk of hyperkalemia without offering extra cardiovascular benefits.

Other options:

Option A: Pharmacologic treatment is indicated for stage 2 hypertension

Option B: Tirzepatide is a GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist used to treat Type 2 Diabetes.

Option C: Glucocorticoids are not indicated and may worsen hypertension.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old female presents to OPD with lethargy, weakness, and persistent low back pain. Blood investigations revealed normochromatic anemia, hypercalcemia. Serum protein electrophoresis showed an M spike. Prognosis is determined by which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serum Beta 2 microglobulin + Albumin

The clinical scenario of a 40-year-old female who presented to OPD with lethargy, weakness, and persistent low back pain, with blood investigations revealing normochromic anemia, hypercalcemia, and serum protein electrophoresis showing M spike, is consistent with the diagnosis of Multiple Myeloma (MM). Serum Beta 2 microglobulin + Albumin is used to determine the prognosis of the MM.

The International Staging System (ISS) is used to assess prognosis in patients with multiple myeloma, with serum β₂-microglobulin serving as the most important prognostic marker.

Multiple myeloma: Malignant neoplasm of plasma cells characterized by:

* Presence of monoclonal immunoglobulin or light chains in the serum and urine

* Bone destruction (lytic lesions)

* Disease of older adults, with a peak age of incidence of 65 to 70 years

Signs and symptoms

* Hypercalcemia, Pathologic fractures/lytic bone lesions, Renal failure, Anemia

* Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray

* Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin

* Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

* Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20% plasma cells (normal is < 5%)

* Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation

Evidence of end-organ damage caused by the underlying plasma cell proliferative disorder: (CRAB features)

* Hypercalcemia: Serum calcium level >1 mg/dL higher than the upper limit of normal or >11 mg/dL

* Renal insufficiency: Creatinine clearance <40 mL/min or serum creatinine >2 mg/dL

* Anemia: Hemoglobin level of >20 g/L (2gm/dl) below the lowest limit of normal, or Hb <10 g/dL

* Bone lesions: One or more lytic lesions on bone radiographs, computed tomography (CT), or positron emission tomography (PET-CT).

Any one or more of :

* Plasma cells in the bone marrow clonally proliferated up to 60% or higher

* The ratio of serum involved to uninvolved free light chains of 100 or greater

* Greater than one focal lesion on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) that is at least >5 mm in size

Treatment includes a combination of lenalidomide/thalidomide (immunomodulatory agents), bortezomib (proteasome inhibitor), and dexamethasone.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old male with septic shock and acute kidney injury (AKI) is hemodynamically unstable. Which of the following is the most appropriate modality of dialysis in this situation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy (CRRT)

The clinical scenario describes a patient with sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (AKI), who is hemodynamically unstable. CRRT is preferred in this setting because it provides slow and continuous removal of solutes and fluids, preventing sudden fluid shifts and hypotension that can occur with intermittent hemodialysis.

It is preferred in the following cases:

* Acute renal failure complicated by hemodynamic instability or heart failure

* Severe volume overload unresponsive to diuretic therapy

* Brain edema

* Hypercatabolism state

* Acute or chronic liver failure as a renal support measure

It is an extracorporeal blood purification therapy intended to substitute for impaired renal function over an extended period of time, aimed at being applied for 24 hours a day. There is no rapid shift of volume and osmolarity with this process as in intermittent hemodialysis. CRRT can utilize convective clearance (continuous venovenous hemofiltration [CVVH]) and diffusive clearance (continuous venovenous hemodialysis [CVVHD]), which offer more stable hemodynamics and continuous solute removal.

Other options:

Option A: IHD, not preferred due to rapid fluid and solute shifts causing hemodynamic instability in critically ill patients.

Option B: EDD is a more frequent(less than <12h) version of IHD and may worsen the hypotension.

Option D: PD is rarely used for AKI in adults and, when hemodialysis is not readily available.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old alcoholic patient with hypertension presents with dizziness, palpitations, and syncopal attacks. ECG shows irregularly irregular rhythm with no visible P waves, and JVP was measured. Which of the following changes is seen on the JVP waveform? JVP- Jugular Venous Pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Absent A wave

The above clinical scenario of a 55-year-old male alcoholic patient with hypertension develops dizziness and palpitations, syncopal attacks, with an ECG showing irregular rhythm with no visible P waves where seen is consistent with the diagnosis of atrial fibrillation, which on the JVP waveform presents as an absent A wave, which corresponds to atrial contraction.

Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained arrhythmia. There is rapid and irregular atrial activation, which is transmitted through the atrioventricular node. The conducted ventricular rate is usually rapid and irregularly irregular. It can vary from 110-160 beats/minute. A pulse deficit is an important clinical finding associated with the condition. This arises due to preload reduction.

Symptoms include palpitations, fatigue, presyncope, and dyspnea. An ECG shows the absence of P waves.

In acute atrial fibrillation with hemodynamic instability, electrical or chemical cardioversion is the first step. The latter is done by intravenous administration of class III antiarrhythmic - ibutilide. In a stable patient, ventricular rate control is the primary aim. This is done by intravenous or oral administration of beta-blockers. Calcium channel blockers such as verapamil and diltiazem can also be used. Another option is to evaluate the presence of a thrombus in the left atrial appendage. This can be done either by transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) or high-resolution CT.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 58-year-old male undergoing chemotherapy for lymphoma, who also has chronic kidney disease (CKD), presents with fatigue, pallor, and exertional breathlessness. Laboratory tests show normocytic normochromic anemia with low hemoglobin and low reticulocyte count. What is the drug of choice for treating his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Darbepoeitin alfa

In the above clinical scenario of a 58-year-old male who has anemia of chronic disease (normocytic normochromic anemia) with low hemoglobin and low retic count, the drug of choice for this condition would be Erythropoiesis Stimulating Agents (ESA) like Darbepoeitin alfa. It is a long-acting ESA that acts on the bone marrow to increase erythropoiesis.

It can lead to a sudden increase in haematocrit, blood viscosity, and peripheral vascular resistance. These can lead to hypertensive episodes, serious thromboembolic events, and occasionally seizures.

Human recombinant erythropoietin, eg, darbepoetin, is the best treatment for anemia in CKD (chronic kidney disease) patients. The anemia of CKD is primarily due to decreased erythropoietin production. Hence, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs, eg, epoetin and darbepoetin) become the mainstay of treatment in anemia of CKD.

However, iron stores must be adequate to ensure a response to ESAs. Since iron deficiency is common in CKD patients, iron therapy is a crucial initial step in their management.

Treatment options for the management of anemia in CKD:

* Recombinant human ESA

* Iron supplementation: Oral preferred, IV given only if GI intolerance to oral therapy.

* Vitamin B12 and folate supplementation

* Blood transfusion: Indicated only in severe anemia and failure to respond to EPO therapy.

Other options:

Option B:  Filgastrim is a granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and is used in chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression in non-myeloid malignancies to increase leukocyte levels.

Option C: Oprelvekin is an IL-11 analog that stimulates megakaryocyte maturation and increases platelet levels.

Option D: Parenteral iron therapy can be used in conjunction with darbepoetin for the treatment of anaemia due to CKD, but it is not the primary choice.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman with metastatic cancer reports moderate bone pain despite taking paracetamol and ibuprofen regularly. What is the next appropriate step according to the WHO analgesic ladder for chronic pain in adults?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Start tramadol and continue NSAIDs

According to the WHO analgesic ladder for chronic pain, the next step would be to start tramadol (mild opioid) and continue the non-opioids.

WHO has developed a 3-step ladder for chronic/cancer pain relief in adults.

The 3 main principles are as follows:

* By the clock: Drugs should be given “by the clock” or “around the clock” rather than “on-demand”.

* By the mouth: The oral route is preferred. If not feasible, the least invasive route should be considered.

* By the ladder: Drugs are given in the following order: Non-opioids → Mild opioids → Strong opioids. Adjuvants are added at any stage of the WHO ladder to relieve anxiety.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 7 year old child is brought to the clinic with complaints of fatigue and poor concentration. The mother reports that the child has been eating non-food items such as soil and paint chips for the past few months. A peripheral blood smear image shows microcytic, hypochromatic red blood cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Iron deficiency anemia

The above clinical scenario of a child with fatigue, poor concentration, and a history of pica (eating soil and paint chips) presents with a peripheral smear showing small RBC with increased central pallor with no basophilic stippling( helps rule out lead poisoning) demonstrates classical features of Iron deficiency anemia(IDA).

The causes of IDA can be inadequate diet, impaired reabsorption, increased requirement, and increased blood loss.

The manifestations of IDA depend upon the underlying cause. In general, IDA presents with koilonychia, alopecia, atrophic changes in the tongue, gastric mucosa, malabsorption and pica (craving for consumption of non-edible materials)

Peripheral smears show small and pale red cells typically described as microcytic (reduced MCV) and hypochromic (enlarged zone of central pallor). Poikilocytosis can be seen in the form of elongated red cells, known as pencil cells. Target cells can be found in cases of severe IDA.

Laboratory findings of IDA are:

* Reduced hemoglobin and hematocrit values. hypochromia, microcytosis, and poikilocytosis.

* Serum iron and ferritin levels are low.

* The total plasma iron-binding capacity, which reflects the elevated transferrin level, is high.

* Low serum iron with increased iron-binding capacity results in a reduction of transferrin saturation to below 15%.

* RBC protoporphyrin levels are increased.

* Bone marrow reveals a mild to moderate increase in erythroid progenitors. The absence of stainable iron in macrophages is a diagnostically significant finding

Option A: In Vitamin B12 deficiency, patients usually present with larger than normal RBC, no history of Pica, hypersegmented neutrophils (image below) and Macrocytes on PBS.

Option B: Thalassemia Major generally presents in infancy, with Microcytic hypochromic anemia as well, requiring multiple blood transfusions, it is a hereditary hemoglobinopathy resulting from deficient synthesis of one or more globin chains. Differentiating IDA and Thalassemia: Both conditions present with microcytosis and anisocytosis, with the Mentzer index being less than 13 (MCV/RBC).

Option C: Lead poisoning causes dry throat, burning abdominal pain, peripheral circulatory collapse, insomnia, paraesthesias, depression, coma, and death. Cerebellar ataxia is common in children with acute lead poisoning. A screening test for lead poisoning is the presence of porphyrinuria, mainly due to coproporphyrin III. Peripheral smear shows basophilic stippling. A Burtonian line may be visible on the gums.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A female patient complains of chest pain after waking up in the morning. Pain is more prevalent in the winter months. Which of the following best describes this patient?
options: Subendocardial ischemia due to increased demand of myocardium
Increased sympathomimetic drive in morning hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ach-induced coronary vasoconstriction

The above clinical scenario of a female patient with chest pain in the morning, worse in winter months, is consistent with the diagnosis of Prinzmetal angina. Prinzmetal angina occurs as a result of an abnormal response, causing Ach-induced coronary vasoconstriction. It may result in transient transmural ischemia. This type of angina is commonly seen in women under 50 years of age and is precipitated by smoking and cocaine use.

Prinzmetal angina occurs as a result of vasospasm of the epicardial coronary artery. It may result in transient transmural ischemia. The cause of this spasm is poorly understood and is suspected to be due to hypercontractility of cardiac smooth muscles. This type of angina is commonly seen in women under 50 years of age and is precipitated by smoking and cocaine use.

The vasospasm leads to transmural ischemia, which is seen on the ECG as transient ST-segment elevation, although there is no atherosclerosis present on angiography.

Depolarization of cardiac myocytes depends primarily on the influx of Ca2+ ions. Ca 2+ antagonists relax arterial smooth muscle, thereby decreasing arterial resistance, blood pressure, and cardiac afterload. Hence, calcium channel blockers such as long-acting nifedipine and amlodipine are employed along with nitrates to alleviate vasospasm.

Treatment: Nitrates and Calcium Channel blockers are used in Prinzmetal angina for endothelium-independent coronary vasodilatation. Beta-blockers are contraindicated in Prinzmetal angina.

Other options:

Option A: Fixed plaque obstruction describes Stable angina, which presents as effort-induced, relieved by rest, type of pain.

Option C: Subendocardial ischemia due to increased demand of the myocardium is the mechanism of unstable angina, which presents as pain that does not subside with rest.

Option D: Increased sympathomimetic drive in morning hours is not the key feature of Prinzmetal angina.

Pearl PF1920: Indications for Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG)

Class I indications for CABG from the American College of Cardiology(ACC) and American Heart Association(AHA).

* Left main disease

* Three-vessel disease with or without proximal LAD disease

* Two vessel disease with proximal LAD disease

* Survivors of sudden cardiac death with presumed ischemia-mediated VT

Other indications for CABG include the following:

* Disabling angina

* Ongoing ischemia in the setting of a non–ST-segment elevation (MI) that is unresponsive to medical therapy

* Poor LV function but with viable, nonfunctioning myocardium above the anatomic defect that can be revascularized

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient after myocardial infarction, develops a broad QRS complex tachycardia. His BP is 120/70 mm Hg. ECG is given below. What is the best management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amiodarone IV

The patient here complaining of chest pain, and palpitations and has ECG changes showing wide QRS complex tachycardia with absent p waves is likely to have acute ventricular tachycardia. Since the patient is stable and has an underlying coronary artery disease the drug of choice is intravenous amiodarone. Intravenous amiodarone is recommended by the AHA/ACC 2015 guidelines for the treatment of hemodynamically stable ventricular tachycardia.

Ventricular tachycardias can be defined as three or more pre-ventricular contractions at a rate >100/minute.

ECG changes include wide QRS complexes, absence of P waves, and ventriculoatrial dissociation. It can be broadly classified as sustained VT or non-sustained VT. Nonsustained VT has QRS complexes lasting <30 seconds while sustained VT lasts for >30 seconds. In monomorphic VT, all QRS complexes look the same. Polymorphic VT has QRS complexes varying in shape or direction in the same lead.

Most monomorphic VT have an underlying cardiac disease. Symptoms of ventricular tachycardia include palpitations, syncope, and shortness of breath.

In a hemodynamically stable patient, amiodarone, procainamide, and lidocaine can be used to treat the condition. In the presence of heart disease, intravenous amiodarone is the drug of choice. In hemodynamically unstable patients, electrical cardioversion is done. Further management depends on the underlying heart condition and frequency of VT. Frequent episodes warrant the use of antiarrhythmics or catheter ablation.

Torsades de Pointes is a type of polymorphic VT occurring with QT prolongation. It can progress to ventricular fibrillation which is treated with defibrillation. Recurrent episodes can be managed with intravenous magnesium sulfate.

Other causes of wide QRS complexes include supraventricular tachycardias with bundle branch block and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

Pearl PF1836: ECG patterns of various ventricular arrhythmias

Ventricular tachycardia

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with QTc prolongation- Torsades de pointes

Ventricular flutter

Ventricular fibrillation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient following a crush injury is passing red color urine due to myoglobinuria. Which of the following will most likely be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hyperkalemia

In this clinical scenario, a patient with a crush injury develops red-colored urine due to myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis. This process results in the release of intracellular potassium, leading to hyperkalemia, and also contributes indirectly to the development of acute kidney injury (AKI).

Rhabdomyolysis is defined as a pathological condition of skeletal muscle cell damage leading to the release of toxic intracellular material into the blood circulation. The causes of rhabdomyolysis include:

* Crush injury

* Hypothyroidism (precipitated by exertion, alcohol, infection)

* Electric shock

* Prolonged seizures

* Malignant hyperthermia

* Exertion

* Drugs like fibrates, statins

* Polymyositis / Dermatomyositis

* McArdle's disease (GSD-5) causes recurrent rhabdomyolysis.

Rhabdomyolysis is a cause of AKI due to myoglobin release from injured muscle due to excessive strenuous exercise, heat stroke, or traumatic crush injuries. Pathogenic factors for AKI due to endogenous toxins include intrarenal vasoconstriction, direct proximal tubular toxicity, and mechanical obstruction of the distal nephron lumen. Patients often present with muscle pain and high-colored urine(myoglobinuria). The following features are also seen:

* High serum creatinine kinase (> 5 times normal)

* High serum myoglobin

* High serum LDH

* Hyperkalemia

* Hypermagnesemia

* Hyperphosphatemia

* Hypocalcemia

* Hyperuricemia

* Once AKI develops, high serum creatinine and urea

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient in the ICU underwent a failed attempt at subclavian catheterization. Following the procedure, the patient developed respiratory distress and unilateral chest retraction. On examination, BP was low and pulse rate was elevated, with decreased breath sounds. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pneumothorax

The above clinical scenario of an ICU patient following a failed attempt of subclavian catheterization, developed respiratory distress and retraction, with low blood pressure, elevated pulse, and decreased breath sounds, is characteristic of one of the complications of the procedure, pneumothorax.

A tension pneumothorax develops when a ‘one-way valve’ air leak occurs either from the lung or through the chest wall. Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any means of escape, completely collapsing and then compressing the afected lung. Common causes of tension pneumothorax are penetrating chest trauma, blunt chest trauma with a parenchymal lung injury and air leak that did not spontaneously close, iatrogenic lung injury (e.g. due to central venepuncture) and mechanical positive-pressure ventilation.

Complications of central vein catheterization are:

* Pneumothorax is more common in subclavian vein catheterization as a result of injury to the underlying pleura.

* Arterial puncture is the most common mechanical complication.

* Cardiac tamponade is the most important life-threatening complication. It occurs as a result of the puncture of the intrapericardial superior vena cava, right atrium, or right ventricle.

* Chylothorax can occur particularly in left subclavian vein catheterization. But it is not the most common.

* Injury to the associated nerves, like brachial plexus, stellate ganglion, phrenic nerve, or vocal cords.

* Thromboembolism- can lead to venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. It is more common with femoral veins.

* Infections- the most common late complication.

A central venous catheter (CVC) is an indwelling device inserted into a large, central vein and advanced until the terminal lumen resides within the inferior vena cava, superior vena cava, or right atrium. It is indicated for the administration of vasopressors, medications, and total parenteral nutrition. It is also useful in procedures like dialysis, plasmapheresis, and interventions such as transvenous pacemaker placement.

Cannulation can be done at various sites, namely the internal jugular, common femoral, and subclavian veins.

The image below shows central venous catheterization:

Other options:

Option B: Displacement of the endotracheal tube typically presents with hypoxia and inadequate ventilation, not chest retraction and hypotension.

Option C: Air embolism occurs when air bubbles enter the pulmonary circulation and are absorbed in large quantities. Severe hypotension and hypoxemia are seen in this condition. The patient is then placed in Trendelenburg's left lateral decubitus position.

Option D: Dislodgement of the endotracheal tube would typically affect bilateral lungs, not just unilateral, leading to difficult ventilation and global hypoxia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with central chest pain, palpitations, and tachycardia. The following changes were seen in the ECG. What is the most likely heart condition? MI - Myocardial infarction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterolateral wall MI

The above clinical scenario of a patient presenting with central chest pain, palpitations, and tachycardia, and ECG showing convex type of ST elevation in lead 1, aVL, V2-6 with reciprocal changes (ST depression) in Lead 2, 3, aVF is consistent with Anterolateral wall MI.

MI occurs when there is severe cardiac muscle ischemia. Severe, acute ischemia causes a change in the membrane potential which shortens the duration of the action potential. This creates a voltage gradient between the normal myocardium and ischemic myocardium causing a flow of current between the two.  This altered flow of current manifests as changes in the ST segment, which represents ventricle repolarization. The change in the ST segment depends on the part of the myocardium involved.

The following protocol must be followed in the management of patients with acute coronary syndrome:

* Stabilization of airway, breathing, and circulation.

* Administration of O2

* Give aspirin 325 mg and clopidogrel

* History and examination, assess cardiac biomarkers.

* Give up to three sublingual nitroglycerin tablets. Add IV nitroglycerin for the persistence of symptoms.

* Treat left heart failure if present with an afterload-reducing agent or loop diuretic.

* Give beta blockers if there are no features of heart failure.

* Give morphine for the persistence of anxiety and discomfort related to MI.

In patients with STEMI, Reperfusion with Percutaneous coronary intervention(PCI) or fibrinolysis (if PCI is unavailable within 120 min). This is followed by antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy.

In patients with NSTEMI, antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is indicated.

Other options:

Option A: Acute pericarditis is an inflammation of the pericardium, also characterized by retrosternal chest pain that is aggravated by deep inspiration and a supine position and relieved by sitting and leaning forward. On auscultation, a pericardial friction rub is heard. On ECG, there is widespread concave type of elevation of the ST segments with depression of the PR segment.

Option C: Anterior Wall MI presents as ST elevation in lead V1-V4.

Option D: Inferior Wall MI presents as ST elevation in lead 2, 3, aVF with characteristic symptoms of Bradycardia and hypotension.

Pearl PF0365: Localisation of MI based on ST elevations in different leads

Extensive anterior - I, aVL, V1-V6

Lateral - I, aVL

Inferior - II, III, aVF

Anteroseptal - V1-V4

Anterolateral - I, aVL, V3-V6

Posterior - ST depression and tall R in V1-V4

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with palpitations, headache, and sweating. His BP is 180/100 mmHg. 24-hour urinary metanephrine values are elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pheochromocytoma

The above clinical scenario of palpitations, headache, and sweating, with BP is 180/100 mmHg, 24-hour urinary metanephrine values are elevated, is consistent with the diagnosis of Pheochromocytoma.

It is a catecholamine-secreting tumor derived from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.It can be sporadic or hereditary. Hereditary pheochromocytoma occurs in association with syndromes such as MEN 2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2), familial paraganglioma syndrome, Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome, and neurofibromatosis (NF) type 1.

Clinical features:

It most commonly presents as a classic triad of intermittent headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating along with hypertension. The patient can also present with anxiety, panic attacks, nausea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and weakness. Symptoms may be precipitated by surgery, pregnancy, position changes, exercise, and medications such as metoclopramide and tricyclic antidepressants.

Investigations:

* Biochemical screening test—measurement of urinary and plasma levels of catecholamines and metanephrines.

* MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor. It is preferred over a CT scan, as the contrast used in CT scans can precipitate paroxysms.

* Other imaging modalities like MIBG scintigraphy and DOPA- or FDG-PET scans are used in identifying the primary tumor as well as the extra-adrenal tumors and metastases.

Surgical resection of the tumor is the definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma. Preoperatively, hypertension is managed initially with alpha-blockers followed by beta-blockers.

Other options:

Option B: Carcinoid Tumor usually presents with flushing, diarrhea, wheezing, and elevated 5-HIAA (not metanephrines).

Option C: Neuroblastoma usually occurs in children, presents with abdominal mass with hypotonia, ataxia, behavioral symptoms and elevated urinary VMA/HVA, not metanephrines.

Option D: Adrenocortical Tumor secretes cortisol/aldosterone/androgens, not catecholamines.

Pearl PF1539: Pheochromocytoma

Features:

* When pheochromocytoma is associated with the MEN syndrome it is rarely malignant.

* Phaeochromocytomas are greyish-pink on the cut surface and are usually highly vascularised.

* Zellbalen cells and nuclei with salt and pepper chromatin are seen.

Factors indicating more chances of malignancy:

* An increased PASS (phaeochromocytoma of the adrenal gland scale score)

* High number of Ki-67-positive cells

* Vascular invasion or a breached capsule

Diagnosis:

* Urinary catecholamine and VMA level assay are most sensitive screening test.

* MRI is the IOC.

* Biopsy and CT Contrast scan are contraindicated in order to avoid Hypertensive crisis.

Treatment:

* Adrenalectomy is preferred TOC.

* Size<5 cm -  Laparoscopic adrenalectomy

* Preop Alpha blockers should be given

* Mitotane should be started as adjuvant or palliative treatment

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with progressive shortness of breath for the last 6 months, accompanied by dry cough. Auscultation reveals bilateral basal end-inspiratory crepitations. There is no history of fever, joint pain, or occupational exposure. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

Progressive dyspnea with dry cough, basal end-inspiratory crepitations, and absence of systemic or occupational features is classic for IPF (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis).

Interstitial lung diseases are characterized by inflammation and fibrosis involving the lung parenchyma. Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive, and ultimately fatal lung disease characterized by fibrosis and scarring of lung tissue, leading to declining lung function and respiratory failure. Clinical features include progressive dyspnoea more common with exertion, dry cough, and basal end-inspiratory crackles or rales on auscultation. Digital clubbing is seen.

Pulmonary function tests will show a restrictive deficit and reduction of TLC, FEV1, and FVC. There is also a reduction in DLCO and may be the first finding seen in PFT. IPF is the most common interstitial lung disease occurring due to an unknown cause. HRCT shows predominant subpleural and basal involvement, in the form of reticulation, honeycombing, and traction bronchiectasis. This is known as the usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern. Note that ground glass opacities are absent in this pattern.

Pirfenidone and Nintedanib slow disease progression by reducing fibrosis. Management is oxygen therapy, pulmonary rehabilitation, and symptom management (e.g., antitussives for cough).

Other options:

Option A: Cor-pulmonale is a complication of chronic lung disease that presents with signs of right heart failure (edema, JVP, hepatomegaly), not with progressive dry cough and basal crepitations.

Option B: Sarcoidosis usually presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, systemic features (like uveitis, skin lesions, arthritis), and not with basal crepitations as in IPF.

Option D: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is linked to a clear history of occupational or environmental antigen exposure (like birds, molds, farming), which is absent in this case. Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis is a lung disease caused by inhaling various antigens, leading to inflammation in the alveoli and small airways. It presents in acute, subacute, and chronic forms, with the acute form characterized by fever, chills, malaise, dyspnea, and cough. Diagnosis requires a thorough patient history, including occupational exposure assessment.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with aplastic anemia undergoes bone marrow transplantation. Within 2 weeks, he presents with complaints of bloody diarrhea. Upon further examination, he was found to have jaundice and blistering rashes on the skin. What is the possible mechanism behind the patient's current clinical picture?
options: Immune cells of the host attacking transplanted tissue
Preformed antibodies of the host attacking transplanted tissue
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transplanted cells attacking host tissues

The given scenario is suggestive of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). The possible mechanism behind the patient's current clinical picture is transplanted cells attacking host tissues.

Transfusion of irradiated RBCs prevents the incidence of GVHD associated with the transfusion.

GVHD occurs when immunologically competent cells or their precursors are transplanted into immunologically compromised recipients. The transferred cells recognize the alloantigens in the host and attack host tissues. It is seen most commonly during hematopoietic stem cell transplantation but may also occur following the transplantation of solid organs.

GVHD may be of two types: acute and chronic.

Acute GVHD occurs within days to weeks after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. It mainly involves the immune system and the epithelia of the skin (in the form of generalized rash), liver (in the form of jaundice), and intestines (in the form of bloody diarrhea). But the affected tissues are not heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes.

Chronic GVHD may follow acute GVHD or may occur insidiously. These patients have extensive skin damage, with the destruction of skin appendages and fibrosis of the dermis, resembling systemic sclerosis. Cholestatic jaundice and esophageal strictures are also common. There will be involution of the thymus and depletion of lymphocytes in the lymph nodes. There will also be recurrent bouts of life-threatening infections. Some may even develop autoimmunity, owing to the grafted CD4+ helper T cells reacting with host B cells and stimulating them, which may result in autoantibody production.

Depletion of donor T cells by irradiation before transfusion can eliminate the occurrence of GVHD. But irradiation also has its adverse effects such as tumor recurrence in leukemic patients, increased incidence of graft failures, and EBV-related B-cell lymphoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with renal disease undergoes a biopsy. On Congo red staining, the deposits show apple-green birefringence under polarized light. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Amyloidosis

The given clinical case of renal biopsy showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light on congo red staining is suggestive of amyloidosis

Amyloidosis refers to extracellular deposits of fibrillar proteins. Abnormal fibrils are produced by the aggregation of misfolded proteins. The fibrillar deposits bind a wide variety of proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans, including heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate, and plasma proteins, notably serum amyloid P component (SAP). Amyloid appears as an amorphous, eosinophilic, hyaline, extracellular substance.

It could be classified as systemic, localized, and hereditary amyloidosis. Microscopically, all types of amyloid deposits are made up of continuous, nonbranching fibrils. A characteristic cross-β-pleated sheet conformation is visualized on X-ray crystallography and infrared spectroscopy.

The stain used for amyloid deposits is congo red staining, which imparts pink to red color to the amyloid under ordinary light and apple-green birefringence under polarised microscopy.

The image shows a congo-red stained biopsy specimen with the following:

(A) Focal positive staining (orange-red) of amorphous extracellular material

(B) Apple-green birefringence under polarized light

The next best step is to determine the type of precursor protein by immunohistochemistry, immunoelectron microscopy, or extraction and biochemical analysis using mass spectrometry.

Other options:

Option A: In Minimal change disease, Biopsy findings include the following:

* Light microscopy- glomeruli appear normal (hence called "minimal change")

* Immunofluorescence studies- no Ig or complement deposits

* Electron microscopy- diffuse effacement of foot processes of visceral epithelial cells/podocytes

Option B: Diabetic nephropathy shows no Congo red positivity.

Option D: Sarcoidosis renal lesions are Congo red–negative for amyloid deposition.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A pregnant female presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Serum prolactin is elevated. MRI shows pituitary adenoma. What is the best management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bromocriptine

The clinical vignette points to a diagnosis of prolactinoma in a pregnant female, and the best drug for managing this condition is bromocriptine.

Pituitary adenomas are benign tumors that arise from hormone-producing cells in the pituitary gland, with lactotrope cell tumors (prolactinomas) being the most common. These tumors can sometimes secrete multiple hormones, such as prolactin, growth hormone, or ACTH.

Tumors <1 cm in diameter and no regional invasion are known as microadenomas. It is more commonly seen in women. Tumors > 1 cm in size are known as macroadenomas. It can be locally invasive. Prolactin levels >200 μg/L are suggestive of prolactinomas.

Women present with features such as amenorrhea, infertility, and galactorrhea. Visual field defects can also be seen. Symptoms in males include impotence, infertility, and loss of libido. An MRI is recommended in all patients who present with hyperprolactinemia.

Microadenomas can be managed with regular monitoring of prolactin levels and MRI scans, if fertility is not a requisite. Oral dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine and cabergoline are used for medical management.

Management of Pituitary Adenoma:

* Asymptomatic microadenoma: The approach is "wait and watch." Repeat an MRI after 6 months. Treatment is initiated if the size increases > 1 cm to become a macroadenoma.

* Symptomatic microadenoma or macroadenoma: The first line of treatment is medical management with dopamine agonists. The drug of choice is cabergoline, administered in weekly doses. An MRI should be repeated after 6 months to assess tumor size. If there is no reduction, the dose can be increased to a maximum of 2 mg/week. Bromocriptine is preferred for pregnant patients.

* Surgical intervention is indicated if there is resistance to medical management (dopamine agonists), unstable pituitary apoplexy, or in pregnancy when there is no response to short-term medical therapy. In these cases, adenoma debulking surgery is performed.

* Radiotherapy: Gamma knife stereotactic radiotherapy is reserved for patients with aggressive prolactinomas that do not respond to the maximum tolerated dose of dopamine agonists and/or surgery.

Other options:

Option A: Cabergoline is more potent dopamine agonist and better tolerated than bromocriptine in non-pregnant patients. However, in pregnancy, bromocriptine is preferred because it has the largest and longest safety data for maternal and fetal outcomes.

Option C: Transsphenoidal surgery  is reserved only for patients who do not respond to medical therapy or if there is acute visual compromise from tumor compression. It is not the first-line treatment in a stable pregnant patient.

Option D: Goserelin is a GnRH agonist used for the treatment of endometriosis, dysfunctional uterine bleeding, and prostate and breast cancer, not in prolactinomas.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of bony deformities. Physical examination revealed wrist widening, cupping. He is asymptomatic otherwise. Laboratory investigation revealed low plasma Vitamin D and serum ALP levels of 1500. What will be the most appropriate immediate management for this boy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin D supplementation

The above clinical scenario of an asymptomatic 8-year-old boy with wrist widening and cupping, with low plasma vitamin D on laboratory investigation, is consistent with Rickets. Treatment of nutritional Rickets includes Vitamin D Supplementation.

Radiograph of wrist showing cupping and fraying is given below

Rickets occurs due to a nutritional deficiency in vitamin D. A Decrease in vitamin D levels leads to decreased calcium and phosphate due to reduced absorption. The decreased calcium stimulates increased parathyroid hormone(PTH) production. ALP level is increased as it is involved in bone mineralization.

Clinical features of rickets include:

* General features include malnourishment, abdominal distension, proximal muscle weakness, etc.

* Head: Softening of the skull bones, called craniotabes, and delayed closure of fontanelles.

* Chest: Rachitic rosary, i.e., widening of the costochondral junctions that give the feeling of rosary beads on palpation. Harrison's groove, a horizontal groove in the lower chest, may appear from the inward pull of the softened ribs by the diaphragm during respiration.

* Vertebral column abnormalities like scoliosis, kyphosis, and lordosis

* In the distal extremities, widening of the wrists and ankles, varus/ valgus deformities, windswept deformity (valgus on the side and varus on the contralateral side), and anterior tibial bowing.

Metabolic bone disorders due to nutritional deficiencies include:

* Vitamin D deficiency leads to Rickets in children

* Osteomalacia- in adults

Treatment:

Vitamin D–dependent rickets is treated long-term with active vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D or calcitriol). The typical starting dose ranges from 0.25 to 2 µg/day, which is gradually reduced after clinical and radiological healing of rickets. During early treatment, ensuring adequate calcium intake is essential to support proper bone mineralization and prevent hypocalcemia.

Option D: Vitamin C supplementation is recommended for children to prevent Scurvy.

Pearl PF2091: Important Clinical Features of Rickets

Pearl PF1660: Radiological features of rickets

Radiological features of rickets:

* Loss of provisional zone of calcification: earliest radiological finding of rickets.

* Delayed appearance of the epiphysis

* Widening of growth plate: normal width of growth is 2-4mm. It is increased in cases of rickets due to excessive accumulation of uncalcified osteoid at the growth plate.

* Cupping of metaphysis: normally metaphysis meets epiphysis as a smooth line of sclerosis. But in rickets the line is absent and the metaphyseal ends appear irregular and the cartilage accumulating in the growth plate creates a depression in the metaphysis causing cupping.

* Fraying: indistinct margins of the metaphysis

* Bowing of diaphysis, with thinning of cortices

* In healing rickets, zone of calcification becomes denser.

The above features are prominent at the growth plates where growth is greatest:

* Knee: distal femur, proximal tibia

* Wrist: especially the ulna

* Anterior rib ends: rachitic rosary

The below image shows bowing of legs in rickets.

Pearl PF2079: Radiological Features of Scurvy

Radiological features of scurvy:

* Generalised osteopenia

* Pencil-point cortex: Cortical thinning

* Periosteal reaction due to subperiosteal hemorrhage

* Scorbutic rosary: Expansion of the costochondral junctions

* Hemarthrosis

* Wimberger ring: Circular, opaque radiological shadow surrounding epiphyseal centers of ossification, which may result from bleeding

* Frenkel line: Dense zone of provisional calcification

* Trummerfeld zone: Lucent metaphyseal band underlying Frankel line

* Pelken spur: Metaphyseal spurs which result in cupping of the metaphysis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly male patient presents with a cough and weight loss for the last 3 months. Biopsy of the lung mass revealed tumor cells that are positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin. Which of the following paraneoplastic syndromes will most likely occur in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. SIADH

The above clinical scenario of an elderly male with cough and weight loss, and chromogranin, synaptophysin positive tumor cells is most consistent with small cell cancer of the lungs. Paraneoplastic syndrome most commonly associated with small cell cancer is SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate Anti-Diuretic Hormone Release).

Small-cell cancer is a highly aggressive cancer that metastasizes early. It is also often associated with smoking and is generally metastasized by the time it gets diagnosed.

SIADH can be associated with several different tumors, such as those of the lung, ovaries, pancreas, bladder, etc. In this condition, ectopic vasopressin is produced by the small-cell lung cancer, which is a neuroendocrine tumor. Ectopic vasopressin increases the anti-diuretic property of the kidney, decreasing renal clearance and leading to SIADH. This causes increased free water retention, leading to hyponatremia.

It is a syndrome characterized by euvolemic hyponatremia due to a primary defect in osmoregulation. The causes of SIADH include neoplasms of the lung, duodenum, pancreas, ovary, head trauma, infections (tuberculosis, meningitis, pneumonia), and drug overdose (vasopressin, desmopressin).

Treatment involves administration of conivaptan or tolvaptan (vasopressin receptor V2 antagonist), demeclocycline, and fluid restriction to less than 500 ml (although this can be difficult). In severe cases, correction of hyponatremia is done by administering IV fluids with hypertonic normal saline along with diuretics such as furosemide (to increase free water clearance).

Other options:

Option A: Hypercalcemia is most commonly associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the lungs due to the release of PTHrp.

Option B: Cushing syndrome is also associated with small cell carcinoma of the lungs due to ectopic ACTH release, but it's not the most common one.

Option C: Gynaecomastia is mostly associated with testicular tumors Leydig cell) or hCG-secreting tumors.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 19-year-old male, chronic smoker, presented with fever, a painful lump over his left cheek just below the ear, and difficulty in swallowing or talking. The patient also complained of mild testicular pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mumps

The clinical features of painful swelling in the parotid region (parotitis) together with testicular pain (orchitis) is most likely suggestive of mumps.

Mumps is a paramyxoviral disease, which spreads by respiratory droplets. It usually affects children. However, there has been an increasing trend in the incidence of mumps in adolescents and young adults. The disease is more serious in adults than in children.

Clinical features:

* Parotitis is the most common presentation. It is often bilateral. Other salivary glands such as submaxillary and sublingual glands may also be involved, but are less likely than parotid.

* Patients complain of earache and find it difficult to eat, swallow, or talk.

* Epididymo-orchitis is the next common presentation. The testis is painful and tender and may enlarge up to several times its normal size.

Complications of Mumps:

* Meningitis or Meningoencephalitis

* Other complications include: Arthritis, oophoritis, nephritis, pancreatitis, thyroiditis and myocarditis.

Diagnosis is made by detection of viral RNA by reverse-transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) or on serology.

Treatment: The disease is self-limiting. Analgesics and application of warm or cold compress over the parotid and testicular swellings may help relieve the symptoms.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient presents with complaints of chronic diarrhea, fatigue, and tiredness. On examination, his nail findings are shown below. Lab investigations show Hb as 8 gm%. Which of the following is the best treatment approach for this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Iron supplements

Since the patient has chronic diarrhea there is malabsorption of nutrients in this patient. He has anemia from his lab investigations and his nail findings suggest koilonychia(spooning of nails) which is a characteristic finding in iron deficiency anemia. Thus the preferred treatment for this patient is iron supplements.

Malabsorption syndrome refers to a spectrum of conditions of various etiologies that arises due to diminished absorption of one or more dietary nutrients.

Anemia may be present when there is defective absorption of iron, folate, or vitamin B12.

The majority of the patients with iron deficiency anemia present with easy fatigability, tachycardia, palpitations, and dyspnea on exertion. Severe deficiency causes skin and mucosal changes like

* smooth tongue

* brittle nails

* koilonychia- spooning of nails

* cheilosis- fissures at the corner of the mouth

* pica- craving for specific foods that are not rich in iron.

Laboratory investigation of iron deficiency anemia

The peripheral smear will show small (microcytic) and pale (hypochromic) cells with an increased area of central pallor. Pencil-shaped cells can be seen which is called poikilocytosis.

Serum iron levels- It represents the amount of circulating iron bound to transferrin. The normal range for the serum iron is 50–150 μg/dL. It is decreased in iron deficiency anemia.

Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC)- It is an indirect measure of the circulating transferrin. The normal levels are 300–360 μg/dL. The levels are increased in IDA.

Transferrin saturation- The normal levels are 25–50%. The levels are decreased in IDA.

Serum ferritin- Free iron is toxic to the body. Therefore it is bound to a protein called apoferritin to form ferritin. Adult males have serum ferritin values averaging 100 μg/L, while adult females have levels averaging 30 μg/L. The serum ferritin level is the most convenient laboratory test to estimate iron stores. It is decreased in IDA.

Evaluation of bone marrow iron stores- can be done by performing bone marrow biopsy and using the Prussian stain to stain the iron stores. It is rarely done these days due to the availability of the serum ferritin estimation tests.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old lady presents with body pain, easy fatigability and problems while standing. Neurological examination revealed loss of vibration sense and proprioception. Investigations revealed a hemoglobin level of 7 gm/dL. Which of the following should be administered for the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vit B12

The given scenario describes megaloblastic anaemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency. Vitamin B12 deficiency may lead to subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord  and the patient needs to be given Vit B12.

Megaloblastic anaemia can be due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. In vitamin B12 deficiency, serum levels of both homocysteine and methylmalonic acid are elevated whereas in folate deficiency, only homocysteine levels are elevated.

Subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord occurs due to defective myelin synthesis which leads to degeneration of the ascending and descending spinal tracts. It presents with symmetrical paraesthesia and progresses to weakness, ataxia and spasticity. It can be treated by administration of vitamin B12.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with distal leg weakness, reduced muscle stretch reflexes, with no complaints of tingling or numbness. On examination, there is atrophy of the muscles below the knee. The following clinical findings are seen and similar history is seen in elder brother. The most probable diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease

The given image shows lack of muscle, high arch of foot, and hammer-toes which, along with the other clinical features mentioned above, are suggestive of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.

Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease (CMT) is the most common type of hereditary neuropathy. CMT is a syndrome of many genetically distinct disorders.

CMT type 1

* Most common form of hereditary neuropathy

* Usually presents in the first to third decade of life with distal leg weakness, e.g., foot drop

* No numbness or tingling

* Reduced sensation to all modalities apparent on examination

* Reduced muscle stretch reflexes

* Atrophy of the muscles below the knee, leading to inverted champagne bottle legs

Diabetic neuropathy, primary amyloidosis, neuropathy associated with Sjogren’s syndrome, and rheumatoid arthritis are acquired forms of neuropathies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with fatigue. She had pallor on physical examination. Lab values are given below. Serum methyl malonyl CoA levels are normal. Which of the following should be administered as a therapy for this patient? Hemoglobin - 9.8 g/dL Platelets - 1,80,000/mm3 Leukocyte count - 7800/mm3 MCV - 106 fl
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Folic acid

This patient has megaloblastic anemia (high MCV). This could be due to various causes, commonly Vitamin B12 or folic acid deficiency. The presence of normal methyl malonyl Co-A favours folic acid deficiency. Thus folic acid has to be given as supplements.

Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is a vitamin B12-dependent enzyme. Its activity is greatly reduced in vitamin B12 deficiency, leading to an accumulation of methylmalonic acid. Whereas in folate deficiency, methylmalonic acid levels are normal. This cab be used to differentiate between megaloblastic anaemia due to folate and vitamin B12 deficiency.

There are two vitamin B12-dependent enzymes:

* Methionine synthase (Homocysteine methyltransferase): Catalyzes the conversion of homocysteine to methionine

* Methylmalonyl CoA mutase: Methylmalonyl CoA, formed as an intermediate in the catabolism of valine, isoleucine and propionyl CoA is converted to succinyl CoA

The folate cycle acts as the link between the functions of folate and vitamin B12, and a deficiency of vitamin B12 can cause a functional deficiency of folate.

Vitamin B12 acts as a cofactor of methionine synthase, an enzyme involved in the regeneration of tetrahydrofolate from methyl-tetrahydrofolate. The decreased activity of methionine synthase in vitamin B12 deficiency results in the accumulation of methyltetrahydrofolate, which cannot be used, resulting in a folate trap.

Causes of megaloblastic anaemia:-

* Cobalamin deficiency/abnormalities of cobalamin metabolism: Nutritional, Malabsorption, absence of intrinsic factor, total/ partial gastrectomy.

* Folate deficiency/ abnormalities of folate metabolism.

* Therapy with antifolate drugs e.g., methotrexate.

* Independent of cobalamin/folate deficiency:

* Acute myeloid leukaemia, myelodysplasia.

questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness for the last 1 month. His eyes are in a down and out position. On examination, Kernig’s and Brudzinski sign is positive. CSF reveals the predominance of mononuclear cells with low glucose and forms cobweb coagulum on standing. MRI shows basal exudates with meningeal enhancement. What is the therapy of choice for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Isoniazid + Rifampicin + Pyrazinamide+ Ethambutol

Given a clinical scenario, CSF findings(low glucose, a predominance of mononuclear cells and cobweb like clot formation) and the MRI findings point towards a likely diagnosis of tubercular meningitis. Antitubercular drugs like isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide+ ethambutol are used in the management of tubercular meningitis.

If a patient presents with features of meningitis or encephalitis for more than 4 weeks duration, it is known as chronic meningitis. Tubercular meningitis predominantly involves the basal portion of the brain and frequently causes cranial nerve palsies (eyes in down and out position indicating III CN palsy). MRI features include meningeal enhancement with basilar exudates.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presented to the medicine OPD with complaints of muscle weakness and blurring of vision following exertion more towards the evening.On examination, the patient had ptosis. The symptoms improved after edrophonium test.The person is likely suffering from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Myasthenia gravis

The clinical scenario along with the symptoms improving with edrophonium is suggestive of myasthenia gravis.

Muscle weakness is a common presentation in patients with myasthenia gravis and cholinergic crisis (excessive dose of anti-ChE drugs). Intravenous injection of edrophonium improves muscular weakness in a patient with myasthenia gravis and not in a case of cholinergic crisis.

Edrophonium, a short-acting anticholinesterase agent is used for diagnosing myasthenia gravis. It is also called the tensilon test.

Initially, 2 mg is administered. If improvements of symptoms do not occur within 45 seconds, an additional 8 mg can be administered. Improvement of strength unaccompanied by lingual fasciculations (generally present in non-myasthenics) is a positive test.

Myasthenia gravis

* A disease characterized by generalized muscle weakness and rapidly developing fatigue of the muscles due to auto-immune damage of the acetylcholine receptors that take place at the post-synaptic membrane.

* The symptoms fluctuate and, after a short rest, recovery follows rapidly in the early stages.

* Ptosis and failure of convergence are early and prominent features.

* A remarkable temporary improvement in the action of the muscles is obtained by injections of Prostigmin or edrophonium intravenously which lead to acetylcholine accumulation.

* The resultant increase in acetylcholine available at the receptor sites leads to an improvement in the muscular function, confirming the diagnosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 5-year-old child has flexible fingers and can even touch the back of his hand with his wrist extended. The child also demonstrates the sign shown in the image below. On auscultation, a click is heard after S1, followed by a late systolic murmur. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

The probable diagnosis of the above scenario is Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) and the image shows Gorlin’s sign which is the ability to touch the tip of the nose with the tip of the tongue. The auscultation finding is of mitral valve prolapse which is a frequent finding in patients with EDS.

The Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (EDS) is a heterogeneous group of heritable connective tissue disorders (HCTDs) characterized by joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility, and tissue fragility.

The following diagnostic criteria have been proposed by the 2017 International Classification of the Ehlers–Danlos Syndromes.

Major criteria:

* Skin hyperextensibility and atrophic scarring

* Generalized joint hypermobility (GJH)

Minor criteria:

* Easy bruising

* Soft, doughy skin

* Skin fragility (or traumatic splitting)

* Molluscoid pseudotumors

* Subcutaneous spheroids

* Hernia (or history thereof)

* Epicanthal folds

* Complications of joint hypermobility (e.g., sprains, luxation/ subluxation, pain, flexible flatfoot)

* Family history of a first-degree relative who meets clinical criteria

Minimal diagnostic criteria for classical EDS:

* Major criterion (1): skin hyperextensibility and atrophic scarring

Plus

* Either major criterion (2): GJH

* And/or: at least three minor criteria

Marfan's Syndrome can have joint hypermobility but it is mainly characterised by skeletal abnormalities, including tall stature, long limbs, and arachnodactyly (long, slender fingers).
Given the presence of Gorlin's sign, along with other features like joint hypermobility, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is the probable diagnosis here.
