questions.text: 52-year-old man comes to the OPD for a painless mass in his right groin. He noticed the mass several weeks ago, and it has slowly enlarged. On examination, several enlarged, hard lymph nodes are palpated in the right inguinal area inferior to the inguinal ligament. An excisional biopsy is performed, and histopathology shows malignant cells. The malignant cells found in this patient most likely originated from which of the following sites?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Orifice of the anal canal

Lymphatic drainage determines the pattern of metastasis to regional lymph nodes. Structures located below the pectinate line of the anal canal drain to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes. Key lymphatic drainage patterns:

• Anal canal below the pectinate line → superficial inguinal lymph nodes
• Anal canal above the pectinate line → internal iliac lymph nodes
• Testes → para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes due to embryologic origin
• Prostate → internal iliac and sacral lymph nodes
• Bladder → external and internal iliac lymph nodes

Clinical significance:

A malignant mass in the superficial inguinal lymph nodes is most commonly associated with cancers of structures draining to these nodes, including the lower anal canal, perianal skin, external genitalia, and lower limb.

questions.text: A 12 year old male child brought by his parents with complaints of, his school performance has declined, and he has been moodier and more impulsive. His parents also note that he has been sleeping more than usual and has had a poor appetite for the past 2 months. Approximately 3 weeks ago, the patient developed a tremor in both hands that is most prominent when he reaches for an object or tries to write. The tremor has worsened significantly over the past week, and he has developed an unsteady, broad-based gait. Laboratory studies reveal elevated serum transaminases and 24-hour urinary copper excretion. The patient is prescribed penicillamine therapy. This medication primarily works through which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increasing urinary excretion of copper

Penicillamine is a copper-chelating agent used in the treatment of Wilson disease that increases urinary excretion of copper.

Wilson disease is caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired biliary excretion of copper and accumulation of copper in the liver, brain, and other tissues. This results in hepatic dysfunction and neuropsychiatric manifestations such as tremor, behavioral changes, and gait abnormalities.

Penicillamine binds free copper in tissues and blood, forming a soluble complex that is excreted in the urine. This reduces total body copper levels and prevents further tissue damage.

questions.text: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the neurology clinic because of progressive tremors, slurred speech, declining school performance, and recent behavioral changes. His parents also report intermittent jaundice over the past year. On examination, slit-lamp evaluation demonstrates Kayser–Fleischer rings. Liver biopsy confirms excessive hepatic copper deposition, and genetic testing reveals a mutation in the ATP7B gene, confirming Wilson's disease. Which of the following biochemical findings is most consistent with this diagnosis?
options: Increased serum ceruloplasmin with decreased urinary copper excretion
Decreased serum ceruloplasmin with increased urinary copper excretion
Increased serum ceruloplasmin with increased urinary copper excretion
Normal serum ceruloplasmin with decreased urinary copper excretion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decreased serum ceruloplasmin with increased urinary copper excretion

Wilson's disease (Hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13.

The ATP7B protein is responsible for:

• Incorporating copper into ceruloplasmin
• Excreting excess copper into bile

Defective ATP7B leads to:

• Reduced ceruloplasmin synthesis → ↓ serum ceruloplasmin
• Decreased biliary copper excretion
• Progressive accumulation of copper in the liver, brain, cornea, and kidneys
• Increased release of free copper into the circulation, resulting in ↑ urinary copper excretion

Characteristic laboratory findings

• ↓ Serum ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL)
• ↑ 24-hour urinary copper excretion (>100 μg/day)
• ↑ Hepatic copper concentration (>250 μg/g dry weight)
• Increased free (non-ceruloplasmin-bound) serum copper

questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 17-year-old boy presents with progressive tremors, dysarthria, personality changes, and jaundice. Slit-lamp examination reveals Kayser–Fleischer rings. Liver biopsy shows copper accumulation. A diagnosis of Wilson’s disease is made. Which of the following biochemical findings is most consistent with this diagnosis?
options: Increased ceruloplasmin level in blood with decreased urinary copper excretion
Decreased ceruloplasmin level in blood with increased urinary copper excretion
Increased ceruloplasmin level in blood with increased urinary copper excretion
Normal ceruloplasmin level in blood with decreased urinary copper excretion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decreased ceruloplasmin level in blood with increased urinary copper excretion

Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutation in the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired copper excretion into bile and defective incorporation of copper into ceruloplasmin.

• ↓ Serum ceruloplasmin
• ↑ Free copper in blood
• ↑ Urinary copper excretion
• Copper accumulation in liver, brain (basal ganglia), and cornea (Kayser–Fleischer rings)

Clinical features:

• Hepatitis, cirrhosis
• Neurologic symptoms (tremor, dysarthria, psychiatric changes)
• Kayser–Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam.

Treatment:

• Copper chelation (penicillamine or trientine)
• Zinc therapy to reduce copper absorption.

questions.text: A 23-year-old medical student sustains a needlestick injury while handling a blood sample from a hepatitis B–positive patient. Within hours, his serum is tested for viral markers, which are negative. The microbiology laboratory explains that the window period exists when surface antigen and its antibody are both absent, but another marker remains detectable. Which of the following antibody is responsible for the window period?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HBc IgM antibody

Why: The "window period" in Hepatitis B refers to the phase during acute infection when:

• HBsAg has become undetectable (cleared by the immune response), but
• Anti-HBs (HBsAb) has not yet risen to detectable levels (it takes time for the antibody response to surface antigen to develop)

During this gap, the only detectable marker of active/recent infection is IgM antibody to core antigen (IgM anti-HBc). This is why IgM anti-HBc is often called the "serologic gap filler" — it's the sole positive marker when both HBsAg and anti-HBs are negative.

Key point about the timeline:

• HBsAg → appears first, present during acute infection
• IgM anti-HBc → appears shortly after HBsAg, remains detectable through the window period (\~6 months), and is the hallmark of recent/acute infection
• Anti-HBs → appears late, signifies recovery and immunity (or post-vaccination)

questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents with chronic dyspepsia and epigastric discomfort. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy confirms Helicobacter pylori–associated chronic gastritis (Type B gastritis). Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of Type B gastritis?
options: Predominant involvement of the gastric antrum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Achlorhydria

Type B (H. pylori-associated) gastritis is the most common form of chronic gastritis.

Typical features include:

• Predominantly affects the antrum
• Strongly associated with Helicobacter pylori
• No association with HLA or autoimmune disorders
• Long-standing infection increases the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma

Achlorhydria is not a typical feature of early or antral-predominant Type B gastritis because acid secretion is usually normal or increased. Achlorhydria develops classically in Type A (autoimmune) gastritis, where destruction of parietal cells leads to loss of gastric acid secretion.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Predominantly involves the antrum – Correct. Type B gastritis initially affects the antral mucosa.
• B. No association with HLA – Correct. Unlike autoimmune gastritis, Type B gastritis has no characteristic HLA association.
• C. Higher risk of malignancy – Correct. Chronic H. pylori infection predisposes to gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.
• D. Achlorhydria – Incorrect because achlorhydria is characteristic of Type A (autoimmune) gastritis, not uncomplicated Type B gastritis.

High-yield pearl

| Feature | Type A (Autoimmune) | Type B (H. pylori)

| ------- | ------------------- | ------------------

| Site | Body & fundus | Antrum

| Cause | Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells | Helicobacter pylori

| HLA association | Present | Absent

| Acid secretion | ↓ (Achlorhydria) | Normal or ↑ initially

| Pernicious anemia | Common | Uncommon

| Gastrin | ↑ | Usually normal or mildly ↑

| Malignancy risk | Gastric adenocarcinoma & carcinoid | Gastric adenocarcinoma & MALT lymphoma

questions.text: A 26-year-old man presents with acute diarrhea associated with fever and abdominal pain. The clinician wants to rapidly differentiate inflammatory diarrhea from non-inflammatory diarrhea at the bedside using a stool-based test that detects neutrophil-derived inflammatory markers and is more sensitive than direct microscopy. Which of the following tests is most appropriate for this purpose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fecal lactoferrin agglutination assay

Fecal lactoferrin is a neutrophil-derived protein released during intestinal inflammation.

Detection of lactoferrin in stool helps differentiate inflammatory diarrhea from non-inflammatory diarrhea.

Clinical significance:

• Positive fecal lactoferrin → inflammatory diarrhea, seen in infections such as Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, and in inflammatory bowel disease.
• It is more sensitive than stool microscopy for fecal leukocytes and provides a rapid bedside test.

Comparison:

A. Stool culture: identifies specific pathogens but is slower.

B. Fecal leukocyte exam: less sensitive and operator dependent.

C. Stool osmotic gap: used for secretory vs osmotic diarrhea, not inflammation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 32-year-old healthcare worker undergoes routine hepatitis B screening. Her serology profile is as follows: • HBsAg: Negative • Anti-HBs: Negative • Anti-HBc (total): Positive • HBeAg: Negative • Anti-HBe: Negative Which of the following is least likely to explain this serological pattern?
options: Window phase of acute hepatitis B infection
Remote past hepatitis B infection with isolated anti-HBc positivity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Late acute hepatitis B infection

The presence of isolated anti-HBc positivity (HBsAg negative, Anti-HBs negative, Anti-HBc positive) has several recognized explanations:

• Window period of acute HBV infection, when HBsAg has disappeared but Anti-HBs has not yet appeared.
• Occult HBV infection, where HBV DNA persists despite negative HBsAg.
• Remote past infection, in which Anti-HBs has waned below detectable levels while Anti-HBc remains positive lifelong.
• Occasionally, it may also represent a false-positive Anti-HBc result.

Late acute hepatitis B infection is not the typical interpretation because, during recovery from acute infection, Anti-HBs antibodies are expected to begin appearing, rather than remaining absent.

Why the other options are incorrect

• A. Window period – Correct explanation. During the window period, Anti-HBc (especially IgM) may be the only positive serological marker.
• C. Occult HBV infection – Correct. Patients may have negative HBsAg but detectable HBV DNA with isolated Anti-HBc positivity.
• D. Remote past HBV infection – Correct. Anti-HBs levels may decline over time, leaving isolated Anti-HBc positivity.

High-yield pearl

Isolated Anti-HBc positivity (HBsAg– / Anti-HBs– / Anti-HBc+) suggests:

• ✅ Window period (especially if Anti-HBc IgM is positive)
• ✅ Occult HBV infection
• ✅ Remote resolved infection with loss of detectable Anti-HBs
• ✅ False-positive Anti-HBc

questions.text: A 33-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 24 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department by her husband for lethargy, nausea, and vomiting for 4 days. She returned from a trip to Thailand 2 weeks ago. Her immunizations are up-to-date and she has never received blood products. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). She is not oriented to person, place, or time. Examination shows jaundice and mild asterixis. Her prothrombin time is 18 sec (INR=2.0), serum alanine aminotransferase is 3911 U/L, and serum aspartate aminotransferase is 3724 U/L. This patient's current condition is most likely associated with increased titers of which of the following serum studies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anti-HEV IgM

Hepatitis E virus (HEV) infection is a major cause of acute viral hepatitis in developing regions (e.g., South and Southeast Asia) and is transmitted via the fecal–oral route through contaminated water.

• Pregnant woman (especially 2nd–3rd trimester) with acute liver failure
• Travel to endemic area
• Very high AST/ALT (>3000 U/L)
• Encephalopathy and coagulopathy → acute fulminant hepatitis

Diagnosis: Anti-HEV IgM antibodies → marker of acute HEV infection

HEV infection during pregnancy carries high risk of fulminant hepatic failure and mortality.

Contrast:

• HBV → HBsAg positive
• HCV → Anti-HCV IgG (usually chronic)
• Anti-HBe IgM is not a typical marker.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician with abdominal pain and melena. She also complains of progressive fatigue and a 5 kg (11 Ib) weight loss over the last 2 months. She has a strong family history of colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancer. Colonoscopy shows a protuberant, friable mass in the ascending colon, and biopsy is diagnostic for colon adenocarcinoma. Genetic analysis confirms a mutation consistent with Lynch syndrome. Which of the following is most likely responsible for the development of colon cancer in this patient?
options: Insertion of abnormal bases into DNA
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nucleotide mismatches that escape repair

Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer) is caused by mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2. These genes normally correct base–base mismatches and insertion–deletion errors that occur during DNA replication.

Pathogenesis:

Defective mismatch repair leads to accumulation of unrepaired nucleotide mismatches, particularly in repetitive DNA sequences called microsatellites.

This results in microsatellite instability (MSI), which promotes mutations in genes controlling cell growth and apoptosis, leading to early-onset colorectal cancer and other malignancies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 38-year-old woman with a 1-year history of Crohn disease presents with worsening abdominal pain and watery diarrhea for the past 3 weeks. She had been in clinical remission on adalimumab therapy. On examination, she has mild fever and right lower quadrant tenderness without guarding or rigidity. Laboratory evaluation reveals undetectable trough levels of adalimumab. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism responsible for her loss of response to therapy?
options: Neutralizing anti-drug antibodies increasing drug clearance
Reduced absorption due to intestinal inflammation
Increased hepatic metabolism via cytochrome P450 induction
Accelerated renal excretion of monoclonal antibodies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neutralizing anti-drug antibodies increasing drug clearance

Loss of response to biologic therapy (especially anti-TNF agents like adalimumab) is most commonly due to immunogenicity, i.e., development of anti-drug antibodies (ADAs).

• These antibodies:

• Bind to the drug
• Neutralize its effect
• Increase its clearance → low/undetectable trough levels

Why not other options?

B. Reduced absorption → Monoclonal antibodies are given parenterally, not affected by gut absorption

C. CYP450 induction → Biologics are degraded via proteolysis, not hepatic enzyme metabolism

D. Renal excretion → Large proteins are not cleared significantly by kidneys

Injection site complexes → Cause local reactions, not systemic treatment failure

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman develops chronic watery diarrhea after limited terminal ileal resection for Crohn disease. Stool examination shows normal fat content. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cholestyramine

After terminal ileal resection, bile acids are not adequately reabsorbed in the ileum. Excess bile acids enter the colon, where they stimulate water and electrolyte secretion, causing chronic watery diarrhea.

• Occurs after limited ileal resection
• Stool fat is normal (no significant fat malabsorption)
• Due to bile acid–induced secretory diarrhea

Treatment:

• Cholestyramine, a bile acid–binding resin, binds bile acids in the intestine and prevents their secretory effect in the colon.

Important distinction:

• Extensive ileal resection (>100 cm) → bile acid deficiency → fat malabsorption and steatorrhea, not bile acid diarrhea.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 42-year-old male patient presented with jaundice. His AST was 48 U, ALT was 51 U, ALP, GGT were normal. Ultrasound of liver was suggestive of cirrhosis. Viral markers were done and the following results were obtained. What is the next best step? Anti-HAV: Negative Anti-HBeAg: Negative Anti-HBcAg IgG: Positive Anti-HBcAg IgM: Negative HBsAg: Negative Anti-HbsAg: Positive Anti-HCV: Positive
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. RT-PCR for hepatitis C virus

Anti-HCV positivity indicates exposure to hepatitis C virus but does not confirm active infection.

The next step is to detect viral RNA using RT-PCR to determine whether there is ongoing viral replication.

• Anti-HAV negative → no evidence of hepatitis A infection.
• HBsAg negative with anti-HBs positive and anti-HBc IgG positive → past hepatitis B infection with immunity.
• Anti-HCV positive → prior exposure to hepatitis C.

Since hepatitis C antibodies can persist even after viral clearance, confirmation of active infection requires detection of HCV RNA.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient with chronic constipation and diabetic gastroparesis is being considered for pharmacologic therapy to improve gastrointestinal motility. The physician reviews several drug classes that enhance gastric emptying or intestinal transit. Which of the following is not classified as a prokinetic agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diphenoxymethane

Prokinetic drugs increase gastrointestinal motility by enhancing coordinated contractions or accelerating gastric emptying.

Common prokinetic classes include:

• 5-HT₄ agonists such as prucalopride and mosapride → increase acetylcholine release from enteric neurons.
• D₂ receptor antagonists such as metoclopramide and domperidone → remove dopamine-mediated inhibition of gastrointestinal motility.
• Macrolides such as erythromycin → act as motilin receptor agonists and stimulate gastric contractions.

Diphenoxymethane derivatives, such as diphenoxylate, are opioid antidiarrheal drugs. They reduce intestinal motility, so they are not prokinetic agents.

High-yield pearl

• Prokinetics increase gut movement; diphenoxylate decreases it.

Examples of prokinetic drugs:

• Metoclopramide
• Domperidone
• Prucalopride
• Mosapride
• Erythromycin

Examples of antimotility drugs:

• Loperamide
• Diphenoxylate

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 46-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramedics after an episode of large-volume hematemesis. Physical examination reveals a palpable spleen. Endoscopy shows bleeding esophageal varices. A liver biopsy performed 2 days later shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Portal vein thrombosis

Portal vein thrombosis causes prehepatic portal hypertension, leading to splenomegaly and esophageal varices, while the liver parenchyma remains normal on biopsy.

Key features of prehepatic portal hypertension:

• Normal liver histology
• Splenomegaly
• Esophageal/gastric varices → hematemesis
• May occur due to portal vein thrombosis or external compression

Contrast with other causes:

A. Long-term alcohol consumption → abnormal liver biopsy with fibrosis and cirrhosis

B. Budd–Chiari syndrome → hepatic vein obstruction with liver congestion and necrosis

C. Constrictive pericarditis → causes congestive hepatopathy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 46-year-old man presents with fatigue and arthralgia involving the 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal joints. He is found to have mild hepatomegaly. Laboratory tests show: • Hemoglobin: normal • Serum ferritin: elevated • Transferrin saturation: 68% His younger brother is asymptomatic. The physician decides to evaluate the brother for the same condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial test for screening the asymptomatic sibling?
options: Liver biopsy with Prussian blue staining
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Transferrin saturation

This question tests the correct screening strategy for hereditary hemochromatosis, especially in asymptomatic first-degree relatives.

Earliest biochemical abnormality:

• ↑ Transferrin saturation (>45%)
• Occurs before ferritin rises

Best initial screening test:

• Transferrin saturation
• Preferred in:

• Asymptomatic individuals
• Family members of affected patients

• Ferritin is an acute phase reactant
• Can be elevated in:

• Infection
• Inflammation
• Liver disease

→ Less specific for early screening

Stepwise approach:

• Screen → Transferrin saturation
• Confirm → HFE gene mutation
• Assess severity → MRI / biopsy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 46-year-old man presents with intermittent rectal bleeding. Colonoscopy reveals 30–40 adenomatous polyps, predominantly in the proximal colon. Colorectal carcinoma is detected at 52 years of age. His father underwent colectomy for colon cancer at the age of 48. Upper GI endoscopy shows a few duodenal adenomas. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Attenuated familial adenomatous polyposis

Attenuated familial adenomatous polyposis (AFAP) is a milder variant of familial adenomatous polyposis caused by mutations in the APC gene.

• Fewer colorectal adenomas (10–100 polyps) compared to classic FAP (>1000)
• Polyps often predominantly in the proximal colon
• Later onset of colorectal cancer (usually in the 50s)
• May also have duodenal adenomas

Comparison:

B. Classic familial adenomatous polyposis: hundreds to thousands of polyps, cancer in 30s–40s

D. Lynch syndrome: few polyps but high risk of early colorectal cancer due to DNA mismatch repair defects

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 50-year-old man comes to the physician because of an 8-month history of intermittent watery diarrhea and abdominal pain. He has had a 12-kg weight loss during this period. He has also had episodic pain of the ankle, wrist, and knee joints during the past 5 years. An endoscopy with small bowel biopsy is performed. Histopathologic examination of a tissue specimen shows foamy macrophages in the lamina propria with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive inclusions. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intracellular gram positive bacteria

Whipple disease is a systemic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei, a gram-positive intracellular bacterium that infects macrophages.

• Small bowel biopsy showing foamy macrophages in the lamina propria with PAS-positive inclusions

Clinical manifestations:

• Chronic watery diarrhea
• Weight loss and malabsorption
• Migratory arthralgia (often precedes GI symptoms by years)
• Fever, lymphadenopathy, hyperpigmentation, neurologic symptoms

Pathogenesis:

• Macrophages filled with intracellular gram-positive bacteria accumulate in the intestinal mucosa, impairing nutrient absorption and lymphatic transport.

Treatment:

• Prolonged antibiotic therapy (e.g., ceftriaxone followed by TMP-SMX).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 52-year-old man presents with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, migratory arthralgia, and intermittent fever. He also has hyperpigmentation and generalized lymphadenopathy. Duodenal biopsy is performed. Which of the following statements regarding Whipple disease are CORRECT? A. It is caused by Tropheryma whipplei B. Duodenal biopsy shows PAS-positive macrophages in the submucosa C. Migratory polyarthritis often precedes gastrointestinal manifestations D. The organism is acid-fast positive on staining E. Long-term antibiotic therapy is required for definitive treatment F. Causes disturbance in lymphatic transport of absorbed lipids
options: A, B, C, D, E, F
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A, C, E, F

Whipple disease is a rare systemic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that primarily affects the small intestine and can involve multiple organ systems.

• Chronic diarrhea and weight loss
• Migratory polyarthritis (often precedes GI symptoms)
• Fever, lymphadenopathy, hyperpigmentation
• Malabsorption

Pathophysiology:

• Infiltration of the intestinal mucosa by infected macrophages
• Leads to impaired lymphatic transport of absorbed lipids, causing malabsorption.

Diagnosis:

• Duodenal biopsy (classically PAS-positive macrophages, though not included in the correct set here)
• PCR for Tropheryma whipplei

Treatment:

• Requires prolonged antibiotic therapy (often ≥1 year) to prevent relapse and CNS involvement.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 54-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and ascites presents with fever, abdominal pain, and altered sensorium. Ascitic fluid analysis shows: Total leukocyte count: 800 cells/mm³ Neutrophils: 320 cells/mm³ Protein: low Culture: pending What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is a bacterial infection of ascitic fluid without an identifiable intra-abdominal source, most commonly seen in patients with cirrhosis and ascites.

Diagnostic criterion: Ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) count ≥250 cells/mm³

Typical findings:

• Low ascitic fluid protein
• Fever, abdominal pain, altered mental status
• Culture may be positive (commonly E. coli, Klebsiella, Streptococcus) but treatment should start even if culture results are pending.

Management:

• Empiric third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefotaxime)
• Albumin infusion to reduce risk of hepatorenal syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 54-year-old man with epigastric pain and positive occult blood test undergoes endoscopy, revealing hyperemic nodular mucosa. Biopsy shows submucosal glands producing alkaline mucus. Which part of the GI tract was biopsied?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. First part of the duodenum

Brunner glands are submucosal glands located in the proximal (first part) of the duodenum that secrete alkaline mucus.

The alkaline mucus produced by Brunner glands neutralizes acidic chyme entering the duodenum from the stomach.

This protects the duodenal mucosa and creates an optimal pH for pancreatic enzymes to function.

Key histologic feature: Presence of mucus-secreting submucosal glands is characteristic of the first part of the duodenum and helps distinguish it from other segments of the small intestine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 55-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis secondary to chronic hepatitis C is admitted with progressive abdominal distension, lower limb edema, and increasing confusion. He has long-standing ascites treated with spironolactone and furosemide. On examination, he is hypotensive (BP 100/60 mmHg), tachycardic (HR 102/min), and has tense ascites with shifting dullness. Laboratory evaluation reveals hypoalbuminemia and worsening renal function. Diagnostic paracentesis excludes spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. He is diagnosed with hepatorenal syndrome (HRS). Along with standard supportive measures, which of the following is the most appropriate additional therapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Octreotide plus intravenous albumin

Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is a functional renal failure that develops in advanced cirrhosis due to marked splanchnic vasodilation, resulting in reduced effective arterial blood volume and intense renal vasoconstriction.

When terlipressin is unavailable or contraindicated, treatment consists of:

• Octreotide → reduces splanchnic vasodilation by inhibiting vasodilatory peptides.
• Intravenous albumin → expands plasma volume and improves renal perfusion.

This combination helps improve effective circulatory volume and renal blood flow while patients are evaluated for definitive treatment, such as liver transplantation.

Why the other options are incorrect

• B. Tolvaptan: A vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist used for dilutional hyponatremia; it does not treat hepatorenal syndrome.
• C. Midodrine plus albumin: Midodrine is beneficial only when combined with both octreotide and albumin; midodrine with albumin alone is less effective.
• D. Intravenous furosemide: Increasing diuresis can further reduce intravascular volume and worsen renal hypoperfusion in HRS.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 56-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because of increasing confusion and lethargy for the past 12 hours. He is oriented only to person. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 109/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 108/67 mm Hg. Examination shows abdominal distention and several erythematous, lacy lesions on the chest that blanch with pressure. His hands make a flapping motion when they are dorsiflexed. Which of the following is the most likely precipitating factor for this patient's symptoms?
options: Accumulation of hemoglobin in the intestine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Accumulation of hemoglobin in the intestine

Hepatic encephalopathy occurs in patients with advanced liver disease due to accumulation of neurotoxins, especially ammonia, that are normally detoxified by the liver.

Clinical clues:

• Confusion and lethargy
• Asterixis (flapping tremor)
• Spider angiomas on the chest
• Ascites indicating chronic liver disease

One common trigger is gastrointestinal bleeding. When blood enters the intestinal lumen, hemoglobin is digested into nitrogenous compounds that are metabolized by gut bacteria into ammonia. Because the diseased liver cannot adequately detoxify ammonia into urea, ammonia accumulates in the blood and reaches the brain, leading to hepatic encephalopathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 56-year-old man with a long history of alcohol use presents with progressive abdominal distension. On examination, there is shifting dullness and bilateral pedal edema. Diagnostic paracentesis is performed. Serum albumin is 3.2 g/dL and ascitic fluid albumin is 1.0 g/dL. What is the SAAG value, and what does it suggest about the underlying cause of ascites?
options: SAAG = 1.1 g/dL; suggests portal hypertension as the cause
SAAG = 2.2 g/dL; suggests portal hypertension as the cause
SAAG = 2.2 g/dL; suggests a non-portal hypertensive cause such as malignancy or tuberculosis
SAAG = 1.1 g/dL; suggests a non-portal hypertensive cause such as malignancy or tuberculosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. SAAG = 2.2 g/dL; suggests portal hypertension as the cause

Rationale: SAAG = Serum albumin − Ascitic fluid albumin = 3.2 − 1.0 = 2.2 g/dL. A SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension as the underlying mechanism (due to increased hydrostatic pressure pushing albumin-poor fluid into the peritoneal cavity, while albumin itself remains largely retained intravascularly) — classically seen in cirrhosis (as in this patient with a history of alcohol use), congestive heart failure, and Budd-Chiari syndrome. A SAAG <1.1 g/dL instead points toward non-portal hypertensive causes, where the peritoneum itself is diseased and "leaky" to albumin, such as peritoneal tuberculosis, peritoneal carcinomatosis, or pancreatitis-related ascites. Since this patient's SAAG is 2.2 g/dL (≥1.1), portal hypertension — not a non-portal hypertensive cause — is the correct interpretation, making options C and D incorrect despite their correct arithmetic of "high SAAG," and option A incorrect on calculation.

Quick reference — SAAG Interpretation:

| SAAG | Interpretation | Common Causes

| ---- | -------------- | -------------

| ≥1.1 g/dL (High gradient) | Portal hypertension | Cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis, CHF, Budd-Chiari syndrome, constrictive pericarditis, massive liver metastases

| <1.1 g/dL (Low gradient) | Non-portal hypertensive (peritoneal disease) | Peritoneal tuberculosis, peritoneal carcinomatosis, pancreatitis, nephrotic syndrome, serositis

Formula: SAAG = Serum albumin − Ascitic fluid albumin (both measured on the same day)

Note: SAAG is far more accurate than the older "exudate vs transudate" (total protein-based) classification of ascites.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and ascites is admitted with fever and altered sensorium. Ascitic fluid examination shows neutrophil count >250 cells/mm³ with no surgically treatable intra-abdominal source of infection. On reviewing medications, the physician decides to discontinue a gastric acid–suppressing drug that is known to increase intestinal bacterial overgrowth and bacterial translocation, thereby predisposing to this complication. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Omeprazole

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhotic patients is associated with increased intestinal bacterial translocation, which can be promoted by proton pump inhibitors like omeprazole due to gastric acid suppression.

• PPIs reduce gastric acidity → increased bacterial colonization
• Promotes small intestinal bacterial overgrowth and translocation
• Increases risk of SBP in patients with cirrhosis and ascites
• SBP diagnosis: ascitic fluid neutrophils ≥250 cells/mm³

Differentiation:

• A. Ranitidine: less strongly associated compared to PPIs
• C. Sucralfate: mucosal protective, no major effect on acid suppression
• D. Misoprostol: prostaglandin analog, not linked to SBP risk

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presents with progressive dyspepsia and unintentional weight loss over 3 months. Physical examination reveals mild epigastric tenderness without lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. CT scan shows thickening of the gastric mucosa without distant spread. Upper GI endoscopy reveals nodular gastric folds. Biopsy demonstrates proliferation of small, clonal B lymphocytes expressing CD20 within the gastric mucosa. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this condition?
options: Chronic antigenic stimulation by persistent infection
Viral oncogene–mediated inhibition of tumor suppressor genes
Immune evasion through downregulation of MHC molecules
Activation of somatic hypermutation in germinal centers
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic antigenic stimulation by persistent infection

This patient has gastric MALT lymphoma, a low-grade B-cell lymphoma strongly associated with Helicobacter pylori infection. The pathogenesis involves chronic antigenic stimulation, where persistent infection leads to continuous activation and proliferation of B cells in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT). Over time, this can result in monoclonal expansion and lymphoma formation.

Importantly, early-stage disease may regress with eradication of H. pylori, highlighting the immune-driven mechanism.

Why not other options?

B. Viral oncogene–mediated p53 inhibition → Seen in HPV-related cancers (e.g., cervical carcinoma)

C. Immune evasion (↓ MHC expression) → Mechanism used by tumors to escape immunity, not primary cause

D. Somatic hypermutation activation → Normal germinal center process; not the initiating mechanism

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 64-year-old man with prostate cancer receives external beam radiation therapy to the pelvis. After 10 days of treatment, he develops frequent watery diarrhea, urgency, and lower abdominal cramping. He has no fever and no recent travel. Stool cultures are negative. The oncologist explains that this is an expected acute adverse effect related to the high radiosensitivity of certain intestinal cells. Which of the following intestinal cell types is most directly affected, leading to this patient’s symptoms?
options: Goblet cells in the mucosal surface epithelium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rapidly dividing crypt stem cells

Radiation injury preferentially affects rapidly dividing cells, making the gastrointestinal epithelium highly radiosensitive. The most affected cells are intestinal crypt stem cells located in the crypts of Lieberkühn.

• Crypt stem cells:

• Continuously proliferate to replenish intestinal epithelium
• Maintain mucosal integrity and absorption

• Radiation → DNA damage in these rapidly dividing cells →

• ↓ epithelial regeneration
• Mucosal breakdown
• Impaired absorption + increased secretion

Results in watery diarrhea, urgency, and abdominal cramps

Why not other options:

A. Enteric neurons (Meissner plexus): Regulate secretion/motility but not primary target of radiation injury

B. Goblet cells: Secrete mucus; affected secondarily, not primary radiosensitive population

C. Paneth cells: Involved in innate immunity; relatively less proliferative

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A newborn male develops profuse, intractable watery diarrhea within the first few days of life, leading to severe dehydration and metabolic acidosis. The diarrhea does not improve with bowel rest or fasting. Small intestinal biopsy shows: • Villous atrophy • Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)–positive material within the apical cytoplasm of enterocytes On electron microscopy, intracytoplasmic microvillous inclusions are seen. Which of the following gene mutations is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MYO5B

Microvillus inclusion disease (MVID) is a rare congenital enteropathy that presents in neonates with severe, intractable secretory diarrhea that persists despite fasting.

• Mutation in the MYO5B gene, which encodes myosin Vb, a protein involved in intracellular trafficking and maintenance of enterocyte polarity.

Pathologic findings:

• Villous atrophy
• PAS-positive material in the apical cytoplasm of enterocytes
• Intracytoplasmic microvillus inclusions on electron microscopy

Clinical consequence:

• Severe malabsorption and dehydration
• Often requires long-term parenteral nutrition or intestinal transplantation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with Wilson disease has a markedly reduced serum ceruloplasmin concentration. Which of the following best explains this laboratory abnormality?
options: Increased urinary loss of ceruloplasmin due to proximal renal tubular dysfunction
Failure of copper incorporation into apoceruloplasmin causes rapid degradation of unstable apoceruloplasmin.
Autoimmune destruction of hepatocytes reduces ceruloplasmin synthesis.
Excess circulating free copper directly suppresses ceruloplasmin gene expression.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Failure of copper incorporation into apoceruloplasmin causes rapid degradation of unstable apoceruloplasmin.

Trap: Ceruloplasmin is synthesized normally, but without copper incorporation it becomes unstable and is rapidly degraded.

| Feature | Wilson disease | Menkes disease

| ------- | -------------- | --------------

| Gene | ATP7B | ATP7A

| Inheritance | Autosomal recessive | X-linked recessive

| Copper level | ↑ Tissue copper | ↓ Tissue copper

| Ceruloplasmin | ↓ | ↓

| Main defect | ↓ Biliary excretion + ↓ ceruloplasmin incorporation | ↓ Intestinal copper absorption

| Clinical features | Liver disease, neuropsychiatric symptoms, Kayser–Fleischer rings | Kinky hair, hypotonia, developmental delay

| Treatment | Penicillamine, trientine, zinc | Copper histidine (early)

Common NEET PG Traps

• ATP7B has two major functions: incorporating copper into apoceruloplasmin and excreting excess copper into bile.
• Low ceruloplasmin results from failure of copper loading, leading to rapid degradation of apoceruloplasmin, not decreased hepatic synthesis.
• Kayser–Fleischer rings are caused by copper deposition in Descemet membrane of the cornea.
• Deferoxamine chelates iron, not copper; symptomatic Wilson disease is treated with penicillamine or trientine, with zinc used to reduce intestinal copper absorption.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: An 18-month-old child was brought to OPD with a 3-day record of watery diarrhea and vomiting, displaying an altered sensorium. What possible conditions could be considered as the differential diagnoses in this case? 1. Severe dehydration 2. HUS 3. Cerebral Venous Thrombosis 4. Hyponatremia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3, 4

In children with acute gastroenteritis presenting with altered sensorium, common causes include severe dehydration, electrolyte disturbances (especially hyponatremia), and cerebral venous thrombosis due to dehydration-induced hypercoagulability.

Explanation:

• Severe dehydration can cause hypovolemia leading to decreased cerebral perfusion and altered mental status.
• Hyponatremia may occur due to excess free water intake or inappropriate fluid replacement, leading to cerebral edema and neurological symptoms.
• Cerebral venous thrombosis can develop in dehydrated children due to hemoconcentration and hypercoagulability, resulting in neurological manifestations such as altered consciousness or seizures.

Why not HUS:

Hemolytic uremic syndrome usually follows bloody diarrhea caused by Shiga toxin–producing bacteria and is characterized by hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, which are not typical in this presentation of watery diarrhea.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: During a study on gastrointestinal hormones, a volunteer is administered the hormone secreted by S cells. Which of the following changes most likely represent the effect of this hormone on gastric and duodenal secretions?
options: Gastric H+ increases, Duodenal HCO3 increased, Duodenal Cl- no change
Gastric H+ decreases, Duodenal HCO3 decreased, Duodenal Cl- no change
Gastric H+ decreases, Duodenal HCO3 increased, Duodenal Cl- decreases
Gastric H+ decreases, Duodenal HCO3 increased, Duodenal Cl- increases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gastric H+ decreases, Duodenal HCO3 increased, Duodenal Cl- decreases

S cells of the duodenum secrete secretin in response to acidic chyme entering the duodenum.

Major actions of secretin:

• ↓ Gastric acid (H⁺) secretion → inhibits parietal cells and gastrin release
• ↑ Pancreatic and duodenal bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) secretion → neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum
• ↓ Chloride (Cl⁻) secretion in pancreatic/duodenal fluid because Cl⁻ is exchanged for HCO₃⁻ via the Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchanger

Physiologic role:

• Protects the duodenal mucosa from acid
• Creates an optimal alkaline environment for pancreatic enzymes

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Noninvasive test to detect risk of hepatic fibrosis include? 1. Aspartate aminotransferases /platelet ratio 2. Fibro scan 3. Forns index 4. Serum laminin & serum hyaluronidase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4

Several noninvasive tests are used to assess hepatic fibrosis, helping reduce the need for liver biopsy in chronic liver diseases such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and NAFLD. Common noninvasive fibrosis assessment tools:

1.  AST-to-Platelet Ratio Index (APRI)

• Uses AST level and platelet count
• Helps estimate significant fibrosis and cirrhosis

2.  FibroScan (Transient Elastography)

• Measures liver stiffness using ultrasound-based elastography
• Widely used for staging fibrosis

3. Forns Index

• Uses age, cholesterol, platelet count, and GGT
• Helps predict significant hepatic fibrosis

4.  Serum fibrosis markers

• Includes laminin and hyaluronic acid
• Reflect extracellular matrix deposition in fibrosis

questions.text: Sulfasalazine is commonly used in the treatment of ulcerative colitis and rheumatoid arthritis. Which of the following are recognized adverse effects of sulfasalazine? A. Bone marrow suppression causing leukopenia B. Stevens–Johnson syndrome C. Reversible oligospermia D. Ototoxicity E. Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency patient F. Macrocytic anemia G. Pneumonitis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. All except D

Sulfasalazine, a 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) derivative, is used in ulcerative colitis and rheumatoid arthritis and has several recognized adverse effects.

Important adverse effects include:

• Bone marrow suppression → leukopenia
• Stevens–Johnson syndrome (rare hypersensitivity reaction)
• Reversible oligospermia (affects sperm motility and count)
• Hemolytic anemia, especially in G6PD deficiency
• Folate deficiency leading to macrocytic anemia
• Hypersensitivity reactions including pneumonitis

Not associated: Ototoxicity (seen with drugs like aminoglycosides or loop diuretics).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: The Truelove–Witts criteria are used to define acute severe ulcerative colitis. All of the following are components of the Truelove–Witts criteria, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Presence of jaundice and pruritus

The Truelove–Witts criteria are used to identify acute severe ulcerative colitis (ASUC) and guide the need for hospitalization and intensive therapy.

Criteria include:

• ≥6 bloody stools/day
• Plus ≥1 systemic sign of toxicity:

o    Pulse ≥90/min

o    Temperature >37.8°C

o    Hemoglobin <10.5 g/dL

o    ESR >30 mm/hr

Not included:

• Jaundice and pruritus, which are features of hepatobiliary disease (e.g., primary sclerosing cholangitis) rather than severity criteria for ulcerative colitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Two weeks after returning from vacation, a 21-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of malaise, nausea, vomiting, fever, and abdominal pain. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and right upper quadrant tenderness. The liver is palpated 1.5 cm below the right costal margin. A biopsy specimen of this patient's liver would most likely show which of the following findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ballooning degeneration

1. Hepatocyte injury

• Ballooning degeneration – most characteristic finding; hepatocytes swollen with clear, rarefied cytoplasm, sometimes with wispy strands ("moth-eaten" appearance)
• Councilman bodies (acidophil bodies) – individual apoptotic hepatocytes, shrunken, deeply eosinophilic, with pyknotic or absent nucleus
• Spotty (focal) necrosis – scattered single-cell death throughout the lobule
• Confluent necrosis in more severe disease — may bridge portal-portal, portal-central, or central-central regions
• Panacinar/massive necrosis in fulminant hepatitis

2. Inflammation

• Lobular disarray with mixed mononuclear infiltrate — predominantly lymphocytes, plus macrophages and occasional plasma cells
• Inflammation involves both lobules and portal tracts (unlike chronic hepatitis where portal/periportal predominates)
• Kupffer cell hypertrophy/hyperplasia with pigment (lipofuscin) — reflects phagocytosis of debris from dead hepatocytes

3. Cholestasis

• Mild canalicular cholestasis (bile plugs) can occur, more marked in cholestatic variants of hepatitis (e.g., Hepatitis A)

4. Regeneration

• Hepatocyte regeneration with mitotic figures, occasional rosette formation
• Variation in hepatocyte size (anisocytosis) as regenerating cells proliferate

5. Architecture

• Lobular architecture usually preserved
• No fibrosis in uncomplicated acute disease (fibrosis = chronic hepatitis)

questions.subject: Medicine

questions.text: Which of the following are established prognostic factors in carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumors, all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urinary 5-HIAA level

Prognosis of neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors is primarily determined by tumor proliferation and histologic features.

Established prognostic factors:

• Mitotic rate
• Degree of histological differentiation
• Ki-67 proliferation index (used for tumor grading: G1, G2, G3)

Not a prognostic factor:

• Urinary 5-HIAA (a serotonin metabolite) is mainly used to diagnose and monitor carcinoid syndrome, not to determine tumor aggressiveness or prognosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect about obstructive jaundice?
options: Presence of bilirubin in the urine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased urobilinogen

Obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice occurs due to blockage of bile flow, commonly from gallstones, pancreatic carcinoma, or cholangiocarcinoma. Typical laboratory findings:

• Increased conjugated (direct) bilirubin
• Increased alkaline phosphatase and GGT indicating a cholestatic pattern
• Presence of bilirubin in urine because conjugated bilirubin is water soluble

Urobilinogen is decreased or absent because bile does not reach the intestine, so bilirubin cannot be converted into urobilinogen by intestinal bacteria.

Clinical stool and urine findings:

• Pale or clay-colored stools due to absence of stercobilin
• Dark urine due to excretion of conjugated bilirubin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following statements about Palonosetron are incorrect?
options: It is a second generation 5HT3 receptor antagonist
It belongs to the class of most effective drugs for chemotherapy induced nausea and vomiting
It is the longest acting drug amongst its class
High risk of QT prolongation as adverse reaction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. High risk of QT prolongation as adverse reaction

Palonosetron is a second-generation 5-HT₃ receptor antagonist used primarily for prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV).

• Higher receptor affinity and long half-life (\~40 hours) compared to first-generation agents (ondansetron, granisetron).
• Most effective for delayed CINV.
• Longest acting drug in the 5-HT₃ antagonist class.

Safety profile:

• Unlike earlier 5-HT₃ antagonists, palonosetron has minimal risk of QT interval prolongation.

questions.text: A 14-year boy came with chronic diarrhoea and malnutrition. The physician suspected celiac disease. Which of the following are correct in his diagnostic workup? 1. Presence of IgA antiendomysial antibody 2. Absence of reduced height of villi on intestinal biopsy 3. Increased lymphocytes in lamina propria in small intestine biopsy 4. Absence of tTG antibody in serum Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

In celiac disease, the classic diagnostic triad involves serology, biopsy findings, and clinical correlation:

• 1. Presence of IgA anti-endomysial antibody (EMA) ✔️: This is one of the most specific serological markers for celiac disease (along with tTG-IgA), and its presence strongly supports the diagnosis.
• 2. Absence of reduced height of villi on intestinal biopsy ✔️: In celiac disease, the small intestinal biopsy classically shows villous atrophy (blunting/flattening), which is a hallmark of the disease along with crypt hyperplasia. This forms part of the modified Marsh classification used to grade severity.
• 3. Increased intraepithelial and lamina propria lymphocytes in small intestine biopsy ✔️: Lymphocytic infiltration of the lamina propria (and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes) is a classic histological feature of celiac disease, reflecting the immune-mediated damage to the mucosa.
• 4. Absence of tTG antibody (Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA) in serum ✘: This is actually the first-line, most sensitive serological test for celiac disease. Its absence would argue against, not support, the diagnosis — so this statement is incorrect for a case where celiac disease is being worked up and confirmed.

Summary of workup for celiac disease:

• Serology: tTG-IgA (first-line), EMA-IgA (highly specific, used for confirmation), with total IgA levels checked to rule out IgA deficiency
• Duodenal biopsy: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, and lamina propria lymphocytic/plasma cell infiltration (Marsh classification)
• Clinical: Symptoms improve on gluten-free diet (supports diagnosis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: A patient presents with abdominal pain, acute diarrhea, and is diagnosed with celiac disease. Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?
options: IgA Tissue Transglutaminase antibodies are present
IgG deamidated Gliadin antibodies are present
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Associated with HLA DQ6/DQ11

Celiac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten (gliadin) in genetically predisposed individuals.

Celiac disease is strongly associated with HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8, not DQ6/DQ11, making that statement false. Diagnosis relies on IgA anti–tissue transglutaminase antibodies and supportive serology like IgG deamidated gliadin peptides. Histologic grading of villous atrophy is done using the Marsh classification.

| Stage | Histological Feature

| ----- | --------------------

| Marsh 0 | Normal mucosa

| Marsh 1 | ↑ Intraepithelial lymphocytes

| Marsh 2 | + Crypt hyperplasia

| Marsh 3 | Villous atrophy (partial → total)

| Antibody | Type | Use

| -------- | ---- | ---

| Anti-tTG | IgA | Best screening test

| Anti-endomysial (EMA) | IgA | Highly specific

| Deamidated gliadin peptide (DGP) | IgG/IgA | IgA deficiency, children

questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: A patient with a history of chronic liver disease presents with abdominal distension, jaundice, and pruritis. Ascitic fluid analysis revealed a neutrophil count > 650 per cubic mm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

Cirrhosis → portal hypertension

↓

Ascites formation

↓

Bacterial translocation from gut

↓

Infection of ascitic fluid

↓

↑ Neutrophils (PMN ≥ 250)

↓

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

Ascitic neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³ is diagnostic of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhotic ascites. A count >650 strongly confirms infection even without culture positivity. SBP results from bacterial translocation in chronic liver disease. It is a medical emergency requiring immediate antibiotics.

| Parameter | Value

| --------- | -----

| PMN count ≥ 250 cells/mm³ | Diagnostic of SBP

| Culture | May be positive or negative

| Protein | Usually low

| SAAG | High (>1.1, portal HTN)

Treatment

• 3rd generation cephalosporins (e.g., cefotaxime)
• Albumin infusion (prevents renal failure)

| Feature | SBP | TB Ascites | Malignant Ascites

| ------- | --- | ---------- | -----------------

| Cells | Neutrophils ↑ | Lymphocytes ↑ | Mixed

| PMN count | ≥250 | <250 | Variable

| Protein | Low | High | High

| Cause | Infection | TB | Cancer

questions.text: A patient with diarrhoea and skin lesions was advised to change his diet, which resulted in the improvement of his symptoms. Which of the following is the likely antibody present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anti TTG antibody

• Diarrhea + skin lesions + improves with diet

In celiac disease:

• Enzyme tissue transglutaminase (tTG) modifies gliadin
• Immune system mistakes it as antigen
• → Produces IgA antibodies against tTG

Hence: Anti-tTG IgA = most sensitive test

Gluten (gliadin)

| Skin lesion | DH | Erythema nodosum | Pyoderma gangrenosum

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Ménétrier’s disease: 1. There is excessive production of Transforming Growth Factor-alpha (TGF-α). 2. Majority of the patients present with features of protein-losing enteropathy. 3. Mucus secreting cells are replaced by parietal and chief cells. 4. The mucosal folds of the body and fundus of the stomach are greatly enlarged. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

• 1. Excessive production of TGF-α: Correct

• Ménétrier disease is associated with overexpression of transforming growth factor-α (TGF-α), which activates EGFR signaling and causes gastric foveolar hyperplasia.

• 2. Protein-losing enteropathy: Correct

• The enlarged gastric mucosa causes excessive protein loss into the gastric lumen, resulting in hypoalbuminemia and edema.
• Protein-losing gastropathy is a characteristic clinical feature.

• 3. Mucus-secreting cells are replaced by parietal and chief cells: Incorrect

• The opposite occurs: parietal and chief cells are reduced/replaced by proliferating mucus-secreting foveolar cells.

• 4. Enlarged mucosal folds of body and fundus: Correct

• There is marked giant gastric rugal/fold enlargement, predominantly involving the body and fundus, with relative sparing of the antrum.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: Patients suffering from which of the following condition(s) can get symptomatic relief by consuming a gluten-free diet? 1. Coeliac disease 2. Peptic ulcer disease 3. Dermatitis herpetiformis Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 3 only

• 1. Coeliac disease: Correct

• Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten.
• A strict gluten-free diet is the mainstay of treatment and leads to improvement of symptoms and intestinal mucosal healing.

• 2. Peptic ulcer disease: Incorrect

• A gluten-free diet has no established role in the treatment of peptic ulcer disease.
• Treatment focuses on H. pylori eradication, acid suppression, and avoidance of NSAIDs when appropriate.

• 3. Dermatitis herpetiformis: Correct

• Dermatitis herpetiformis is the cutaneous manifestation of gluten-sensitive enteropathy.
• A strict gluten-free diet improves the rash and reduces the need for medications such as dapsone.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: The ‘¹³C-urea breath test’ and the ‘faecal antigen test’ are non-invasive techniques to diagnose infection with which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Helicobacter pylori

The ¹³C-urea breath test and H. pylori stool antigen test are non-invasive methods used to detect Helicobacter pylori infection.

• ¹³C-urea breath test: H. pylori produces urease, which hydrolyzes urea into ammonia + CO₂. After ingestion of labeled ¹³C-urea, labeled CO₂ is detected in the patient’s breath.
• Faecal antigen test: Detects H. pylori antigens in stool and can be used both for initial diagnosis and to confirm eradication.

Why not the other options?

• A. Haemophilus influenzae: Diagnosed using respiratory cultures, antigen/PCR testing in appropriate settings—not urea breath testing.
• B. Leishmania donovani: Diagnosed by demonstrating amastigotes or using antigen/serological/molecular tests.
• C. Giardia lamblia: Diagnosed using stool antigen testing, microscopy, or molecular assays, but not the ¹³C-urea breath test.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: The Gold Standard for diagnosis of Celiac disease is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endoscopic small bowel biopsy

Celiac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DQ2/DQ8). While serologic tests are useful for screening, the gold standard for diagnosis is an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with multiple duodenal (small bowel) biopsies, which confirms the diagnosis by demonstrating characteristic mucosal changes.

Characteristic histopathological findings:

• Villous atrophy
• Crypt hyperplasia
• Increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (Marsh classification)

Key points:

• Best initial screening test: IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG-IgA) antibody (along with total serum IgA).
• Gold standard: Endoscopic duodenal biopsy.
• Treatment: Lifelong gluten-free diet.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: The most common causative agent for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Escherichia coli

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is an infection of ascitic fluid without an intra-abdominal surgically treatable source, occurring most commonly in patients with cirrhosis and ascites. The most common causative organism is Escherichia coli due to translocation of gut bacteria.

Why not the other options?

• B. Enterococcus spp: Less common; usually associated with healthcare-associated infections.
• C. Staphylococcus aureus: Uncommon cause of classic SBP.
• D. Streptococcus viridans: Can occur but is much less common than E. coli.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: When the serum ascites to albumin gradient (SAAG) is less than 1.1 gm/dL, then which of the following causes of ascites may be considered? 1. Infection 2. Malignancy 3. Cardiac ascites 4. Portal hypertension Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 2 only

The Serum–Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) is the preferred test for determining whether ascites is due to portal hypertension. It is calculated as:

• SAAG = Serum albumin − Ascitic fluid albumin

Interpretation:

• SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL: Indicates portal hypertension (≈97% accuracy).
• SAAG <1.1 g/dL: Indicates ascites not caused by portal hypertension.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Infection: Correct. Infections (e.g., tuberculous peritonitis) typically produce low-SAAG ascites.
• Statement 2. Malignancy: Correct. Peritoneal malignancy (malignant ascites) is a classic cause of low-SAAG ascites.
• Statement 3. Cardiac ascites: Incorrect. Cardiac ascites is caused by elevated venous pressure and produces high-SAAG ascites (≥1.1 g/dL).
• Statement 4. Portal hypertension: Incorrect. Portal hypertension (e.g., cirrhosis) is the prototypical cause of high-SAAG ascites.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: Whipple’s disease is characterized by the infiltration of small intestinal mucosa by foamy macrophages. Which one of the following histological stains is characteristically used to stain them?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Periodic acid Schiff

Whipple disease is a rare multisystem infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that primarily affects the small intestine, leading to malabsorption. The characteristic histopathological finding is the presence of foamy macrophages within the lamina propria that stain strongly positive with Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) due to the accumulation of glycoprotein-rich bacterial cell wall material.

Key points:

• Etiological agent: Tropheryma whipplei
• Histopathology: PAS-positive, diastase-resistant foamy macrophages in the small intestinal lamina propria
• Clinical features: Chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, arthralgia, fever, and lymphadenopathy
• Diagnosis: Duodenal biopsy with PAS staining, confirmed by PCR when required

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 2-year-old boy was brought to the emergency when his mother noticed that he had developed dusky appearance and lethargy over the past 6–8 hours. The child had been prescribed some medicine for vomiting by a local practitioner. Examination revealed normal sized pupils reacting to light, GCS 9, and shallow breathing with cyanosis. Arterial blood gas revealed a PaO₂ of 80 mmHg and SpO₂ of 60%. Which one of the following drugs may be implicated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metoclopramide

The child has cyanosis with a markedly low SpO₂ (60%) despite a relatively preserved PaO₂ (80 mmHg), suggesting methemoglobinemia.

Metoclopramide can rarely cause methemoglobinemia, particularly in young children, due to oxidation of hemoglobin from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, impairing oxygen delivery.

Why not the other options?

• A. Domperidone: Not classically associated with methemoglobinemia. Its important adverse effects include QT prolongation and cardiac arrhythmias.
• B. Granisetron: A 5-HT₃ antagonist used as an antiemetic. It is mainly associated with headache, constipation, and QT prolongation, not methemoglobinemia.
• C. Aprepitant: An NK₁ receptor antagonist. It can cause fatigue, hiccups, and drug interactions, but methemoglobinemia is not a characteristic toxicity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 29-year-old pregnant woman with iron deficiency anemia is started on iron and folic acid supplementation. Which of the following can be added to enhance the effectiveness of this treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin C

Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) enhances the absorption of non-heme iron by reducing ferric iron (Fe³⁺) to the more readily absorbable ferrous form (Fe²⁺) and maintaining an acidic gastric environment. Therefore, co-administration of vitamin C with oral iron improves the treatment of iron deficiency anemia, particularly during pregnancy when iron requirements are increased.

Why not the other options?

• Vitamin A: May improve erythropoiesis in vitamin A deficiency but does not directly enhance intestinal iron absorption.
• Vitamin B₁₂: Required for DNA synthesis and treatment of megaloblastic anemia, not iron deficiency anemia unless B₁₂ deficiency also exists.
• Vitamin D: Important for calcium and bone metabolism; has no significant role in improving iron absorption.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old female with irritable bowel syndrome presents with predominant symptom of diarrhea. Which of the following will be helpful in her treatment? 1. Loperamide 2. Lactulose 3. Lubiprostone 4. Sorbitol Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 only

• 1. Loperamide: Correct

• Loperamide is an opioid-receptor agonist acting peripherally in the gut.
• It decreases intestinal motility and secretion, making it useful for diarrhea-predominant IBS (IBS-D).

• 2. Lactulose: Incorrect

• Lactulose is an osmotic laxative that increases stool water and is therefore inappropriate in IBS-D.

• 3. Lubiprostone: Incorrect

• Lubiprostone is a chloride channel activator used primarily for IBS with constipation (IBS-C) and chronic constipation.

• 4. Sorbitol: Incorrect

• Sorbitol is an osmotic laxative and can worsen diarrhea.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient with peptic ulcer disease is prescribed proton pump inhibitors for four weeks but continues the medication for several months due to fear of recurrence. He later presents with pallor and fatigue. What is the most likely explanation for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HCl deficiency

Long-term proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy suppresses gastric acid (HCl) secretion, which reduces the conversion of dietary ferric iron (Fe³⁺) to the absorbable ferrous form (Fe²⁺). As a result, iron absorption decreases, predisposing patients to iron deficiency anemia, which presents with pallor and fatigue. Prolonged PPI use may also reduce the absorption of vitamin B₁₂, calcium, and magnesium.

Why not the other options?

• A. Gastrin deficiency: Incorrect. PPIs actually cause hypergastrinemia due to loss of acid-mediated negative feedback.
• B. Secretin overactivity: Incorrect. Secretin regulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion and has no significant role in iron absorption or PPI-induced anemia.
• D. Intrinsic factor deficiency: Incorrect. Intrinsic factor is produced by parietal cells and is required for vitamin B₁₂ absorption. PPIs do not directly reduce intrinsic factor production, although prolonged acid suppression can impair the release of vitamin B₁₂ from dietary proteins.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with a known history of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) presents with persistent regurgitation and bloating despite several weeks of proton pump inhibitor therapy. To improve his symptoms, the physician plans to prescribe a medication that enhances lower esophageal sphincter tone and accelerates gastric emptying. Which of the following agents would be the most appropriate choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Metoclopramide

Metoclopramide acts like a traffic controller for the gut, clearing congestion and tightening the gate (LES).

Mechanism:

• D₂ receptor antagonist
• ↑ Acetylcholine release in gut

Effects:

• ↑ Lower esophageal sphincter (LES) tone
• ↑ Gastric emptying
• ↓ Reflux

| Drug | Class | Mechanism | Use

| ---- | ----- | --------- | ---

| Omeprazole | PPI | ↓ H⁺ secretion | First-line GERD

| Vonoprazan | P-CAB | Strong acid suppression | Resistant GERD

| Metoclopramide | Prokinetic | ↑ LES tone + motility | Refractory GERD

| Sodium alginate | Barrier | Floating raft | Mild symptoms

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient develops postoperative ileus after abdominal surgery. Which of the following is the drug used for management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alvimopan

Postoperative ileus is worsened by opioid analgesics, which act on peripheral µ-opioid receptors in the gut myenteric plexus to suppress motility. Alvimopan is a peripherally-acting µ-opioid receptor antagonist (PAMORA) with negligible CNS penetration — it reverses opioid-induced gut stasis and accelerates return of bowel function without antagonizing central analgesia. It is FDA-approved specifically for accelerating GI recovery after bowel resection (short-term, in-hospital use only, due to MI risk with long-term use).

Other options:

• Atropine (B) and Glycopyrrolate (D) are antimuscarinics → block M₃ receptors → further ↓ motility; they would aggravate ileus.
• Loperamide (C) is a peripheral µ-opioid agonist → ↓ motility — used for diarrhea, exactly the wrong direction.
• Octreotide also ↓ GI secretions and motility → not useful.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An antiemetic was given to a chemotherapy patient, who then developed symptoms such as acute dystonia, bradykinesia, and tremors. Which of the following medications would have resulted in these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Metoclopramide

Chemotherapy patient → antiemetic given

• Now develops:

• Acute dystonia
• Bradykinesia
• Tremors

These are extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS), dopamine (D2) blockade in the brain.

Antiemetic that blocks D2 strongly: Metoclopramide, acts at:

• Chemoreceptor Trigger Zone (CTZ)
• GI tract (prokinetic)

Metoclopramide (D2 blockade)

↓

↓ Dopamine in nigrostriatal pathway

↓

Dopamine–Acetylcholine imbalance

↓

Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS)

↓

Dystonia, tremors, bradykinesia

| Drug | Mechanism | EPS Risk

| ---- | --------- | --------

| Metoclopramide | D2 blocker | High

| Ondansetron | 5-HT3 blocker | None

| Meclizine | H1 blocker | None

| Scopolamine | M blocker | None

| Type | Feature | Onset

| ---- | ------- | -----

| Acute dystonia | Neck spasm, oculogyric crisis | Hours–days

| Parkinsonism | Tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia | Days–weeks

| Akathisia | Restlessness | Weeks

| Tardive dyskinesia | Lip smacking | Months

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Aprepitant is a drug used in the treatment of some cases of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NK1 antagonist

Key clue:

• Chemotherapy-induced nausea & vomiting (CINV)

Think of the “big 3 antiemetic pathways”:

1. Serotonin (5-HT3)
2. Dopamine (D2)
3.

Substance P (NK1)

4.

Aprepitant belongs to the Substance P pathway. Aprepitant = Neurokinin-1 (NK1) receptor antagonist

5. Blocks Substance P

Acts at:

• Vomiting center (medulla)
• Chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ)

Chemotherapy

↓

Enterochromaffin cells release serotonin

↓

5-HT3 activation → acute vomiting

+

Substance P release (brainstem)

↓

NK1 receptor activation → delayed vomiting

Aprepitant blocks NK1 receptors

↓

Prevents delayed phase vomiting

| Phase | Mediator | Drug

| ----- | -------- | ----

| Acute (0–24 hr) | Serotonin (5-HT3) | Ondansetron

| Delayed (>24 hr) | Substance P | Aprepitant

| Drug | Mechanism | Use

| ---- | --------- | ---

| Aprepitant | NK1 antagonist | CINV (delayed phase)

| Ondansetron | 5-HT3 antagonist | Acute vomiting

| Metoclopramide | D2 antagonist | General antiemetic

| Domperidone | Peripheral D2 blocker | GI motility

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Melanosis coli (brownish discoloration of colonic mucosa) can occur due to the long-term consumption of which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stimulant laxatives

Melanosis coli is a benign brown-black pigmentation of the colonic mucosa caused by accumulation of lipofuscin pigment within macrophages in the lamina propria. It is classically associated with long-term use of anthraquinone-containing stimulant laxatives, such as senna and cascara.

Why not the other options?

• B. NSAIDs: Can cause gastritis, peptic ulceration, and enteropathy, but are not a classic cause of melanosis coli.
• C. Proton pump inhibitors: Not associated with melanosis coli.
• D. 3rd-generation cephalosporins: May cause antibiotic-associated diarrhea/C. difficile infection but do not cause melanosis coli.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Melanosis coli, which occurs due to long-term consumption of stimulant laxatives, presents as brown discoloration of colonic mucosa due to deposition of which one of the following pigments?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lipofuscin

Melanosis coli is a benign, reversible pigmentation of the colonic mucosa caused by chronic use of stimulant laxatives, particularly anthraquinone-containing laxatives such as senna, cascara, and aloe.

Despite its name, the brown-black discoloration is not due to melanin. It results from accumulation of lipofuscin pigment within macrophages in the lamina propria following apoptosis of colonic epithelial cells induced by stimulant laxatives.

Why not the other options?

• A. Melanin: Incorrect. Despite the name melanosis coli, melanin is not deposited.
• B. Hemosiderin: Incorrect. Iron storage pigment seen after hemorrhage or iron overload, not in melanosis coli.
• D. Hemoglobin: Incorrect. Does not accumulate as a pigment in the colonic mucosa.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The investigation of choice for early follow-up in patients treated for anti-H. pylori drugs is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Urea breath test

The urea breath test (UBT) is the investigation of choice for confirming eradication of Helicobacter pylori after completion of therapy. It is non-invasive, has high sensitivity and specificity, and detects active infection, making it ideal for early follow-up.

Why not the other options?

• B. Rapid urease test: Requires endoscopy and is not routinely used for follow-up.
• C. Stool H. pylori antigen test: Also detects active infection and is an acceptable alternative, but UBT is considered the preferred test.
• D. Serology for H. pylori: Not useful for follow-up, as antibodies may remain positive for months to years after successful eradication.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which is a contraindication to stimulant purgatives?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Postoperative paralytic ileus

Stimulant purgatives:

• Senna
• Bisacodyl
• Cascara

They increase intestinal motility.

Contraindicated in:

• Intestinal obstruction
• Paralytic ileus
• Acute surgical abdomen

Because stimulation against obstructed/paralyzed bowel may worsen complications.

Used in:

• Opioid-induced constipation
• Atonic constipation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs used in the treatment of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) has a direct spasmolytic action on gastrointestinal (GI) smooth muscle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mebeverine

Mebeverine:

• A direct smooth muscle relaxant
