• Works independently of autonomic receptors

Mechanism of Action

• Blocks sodium channels in smooth muscle
• Reduces calcium influx indirectly
• → Decreases contractility
• → Relieves intestinal spasm

| Type of Drug | Example | Mechanism

| ------------ | ------- | ---------

| Direct spasmolytic | Mebeverine | Acts directly on muscle

| Anticholinergic | Dicyclomine, Scopolamine | Blocks M receptors

| Antisecretory | Racecadotril | ↓ intestinal secretion

| Drug | Mechanism | IBS Role | Side Effects

| ---- | --------- | -------- | ------------

| Mebeverine | Direct muscle relaxant | Best for pain/spasm | Minimal

| Dicyclomine | Anticholinergic | Useful | Anticholinergic effects

| Scopolamine | Anticholinergic | Limited | CNS + anticholinergic

| Racecadotril | ↓ secretion | Diarrhea | Minimal

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is correct treatment of peptic ulcer associated with H. pylori?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Omeprazole, Clarithromycin and Metronidazole

H. pylori peptic ulcer requires triple therapy with a proton pump inhibitor plus two antibiotics.

• Colonizes gastric mucosa
• Produces urease → ammonia → mucosal damage

• Causes:

• Chronic gastritis
• Peptic ulcer

Standard Triple Therapy

• PPI (e.g., Omeprazole)
• Clarithromycin
• Amoxicillin (or Metronidazole if penicillin allergy)

Important Tests:

• Urea breath test
• Stool antigen test

Complications of H. pylori:

• Gastric carcinoma
• MALT lymphoma

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements about Lafutidine is incorrect? 1. Increases gastric mucosal blood flow 2. Acts as an H₂ receptor antagonist 3. Decreases nitric oxide production 4. Increases somatostatin secretion+
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3 only

Lafutidine is a second-generation H₂ receptor antagonist used for:

• Peptic ulcer disease
• GERD
• Gastritis
• Stress ulcer prophylaxis

What makes it special is that it has both acid-suppressing and mucosal-protective actions.

Correct answer is C because lafutidine is an H₂ receptor antagonist that enhances mucosal defense by increasing gastric mucosal blood flow and stimulating protective mediators. It is known to promote nitric oxide–mediated mucosal protection rather than decrease nitric oxide production. Protective effects include:

| Effect | Mechanism

| ------ | ---------

| ↑ Gastric mucosal blood flow | via nitric oxide

| ↑ Prostaglandin synthesis | mucosal protection

| ↑ Somatostatin secretion | inhibits gastrin

| ↑ Mucus secretion | barrier protection

Thus it protects gastric mucosa beyond acid suppression.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct with regard to peptic ulcer prophylaxis?
options: Stress ulceration during clinical illness is uncommon
Ulcer prophylaxis should be continued once absorption of enteral feed is established
Proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) are effective at reducing the incidence of ulceration
PPIs when used with antibiotics may decrease the risk of Clostridium difficile infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) are effective at reducing the incidence of ulceration

Stress ulcer prophylaxis is indicated in critically ill patients at high risk (e.g., mechanical ventilation >48 hours, coagulopathy, severe burns, traumatic brain injury). Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) effectively reduce the incidence of stress-related gastric and duodenal ulceration and upper GI bleeding.

Why not the other options?

• A. Stress ulceration during clinical illness is uncommon: Stress-related mucosal injury is common in critically ill patients, not uncommon.
• B. Ulcer prophylaxis should be continued once absorption of enteral feed is established: Ulcer prophylaxis should be discontinued once adequate enteral feeding is established, as enteral nutrition itself is protective.
• D. PPIs when used with antibiotics may decrease the risk of Clostridium difficile infection: PPIs increase, rather than decrease, the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, especially when used with antibiotics.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding peptic ulceration is not correct?
options: Most peptic ulcers are caused by Helicobacter pylori or NSAIDs.
Gastric ulcers are more common than duodenal ulcers
Gastric antisecretory agents and H. pylori eradication therapy are the mainstays of treatment.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gastric ulcers are more common than duodenal ulcers

• (a) Most peptic ulcers are caused by Helicobacter pylori or NSAIDs: Correct. The two major causes of peptic ulcer disease are H. pylori infection and NSAID use.
• (b) Gastric ulcers are more common than duodenal ulcers: Incorrect: Duodenal ulcers are generally more common than gastric ulcers.
• (c) Gastric ulcers may be malignant: Correct. A gastric ulcer may be malignant, so gastric ulcers require appropriate evaluation, often including biopsy.
• (d) Gastric antisecretory agents and H. pylori eradication therapy are the mainstays of treatment: Correct: Treatment includes acid suppression (usually PPI) and H. pylori eradication when infection is present, along with removal of offending factors such as NSAIDs when possible.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Why is atropine mixed with diphenoxylate in combination medications?
options: Atropine decreases the adverse effect of diphenoxylate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. To prevent abuse of diphenoxylate

Diphenoxylate + Atropine (e.g., Lomotil)

• Diphenoxylate → opioid derivative (antidiarrheal)
• Atropine → anticholinergic (very low dose in combo)

Diphenoxylate is an opioid that can cause euphoria in high doses. A small amount of atropine is added to produce unpleasant anticholinergic effects if overdosed. This discourages intentional misuse while preserving antidiarrheal action. The combination is designed as an abuse-deterrent formulation.

Diphenoxylate taken in high dose

↓

Atropine also increases

↓

Anticholinergic toxicity

↓

Unpleasant symptoms

↓

Discourages abuse

| Component | Role

| --------- | ----

| Diphenoxylate | Antidiarrheal (opioid)

| Atropine | Abuse deterrent

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: With regard to Helicobacter pylori eradication in peptic ulcer disease, consider the following statements: 1. Proton-pump inhibitor is taken with two antibiotics. 2. Treatment is prescribed for at least 7 days. 3. Treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection leads to vitamin B12 deficiency. 4. Patients requiring long-term NSAIDs should undergo Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy to reduce ulcer risk. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy is recommended for patients with H. pylori-associated peptic ulcer disease to promote ulcer healing, prevent recurrence, and reduce the risk of complications.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Proton-pump inhibitor is taken with two antibiotics: Correct. Standard eradication therapy consists of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) combined with two antibiotics (e.g., clarithromycin with amoxicillin or metronidazole) or bismuth-based quadruple therapy.
• Statement 2. Treatment is prescribed for at least 7 days: Correct. Treatment is prescribed for at least 7 days, although 10–14 days (preferably 14 days) is currently recommended because of higher eradication rates.
• Statement 3. Treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection leads to vitamin B12 deficiency: Incorrect. H. pylori eradication does not cause vitamin B₁₂ deficiency. In fact, chronic H. pylori infection can lead to atrophic gastritis and impaired vitamin B₁₂ absorption, and eradication may improve B₁₂ status.
• Statement 4. Patients requiring long-term NSAIDs should undergo Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy to reduce ulcer risk: Correct. Patients who require long-term NSAID therapy should be tested for and treated for H. pylori infection, as eradication reduces the risk of NSAID-associated peptic ulcers.

Current first-line regimens:

• Bismuth quadruple therapy (preferred in many regions): PPI + Bismuth + Tetracycline + Metronidazole
• Concomitant therapy: PPI + Amoxicillin + Clarithromycin + Metronidazole

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following about the enteric nervous regulation system is false? 1. Interstitial cells of Cajal are pacemakers 2. It can function independently of the brain and spinal cord 3. All the afferents are from the vagus nerve 4. Myenteric plexus is in the Lamina propria
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3, 4

The Enteric Nervous System (ENS) is like a quiet maestro conducting digestion:

• Coordinates motility, secretion, and blood flow
• Works independently of CNS (but can be modulated by it)

Can function independently of CNS input. Interstitial cells of Cajal act as pacemakers generating slow waves. Afferents are not exclusively vagal; significant intrinsic and spinal afferents exist.

| Feature | Myenteric (Auerbach) | Submucosal (Meissner)

| ------- | -------------------- | ---------------------

| Location | Between muscle layers | Submucosa

| Function | Motility | Secretion, blood flow

| Extent | Entire GI tract | Mainly small intestine

Clinical correlations

| Disease | Defect

| ------- | ------

| Hirschsprung disease | Absence of ganglion cells

| Achalasia | Loss of inhibitory neurons

| IBS | Dysregulated ENS

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following gastrointestinal secretions contain bicarbonate? 1. Stomach 2. Saliva 3. Duodenal 4. Ileal Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3, 4

All four secretions can contain bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻):

| GI secretion | Key point

| ------------ | ---------

| 1. Stomach | Surface mucous cells secrete HCO₃⁻, forming the gastric mucosal bicarbonate barrier

| 2. Saliva | Contains HCO₃⁻, important for buffering

| 3. Duodenal | Brunner glands and pancreatic/biliary secretions provide abundant HCO₃⁻ to neutralize gastric acid

| 4. Ileal | Intestinal epithelial secretion contains HCO₃⁻; Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange contributes to intestinal bicarbonate handling

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following sites has the least concentration of sodium ions in the fluid?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Salivary glands

GI secretions are not static liquids. They get modified along ducts and segments like a river changing chemistry as it flows.

Saliva is the only GI fluid that becomes hypotonic

→ meaning Na⁺ gets reabsorbed more than water

Acinar cells → Secrete isotonic fluid (Na⁺ high)

↓

Ductal cells → Reabsorb Na⁺ & Cl⁻

↓

Final saliva → Hypotonic (Na⁺ ↓↓↓, K⁺ ↑)

Ducts are impermeable to water

→ Na⁺ leaves, water cannot follow → dilution happens

| Site | Na⁺ Concentration | Key Feature

| ---- | ----------------- | -----------

| Saliva | Lowest | Hypotonic

| Stomach | Moderate | HCl secretion dominates

| Duodenum | Higher | Mixing with pancreatic juice

| Ileum | Near isotonic | Absorption ongoing

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following hormones is responsible for gallbladder contraction and release of bile into duodenum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cholecystokinin

Cholecystokinin (CCK) is a hormone secreted by the I cells of the duodenum and jejunum in response to fatty acids and amino acids in the intestinal lumen. It is the principal hormone responsible for gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, facilitating the release of bile into the duodenum for fat digestion.

• Secretin: Stimulates bicarbonate-rich secretion from the pancreas and bile ducts; does not cause gallbladder contraction.
• Gastrin: Stimulates gastric acid secretion and gastric mucosal growth.
• Cholecystokinin (CCK): Contracts the gallbladder, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, stimulates enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion, and slows gastric emptying.
• Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP): Relaxes gastrointestinal smooth muscle and increases intestinal water and electrolyte secretion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with ulcerative colitis is experiencing three episodes of bleeding in stools per day but is otherwise stable. What is the appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 5-Aminosalicylic acid

Mild ulcerative colitis with limited bleeding and stable vitals is treated with 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) as first-line therapy. It acts locally to reduce mucosal inflammation and induces remission. Steroids and immunomodulators are reserved for moderate–severe or refractory disease. 5-ASA is standard initial treatment in mild UC. Mechanism of Action-

Inhibits:

• Cyclooxygenase (COX)
• ↓ Prostaglandins

Reduces local inflammation in colon

| Severity | Clinical features | Treatment

| -------- | ----------------- | ---------

| Mild–moderate | ≤4–6 stools/day, minimal systemic signs | 5-ASA ✔

| Moderate–severe | Frequent stools + systemic symptoms | Steroids

| Severe | Toxic megacolon risk | IV steroids / biologics

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Among the extra intestinal manifestations of Crohn’s disease, which one of the following is related to the disease activity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Eye complications (Iritis/Uveitis)

• Extraintestinal manifestations (EIMs) occur in 25–40% of patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Some manifestations parallel intestinal disease activity, while others occur independently.
• Eye manifestations (episcleritis, iritis, uveitis) are commonly associated with active Crohn’s disease and may improve with treatment of the intestinal inflammation.

Why not other options?

• B. Renal calculi

• Not related to disease activity.
• Occur due to hyperoxaluria from ileal disease or resection.

• C. Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)

• Usually independent of bowel disease activity.
• More commonly associated with ulcerative colitis than Crohn’s disease.

• D. Chronic active hepatitis:

• Not directly related to Crohn’s disease activity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding inflammatory bowel disease: 1. Ulcerative colitis (UC) involves terminal ileum and rarely causes proctitis. 2. Cobblestone appearance of bowel is seen in Crohn’s disease. 3. Skip lesions are a characteristic of ulcerative colitis but never seen in Crohn’s disease. 4. Ulcerative colitis is more common in smokers than non-smokers. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 only

Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, skip lesions, and a cobblestone appearance, and can involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus. Ulcerative colitis (UC) causes continuous mucosal inflammation, beginning in the rectum (proctitis) and extending proximally.

• 2. Cobblestone appearance of bowel is seen in Crohn’s disease ✔️: Cobblestone appearance is a classic feature of Crohn disease.

Why are the other statements incorrect?

• 1. Ulcerative colitis (UC) involves terminal ileum and rarely causes proctitis ❌: UC always involves the rectum and rarely involves the terminal ileum (except backwash ileitis in extensive disease).
• 3. Ulcerative colitis is more common in smokers than non-smokers ❌: Skip lesions are characteristic of Crohn disease, not UC.
• 4. Ulcerative colitis is more common in smokers than non-smokers ❌: Smoking increases the risk of Crohn disease, whereas it is protective against UC.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In contrast to Ulcerative Colitis, which of the following statements regarding Crohn's disease is true?
options: There is no increased risk of colon cancer
Continuous involvement rather than skip lesions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perianal fistulas are frequent

Crohn disease causes transmural inflammation, leading to fissures, abscesses, and frequent perianal fistulas. It shows skip lesions and has an increased colorectal cancer risk with long-standing colonic involvement.

| Feature | Crohn | UC

| ------- | ----- | ---

| Pattern | Skip lesions | Continuous

| Depth | Transmural | Mucosal

| Fistula | Common | Rare

| Perianal disease | Common | Rare

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Onion skin fibrosis on histopathology is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Primary sclerosing cholangitis

Onion-skin” periductal concentric fibrosis is the histologic hallmark of primary sclerosing cholangitis.

Unknown trigger (autoimmune + gut-liver axis)

↓

Chronic inflammation of intra & extrahepatic bile ducts

↓

Periductal fibrosis (concentric layers)

↓

Bile duct strictures (“beading”)

↓

Cholestasis → cirrhosis → liver failure

It reflects chronic inflammatory obliteration of intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts leading to multifocal strictures. Primary biliary cirrhosis shows portal granulomas and ductopenia, not onion-skin fibrosis. This classic pattern is a high-yield buzzword for PSC.

Small bile duct showing an “onion-skin” type of periductal fibrosis

Beaded bile ducts in primary sclerosing cholangitis

| Feature | PSC | PBC

| ------- | --- | ---

| Ducts involved | Intra + extrahepatic | Small intrahepatic

| Histology | Onion-skin fibrosis | Florid duct lesion

| Antibody | p-ANCA | AMA

| Association | Ulcerative colitis | Autoimmune diseases

| Imaging | Beading | Normal early

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The Truelove and Witt criteria are used for assessing which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute severe ulcerative colitis

Truelove and Witt's Criteria for Severity of Ulcerative Colitis

Acute Severe UC: ≥6 bloody stools/day + ≥1 systemic toxicity sign:

• Tachycardia (>90)
• Fever (>37.8°C)
• Anemia (Hb <10.5)
• Raised ESR (>30)

| Step | Treatment

| ---- | ---------

| 1 | Hospitalization

| 2 | IV corticosteroids (1st line)

| 3 | If no response (3–5 days) → Cyclosporine / Infliximab

| 4 | Surgery (colectomy) if refractory

Should also learn Montreal grading for Crohn’s disease; maybe asked in future:

1. Age at Onset

• A1: < 16 years
• A2: 17–40 years
• A3: > 40 years

2. Disease Location

• L1: Ileal
• L2: Colonic
• L3: Ileocolonic
• L4: Isolated upper GI disease*

L4 is a modifier and can be added to L1–L3 if upper GI involvement is present.

3. Disease Behavior

• B1: Non-stricturing, non-penetrating (inflammatory)
• B2: Stricturing
• B3: Penetrating
• p (modifier): Perianal disease

‘p’ is added to B1–B3 if perianal disease is present.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which JAK inhibitor drug is recommended for moderate to severe ulcerative colitis in a patient who is not responding well to TNF-alpha blockers?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tofacitinib

Tofacitinib:

• Class: JAK inhibitor (Janus kinase inhibitor)
• Type: Oral small molecule (unlike biologics which are injectable)

Mild UC

↓

5-ASA (Mesalamine)

↓ (if not controlled)

Steroids

↓

Moderate–Severe UC

↓

Anti-TNF (Infliximab)

↓ (failure)

Tofacitinib / Vedolizumab / Ustekinumab

| Drug | Class | Mechanism | Use in IBD

| ---- | ----- | --------- | ----------

| Infliximab | Anti-TNF | Blocks TNF-α | UC, Crohn

| Etanercept | Anti-TNF | TNF receptor fusion protein | ❌ Not in IBD

| Vedolizumab | Anti-integrin | Blocks gut lymphocyte entry | UC, Crohn

| Ustekinumab | Anti IL-12/23 | ↓ Th1/Th17 | UC, Crohn

| Tofacitinib | JAK inhibitor | Blocks cytokine signaling | UC (oral)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following biologic agents used in the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease acts by inhibiting the enzyme 'Janus Kinase'?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tofacitinib

Tofacitinib is an oral targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (tsDMARD) that acts by inhibiting Janus kinase (JAK) enzymes, primarily JAK1 and JAK3. This blocks the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, thereby reducing the production of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines involved in immune-mediated diseases.

In inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), tofacitinib is approved for the treatment of moderate to severe ulcerative colitis in patients who have had an inadequate response or intolerance to conventional therapy or anti-TNF agents.

Why not the other options?

• A. Infliximab: A chimeric monoclonal antibody against TNF-α; used in Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.
• B. Adalimumab: A fully human monoclonal antibody against TNF-α.
• C. Vedolizumab: A monoclonal antibody against α4β7 integrin, preventing lymphocyte migration specifically into the gastrointestinal tract.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Integrated Gi Hpb
questions.text: The serologic marker detectable during the ‘window’ period of hepatitis B infection is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anti-HBc IgM

The window period of hepatitis B infection is the interval when HBsAg has disappeared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared. During this period, the only reliable serological marker is anti-HBc IgM.

Why not the other options?

• A. Anti-HBsAb: Appears after the window period, indicating recovery or vaccination.
• B. Anti-HBc IgG: Appears later and persists lifelong; not the marker of the window period.
• D. HBeAg: Marker of active viral replication and high infectivity, not specific for the window period.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 42-year-old man with history of alcohol dependency presents with progressive abdominal distension. Abdominal examination reveals shifting dullness. Which one of the following is the most appropriate drug to relieve this abdominal distension?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Spironolactone

The patient has ascites secondary to alcoholic liver cirrhosis with portal hypertension, as suggested by progressive abdominal distension and shifting dullness. The first-line pharmacological treatment for cirrhotic ascites is spironolactone, an aldosterone antagonist, because secondary hyperaldosteronism is the primary mechanism of sodium and water retention in cirrhosis.

In liver cirrhosis:

• Portal hypertension causes splanchnic vasodilation and reduced effective arterial blood volume.
• This activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), leading to secondary hyperaldosteronism.
• Spironolactone blocks aldosterone, promoting sodium excretion and reducing ascites.

Why not the other options?

• A. Octreotide: Used in acute variceal bleeding and some cases of hepatorenal syndrome, not for routine management of ascites.
• B. Propranolol: A non-selective β-blocker used for primary and secondary prophylaxis of esophageal variceal bleeding, not for treating ascites.
• C. Lactulose: Used for the treatment and prevention of hepatic encephalopathy by reducing ammonia absorption; it does not relieve ascites.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic presented with abdominal pain, jaundice and weight loss. He has hypoglycemia and elevated alpha fetoprotein levels (600ng/ml) but has normal AST and ALT. Which of the following is a likely diagnosis of the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hepatocellular carcinoma

• Chronic alcoholic → chronic liver disease risk
• Abdominal pain + jaundice + weight loss → malignancy suspicion
• Hypoglycemia → paraneoplastic clue
• AFP = 600 ng/ml → tumor marker (normal: 10-25)
• Normal AST/ALT → not active hepatitis

Put together → Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)

Classic Triad of HCC:

• Weight loss
• Abdominal pain
• Liver mass

Other Paraneoplastic Features:

• Hypoglycemia
• Polycythemia (↑ EPO)
• Hypercalcemia

Imaging Hallmark:

• Arterial phase enhancement + venous washout (CT/MRI)

| Feature | HCC | Cirrhosis | Hepatitis | Cholangiocarcinoma

| ------- | --- | --------- | --------- | ------------------

| AFP | ↑↑ | Normal | Normal | Normal

| AST/ALT | Normal/slightly ↑ | Mild ↑ | ↑↑ | Mild ↑

| Hypoglycemia | Yes | No | No | No

| Cause | Cirrhosis | Alcohol, viral | Infection | Bile duct malignancy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a history of consumption of 2-3 drinks per week comes with complaints of right upper quadrant discomfort. He has grade 2 steatosis. His BMI was 29 kg/m² and AST and ALT levels were slightly elevated. What would you advise him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lifestyle modification and weight loss

This is metabolic liver disease, not alcohol-driven.

Pathogenesis:

• Insulin resistance → ↑ lipolysis
• Fat accumulation in liver (steatosis)
• Oxidative stress → inflammation → NASH → fibrosis

First-line therapy is weight reduction through diet and exercise, which improves steatosis and transaminases.

Key interventions:

• Weight loss (≥7–10% body weight)
• Exercise
• Diet control (low sugar, low fat)

This can:

• Reverse steatosis
• Improve inflammation
• Prevent progression to cirrhosis

Drugs like vitamin E or pioglitazone are reserved for NASH not responding to lifestyle modification.

Resmetirom (VERY IMPORTANT – 2024 FDA approval)

• Class: Selective thyroid hormone receptor-β (THR-β) agonist
• Mechanism: ↓ hepatic lipogenesis + ↑ β-oxidation → ↓ liver fat
• Indication: Noncirrhotic NASH (MASH) with fibrosis (F2–F3)
• Benefit: Improves steatosis + inflammation + fibrosis (histologic improvement)
• Adverse effects: Diarrhea, pruritus, mild ↑ LFTs
• Key point: First FDA-approved drug for NASH (2024)

Vitamin E (classic NEET favorite)

• Dose: 800 IU/day
• Indication: Non-diabetic NASH patients
• Benefit: Improves steatosis & inflammation (NOT fibrosis)
• Caution: ↑ risk of prostate cancer & hemorrhagic stroke (long-term)

Pioglitazone

• Class: PPAR-γ agonist
• Indication: NASH (especially diabetics)
• Effect: Improves steatosis + inflammation ± fibrosis
• Side effects: Weight gain, edema, CHF risk

GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., Semaglutide)

• Weight loss → ↓ liver fat
• Improves NASH resolution (fibrosis benefit less clear)
• Not officially approved for NASH yet (exam trap)

Obeticholic acid

• FXR agonist
• Improves fibrosis
• Not FDA approved yet (important MCQ trap)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with chronic liver disease presented with jaundice and melena. On examination, there is ascites and mild hepatosplenomegaly. Which of the following is not part of the management of his encephalopathy?
options: Beta blocker to stop variceal bleed
Ascitic tap to rule out SBP
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Beta blocker to stop variceal bleed

• Jaundice → hepatocellular dysfunction
• Melena → variceal bleed (precipitating factor)
• Ascites → portal hypertension
• Hepatosplenomegaly → chronicity

Most important: This patient is at high risk of hepatic encephalopathy (HE)

Hepatic encephalopathy management focuses on identifying precipitating factors like GI bleed, SBP, and renal failure. Ascitic tap is essential to rule out SBP, and evaluation for hepatorenal syndrome is required.

Liver failure / portosystemic shunting

↓

Ammonia not detoxified (NH3 ↑)

↓

Crosses BBB

↓

Astrocyte swelling (glutamine ↑)

↓

Cerebral edema + neurotransmitter imbalance

↓

Hepatic encephalopathy

HE Management-  You don’t treat HE directly first, you identify and treat precipitating factors

Common Precipitating Factors:

• GI bleed
• Infection (SBP)
• Renal failure (HRS)
• Electrolyte imbalance

| Phase | Treatment

| ----- | ---------

| Acute bleed | Octreotide / Terlipressin

| Stabilization | Endoscopic band ligation

| Prevention | Beta blockers

| Drug | Mechanism

| ---- | ---------

| Lactulose | ↓ ammonia absorption (acidifies gut)

| Rifaximin | ↓ gut bacteria producing ammonia

Important points:

1. GI bleed = MOST common trigger of HE

• Blood → protein → ammonia ↑

2. Asterixis = hallmark sign

• “Flapping tremor”

3. Serum ammonia levels

• Helpful but NOT always correlating with severity

4. Always do diagnostic paracentesis in ascites + deterioration

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young lady presents with jaundice and pruritus. She is antimitochondrial antibody positive and ANA negative. Biopsy shows portal inflammation and ductular proliferation with lymphocytic infiltrate. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary biliary cholangitis

A chronic autoimmune cholestatic liver disease characterized by:

• Destruction of intrahepatic small bile ducts
• Leads to cholestasis → bile accumulation → liver damage

Think of bile ducts slowly “vanishing” under immune attack

A florid duct lesion in a primary biliary cholangitis patient. A chronic inflammatory infiltrate made of lymphocytes and plasma cells surrounds and destroys the bile duct.

| Feature | PBC | PSC | AIH

| ------- | --- | --- | ---

| Gender | Female | Male | Female

| Antibody | AMA | p-ANCA | ANA, ASMA

| Ducts involved | Intrahepatic | Intra + extrahepatic | Hepatocytes

| Disease type | Cholestatic | Cholestatic | Hepatocellular

| Association | Autoimmune | IBD (UC) | Autoimmune

| Imaging | Normal early | Beading of ducts | Normal

| Treatment | Role

| --------- | ----

| Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) | First-line

| Obeticholic acid | Second-line

| Liver transplant | Advanced disease

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Carotenoderma, due to ingestion of excessive amounts of carotene-containing fruits and vegetables, can be distinguished from jaundice by sparing of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sclerae

Carotenoderma results from excessive intake of β-carotene-rich foods (e.g., carrots, pumpkin, sweet potatoes). It causes yellow-orange discoloration of the skin, especially over the palms, soles, and nasolabial folds, but spares the sclerae, distinguishing it from jaundice, in which scleral icterus is the earliest clinical sign.

Why not the other options?

• A. Palms: Commonly affected in carotenoderma.
• B. Soles: Commonly affected in carotenoderma.
• C. Nasolabial folds: May also show yellow discoloration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to jaundice: 1. Presence of scleral icterus indicates a serum bilirubin level of at least 3 mg/dL. 2. If the examiner suspects scleral icterus, second site to examine is underneath the tongue. 3. In long-standing jaundice, skin may become green due to reduction of bilirubin to biliverdin. 4. Sclerae have a particular affinity for bilirubin due to its high elastin content. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4 only

Jaundice becomes clinically apparent when serum bilirubin exceeds approximately 2–3 mg/dL. Scleral icterus is the earliest clinical sign because the sclera is rich in elastin, which has a high affinity for bilirubin. If scleral icterus is doubtful, the undersurface of the tongue (sublingual mucosa) should be examined, as it is another early site of bilirubin deposition.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Presence of scleral icterus indicates a serum bilirubin level of at least 3 mg/dL ✔️: Clinically, scleral icterus is usually evident when bilirubin is \~2–3 mg/dL.
• 2. If scleral icterus is suspected\, examine underneath the tongue ✔️: The sublingual mucosa is an early site for detecting jaundice.
• 3. In long-standing jaundice\, skin may become green due to reduction of bilirubin to biliverdin ❌: The green discoloration is due to oxidation of bilirubin to biliverdin, not reduction.
• 4. Sclerae have a particular affinity for bilirubin due to high elastin content ✔️: Correct.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a patient who has undergone gastrectomy, vitamin supplementation required is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vit B12

1. Parietal cells (stomach) produce:

• Intrinsic Factor (IF)
• HCl

2. Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin):

• Comes from diet (animal products)
• Initially binds to R-protein (haptocorrin)

3. In duodenum:

• Pancreatic enzymes free B12
• B12 binds to Intrinsic Factor

4. Terminal ileum:

• IF-B12 complex absorbed via specific receptors

Gastrectomy removes parietal cells that produce intrinsic factor, which is essential for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Loss of intrinsic factor leads to B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anemia if not supplemented.

Dietary B12

↓

Binds R-protein (stomach)

↓

Pancreatic enzymes release B12 (duodenum)

↓

Binds Intrinsic Factor

↓

Terminal ileum absorption

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Anemia | Megaloblastic (↑ MCV)

| Neurological signs | Subacute combined degeneration

| Glossitis | “Beefy red tongue”

| Lab | ↓ B12, ↑ homocysteine, ↑ methylmalonic acid

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Poorly absorbed antibiotics are often used as adjunctive therapies in patients with hepatic encephalopathy. These may include:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Neomycin or Rifaximin

Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a reversible neuropsychiatric complication of advanced liver disease caused primarily by the accumulation of ammonia and other gut-derived neurotoxins. Poorly absorbed oral antibiotics are used as adjuncts to lactulose to reduce intestinal ammonia production by suppressing ammonia-producing gut bacteria.

Key points:

• Rifaximin is the preferred poorly absorbed antibiotic for the prevention of recurrent hepatic encephalopathy.
• Neomycin is an alternative agent but is used less frequently due to the risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
• Lactulose remains the first-line therapy, while rifaximin is added in patients with recurrent episodes or inadequate response.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The single most important treatment and prognostic factor in alcohol-related liver disease is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cessation of alcohol consumption

Complete abstinence from alcohol is the single most important treatment and the strongest predictor of long-term survival in patients with alcohol-related liver disease (ALD), irrespective of the stage of liver disease. Abstinence halts ongoing hepatocyte injury, improves liver function, reduces portal hypertension, and decreases the risk of progression to cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation, and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Why not the other options?

• A. N-acetylcysteine (NAC): Primarily used for acetaminophen toxicity; may be used as an adjunct in severe alcoholic hepatitis with corticosteroids but is not the cornerstone of treatment.
• C. Liver transplantation: Reserved for end-stage liver disease or selected patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis who fail medical therapy; it is not the first-line treatment.
• D. High-dose vitamin E: Has a role in selected patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), not alcohol-related liver disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of resmetirom used in MASH?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thyroid hormone receptor-β agonist

• Resmetirom is a selective Thyroid hormone receptor beta (THR-β) agonist
• Used in: MASH (Metabolic syndrome associated steatohepatitis) with fibrosis

Mechanism:

Activation of hepatic THR-β:

• Increases lipid metabolism
• Reduces hepatic fat accumulation
• Improves steatohepatitis

Important point:

• THR-β selectivity minimizes cardiac adverse effects associated with THR-α stimulation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are correct with regard to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency? 1. Prolonged jaundice in neonatal period. 2. Pulmonary emphysema in adulthood. 3. Panniculitis is seen rarely. 4. Autosomal dominant disorder. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency is an autosomal codominant disorder caused by mutations in the SERPINA1 gene. Deficiency of AAT results in uninhibited neutrophil elastase activity, causing panacinar emphysema, while accumulation of abnormal AAT in hepatocytes leads to liver disease.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Prolonged jaundice in neonatal period ✔️ – Due to neonatal cholestasis from liver involvement.
• 2. Pulmonary emphysema in adulthood ✔️ – Typically early-onset panacinar emphysema, especially in the lower lobes.
• 3. Panniculitis is seen rarely ✔️ – An uncommon but recognized manifestation.
• 4. Autosomal dominant disorder ❌ – Incorrect. It is autosomal codominant (not autosomal dominant).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are precipitating factors for hepatic encephalopathy? 1. Hypokalemia 2. Septicemia 3. Increased dietary protein load Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a potentially reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome seen in patients with advanced liver disease or portosystemic shunting. It is most commonly precipitated by factors that increase ammonia production, decrease ammonia clearance, or worsen cerebral susceptibility to ammonia.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Hypokalemia: Correct. Hypokalemia increases renal ammonia production and promotes metabolic alkalosis, facilitating ammonia entry into the brain, thereby precipitating HE.
• Statement 2. Septicemia: Correct. Septicemia (infection) is a common precipitating factor due to increased catabolism and systemic inflammation.
• Statement 3. Increased dietary protein load: Correct. Increased dietary protein load (especially in susceptible patients) increases intestinal ammonia production and can precipitate HE.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs can cause granulomatous liver injury? 1. Carbamazepine 2. Allopurinol 3. Diltiazem 4. Acetaminophen Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Granulomatous hepatitis is a rare form of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) characterized by hepatic granuloma formation. Common offending drugs include carbamazepine, allopurinol, diltiazem, sulfonamides, phenytoin, and quinidine.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Carbamazepine ✔️ – Recognized cause of granulomatous hepatitis.
• 2. Allopurinol ✔️ – Can cause hypersensitivity syndrome with granulomatous liver injury.
• 3. Diltiazem ✔️ – An established cause of granulomatous hepatitis.
• 4. Acetaminophen (Paracetamol) ❌ – Causes dose-dependent centrilobular (zone 3) hepatic necrosis, not granulomatous hepatitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following medications is most commonly associated with cholestasis in the absence of significant portal inflammation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Estrogens/ Androgens

Estrogens and anabolic androgens classically cause bland cholestasis with canalicular bile stasis and minimal portal inflammation.

Estrogens / anabolic steroids

↓

Inhibit bile salt export pump (BSEP)

↓

Impaired bile flow

↓

Bile accumulation in hepatocytes & canaliculi

↓

Cholestasis (without inflammation)

Micrograph showing bile (yellow) stasis in liver tissue, i.e. cholestasis.

Bland Cholestasis- bile stasis + no inflammation

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| Bile stasis | Present

| Inflammation | Minimal/absent

| Hepatocyte injury | Mild

| Portal inflammation | Absent

Seen classically with:

• Estrogens (OCPs, pregnancy)
• Anabolic steroids

This pattern presents with pruritus and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia without marked hepatocellular injury. Amoxicillin-clavulanate produces cholestatic hepatitis with inflammation, and acetaminophen/isoniazid cause hepatocellular necrosis. Hence steroid hormones are the classic cause of non-inflammatory cholestasis.

| Drug | Pattern | Key Feature

| ---- | ------- | -----------

| Acetaminophen | Hepatocellular | Centrilobular necrosis

| Isoniazid | Hepatocellular | Viral hepatitis-like

| Amox-clav | Cholestatic hepatitis | Inflammation present

| Estrogens | Bland cholestasis | No inflammation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are correct for obesity? 1. Adiponectin levels are reduced in obesity. 2. Orlistat is a reversible inhibitor of lipase used for the treatment of obesity. 3. Liraglutide used for T2DM management can cause weight gain and not recommended in obese patients with T2DM. 4. Bariatric surgery is recommended in obese patients with BMI > 30 kg/m² for long-term benefits. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 2 only

Obesity is associated with decreased adiponectin levels, and pharmacological therapy includes orlistat, a reversible inhibitor of gastric and pancreatic lipases, which reduces fat absorption.

Why are the statements incorrect?

• 3. Liraglutide used for T2DM management can cause weight gain and not recommended in obese patients with T2DM: Incorrect. Liraglutide (GLP-1 receptor agonist) causes weight loss and is recommended in obese patients with T2DM.
• 4. Bariatric surgery is recommended in obese patients with BMI >30 kg/m² for long-term benefits: Incorrect. The conventional indication is BMI ≥40 kg/m², or ≥35 kg/m² with obesity-related comorbidities (though some newer diabetes guidelines consider surgery at lower BMI in selected patients).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is a predictor of liver fibrosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. AST-to-Platelet Ratio Index

APRI (AST-to-Platelet Ratio Index) is a commonly used non-invasive marker for assessing hepatic fibrosis, particularly in chronic viral hepatitis. APRI combines:

• AST elevation, reflecting hepatocellular injury
• Platelet count, which tends to decrease with advancing fibrosis due to portal hypertension and splenic sequestration

Thus, a higher APRI suggests a greater likelihood of significant hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Serum transaminase levels: Indicate hepatocellular injury, but the degree of AST/ALT elevation does not reliably correlate with the extent of fibrosis.
• C. Coagulation profile: PT/INR reflects hepatic synthetic dysfunction, particularly in advanced liver disease, but is not a specific fibrosis marker.
• D. Serum albumin and pre-albumin: Reflect synthetic/nutritional status and may decrease in advanced liver disease but are not specific predictors of fibrosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is correctly matched regarding classification of portal hypertension according to site of vascular obstruction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pre-hepatic presinusoidal – Portal vein thrombosis

Portal hypertension is defined as an increase in the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) >5 mmHg (clinically significant when ≥10 mmHg). It is classified according to the site of vascular obstruction into pre-hepatic, intrahepatic (presinusoidal, sinusoidal, postsinusoidal), and post-hepatic causes.

Portal vein thrombosis is the classic example of pre-hepatic presinusoidal portal hypertension.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sinusoidal – Veno-occlusive disease: Veno-occlusive disease (sinusoidal obstruction syndrome) is a postsinusoidal intrahepatic cause, not sinusoidal.
• C. Intrahepatic presinusoidal – Cirrhosis: Cirrhosis is the most common cause of sinusoidal portal hypertension, not presinusoidal.
• D. Post-hepatic postsinusoidal – Schistosomiasis:

• Schistosomiasis causes intrahepatic presinusoidal portal hypertension due to periportal fibrosis.
• Post-hepatic causes include Budd-Chiari syndrome, inferior vena cava obstruction, and constrictive pericarditis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presents with recurrent abdominal pain and a history of blood in stools. On examination, there are dark pigmented spots on his lips and oral mucosa. Endoscopy shows multiple hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome

Classic Triad of Peutz–Jeghers Syndrome

1. Hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine (especially jejunum)

2. Mucocutaneous pigmentation

• Dark spots on lips
• Oral mucosa
• Perioral skin

3. Adolescent onset with GI bleeding or abdominal pain

These findings together are diagnostic of PJS.

The hamartomatous polyps can cause:

• GI bleeding
• Recurrent abdominal pain
• Intussusception (very common complication in PJS)

The pigmentation occurs due to melanin deposition in mucocutaneous areas.

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is caused by mutation in the: STK11 (LKB1) tumor suppressor gene

Inheritance pattern: Autosomal dominant.

A) Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)

• Caused by APC gene mutation
• Hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps
• No mucocutaneous pigmentation

C) Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome

• Hamartomatous polyps but mainly in colon
• No characteristic mucocutaneous pigmentation

D) Cronkhite–Canada Syndrome

• Non-hereditary
• Occurs in older adults
• Associated with alopecia, nail changes, and diarrhea

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In familial adenomatous polyposis, which of the following all are true? 1. Presence of >100 colorectal polyps 2. Positive family history 3. Autosomal recessive inheritance 4. Genetic mutation on chromosome 5 Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Why is B correct?

• 1. Presence of >100 colorectal polyps: Correct. Classical FAP is defined by the presence of more than 100 adenomatous colorectal polyps.
• 2. Positive family history: Correct. Since FAP is autosomal dominant, most patients have a positive family history (although \~20–30% arise from new mutations).
• 4. Genetic mutation on chromosome 5: Correct. Mutation occurs in the APC gene on chromosome 5q21.

Incorrect statement:

• 3. Autosomal recessive inheritance: Incorrect. FAP is autosomal dominant.

• (Autosomal recessive polyposis is MUTYH-associated polyposis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are true? 1. Presents as multiple hamartomatous polyps in the GIT 2. Histology shows arborising smooth muscle bundles 3. It is an autosomal recessive condition 4. Extra-intestinal manifestations of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome include hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant hamartomatous polyposis syndrome caused by a mutation of the STK11/LKB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 19p13.3.

1. Presents as multiple hamartomatous polyps in the GIT — TRUE

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is characterized by:

• Multiple hamartomatous polyps
• Mainly in the small intestine (especially jejunum), but can occur throughout GIT.

2. Histology shows arborising smooth muscle bundles — TRUE

This is the classic histological hallmark of Peutz-Jeghers polyps.

Histology:

• Tree-like (“arborizing”) branching smooth muscle extending into the polyp.

3. It is an autosomal recessive condition — FALSE

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is:

• Autosomal dominant
• Usually due to mutation in STK11/LKB1 tumor suppressor gene.

4. Extra-intestinal manifestations include hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium — FALSE

Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) is associated with:

Familial adenomatous polyposis

—not Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

Important Differential Diagnosis

| Syndrome | Polyp Type | Gene | Key Feature

| -------- | ---------- | ---- | -----------

| PJS | Hamartomatous | STK11 | Mucocutaneous pigmentation

| Juvenile polyposis | Hamartomatous | SMAD4/BMPR1A | Juvenile retention polyps

| FAP | Adenomatous | APC | CHRPE, colon cancer

| Cowden syndrome | Hamartomatous | PTEN | Trichilemmomas, breast/thyroid cancer

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Peutz–Jeghers syndrome are true 1. Heterogeneous loss of function of the STK11 gene 2. Presents as multiple hamartomatous polyps in the GIT 3. Histology shows arborising smooth muscle bundles 4. It is an autosomal recessive condition 5. Extra-intestinal manifestations of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome include hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, and 3

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is due to loss-of-function mutation of the STK11 tumor suppressor gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. It presents with multiple hamartomatous GI polyps showing classic arborizing smooth muscle bundles on histology. Retinal pigment hypertrophy is seen in familial adenomatous polyposis, not Peutz–Jeghers.

| Feature | Peutz–Jeghers | FAP

| ------- | ------------- | ---

| Gene | STK11 | APC

| Inheritance | AD | AD

| Polyp type | Hamartomatous | Adenomatous

| Histology | Arborizing smooth muscle | Dysplastic epithelium

| Cancer risk | Moderate–high (extraintestinal) | Very high (colon)

| Extra features | Mucocutaneous pigmentation | CHRPE (retinal lesions)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old pregnant woman is found to be HBsAg positive with high HBV DNA levels on routine antenatal screening. She has no clinical features of liver failure. What is the most appropriate management during pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tenofovir

Pregnant women with chronic hepatitis B infection and high HBV DNA levels (>200,000 IU/mL) should receive tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) during the third trimester (typically from 28–32 weeks of gestation) to reduce the risk of mother-to-child (vertical) transmission. Tenofovir is the preferred antiviral in pregnancy because of its efficacy and favorable safety profile.

• Neonatal prophylaxis: Hepatitis B vaccine + Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth is essential to further reduce vertical transmission.
• Breastfeeding: Permitted after appropriate neonatal immunoprophylaxis; tenofovir is considered compatible with breastfeeding.

Why not the other options?

• A. Pegylated interferon: Contraindicated in pregnancy due to its antiproliferative and teratogenic effects.
• C. Zidovudine: Used for HIV, not for prevention of HBV transmission.
• D. Acyclovir: Active against HSV and VZV; it has no role in the management of chronic hepatitis B.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old male is found to be positive for HBsAg and HBeAg and is diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B. The viral load of the patient was 2 x 10^5 IU/mL and ALT is found to be doubled. What is the appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tenofovir

Chronic HBV (HBsAg > 6 months)

↓

Check HBeAg + HBV DNA + ALT

↓

High DNA + ↑ ALT

HBV DNA >2000IU/ml

↓

Start antiviral therapy

↓

Tenofovir + Entecavir x 12wks

Tenofovir:

🔹 Class: Nucleotide analog (reverse transcriptase inhibitor)

🔹 Action:

• Inhibits HBV DNA polymerase
• → Stops viral replication

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man had an episode of jaundice due to HBV one year back. On follow-up now, he has normal levels of liver enzymes. His current profile is shown. • HBsAg: Positive • HBeAg: Negative • Anti-HBe: Positive • Anti-HBc IgG: Positive • Anti-HBc IgM: Negative • HBV DNA: Low • ALT: Normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chronic Hepatitis B

Key interpretation of markers:

• HBsAg positive (>1 year) → Chronic infection
• HBeAg negative + Anti-HBe positive → Low replication
• Anti-HBc IgG positive, IgM negative → Chronic (not acute)
• HBV DNA low + ALT normal → Inactive carrier state

Why not others?

• Resolved infection: HBsAg would be negative, Anti-HBs positive
• Acute HBV: Anti-HBc IgM positive
• Chronic Hep B (active): ↑ ALT, high HBV DNA, often HBeAg + (Negative HBeAg in Pre-core mutant)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A health worker had a needle stick injury. While handling a chronic Hepatitis B case. She has taken 2 complete schedules (6 doses) of HBV vaccination. She was tested and was diagnosed as a non-responder to vaccination 3 months back, What is the most appropriate management in this case:
options: Give 2 doses of HBIG one now and another 4 weeks later
Give HBV vaccination starting now, after 4-6 weeks, check HBV titres and decide on giving HBIG
HBIG single dose with HBV vaccination (first dose beginning now)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Give 2 doses of HBIG one now and another 4 weeks later

A documented vaccine non-responder exposed to an HBsAg-positive source requires passive immunization only. Two doses of HBIG are given: one immediately and another at 1 month, as further vaccination is ineffective in proven non-responders. HBIG provides immediate anti-HBs protection after high-risk exposure. Revaccination strategies are used only in unknown or incomplete responders, not confirmed non-responders.

| Criteria | Meaning

| -------- | -------

| Anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL | No protective immunity

| After 2 full vaccine series | True non-responder

Non-responder : anti-HBs < 10 after 2 full series

What to do: HBIG × 2 doses: 4 weeks apart; No further vaccine

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A man presents with deranged LFT. The serum viral markers are given below: • Anti-HAV IgM - Non-reactive • Anti-HAV-IgG - Reactive • HBsAg - Non-reactive • Anti-HBc total/IgG - Reactive • Anti-HBc IgM - Non-reactive • Anti-HCV IgM - Non-reactive • Anti-HCV IgG - Reactive • Anti-HEV IgM - Non-reactive • Anti-HEV IgG - Non-reactive Which of the following statements is not correct about his condition?
options: Chronic Hepatitis B infection, HBV DNA titres should be done by real time PCR
HBV infection in the remote past
HCV RNA quantitative testing should be done
Past HAV infection or received vaccine for HAV
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic Hepatitis B infection, HBV DNA titres should be done by real time PCR

| Marker | Result | Meaning

| ------ | ------ | -------

| Anti-HAV IgM | ❌ | No acute HAV

| Anti-HAV IgG | ✅ | Past infection / vaccination

| HBsAg | ❌ | No active HBV

| Anti-HBc IgG (total) | ✅ | Past HBV exposure

| Anti-HBc IgM | ❌ | No acute HBV

| Anti-HCV IgM | ❌ | No acute HCV

| Anti-HCV IgG | ✅ | Exposure to HCV

| Anti-HEV IgM/IgG | ❌ | No HEV

HBsAg negative + Anti-HBc IgG positive = past HBV infection, NOT chronic infection.

Important Points:

1. Anti-HBc IgG NEVER appears after vaccination

So if it’s present → natural infection occurred

2. Window period (HBV)

• HBsAg negative
• Anti-HBs negative
• ONLY Anti-HBc IgM positive

3. HCV has NO vaccine

• So IgG always = infection exposure

4. ALT elevation in HCV

• Can be mild, fluctuating, or silent

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient's Hepatitis B virus serology panel shows HBsAg +ve, Anti-HBc IgM +ve, HBeAg –ve, Anti-HBs –ve. Choose the correct diagnosis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute hepatitis

• The single most decisive marker here is Anti-HBc IgM, which is the specific serological marker of recent/acute HBV infection (appears within weeks of HBsAg and persists \~6 months). Its presence, together with HBsAg positivity (active viral surface antigen) and absent anti-HBs (no recovery/immunity), confirms acute hepatitis B.
• The HBeAg-negative status does not exclude acute infection — it may reflect the late/resolving phase of acute illness (HBeAg is transient, appearing early and disappearing before HBsAg) or infection with a precore mutant strain, which cannot produce HBeAg despite active replication.

Other options:

• B. Chronic hepatitis → requires HBsAg persisting >6 months with Anti-HBc IgG (not IgM) positive.
• C. Window period → HBsAg negative and anti-HBs negative, with Anti-HBc IgM the ONLY positive marker — here HBsAg is positive, so it is excluded.
• D. Vaccination → isolated Anti-HBs positive; all core markers and HBsAg negative (vaccine contains only surface antigen).

Pearl:

• Anti-HBc IgM = acute infection / window period
• Anti-HBc IgG + Anti-HBs = past natural infection with recovery
• Anti-HBs alone = vaccination
• HBsAg > 6 months = chronic carrier

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A person had undergone the serology for suspected hepatitis B infection. His/her serology shows the presence of HBs antigen and also IgG anti-HBc along with the presence of anti-HBe, while HBe antigen is negative. Which one of the following diagnoses is the correct interpretation of the serology results?
options: Chronic hepatitis B infection with active viral replication
Chronic hepatitis B infection with low viral replication
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chronic hepatitis B infection with low viral replication

The serology shows:

• HBsAg positive → Current hepatitis B infection.
• IgG anti-HBc positive → Indicates previous/current natural HBV infection; it is not produced after vaccination.
• HBeAg negative → Active viral replication is not strongly indicated.
• Anti-HBe positive → Suggests seroconversion from HBeAg to anti-HBe, usually associated with reduced viral replication.

Therefore, the pattern is most consistent with chronic HBV infection with low viral replication.

Why not the other options?

• (a) Active hepatitis B infection: Too nonspecific. The presence of HBsAg confirms infection, but the HBeAg-negative/anti-HBe-positive pattern specifically suggests lower replication.
• (b) Chronic HBV with active viral replication: Typically associated with HBeAg positivity and high HBV DNA. However, HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis can occasionally have active replication due to precore/core promoter mutations, so HBV DNA is required for definitive assessment.
• (c) Chronic HBV with low viral replication — Correct: HBsAg +, IgG anti-HBc +, HBeAg −, anti-HBe + is the classic exam pattern.
• (d) Recovery/vaccination: Recovery requires HBsAg negativity and anti-HBs positivity. Vaccination produces anti-HBs only, without anti-HBc.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In serological investigation of hepatitis B virus infection, presence of hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg) is an indicator of:
options: Active replication of virus in the liver
Chronic infection with hepatitis B virus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Active replication of virus in the liver

Hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg) is a marker of active HBV replication and high infectivity. Its presence indicates that the virus is actively replicating in hepatocytes and the patient has a high risk of transmitting the infection.

Why not the other options?

• B. Acute liver failure: HBeAg indicates viral replication, not the severity of liver damage.
• C. Chronic infection with hepatitis B virus: Chronic HBV is diagnosed by HBsAg positivity for >6 months; HBeAg may be positive or negative.
• D. Inactive carrier phase of infection: Characterized by HBeAg negativity, anti-HBe positivity, low/undetectable HBV DNA, and normal ALT.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Simultaneous infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis D virus (HDV) followed by full recovery is associated with appearance of:
options: Low titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgM type
Low titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgA type
High titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgM type
High titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgG type
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. High titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgG type

In simultaneous HBV–HDV coinfection, most patients recover completely and clear both viruses. After recovery, anti-HDV IgM disappears, while anti-HDV IgG antibodies appear and persist, indicating past infection and immunity.

Why not the other options?

• A. Low titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgM type: IgM is a marker of acute infection and disappears after recovery.
• B. Low titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgA type: IgA antibodies are not used in the serological diagnosis of HDV.
• C. High titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgM type: Suggest ongoing acute or active infection, not recovery.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The blood investigation of a patient is given below. What is the probable diagnosis? • HBsAg - NR, • Anti HBs - NR, • Anti HBc IgM - NR, • Anti HBc total - positive, • HBeAg - NR, • Anti HBe – NR (NR – Non reactive)
options: Acute HBV infection in window period
HBV infection in the remote past, completely recovered
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HBV infection in the remote past, completely recovered

| Marker | Result | Meaning

| ------ | ------ | -------

| HBsAg | ❌ Negative | No current infection

| Anti-HBs | ❌ Negative | No protective antibodies detected

| Anti-HBc IgM | ❌ Negative | No acute infection

| Anti-HBc total | ✅ Positive | Past exposure to HBV

| HBeAg | ❌ Negative | No active replication

| Anti-HBe | ❌ Negative | No seroconversion marker

The ONLY marker positive = Anti-HBc total

This means:

• Patient was exposed to HBV sometime in the past
• Not acute (IgM negative)
• Not current infection (HBsAg negative)

Hence → Remote past infection, recovered

| Condition | HBsAg | Anti-HBs | Anti-HBc IgM | Anti-HBc IgG

| --------- | ----- | -------- | ------------ | ------------

| Acute infection | + | - | + | +

| Window period | - | - | + | +

| Chronic infection | + | - | - | +

| Vaccinated | - | + | - | -

| Past infection (resolved) | - | ± | - | +

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following anti-HIV drugs is effective in treatment of hepatitis B?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lamivudine

Lamivudine is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor active against both HIV and hepatitis B virus. It inhibits HBV DNA polymerase and is used in chronic HBV therapy. Protease inhibitors and integrase inhibitors have no activity against HBV. Dual antiviral activity is the key exam clue for lamivudine.

| Drug | Class | HBV Activity

| ---- | ----- | ------------

| Lamivudine | NRTI | ✅

| Tenofovir | NRTI | ✅

| Emtricitabine | NRTI | ✅

| Entecavir | HBV drug | ❌ HIV

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are the risk factors for the acquisition of hepatitis C infection? 1. Faeco-oral transmission 2. Intravenous drug abuse 3. Vertical transmission 4. Sharing toothbrush and razors Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is transmitted primarily through blood exposure. The major risk factors include intravenous drug use, vertical (mother-to-child) transmission, and sharing blood-contaminated personal items such as razors and toothbrushes.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Faeco-oral transmission ❌: Incorrect. This is the route for Hepatitis A and E, not HCV.
• 2. Intravenous drug abuse ✔️: Major risk factor.
• 3. Vertical transmission ✔️: Occurs, especially if the mother has a high viral load or HIV coinfection.
• 4. Sharing toothbrush and razors ✔️: Can transmit HCV through blood contamination.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B with pegylated interferon (PEG-IFN)? 1. PEG-IFN is poorly tolerated compared to nucleoside analogues. 2. Resistance to treatment with PEG-IFN is more common than with nucleoside analogues. 3. PEG-IFN is not useful in patients with cirrhosis. 4. PEG-IFN is administered once weekly for 48 weeks. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3 and 4

Pegylated interferon (PEG-IFN) in chronic hepatitis B:

• Statement 1. PEG-IFN is poorly tolerated compared to nucleoside analogues: True. PEG-IFN is associated with significant adverse effects (flu-like symptoms, fatigue, depression, cytopenias, thyroid dysfunction), making it less well tolerated than oral nucleos(t)ide analogues such as entecavir or tenofovir.
• Statement 2. Resistance to treatment with PEG-IFN is more common than with nucleoside analogues: False. Viral resistance does not develop to interferon. In contrast, resistance can occur with some nucleos(t)ide analogues (especially older agents like lamivudine), although tenofovir and entecavir have a high barrier to resistance.
• Statement 3. PEG-IFN is not useful in patients with cirrhosis: True. PEG-IFN is contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis and is generally not recommended in cirrhotic patients because of the risk of hepatic decompensation. It is mainly used in selected non-cirrhotic or compensated patients.
• Statement 4. PEG-IFN is administered once weekly for 48 weeks: True. The standard regimen is pegylated interferon alfa administered once weekly for 48 weeks.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following viruses spreads predominantly through water?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HAV (Hepatitis A Virus)

Hepatitis A virus spreads by the fecal–oral route, classically through contaminated water and food. It causes acute, self-limited hepatitis and is linked to poor sanitation and outbreaks. In contrast, HBV, HCV, and HDV are transmitted parenterally via blood or body fluids. Waterborne transmission is a key epidemiologic hallmark of HAV.

| Feature | HAV | HBV | HCV | HDV | HEV

| ------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---

| Transmission | Feco-oral | Blood/sexual | Blood | Blood | Feco-oral

| Chronicity | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ (high) | ✅ | ❌ (except pregnancy severe)

| Envelope | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌

| Vaccine | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | (via HBV) | ❌

| Special note | Waterborne outbreaks | Vertical transmission | Silent chronic | Needs HBV | Severe in pregnancy

• HAV & HEV = Enterically transmitted
• HBV, HCV, HDV = Parenteral
• HAV:

• No carrier state
• No chronic hepatitis
• Lifelong immunity after infection

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is not a risk factor for the acquisition of chronic hepatitis C?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sharing food

Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is primarily transmitted through blood-to-blood exposure. Sharing food does not transmit HCV.

Why the other options are risk factors?

• A. Intravenous drug abuse: Correct risk factor

• Sharing contaminated needles or injection equipment is a major route of HCV transmission.

• B. Unscreened infected blood transfusion: Correct risk factor

• Transfusion of HCV-contaminated blood can transmit infection, particularly in settings where blood screening is inadequate.

• C. Vertical transmission: Correct risk factor

• HCV can be transmitted from an infected mother to her infant, although the risk is relatively low.

• D. Sharing food: Not a risk factor

• HCV is not spread through food, water, coughing, sneezing, or casual contact.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A 30-year-old female patient came to the outpatient department with complaints of neck swelling. She gives a history of weight loss and palpitations. On examination, she has exophthalmos and a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland. What are the essential investigations that should be done for the patient?

1. Thyroid scan
2. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC)
3. Thyroid function tests
4. Ultrasound of neck
5. Anti-thyroid antibody
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3, 4 and 5 only

The given clinical scenario of a female patient presenting with weight loss, palpitations, exophthalmos, and diffusely enlarged thyroid gland is suggestive of Graves' disease.

The essential investigations in this patient would be thyroid function tests, ultrasound of the neck, thyroid scan, and anti-thyroid antibody. FNAC is not an essential investigation in this condition. FNAC should be done on nodules that are not classified as fully benign on ultrasound.

The hyperthyroidism of Graves’ disease is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) synthesized by lymphocytes in the thyroid gland as well as in bone marrow and lymph nodes. TSI antibodies cause stimulation of the thyroid gland causing features of hyperthyroidism.

Symptoms include hyperactivity, heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, weakness, weight loss, increased appetite, and diarrhea.

Signs include tachycardia, goiter, tremor, muscle weakness, and atrial fibrillation in the elderly.

Thyroid ophthalmopathy seen in one-third of patients with Grave’s disease.

NO SPECS scoring system as describe below can be used to evaluate ophthalmopathy.

• No signs or symptoms
• Only signs (lid retraction, or lag)
• Soft tissue involvement (periorbital edema)
• Proptosis
• Extraocular muscle involvement
• Corneal involvement
• Sight loss

Thyroid dermopathy usually occurs in the presence of moderate or severe ophthalmopathy. It primarily manifests as noninflamed, indurated plaques with a deep pink or purple color and an "orange skin" appearance, commonly found on the anterior and lateral aspects of the lower leg (known as pretibial myxedema).

Investigations done in a patient with Graves' disease include:

• Thyroid function tests- TSH levels are decreased with or without elevated T3 and T4 levels.
• Anti-thyroid antibodies- Elevated levels of TSH receptor antibodies are diagnostic of Graves' disease. Other antibodies like anti-Tg and anti-TPO are elevated in most of the patients.
• Ultrasound of the neck is performed to evaluate vascularity, echogenicity, nodules, and clinical landmarks for surgical planning.
• A radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) scan (thyroid scan) should be performed and a diffuse uptake confirms the diagnosis of Graves' disease. It is also useful to differentiate TSI-negative Graves disease from toxic nodular disease based on diffuse or nodular uptake patterns.
• CT or MRI scans of the orbits are useful to evaluate Graves’ ophthalmopathy.

Hyperthyroidism can be treated by antithyroid drugs, radioiodine treatment (I131), or thyroidectomy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old female patient with class II pulmonary hypertension presents with a negative vasoreactivity test. Which of the following is used in the next step of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ambrisentan

In a patient with class II pulmonary hypertension (low risk) with a negative vasoreactivity test, the next best step of management is to start on ambrisentan (endothelin receptor antagonist)

Pulmonary artery hypertension (PAH) is defined as mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mmHg with a pulmonary vascular resistance of ≥3 wood units.

Exertional dyspnea, chest pain, fatigue, and lightheadedness are common early symptoms. With the progression of the disease, right ventricular dysfunction occurs which causes syncope, abdominal distention, ascites, and peripheral edema.

Vasoreactivity testing involves the administration of inhaled nitric oxide, IV epoprostenol, IV adenosine, or inhaled iloprost. The test is considered positive if the mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAH) decreases by ≥ 10 mmHg leading to mPAH ≤ 40 mmHg, without a decrease in cardiac output (CO).

In case of a positive vasoreactivity test, calcium channel blockers are indicated. Long-acting nifedipine, diltiazem or amlodipine can be used.

If the vasoreactivity test is negative,

• For patients with lower risk (class II, III) based on clinical assessment, oral therapy with endothelin receptor antagonists like ambrisentan, sitaxsentan, bosentan, or phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors (PDE-5 I's) like sildenafil, tadalafil is the first line of therapy.
• For patients with higher risk (those with advanced heart failure or syncope, class IV) based on clinical assessment, continuous treatment with iv prostacyclins (epoprostenol or treprostinil) would be the first line of therapy.

Lung transplantation and/or atrial septostomy are reserved for patients who progress despite optimal medical treatment.

The treatment algorithm for pulmonary hypertension is given below:

Revised WHO classification of pulmonary hypertension:

• Group I: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH)
• Group II: Pulmonary hypertension with left heart disease
• Group III: Pulmonary hypertension associated with lung diseases and/or hypoxemia
• Group IV: Pulmonary hypertension due to chronic thrombotic and/or embolic disease (CTEPH)
• Group V: Pulmonary hypertension due to miscellaneous causes

The table below provides guidance on the prognosis of PAH.
