• TB meningitis: ↓ glucose, high protein, lymphocytes
• Cryptococcus: ↓ glucose, high opening pressure (immunocompromised)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 44-year-old man comes to the OPD due to several weeks of difficulty walking and frequent falls. He also reports episodes of sharp, stabbing pain in his extremities. Deep-tendon reflexes are absent at the knee and ankle bilaterally. Proprioception and vibration sensation are reduced throughout the lower extremities. He has a wide-based gait and a positive Romberg sign. Which of the following diagnostic findings is most likely associated with this patient's current symptoms?
options: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture growing acid-fast bacilli
CSF PCR positive for herpes virus
Encapsulated yeasts on CSF India ink preparation
Reactive VDRL tests on CSF samples
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Reactive VDRL tests on CSF samples

Loss of proprioception and vibration, areflexia, sensory ataxia, lightning-like pains, and positive Romberg sign, areflexia in lower limbs, possible argyll robertson pupil are classic for tabes dorsalis, a late manifestation of neurosyphilis.

Pathophysiology:

• Degeneration of posterior columns and dorsal roots
• Leads to sensory ataxia and neuropathic pain

Diagnostic finding:

• Reactive VDRL in CSF confirms neurosyphilis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 47-year-old man is diagnosed with primary progressive multiple sclerosis (PPMS) after experiencing gradually worsening gait difficulty and lower-limb spasticity over the past 2 years without distinct relapses or remissions. MRI brain and spine show demyelinating lesions consistent with multiple sclerosis. Which of the following disease-modifying therapies has been shown to slow disability progression in patients with primary progressive multiple sclerosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ocrelizumab

Ocrelizumab is a humanized anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that depletes B lymphocytes. It is the first and currently the only FDA-approved disease-modifying therapy shown to reduce disability progression in Primary Progressive Multiple Sclerosis (PPMS).

It works by:

• Depleting CD20-positive B cells
• Reducing CNS inflammation and demyelination
• Slowing progression of neurological disability

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Natalizumab – An α4-integrin inhibitor that prevents leukocyte migration across the blood-brain barrier. It is used for relapsing forms of MS, not PPMS.
• C. Siponimod – A sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulator approved for active secondary progressive MS (SPMS) and relapsing MS, not PPMS.
• D. Rituximab – An anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody used off-label in MS but is not approved for PPMS.

High-yield pearl

Disease-modifying drugs in Multiple Sclerosis:

| MS subtype | Drug with key indication

| ---------- | ------------------------

| Primary Progressive MS (PPMS) | ✅ Ocrelizumab

| Relapsing-Remitting MS (RRMS) | Interferon-β, Glatiramer, Dimethyl fumarate, Fingolimod, Natalizumab, Ocrelizumab

| Active Secondary Progressive MS (SPMS) | Siponimod

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 47-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a stab wound to the back. Neurologic exam shows loss of vibration and proprioception on the right side below the level of the umbilicus. She also has spastic weakness in the right leg and loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side beginning two levels below the lesion. Which of the following best describes this spinal cord syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Brown-Séquard syndrome

The clinical picture is characteristic of Brown-Séquard syndrome, caused by hemisection of one side of the spinal cord (commonly due to penetrating trauma like stab injury).

Ipsilateral (same side as lesion):

• Loss of vibration & proprioception → dorsal column involvement
• Spastic paralysis/weakness → corticospinal tract involvement

Contralateral (opposite side):

• Loss of pain & temperature beginning 1–2 levels below lesion → due to crossing of spinothalamic tract

Tract-wise Understanding:

• Dorsal columns: ascend ipsilaterally → loss on same side
• Corticospinal tract: descends ipsilaterally → ipsilateral UMN signs
• Spinothalamic tract: crosses within 1–2 levels → contralateral loss

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 5 year old patient presents to the OPD with dysphagia, dysarthria, and dysphonia. On examination, brisk jaw jerk is seen. What is the possible localisation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Corticobulbar tracts

Dysphagia, dysarthria, dysphonia with a brisk jaw jerk indicate an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion of bulbar muscles, localizing to the corticobulbar tracts (from motor cortex to cranial nerve nuclei (V, VII, IX, X, XII).

Features of corticobulbar (UMN) lesion:

• Dysarthria, dysphagia, dysphonia
• Brisk jaw jerk
• Spastic tongue
• Emotional lability (pseudobulbar affect)

Differentiation:

• LMN bulbar palsy → absent jaw jerk, fasciculations
• Corticospinal tract lesion → limb weakness, not isolated bulbar signs
• V3 nerve lesion → weak mastication, reduced jaw jerk

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of lower leg weakness, swallowing difficulty, and drooling of saliva. He has not yet received any childhood vaccinations. Two days after admission, the patient de velops shortness of breath. Pulse oximetry shows an oxygen saturation of 64%. Despite resuscitative efforts, the patient dies of respiratory failure. At autopsy, examination of the spinal cord shows destruction of the anterior horn cells. Neurological examination of this patient would have most likely shown which of the following findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyporeflexia

Destruction of anterior horn cells (as seen in poliomyelitis) produces a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion. Poliovirus infects anterior horn cells of spinal cord leading to asymmetric flaccid paralysis and respiratory muscle failure.

Features of LMN lesion:

• Flaccid paralysis
• Hyporeflexia/areflexia
• Hypotonia
• Muscle atrophy and fasciculations
• No sensory loss (pure motor involvement)

Differentiation:

A. Positive Babinski sign & B. Clasp knife spasticity: UMN lesions

D. Sensory loss: Not seen in polio (motor neurons only)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to recurrent, generalized tonic-clonic seizures over the past 24 hours. He takes no medications and has no family history of epilepsy. The patient's temperature is 39.4⁰C (103⁰F), blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 112/min, and respirations are 10/min. During the examination, the patient suddenly develops sustained, generalized tonic-clonic convulsions without fully regaining consciousness between episodes. Which of the following describes the mechanism of action of the most appropriate initial therapy for his seizures?
options: Blockade of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
Blockade of presynaptic voltage-gated sodium channels
Inhibition of vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Enhanced postsynaptic chloride influx

This child has status epilepticus (continuous seizures without regaining consciousness). The initial treatment is a benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam/diazepam or IM midazolam).

Mechanism of action of benzodiazepines:

• Bind to GABA-A receptors
• Increase frequency of chloride channel opening
• Cause enhanced postsynaptic Cl⁻ influx → neuronal hyperpolarization → rapid seizure termination

Stepwise management of status epilepticus:

1. First-line: Benzodiazepines → enhance GABA-mediated Cl⁻ influx
2. Second-line: Phenytoin/fosphenytoin, valproate, levetiracetam
3. Refractory: Phenobarbital, propofol, midazolam infusion

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted with sudden-onset weakness of the right upper and lower limbs. MRI of the brain confirms an acute infarction involving the left internal capsule. Initially, the affected limbs are flaccid, but 2 weeks later he develops increased muscle tone, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and an extensor plantar response. Which of the following best explains the development of spasticity in this patient?
options: Degeneration of α-motor neurons in the anterior horn
Loss of cerebellar inhibitory influence on muscle tone
Loss of corticospinal inhibition of spinal reflex circuits
Dysfunction of basal ganglia motor pathways
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Loss of corticospinal inhibition of spinal reflex circuits

An internal capsule infarct damages the corticospinal (pyramidal) tract, producing an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion.

Immediately after the stroke, patients often experience spinal shock, characterized by:

• Flaccid paralysis
• Hypotonia
• Hyporeflexia

Over the next few weeks, loss of descending inhibitory input from the corticospinal tract leads to:

• Hyperexcitability of spinal stretch reflexes
• Increased γ-motor neuron activity
• Increased muscle tone (spasticity)
• Hyperreflexia
• Clonus
• Babinski sign

Thus, spasticity results from loss of corticospinal inhibition of spinal reflex arcs.

Why the other options are incorrect

• A. Loss of α-motor neurons in anterior horn: Causes a lower motor neuron lesion, leading to flaccid paralysis, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and hyporeflexia.
• B. Loss of cerebellar inhibitory control on muscle tone: Produces hypotonia, ataxia, dysmetria, and intention tremor, not spasticity.
• D. Damage to basal ganglia motor pathways: Results in movement disorders such as rigidity, bradykinesia, chorea, or dystonia rather than the velocity-dependent spasticity of UMN lesions.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with progressive weakness of both upper and lower limbs. Examination reveals muscle wasting with fasciculations, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses. Sensory examination is normal. Cranial nerve examination later shows dysarthria. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by simultaneous upper and lower motor neuron degeneration with no sensory loss.

• Lower motor neuron signs: Muscle wasting, fasciculations, weakness
• Upper motor neuron signs: Hyperreflexia, spasticity, extensor plantar (Babinski)
• Bulbar involvement: Dysarthria, dysphagia (late feature)
• Sensory system: Typically normal

Differentiation:

• Cervical spondylotic myelopathy: UMN signs + sensory deficits/radicular pain
• Multiple sclerosis: CNS lesions with sensory/visual involvement
• CIDP: Pure LMN-type peripheral neuropathy with sensory loss, areflexia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 55-year-old, previously healthy man is brought to the OPD by his wife after being forced into early retirement due to poor work performance. The patient was a financial planner but began missing important deadlines and mismanaging his client's accounts 6 months ago. He became more irritable during this time and started to curse at and insult his coworkers when they expressed concern about his performance. The patient has also become verbally abusive toward his wife but appears indifferent to the hurt he causes. She has had to take over the finances and grocery shopping. She adds, "My husband has developed quite the sweet tooth. He eats almost two boxes of cookies a day now." Physical examination is unremarkable. This patient is most likely to have which of the following neuropathologic findings?
options: Cytosolic vacuolation of neurons and glia with prion inclusions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aggregations of phosphorylated tau protein

Early-onset behavioral changes with personality disturbance, disinhibition, social inappropriateness, apathy, poor judgment, and hyperorality (e.g., increased sweet intake) are classic for frontotemporal dementia (FTD).

Neuropathology:

• Characterized by Pick bodies → intracellular inclusions of hyperphosphorylated tau protein
• Predominant degeneration of frontal and anterior temporal lobes

Differentiation:

• Alzheimer disease: β-amyloid plaques + tau tangles; early memory loss
• Lewy body dementia: α-synuclein inclusions, hallucinations, parkinsonism
• Prion disease: Rapid dementia + spongiform change.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 56-year-old man presents with an 18-month history of gradually progressive weakness affecting both his upper and lower limbs. He has difficulty buttoning his shirt, climbing stairs, and walking long distances. Examination reveals marked muscle wasting with fasciculations in the upper limbs, spasticity, brisk deep tendon reflexes, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Sensory examination is completely normal. A few months later, he develops dysarthria and dysphagia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)

The patient has the classical features of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), a progressive motor neuron disease characterized by simultaneous involvement of:

• Upper motor neurons (UMN)
• Lower motor neurons (LMN)

with no sensory deficits.

Key clinical clues

• Progressive weakness
• LMN signs

• Muscle wasting
• Fasciculations
• Weakness

• UMN signs

• Hyperreflexia
• Spasticity
• Extensor plantar (Babinski) response

• Bulbar involvement

• Dysarthria
• Dysphagia
• Tongue wasting and fasciculations (later)

• Sensory examination is normal

The coexistence of UMN + LMN signs with preserved sensation is the hallmark of ALS.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 58-year-old man is in the intensive care unit (ICU) following treatment for septic shock due to pneumonia. He required mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support for 10 days but is now hemodynamically stable. The patient is alert, oriented, and able to follow commands. However, the nurse reports that he has developed diffuse weakness and is unable to move his limbs effectively during physical therapy. On examination, there is symmetric weakness of all extremities, more pronounced in the lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes are markedly reduced throughout. Sensory examination reveals mild distal loss of pinprick and vibration sense. Cranial nerves are intact. Laboratory studies show normal electrolytes, glucose, and creatine kinase levels. Which of the following best explains this patient’s weakness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Axonal injury from microvascular inflammation

This patient has ICU-acquired weakness, most consistent with Critical illness polyneuropathy, a common complication of sepsis and prolonged ICU stay.

• Caused by axonal degeneration of peripheral nerves due to:

• Microvascular inflammation
• Endothelial dysfunction
• Impaired oxygen delivery to nerves

Leads to diffuse symmetric weakness

Clinical Features:

• Symmetric limb weakness (lower limbs > upper limbs)
• Reduced/absent deep tendon reflexes
• Mild distal sensory loss
• Cranial nerves spared
• Occurs in critically ill patients (sepsis, ventilation)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old male presents to the casualty with chest pain radiating to the back. He is diagnosed with a type A aortic dissection and undergoes emergent open repair. During the postoperative period, he develops thoracic back pain and an inability to move his bilateral lower extremities. Pinprick testing reveals bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the level of the xiphoid process. Injury to which of the following arteries most likely explains this patient’s clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Artery of Adamkiewicz

This is a classic anterior spinal cord syndrome after aortic surgery

Clinical clue:

• Type A aortic dissection → open repair
• Post-op:

o   Bilateral lower limb paralysis

o   Bilateral loss of pain & temperature below xiphoid

o   Acute thoracic back pain

This points towards Anterior spinal cord infarction.

The artery of Adamkiewicz is the principal blood supply to the anterior spinal artery in the thoracolumbar region.

• It typically arises between T9 and T12 but can originate anywhere from T8 to L2.
• In aortic dissection or during surgical repair, disruption of blood flow to this artery can cause anterior spinal artery syndrome

What structure is damaged?

The anterior 2/3 of spinal cord contains:

• Corticospinal tracts → motor paralysis
• Spinothalamic tracts → loss of pain & temperature
• Anterior horn cells

Dorsal columns are spared (not mentioned → vibration/proprioception likely intact). So we’re dealing with ischemia of the anterior spinal artery system.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive weakness in his arms and legs. Neurological examination shows muscle atrophy, fasciculations, decreased muscle tone, and hyporeflexia. Sensory examination is normal. Electromyography demonstrates loss of motor unit potentials. Biopsy of the spinal cord reveals degeneration of neurons located in the ventral horn that directly innervate extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers. Which of the following best describes the type of neuron affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alpha motor neurons

The clinical picture (progressive weakness, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, hypotonia, hyporeflexia with preserved sensation) indicates a pure lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion.

• Alpha motor neurons:

• Located in the anterior (ventral) horn of the spinal cord
• Directly innervate extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers
• Responsible for force generation and voluntary movement

Degeneration of these neurons leads to:

• Flaccid paralysis
• Muscle wasting (atrophy)
• Fasciculations
• Reduced reflexes

Why not other options:

B. Gamma motor neurons:

• Innervate intrafusal fibers (muscle spindles)
• Regulate muscle tone, not primary force generation

C. Preganglionic sympathetic neurons:

• Part of autonomic nervous system
• Not involved in skeletal muscle contraction

D. Renshaw cells:

• Inhibitory interneurons
• Modulate motor neuron activity, not directly innervate muscle

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden onset vertigo, dysphagia, hoarseness of voice, and vomiting. On examination he has loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side of the face and right side of the body. There is ipsilateral ptosis and miosis. Motor power in the limbs is normal. Occlusion of which of the following arteries is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior inferior cerebellar artery

Occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, characterized by vertigo, vomiting, dysphagia, hoarseness, ipsilateral loss of facial pain and temperature sensation, contralateral loss of body pain and temperature sensation, and ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). Motor strength is typically preserved because the corticospinal tract is spared.

Why not the other options?

• A. AICA – classically causes lateral pontine syndrome with facial paralysis (CN VII involvement).
• C. Superior cerebellar artery – primarily causes cerebellar signs without the classic nucleus ambiguus involvement.
• D. Anterior spinal artery – causes medial medullary syndrome with contralateral hemiparesis and ipsilateral hypoglossal palsy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with sudden-onset weakness of the right upper and lower limbs associated with deviation of the angle of the mouth to the left. On neurological examination, power is 2/5 in the right upper and lower limbs, with increased tone and exaggerated deep-tendon reflexes on the right side. The plantar reflex is elicited as demonstrated in the accompanying video on the right foot. Based on the clinical findings and the response demonstrated in the video, which of the following is the most likely site of the lesion?
options: Right corticospinal tract above the pyramidal decussation
Left corticospinal tract above the pyramidal decussation
Right anterior horn cells of the spinal cord
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left corticospinal tract above the pyramidal decussation

• The video demonstrates a positive Babinski sign (extensor plantar response) in the right foot—dorsiflexion of the great toe with fanning of the other toes.
• In an adult, this indicates an upper motor neuron/corticospinal tract lesion. Because the patient has right-sided UMN findings, a lesion above the pyramidal decussation will be on the contralateral (left) side.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 62-year-old man with small cell lung carcinoma presents with confusion and generalized tonic–clonic seizures. Laboratory investigations reveal hyponatremia, low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine, and euvolemic status . He requires long-term antiepileptic therapy. Which of the following antiepileptic drugs is most appropriate in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phenobarbital

In patients with SIADH-related hyponatremia (classically seen with small cell lung carcinoma), antiepileptic drugs that worsen hyponatremia must be avoided.

• Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine can induce or worsen SIADH, leading to further hyponatremia → contraindicated
• Phenytoin may reduce ADH release but is not preferred for long-term control in this setting
• Phenobarbital does not worsen hyponatremia and is safer for long-term seizure control in SIADH

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 62-year-old, right-handed man is evaluated for an episode of left leg weakness that spontaneously resolved within 30 minutes of onset. The patient also has had transient vision loss in the right eye. Medical history is significant for hypertension and diabetes mellitus. Evaluation reveals an atherosclerotic plaque in the extracranial portion of the supplying artery. During percutaneous stenting, the vascular catheter is inserted into the right common femoral artery and gradually advanced to the level of the aortic arch. Which of the following is the most likely path of the catheter before stenting of the culprit lesion can be performed?
options: Aorta - brachiocephalic artery - common carotid artery - external carotid artery
Aorta - brachiocephalic artery - common carotid artery - internal carotid artery
Aorta - common carotid artery - external carotid artery
Aorta - common carotid artery - internal carotid artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aorta - brachiocephalic artery - common carotid artery - internal carotid artery

Transient monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax) and contralateral limb weakness suggest atherosclerotic disease of the internal carotid artery (ICA) supplying the retina and anterior cerebral circulation.

Anatomical pathway for right ICA stenting from femoral artery:

1. Femoral artery → abdominal aorta → thoracic aorta → aortic arch
2. From arch → brachiocephalic trunk (on right side)
3. Brachiocephalic trunk → right common carotid artery
4. Common carotid → right internal carotid artery (culprit vessel)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 63-year-old man presents with progressive memory loss and disorientation over the past 2 years. His wife reports that he often forgets the names of family members and has become increasingly dependent on her for daily activities. MRI of the brain shows diffuse cortical atrophy, most pronounced in the hippocampus and temporal lobes. On histopathology, numerous amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles are seen. Activated glial cells surrounding the plaques are identified as the major source of inflammatory cytokines in this disease. Which of the following cell types is most responsible for this inflammatory response?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Microglia

The clinical picture is consistent with Alzheimer disease, characterized by:

• Progressive memory loss
• Hippocampal and temporal lobe atrophy
•

Amyloid plaques (Aβ) and neurofibrillary tangles (tau)

•

Microglia are the primary immune effector cells of the CNS:

• Derived from mesoderm (yolk sac macrophages)
• Function as phagocytes and antigen-presenting cells
• Become activated around amyloid plaques

• Microglia:

• Surround amyloid plaques
• Release pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6)
• Contribute to chronic neuroinflammation and neuronal damage

Hence, they are the major source of inflammatory response

Why not other options:

A. Astrocytes:

• Provide metabolic and structural support
• Can contribute to inflammation, but not primary immune cells

B. Oligodendrocytes: Responsible for myelination in CNS

D. Schwann cells: Myelinate peripheral nervous system (PNS), not CNS

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 65 year old patient has normal fluency and repetition of speech but impaired naming and comprehension. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transcortical sensory aphasia

Transcortical sensory aphasia presents with:

• Fluent speech
• Impaired comprehension
• Impaired naming
• Preserved repetition (key distinguishing feature)

Lesion in temporoparietal junction or watershed area around Wernicke’s area.

Differentiation:

• Wernicke aphasia: Poor comprehension + poor repetition
• Conduction aphasia: Poor repetition with relatively intact comprehension
• Transcortical motor aphasia: Nonfluent speech but preserved repetition

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman is evaluated for worsening urinary urgency and incontinence. The patient has had no abdominal pain, dysuria, or changes in urinary frequency. The patient feels unsteady while ambulating and walks slowly with small steps. Her family also reports that she has become forgetful and has difficulty planning and executing various activities that she used to perform regularly. MRI of the brain reveals chronic white matter changes with no infarction, hemorrhage, or mass lesions. There is diffuse ventriculomegaly with no sulcal enlargement. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's urinary incontinence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stretching of descending cortical fibers

This patient has the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH):

• Gait disturbance (magnetic/shuffling gait)
• Urinary incontinence/urgency
• Cognitive decline (executive dysfunction)

Pathophysiology of urinary incontinence in NPH:

• Ventriculomegaly with normal sulfi causes stretching of periventricular white matter
• Specifically affects descending frontal cortical fibers that normally inhibit the micturition reflex
• Loss of cortical inhibition → detrusor overactivity → urgency and incontinence

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 67-year-old woman develops a stroke involving the right side of the brain. Weeks later, she presents with severe, persistent burning and aching pain involving the left side of her body, accompanied by hyperalgesia and allodynia. Sensory examination reveals impaired pain and temperature sensation initially, followed by distressing spontaneous pain. Motor power is relatively preserved.Which of the following is the most likely location of her initial infarct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus

Central post-stroke pain (Dejerine–Roussy syndrome) classically occurs after infarction of the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus, which relays pain and temperature from the contralateral body.

Anatomy correlation:

• VPL nucleus: Sensory input from body (spinothalamic + medial lemniscus)
• VPM nucleus: Sensory input from face
• Lateral geniculate body: Vision
• Pulvinar: Visual attention/integration

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 68-year-old man with a long-standing history of poorly controlled hypertension presents with progressive cognitive decline, gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence. Neurological examination reveals upper motor neuron signs. MRI brain shows diffuse periventricular white-matter changes. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Binswanger disease

Binswanger disease (subcortical leukoencephalopathy) is a form of vascular dementia caused by chronic hypertension leading to small-vessel ischemic damage of deep white matter.

MRI shows diffuse periventricular and deep white-matter hyperintensities due to chronic ischemia.

• Progressive cognitive decline (subcortical dementia)
• Gait disturbance
• Urinary incontinence
• Upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, spasticity)

Differentiation:

• Binswanger disease: HTN + UMN signs + white-matter lesions
• Normal pressure hydrocephalus: Triad present but ventriculomegaly without marked white-matter ischemia
• Alzheimer disease: Cortical dementia, memory first, no early UMN signs
• Lewy body dementia: Visual hallucinations + parkinsonism + fluctuating cognition

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive lower back pain radiating to both thighs. The pain is aggravated by walking and prolonged standing, forcing him to stop after a short distance. He reports significant relief when bending forward or sitting, such as when leaning over a shopping cart. He also describes occasional numbness in his legs. On examination Motor strength and Sensory examination is unremarkable. Peripheral pulses are intact and symmetric. Which of the following structures is most likely responsible for this patient’s symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ligamentum flavum

Lumbar spinal stenosis is characterized by neurogenic claudication, presenting as bilateral leg pain, numbness, or weakness worsened by walking or spinal extension and relieved by flexion (e.g., leaning forward— “shopping cart sign”). This occurs due to degenerative narrowing of the spinal canal, most commonly from hypertrophy and infolding of the ligamentum flavum, which compresses the cauda equina or nerve roots.

• It forms the posterior wall of the spinal canal
• With aging, it becomes thickened and loses elasticity
• Leads to canal narrowing during extension, explaining symptom pattern

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. Posterior longitudinal ligament:

• Lies anterior to the spinal cord (posterior to vertebral bodies)
• More commonly involved in disc herniation-related pathology, not primary stenosis

• B. Interspinous ligament:

• Located between spinous processes
• Does not significantly contribute to canal narrowing

• D. Iliolumbar ligament:

• Stabilizes L5 to ilium
• Not part of the spinal canal → no role in stenosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 70-year-old right-handed man is brought to the emergency department due to sudden onset of right-sided weakness and urinary incontinence that began about 10 hours ago. On examination, there is 4/5 strength in the right upper extremity, 1/5 strength in the right lower extremity, and a Babinski sign on the right side. Sensation is decreased throughout the right foot and leg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left Anterior cerebral artery stroke

The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies the medial surface of frontal and parietal lobes, which control lower limb motor and sensory function and bladder control.

Key features of ACA stroke:

• Contralateral lower limb weakness > upper limb weakness
• Contralateral sensory loss in leg
• Urinary incontinence (medial frontal micturition center involvement)
• Behavioral changes/abulia (frontal lobe)

Differentiation:

B. Lacunar stroke: Pure motor/sensory without cortical signs

C. Left MCA stroke: Face/arm > leg weakness + aphasia/neglect

D. Right ACA stroke: Would affect left side

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 71-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension and atrial fibrillation is brought to the emergency department after sudden onset of weakness. His wife reports that while he was reading the newspaper, he suddenly dropped it, slumped to the side, and was unable to move his right arm or face. On arrival, he is alert but has dense right-sided hemiparesis. Neurological examination shows both eyes deviated to the left. He is unable to voluntarily look to the right, though extraocular muscles are otherwise intact. Sensory examination is normal. Which of the following brain regions is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left frontal eye field

The clinical picture is of a left middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke with:

• Contralateral (right-sided) hemiparesis
• Gaze deviation toward the side of the lesion (left)
• Inability to voluntarily look to the right

Frontal eye field controls contralateral horizontal gaze:

• Left frontal eye field → drives gaze to the right
• Right frontal eye field → drives gaze to the left

Mechanism in this Case: Lesion in left frontal eye field:

• Loss of ability to look right
• Unopposed activity of right frontal eye field
• Eyes deviate toward the lesion (left side)

Classic finding: “Eyes look toward the lesion in destructive cortical lesions (MCA stroke)”

Why not other options:

B. Right frontal eye field: Would cause gaze deviation to the right, not left

C. Left abducens nucleus: Causes ipsilateral gaze palsy (cannot look left), not seen here

D. Right medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF):

• Causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)
• Characterized by impaired adduction, not gaze deviation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 72-year-old right-handed man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department after his wife noticed he was speaking unusually. He appears alert and follows both simple and complex commands, such as “touch your left ear with your right hand.” When asked open-ended questions (eg, “What did you eat for breakfast?”), his responses are slow and effortful, consisting of short phrases. However, when the examiner asks him to repeat the phrase “The dog chased the ball,” he does so without difficulty. Writing shows the same halting pattern. Neurological examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Transcortical motor aphasia

• The patient has Transcortical motor aphasia, characterized by:

• Nonfluent, effortful speech
• Preserved comprehension
• Intact repetition

• Lesion in left frontal lobe anterior/superior to Broca’s area
• Arcuate fasciculus is spared → allows repetition to remain intact

Clinical Features:

• Speech:

• Slow, reduced output
• Short, effortful phrases

• Comprehension: Normal (follows complex commands)
• Repetition: Preserved (hallmark feature)

Why not other options:

A. Broca’s aphasia: Nonfluent speech with impaired repetition

B. Wernicke’s aphasia: Fluent but impaired comprehension and repetition

D. Transcortical sensory aphasia: Fluent speech, poor comprehension, but preserved repetition

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A highly agitated 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his family because he is unable to effectively communicate. He speaks clearly and with conviction but his sentences are incomprehensible. He does not appear to understand the doctor's questions, does not follow oral or written instructions, and cannot repeat simple phrases. Branch occlusion of which of the following arteries is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Left Middle cerebral artery-inferior division

Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension and impaired repetition indicates Wernicke aphasia. Patient often unaware of deficit.

• Wernicke area → posterior superior temporal gyrus
• Dominant hemisphere (usually left)
• Vascular supply: Inferior division of left middle cerebral artery (MCA)

Why not other options:

A. Right MCA – superior division: Non-dominant side → neglect, visuospatial deficits; superior division → Broca area, not Wernicke.

B. Right MCA – inferior division: Causes neglect and visuospatial problems (non-dominant hemisphere), not aphasia.

C. Left MCA – superior division: Affects Broca area → nonfluent aphasia with intact comprehension, opposite of this case.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A motorcyclist suffered a head injury 6 months back and presents with persistent memory deficits following injury. Choose the most appropriately matched option related to memory?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial temporal lobe - Declarative memory

The medial temporal lobe, especially the hippocampus, is essential for formation of declarative (explicit) memory — facts and events.

Types of memory & localization:

• Declarative (explicit) memory: facts, events → hippocampus & medial temporal lobe
• Procedural (implicit) memory: skills, habits → basal ganglia & cerebellum
• Associative/semantic memory storage: neocortex
• Emotional memory: amygdala

Clinical correlation:

Damage to medial temporal lobe (e.g., head injury) → anterograde amnesia with impaired formation of new declarative memories.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A neurophysiology experiment studies inhibition of α-motor neurons mediated by slow synaptic transmission. It is observed that activation of certain receptors leads to intracellular enzyme activation, resulting in an increased number and activity of inhibitory synaptic channels, thereby producing an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP). Which of the following best explains this mechanism?
options: Direct opening of ligand-gated Na⁺ channels
Activation of receptor-linked enzyme system increasing inhibitory channel activity
Rapid influx of Ca²⁺ through NMDA receptors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Activation of receptor-linked enzyme system increasing inhibitory channel activity

• Slow synaptic transmission in the CNS is mediated by metabotropic (G-protein–coupled) receptors, which act via second messenger systems rather than directly opening ion channels.
• In this mechanism:

• Neurotransmitter binds to a G-protein–coupled receptor (GPCR)
• This activates an intracellular enzyme system (e.g., adenylate cyclase or phospholipase C)
• Leads to second messenger formation (cAMP, IP₃/DAG)
• Results in modulation (↑ number/activity) of inhibitory ion channels (commonly Cl⁻ or K⁺ channels)
• Produces a slow, prolonged inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP)

Why not other options:

A. Direct opening of ligand-gated Na⁺ channels: Causes fast EPSP (excitatory), not inhibitory

C. Rapid influx of Ca²⁺ through NMDA receptors: Produces excitatory effects and synaptic plasticity (LTP)

D. Closure of Cl⁻ channels: Would reduce inhibition → excitatory effect, opposite of IPSP

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient in convulsive status epilepticus continues to seize despite adequate benzodiazepine therapy. The next drug of choice is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phenytoin / Fosphenytoin

Management of convulsive status epilepticus follows a stepwise protocol:

1. First-line: Rapid-acting benzodiazepine

• IV lorazepam, diazepam, or IM midazolam

2. Second-line (if seizures persist):

• IV phenytoin or fosphenytoin → stabilizes neuronal membranes by blocking voltage-gated Na⁺ channels

3. Third-line (refractory status):

• Phenobarbital, levetiracetam, valproate

4. Super-refractory:

• General anesthesia (propofol, midazolam infusion

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient presents with fever, neck rigidity and altered sensorium. The resident was instructed to perform a lumbar puncture on this patient. What is the correct order of managing this patient? 1. Place IV cannula and give fluids at 40 mL/h 2. Start injection ceftriaxone 3. Fundoscopy 4. Perform guarded lumbar puncture
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3, 4, 2

In suspected acute bacterial meningitis, lumbar puncture must be performed safely after ruling out raised intracranial pressure to prevent brain herniation.

Correct sequence of management:

• Stabilize patient first → secure IV access and start fluids
• Fundoscopy → check for papilledema (sign of raised ICP)
• Guarded lumbar puncture → if no signs of raised ICP
• Start antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) immediately after CSF collection

Always rule out raised intracranial pressure before LP to avoid herniation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient sustains a knife wound causing hemisection of the spinal cord at T10 (Brown-Séquard syndrome). Below the level of the lesion, what pattern of sensory loss would be expected?
options: Ipsilateral loss of pain/temperature and contralateral loss of vibration/proprioception
Ipsilateral loss of vibration/proprioception/fine touch and contralateral loss of pain/temperature
Bilateral loss of all sensory modalities below the level of the lesion
Ipsilateral loss of both pain/temperature and vibration/proprioception
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ipsilateral loss of vibration/proprioception/fine touch and contralateral loss of pain/temperature

| Tract | Site of 2nd-order decussation | Effect of spinal hemisection (below lesion)

| ----- | ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------

| Dorsal column | Medulla | Ipsilateral loss (vibration, proprioception, fine touch)

| Spinothalamic | Spinal cord (near level of entry) | Contralateral loss (pain, temperature)

| Corticospinal | Medulla (pyramidal decussation) | Ipsilateral UMN signs

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with a posterior cortical lesion is unable to perceive more than one object at a time, has difficulty accurately reaching for objects under visual guidance, and shows impaired voluntary eye movements despite normal ocular motility. This constellation of findings is best described as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Balint syndrome

Balint syndrome results from bilateral parieto-occipital (posterior cortical) lesions and is characterized by a classic triad:

1. Simultanagnosia: Inability to perceive more than one object at a time
2. Optic ataxia: Difficulty reaching for objects using visual guidance
3. Oculomotor (ocular) apraxia: Impaired voluntary eye movements despite normal ocular motility

Exam differentiation:

• Gerstmann syndrome: Dominant parietal lesion → acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, L–R disorientation
• Anton syndrome: Cortical blindness with denial of blindness
• Visual agnosia: Cannot recognize objects but vision intact; no optic ataxia or gaze apraxia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with chronic alcoholism develops memory impairment related to hypothalamic damage. Which structure is classically involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mammillary bodies

Chronic alcoholism can cause thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, leading to Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome, which primarily damages the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus.

Damage results in Korsakoff psychosis characterized by:

• Severe anterograde amnesia
• Confabulation
• Memory impairment

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with hypothalamic damage develops loss of pulsatile secretion of a hormone, leading to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, while other pituitary axes are relatively preserved. Which neuronal population is most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kisspeptin–neurokinin B–dynorphin neurons

Pulsatile secretion of GnRH from the hypothalamus is essential for normal LH and FSH release and reproductive function.

This pulsatility is generated by Kisspeptin–Neurokinin B–Dynorphin (KNDy) neurons located in the arcuate nucleus.

• Kisspeptin: Stimulates GnRH neuron activity
• Neurokinin B: Promotes synchronized pulsatile firing
• Dynorphin: Provides inhibitory feedback to regulate pulse frequency

Damage to KNDy neurons → loss of GnRH pulsatility → hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with relatively preserved other pituitary axes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with long-standing liver cirrhosis develops confusion and altered level of consciousness. Blood ammonia levels are markedly elevated. The toxin primarily affects astrocytes leading to increased production of which substance causing cerebral edema?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glutamine

• This condition is Hepatic encephalopathy.
• Mechanism:

• Liver failure → ammonia not detoxified
• Ammonia enters brain
• Astrocytes convert ammonia + glutamate → glutamine
• Glutamine accumulation causes astrocyte swelling and cerebral edema

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Ablation of Brodmann area 1 leads to loss of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tactile discrimination and two-point discrimination

Brodmann areas 3, 1, and 2 form the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus, each with specialized sensory functions:

• Area 3: Main receiving area for pain, temperature, and crude touch
• Area 1: Responsible for tactile localization, texture perception, and two-point discrimination
• Area 2: Integrates size, shape, and proprioceptive information

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the factors would suggest a higher risk for a patient with TIA developing stroke in the future according to ABCD2 scoring except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Duration of symptoms 5 mins

ABCD₂ components:

• A – Age ≥60 years → 1 point
• B – Blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg → 1 point
• C – Clinical features:

o    Unilateral weakness → 2 points

o    Speech impairment (without weakness) → 1 point
• D – Duration of symptoms:

o    ≥60 min → 2 points

o    10–59 min → 1 point

o    <10 min → 0 points
• D – Diabetes mellitus → 1 point

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following are subcortical dementias, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pick’s disease

Subcortical dementias primarily affect the basal ganglia, thalamus, brainstem, and white matter, leading to psychomotor slowing, impaired attention, executive dysfunction, and mood changes rather than early aphasia or apraxia.

Examples include:

• Parkinson’s disease dementia
• Huntington disease
• Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP)

Pick’s disease (Frontotemporal dementia) is a cortical dementia, characterized by early personality changes, behavioral disinhibition, and language impairment due to frontal and temporal lobe degeneration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following statements about NMDA receptors are true except:
options: They are blocked by Mg²⁺ at resting potential
They mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. They mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission

NMDA receptors are glutamate-gated ion channels involved in synaptic plasticity, learning, and memory. They have unique properties compared with other excitatory receptors.

Key features:

• Permeable to Ca²⁺, Na⁺, and K⁺
• Blocked by Mg²⁺ at resting membrane potential
• Require both glutamate binding and postsynaptic depolarization to remove the Mg²⁺ block
• Produce slow excitatory postsynaptic responses

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All the following statements are true regarding Miller-Fisher syndrome except?
options: Associated with areflexia of the limbs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type of axonal neuropathy

Miller–Fisher syndrome (MFS) is a rare variant of Guillain–Barré syndrome characterized by the classic triad: Ophthalmoplegia, Ataxia and Areflexia.

Key associations:

• Strongly associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies
• Usually follows a preceding infection
• Considered a demyelinating neuropathy, not primarily axonal

Why option B is incorrect:

MFS is classically a demyelinating immune-mediated neuropathy, whereas axonal forms are seen in variants like AMAN/AMSAN of GBS.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: An intensivist is evaluating a patient for brain stem death in the ICU. Presence of which of the following features maybe seen in this patient even if brain dead? 1. Cremasteric reflex 2. Decorticate and decerebrate posturing 3. HR 110bpm 4. SBP of 110 mmHg 5. Positive corneal reflex
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3 and 4

Brain stem death is defined as the irreversible loss of all brain stem functions, including consciousness, brain stem reflexes, and the ability to breathe spontaneously. However, spinal cord–mediated reflexes and autonomic functions may persist despite brain stem death.

Why the correct answer is D (1, 3 and 4):

• Cremasteric reflex – a spinal reflex that may persist.
• Heart rate of 110 bpm – cardiac activity can continue due to intrinsic pacemaker activity and residual autonomic influences.
• SBP of 110 mmHg – blood pressure may be maintained temporarily with ongoing cardiovascular support.

Why not the other options?

• Decorticate and decerebrate posturing indicate residual brain/brainstem function and are not compatible with established brain stem death.
• Corneal reflex is a brain stem reflex (CN V and VII) and must be absent in brain stem death.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Ataxia due to vitamin E deficiency most closely resembles which of the following neurological conditions?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (SACD)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Friedreich’s ataxia

Vitamin E deficiency–related ataxia produces a neurological picture that closely mimics Friedreich’s ataxia due to degeneration of the posterior columns, spinocerebellar tracts, and peripheral nerves.

Common features with Friedreich’s ataxia:

• Progressive cerebellar ataxia
• Loss of proprioception and vibration sense
• Areflexia
• Peripheral neuropathy
• Dysarthria

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Cortical homunculus representation of the body in the cerebrum is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vertical

The cortical homunculus represents somatotopic organization of the body on the primary motor and sensory cortex (precentral and postcentral gyri).

Orientation:

• Arranged vertically along the central sulcus
• From medial → lateral:

o    Lower limb (paracentral lobule)

o    Trunk

o    Upper limb

o    Face and tongue (most lateral)
• Areas needing fine control (hands, lips) have larger cortical representation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: During a spinal cord electrophysiology experiment, stimulation of an α-motor neuron produces a brief burst of activity followed by suppression of firing in the same motor neuron pool. This inhibitory effect is mediated by an interneuron that is excited by acetylcholine released from recurrent axon collaterals of the motor neuron. Which neurotransmitter released from this interneuron is primarily responsible for the inhibition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glycine

• The interneuron described is the Renshaw cell.
• Mechanism:

• α-motor neuron releases acetylcholine
• Activates Renshaw cell via nicotinic receptors
• Renshaw cell releases glycine
• Produces recurrent inhibition of α-motor neurons

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: If you see the word "yellow," you'll likely recognize "banana" faster than "television" because yellow and banana are more closely linked in memory. Which of the following structures is this concept dependent on?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neocortex

Faster recognition of related concepts (e.g., “yellow” → “banana”) demonstrates semantic memory and associative priming, which depend primarily on the neocortex which Stores long-term semantic knowledge, language, and conceptual associations.

Responsible for linking related concepts and meaning-based memory retrieval

Differentiation:

• Hippocampus: Formation of new episodic memories
• Amygdala: Emotional memory/fear processing
• Striatum: Procedural memory and habit learning

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: In isolated Gerstman’s syndrome, the damage is in :
options: Superior parietal lobule of the dominant hemisphere
Inferior parietal lobule of the dominant hemisphere
Superior parietal lobule of the non-dominant hemisphere
Inferior parietal lobule of the non-dominant hemisphere
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inferior parietal lobule of the dominant hemisphere

Gerstmann syndrome results from a lesion in the inferior parietal lobule (angular gyrus) of the dominant hemisphere (usually left).

Classic tetrad:

• Agraphia
• Acalculia
• Finger agnosia
• Left–right disorientation

Exam tip:

• Dominant inferior parietal lesion → Gerstmann syndrome
• Non-dominant parietal lesion → hemineglect, constructional apraxia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Match List I (Drugs) with List II (Primary mechanism of action) List I – Drugs A. Ethosuximide B. Levetiracetam C. Lacosamide D. Vigabatrin E. Perampanel List II – Mechanism 1. Inhibition of synaptic vesicle protein involved in neurotransmitter release 2. Irreversible inhibition of GABA transaminase 3. Blockade of slow inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels 4. Non-competitive AMPA receptor antagonism 5. Blockade of thalamic pacemaker currents
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A-5, B-1, C-3, D-2, E-4

Antiepileptic drugs are frequently tested by their unique primary mechanisms of action, which target ion channels, neurotransmitter release, or excitatory/inhibitory pathways.

• Ethosuximide: Blocks T-type Ca²⁺ (thalamic pacemaker) currents → drug of choice for absence seizures
• Levetiracetam: Inhibits synaptic vesicle protein SV2A → ↓ neurotransmitter release
• Lacosamide: Enhances slow inactivation of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
• Vigabatrin: Irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase → ↑ GABA levels
• Perampanel: Non-competitive AMPA receptor antagonist → ↓ glutamate-mediated excitation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Match the following genes associated with Alzheimer’s disease with their chromosomes List I (Gene) A. APOE (ε2 / ε4) B. Presenilin-1 (PSEN-1) C. Presenilin-2 (PSEN-2) D. LRP1 E. APP (Amyloid precursor protein) List II (Chromosome) 1.Chromosome 1 2.Chromosome 12 3.Chromosome 14 4.Chromosome 19 5.Chromosome 21
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A-4,B-3, C-1 D-2 E-5

Key genes implicated in Alzheimer’s disease are frequently tested with their chromosomal locations:

A. APP (Amyloid precursor protein) → 4. Chromosome 21

• Explains early Alzheimer’s in Down syndrome (trisomy 21)

B. Presenilin-1 (PSEN-1) → 3. Chromosome 14

• Most common cause of early-onset familial Alzheimer’s

C. Presenilin-2 (PSEN-2) → 1. Chromosome 1

D. APOE (ε4 risk allele) → 2. Chromosome 19

• Strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer’s

E. LRP1 → 5. Chromosome 12

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Match the neurotransmitter with its correct receptor type:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GABA-A – Ionotropic

Neurotransmitter receptors are broadly classified into ionotropic (ligand-gated ion channels) and metabotropic (G-protein-coupled receptors, GPCRs). GABA-A receptors are ionotropic chloride channels, producing rapid inhibitory neurotransmission in the CNS.

• GABA-A receptor is a ligand-gated Cl⁻ channel.
• Activation causes Cl⁻ influx, leading to neuronal hyperpolarization and rapid inhibition.
• Targeted by benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and zolpidem.

Why not other options?

• B. Glycine – G-Protein Coupled Receptor: Glycine receptor is ionotropic (Cl⁻ channel), not GPCR.
• C. Nicotinic – G-Protein Coupled Receptor: Nicotinic receptor is ionotropic (Na⁺/K⁺ channel), not GPCR.
• D. GABA-B – Ionotropic: GABA-B is Gi-coupled GPCR, not ionotropic.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Thalidomide should not be used in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HIV-assosiated peripheral neuropathy

Thalidomide is an immunomodulatory drug used for several inflammatory and dermatologic conditions but is contraindicated in peripheral neuropathy because it can cause or worsen neuropathy.

Uses of thalidomide:

• Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) – drug of choice
• Behçet syndrome (oral/genital ulcers)
• HIV-associated aphthous ulcers
• Multiple myeloma

Major adverse effects:

• Peripheral neuropathy (dose-related, often irreversible)
• Severe teratogenicity (phocomelia)
• Sedation, constipation, thrombosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: The Westphal variant of Huntington’s disease is most closely related to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parkinson’s disease

The Westphal variant is a juvenile form of Huntington’s disease characterized predominantly by parkinsonian features rather than chorea. Key features of Westphal variant:

• Early onset (juvenile HD)
• Rigidity and bradykinesia (parkinsonism)
• Dystonia
• Seizures common
• Rapid progression
• Often associated with paternal transmission and larger CAG repeat expansion

Comparison:

• Adult Huntington’s: Chorea, behavioral changes, dementia
• Westphal variant: Parkinsonism-dominant → resembles Parkinson’s disease

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: What would be seen if the central part of the cord was involved? 1. LMN lesion of trunk and UMN of lower limbs. 2. UMN lesion of trunk and LMN of lower limbs. 3. Bladder and bowel involvement. 4. Posterior tract involvement.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1 and 3

Lesions involving the central part of the spinal cord (e.g., central cord syndrome, syringomyelia) affect structures in a characteristic pattern.

Key features:

• LMN signs at level of lesion (anterior horn cells) → flaccid weakness of trunk/segmental muscles
• UMN signs below lesion (corticospinal tract) → spasticity in lower limbs
• Autonomic involvement → early bladder and bowel dysfunction

Posterior columns are located posteriorly → often preserved initially

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which neuropeptide has an orexigenic effect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neuropeptide Y

Neuropeptide Y (NPY) is one of the most potent orexigenic (appetite-stimulating) neuropeptides in the hypothalamus. It is released by neurons in the arcuate nucleus and promotes food intake while reducing energy expenditure.

• NPY stimulates hunger and feeding behavior.
• Its activity increases during fasting and states of negative energy balance.
• It works together with Agouti-related peptide (AgRP) to promote appetite.

Why not the others?

• A. MSH (α-MSH) → Suppresses appetite via melanocortin receptors.
• B. Leptin → Satiety hormone released from adipocytes; inhibits NPY neurons.
• D. CRH → Decreases appetite and is associated with stress-induced anorexia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following anti-obesity drugs is a selective 5-HT2C receptor agonist?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lorcaserin

Lorcaserin is a selective 5-HT₂C (serotonin) receptor agonist that promotes weight loss by activating pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons in the hypothalamus, thereby increasing satiety and reducing food intake.

• Lorcaserin selectively stimulates 5-HT₂C receptors in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus.
• This activates the melanocortin pathway, leading to:

• Increased satiety
• Reduced appetite
• Decreased caloric intake

| Drug | Mechanism of Action

| ---- | -------------------

| Lorcaserin | Selective 5-HT₂C receptor agonist

| Orlistat | Inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipases

| Phentermine | Sympathomimetic; increases norepinephrine release

| Topiramate | Enhances GABA activity and suppresses appetite (mechanism not fully understood)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of Klüver–Bucy syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hyperactivity

Klüver–Bucy syndrome results from bilateral lesions of the amygdala and anterior temporal lobes, classically following herpes simplex encephalitis, bilateral temporal lobectomy, trauma, or stroke.

Characteristic features include:

• ✅ Hypersexuality
• ✅ Hyperorality (placing objects in the mouth)
• ✅ Hyperphagia
• ✅ Hypermetamorphosis (compulsive exploration of visual stimuli)
• ✅ Placidity (loss of fear and aggression)
• ✅ Visual agnosia (psychic blindness)

Hyperactivity is not a defining feature of Klüver–Bucy syndrome.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Hypersexuality – A classic manifestation due to loss of amygdala-mediated behavioral inhibition.
• C. Hypermetamorphosis – Excessive curiosity and irresistible urge to explore environmental stimuli; a hallmark feature.
• D. Placidity – Patients become unusually calm and lose normal fear and aggressive responses because of bilateral amygdala damage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following neurotransmitter–peptide combinations originates predominantly from neurons of the arcuate nucleus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. POMC – α-MSH

The arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus plays a central role in appetite and energy homeostasis and contains POMC (pro-opiomelanocortin) neurons.

• POMC neurons produce α-MSH (alpha-melanocyte–stimulating hormone)
• α-MSH acts on melanocortin receptors (MC4) in the hypothalamus to suppress appetite and increase satiety

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 32-year-old man presents with history of recurrent jaundice over the previous decade. Family gives history of the patient having episodes of facial grimacing. Which one of the following is a clinical clue to the diagnosis?
options: Adenoma sebaceum in the mid face
Osler’s nodes at the finger tips
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Kayser-Fleisher rings in the cornea

The combination of recurrent jaundice and facial grimacing (orofacial dystonia) in a young adult is highly suggestive of Wilson’s disease (hepatolenticular degeneration). A key clinical clue is the presence of Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings, which are brownish-green deposits of copper in Descemet’s membrane of the cornea, best detected by slit-lamp examination.

Why not the other options?

• A. Adenoma sebaceum in the mid face: Seen in Tuberous sclerosis.
• B. Erythema nodosum on the skin: Associated with sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, tuberculosis, and streptococcal infections.
• D. Osler’s nodes at the fingertips: Painful nodules seen in infective endocarditis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A clinical assessment video shows a 7-year-old girl with continuous, slow, writhing involuntary movements involving the hands and fingers. What is the correct semiological term?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Athetosis

Athetosis is a hyperkinetic movement disorder characterized by continuous, slow, sinuous, writhing involuntary movements, predominantly affecting the distal limbs (hands and fingers). These movements often worsen during voluntary activity and disappear during sleep.

The video description of continuous, slow, writhing movements of the hands and fingers is classic for athetosis.

Why not the other options?

• B. Hemiballismus: Characterized by violent, flinging, large-amplitude movements of one side of the body, usually due to a lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus.
• C. Chorea: Consists of rapid, irregular, jerky, dance-like movements that flow randomly from one body part to another.
• D. Myoclonus: Characterized by sudden, brief, shock-like muscle jerks, not slow writhing movements.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is presented with a staggering gait and nystagmus after a road traffic accident. Which lobe of cerebellum is affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Flocculonodular

Staggering gait with nystagmus indicates involvement of the vestibulocerebellum.

The flocculonodular lobe controls balance, posture, and eye movements via vestibular connections.

Lesions cause truncal ataxia, vertigo, and nystagmus with a positive Romberg sign.

Anterior lobe causes limb ataxia, and vermis affects axial posture without prominent eye signs.

| Structure | Function | Lesion Feature

| --------- | -------- | --------------

| Flocculonodular | Balance + eye movement | ⭐ Ataxia + nystagmus

| Anterior lobe | Posture | Gait disturbance

| Posterior lobe | Fine movement | Limb ataxia

| Vermis | Trunk control | Truncal instability

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All of the following disorders are associated with dystonia and basal ganglia involvement. Which among the following needs to be diagnosed/excluded as it requires a distinctly different treatment approach compared to the others?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Wilson disease

Wilson disease is an important treatable cause of dystonia and basal ganglia dysfunction. Therefore, it should always be actively excluded in any young patient presenting with dystonia, movement disorders, or unexplained liver disease, as early copper-chelating therapy can halt disease progression, unlike most other neurodegenerative disorders with brain iron accumulation.

• Wilson disease is caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to copper accumulation in the liver, basal ganglia, and cornea.
• Specific treatment includes:

• D-Penicillamine or Trientine (copper chelators)
• Zinc therapy to reduce intestinal copper absorption

Why not the other options?

• A. Pantothenate Kinase-Associated Neurodegeneration (PKAN): A form of NBIA (Neurodegeneration with Brain Iron Accumulation); treatment is mainly supportive.
• B. PLA2G6-Associated Neurodegeneration (PLAN): Another NBIA disorder with no disease-modifying therapy.
• D. Kufor-Rakeb syndrome: A juvenile Parkinsonism syndrome (ATP13A2 mutation); managed symptomatically with dopaminergic therapy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Circuits between the basal ganglia and the motor cortex constitute the extrapyramidal system which controls muscle tone, body posture and the initiation of movement. Lesions of the extrapyramidal system present clinically with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tremor and rigidity

The extrapyramidal system comprises the basal ganglia and their neural connections, which regulate muscle tone, posture, and the initiation and smooth coordination of voluntary movements. Unlike pyramidal tract lesions, extrapyramidal lesions do not cause muscle weakness; instead, they present with abnormal involuntary movements and altered muscle tone, classically tremor and rigidity.

• Clinical features of extrapyramidal lesions:

• Resting tremor
• Rigidity (lead-pipe/cogwheel)
• Bradykinesia
• Postural instability
• Chorea, athetosis, dystonia

• Common causes:

• Parkinson disease
• Huntington disease
• Wilson disease
• Drug-induced extrapyramidal syndrome (antipsychotics, metoclopramide)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following clinical features: 1. Hypomimia 2. Dysphonia 3. Festination gait 4. Cogwheel rigidity Which of the features given above are generally present in Parkinsonism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Parkinsonism is a hypokinetic movement disorder resulting from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia. It is clinically characterized by bradykinesia, along with resting tremor, rigidity, and postural instability, and is associated with several characteristic motor features.

• Cardinal features: Bradykinesia (mandatory), resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, and postural instability.
• Hypomimia (masked facies): Reduced facial expression due to facial bradykinesia.
• Hypophonia/Dysphonia: Soft, monotonous speech.
• Festination gait: Short, rapid, shuffling steps with difficulty stopping.
• Other features:

• Micrographia
• Stooped posture
• Reduced arm swing
• Freezing of gait
• Decreased blinking

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Out of the following areas of brain, which area is most commonly affected on brain imaging in Wilson’s disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Basal ganglia

Wilson’s disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired biliary copper excretion and excessive copper accumulation. The basal ganglia, particularly the putamen, are the most commonly affected structures on brain MRI, explaining the characteristic movement disorders seen in the disease.

• Basal ganglia, especially the putamen, show the most frequent MRI abnormalities.
• MRI may demonstrate:

• Bilateral symmetric T2 hyperintensities in the putamen
• Globus pallidus involvement
• Caudate nucleus involvement
• Thalamic and brainstem involvement in advanced disease
• “Face of the giant panda” sign in the midbrain (classic MRI finding).

Why not the other options?

• A. Cerebellum – May be involved in advanced disease but is not the most commonly affected area.
• B. Sub-cortex – White matter involvement is less common than basal ganglia involvement.
• C. Thalamus – Can be affected but less frequently than the basal ganglia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Tremors at rest seen in Parkinsonism are due to which of the following basal ganglia pathway changes?
options: Inhibition of globus pallidus interna by putamen
Loss of inhibitory discharge from globus pallidus interna
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Loss of inhibitory discharge from globus pallidus interna

Normal circuit

• Substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) releases dopamine onto the striatum (caudate + putamen).
• Dopamine acts on two different receptor populations in the striatum:
• D1 receptors → excite the direct pathway (striatum → GPi/SNr directly)
• D2 receptors → inhibit the indirect pathway (striatum → GPe → STN → GPi/SNr)
• Net effect of dopamine: it facilitates the direct pathway and suppresses the indirect pathway — both actions reduce GPi output, which disinhibits the thalamus, which increases excitatory drive to the motor cortex. More dopamine = more movement.

In Parkinsonism

• SNpc degenerates → dopamine loss.
• Loss of D1 stimulation → direct pathway underactive.
• Loss of D2 inhibition → indirect pathway becomes overactive (disinhibited GPe→STN drive increases, STN excites GPi even more).
• Both effects push in the same direction: GPi/SNr becomes hyperactive, firing more inhibitory (GABAergic) output onto the thalamus.
• This excessive inhibitory discharge from GPi suppresses the thalamocortical pathway → bradykinesia/rigidity.

Why option C is correct for tremor specifically

The classic teaching (and the one tested here) is that the resting tremor of Parkinsonism results from loss of the normal inhibitory (GABAergic) discharge from GPi disrupting the ordinary tonic inhibitory tone on thalamic/brainstem motor circuits, unmasking abnormal oscillatory (pacemaker) activity in the thalamus and basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop that generates the rhythmic 4–6 Hz tremor.

Why the distractors are wrong

• A) Hyperdirect pathway inhibition — the hyperdirect pathway (cortex → STN directly) is involved in rapid movement-stopping/impulse control, not classically tied to resting tremor generation.
• B) Inhibitory discharge from GPi by putamen — this describes the normal direct pathway action (striatum inhibits GPi), not the pathological change; it also reverses the direction of causation (GPi doesn't get inhibited more, it gets inhibited less due to dopamine loss).
• D) Excitation of GPe — dopamine loss actually disinhibits GPe activity onto STN in the classic model, but GPe itself isn't "excited" in a way that directly explains tremor; it's a downstream consequence, not the primary mechanistic answer being tested.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are clinical features of Parkinson’s disease? I. Reduced eye blinking II. Drooling of saliva III. Soft voice IV. Macrographia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dopamine deficiency in the nigrostriatal pathway. It is characterized by both motor and non-motor symptoms.

The classic motor features are:

• Bradykinesia (essential feature) ⭐
• Resting tremor
• Rigidity
• Postural instability

The following are characteristic clinical features of Parkinson’s disease:

• I. Reduced eye blinking: Due to facial bradykinesia, producing a masked facies (hypomimia).
• II. Drooling of saliva: Caused by reduced spontaneous swallowing, not excessive saliva production.
• III. Soft voice (Hypophonia): Speech becomes soft, monotonous, and low in volume.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Macrographia: Parkinson’s disease causes micrographia (progressively smaller handwriting), which is a classic feature due to bradykinesia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A comatose patient after sustaining severe head injury has been admitted in neurosurgical ICU. Which of the following parameters should ideally be maintained in this patient? 1. pCO₂ = 4.5–5.0 kPa (33–38 mmHg) 2. MAP = 80–90 mmHg 3. pO₂ > 11 kPa (>80 mmHg) 4. Na⁺ <130 mEq/L Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

In severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), the goal is to prevent secondary brain injury by maintaining adequate oxygenation, cerebral perfusion, and normocapnia.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. pCO₂ = 4.5–5.0 kPa (33–38 mmHg): Correct. Normocapnia is maintained; prolonged hyperventilation is avoided.
• 2. MAP = 80–90 mmHg: Correct. Adequate MAP is required to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP).
• 3. pO₂ >11 kPa (>80 mmHg): Correct. Hypoxia must be avoided.
• 4. Na⁺ <130 mEq/L: Incorrect. Hyponatremia worsens cerebral edema. Serum sodium should be maintained in the normal or slightly high range.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following clinical features: 1. Raised ICP 2. Seizures 3. Focal deficit 4. Headache Which of the above clinical features are related to most brain tumours?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Why is A correct?

• 1. Raised ICP ✓

• Brain tumors increase intracranial pressure by mass effect, cerebral edema, or obstruction of CSF pathways, leading to headache, vomiting, papilledema, and altered consciousness.

• 2. Seizures ✓

• Seizures are a common presenting feature, especially in supratentorial tumors, due to cortical irritation.

• 3. Focal deficit ✓

• Depending on the tumor location, patients may develop hemiparesis, aphasia, visual field defects, cranial nerve palsies, or cerebellar signs.

• 4. Headache ✓

• Headache is one of the most frequent symptoms, typically worse in the early morning or aggravated by coughing, sneezing, or straining due to raised ICP.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What are the components to establish the diagnosis of Brain Death? I. Absent brain stem reflexes II. Apnoea in presence of elevated PCO₂ III. Hypothermia IV. Irreversible and unresponsive coma Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

Brain death is defined as the irreversible cessation of all functions of the entire brain, including the brainstem. It is a clinical diagnosis that requires demonstration of irreversible coma, absence of all brainstem reflexes, and apnea despite adequate stimulation by elevated carbon dioxide (CO₂) after excluding reversible causes.

• I. Absent brainstem reflexes ✔

• Essential for the diagnosis.
• Includes absent:

• Pupillary light reflex
• Corneal reflex
• Oculocephalic reflex (doll’s eye)
• Oculovestibular reflex (caloric test)
• Gag reflex
• Cough reflex

• II. Apnea in the presence of elevated PCO₂ ✔

• Demonstrated by the apnea test.
