• Absence of spontaneous respiratory effort despite PaCO₂ ≥60 mmHg or an increase of ≥20 mmHg above baseline confirms loss of medullary respiratory drive.

• III. Hypothermia ✘

• Hypothermia is not a criterion for brain death.
• In fact, hypothermia must be excluded before testing because it can suppress brain function.
• Core temperature should generally be ≥36°C before assessment.

• IV. Irreversible and unresponsive coma ✔

• The patient must be in a known irreversible coma with no response to painful stimuli.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are the aetiological factors associated with a communicating hydrocephalus? I. Post haemorrhagic II. Lesions within the ventricle III. CSF infection IV. Raised CSF protein Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

Communicating hydrocephalus occurs when there is impaired absorption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) at the arachnoid villi (granulations) despite patent ventricular pathways. Since the ventricular system communicates freely with the subarachnoid space, all ventricles enlarge uniformly.

The following conditions cause communicating hydrocephalus:

• I. Post-haemorrhagic: Subarachnoid or intraventricular hemorrhage causes blood products to obstruct the arachnoid granulations, reducing CSF absorption.
• III. CSF infection: Meningitis causes inflammation and fibrosis of the arachnoid villi, impairing CSF absorption.
• IV. Raised CSF protein: High CSF protein (e.g., in Guillain-Barré syndrome, spinal tumors, chronic meningitis) increases CSF viscosity and interferes with absorption.

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Lesions within the ventricle: Intraventricular lesions (e.g., colloid cyst, intraventricular tumor) obstruct CSF flow and cause non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus, not communicating hydrocephalus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 20-year-old male presents with sudden onset severe headache and vomiting. On examination, he has neck stiffness. A CT scan of the brain shows hydrocephalus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Subarachnoid Haemorrhage

The classic triad here is:

• Sudden onset severe headache ("thunderclap headache" — worst headache of life)
• Neck stiffness (meningeal irritation)
• Young patient (20-year-old)

This points strongly to SAH, most commonly caused by rupture of a berry (saccular) aneurysm.

Why the other options are wrong

| Option | Why eliminated

| ------ | --------------

| A - Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus | Occurs in elderly with classic triad: dementia, gait disturbance, urinary incontinence — not sudden headache

| B - Bacterial Meningitis | Can cause neck stiffness, but headache is gradual, fever is prominent, and CT rarely shows hydrocephalus acutely

| C - Viral Encephalitis | Presents with altered consciousness, fever, seizures — not sudden thunderclap headache

Key Exam Points

• SAH = "worst headache of life" + neck stiffness + young patient
• CT shows hyperdense (white) blood in basal cisterns
• If CT negative → do lumbar puncture (xanthochromia)
• Most common cause: berry aneurysm (Circle of Willis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old lady presented with complaint of chronic daily headache. She has prior history of migraine but is increasingly unrelieved with analgesics. She has history of using Sumatriptan almost daily since the last three weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medication overuse headache

Medication Overuse Headache (MOH), also known as rebound headache, is a secondary chronic headache disorder caused by the frequent use of acute headache medications in patients with a pre-existing primary headache disorder, most commonly migraine. Instead of relieving headache, excessive use of these medications perpetuates a cycle of chronic daily headache.

• Occurs in patients with pre-existing migraine or tension-type headache.
• Suspect MOH in patients with headache on ≥15 days/month and regular overuse of acute headache medications for >3 months.
• Common offending drugs:

• Triptans (e.g., Sumatriptan)
• NSAIDs
• Paracetamol
• Opioids
• Ergot derivatives
• Combination analgesics

• Treatment:

• Discontinue the overused medication (abruptly for most drugs; gradual taper for opioids/barbiturates).
• Initiate or optimize preventive migraine therapy.
• Patient education to avoid recurrence.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 25-year-old female patient with diagnosed recurrent migraine despite Sumatriptan, has 3-5 episodes/week and presents with features of anxiety and palpitations. There is no clinical neck swelling, no history of coronary artery disease; however, there is a family history of CHD. She reports experiencing chest tightness after taking the medication. What is the most appropriate agent to add for migraine prophylaxis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Propranolol

| Clue | Meaning

| ---- | -------

| 3–5 episodes/week | Needs prophylaxis

| Chest tightness after sumatriptan | Triptan side effect (vasoconstriction)

| Anxiety + palpitations | Sympathetic overactivity

| Family history of CHD | Avoid excessive vasoconstrictors

This patient has frequent migraines (≥3–5/week) requiring prophylactic therapy.

Propranolol, a non-selective beta blocker, is effective for migraine prevention and also helps anxiety and palpitations.

Chest tightness with sumatriptan suggests triptan intolerance, so adding another triptan or ergotamine is inappropriate.

Topiramate is an alternative, but beta blockers are preferred here given associated anxiety and autonomic symptoms.

| Drug | Role | Key Feature

| ---- | ---- | -----------

| Propranolol | ⭐ Prophylaxis | Good for anxiety

| Topiramate | Prophylaxis | Cognitive side effects

| Naratriptan | Acute | Vasoconstriction

| Ergotamine | Acute | Strong vasoconstrictor

Start Prophylaxis-

• ≥4 attacks/month
• Severe disability
• Poor response to acute therapy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with brief episodes of lancinating unilateral facial pain involving the buccal distribution. Pain is triggered by washing the face with cold water. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Trigeminal neuralgia

Trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) is characterized by recurrent episodes of sudden, severe, electric shock-like or lancinating unilateral facial pain occurring in the distribution of one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve (CN V). The pain is typically triggered by innocuous stimuli, such as washing the face, brushing teeth, shaving, chewing, talking, or exposure to cold air or water.

The maxillary (V2) division is the most commonly affected, followed by the mandibular (V3) division.

Why not the other options?

• A. Migraine: Causes prolonged throbbing headache lasting 4–72 hours with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia, not brief facial pain.
• B. Medication overuse headache: Chronic daily headache due to excessive use of analgesics, not paroxysmal facial pain.
• C. Chronic paroxysmal hemicrania: Causes short unilateral headaches with autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, conjunctival injection), responds dramatically to indomethacin, and does not follow the trigeminal nerve distribution.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 72-year-old patient with a confirmed diagnosis of mild to moderate Alzheimer's dementia has shown aversion and non-compliance to oral medications. The patient's caregiver reports difficulty in administering the oral drugs due to the patient's refusal to swallow pills. Considering the need for continued treatment, which of the following medications could be prescribed in a form that does not require oral administration?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rivastigmine

Core issue: ↓ Acetylcholine in brain (basal forebrain degeneration)

Strategy: Increase cholinergic transmission

| Class | Drugs

| ----- | -----

| Cholinesterase inhibitors | Donepezil, Rivastigmine, Galantamine

| NMDA antagonist | Memantine

Rivastigmine is available as a transdermal patch, making it suitable for patients who cannot take oral medications.

It is a cholinesterase inhibitor used in mild to moderate Alzheimer’s dementia.

The patch provides steady drug delivery and improves compliance.

Memantine, donepezil, and galantamine are primarily administered orally.

| Drug | Class | Route | Special Feature

| ---- | ----- | ----- | ---------------

| Rivastigmine | AChE inhibitor |  Patch | Non-oral option

| Donepezil | AChE inhibitor | Oral | Once daily

| Galantamine | AChE inhibitor | Oral | Dual action

| Memantine | NMDA antagonist | Oral | Moderate–severe

Patch Advantage

• Steady drug delivery
• Fewer GI side effects
• Better compliance

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A female patient presents to you with a unilateral headache. It is associated with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia. What is the best drug for acute management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sumatriptan

This presentation is classic migraine with unilateral headache, nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia.

Trigger

↓

Trigeminal nerve activation

↓

CGRP release

↓

Vasodilation + inflammation

↓

Migraine pain

Sumatriptan is the drug of choice for acute abortive treatment, acting as a 5-HT₁B/1D agonist. It causes cranial vasoconstriction and inhibits trigeminal neuropeptide release.

| Drug | Role | Use

| ---- | ---- | ---

| Sumatriptan | Abortive | Acute migraine

| Flunarizine | Prophylaxis | Prevention

| Propranolol | Prophylaxis | Prevention

| Topiramate | Prophylaxis | Prevention

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with migraine is treated with a triptan for an acute attack. Triptans exert their therapeutic effect by acting on which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5-HT1B/5-HT1D receptor

Triptans (e.g., sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan) are selective 5-HT₁B/5-HT₁D receptor agonists and are the first-line drugs for the acute treatment of moderate-to-severe migraine attacks. They relieve migraine by causing cranial vasoconstriction, inhibiting the release of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and other vasoactive neuropeptides, and blocking pain transmission in the trigeminovascular system.

Why not the other options?

• A. 5-HT₁A receptor: Involved mainly in mood regulation and anxiety; not the target of triptans.
• C. 5-HT₂A receptor agonist: Activation is not used in migraine therapy; methysergide is a 5-HT₂ receptor antagonist, historically used for migraine prophylaxis.
• D. 5-HT₃ receptor antagonist: Drugs such as ondansetron block 5-HT₃ receptors and are used as antiemetics, not as antimigraine agents.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An 80-year-old woman presents with a progressive decline in daily activity. She gives a history of staring into space with frequent visual hallucinations. Pathology reveals Lewy bodies in neurons. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Parkinson’s Disease

| Feature | Interpretation

| ------- | --------------

| Progressive decline | Dementia

| Visual hallucinations | characteristic of Lewy body disorders

| “Staring into space” | Fluctuating cognition

| Lewy bodies | α-synuclein pathology

Lewy bodies (α-synuclein inclusions) in neurons are characteristic of Parkinson’s disease.

Lewy body (LB) pathology. LBs are eosinophilic intraneuronal inclusions.

Progressive decline in daily activities with visual hallucinations and staring spells suggests Parkinson’s disease with dementia.

Visual hallucinations are common in advanced PD due to cortical Lewy body involvement.

| Feature | DLB | Parkinson’s

| ------- | --- | -----------

| Dementia | Early | Late

| Hallucinations | ⭐ Prominent | Less common

| Motor symptoms | Mild | Prominent

| Pathology | Lewy bodies | Lewy bodies

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding cluster headache: 1. The headaches are periodic, beginning at the same time for weeks at a stretch. 2. Patients experience severe unilateral periorbital pain which typically lasts from 30–90 minutes. 3. The headache is accompanied with autonomic features such as ipsilateral tearing, nasal congestion and conjunctival injection. 4. Subcutaneous injection of Sumatriptan or inhalation of 100% oxygen may be beneficial in halting acute attacks. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Cluster headache is a primary trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia (TAC) characterized by recurrent attacks of excruciating unilateral periorbital or temporal pain, accompanied by ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptoms. Attacks occur in clusters, often at the same time each day for weeks, followed by prolonged remission.

• Pain: Severe unilateral periorbital/temporal pain lasting 15–180 minutes (typically 30–90 minutes).
• Periodic pattern: Attacks occur at the same time daily for weeks (“cluster period”).
• Associated autonomic features:

• Ipsilateral lacrimation
• Conjunctival injection
• Nasal congestion/rhinorrhea
• Ptosis and miosis (partial Horner syndrome)

• Patients are typically restless or agitated during an attack (unlike migraine, where patients prefer to lie still).

Treatment

• Acute attack:

• 100% oxygen inhalation
• Subcutaneous sumatriptan

• Prevention:

• Verapamil (first-line prophylaxis)
• Lithium or topiramate in selected cases

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Transient Global Amnesia (TGA): 1. TGA mainly affects middle-aged persons who present with abrupt, discrete loss of anterograde memory lasting for few hours. 2. During the episode, the patients are unable to record new memories resulting in repetitive questioning. 3. Consciousness is impaired during the episode and the patient is unable to perform even simple motor functions. 4. After 4–6 hours, memory function and behaviour return to normal but the patient has complete and persistent amnesia for the duration of the episode. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Transient Global Amnesia (TGA) is a benign, self-limiting neurological syndrome characterized by the sudden onset of profound anterograde amnesia, with variable retrograde amnesia, lasting up to 24 hours (typically 4–6 hours). During the episode, consciousness, personal identity, language, and other cognitive and motor functions are preserved. Patients are unable to form new memories, leading to repetitive questioning, and recover completely except for persistent amnesia for the duration of the episode.

• Typical age: Middle-aged and elderly adults (50–70 years).
• Hallmark feature: Sudden anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning.
• Consciousness and higher cortical functions remain intact.
• No focal neurological deficits or seizures.
• Duration: Usually 4–6 hours, always <24 hours.
• Recovery: Complete recovery with permanent memory gap for the episode.
• MRI brain: May show small punctate diffusion-restricted lesions in the hippocampus on DWI after 24–72 hours.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) includes which of the following? 1. Asymptomatic neurocognitive disorder 2. Minor neurocognitive disorder 3. HIV-associated dementia Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) is a spectrum of cognitive impairment caused by HIV infection of the CNS. According to the Frascati criteria, HAND includes:

• Asymptomatic Neurocognitive Impairment (ANI)
• Mild Neurocognitive Disorder (MND) (previously called minor neurocognitive disorder)
• HIV-Associated Dementia (HAD)

Why are the other statements correct?

• 1. Asymptomatic neurocognitive disorder ✔️: Included in HAND.
• 2. Minor (Mild) neurocognitive disorder ✔️: Included in HAND.
• 3. HIV-associated dementia ✔️: Most severe form of HAND.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the first line therapy for aborting the acute attack of cluster headache?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 100% oxygen

Cluster Headache?

• A type of Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgia (TAC)
• Characterized by:

• Severe unilateral orbital/temporal pain
• Associated autonomic symptoms:

• Lacrimation
• Nasal congestion
• Ptosis

Often called “suicide headache” due to intensity

Oxygen works by-

• Causes cerebral vasoconstriction
• Reduces trigeminal nerve activation
• Modulates hypothalamic activity

Result:

• Rapid pain relief within 10–15 minutes

| Drug | Role | Use in Cluster Headache

| ---- | ---- | -----------------------

| Oxygen | Vasoconstriction | First-line acute

| Sumatriptan | 5-HT agonist | Acute (2nd line)

| Lithium | Mood stabilizer |  Prophylaxis only

| Topiramate | AED |  Prophylaxis only

| Feature | Cluster | Migraine

| ------- | ------- | --------

| Behavior | Restless | Wants to lie down

| Autonomic signs | Prominent | Mild/absent

| Duration | Short (minutes–hours) | Long (hours–days)

| Oxygen response | Excellent | No role

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are causes of reversible dementia? I. Hypothyroidism II. Vitamin B12 deficiency III. Dementia with Lewy body IV. Thiamine deficiency Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

Reversible (treatable) dementias are conditions in which cognitive impairment improves or stabilizes with appropriate treatment. Identifying these causes is essential because they should be excluded before diagnosing a primary neurodegenerative dementia such as Alzheimer’s disease.

• I. Hypothyroidism ✅

• Hypothyroidism can cause memory impairment, slowed thinking, depression, and dementia-like symptoms, which often improve with thyroxine replacement.

• II. Vitamin B12 deficiency ✅

• Vitamin B12 deficiency causes cognitive impairment, peripheral neuropathy, and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. Early treatment with vitamin B12 can reverse neurological and cognitive deficits.

• III. Dementia with Lewy body ❌

• Dementia with Lewy bodies is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder and is not a reversible cause of dementia.

• IV. Thiamine deficiency ✅

• Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency can cause Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, particularly in chronic alcoholics. Early thiamine replacement can prevent progression and may improve cognitive function.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are clinical features of Fronto-Temporal dementia? I. Personality change II. Language disturbance III. Memory may be preserved in early stages IV. Anti-cholinesterases are the drug of choice for treatment Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by degeneration of the frontal and/or temporal lobes. It is the second most common cause of early-onset dementia (<65 years) after Alzheimer’s disease.

• I. Personality change ✅

• One of the earliest and most characteristic features.
• Patients develop disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, socially inappropriate behavior, compulsive behavior, and poor judgment.

• II. Language disturbance ✅

• FTD commonly presents as Primary Progressive Aphasia (PPA) with impaired speech production, word finding, or language comprehension.

• III. Memory may be preserved in early stages ✅

• Episodic memory is often relatively preserved initially, distinguishing FTD from Alzheimer’s disease.

• IV. Anti-cholinesterases are the drug of choice for treatment ❌

• Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) are not effective in FTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
• Management is mainly supportive, with SSRIs often used for behavioral symptoms.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are clinical features of migraine? I. It is associated with dilatation of extracranial vessels II. Common migraine is seen without aura III. Aura is most often visual
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Migraine is a primary headache disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of moderate to severe, usually unilateral, throbbing headache, often associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia. It is believed to result from activation of the trigeminovascular system, leading to release of vasoactive neuropeptides such as calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), which causes vasodilatation of extracranial vessels and neurogenic inflammation.

All three statements are correct:

• I. It is associated with dilatation of extracranial vessels
• II. Common migraine is seen without aura (Migraine without aura accounts for 80–85% of cases)
• III. Aura is most often visual (e.g., scintillating scotoma, flashing lights, zig-zag lines.)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are features of Alzheimer’s disease? I. It is a disorder of cerebral cortical function II. Only short term memory is affected III. Patients deny that there is anything wrong IV. Depression is commonly present Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia and is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cortical neuronal degeneration, leading to impairment of memory, language, executive function, visuospatial skills, and behavior.

• I. It is a disorder of cerebral cortical function. ✔

• Alzheimer’s disease primarily affects the cerebral cortex, especially the hippocampus, temporal, and parietal lobes, resulting in progressive cognitive decline.

• II. Only short-term memory is affected. ✘

• Initially, short-term (recent) memory is affected, but as the disease progresses, long-term memory and other cognitive domains are also impaired.

• III. Patients deny that there is anything wrong. ✔

• Many patients exhibit anosognosia, a lack of awareness or denial of their cognitive deficits, particularly in the early and moderate stages.

• IV. Depression is commonly present. ✔

• Depression is a common neuropsychiatric manifestation and may occur early in the course of Alzheimer’s disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are inherited causes of dementia? 1. Alzheimer’s disease 2. Huntington’s disease 3. Wilson’s disease 4. Punch-drunk syndrome Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Inherited dementias are caused by genetic disorders that lead to progressive cognitive decline. Important inherited causes include familial Alzheimer’s disease, Huntington’s disease, and Wilson’s disease, whereas punch-drunk syndrome (chronic traumatic encephalopathy) is an acquired neurodegenerative disorder resulting from repetitive head trauma.

Why is A correct?

• 1. Alzheimer’s disease✅: Familial early-onset Alzheimer’s disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern due to mutations in APP, Presenilin-1 (PSEN1), and Presenilin-2 (PSEN2).
• 2. Huntington’s disease✅: An autosomal dominant disorder caused by CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene, presenting with dementia, chorea, and psychiatric symptoms.
• 3. Wilson’s disease✅: An autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism (ATP7B mutation) that can cause cognitive decline, psychiatric manifestations, and dementia.

Incorrect option:

• 4. Punch-drunk syndrome❌: Also known as chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), it is caused by repetitive head injury, not inheritance.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following best describes memantine’s mechanism of action in the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NMDA receptor antagonist

Memantine improves symptoms in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer’s disease by acting as a non-competitive NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptor antagonist. It reduces excessive glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity, which contributes to neuronal injury and cognitive decline, while preserving normal synaptic transmission.

Why not the other options?

• A. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition: Mechanism of donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, which increase acetylcholine levels in the brain and are primarily used for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer’s disease.
• C. Blockade of A-beta amyloid: Mechanism of anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies such as lecanemab and donanemab, which target amyloid plaques.
• D. Dopamine D₂ receptor antagonism: Mechanism of antipsychotic drugs (e.g., haloperidol, risperidone); not used to treat the cognitive symptoms of Alzheimer’s disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a marker of Alzheimer disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amyloid beta plaque

Alzheimer disease is characterized by extracellular amyloid-β plaque deposition in the cerebral cortex. Two pathological signatures:

1. Amyloid beta (Aβ) plaques → extracellular
2. Neurofibrillary tangles (tau protein) → intracellular

These plaques are derived from abnormal processing of amyloid precursor protein.

Amyloid precursor protein (APP)

↓ (β & γ secretase)

Amyloid β accumulation

↓

Extracellular plaques

↓

Neurotoxicity + synaptic dysfunction

↓

Cognitive decline

α-Synuclein is seen in Parkinson disease, GFAP marks astrocytes, and desmin is a muscle intermediate filament.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT indicative of underlying serious pathology in headache?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chronic Cocaine use

“Red flag headache”-

These are features suggesting secondary headache (dangerous cause), not primary headache like migraine.

| Letter | Meaning | Example

| ------ | ------- | -------

| S | Systemic symptoms | Fever, cancer

| N | Neurological deficit | Weakness, confusion

| O | Onset sudden | Thunderclap

| O | Older age (>50) | GCA, tumor

| P | Progression | Worsening over weeks

Headache presentation

↓

Check for SNOOP features

↓

If present → Secondary cause likely

↓

Urgent evaluation (imaging, labs)

| Feature | Red Flag? | Why

| ------- | --------- | ---

| Age >50 | ✅ Yes | GCA, malignancy

| Temporal tenderness | ✅ Yes | GCA

| Chronic cocaine use | ❌ Not alone | Needs associated features

| Progressive headache | ✅ Yes | Tumor, SOL

Giant Cell Arteritis-

| Feature | Finding

| ------- | -------

| Age | >50

| Pain | Temporal

| Associated | Jaw claudication

| Lab | ↑ ESR

| Risk | Blindness

Treat immediately with steroids

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Rimegepant is true? 1. It is a partial agonist of the CGRP receptor 2. It causes vasoconstriction 3. It is given via the subcutaneous route 4. It is used in the acute management of migraine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 4 only

Rimegepant:

Rimegepant is a “gepant” class drug:

• A CGRP (Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide) receptor antagonist

During migraine:

• CGRP released from trigeminal nerve endings

→ Causes:

• Vasodilation
• Neurogenic inflammation
• Pain transmission

| Feature | Rimegepant | Triptans (e.g., Sumatriptan) | CGRP mAbs

| ------- | ---------- | ---------------------------- | ---------

| Mechanism | CGRP receptor antagonist | 5-HT1B/1D agonist | CGRP ligand/receptor block

| Vasoconstriction | ❌ No | ✅ Yes | ❌ No

| Route | Oral | Oral / SC / nasal | SC / IV

| Use | Acute ± preventive | Acute | Preventive

| CV safety | Safe | Contraindicated | Safe

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is a secondary cause of headache?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Medication overuse headache

Headaches are classified into primary and secondary headaches according to the International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3).

• Primary headaches are disorders in which the headache itself is the disease (e.g., migraine, tension-type headache, trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias).
• Secondary headaches occur as a consequence of another condition, including medication overuse, infections, trauma, vascular disorders, or intracranial pathology.

Medication overuse headache (MOH) is the most common secondary chronic daily headache, resulting from the frequent use of acute headache medications.

Why not the other options?

• A. Migraine: A primary headache disorder.
• B. Tension-type headache: The most common primary headache.
• C. Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia: A group of primary headache disorders, including cluster headache, paroxysmal hemicrania, and SUNCT.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the role of caffeine in wakefulness?
options: Blocks adenosine action and causes wakefulness
Activates locus coeruleus and cause wakefulness
No role in maintaining wakefulness if taken 1hr before sleep
Activates histamine release and prevents sleep
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Blocks adenosine action and causes wakefulness

Caffeine = adenosine receptor antagonist → removes “sleep pressure” → promotes wakefulness

Caffeine promotes wakefulness by blocking adenosine receptors, particularly A₁ and A₂A, in the brain. Adenosine normally accumulates during wakefulness and induces sleepiness; its blockade reduces sleep drive.

Thus, caffeine causes increased alertness and delayed sleep onset.

| Time awake | Adenosine level | Effect

| ---------- | --------------- | ------

| Morning | Low | Alert

| Afternoon | Moderate | Slight fatigue

| Night | High | Sleep drive ↑

Caffeine does NOT reduce adenosine, it just blocks its effect

| Neurotransmitter | Source | Role

| ---------------- | ------ | ----

| Adenosine | ATP metabolism | Promotes sleep

| Norepinephrine | Locus coeruleus | Arousal

| Histamine | Tuberomammillary nucleus | Wakefulness

| Dopamine | VTA | Alertness

| Orexin | Hypothalamus | Stabilizes wakefulness

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which centre in the brain is responsible for producing fever during infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Preoptic Nucleus

Temperature is controlled in the anterior hypothalamus, specifically:

Preoptic nucleus (Preoptic area)

During infection:

• Bacteria/viruses → release exogenous pyrogens
• These trigger immune cells → release IL-1, TNF, IL-6

These cytokines act on hypothalamus:

Infection

↓

Pyrogens (IL-1, TNF, IL-6)

↓

↑ Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2)

↓

Acts on Preoptic Nucleus

↓

↑ Set-point temperature

↓

Heat Conservation + Heat Production

↓

Fever

| Option | Structure | Function | Why Correct/Incorrect | Key Exam Point

| ------ | --------- | -------- | --------------------- | --------------

| A | Paraventricular nucleus | ADH, oxytocin, autonomic | Not temperature regulator | Endocrine nucleus

| B | Dorsomedial nucleus | Feeding, circadian | No fever role | Behavioral regulation

| C | Preoptic nucleus | Thermoregulation | Controls fever set point | Fever center

| D | Cerebellum | Coordination | No role in fever | Motor control

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following areas of the brain are correctly matched with the neurotransmitters they release? 1. Substantia nigra - Dopamine 2. Locus ceruleus - Acetylcholine 3. Raphe nucleus - Serotonin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 3

| Nucleus | Neurotransmitter | Function | Clinical Correlation

| ------- | ---------------- | -------- | --------------------

| Substantia nigra | Dopamine | Movement | Parkinson disease

| Locus ceruleus | Norepinephrine | Arousal, attention | Anxiety, stress

| Raphe nuclei | Serotonin | Mood, sleep | Depression

| Basal nucleus of Meynert | Acetylcholine | Memory | Alzheimer disease

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following brain regions is primarily associated with the processing of explicit memory?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hippocampus

| Type | Example | Brain Region

| ---- | ------- | ------------

| Explicit | Facts, events | Hippocampus

| Implicit (procedural) | Skills | Cerebellum, basal ganglia

Declarative / Explicit Memory:

• Semantic (factual):

• Prefrontal cortex
• Temporal cortex (lateral and anterior)

• Episodic (events):

• Hippocampus
• Medial temporal lobe
• Neocortex

Nondeclarative / Implicit Memory:

• Procedural (skills, habits):

• Striatum
• Cerebellum
• Motor cortex

• Priming and perceptual:

• Neocortex

• Associative learning (classical conditioning):

• Amygdala
• Cerebellum

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following hypothalamic nuclei are responsible for leptin resistance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arcuate nucleus

Leptin is the body’s “fat thermostat hormone”

• Secreted by adipocytes
• Tells the brain: “We have enough energy, stop eating.”

But in obesity- Leptin is high, yet appetite persists → leptin resistance

The arcuate nucleus is the main hypothalamic leptin-sensing center containing POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons. Leptin resistance arises from impaired signaling in this nucleus, leading to failure of appetite suppression. It integrates peripheral energy signals.

| Nucleus | Function | Lesion Effect

| ------- | -------- | -------------

| Arcuate | Leptin integration | Leptin resistance

| Lateral | Hunger center | ↓ eating

| Ventromedial | Satiety center | Hyperphagia

| Paraventricular | Autonomic/endocrine control | Dysregulation

Extra Edge Points

1. POMC → α-MSH → acts on MC4 receptor → satiety
2. NPY = strongest appetite stimulant
3. AgRP blocks melanocortin receptors → promotes eating

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old college student presents to the emergency department with a 1-day history of high-grade fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and a petechial rash. Neurological examination reveals positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs. The diagnosis of meningococcal meningitis is suspected. Which of the following medications is the drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis of close contacts of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rifampicin

This presentation is classic for meningococcal meningitis (fever, neck stiffness, petechial rash).

Close contacts are at high risk due to nasopharyngeal carriage of Neisseria meningitidis.

Rifampicin is the drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis, as it eradicates nasopharyngeal carriage.

| Drug | Role in Meningococcal Prophylaxis

| ---- | ---------------------------------

| Rifampicin | First-line

| Ciprofloxacin | Alternative

| Ceftriaxone | Alternative

| Others | ❌ Not used

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with low-grade fever, headache, and malaise for the past 2 weeks. Lumbar puncture is performed. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis reveals lymphocytic predominance and low glucose levels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tubercular meningitis

Differentiate the common causes of meningitis based on CSF analysis. Tubercular meningitis (TBM) typically presents with a subacute onset (days to weeks) of fever, headache, and malaise. CSF classically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose, reflecting chronic granulomatous inflammation caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Bacterial meningitis: Usually presents acutely with neutrophilic predominance, markedly low glucose, and very high protein.
• B. Viral meningitis: CSF shows lymphocytic predominance, but glucose is usually normal with only mildly elevated protein.
• D. Fungal meningitis: Can also show lymphocytic pleocytosis with low glucose, but it is more commonly seen in immunocompromised patients (e.g., cryptococcal meningitis), whereas the clinical presentation here is most typical of TBM.

High-yield Pearl

| Type of Meningitis | Cells | Protein | Glucose

| ------------------ | ----- | ------- | -------

| Bacterial | Neutrophils ↑ | ↑↑ | ↓↓

| Viral | Lymphocytes ↑ | Mild ↑ | Normal

| Tubercular | Lymphocytes ↑ | ↑↑ | ↓

| Fungal | Lymphocytes ↑ | ↑ | ↓

Exam Tip:

• Subacute meningitis + Lymphocytic CSF + Low glucose = Think Tubercular meningitis.
• Acute meningitis + Neutrophils + Very low glucose = Bacterial meningitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old male patient presented with complaints of drowsiness and was admitted for evaluation. Sodium was found to be 98 mEq/L, which was corrected to 110 mEq/L with 3% saline in 24 hours. The patient recovered for a while and had an altered sensorium later. Now, he developed quadriparesis and bilateral conjugate gaze palsy. Which is the investigation to be done in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MRI brain

| Clue | Interpretation

| ---- | --------------

| Severe hyponatremia (Na⁺ = 98) | Chronic adaptation likely

| Rapid correction with hypertonic saline |  Risk factor

| Initial improvement → then deterioration | Classic biphasic course

| Quadriparesis + gaze palsy | Brainstem (pons) involvement

Rapid correction of severe hyponatremia predisposes to osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis).

Features like delayed altered sensorium, quadriparesis, and bilateral gaze palsy are classic for pontine involvement.

Chronic hyponatremia

↓

Brain adapts (↓ osmoles)

↓

Rapid Na⁺ correction

↓

Extracellular osmolality ↑

↓

Water leaves neurons

↓

Cell shrinkage + myelin damage

↓

Demyelination (pons)

| Feature | CPM (ODS)

| ------- | ---------

| Cause | Rapid Na⁺ correction

| Site | Pons

| Symptoms | Quadriparesis, gaze palsy

| Best test | ⭐ MRI brain

| CSF | Normal

The investigation of choice is MRI brain, which shows pontine hyperintensities on T2/FLAIR.

CSF and EEG are non-diagnostic, and BAEP is not useful for confirming demyelination.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 42-year-old labourer developed a sudden, severe and persistent headache, accompanied by vomiting and neck pain. He was evaluated at the nearest hospital where an emergency computed tomography was negative for stroke. Which one of the following investigations is best to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lumbar puncture after 12 hours

The presentation is highly suggestive of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH): sudden, severe “thunderclap” headache with vomiting and neck pain/meningism. A CT scan may be negative, particularly when performed after the early period. In a patient with persistent clinical suspicion and a negative CT, lumbar puncture can demonstrate RBCs and xanthochromia in the CSF.

The question specifically specifies LP after 12 hours, which is important because xanthochromia becomes detectable several hours after the hemorrhage.

Why not the others?

• A. EEG: Used to evaluate seizures/epileptiform activity; does not confirm SAH.
• B. Carotid Doppler: Evaluates carotid stenosis; not useful for diagnosing SAH.
• D. Upper GI endoscopy: Has no role in evaluating thunderclap headache.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presents with fever, headache, cranial nerve palsy, and hydrocephalus. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination shows low glucose, elevated protein, and predominant lymphocytosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tuberculous meningitis

Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is a subacute or chronic meningitis caused by hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to the meninges. It classically involves the basal meninges, leading to cranial nerve palsies, hydrocephalus, and vasculitis with cerebral infarction.

• The combination of fever, headache, cranial nerve palsy, hydrocephalus, and CSF findings of low glucose, high protein, and lymphocytic pleocytosis is characteristic of tuberculous meningitis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Pyogenic meningitis: Acute presentation with neutrophilic predominance, markedly elevated protein, and low glucose.
• C. Fungal meningitis: Usually occurs in immunocompromised patients and has similar CSF findings but is less commonly associated with basal meningeal involvement and cranial nerve palsies in children.
• D. Viral meningitis: Typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis but normal CSF glucose with only mildly elevated protein.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic sinusitis is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of high-grade fever, severe headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, and two episodes of vomiting. On examination, he is confused and febrile (39.5 °C), with neck rigidity and a positive Kernig’s sign. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 104/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Fundoscopic examination shows no papilledema. Empirical antibiotic therapy is planned prior to lumbar puncture. Which of the following is the most appropriate empirical treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin

Acute bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency that requires immediate empiric intravenous antibiotics, ideally after obtaining blood cultures and before lumbar puncture if the LP is expected to be delayed. In adults with suspected community-acquired bacterial meningitis, ceftriaxone plus vancomycin provides broad coverage against the two most common pathogens—Streptococcus pneumoniae (including penicillin- and cephalosporin-resistant strains) and Neisseria meningitidis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Meropenem alone: Has broad-spectrum activity but is not recommended as first-line empiric monotherapy for community-acquired meningitis.
• C. Vancomycin alone: Covers resistant Gram-positive organisms but lacks adequate Gram-negative coverage, including N. meningitidis.
• D. Clindamycin: Has poor CSF penetration and inadequate activity against the common causes of bacterial meningitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient presents with fever and nuchal rigidity. His CSF analysis reveals low sugar, elevated WBCs and Cryptococcal antigen positivity. Which of the following is used in the initial management of this condition? 1. Amphotericin B + Flucytosine 2. Amphotericin B + Fluconazole 3. Fluconazole 4. Liposomal Amphotericin B + Itraconazole
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 only

• Fever + neck stiffness + CSF:

• ↓ Glucose
• ↑ WBCs
• Cryptococcal antigen positive

Diagnosis: Cryptococcal meningitis

(most commonly due to Cryptococcus neoformans infection)

• Inhaled yeast → lungs → hematogenous spread

→ CNS invasion

→ thick polysaccharide capsule prevents immune clearance

| Parameter | Finding

| --------- | -------

| Opening pressure | ↑↑ (very high)

| Glucose | ↓

| Protein | ↑

| Cells | Lymphocytic predominance

Diagnostic Clues

• India ink stain → encapsulated yeast
• Cryptococcal antigen test → highly sensitive

Treatment-

Cryptococcal Meningitis

↓

INDUCTION (2 weeks)

→ Amphotericin B + Flucytosine

↓

CONSOLIDATION (8 weeks)

→ Fluconazole (high dose)

↓

MAINTENANCE

→ Fluconazole (low dose)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with high-grade fever, headache, and altered sensorium. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination reveals low glucose, high protein, and a marked increase in polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute bacterial meningitis

| Parameter | Finding | Interpretation

| --------- | ------- | --------------

| Glucose | ↓ Low | Consumed by bacteria + neutrophils

| Protein | ↑ High | BBB disruption + inflammation

| Cells | ↑ PMNs (neutrophils) | Acute pyogenic response

Common organisms (age-wise)

• Neonates → E. coli, GBS
• Young adults → Neisseria meningitidis
• Elderly → Streptococcus pneumoniae

| Feature | Bacterial | Viral | Tubercular | SAH

| ------- | --------- | ----- | ---------- | ---

| Cells | Neutrophils | Lymphocytes | Lymphocytes | RBCs

| Glucose | ↓↓↓ | Normal | ↓ | Normal

| Protein | ↑↑ | Mild ↑ | ↑↑↑ | Mild ↑

| CSF appearance | Turbid | Clear | Cobweb clot | Bloody

| Onset | Acute | Subacute | Chronic | Sudden

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Regarding Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) in children, which of the following statements is false?
options: Plasmapheresis is not effective in GBS
IV immunoglobulins are the first line of treatment
Areflexia in the weaker arm is included in diagnostic criteria
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Plasmapheresis is not effective in GBS

Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)-

• Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP)
• Immune-mediated attack on peripheral nerve myelin
• Often follows:

• Infection (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni)

Infection (e.g., Campylobacter)

↓

Molecular mimicry

↓

Autoantibodies against myelin

↓

Demyelination of peripheral nerves

↓

↓ Nerve conduction

↓

Ascending weakness + areflexia

A. Plasmapheresis is not effective in GBS

• Plasmapheresis IS effective
• Removes circulating antibodies
• Used in:

• Severe GBS
• Refractory cases

So, statement is FALSE

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis based on the CSF profile: Appearance: Opalescent Opening pressure: Raised Cell count: 500 cells/µL, predominantly lymphocytes Protein: Elevated Glucose: Reduced (<40 mg/dL) Chloride: Decreased
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tubercular meningitis

Why this is TB meningitis (Key Pattern)

• ↑ Protein + ↓ Glucose + Lymphocytic predominance → classic TB CSF

| Parameter | Normal | Bacterial | Viral | Fungal | TB | Autoimmune

| --------- | ------ | --------- | ----- | ------ | --- | ----------

| Appearance | Clear | Cloudy / Turbid | Clear | Clear / fibrin web | Clear / fibrin web | Clear

| Opening Pressure | 5–20 | Elevated | Normal or slightly elevated | Elevated | Variable | Normal

| Leukocytes (/µL) | <5 | >1\,000 | 25–2,000 | 10–1,000 | 10–1,000 | 10–1,000

| Differential | — | Neutrophil predominant | Early: Neutrophil Late: Lymphocytic | Lymphocyte predominant | Lymphocyte predominant | Lymphocyte predominant

| Glucose (mg/dL) | 45–85 | Low | Low / Normal | Low | Low | Normal

| Protein (mg/dL) | 15–45 | High | High | High | Very high | High

| Cultures | Negative | Positive | Negative | Positive (fungal) | Positive (AFB) | Negative

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which autoimmune disorder involves antibodies against post-synaptic ACh receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Myasthenia gravis

Normal Neuromuscular Transmission

Motor nerve impulse

↓

ACh released into synaptic cleft

↓

ACh binds to post-synaptic receptors

↓

Muscle depolarization

↓

Muscle contraction

Myasthenia gravis is caused by autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. This leads to fatigable muscle weakness that worsens with activity and improves with rest. Common muscles involved:

• Extraocular → ptosis, diplopia
• Facial muscles
• Proximal limb muscles

Classic Associations

• Thymoma (very important exam point)

| Disease | Site of lesion | Antibody target | Key feature

| ------- | -------------- | --------------- | -----------

| Myasthenia gravis | Post-synaptic NMJ | ACh receptors |  Weakness ↑ with use

| Lambert-Eaton | Pre-synaptic NMJ | Ca²⁺ channels | Weakness ↓ with use

| Multiple sclerosis | CNS myelin | Myelin | CNS deficits

| Guillain-Barré | Peripheral nerves | Myelin | Ascending paralysis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are the clinical features of multiple sclerosis? 1. Loss or blurring of vision 2. Tingling in limbs on neck flexion 3. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures 4. Gait ataxia Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 4

• 1. Loss or blurring of vision: Correct

• Commonly due to optic neuritis, a classic presentation of multiple sclerosis.
• Typically causes painful, unilateral visual loss with impaired color vision.

• 2. Tingling in limbs on neck flexion: Correct

• This is Lhermitte sign: an electric-shock-like sensation radiating down the spine or limbs on neck flexion.
• Indicates involvement of the cervical spinal cord.

• 3. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures: Incorrect. Seizures can occur in MS but are uncommon and are not considered a characteristic clinical feature.
• 4. Gait ataxia: Correct. Results from cerebellar or cerebellar pathway involvement and is a recognized manifestation of MS.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are the features of post-lumbar puncture headache? 1. Dull aching occipitofrontal headache. 2. Worse on waking but improves during the day. 3. Recumbency usually improves the headache within minutes. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 3 only

Post-lumbar puncture headache (PLPH) is caused by CSF leakage through the dural puncture site, leading to intracranial hypotension. It is typically a dull occipitofrontal headache that is postural—worsens on sitting or standing and improves rapidly on lying down (recumbency).

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Dull aching occipitofrontal headache ✔️ – Characteristic feature.
• 2. Worse on waking but improves during the day ❌ – Incorrect. The headache is worse in the upright position and improves when lying down, irrespective of the time of day.
• 3. Recumbency usually improves the headache within minutes ✔️ – Classical feature due to restoration of CSF pressure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common presenting symptom in patients with Multiple Sclerosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sensory Disturbances

Multiple sclerosis most commonly presents initially with sensory disturbances such as numbness, paresthesia, or sensory loss.

These symptoms result from demyelination of sensory pathways in the CNS.

Motor deficits, ataxia, and cranial nerve involvement usually occur later in the disease course.

Thus, sensory symptoms are the earliest and most common presenting feature.

Classic Early Presentation Triad

1.     Sensory symptoms (most common)

2.     Optic neuritis (painful vision loss)

3.     Motor weakness

Initial Symptoms of Multiple Sclerosis (MS)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements about Multiple Sclerosis are incorrect? A) 70% of patients with MS develop Optic Neuritis during the course of illness B) Oral steroids are first line for acute relapses C) Loss of colour and depth perception is proportional to loss of visual acuity D) Fundus examination can be normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A, B, C

In multiple sclerosis, optic neuritis occurs in \~50%, not 70%, making statement A incorrect.

Autoimmune attack on optic nerve myelin

↓

Demyelination of optic nerve fibers

↓

↓ Conduction velocity

↓

Visual symptoms:

- Blurring of vision

- Pain on eye movement

- Color vision loss (early)

↓

Fundus initially normal (retrobulbar neuritis)

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| Vision loss | Subacute, unilateral

| Pain | On eye movement

| Color vision | Earliest affected

| Pupillary reflex | RAPD (Marcus Gunn pupil)

| Fundus | Normal initially

Acute relapses are treated with IV methylprednisolone, not oral steroids, so B is incorrect.

In optic neuritis, loss of color vision (red desaturation) is disproportionately greater than visual acuity loss, making C incorrect.

Fundus can be normal (retrobulbar neuritis), so D is correct; hence A, B, C are incorrect.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following distinguishes axonal degeneration from segmental demyelination on electrophysiological studies?
options: Distal latency is normal in axonal degeneration and prolonged in segmental demyelination
Conduction velocity is slow in axonal degeneration and normal in segmental demyelination
Conduction block is present in axonal degeneration and absent in segmental demyelination
Temporal dispersion is prominent in axonal degeneration and absent in segmental demyelination
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Distal latency is normal in axonal degeneration and prolonged in segmental demyelination

Nerve conduction studies (NCS) help differentiate axonal neuropathies from demyelinating neuropathies based on characteristic electrophysiological findings.

A. Distal latency is normal in axonal degeneration and prolonged in segmental demyelination: True

• Axonal degeneration: Myelin is relatively preserved, so distal latency is usually normal or only mildly prolonged.
• Segmental demyelination: Loss of myelin markedly slows impulse conduction, resulting in prolonged distal latency.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Conduction velocity is slow in axonal degeneration and normal in segmental demyelination: False

• Axonal neuropathy: Conduction velocity is normal or only mildly reduced.
• Demyelinating neuropathy: Conduction velocity is markedly slowed.

• C. Conduction block is present in axonal degeneration and absent in segmental demyelination: False

• Conduction block is a hallmark of demyelinating neuropathies (e.g., Guillain–Barré syndrome, CIDP), not axonal degeneration.

• D. Temporal dispersion is prominent in axonal degeneration and absent in segmental demyelination: False.

• Temporal dispersion occurs due to uneven demyelination causing variable conduction velocities among nerve fibers.
• It is characteristic of segmental demyelination, not axonal degeneration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: While doing a lumbar puncture, the following structures are pierced: 1. Ligamentum flavum 2. Supraspinous ligament 3. Interspinous ligament 4. Dura mater 5. Arachnoid mater 6. Epidural space 7. Subdural space Arrange them in the sequence in which they are pierced.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2–3–1–6–4–7–5

Lumbar puncture is performed by advancing the needle through the midline structures of the lumbar spine until it reaches the subarachnoid space to obtain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Knowledge of the anatomical layers traversed is essential for safe and accurate needle placement.

The structures are pierced in the following sequence:

1. Supraspinous ligament
2. Interspinous ligament
3. Ligamentum flavum
4. Epidural space
5. Dura mater
6. Subdural space (potential space)
7. Arachnoid mater → Needle enters the subarachnoid space containing CSF.

Hence, the correct sequence is: 2 → 3 → 1 → 6 → 4 → 7 → 5

Why not the other options?

• The other sequences incorrectly place the arachnoid before the dura, omit the epidural space, or reverse the order of the ligaments.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy with generalized tonic–clonic seizures has been receiving multiple antiepileptic drugs for the past 3 weeks. He now presents with high-grade fever, a painful erythematous rash, and petechial lesions on the lips, raising concern for a severe drug-induced cutaneous reaction. Which of the following antiepileptic drugs can be safely continued in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Clobazam

Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS)/Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) is a rare but life-threatening Type IV (T-cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction most commonly triggered by aromatic antiepileptic drugs such as phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, and lamotrigine. The immediate management is prompt withdrawal of the offending drug. Clobazam, a benzodiazepine, is not associated with SJS/TEN and can be safely used as an alternative antiepileptic in this setting.

Why not the other options?

• A. Phenytoin: High risk of SJS/TEN; should be discontinued immediately.
• B. Valproate: Although the risk is much lower than with aromatic AEDs, it is not preferred as the best answer in a patient with suspected severe cutaneous adverse reaction, especially if combination therapy was being used.
• C. Lamotrigine: Well-known cause of SJS/TEN, particularly with rapid dose escalation or concomitant valproate use.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy has generalized tonic-clonic seizures for 35 minutes. He received buccal midazolam, but seizures continue. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Start fosphenytoin

• This patient has convulsive status epilepticus (>30 minutes; treatment begins much earlier).
• Management follows a time-based algorithm:

• 0–5 min: Stabilization (ABC, glucose, electrolytes)
• 5–20 min: Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, diazepam, buccal/intranasal midazolam)
• 20–40 min: Second-line antiseizure medication

• Since he has already received a benzodiazepine and is still seizing at 35 minutes, he requires a second-line non-benzodiazepine.
• Recommended agents include IV fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, or valproate.
• Fosphenytoin is preferred over phenytoin because it has fewer infusion-related adverse effects.
• Phenobarbital is generally reserved for refractory cases or neonatal seizures.

Status epilepticus timeline

• 0–5 min: Stabilization
• 5–20 min: Benzodiazepines
• 20–40 min: Fosphenytoin/Levetiracetam/Valproate
• >40 min: Refractory status → anesthetic infusion (midazolam, propofol, thiopentone)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old male with a known history of generalized tonic-clonic seizures is on long-term carbamazepine therapy. He recently developed a sore throat and was prescribed erythromycin by a local physician. Two days later, he presents to the emergency department with complaints of dizziness, diplopia, ataxia, and confusion. What is the most likely explanation for his symptoms?
options: Refractory seizures due to pharmacodynamic resistance
Carbamazepine toxicity due to drug interaction
Erythromycin toxicity due to enzyme induction
Decreased absorption of carbamazepine leading to subtherapeutic levels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Carbamazepine toxicity due to drug interaction

• Carbamazepine is metabolized in the liver by CYP3A4
• Erythromycin = strong CYP3A4 inhibitor

So, when erythromycin is added:

• ↓ metabolism of carbamazepine
• ↑ plasma levels
• → toxicity

Features of Carbamazepine Toxicity

• Dizziness
• Diplopia
• Ataxia
• Nystagmus
• Confusion

| Option | Mechanism | Expected Effect | Why Correct/Incorrect | Key Exam Point

| ------ | --------- | --------------- | --------------------- | --------------

| A | Resistance | ↑ seizures | ❌ No seizures here | Wrong clinical picture

| B | CYP inhibition | ↑ CBZ levels | ✅ Correct | Classic interaction

| C | Enzyme induction | ↓ drug levels | ❌ Wrong mechanism | Erythromycin = inhibitor

| D | ↓ absorption | ↓ CBZ levels | ❌ Opposite effect | Would cause seizures

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old man reports arm and hand weakness and numbness after sleeping with his arm over a chair post heavy drinking. What is the correct order of susceptibility of different nerve Fibers to pressure?
options: A Fiber is less susceptible than B Fibers
B Fiber is more susceptible than A Fibers
C Fiber is less susceptible than B Fibers
C Fiber is more susceptible than A Fibers
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C Fiber is less susceptible than B Fibers

Pressure neuropathy preferentially affects larger, myelinated Fibers.

B Fibers (preganglionic autonomic, myelinated) are more susceptible to pressure than C Fibers (unmyelinated).

C Fibers are relatively resistant to compression and hypoxia.

| Fiber | Myelination | Size | Function

| ----- | ----------- | ---- | --------

| A Fibers | Heavy | Large | Motor, proprioception

| B Fibers | Light | Small | Autonomic

| C Fibers | None | Very small | Pain, temperature

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 29-year-old man sustains a hemisection injury of the spinal cord after a penetrating back trauma. On neurological examination, he has loss of pain and temperature sensation on the side opposite to the lesion below the level of injury, while vibration sense remains intact. Which ascending sensory pathway is primarily responsible for transmitting the affected sensations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spinothalamic tract

The spinothalamic tract (anterolateral system) carries pain, temperature, and crude touch sensations from the body. Primary sensory neurons enter the spinal cord, synapse in the dorsal horn, and second-order neurons cross (decussate) within 1–2 spinal segments through the anterior white commissure before ascending contralaterally to the thalamus. Consequently, spinal cord lesions involving this tract cause contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the level of the lesion.

Why not the other options?

• B. Dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway: Carries fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception; fibers ascend ipsilaterally and decussate in the medulla.
• C. Spinocerebellar tract: Conveys unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum for coordination of movement.
• D. Fasciculus gracilis: Part of the dorsal column system that carries fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception from the lower limb and lower trunk, not pain and temperature.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy presents to the emergency room with seizures. He has been receiving oral phenytoin since the age of 6 months and has a history of epileptic spasms despite therapy. Examination reveals some hypopigmented lesions over the chest. MRI brain shows subependymal nodules. Which one of the following is the best anti-epileptic drug for him after stabilization in the emergency room?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Oral Vigabatrin

The child most likely has tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), suggested by:

• Hypopigmented “ash-leaf” macules
• Subependymal nodules on MRI
• Epileptic spasms beginning in infancy
• Persistent seizures despite phenytoin

Vigabatrin is the preferred first-line treatment for infantile spasms associated with tuberous sclerosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Phenytoin: Not effective as first-line therapy for infantile spasms and has already failed in this patient.
• B. Zonisamide: May have antiseizure activity but is not the preferred treatment for TSC-associated infantile spasms.
• C. Topiramate: Can be used as an adjunct in refractory epilepsy but is not first-line for TSC-associated infantile spasms.
• D. Vigabatrin: Drug of choice for infantile spasms associated with tuberous sclerosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old female notices weakness in her right hand and difficulty while kneading dough. On examination, right arm tone and power are decreased, and reflexes are sluggish. What is the site of the lesion?
options: Posterior limb of the internal capsule
Right corticospinal tract in cervical cord
Anterior horn cell of the cervical spinal cord
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anterior horn cell of the cervical spinal cord

| Finding | What it tells you

| ------- | -----------------

| Decreased tone (hypotonia) | LMN sign

| Decreased power | Non-localizing (both UMN/LMN)

| Sluggish reflexes (hyporeflexia) | LMN sign

Hypotonia + hyporeflexia = Lower Motor Neuron lesion. The only option that produces an LMN picture is the anterior horn cell. All three distractors are UMN sites and would give the opposite pattern — hypertonia + hyperreflexia.

Distractor-by-distractor analysis

| Option | Site | Tract level | Signs it would produce | Verdict

| ------ | ---- | ----------- | ---------------------- | -------

| A | Posterior limb of internal capsule | UMN | Contralateral spastic hemiparesis, ↑ tone, ↑ reflexes, Babinski + | ✗ Wrong sign pattern; also gives face + arm + leg, not isolated arm

| B | Right corticospinal tract, cervical cord | UMN | Ipsilateral (below decussation) spastic weakness, ↑ tone, ↑ reflexes | ✗ UMN pattern

| C | Anterior horn cell, cervical cord | LMN | Segmental flaccid weakness, ↓ tone, ↓ reflexes, wasting, fasciculations | ✓ Matches vignette

| D | Left medullary pyramid | UMN | Contralateral (right) spastic weakness, ↑ tone, ↑ reflexes | ✗ Correct side, wrong sign pattern

High-yield pearl (UMN vs LMN)

| Feature | UMN | LMN

| ------- | --- | ---

| Tone | ↑ (spastic) | ↓ (flaccid)

| Reflexes | ↑ (brisk) | ↓ / absent

| Plantar | Extensor (Babinski +) | Flexor / absent

| Wasting | Minimal (disuse only) | Marked, early

| Fasciculations | Absent | Present

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old man had a RTA and was admitted to a hospital. After a few days, he had an exaggerated right-sided extensor plantar reflex and knee jerk. What other finding would be seen?
options: Atrophy of the right lower limb
Loss of proprioception in the left leg
Ankle clonus in the right foot
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ankle clonus in the right foot

Exaggerated knee jerk and extensor plantar response indicate an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion on the right side.

| Finding | Interpretation

| ------- | --------------

| Exaggerated knee jerk | Hyperreflexia

| Extensor plantar reflex |  Babinski sign

| Same side (right) | Localized lesion

UMN lesions are associated with spasticity and clonus due to loss of inhibitory control.

Sudden stretch (ankle dorsiflexion)

↓

Exaggerated reflex contraction

↓

Repeated oscillations

↓

Clonus

Hence, ankle clonus in the right foot is an expected finding.

| Feature | UMN Lesion | LMN Lesion

| ------- | ---------- | ----------

| Reflexes | ↑ | ↓

| Babinski | ✅ | ❌

| Clonus | ✅ | ❌

| Fasciculations | ❌ | ✅

| Atrophy | Mild | Severe

Atrophy and fasciculations are LMN signs, and proprioceptive loss suggests dorsal column involvement.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old man was found to have weakness of the right shoulder and arm 6 hours before presentation. This was followed by weakness of the ipsilateral leg, then left leg, followed by left arm (around-the-clock pattern). Where in the neuraxis is the lesion likely to be present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Foramen magnum

The “around-the-clock” pattern of progressive weakness is a classic localizing sign of a foramen magnum/cervicomedullary junction lesion. The characteristic sequence is: Ipsilateral arm → ipsilateral leg → contralateral leg → contralateral arm

This occurs because corticospinal fibers are decussating at the cervicomedullary junction, with fibers destined for the legs crossing caudal to those destined for the arms. A compressive lesion progressively involves these crossing fibers.

Why not the others?

• A. Cerebral cortex: Usually produces contralateral weakness, often with cortical signs such as aphasia, neglect, seizures, or sensory deficits.
• C. Midbrain: Can produce crossed cranial nerve and long-tract findings but does not produce the characteristic around-the-clock progression.
• D. Pons: Can produce crossed cranial nerve and corticospinal tract signs, but the described sequential four-limb pattern specifically localizes to the foramen magnum.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with a stab wound to the back. He has loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception in the left leg below the lesion. Which tract is affected on the left side?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway

• The dorsal column carries fine touch, vibration, and proprioception.
• These fibers ascend ipsilaterally in the spinal cord.
• Therefore, a left hemisection causes ipsilateral loss of these sensations below the lesion.
• Pain and temperature fibers cross within 1–2 spinal segments via the anterior white commissure.
• Hence, pain and temperature are lost contralaterally below the lesion.
• Motor weakness also occurs ipsilaterally due to corticospinal tract involvement.
• Dorsal columns decussate only in the medulla.
• Spinothalamic fibers decussate within the spinal cord.
• Classic triad: Ipsilateral motor + dorsal column loss with contralateral pain/temperature loss.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 46-year-old male presents to the ER with the acute onset of ataxia. Neurological examination shows loss of pain and temperature sensation from the face on the left side and loss of pain and temperature sensation from the right half of the body. He also has dysarthria, dysphagia, and diminished gag reflex with ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the left. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lateral medullary syndrome

| Finding | Side | Structure involved

| ------- | ---- | ------------------

| Face pain/temp loss | Left | Spinal trigeminal nucleus

| Body pain/temp loss | Right | Spinothalamic tract

| Dysphagia, dysarthria, ↓ gag | Left | Nucleus ambiguus (CN IX, X)

| Ataxia | Left | Inferior cerebellar peduncle

| Ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis | Left | Sympathetic fibers (Horner’s)

Ipsilateral face + contralateral body pain loss + Cranial nerve IX, X involvement + Horner’s syndrome

This combination = Wallenberg syndrome

PICA infarction

↓

Lateral medulla damage

↓

Multiple structure involvement:

↓

Spinal trigeminal nucleus → Ipsilateral face pain loss

Spinothalamic tract → Contralateral body pain loss

Nucleus ambiguus → Dysphagia, dysarthria

Sympathetic fibers → Horner’s syndrome

Cerebellar peduncle → Ataxia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 5-year-old child has a 2-year history of episodic behavioural arrest, picking movements of the right hand, and piloerection. Which of the following is the correct combination of the diagnosis and semiology? 1. Focal seizure with intact awareness 2. Focal seizure with impaired awareness 3. Frontal lobe semiology 4. Temporal lobe semiology
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 4

Focal seizures with impaired awareness (formerly complex partial seizures) arising from the temporal lobe typically present with behavioral arrest, impaired awareness, automatisms (e.g., picking, lip-smacking), and autonomic symptoms such as piloerection, epigastric rising sensation, or tachycardia.

• The child has:

• Behavioral arrest → impaired awareness
• Picking movements of the right hand → automatisms
• Piloerection → autonomic manifestation

• These features are classic for a focal seizure with impaired awareness of temporal lobe origin.

Why not the other options?

• A. 1,4 (Focal seizure with intact awareness + Temporal lobe): Incorrect because behavioral arrest indicates impaired awareness.
• B. 1,3 (Focal seizure with intact awareness + Frontal lobe): Incorrect; frontal lobe seizures are usually brief, hypermotor, and awareness may be preserved.
• C. 2,3 (Focal seizure with impaired awareness + Frontal lobe): Incorrect; automatisms and autonomic features such as piloerection are more typical of temporal lobe epilepsy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 52-year-old male presents with progressive weakness in the lower limbs, difficulty in walking, and tingling sensations in hands and feet. On examination, there is spasticity, increased deep tendon reflexes, along with impaired vibration and position sense. Which of the following best explains this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin B12 deficiency

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency causes a combination of hematological and neurological manifestations, making it a key exam diagnosis when both are present.

• B12 is required for:

o    DNA synthesis → deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia (pallor)

o    Myelin synthesis → deficiency leads to demyelination of the spinal cord

Neurological features (important clue):

• Subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord

o    Involves posterior columns → loss of vibration & position sense

o    Involves lateral corticospinal tracts → UMN signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia)

• Peripheral neuropathy → paresthesia, numbness

Why other options are incorrect:

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS): Core pathology: Mixed UMN + LMN degeneration

• Anterior horn cells (LMN) → atrophy, fasciculations
• Lateral corticospinal tracts (UMN) → spasticity, hyperreflexia
• No sensory involvement

Pattern:

→ Anterior horn + lateral columns

→ Pure motor disease

Poliomyelitis: Core pathology: Viral destruction of LMN

• Anterior horn cells only
• Leads to flaccid paralysis

Vitamin E deficiency: Core pathology: Axonal degeneration

• Dorsal columns → proprioceptive loss
• Spinocerebellar tracts → ataxia
• Peripheral neuropathy common

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant presents with sudden, brief spasms involving flexion of the neck, trunk, and limbs occurring in clusters. EEG reveals a hypsarrhythmia pattern. What is the first-line treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ACTH

A 6-month-old infant with clustered flexor spasms and a hypsarrhythmia pattern on EEG is characteristic of infantile spasms (West syndrome). This is an age-specific epileptic encephalopathy requiring urgent treatment to prevent neurodevelopmental deterioration.

• Classic triad:
• Infantile spasms (sudden flexion/extension movements in clusters)
• Hypsarrhythmia on EEG (chaotic, high-amplitude disorganized pattern)
• Developmental delay or regression
• Peak onset: 3–8 months of age
• First-line treatment: ACTH (or oral steroids); vigabatrin is preferred in tuberous sclerosis
• Drugs like valproate, ethosuximide, and carbamazepine are not effective for this condition

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure after high grade fever. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diazepam

This is a febrile seizure presenting as a generalized tonic–clonic seizure in a child with high-grade fever. The immediate management is benzodiazepine administration to abort the seizure.

Diazepam (IV/rectal) is the drug of choice for acute control.

Diazepam given

↓

Binds GABA-A receptor

↓

↑ Cl⁻ influx into neuron

↓

Hyperpolarization

↓

↓ Neuronal firing

↓

Seizure stops

Phenytoin, valproate, and ethosuximide are not used for immediate termination of febrile seizures.

| Drug | Role | Use

| ---- | ---- | ---

| Diazepam | ⭐ First-line | Acute seizure

| Phenytoin | Second-line | Status epilepticus

| Valproate | Maintenance | Chronic seizures

| Ethosuximide | Specific | Absence seizures

Febrile Seizure-

| Feature | Finding

| ------- | -------

| Age | 6 months–5 years

| Type | Generalized

| Prognosis | Good

| Recurrence | Possible

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 62-year-old patient presents with left-sided arm and leg weakness, right-sided facial paralysis, and horizontal gaze palsy. Based on the clinical presentation, which of the following is most consistent with the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Foville syndrome

| Finding | Structure Involved

| ------- | ------------------

| Left arm & leg weakness | Contralateral corticospinal tract

| Right facial paralysis | Facial nerve nucleus (VII)

| Horizontal gaze palsy | PPRF / Abducens nucleus (VI)

Lesion in dorsal pons

↓

Facial nucleus (VII) affected

↓

Ipsilateral facial paralysis

↓

PPRF / Abducens nucleus affected

↓

Horizontal gaze palsy

↓

Corticospinal tract affected

↓

Contralateral hemiparesis

This presentation shows a pontine lesion with ipsilateral facial paralysis, horizontal gaze palsy, and contralateral hemiparesis.

Foville syndrome involves the pontine tegmentum, affecting the facial nerve nucleus, PPRF/abducens nucleus, and corticospinal tract.

This explains facial weakness and gaze palsy on one side with opposite limb weakness.

Millard–Gubler lacks gaze palsy, Wallenberg spares motor tracts, and locked-in syndrome causes quadriplegia without facial palsy.

| Syndrome | Location | Key Features

| -------- | -------- | ------------

| Foville | Dorsal pons |  Facial palsy + gaze palsy + contralateral weakness

| Millard-Gubler | Ventral pons | Facial palsy + contralateral weakness

| Locked-in | Ventral pons | Quadriplegia, conscious

| Wallenberg | Lateral medulla | Dysphagia, ataxia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 9-month-old infant is brought to the pediatric clinic with a history of sudden, jerky movements of the limbs. EEG shows a chaotic high-amplitude background with multifocal spikes, consistent with hypsarrhythmia. What is the treatment of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ACTH

All clues point to Infantile Spasms (West Syndrome):

| Clue | Meaning

| ---- | -------

| Age: 9 months | Peak age (3–12 months)

| Sudden jerky movements | Flexor/extensor spasms

| EEG: Hypsarrhythmia | Chaotic, disorganized pattern

Diagnosis = West Syndrome

Hypsarrhythmia-

• Highly chaotic EEG pattern
• High-amplitude slow waves
• Multifocal spikes

ACTH (Adrenocorticotropic hormone):

• Reduces corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH)
• CRH is pro-convulsant in infants

So ACTH:

• Suppresses abnormal neuronal excitability
• Helps normalize EEG

| Drug | Mechanism | Uses | Role in Infantile Spasms

| ---- | --------- | ---- | ------------------------

| Ethosuximide | T-type Ca²⁺ block | Absence seizures |  No role

| Valproate | ↑ GABA | Generalized seizures |  Not first-line

| ACTH | ↓ CRH | Infantile spasms | ✅ Gold standard

| Lorazepam | ↑ GABA (benzodiazepine) | Status epilepticus |  No role

Alternative Treatment

• Vigabatrin

• Especially in Tuberous Sclerosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A child with Dravet syndrome is started on fenfluramine. What monitoring is required?
options: Cardiac evaluation for valvular heart disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cardiac evaluation for valvular heart disease

Fenfluramine was previously used as an anti-obesity drug and became associated with:

• Valvular heart disease
• Pulmonary hypertension

Now used in: Dravet syndrome

Therefore:

Patients require:

• Baseline echocardiography
• Periodic cardiac monitoring

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A newborn presents with generalized tonic-clonic and myoclonic seizures. What is the first-line anticonvulsant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phenobarbitone

• Initial management includes correction of reversible metabolic causes:

• Hypoglycemia
• Hypocalcemia
• Hypomagnesemia

• If seizures persist, IV phenobarbitone is the first-line antiepileptic.
• Loading dose: 20 mg/kg IV.
• Additional doses may be given up to 40 mg/kg if needed.
• Phenytoin or levetiracetam may be used as second-line agents.
• Midazolam infusion is reserved for refractory seizures.
• Continuous EEG monitoring is recommended in persistent seizures.
• Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy is the commonest cause of neonatal seizures.
• First-line drug = Phenobarbitone.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with altered sensorium and his BP was 220/110 mmHg. He also had one episode of vomiting and on examination has weakness in the left upper and lower limbs. Which of the following is incorrect?
options: BP should be checked multiple times before administering anti-hypertensives
