In haemorrhagic stroke, you should aggressively treat with intravenous anti-hypertensives
In haemorrhagic stroke, BP should be reduced to 160/100 mmHg with anti-hypertensives
BP should be reduced immediately to less than 140/90 mmHg in ischemic stroke
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. BP should be reduced immediately to less than 140/90 mmHg in ischemic stroke

• BP: 220/110 mmHg
• Vomiting + altered sensorium
• Focal weakness

Strong suspicion: acute stroke (likely hemorrhagic, but could be ischemic initially)

In ischemic stroke:

• Brain tissue = ischemic penumbra
• Blood flow is already compromised

If you rapidly lower BP:

• ↓ Cerebral perfusion
• Penumbra → infarction

Ischemic stroke

↓

Reduced cerebral perfusion

↓

Body increases BP (compensatory)

↓

Maintains blood flow to penumbra

↓

If BP lowered aggressively

↓

↓ Perfusion → infarct expansion

| Feature | Ischemic Stroke | Hemorrhagic Stroke

| ------- | --------------- | ------------------

| BP role | Maintain perfusion | Prevent bleeding

| BP management | Permissive HTN | Aggressive control

| Target BP | Usually <220/120 | \~160/100

| Immediate reduction | ❌ No | ✅ Yes

| Situation | BP Target

| --------- | ---------

| Ischemic stroke (no thrombolysis) | <220/120

| Before thrombolysis | <185/110

| Hemorrhagic stroke | \~160 systolic

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with right-sided weakness, aphasia, and irregularly irregular pulse for last 2 hours. On CT brain, no hemorrhage can be seen. What should be the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. rtPA

Symptoms suggest acute ischemic stroke:

| Symptom | Brain area involved

| ------- | -------------------

| Aphasia | Left hemisphere

| Right-sided weakness | Left motor cortex

The irregularly irregular pulse suggests: Atrial fibrillation

AF is the most common cause of cardioembolic stroke.

CT brain shows no hemorrhage, and symptom onset is within the thrombolysis window (≤4.5 hours). The patient presented within 2 hours.

IV thrombolysis is indicated if:

| Condition | Requirement

| --------- | -----------

| Ischemic stroke | Yes

| Time window | <4.5 hours

| CT scan | No hemorrhage

All criteria are satisfied.

Thus, IV rtPA is the treatment of choice. rtPA converts: Plasminogen → Plasmin

Plasmin dissolves fibrin clots.

Anticoagulation (warfarin/LMWH) is started later, not in the hyperacute phase.

(A) Warfarin

Used for long-term anticoagulation in AF, but not in acute stroke treatment.

B) Transesophageal echocardiography

Used to detect cardiac thrombus, but not the immediate priority.

D) LMWH

Anticoagulation is not recommended immediately in acute ischemic stroke because of bleeding risk.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with worsening back pain and weakness in the lower limbs. Which of the following would not support the diagnosis of compressive myelopathy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Normal cremasteric reflex

Findings that SUPPORT compressive myelopathy:

• Babinski positive → classic UMN sign
• Knee clonus → hyperreflexia → UMN
• (Later stage) ↑ tone (spasticity)

Correct answer B) Normal cremasteric reflex → does NOT support

• Cremasteric reflex = L1–L2 spinal segment
• In spinal cord compression, segmental reflexes are often:

• Lost at the level of lesion
• Exaggerated below

• So a normal reflex argues against cord involvement at that level

C) Hypotonia → can be present early

• In acute spinal cord compression (spinal shock phase):

• Hypotonia
• Hyporeflexia

• Later → becomes spastic (UMN)
• So hypotonia does not exclude compressive myelopathy

| Feature | UMN Lesion (Myelopathy) | LMN Lesion

| ------- | ----------------------- | ----------

| Tone | ↑ Hypertonia (spastic) | ↓ Hypotonia

| Reflexes | ↑ Hyperreflexia | ↓ Hyporeflexia

| Babinski | Positive | Negative

| Clonus | Present | Absent

| Muscle atrophy | Mild (disuse) | Marked

| Fasciculations | Absent | Present

Spinal Shock vs Chronic Myelopathy

| Phase | Findings

| ----- | --------

| Acute | Hypotonia + areflexia

| Chronic | Hypertonia + hyperreflexia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a mood disorder has been on medication and presents with new-onset liver dysfunction and hyperammonaemia. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Valproate

Valproate commonly causes hepatotoxicity and hyperammonemia due to inhibition of the urea cycle.

Valproate

↓

Inhibits mitochondrial β-oxidation

↓

↓ N-acetylglutamate

↓

↓ Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase-1 (CPS-1)

↓

Impaired urea cycle

↓

↑ Ammonia (hyperammonemia)

This can lead to valproate-induced encephalopathy even with normal liver enzymes.

The risk is higher with long-term use and in patients with metabolic vulnerability.

↑ Ammonia

↓

Crosses BBB

↓

Converted to glutamine in astrocytes

↓

Osmotic swelling

↓

Cerebral edema

↓

Encephalopathy (confusion, altered sensorium)

| Drug | Key Side Effect | Liver | Ammonia

| ---- | --------------- | ----- | -------

| Valproate | Hepatotoxicity | ✅ Yes | ✅ ↑

| Lamotrigine | SJS | ❌ | ❌

| Carbamazepine | SIADH, aplasia |  Mild | ❌

| Topiramate | Cognitive issues | ❌ | ❌

Valproate Toxicity Clues

| Feature | Finding

| ------- | -------

| CNS | Confusion, lethargy

| Liver | ↑ LFTs

| Metabolic | ↑ Ammonia

| Severe | Encephalopathy

Management Insight

• Stop valproate
• Give L-carnitine

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus complains of numbness and burning sensations in the extremities. On examination he has absent ankle reflexes and has no sensation to touch, vibration, or pain in his lower limbs. The loss of sensation in his extremities has a stocking distribution. What type of neuropathy is associated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Symmetric distal polyneuropathy

| Finding | Meaning

| ------- | -------

| Burning + numbness | Neuropathic pain

| Absent ankle reflex | Peripheral neuropathy

| Loss of vibration + touch + pain | Large + small fiber involvement

| Stocking distribution |  Distal symmetric pattern

| Diabetes | Most common cause

Type 2 diabetes commonly causes symmetric distal polyneuropathy, the most frequent diabetic neuropathy.

It presents with stocking-glove sensory loss, involving pain, vibration, touch, and absent ankle reflexes.

Symptoms include burning, numbness, and paresthesias, starting distally and progressing proximally.

Autonomic and focal neuropathies have different clinical patterns.

| Feature | DSPN | Mononeuropathy | Autonomic | Proximal

| ------- | ---- | -------------- | --------- | --------

| Distribution | Symmetric distal | Single nerve | Systemic | Proximal

| Sensory loss | ✅ Yes | Limited | ❌ | ❌

| Reflexes | ↓ | Variable | ❌ | Variable

| Pain | Burning | Localized | ❌ | Deep pain

| Diabetes link | ⭐ Strong | Possible | Strong | Strong

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A person after sleeping overnight with the arm under his head now experiences paresis but no numbness in the morning. Which of the following is the best explanation for it?
options: C Fibers are more sensitive to pressure than A Fibers
A Fibers are more sensitive to hypoxia than B Fibers
A Fibers are more susceptible to pressure changes than C Fibers
A Fibers are more susceptible to hypoxia than C Fibers
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A Fibers are more susceptible to pressure changes than C Fibers

• Sleeping with arm under head → prolonged nerve compression
• Morning:

• ✅ Paresis (motor weakness)
• ❌ No numbness (sensory preserved)

So: Motor Fibers affected > Sensory Fibers

| Fiber Type | Function | Myelination | Diameter | Vulnerability

| ---------- | -------- | ----------- | -------- | -------------

| A Fibers (Aα, Aβ) | Motor + proprioception | Heavily myelinated | Large |  Highly sensitive to pressure

| B Fibers | Autonomic | Lightly myelinated | Small | Moderate

| C Fibers | Pain, temperature | Unmyelinated | Very small |  Resistant to pressure

• A Fibers = thick
• C Fibers = thin

When compressed:

• Large myelinated Fibers (A Fibers)

→ Myelin sheath + large size = more susceptible to deformation + ischemia
• Small unmyelinated Fibers (C Fibers)

→ Minimal structure = more resilient to compression

| Feature | A Fibers | B Fibers | C Fibers

| ------- | -------- | -------- | --------

| Myelination | Heavy | Light | None

| Diameter | Large | Small | Very small

| Function | Motor, proprioception | Autonomic | Pain, temperature

| Conduction speed | Fastest | Intermediate | Slowest

| Pressure sensitivity |  Highest | Moderate | Lowest

| Clinical effect in compression | Weakness first | Autonomic later | Pain last

• “Pain lost first” → NOT compression → think ischemia/toxin
• “Motor loss first” → think compression neuropathy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman suffered from sunburn after enjoying a vacation on a beach. Now while taking a shower lukewarm water (40-degree Celsius) touches her back causing her to feel pain. What type of receptors are activated by lukewarm water and what causes her to feel pain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Innocuous thermal receptor – allodynia

Lukewarm water (40 °C) normally activates innocuous thermal receptors, not nociceptors.

After sunburn, peripheral sensitization lowers the pain threshold of sensory pathways.

As a result, a normally non-painful stimulus is perceived as pain, termed allodynia.

Sunburn → inflammation

↓

Release of mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin)

↓

↓ Threshold of nociceptors

↓

Non-painful stimuli now activate pain pathways

↓

Allodynia

| Feature | Allodynia | Hyperalgesia

| ------- | --------- | ------------

| Stimulus | Non-painful | Painful

| Response | Pain | Exaggerated pain

| Example | Sunburn + warm water | Pinprick → severe pain

Hyperalgesia refers to exaggerated pain to a painful stimulus, which is not the case here.

| Term | Meaning

| ---- | -------

| Allodynia | Pain from non-painful stimulus

| Hyperalgesia | Increased pain from painful stimulus

| Analgesia | No pain

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: After a right limb amputation, the patient is experiencing severe pain (phantom limb). What is the mechanism behind this?
options: Projection of adjacent fibers to overlap to right sensory cortex
Projection of adjacent fibers to overlap to left sensory cortex
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Projection of adjacent fibers to overlap to left sensory cortex

Phantom limb pain occurs due to cortical reorganization after amputation.

Adjacent sensory areas invade the contralateral (left) primary somatosensory cortex representing the amputated right limb.

Stimulation of these neighboring regions is misinterpreted as pain from the missing limb.

• Pain perceived in an amputated limb
• Due to central (cortical) mechanisms, not peripheral input

Thus, projection of adjacent fibers overlapping the left sensory cortex explains the phenomenon.

Limb amputated

↓

No sensory input from that region

↓

Adjacent cortical areas expand

↓

They “invade” the vacant area

↓

Misinterpretation of signals

↓

Phantom sensation / pain

| Concept | Phantom Limb

| ------- | ------------

| Side affected | Contralateral cortex

| Mechanism | Cortical reorganization

| Key event | Adjacent area overlap

| Type | Central phenomenon

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An 8-month-old infant has prolonged recurrent febrile seizures progressing to status epilepticus, developmental delay, and generalized epilepsy. Genetic analysis reveals a de novo mutation in the SCN1A gene. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dravet syndrome

Dravet syndrome (Severe Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy) is a rare developmental and epileptic encephalopathy caused in approximately 80% of cases by a de novo mutation in the SCN1A gene, which encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel (NaV1.1).

• Onset in the first year of life (typically 4–12 months)
• Prolonged febrile seizures or hemiclonic seizures as the initial presentation
• Recurrent seizures progressing to status epilepticus
• Developmental slowing or regression after seizure onset
• Multiple seizure types (myoclonic, generalized tonic-clonic, focal, atypical absence)
• Drug-resistant epilepsy

Treatment:

• Preferred: Valproate, clobazam, stiripentol, topiramate, fenfluramine, or cannabidiol
• Avoid sodium channel blockers (e.g., carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine) as they can worsen seizures.

Why not the other options?

• B. Lennox–Gastaut syndrome: Onset at 1–8 years, characterized by multiple seizure types, cognitive impairment, and slow spike-and-wave EEG; not associated with SCN1A mutations.
• C. West syndrome: Presents at 3–12 months with infantile spasms, developmental regression, and hypsarrhythmia on EEG.
• D. Benign febrile seizures: Brief, generalized febrile seizures in neurologically normal children with normal development; no progression to epilepsy or developmental delay.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following with regard to trigger factors for seizures: 1. Flickering lights 2. Recreational drug misuse 3. Non-compliance to treatment with antiepileptic drugs 4. Sleep deprivation Which of the factors given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Seizure triggers are factors that lower the seizure threshold and can precipitate seizures in susceptible individuals, especially those with epilepsy. Identifying and avoiding these triggers is an important component of long-term seizure management.

• Common seizure triggers:

• Sleep deprivation
• Missed doses/non-compliance with antiepileptic drugs
• Flickering or flashing lights (photosensitive epilepsy)
• Alcohol or recreational drug misuse/withdrawal
• Fever (especially in children)
• Emotional stress
• Metabolic disturbances (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia)

• Photosensitive epilepsy is most commonly triggered by:

• Flashing lights
• Video games
• Television or strobe lights

• The most common cause of breakthrough seizures in known epileptic patients is poor compliance with antiepileptic medication.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Contralateral homonymous lower quadrantanopia is the type of visual loss seen when the lesion is located at which one of the following anatomical locations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Parietal lobe

A contralateral homonymous lower quadrantanopia (“pie on the floor”) results from a lesion involving the parietal lobe, specifically the superior optic radiations. These fibers carry visual information from the inferior visual field, and damage produces loss of the contralateral lower quadrant of the visual field.

High-Yield Pearls

• Parietal lobe (Superior optic radiations): Contralateral homonymous lower quadrantanopia (“Pie on the floor”). ⭐
• Temporal lobe (Meyer’s loop/Inferior optic radiations): Contralateral homonymous upper quadrantanopia (“Pie in the sky”). ⭐
• Occipital lobe: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing. ⭐
• Optic chiasm: Bitemporal hemianopia (classically due to pituitary adenoma). ⭐
• Optic tract: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Focal seizures may be associated with which of the following? 1. Jacksonian march 2. Todd’s paralysis 3. Epilepsia partialis continua Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Focal (partial) seizures originate from a localized region of one cerebral hemisphere and may remain focal or progress to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures. They are associated with several characteristic clinical phenomena.

• 1. Jacksonian march: True.

• Refers to the orderly spread of clonic movements from one body part to adjacent parts (e.g., fingers → hand → arm → face) due to the sequential spread of epileptic activity along the primary motor cortex.

• 2. Todd’s paralysis: True.

• A transient focal neurological deficit (usually weakness) occurring after a focal motor seizure.
• Typically lasts minutes to 48 hours and resolves completely.
• It may mimic an acute stroke but is self-limiting.

• 3. Epilepsia partialis continua: True.

• A rare form of focal motor status epilepticus characterized by continuous or repetitive focal clonic muscle jerks involving one part of the body for hours, days, or even longer, with preserved awareness in many patients.
• Common causes include Rasmussen encephalitis, stroke, cortical dysplasia, tumors, and metabolic disorders.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In the below question mechanical receptors are given with their functions. Choose the correctly matched pair.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pacinian Corpuscle - Fast Vibration

Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors that detect high-frequency (fast) vibration.

They have large receptive fields and respond best to sudden pressure changes.

Ruffini endings sense stretch, Meissner corpuscles mediate light touch, and Merkel discs detect form and texture.

| Receptor | Adaptation | Function | Receptive Field

| -------- | ---------- | -------- | ---------------

| Pacinian | Rapid | ⭐ Vibration | Large

| Meissner | Rapid | Light touch | Small

| Merkel | Slow | Fine touch | Small

| Ruffini | Slow | Stretch | Large

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Interventional technique used for the management of cerebral aneurysm:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coiling

Cerebral Aneurysm-

• Localized dilatation of an artery (usually at branch points in Circle of Willis)
• Most common: Berry (saccular) aneurysm
• Risk: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) → sudden “worst headache of life”

Treatment Goal- Exclude aneurysm from circulation WITHOUT blocking parent artery

Cerebral aneurysm → Endovascular coiling is the standard minimally invasive treatment to prevent rupture/rebleed

| Feature | Coiling | Surgical Clipping

| ------- | ------- | -----------------

| Approach | Endovascular | Open surgery

| Invasiveness | Minimal | High

| Recovery | Faster | Slower

| Recurrence | Slightly higher | Lower

Clinical Insight

• After SAH:

• Secure aneurysm ASAP → coiling/clipping

• Prevents:

• Rebleeding (highest risk in first 24 hrs)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Lamotrigine is drug of choice for which seizure type?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tonic-clonic seizures

Lamotrigine is a broad-spectrum antiepileptic.

Major mechanism:

• Blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
• Decreases glutamate release

Particularly useful in:

• Generalized tonic-clonic seizures
• Focal seizures

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: LMN (Lower Motor Neuron) lesion is associated with which one of the following? 1. Reduced muscle tone 2. Spastic paralysis 3. Babinski signs positive 4. Fasciculation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 4

Lower Motor Neuron (LMN)

LMNs are the final common pathway:

• From anterior horn cell → peripheral nerve → muscle

If this pathway is damaged → muscle loses direct neural input

After LMN injury-

• Muscle becomes denervated
• No trophic support → atrophy
• Spontaneous discharges → fasciculations
• Loss of stretch reflex → hypotonia

| Feature | LMN Lesion | UMN Lesion

| ------- | ---------- | ----------

| Tone | ↓ Hypotonia | ↑ Hypertonia

| Paralysis | Flaccid | Spastic

| Reflexes | ↓ / absent | ↑ exaggerated

| Babinski | ❌ Absent | ✅ Present

| Muscle bulk | Atrophy (early) | Mild atrophy (late)

| Fasciculations | ✅ Present | ❌ Absent

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The most common site of a berry aneurysm in the circle of Willis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior cerebral artery

Most common berry aneurysm site = Anterior communicating artery (ACoA)

(which connects the anterior cerebral arteries)

Berry (Saccular) Aneurysm-

• Small, rounded outpouching at arterial bifurcations
• Caused by:

• Congenital weakness of vessel wall (tunica media defect)

• Strongly associated with:

• Hypertension
• Polycystic kidney disease

B) Vertebral artery

• Rare site for berry aneurysm
• More associated with:

• Dissections
• Posterior circulation strokes

C) Posterior cerebral artery

• Much less common
• PCA aneurysms are rare compared to ACoA/PCom

D) Basilar artery

• Can have aneurysms (especially tip of basilar)
• But not the most common

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Typical absence seizures are characterized by:
options: Abrupt 3 Hz spike-and-slow wave discharges on EEG
Multifocal structural abnormalities of the brain
Less responsiveness to anticonvulsants as compared to atypical absence seizures
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abrupt 3 Hz spike-and-slow wave discharges on EEG

Typical absence seizures are generalized non-motor seizures characterized by brief episodes of impaired consciousness with sudden onset and abrupt termination.

A. Abrupt 3 Hz spike-and-slow wave discharges on EEG:

• This is the classic EEG finding in typical absence seizures.
• EEG shows generalized, symmetric 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges, usually precipitated by hyperventilation.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Postictal confusion in children: False.

• There is no postictal confusion.
• Children resume normal activity immediately after the seizure.

• C. Multifocal structural abnormalities of the brain: False.

• Typical absence seizures are idiopathic (genetic) generalized epilepsies.
• Neuroimaging is usually normal, with no structural brain lesions.

• D. Less responsiveness to anticonvulsants as compared to atypical absence seizures: False.

• Typical absence seizures generally respond very well to treatment, especially ethosuximide (drug of choice for pure absence seizures), valproate, or lamotrigine.
• Atypical absence seizures are usually more difficult to control and often occur in children with underlying neurological impairment (e.g., Lennox–Gastaut syndrome).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Upper motor neuron lesions are characterized by which of the following? 1. Increased tone (spasticity) 2. Hyperreflexia 3. Absent plantar response 4. Motor weakness Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) lesions result from damage to the corticospinal (pyramidal) tract above the anterior horn cell. Loss of inhibitory control over spinal reflexes leads to spasticity, hyperreflexia, pathological reflexes, and weakness.

• 1. Increased tone (spasticity) ✓

• UMN lesions cause spasticity, a velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone due to loss of descending inhibitory pathways.

• 2. Hyperreflexia ✓

• Deep tendon reflexes become exaggerated because of increased spinal reflex activity.

• 3. Absent plantar response ✗

• The plantar response is not absent. Instead, UMN lesions produce an extensor plantar response (Babinski sign).

• 4. Motor weakness ✓

• UMN lesions produce spastic weakness, predominantly affecting antigravity muscles.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: When comparing oxcarbazepine and carbamazepine, which of the following adverse effects is more commonly associated with oxcarbazepine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyponatremia

Oxcarbazepine is more commonly associated with hyponatremia due to SIADH-like effect.

Oxcarbazepine vs Carbamazepine

Both:

• Block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
• Used in focal seizures

BUT they differ in side-effect.

Oxcarbazepine

↓

↑ ADH effect (SIADH-like)

↓

↑ Water reabsorption in kidney

↓

Dilution of sodium

↓

Hyponatremia

Clinical Consequence Flow-

↓ Serum sodium

↓

Cellular swelling (brain)

↓

Headache, confusion

↓

Seizures (paradoxical!)

| Advantage | Reason

| --------- | ------

| Less enzyme induction | Fewer drug interactions

| Safer hematologically | Less bone marrow suppression

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which antiepileptic drug specifically enhances the inactivation phase of voltage-gated slow sodium channels, helping to stabilize hyperexcitable neurons?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lacosamide

Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels have 3 states:

1. Resting (closed)
2. Open (activated)
3. Inactivated

There are TWO types of inactivation:

• Fast inactivation (milliseconds)
• Slow inactivation (longer, stabilizing phase)

Lacosamide selectively enhances SLOW inactivation

• Keeps neurons in a non-excitable state longer
• Prevents repetitive firing
• Stabilizes hyperexcitable neuronal membranes

| Drug | Mechanism | Na⁺ Channel Effect |

| ---- | --------- | ------------------ | ---

| Lacosamide | Enhances slow inactivation | Keeps channels inactive longer |

| Phenytoin | Blocks fast inactivation | Prevents rapid firing |

| Lamotrigine | Fast inactivation + ↓ glutamate | Dual action |

| Felbamate | NMDA antagonist | No Na⁺ effect |

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are contraindications to thrombolysis in acute ischemic stroke? 1. Recent head injury 2. Recent myocardial infarction 3. Hypertension > 150/100 mmHg 4. Gastrointestinal bleeding in the last 3 weeks Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Intravenous thrombolysis (alteplase/tenecteplase) is used in eligible patients with acute ischemic stroke after excluding contraindications that increase the risk of bleeding.

• 1. Recent head injury: True.

• Recent severe head trauma (within the previous 3 months) is a contraindication due to the high risk of intracranial hemorrhage.

• 2. Recent myocardial infarction: True.

• Recent MI (especially within the past 3 months) is considered a contraindication/major relative contraindication because of the risk of myocardial wall rupture, hemopericardium, and embolization, particularly after a large anterior transmural MI.

• 3. Hypertension > 150/100 mmHg: False.

• This blood pressure is not a contraindication.
• Thrombolysis can be given if BP is ≤ 185/110 mmHg before treatment and maintained < 180/105 mmHg for the next 24 hours.
• Therefore, 150/100 mmHg is within the acceptable range.

• 4. Gastrointestinal bleeding in the last 3 weeks: True.

• Recent gastrointestinal or genitourinary bleeding (within 21 days) is a contraindication because of the increased risk of major hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are trigger factors for seizures? I. Sleep deprivation II. Missed doses of antiepileptic drugs III. Recreational drug misuse IV. Physical exhaustion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, II, III and IV

Seizure triggers are factors that lower the seizure threshold in individuals with epilepsy, increasing the likelihood of seizure occurrence. Identifying and avoiding these triggers is an essential part of epilepsy management.

All the factors listed are recognized seizure triggers:

• I. Sleep deprivation
• II. Missed doses of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs)
• III. Recreational drug misuse (e.g., cocaine, amphetamines, MDMA)
• IV. Physical exhaustion

Each of the listed factors can precipitate seizures by increasing neuronal excitability or reducing seizure threshold.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of gabapentin?
options: Binding to and blockade of the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Binding to and blockade of the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels

Gabapentin exerts its anticonvulsant and analgesic effects by binding to the α2δ subunit of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, thereby reducing calcium influx into nerve terminals. This decreases the release of excitatory neurotransmitters such as glutamate, substance P, and norepinephrine, making it effective in neuropathic pain and focal seizures. Despite its structural similarity to GABA, gabapentin does not act on GABA receptors.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sodium channel blockade: Mechanism of phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, and lacosamide.
• C. Opioid receptor blockade: Mechanism of naloxone and naltrexone.
• D. NMDA receptor antagonism: Mechanism of ketamine, memantine, and dextromethorphan, not gabapentin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is not given in status epilepticus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ethosuximide

Status Epilepticus:

• Continuous seizure activity >5 minutes OR
• Recurrent seizures without regaining consciousness

It’s a neurological emergency → risk of:

• Neuronal injury
• Hypoxia
• Death

1. Immediate suppression (fastest acting)

→ Benzodiazepines (IV Lorazepam)

2. Stabilization (prevent recurrence)

→ Longer-acting anticonvulsants

3. Refractory phase

→ Anesthetics (propofol, midazolam infusion)

Ethosuximide Fails in SE

• Works on thalamic pacemaker activity
• SE involves diffuse cortical excitation
• Ethosuximide → ONLY absence seizures

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following features are present in Locked-in syndrome? 1. Cerebral cortex is intact. 2. Bilateral motor tracts are damaged. 3. Some response to verbal stimuli may be present. 4. Limb movement occurs in response to noxious stimuli. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Locked-in syndrome results from bilateral ventral pontine lesions that interrupt corticospinal and corticobulbar pathways while preserving consciousness and cognitive function. Patients are typically quadriplegic and unable to speak but retain vertical eye movements and blinking for communication.

1. Cerebral cortex is intact: Correct

• In locked-in syndrome, consciousness and cognitive function are preserved because the cerebral cortex remains intact.

2. Bilateral motor tracts are damaged: Correct

• Usually caused by a lesion of the ventral pons, affecting the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts.
• This produces quadriplegia and anarthria.

3. Some response to verbal stimuli may be present: Correct

• The patient is conscious and can generally understand verbal commands, although they cannot respond normally because of paralysis.

4. Limb movement occurs in response to noxious stimuli: Incorrect

• Voluntary limb movement is absent due to bilateral corticospinal tract damage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Brisk reflexes

UMNs originate in:

• Motor cortex (precentral gyrus)
• Descend via corticospinal tracts
• Synapse on lower motor neurons (LMN) in anterior horn

Their main role:

Modulate + inhibit reflex activity

When UMN is damaged →

Inhibitory control is lost

So spinal reflex arcs become:

• Overactive
• Unchecked
• Hyper-excitable

Normally:

• Stretch reflex → moderated by descending inhibition

In UMN lesion:

• No inhibition
• Reflex arc becomes exaggerated

Result:

• Hyperreflexia (brisk reflexes)
• Clonus (advanced cases)
• Spasticity (velocity-dependent ↑ tone)

| Feature | UMN Lesion | LMN Lesion

| ------- | ---------- | ----------

| Tone | ↑ (Spastic) | ↓ (Flaccid)

| Reflexes | ↑ (Hyperreflexia) | ↓ (Hyporeflexia)

| Plantar reflex | Extensor (Babinski +) | Flexor/absent

| Fasciculations | ❌ Absent | ✅ Present

| Muscle bulk | Mild atrophy (disuse) | Severe atrophy

| Clonus | May be present | Absent

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is involved in Static Two-point discrimination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Merkel disk

Static Two-Point Discrimination:

It is the ability to distinguish two closely spaced points applied simultaneously on the skin WITHOUT movement.

Requires:

• High spatial resolution
• Precise localization
• Sustained response

It is mediated by Merkel disks, which are slowly adapting mechanoreceptors with small receptive fields.

Slowly adapting (SA-I)

• Small receptive fields → high precision
• Located in basal epidermis
• Detect:

• Edges
• Shape
• Fine details (e.g., reading Braille)

They fire continuously as long as the stimulus is present → perfect for static touch discrimination

They are specialized for detecting edges, form, and texture.

Meissner corpuscles mediate dynamic touch, Pacinian vibration, and Ruffini stretch.

| Receptor | Adaptation | Receptive Field | Function | Static 2-Point?

| -------- | ---------- | --------------- | -------- | ---------------

| Merkel (SA-I) | Slow | Small | Fine touch, edges | ✅ YES

| Meissner (RA) | Rapid | Small | Light touch, flutter | ❌ No

| Pacinian (RA) | Rapid | Large | Vibration, deep pressure | ❌ No

| Ruffini (SA-II) | Slow | Large | Skin stretch | ❌ No

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements about barbiturates and benzodiazepines is correct?
options: Both act on GABA chloride channels
Benzodiazepines increase the duration of chloride channel opening
Barbiturates are used to treat acute anxiety
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Both act on GABA chloride channels

| Drug Class | Mechanism

| ---------- | ---------

| Benzodiazepines | ↑ Frequency of Cl⁻ channel opening

| Barbiturates | ↑ Duration of Cl⁻ channel opening

| Both | Enhance GABA action → CNS depression

Both benzodiazepines and barbiturates act on the GABA_A receptor–chloride ion channel complex. Benzodiazepines increase the frequency of chloride channel opening, while barbiturates increase the duration. Both act on the same receptor (GABA-A) but at different sites.

Flumazenil antagonizes benzodiazepines only, not barbiturates.

Barbiturates are not preferred for acute anxiety due to narrow therapeutic index and respiratory depression risk.

| Feature | Benzodiazepines | Barbiturates

| ------- | --------------- | ------------

| Receptor | GABA-A | GABA-A

| Action | ↑ Frequency | ↑ Duration

| GABA required? | Yes | No (high dose)

| Safety | High | Low

| Antidote | Flumazenil | None

| Uses | Anxiety, seizures | Epilepsy (rare now), anesthesia

| Toxicity | Mild CNS depression | Severe respiratory depression

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding the use of benzodiazepines in the initial management of status epilepticus? I. Upto two doses may be used 5 minutes apart, if seizures are not controlled II. For Lorazepam, only a single dose should be used, even if seizures are not controlled III. Dose of midazolam at this stage is 1–15 μg/kg/min infusion IV. Dose of both lorazepam and midazolam is 0.1 mg/kg Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I and IV

Status epilepticus (SE) is a neurological emergency requiring immediate administration of benzodiazepines as first-line therapy. If seizures persist after the initial dose, a second dose may be administered after 5 minutes before proceeding to second-line antiseizure medications.

Why is B correct?

• I. Up to two doses may be used 5 minutes apart, if seizures are not controlled. ✔

• Correct.
• If seizures continue after the first benzodiazepine dose, one repeat dose can be given after 5 minutes.

• II. For Lorazepam, only a single dose should be used, even if seizures are not controlled. ✘

• Incorrect.
• A second dose of lorazepam may be given if seizures persist.

• III. Dose of midazolam at this stage is 1–15 μg/kg/min infusion. ✘

• Incorrect.
• Midazolam infusion is used for refractory status epilepticus, not during the initial management.
• Initial therapy uses a bolus dose.

• IV. Dose of both lorazepam and midazolam is 0.1 mg/kg. ✔

• Correct.
• Lorazepam: 0.1 mg/kg IV (maximum 4 mg/dose).
• Midazolam: 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV (or 0.2 mg/kg IM if IV access is unavailable). For exam purposes, 0.1 mg/kg is accepted.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding fosphenytoin and phenytoin?
options: At high doses in elderly patients, it causes cardiotoxicity and in younger patients’ nephrotoxicity
Adverse effects can be avoided if the dose is kept less than 250 mg phenytoin sodium equivalents
It is given to all seizure patients in emergency irrespective of CNS adverse effects and hypotension
High oral dose of phenytoin can result in cerebellar degeneration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. High oral dose of phenytoin can result in cerebellar degeneration

Fosphenytoin is a water‑soluble prodrug of phenytoin given IV or IM (no oral form). It is used acutely for status epilepticus or neurosurgical seizure prophylaxis.

Doses are expressed in “phenytoin equivalents” (PE): e.g. 75 mg fosphenytoin = 50 mg phenytoin. Typical IV loading is 15–20 mg PE/kg (e.g. 1000–1500 mg PE in adults) at a max infusion rate of 150 mg PE/min. Hence, Option B is wrong.

Option A and C. Its adverse‐effect profile mirrors phenytoin’s: CNS (nystagmus, ataxia, sedation), and serious cardiovascular toxicity if infused too rapidly. Fosphenytoin can indeed cause serious cardiotoxicity in high doses, especially in elderly patients. The claim about nephrotoxicity in younger patients lacks evidence and is not a recognized phenomenon.

Cerebellar degeneration is associated with chronic phenytoin use, so that seems to be the best answer.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following childhood epileptic disorders often needs long-term treatment with antiepileptic drugs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy

Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) is a genetic generalized epilepsy syndrome that typically begins during adolescence (12–18 years). It is characterized by the triad of:

• Myoclonic jerks (especially soon after awakening) ⭐
• Generalized tonic-clonic seizures
• Absence seizures (in about one-third of patients)

Unlike many childhood epilepsy syndromes, JME usually requires lifelong or long-term antiepileptic therapy, as seizures commonly recur after discontinuation of medication.

Why not the other options?

• A. Benign neonatal seizures: Usually self-limiting and often resolve spontaneously without long-term therapy.
• B. Febrile seizures: Simple febrile seizures are benign and do not require long-term antiepileptic drugs. ⭐
• C. Benign rolandic epilepsy (Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes): Has an excellent prognosis and usually remits spontaneously by adolescence; long-term treatment is often unnecessary.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is a childhood onset epilepsy syndrome characterized by multiple seizure types, developmental delay and slow (<3 Hz) spike-and-wave discharges on an electroencephalogram?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lennox–Gastaut Syndrome

Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (LGS) is a severe childhood-onset epileptic encephalopathy characterized by:

• Multiple seizure types — especially tonic seizures and atonic (“drop”) attacks
• Developmental/cognitive impairment
• Characteristic EEG showing slow (<3 Hz) generalized spike-and-wave discharges, typically around 1.5–2.5 Hz
• Abnormal background activity

Why not the others?

• A. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: Adolescent onset; myoclonic jerks, generalized tonic-clonic seizures and absence seizures; EEG shows 3–6 Hz generalized spike/polyspike-and-wave.
• C. Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy: Focal seizures with temporal lobe features; EEG may show temporal sharp waves, not generalized slow spike-and-wave.
• D. Rasmussen syndrome: Childhood-onset progressive unilateral cerebral hemispheric inflammation, causing focal seizures, hemiparesis, and cognitive decline.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following oral drugs may be used in the management of super-refractory status epilepticus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Topiramate

Super-refractory status epilepticus (SRSE) is defined as status epilepticus that continues or recurs for ≥24 hours despite treatment with intravenous anesthetic agents, including recurrence after attempts to withdraw anesthesia. Management requires intensive care, continuous EEG monitoring, treatment of the underlying cause, and the addition of multiple antiseizure medications.

Oral (or enteral) Topiramate is one of the commonly used adjunctive drugs in the management of SRSE.

Why is D correct?

• Topiramate is a broad-spectrum antiseizure medication that can be administered orally or via a nasogastric tube in patients with SRSE.
• It has multiple mechanisms of action:

• Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels
• Enhances GABA-mediated inhibition
• Antagonizes AMPA/kainate glutamate receptors
• Weak carbonic anhydrase inhibitor

• It is frequently used as an adjunct when seizures remain uncontrolled despite standard therapy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Clonazepam: A benzodiazepine used for certain seizure disorders but not routinely used for SRSE.
• B. Clobazam: May be used as adjunctive therapy in refractory epilepsy but is not the preferred oral agent classically used for SRSE.
• C. Lamotrigine: Requires slow dose titration due to the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, making it unsuitable for acute management of SRSE.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following refers to agraphesthesia?
options: Inability to identify common objects by palpation recognising their shape, texture and size
Inability to recognize with eyes closed, letters or numbers drawn by the examiner’s fingertip on the palm of the hand
Inability to discriminate two points set 3 mm apart on fingertips
Inability to stand and walk with both the eyes closed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inability to recognize with eyes closed, letters or numbers drawn by the examiner’s fingertip on the palm of the hand

• Agraphesthesia is the inability to recognize letters, numbers, or symbols traced on the skin when the patient’s eyes are closed.
• It is a cortical sensory deficit, usually due to a lesion of the contralateral parietal cortex.

Why not the others?

• A. Astereognosis: Inability to identify a familiar object by touch despite intact primary sensation.
• C. Impaired two-point discrimination: Deficit in cortical sensory discrimination; commonly tested on fingertips.
• D. Positive Romberg sign: Inability to maintain standing with eyes closed, suggesting impaired proprioception or vestibular function.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which statement regarding lamotrigine is not true?
options: Clearance reduced in severe hepatic impairment
Dizziness and ataxia are adverse effects
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Undergoes significant enterohepatic circulation

A. Primarily metabolized by glucuronidation: True. Lamotrigine is mainly metabolized via: Hepatic glucuronidation

B. Clearance reduced in severe hepatic impairment: True. Severe liver disease:

• Reduces clearance
• Requires dose adjustment

C. Undergoes significant enterohepatic circulation: False. Lamotrigine does not undergo significant enterohepatic circulation.

D. Dizziness and ataxia are adverse effects: True. Common adverse effects:

• Dizziness
• Diplopia
• Ataxia
• Rash/SJS

Reference: Katzung Pharmacology:

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department with vomiting, abdominal pain, and altered sensorium. His ABG report shows: pH 7.18, PaCO2 18 mmHg, HCO3⁻ 8 mEq/L. Serum electrolytes show Na⁺ 138 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 96 mEq/L, K⁺ 5.2 mEq/L. What is the most likely acid-base disturbance, and which value best supports this interpretation?
options: Simple respiratory alkalosis; based on the markedly low PaCO2
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation; anion gap = 34 mEq/L
Normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis; anion gap = 8 mEq/L
Mixed respiratory and metabolic alkalosis; based on low PaCO2 and low HCO3⁻
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation; anion gap = 34 mEq/L

Rationale: The anion gap is calculated as Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO3⁻) = 138 − (96 + 8) = 34 mEq/L, markedly elevated above the normal range (8–12 mEq/L), confirming a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) — consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis in this patient (accumulation of ketoacid anions like β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate). The low pH (7.18) confirms acidemia, and the markedly reduced PaCO2 (18 mmHg) reflects appropriate respiratory compensation (Kussmaul breathing) attempting to blow off CO2 and raise pH back toward normal — this is expected, not a separate primary respiratory disorder, so option A is incorrect. Using Winter's formula to check compensation adequacy: expected PaCO2 = 1.5(HCO3⁻) + 8 ± 2 = 1.5(8) + 8 = 20 ± 2 (i.e., 18–22 mmHg) — the patient's PaCO2 of 18 falls within this expected range, confirming appropriate (not mixed) compensation. Option C is incorrect because the anion gap is clearly elevated, not normal; option D incorrectly identifies the primary disturbance as alkalosis, when the markedly acidic pH confirms acidosis is primary.

Quick reference — Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis Workup:

| Step | Calculation/Concept

| ---- | -------------------

| Anion gap | Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO3⁻); normal = 8–12 mEq/L

| HAGMA causes (MUDPILES) | Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Propylene glycol/Paraldehyde, Iron/INH, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates

| Expected respiratory compensation (Winter's formula) | Expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3⁻ + 8 (±2)

| If measured PaCO2 > expected | Concurrent primary respiratory acidosis

| If measured PaCO2 < expected | Concurrent primary respiratory alkalosis

| Delta-delta gap (Δgap/ΔHCO3⁻) | Identifies a coexisting normal AG acidosis or metabolic alkalosis hiding behind a HAGMA

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 22-year-old female with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with polyuria, polydipsia, vomiting, abdominal pain, and deep, rapid breathing for one day. She is dehydrated and has a fruity breath odor. Her random blood glucose is 400 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis shows: pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 20 mmHg, and HCO₃⁻ 14 mEq/L. What is the most likely acid–base disorder?
options: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory acidosis
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) produces a high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to the accumulation of ketoacids (β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate) resulting from absolute insulin deficiency. The body compensates by hyperventilation (Kussmaul respiration), leading to a fall in PaCO₂ as a form of respiratory compensation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory acidosis: Incorrect. DKA causes a high anion gap acidosis, and patients hyperventilate rather than retain CO₂.
• C. Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation: Incorrect. Vomiting can cause metabolic alkalosis, but the predominant disturbance in DKA is metabolic acidosis.
• D. Respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation: Incorrect. The primary abnormality is metabolic, not respiratory.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 23-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department with confusion and generalized weakness. He reports missing multiple doses of insulin over the past few days due to poor oral intake following an episode of diarrhea. On examination, he is dehydrated and has deep, rapid breathing with a fruity odor to his breath. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals metabolic acidosis. Which of the following changes in urine chemistry is most likely to be seen in this patient?
options: Increased urine pH, increased bicarbonate excretion, decreased ammonium excretion
Increased urine pH, decreased bicarbonate excretion, increased ammonium excretion
Decreased urine pH, decreased bicarbonate excretion, decreased ammonium excretion
Decreased urine pH, decreased bicarbonate excretion, increased ammonium excretion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreased urine pH, decreased bicarbonate excretion, increased ammonium excretion

This patient has diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) causing high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

Renal compensation:

• Kidneys try to excrete excess acid (H⁺)
• Increase ammonium (NH₄⁺) excretion to buffer H⁺
• Reabsorb bicarbonate → ↓ urinary HCO₃⁻ loss
• Urine becomes acidic (↓ pH)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with progressive shortness of breath over the past few weeks. Her vital signs are stable, and oxygen saturation is normal. Which acid–base disturbance best explains this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Respiratory Alkalosis due to hyperventilation

Normal pregnancy is associated with physiological hyperventilation due to progesterone-mediated stimulation of the respiratory center, leading to increased alveolar ventilation. This causes a chronic compensated respiratory alkalosis, characterized by decreased PaCO₂, a mild rise in pH, and renal compensation with increased bicarbonate excretion.

Why not the other options?

• A. Metabolic alkalosis due to hyperventilation: Hyperventilation causes a primary respiratory, not metabolic, disturbance.
• B. Metabolic acidosis due to hypoventilation: Hypoventilation causes respiratory acidosis, not metabolic acidosis.
• D. Respiratory acidosis due to hypoventilation: Pregnancy is associated with hyperventilation, making respiratory acidosis unlikely in a healthy pregnant woman.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to progressive confusion and lethargy over the past several hours. The patient has no significant medical history but he has been depressed since a recent breakup with his girlfriend. He works at an automotive repair shop, and one of his coworkers reported seeing the patient consume antifreeze prior to symptom onset. Blood pressure is 110/66 mmHg, pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 24/min. Bilateral costovertebral angles are tender to percussion. Bladder catheterization yields a small amount of bloody urine. Which of the following is most likely to be seen on this patient's arterial blood gas analysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. pH 7.3, pO2 95, pCO2 24, HCO3 19

Ethylene glycol (antifreeze) poisoning causes high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to metabolism into glycolic and oxalic acids. This leads to:

• ↓ pH (acidemia)
• ↓ HCO₃⁻ (metabolic acidosis)
• Compensatory ↓ pCO₂ from hyperventilation
• Normal PaO₂

Oxalate crystal deposition in kidneys causes flank pain, hematuria, and acute kidney injury.

Thus, ABG shows metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with complaints of nausea, diarrhea, and vomiting. Upon further investigation, arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis reveals the following: pH: 7.55, PCO2: 50 mmHg, HCO3-: 44 mmol/L. Given these findings, which of the following conditions is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metabolic Alkalosis

ABG shows alkalemia (pH 7.55) with markedly elevated bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻ 44 mmol/L), indicating a primary metabolic process.

The raised PCO₂ (50 mmHg) represents appropriate respiratory compensation via hypoventilation.

• pH = 7.55 → Alkalemia
• HCO₃⁻ = 44 mmol/L (↑) → pushes pH up
• PCO₂ = 50 mmHg (↑) → would push pH down (compensation)

HCO₃⁻ = 44 → (44−24)=20

• 0.7 × 20 = 14
• Expected PCO₂ ≈ 54 ± 5 → 49–59 mmHg

Observed PCO₂ = 50 mmHg

Appropriate respiratory compensation

Thus, the diagnosis is metabolic alkalosis, commonly due to gastric acid loss from vomiting

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 4-week-old, full-term boy is brought to the emergency department due to vomiting. His parents describe the emesis as undigested formula without blood or bile. The vomiting occurs after feeds and has increased in frequency and force over the past 3 days. Examination shows a sunken anterior fontanelle and dry mucous membranes. Arterial blood gas analysis is most likely to reveal which of the following sets of values?
options: pH 7.29, PaCO2 30, HCO3 14, Anion gap elevated
pH 7.30, PaCO2 50, HCO3 28, Anion gap normal
pH 7.48, PaCO2 46, HCO3 34, Anion gap normal
pH 7.53, PaCO2 22, HCO3 22, Anion gap normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. pH 7.48, PaCO2 46, HCO3 34, Anion gap normal

Projectile, non-bilious vomiting in a 4-week-old infant suggests hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

Loss of gastric HCl leads to metabolic alkalosis with:

• ↑ pH
• ↑ HCO₃⁻
• Compensatory ↑ PaCO₂ (respiratory hypoventilation)
• Normal anion gap
• Often associated with hypokalemia and hypochloremia

Thus, persistent vomiting of gastric contents causes hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 40-year-old male presents with altered mental status, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypertension after consuming an unknown substance. On evaluation, he has high anion gap metabolic acidosis and hypocalcemia. Which of the following is likely to be the reason for his presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ethylene glycol

Ethylene glycol poisoning causes high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to accumulation of glycolic and oxalic acids.

Oxalic acid chelates calcium, leading to hypocalcemia and calcium oxalate crystal deposition.

This explains altered mental status, tachypnea (Kussmaul breathing), and cardiovascular instability.

| Finding | Mechanism

| ------- | ---------

| Altered mental status | CNS toxicity

| Tachypnea | Compensation for metabolic acidosis

| Tachycardia | Stress response

| Hypertension | Early sympathetic response

| Hypocalcemia | Ca²⁺ bound by oxalate

| High AG acidosis | Organic acids accumulate

Methanol causes visual symptoms, iron causes GI hemorrhage and acidosis without hypocalcemia, and digoxin causes arrhythmias without metabolic acidosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 45-year-old man has the following serum electrolyte values during evaluation: • Na⁺: 130 mmol/L • Cl⁻: 84 mmol/L • HCO₃⁻: 16 mmol/L What is the calculated anion gap for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 30

Anion gap is calculated as Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻).

Substituting values: 130 − (84 + 16) = 130 − 100 = 30.

Thus, the calculated anion gap is 30, indicating a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

| Anion Gap | Value | Meaning

| --------- | ----- | -------

| Normal | 8–12 | No excess acids

| Mild ↑ | 12–20 | Early acidosis

| High ↑ | >20 |  Accumulation of acids

High Anion Gap-

| Letter | Cause

| ------ | -----

| G | Glycols (ethylene glycol, propylene glycol)

| O | Oxoproline (chronic paracetamol use)

| L | L-lactate (shock, sepsis)

| D | D-lactate

| M | Methanol

| A | Aspirin

| R | Renal failure (uremia)

| K | Ketoacidosis (DKA, starvation)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 55-year-old patient presents with shortness of breath. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals the following- pH: 7.22, PaCO₂: 66 mmHg PaO₂: 45 mmHg HCO₃⁻: 26 mEq/L. What is the most likely acid-base disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Respiratory acidosis

Low pH (7.22) with markedly elevated PaCO₂ (66 mmHg) indicates a primary respiratory acidosis.

Near-normal bicarbonate (26 mEq/L) suggests minimal or no metabolic compensation, consistent with an acute process.

Acidemia (↓ pH)

+

↑ PaCO₂ (primary abnormality)

+

Normal HCO₃⁻ (no compensation)

Severe hypoxemia further supports hypoventilation as the underlying cause.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with progressive dyspnea. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals: • pH: 7.32 • PaCO₂: 60 mmHg • HCO₃⁻: 30 mmol/L Which of the following represents the primary acid–base disorder in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chronic respiratory acidosis

| Condition | PaCO₂ ↑ | HCO₃⁻ Change | Mechanism

| --------- | ------- | ------------ | ---------

| Acute respiratory acidosis | ↑ | ↑ slightly (\~+1 per 10 CO₂) | Buffer systems

| Chronic respiratory acidosis | ↑ | ↑↑ more (\~+4 per 10 CO₂) | Renal compensation

Low pH with elevated PaCO₂ indicates primary respiratory acidosis.

The elevated bicarbonate (30 mmol/L) reflects renal compensation, which develops over time.

This pattern is typical of chronic respiratory acidosis seen in long-standing COPD.

1. COPD = classic chronic respiratory acidosis

• “CO₂ retainers”
• Often have compensated pH (\~near normal)

2. Oxygen therapy caution

In COPD:

• High O₂ → ↓ respiratory drive → ↑ CO₂ retention

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with small cell lung carcinoma presents with confusion and seizures. Laboratory findings show: • Serum sodium: 112 mEq/L • Serum osmolality: Low • Urine osmolality: High Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypertonic saline (3% NaCl)

Symptomatic severe hyponatremia (e.g., confusion, seizures) due to SIADH, commonly associated with small cell lung carcinoma, is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment with hypertonic saline (3% NaCl). Hypertonic saline rapidly raises serum sodium and reduces the risk of cerebral edema and herniation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Fluid restriction – first-line for chronic or mild SIADH but too slow in patients with severe neurologic symptoms.
• C. Demeclocycline – used for long-term management of chronic SIADH; not appropriate for acute emergencies.
• D. Tolvaptan – may be used in selected cases of euvolemic hyponatremia but is not the initial treatment for symptomatic severe hyponatremia with seizures.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 60-year-old with a history of COPD is brought to the ER with worsening dyspnea. ABG was done and pH was 7.3, pCO2 was 60 mmHg with HCO3- being 26 mEq/L. Which of the following is seen in this patient?
options: Respiratory acidosis, hyperventilation, inadequate metabolic compensation
Respiratory alkalosis, hypoventilation, inadequate metabolic compensation
Respiratory acidosis, hypoventilation, inadequate metabolic compensation
Respiratory acidosis, hypoventilation, adequate metabolic compensation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Respiratory acidosis, hypoventilation, adequate metabolic compensation

In COPD:

• Air trapping + ↓ alveolar ventilation
• CO₂ cannot be expelled → hypercapnia
• Leads to respiratory acidosis

Low pH (7.3) with elevated pCO₂ (60 mmHg) indicates primary respiratory acidosis due to hypoventilation, typical in COPD exacerbation.

Expected Compensation Rules:

| Condition | Expected HCO₃⁻ change

| --------- | ---------------------

| Acute respiratory acidosis | ↑ 1 mEq/L per 10 mmHg CO₂ rise

| Chronic respiratory acidosis | ↑ 4 mEq/L per 10 mmHg CO₂ rise

Bicarbonate is elevated (26 mEq/L; should be 24 + 2 = 26 mEq/L, considering acute-on-chronic COPD changes), indicating adequate metabolic compensation for the degree of hypercapnia.

Thus, this represents acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis with hypoventilation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 70-year-old unconscious patient is brought to the emergency department. Laboratory results show: • Serum Na⁺: 160 mEq/L • Serum osmolality: Increased • Urine osmolality: 90 mOsm/kg The patient is producing large volumes of dilute urine. Which of the following is the most likely cause of hypernatremia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Central diabetes insipidus

Central diabetes insipidus (DI) is characterized by deficient secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), resulting in the inability of the kidneys to concentrate urine. This leads to excretion of large volumes of dilute urine, causing excessive free-water loss, hypernatremia, and increased serum osmolality.

In this patient:

• Serum Na⁺ = 160 mEq/L → Hypernatremia
• Increased serum osmolality → Water deficit
• Urine osmolality = 90 mOsm/kg → Inappropriately dilute urine
• Polyuria → Suggests diabetes insipidus

These findings are most consistent with central diabetes insipidus.

Why not the others?

• B. SIADH → Hyponatremia, low serum osmolality, concentrated urine.
• C. Primary hyperaldosteronism → Mild hypernatremia may occur, but marked polyuria with very dilute urine is not typical.
• D. Vomiting-induced dehydration → Kidneys conserve water, producing concentrated urine (high urine osmolality), not dilute urine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A man goes trekking at a high altitude. Due to the physiological response to decreased atmospheric oxygen tension, which of the following primary acid–base disturbances is most likely to develop in this individual?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Respiratory alkalosis

At high altitude, reduced atmospheric oxygen tension causes hypoxemia, which stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors. At High Altitude

| Parameter | Change

| --------- | ------

| pH | ↑ (alkalosis)

| pCO₂ | ↓

| HCO₃⁻ | Initially normal → later ↓ (renal compensation)

This leads to hyperventilation, resulting in excessive CO₂ washout.

The primary acid–base disturbance is therefore respiratory alkalosis.

| Phase | Mechanism | ABG

| ----- | --------- | ---

| Acute (hours) | Hyperventilation | Respiratory alkalosis

| Chronic (days) | Kidney excretes HCO₃⁻ | Compensated alkalosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A patient arrives at the emergency department presenting with symptoms of abdominal pain, vomiting, tachypnea, and tachycardia. Laboratory results are as follows: pH: 7.34, Sodium: 135 mmol/L, Potassium: 5 mmol/L, Bicarbonate: 12 mmol/L, Chloride: 92 mmol/L, RBS: 450 mg/dL. Given these laboratory findings, which of the following statements best describes the patient's acid-base status?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (HAGMA)

pH 7.34 with low bicarbonate (12 mmol/L) indicates a primary metabolic acidosis.

Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO₃) = 135 − (92 + 12) = 31, which is markedly elevated.

Severe hyperglycemia with abdominal pain and tachypnea is classic for diabetic ketoacidosis, a cause of high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

1.

anion gap increases:

2.

Ketone bodies:

• β-hydroxybutyrate
• Acetoacetate

These are unmeasured anions

1. tachypnea occurs because:

Respiratory compensation

• Blows off CO₂
•

Tries to increase pH

Kussmaul respiration

•

Potassium paradox:

•

Serum K⁺ = 5 (normal/high)

• But:

• Total body potassium = LOW

Due to:

• Insulin deficiency

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A patient is brought to the emergency department in a state of shock. Arterial blood gas analysis shows: pH 7.2, PCO₂ 25 mmHg, and HCO₃⁻ 20 mEq/L. Which of the following best describes this patient’s acid–base status?
options: Respiratory Alkalosis with compensated Metabolic Acidosis
Mixed Respiratory Acidosis with Metabolic Alkalosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Metabolic Acidosis with Respiratory Alkalosis

Shock commonly causes lactic acidosis due to tissue hypoperfusion and anaerobic metabolism, resulting in a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. The body’s immediate compensatory response is hyperventilation, which lowers PaCO₂ (respiratory compensation) in an attempt to restore blood pH. Thus, the ABG pattern of ↓ pH, ↓ HCO₃⁻, and ↓ PaCO₂ is consistent with metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Metabolic alkalosis with compensated respiratory acidosis: Would show ↑ pH and ↑ HCO₃⁻, not acidemia.
• C. Respiratory alkalosis with compensated metabolic acidosis: In respiratory alkalosis, the primary abnormality is low PaCO₂ with elevated pH.
• D. Mixed respiratory acidosis with metabolic alkalosis: Would present with ↑ PaCO₂ and ↑ HCO₃⁻, not the findings seen here.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A patient presents with a 2-day history of watery diarrhea (5–6 episodes per day). Arterial blood gas analysis shows decreased PCO₂. Which of the following findings is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ↓ pH, ↓ HCO₃⁻, ↑ Cl⁻

Diarrhea causes a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis due to excessive loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid. The fall in serum HCO₃⁻ leads to metabolic acidosis (↓ pH), while compensatory hyperventilation (Kussmaul respiration) lowers PCO₂. To maintain electroneutrality, chloride is retained by the kidneys, resulting in hyperchloremia.

Why not the other options?

• A. ↑ pH, ↑ HCO₃⁻, ↑ Cl⁻: Suggests metabolic alkalosis, which is inconsistent with bicarbonate loss in diarrhea.
• C. ↑ pH, ↑ HCO₃⁻, ↓ Cl⁻: Typical of vomiting-induced hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.
• D. ↓ pH, ↑ HCO₃⁻, ↑ Cl⁻: Elevated bicarbonate would not be seen in metabolic acidosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A patient with a history of smoking presents to the emergency with a complaint of breathlessness for the last two days. On examination, he was found to be cyanosed and had bilateral rhonchi. ABG was done, which shows: • pH: 7.12 • PaCO₂: 80 mmHg • PaO₂: 46 mmHg • HCO₃⁻: 29 mEq/L Based on the history, clinical examination and ABG finding, the most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. COPD exacerbation

The clinical picture of a chronic smoker with acute worsening breathlessness, bilateral rhonchi, cyanosis, severe hypoxemia, and hypercapnia strongly suggests an acute exacerbation of COPD causing acute-on-chronic respiratory failure.

| Parameter | Value | Interpretation

| --------- | ----- | --------------

| pH | 7.12 | Severe acidemia

| PaCO₂ | 80 mmHg | Markedly elevated → respiratory acidosis

| HCO₃⁻ | 29 mEq/L | Mildly elevated → chronic renal compensation

| PaO₂ | 46 mmHg | Severe hypoxemia

The markedly elevated PaCO₂ with elevated HCO₃⁻ suggests acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis, typical of a COPD exacerbation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Pulmonary embolism: Usually causes hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis due to hyperventilation → ↓ PaCO₂.
• B. Pneumonia: Can cause hypoxemia, but the prominent severe hypercapnia with rhonchi in a smoker strongly favors COPD exacerbation.
• D. Pulmonary fibrosis: Typically causes restrictive lung disease with hypoxemia; hypercapnia is generally a late finding.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A woman presents after 4 days of a flu-like illness associated with poor oral intake and repeated vomiting. She reports dizziness and unsteadiness when standing. Arterial blood gas analysis shows: • pH: 7.50 • PaCO₂: 53 mmHg Which of the following best explains the underlying acid–base disturbance?
options: Reduced hydrogen ion secretion in the distal nephron
Increased bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Volume depletion causing increased distal hydrogen ion secretion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Volume depletion causing increased distal hydrogen ion secretion

The patient has metabolic alkalosis with appropriate respiratory compensation:

• Elevated pH → alkalemia
• Elevated PaCO₂ → compensatory hypoventilation

Repeated vomiting causes loss of gastric hydrochloric acid, producing metabolic alkalosis. In addition, poor intake and vomiting lead to volume and chloride depletion.

Volume depletion activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, causing:

• Increased proximal sodium and bicarbonate reabsorption
• Increased distal sodium reabsorption
• Increased hydrogen and potassium secretion by the collecting duct

This maintains and worsens the metabolic alkalosis, a process called contraction alkalosis.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Excessive antacid use: Can cause metabolic alkalosis, but repeated vomiting with volume depletion is the more likely cause.
• B. Decreased distal hydrogen excretion: Would promote acidosis rather than alkalosis.
• C. Increased proximal bicarbonate reabsorption: Occurs in volume depletion, but the option does not fully describe the key aldosterone-mediated increase in distal hydrogen secretion.

High-yield pearl

• Vomiting → loss of H⁺ and Cl⁻ + volume contraction → RAAS activation → increased distal H⁺ secretion → metabolic alkalosis.
• Expected respiratory compensation: Expected PaCO₂ ≈ 0.7 × rise in HCO₃⁻ + 40 ± 2 mmHg

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: An elderly patient presents with increased frequency of breathing and weakness. ABG is given. What is the likely diagnosis? • pH = 7.3 • pCO₂ = 44 mmHg • pO₂ = 85 mmHg • HCO₃⁻ = 16 mEq/L • Na⁺ = 132 mEq/L • Cl⁻ = 86 mEq/L • Base excess = -12 mEq/L
options: Acute metabolic alkalosis with AG 16 mEq/L
Acute respiratory acidosis with AG 16 mEq/L
Acute metabolic acidosis with AG 30 mEq/L
Chronic Respiratory acidosis with AG 30 mEq/L
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute metabolic acidosis with AG 30 mEq/L

Low pH with markedly reduced HCO₃⁻ (16 mEq/L) indicates primary metabolic acidosis.

Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) = 132 − (86 + 16) = 30 mEq/L, which is elevated.

Near-normal pCO₂ reflects early/partial respiratory compensation, confirming acute high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

| Parameter | Finding

| --------- | -------

| pH | ↓ (acidemia)

| HCO₃⁻ | ↓ → metabolic cause

| pCO₂ | not appropriately ↓

| AG | 30 (high)

Acidemia (↓ pH)

↓

Check HCO₃⁻ → LOW → Metabolic acidosis

↓

Calculate AG → HIGH (30)

↓

Check compensation (Winter’s formula)

↓

pCO₂ higher than expected → Acute / inadequate compensation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Consider the following regarding salicylate poisoning: I. Arterial pH of 7.25, anion gap of 18 mmol/L II. Arterial pH of 7.25, anion gap of 10 mmol/L III. pCO₂ of 20 mmHg IV. pCO₂ of 48 mmHg Which disturbance is likely to be encountered?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I and III

Salicylate (aspirin) poisoning produces a mixed acid-base disorder. Initially, salicylates stimulate the medullary respiratory center, causing primary respiratory alkalosis. As toxicity progresses, accumulation of salicylic acid, lactic acid, and ketoacids leads to high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA).

Therefore, severe salicylate poisoning is characterized by:

• Low arterial pH
• High anion gap metabolic acidosis
• Low pCO₂ due to compensatory hyperventilation (and respiratory center stimulation)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Evaluate the arterial blood gas with the following findings: pH 7.26, PaCO₂ - 16 mm Hg, HCO₃ - 8, Na⁺ 135, Cl⁻ - 108, K⁺ - 4.2.
options: Metabolic acidosis with compensatory respiratory alkalosis with high anion gap
Respiratory acidosis with compensatory metabolic alkalosis with low anion gap
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Metabolic acidosis with compensatory respiratory alkalosis with high anion gap

Low pH with markedly reduced HCO₃⁻ (8 mEq/L) indicates primary metabolic acidosis.

PaCO₂ is appropriately low (16 mmHg), showing respiratory compensation.

Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) = 135 − (108 + 8) = 19, confirming high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

| Value | Meaning

| ----- | -------

| Normal | 8–12

| This case: 19 | 🔺 High anion gap

| Cause | Example

| ----- | -------

| Lactic acidosis | Shock, sepsis

| Ketoacidosis | DKA

| Renal failure | Uremia

| Toxins | Methanol, ethylene glycol

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (HAGMA) is not caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diarrhea

If new acids enter the blood:

• H⁺ consumes HCO₃⁻
• Unmeasured anions rise

→ Anion gap increases

High anion gap metabolic acidosis results from accumulation of unmeasured acids such as ketones, lactate, or retained uremic toxins.

DKA, acute renal failure, and inborn errors of metabolism all cause HAGMA.

Diarrhea causes normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis due to bicarbonate loss.

| Feature | HAGMA | NAGMA

| ------- | ----- | -----

| Cause | Acid accumulation | HCO₃⁻ loss

| Cl⁻ | Normal | ↑

| Examples | DKA, AKI, toxins | Diarrhea, RTA

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Identify the acid base disorder in a patient with the following values: pH- 7.2 and pCO2 – 80 mm Hg?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Respiratory acidosis

Interpretation of acid–base disorders is based on pH and pCO₂:

• Normal pH: 7.35–7.45
• Normal pCO₂: 35–45 mm Hg

In this case:

• pH = 7.2 → Acidemia
• pCO₂ = 80 mm Hg → Markedly elevated (hypercapnia)

An increased pCO₂ indicates CO₂ retention, which shifts the equilibrium toward carbonic acid formation, lowering pH.

Common causes of respiratory acidosis: Hypoventilation (e.g., COPD, airway obstruction, CNS depression)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Metabolic acidosis: ↓ pH with ↓ HCO₃⁻ (not given; pCO₂ usually compensatorily low)
• Metabolic alkalosis: ↑ pH with ↑ HCO₃⁻
• Respiratory alkalosis: ↑ pH with ↓ pCO₂

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Interpret the following arterial blood gas (ABG) values: pH: 7.20 PaO₂: 69 mmHg PaCO₂: 30 mmHg HCO₃⁻: 15 mEq/L What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Metabolic acidosis with compensatory respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis with additional respiratory acidosis
Metabolic acidosis with additional respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis with compensatory metabolic acidosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Metabolic acidosis with compensatory respiratory alkalosis

Stepwise ABG interpretation:

• pH 7.20 → acidemia
• HCO₃⁻ 15 (low) → primary metabolic acidosis
• PaCO₂ 30 (low) → lungs are blowing off CO₂ → respiratory compensation

There is no evidence of an additional respiratory disorder. Since PaCO₂ is reduced in the appropriate direction for compensation, the correct interpretation is Metabolic acidosis with compensatory respiratory alkalosis.

Low PaO₂ (69 mmHg) indicates mild hypoxemia but does not change the primary acid–base diagnosis.

Expected PaCO₂ by Winter’s formula:

(1.5 × HCO₃⁻) + 8 ± 2 = 30.5 ± 2, which matches the measured PaCO₂ (30)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Interpret the given ABG analysis: • pH = 7.2 • pCO₂ = 25 mmHg • HCO₃⁻ = 16 mEq/L • Anion gap = 12
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NAGMA

The ABG demonstrates primary metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation. The low pH (7.2) indicates acidemia, while the low HCO₃⁻ (16 mEq/L) identifies the primary disorder as metabolic acidosis. The normal anion gap (12 mEq/L; normal: 8–12) classifies it as non-anion gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA), also known as hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. The low pCO₂ (25 mmHg) represents appropriate respiratory compensation through hyperventilation.

Stepwise ABG Interpretation:

1. pH = 7.2 → Acidemia
2. HCO₃⁻ = 16 mEq/L (low) → Primary metabolic acidosis
3. pCO₂ = 25 mmHg (low) → Respiratory compensation
4. Anion gap = 12 (normal) → Non-anion gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA)

Winter’s Formula (Assessing Compensation):

Expected pCO₂ = (1.5 × HCO₃⁻) + 8 ± 2

= (1.5 × 16) + 8

= 32 ± 2 mmHg (30–34 mmHg)

The measured pCO₂ is 25 mmHg, which is lower than expected, suggesting an additional respiratory alkalosis may be present. However, the primary disorder remains NAGMA.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Nebulized salbutamol is used in the management of which of the following electrolyte abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hyperkalemia

Nebulized salbutamol (β₂-adrenergic agonist) is used as an adjunct in the emergency management of hyperkalemia. It lowers serum potassium by stimulating the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump, thereby shifting potassium from the extracellular fluid into cells. It acts rapidly but does not remove potassium from the body.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Hypernatremia: Managed with free water replacement or hypotonic fluids, not salbutamol.
• C. Hyponatremia: Treated according to severity with fluid restriction, hypertonic saline, or vasopressin antagonists, depending on the cause.
• D. Hypomagnesemia: Treated with oral or intravenous magnesium replacement.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: PTH is increased in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia

Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) is due to an inactivating mutation of the calcium-sensing receptor, causing the parathyroid glands to perceive serum calcium as low.

This leads to inappropriately normal or increased PTH levels despite hypercalcemia.

Immobility, vitamin D toxicity, and thiazides cause hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH.

Option A: Immobility

• Causes:

• ↑ Bone resorption → ↑ Serum calcium

• Feedback:

• High Ca²⁺ → suppresses PTH

✔ So PTH ↓

•

Option C: Vitamin D toxicity

• Mechanism:

• ↑ Ca absorption from gut

• Result:

• ↑ Serum Ca²⁺ → suppresses PTH
•

Option D: Thiazide diuretics

• Mechanism:

• ↑ Ca reabsorption in distal tubule

• Result:

• Mild hypercalcemia → ↓ PTH

| Feature | FHH | Primary Hyperparathyroidism

| ------- | --- | ---------------------------

| Serum Ca | ↑ | ↑
