| PTH | Normal / ↑ | ↑↑

| Urinary Ca | ↓ (key!) | ↑

| Cause | CaSR mutation | Parathyroid adenoma

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: The hyponatremia in a hypovolemic patient in case of severe diarrhea is due to:
options: Decreased reabsorption of sodium from kidney
Decreased absorption of sodium from the gut
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased secretion of antidiuretic hormone

Severe diarrhea causes extrarenal loss of sodium and water, leading to hypovolemia. The resulting decrease in effective circulating volume stimulates non-osmotic release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). ADH promotes water reabsorption in the collecting ducts, causing retention of free water that exceeds sodium retention, thereby producing dilutional hyponatremia.

Although the kidneys conserve sodium by activating the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS), the marked increase in ADH-mediated water retention is the primary mechanism responsible for the low serum sodium concentration.

Why the other options are incorrect

• A. Decreased reabsorption of sodium from kidney – Incorrect. In hypovolemia, the kidneys increase sodium reabsorption under the influence of aldosterone.
• B. Decreased absorption of sodium from the gut – Incorrect. Diarrhea causes sodium loss, not impaired intestinal absorption.
• D. Decreased secretion of aldosterone – Incorrect. Hypovolemia stimulates increased, not decreased, aldosterone secretion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: The statements below mention about the anion gap in different conditions. Select the true statements. 1. Starvation: Increase 2. Diabetic ketoacidosis: Increase 3. Severe vomiting: Increase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, and 2

Normal ≈ 8–12 mEq/L

Anion gap increases when unmeasured acids accumulate

These acids donate H⁺ → consume HCO₃⁻ → gap widens

Starvation leads to ketosis with accumulation of organic acids, causing an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis.

Diabetic ketoacidosis is a classic cause of high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to ketone bodies.

Severe vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis with normal anion gap, not an increased anion gap.

| Condition | Primary Disorder | Anion Gap | Mechanism

| --------- | ---------------- | --------- | ---------

| Starvation | Metabolic acidosis | ↑ | Ketone bodies

| DKA | Metabolic acidosis | ↑ | Ketoacids

| Vomiting | Metabolic alkalosis | Normal | Loss of H⁺ (not acid accumulation)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: What type of electrolyte imbalance is seen in refeeding syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypophosphatemia

Refeeding syndrome is a potentially life-threatening metabolic complication that occurs when nutrition, particularly carbohydrates, is rapidly reintroduced after prolonged starvation or severe malnutrition. The resulting insulin surge drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, leading to profound hypophosphatemia, the hallmark electrolyte abnormality of refeeding syndrome.

• During starvation, total body phosphate stores become depleted.
• Refeeding with carbohydrates increases insulin secretion, which:

• Stimulates cellular uptake of glucose
• Drives phosphate into cells for ATP production

• This results in severe hypophosphatemia, which is the earliest and most characteristic laboratory finding.

Why not the other options?

• A. Hyperkalemia: Incorrect. Refeeding causes hypokalemia, as potassium shifts intracellularly under the influence of insulin.
• B. Hyponatremia: Incorrect. May occur due to fluid retention but is not the hallmark abnormality.
• C. Hypomagnesemia: Incorrect. Commonly occurs in refeeding syndrome but is less characteristic than hypophosphatemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Which of the following are used in calculating the serum osmolality? 1. Serum sodium 2. Glucose 3. Calcium 4. Blood urea nitrogen Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Serum osmolality reflects the concentration of osmotically active particles in plasma and is primarily determined by serum sodium, glucose, and blood urea nitrogen (BUN). It is useful in the evaluation of electrolyte disorders, dehydration, poisoning, and acid–base disturbances.

Why is B correct?

• 1. Serum sodium✅: The major determinant of serum osmolality.
• 2. Glucose✅: Significantly contributes to osmolality, especially in hyperglycemia.
• 4. Blood urea nitrogen (BUN)✅: Included in the calculated serum osmolality, although urea is an ineffective osmole because it freely crosses cell membranes.

Incorrect statement:

• 3. Calcium❌: Although physiologically important, calcium contributes negligibly to serum osmolality and is not included in the calculation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Which of the following are used in the management of hyperkalemia? 1. 10% calcium gluconate intravenously 2. Regular insulin and intravenous glucose 3. Nebulized ipratropium bromide 4. Intravenous sodium bicarbonate Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Hyperkalemia is a life-threatening electrolyte disturbance because of its potential to cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias. Emergency management involves stabilizing the cardiac membrane, shifting potassium into cells, and removing excess potassium from the body.

Why is B correct?

• 1. 10% Calcium gluconate intravenously✅: Stabilizes the myocardial cell membrane, reducing the risk of life-threatening arrhythmias. It does not lower serum potassium levels.
• 2. Regular insulin and intravenous glucose✅: Insulin activates the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump, driving potassium into cells. Glucose is given to prevent hypoglycemia.
• 4. Intravenous sodium bicarbonate✅: Particularly useful in hyperkalemia associated with metabolic acidosis, as it promotes intracellular potassium movement.

Incorrect statement:

• 3. Nebulized ipratropium bromide❌: Ipratropium has no role in treating hyperkalemia. The inhaled drug used is nebulized salbutamol (β₂-agonist), which shifts potassium intracellularly.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Which of the following can be used for the management of severe hyperkalaemia? I. Intravenous calcitonin II. Intravenous sodium bicarbonate III. Oral sodium polystyrene sulphonate IV. Intravenous calcium gluconate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II, III and IV

Severe hyperkalemia (especially K⁺ ≥6.5 mEq/L, ECG changes, or symptomatic patients) is a medical emergency because it can cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias. Management involves:

1. Stabilizing the cardiac membrane
2. Shifting potassium into cells
3. Removing potassium from the body

Why is B correct?

• I. Intravenous calcitonin ❌

• Incorrect. Calcitonin is used for hypercalcemia, not hyperkalemia.

• II. Intravenous sodium bicarbonate ✅

• Useful especially in patients with metabolic acidosis by promoting intracellular potassium shift.

• III. Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate ✅

• Removes potassium from the body through the gastrointestinal tract by exchanging sodium for potassium.
• (Newer agents such as patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate are increasingly preferred for non-emergency potassium removal.)

• IV. Intravenous calcium gluconate ✅

• First drug given in hyperkalemia with ECG changes.
• Stabilizes the cardiac membrane but does not lower serum potassium.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is most likely based on the lab values shown - Blood pH 7.28, Na 138 mEq/L, K 2.8 mEq/L, Cl 113 mEq/L, HCO3 12 mEq/L, BUN 3 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.2 mg/dL. Urinalysis showed a urinary pH of 9. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type 1 RTA

Low pH with low HCO₃⁻ (12 mEq/L) indicates metabolic acidosis with normal renal function.

Marked hyperchloremia, hypokalemia, and inappropriately alkaline urine (pH 9) indicate failure of distal H⁺ secretion.

Metabolic acidosis

↓

Normal AG → RTA

↓

Check K⁺ → LOW

↓

Check urine pH → HIGH (>5.5)

↓

Type 1 (Distal) RTA

This is characteristic of distal (Type 1) renal tubular acidosis, which is associated with hypokalemia and high urine pH.

| Feature | Type 1 (Distal) | Type 2 (Proximal) | Type 4

| ------- | --------------- | ----------------- | ------

| Defect | ↓ H⁺ secretion | ↓ HCO₃⁻ reabsorption | ↓ Aldosterone

| Urine pH | >5.5 (alkaline) | <5.5 (later) | <5.5

| K⁺ | Low | Low | More

| Stones | Common | Rare | No

| AG | Normal | Normal | Normal

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Which of the following crystalloid infusions, when given in large quantities, is likely to cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NS

Large-volume infusion of normal saline (0.9% NaCl) delivers excess chloride relative to sodium. Large-volume normal saline → ↑Cl⁻ → ↓HCO₃⁻ → hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (normal anion gap)

This increases plasma chloride, causing bicarbonate dilution and a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis.

| Fluid | Key Composition | Effect on Acid-Base

| ----- | --------------- | -------------------

| NS (0.9%) | High Cl⁻ | Causes acidosis

| Ringer Lactate | Lactate → HCO₃⁻ | Alkalinizing

| D5W | Free water | Neutral

| DNS | Dextrose + NS | Mild acidosis possible but less prominent

Ringer lactate is balanced, D5W is free water, and DNS does not cause significant hyperchloremia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Which of the following is seen during rapid ascent to high altitude?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Respiratory alkalosis

High altitude → ↓ O₂ (Hypoxia)

↓

Peripheral chemoreceptor stimulation

↓

Hyperventilation

↓

↓ CO₂ (Hypocapnia)

↓

↑ pH

↓

Respiratory Alkalosis

Rapid ascent to high altitude causes hypoxemia, which stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors.

This leads to hyperventilation, causing excessive CO₂ washout and resulting in respiratory alkalosis.

Renal compensation with bicarbonate loss occurs later.

| Phase | Change

| ----- | ------

| Immediate (hours) | Respiratory alkalosis

| After 2–3 days | Renal compensation → ↓ HCO₃⁻

| Long-term | ↑ RBC, ↑ 2,3-BPG

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common regulatory mechanism of magnesium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renal reabsorption

Magnesium homeostasis is primarily regulated by renal reabsorption, especially in the thick ascending limb and distal convoluted tubule. The kidneys adjust magnesium excretion according to body needs, making renal handling the most important regulatory mechanism.

| Nephron Segment | % Reabsorbed | Mechanism

| --------------- | ------------ | ---------

| PCT | \~15–20% | Passive (paracellular)

| Thick Ascending Limb (TAL) | \~60–70% (MOST IMPORTANT) | Paracellular via lumen-positive potential

| DCT | \~5–10% | Active (TRPM6 channels)

Dietary intake, intestinal absorption, and bone stores play lesser roles in moment-to-moment regulation.

| Option | Verdict | Explanation |

| ------ | ------- | ----------- | ---

| A) Dietary intake | ❌ | Intake affects levels but not regulation |

| B) Intestinal absorption | ❌ | Limited adaptive control |

| C) Renal reabsorption | ✅ | Primary regulator via nephron control |

| D) Bone resorption | ❌ | Storage site, not dynamic regulator |

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding hypernatremia in children? I. Diabetes insipidus due to a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) may cause hypernatremia II. Addison disease may be associated with hypernatremia III. Use of boiled skimmed milk can lead to hypernatremia IV. Use of lactulose can lead to hypernatremia Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, III and IV

Hypernatremia is defined as a serum sodium concentration >145 mEq/L and usually results from water deficit exceeding sodium loss or, less commonly, excessive sodium intake. In children, the common causes include gastrointestinal water loss, diabetes insipidus, osmotic diarrhea, and improper infant feeding practices.

Why is A correct?

• I. Diabetes insipidus due to a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) may cause hypernatremia. ✔

• Correct.
• Central diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency) causes excessive free water loss, resulting in polyuria, dehydration, and hypernatremia.

• II. Addison disease may be associated with hypernatremia. ✘

• Incorrect.
• Addison disease causes hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension due to aldosterone deficiency.

• III. Use of boiled skimmed milk can lead to hypernatremia. ✔

• Correct.
• Feeding infants with boiled skimmed milk or improperly prepared concentrated feeds increases the renal solute load and predisposes to hypernatremic dehydration.

• IV. Use of lactulose can lead to hypernatremia. ✔

• Correct.
• Lactulose can cause osmotic diarrhea, leading to excessive free water loss and hypernatremia if fluids are not adequately replaced.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding management of hyperkalemia in a child? I. Intravenous calcium (gluconate or chloride) is given to enhance cellular uptake of potassium II. Beta adrenergic agonists (salbutamol or terbutaline) are used to stabilize myocardial cell membrane III. Regular insulin and glucose given intravenously enhance cellular uptake of potassium IV. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate enhances total body potassium elimination Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. III and IV

Hyperkalemia is a potentially life-threatening electrolyte emergency because it can cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias. Management involves three key principles:

1. Stabilize the cardiac membrane
2. Shift potassium into cells
3. Remove potassium from the body

Why is D correct?

• I. Intravenous calcium (gluconate or chloride) is given to enhance cellular uptake of potassium. ✘

• Incorrect.
• IV calcium does not lower serum potassium.
• It stabilizes the myocardial cell membrane, reducing the risk of life-threatening arrhythmias.

• II. Beta-adrenergic agonists (salbutamol or terbutaline) are used to stabilize myocardial cell membrane. ✘

• Incorrect.
• β₂-agonists shift potassium into cells by stimulating the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump.
• They do not stabilize the cardiac membrane.

• III. Regular insulin and glucose given intravenously enhance cellular uptake of potassium. ✔

• Correct.
• Insulin activates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, driving potassium into cells.
• Glucose is administered to prevent hypoglycemia.

• IV. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate enhances total body potassium elimination. ✔

• Correct.
• It is a cation-exchange resin that binds potassium in the intestine and increases fecal potassium excretion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: 21-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to diffuse muscle aches and weakness. He has also noticed darkening of his urine. he patient recently joined the military and was participating in rigorous training exercises in hot weather earlier in the day. Laboratory results are as follows: Sodium: 136 mEq/L Potassium: 5.6 mEq/L Bicarbonate: 18 mEq/L Creatinine: 2.0 mg/dL CK: 22,000 U/L (normal: 30-170) Which of the following urine microscopy is most likely present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Granular casts

Severe muscle injury with markedly elevated CK and dark urine after strenuous exercise indicates rhabdomyolysis. Myoglobin released from muscle causes acute tubular necrosis (ATN) and acute kidney injury.

Urine microscopy in ATN shows muddy brown granular casts formed from necrotic tubular epithelial cells and protein debris. Thus, rhabdomyolysis-associated AKI is characterized by granular casts on urine microscopy.

Why not other options:

A. Dysmorphic RBCs: Glomerulonephritis.

B. Eosinophils: Acute interstitial nephritis.

D. Waxy casts: Chronic kidney disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: 38-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to vomiting blood. After appropriate resuscitation measures, he undergoes upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, which reveals a bleeding duodenal ulcer. During hospital day 2, the patient develops decreased urine output. Serum creatinine rises to 3.0 mg/dL from a baseline of 1.2 mg/dL. Renal biopsy shows patchy epithelial necrosis of the tubules, intratubular casts. Supportive care is provided. Several days later, his urine output significantly increases, and serum creatinine levels decline. Over the next few days, this patient is at highest risk for which of the following complications?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypokalemia

This patient developed acute tubular necrosis (ATN) due to hypovolemia from GI bleeding.

ATN progresses through phases:

1.      Initiation phase – rise in creatinine

2.      Maintenance (oliguric) phase – low urine output

3.      Recovery (polyuric) phase – ↑ urine output due to tubular dysfunction

During the polyuric recovery phase, impaired tubular reabsorption leads to excessive loss of electrolytes, especially potassium, placing the patient at risk for hypokalemia (and dehydration). Thus, the major complication during recovery from ATN is hypokalemia.

Electrolyte Changes – Oliguric vs Diuretic Phase

| Parameter | Oliguric Phase | Diuretic Phase

| --------- | -------------- | --------------

| Urine output | ↓ (<400 mL/day) | ↑↑ (3–5 L/day)

| Potassium | ↑ Hyperkalemia | ↓ Hypokalemia ⭐

| Sodium | ↑ Hypernatremia/normal | ↓ Hyponatremia

| Phosphate | ↑ Hyperphosphatemia | ↓ Hypophosphatemia

| Creatinine | ↑↑ Rising | ↓ Slowly falling

| BUN | ↑↑ | ↓ Slowly falling

| Volume status | Overloaded | Depleted (if losses not replaced)

| pH | Metabolic acidosis | Improving/normal

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presented with follicular tonsillitis, for which antibiotics were prescribed. In a few days, the child developed flank pain and rash. Peripheral blood demonstrated eosinophilia, and urinalysis showed WBC casts. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Allergic Interstitial Nephritis

Recent antibiotic exposure followed by flank pain, rash, and eosinophilia is classic for drug-induced allergic interstitial nephritis.

Urinalysis showing WBC casts reflects interstitial inflammation rather than glomerular disease.

Drug exposure (e.g., antibiotics)

↓

Type IV hypersensitivity reaction

↓

Interstitial inflammation + edema

↓

Eosinophil infiltration

↓

Tubular injury

↓

WBC casts in urine

↓

Acute Interstitial Nephritis

Pyelonephritis causes neutrophilia and fever, Berger disease presents with hematuria, and uncomplicated UTI lacks eosinophilia and casts.

| Option | Key Features | Why Right/Wrong

| ------ | ------------ | ---------------

| A) AIN | Drug + rash + eosinophilia + WBC casts | ✅ Classic

| B) Pyelonephritis | Fever, bacteria, neutrophils | ❌ No eosinophilia

| C) Berger disease (IgA) | Hematuria post-URI | ❌ No rash/eosinophilia

| D) UTI | Dysuria, bacteria | ❌ No systemic hypersensitivity

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old male with a history of hypertension and diabetes, recently diagnosed with end-stage renal disease (stage 5) and on hemodialysis, seeks dietary advice. Which of the following characterizes the ideal feed for him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Low volume, high calories

•

In patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on hemodialysis, the ideal diet is low volume and high calorie.

•

Fluid intake must be restricted to prevent volume overload, hypertension, and pulmonary edema, while adequate calories are required to prevent protein-energy malnutrition and maintain nutritional status.

•

Thus, feeds should be calorie-dense with restricted fluid volume and controlled sodium, potassium, and phosphorus intake.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old man is hospitalized for acute chest pain and undergoes PCI. His serum creatinine is unchanged 3 days post-procedure, but from day 4 slowly rises to a peak of 2.4 mg/dL. Urinalysis demonstrates no proteinuria or red blood cells, and a few granular casts are present. Serum complement is low. Blood counts show eosinophilia. Which one of the following is likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Atheroembolic disease

Subacute rise in creatinine several days after PCI, with minimal urinary findings (few granular casts), low complement levels, and peripheral eosinophilia is characteristic of atheroembolic renal disease due to cholesterol crystal embolization from disrupted atherosclerotic plaques during vascular procedures. It typically presents with delayed AKI (days to weeks), systemic inflammatory features, and complement consumption.

Why not other options:

A. Allergic interstitial nephritis: Drug-induced; shows fever, rash, eosinophiluria, WBC casts — complements usually normal.

B. Contrast-induced nephropathy: Occurs within 24–72 hrs after contrast, no eosinophilia or low complement.

D. RPGN: Has hematuria, proteinuria, RBC casts and rapid severe renal failure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 74-year-old man with congestive heart failure (CHF) on intravenous furosemide develops acute kidney injury (AKI) with serum creatinine rising from 1.0 to 2.1 mg/dL. Laboratory findings show: Urine Na⁺: 45 mEq/L Urine creatinine: 55 mg/dL Which of the following tests best distinguishes prerenal azotemia from acute tubular necrosis (ATN) in the setting of diuretic use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fractional excretion of urea (FeUrea)

In patients receiving loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide), the fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) becomes unreliable because diuretics increase urinary sodium excretion.

In this setting, fractional excretion of urea (FeUrea) is preferred to distinguish:

• Prerenal azotemia → FeUrea < 35%
• Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) → FeUrea > 50%

Urea reabsorption occurs mainly in the proximal tubule and is less affected by diuretics, making FeUrea the best test to differentiate prerenal AKI from ATN when diuretics are used.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with CKD with refractory hypertension is brought to the casualty with dizziness. His BP was found to be 200/120 mmHg. His BUN was 50 mg/dl and creatinine was 3 mg/dl. Potassium was 6 mEq/L. Which of the following is an indication of emergency hemodialysis?
options: Severe acidosis with elevated BUN and creatinine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Severe acidosis with elevated BUN and creatinine

Emergency Hemodialysis-

| Letter | Indication | Explanation

| ------ | ---------- | -----------

| A | Acidosis | Severe metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.1) not responding to treatment

| E | Electrolytes | Severe hyperkalemia (usually >6.5 mEq/L or with ECG changes)

| I | Intoxication | Dialyzable toxins (methanol, lithium, etc.)

| O | Overload | Fluid overload refractory to diuretics

| U | Uremia | Symptoms like encephalopathy, pericarditis

Emergency hemodialysis is indicated in CKD patients with severe metabolic acidosis associated with azotemia, reflecting life-threatening internal milieu disturbance.

Hypertension alone is managed medically, and K⁺ = 6 mEq/L without ECG changes is not an absolute indication.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with long-standing chronic kidney disease develops secondary hyperparathyroidism. The major stimulus for increased parathyroid hormone secretion is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decreased calcitriol production

• In Chronic kidney disease:

• Kidney cannot convert vitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol).
• This decreases intestinal calcium absorption.
• Result: Hypocalcemia → stimulation of Parathyroid hormone secretion.
• Also phosphate retention contributes, but loss of calcitriol is the primary mechanism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: According to KDIGO staging of chronic kidney disease (CKD), what is the GFR range for stage 3b?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 30–44 mL/min/1.73m²

KDIGO classifies CKD stage 3b as an eGFR of 30–44 mL/min/1.73 m².

Stage 3 is subdivided into 3a (45–59) and 3b (30–44) due to differing risks of progression and complications.

Higher values represent earlier stages, while 15–30 corresponds to stage 4.

GFR ranges for CKD staging:

• Stage 1: >90 mL/min/1.73m²
• Stage 2: 60–89 mL/min/1.73m²
• Stage 3a: 45–59 mL/min/1.73m²
• Stage 3b: 30–44 mL/min/1.73m²
• Stage 4: 15–29 mL/min/1.73m²
• Stage 5: <15 mL/min/1.73m²

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: According to the KDIGO criteria, acute kidney injury (AKI) can be diagnosed based on urine output when it is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. < 0.5 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours

KDIGO AKI definition includes:

• ↑ Serum creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dL in 48 hours, or
• ↑ Serum creatinine ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or
• Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours

KDIGO Staging of AKI

Stage 1

• Creatinine: 1.5–1.9 × baseline OR ↑ ≥0.3 mg/dL
• Urine output: <0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6–12 hrs

Stage 2

• Creatinine: 2.0–2.9 × baseline
• Urine output: <0.5 mL/kg/hr ≥12 hrs

Stage 3

• Creatinine: ≥3 × baseline OR ≥4 mg/dL OR dialysis initiation
• Urine output: <0.3 mL/kg/hr ≥24 hrs OR anuria ≥12 hrs

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All of the following are indications for initiating dialysis in a patient with renal failure, except:
options: Severe metabolic acidosis not responding to medical therapy
Asymptomatic elevation of serum creatinine to 5 mg/dL
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Asymptomatic elevation of serum creatinine to 5 mg/dL

Indications for dialysis are based on clinical complications, not serum creatinine level alone.

Classic indications can be remembered by AEIOU:

• Acidosis: severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.1–7.2) refractory to therapy
• Electrolyte imbalance: refractory hyperkalemia (>6.5 mEq/L)
• Intoxication: certain drug/toxin overdoses
• Overload: pulmonary edema unresponsive to diuretics
• Uremic symptoms: encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding

An asymptomatic rise in creatinine alone is not an indication for dialysis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Calcium resonium, which is used to treat hyperkalaemia over a short-term in chronic kidney disease, is associated with the development of which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bowel necrosis

• Calcium resonium (calcium polystyrene sulfonate) is a cation-exchange resin used to treat hyperkalemia by exchanging calcium for potassium in the gastrointestinal tract, thereby increasing fecal potassium excretion.
• A rare but serious complication is intestinal injury, including bowel necrosis, particularly when used with sorbitol. It can also cause constipation and gastrointestinal obstruction.

Why not the other options?

• A. Prostatomegaly: Not associated with calcium resonium.
• B. Myocarditis: Not a recognized adverse effect.
• C. Renal artery stenosis: Not associated with potassium-binding resins.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Dialysis will be effective for which of the following? 1. Seizures 2. Metabolic acidosis 3. Peripheral neuropathy 4. Uremic pericarditis 5. Hyperkalemia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 4, 5

Dialysis is effective in treating acute, life-threatening complications of uremia, including:

• Seizures (uremic encephalopathy)
• Severe metabolic acidosis
• Uremic pericarditis
• Refractory hyperkalemia

However, peripheral neuropathy is a chronic complication of uremia and does not improve immediately with dialysis.

Thus, dialysis is effective for 1, 2, 4, and 5, but not for chronic uremic neuropathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In an experimental model of acute kidney injury, renal perfusion is transiently reduced, leading to sublethal ischemic injury of tubular epithelial cells. Renal function is later restored after reperfusion. Which of the following is the earliest cellular change that occurs in renal tubular epithelial cells during the ischemic phase?
options: Activation of apoptotic pathways with caspase activation
Disruption of the tubular basement membrane
Loss of epithelial cell polarity with redistribution of membrane proteins
Necrosis and sloughing of tubular epithelial cells into the lumen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Loss of epithelial cell polarity with redistribution of membrane proteins

In ischemic acute tubular injury, the earliest cellular event is loss of epithelial cell polarity, characterized by redistribution of membrane proteins such as Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase from the basolateral to the apical surface. This disrupts vectorial transport of sodium, leading to impaired tubular reabsorption and early functional decline, even before structural damage occurs. Importantly, this stage represents reversible injury, and timely reperfusion can restore normal function.

As ischemia persists, injury progresses in a predictable sequence: cytoskeletal disruption → apoptosis → necrosis and sloughing of epithelial cells → tubular obstruction and back-leak → basement membrane damage (late and severe).

Why not other options?

A. Activation of cytoplasmic caspases (Apoptosis) → Occurs after initial reversible injury; represents progression to programmed cell death, not the earliest event

B. Damage to tubular basement membrane → Late finding, seen in severe or prolonged ischemia; associated with poor recovery

D. Necrosis and sloughing of epithelial cells → Occurs after loss of polarity and cytoskeletal damage; leads to tubular obstruction and is not an early change

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In multiple myeloma, monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains combine with Tamm–Horsfall protein precipitate in the renal tubules which leads to the development of which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cast nephropathy

In multiple myeloma, excessive production of monoclonal free immunoglobulin light chains (Bence Jones proteins) leads to their filtration through the glomerulus. In the distal nephron, these light chains bind to Tamm–Horsfall protein (uromodulin) and form obstructing light-chain casts. This causes tubular obstruction and direct tubular injury, producing myeloma cast nephropathy, also called myeloma kidney.

Why not the other options?

• A. IgA nephropathy: Caused by deposition of IgA-containing immune complexes in the mesangium; not due to light-chain/Tamm–Horsfall protein casts.
• C. Membranous glomerulonephritis: Characterized by subepithelial immune-complex deposition and diffuse glomerular basement membrane thickening.
• D. Interstitial nephritis: Usually caused by drugs, infections, or systemic diseases and produces interstitial inflammatory infiltrates, rather than light-chain casts.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Kidney damage and Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) value between 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m² are found in which stage of Chronic Kidney Disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stage 4 (severe)

Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is defined as kidney damage and/or a decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m²) persisting for ≥3 months. CKD is classified into five stages based on the estimated GFR (eGFR) according to the KDIGO guidelines.

A patient with an eGFR of 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m² has Stage 4 CKD (Severe reduction in GFR).

Why not the other options?

• A. Stage 2 (Mild): GFR 60–89 mL/min/1.73 m² with evidence of kidney damage.
• B. Stage 3A (Mild to moderate): GFR 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m².
• D. Stage 5 (Kidney failure): GFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² or dialysis-dependent.

| Stage | eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²) | Description

| ----- | --------------------- | -----------

| G1 | ≥90 | Normal/high GFR (with evidence of kidney damage)

| G2 | 60–89 | Mild decrease

| G3a | 45–59 | Mild to moderate decrease

| G3b | 30–44 | Moderate to severe decrease

| G4 ⭐ | 15–29 | Severe decrease in GFR

| G5 | <15 | Kidney failure (ESKD)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Peritoneal dialysis is associated with all of the following complications except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Weight loss

Peritoneal dialysis (PD) complications include:

• Peritonitis → most common and serious complication
• Poor filtration / inadequate clearance → especially in large or long-term patients
• Hyperglycemia → due to absorption of glucose-containing dialysate
• Weight loss is NOT typical

PD commonly causes weight gain, not loss, due to:

• Glucose absorption
• Increased caloric load
• Fluid retention

| Feature | PD | HD

| ------- | --- | ---

| Access | Peritoneal catheter | AV fistula/graft

| Frequency | Daily (continuous) | 3×/week

| Hemodynamic stability | ✅ Better | ❌ More fluctuation

| Residual renal function | ✅ Better preserved | ❌ Faster loss

| Peritonitis risk | ✅ Higher | Lower

| Weight change | ↑ Weight GAIN | Variable

| Protein loss | ✅ Higher | Lower

| Preferred in | Diabetics, children, remote areas | High-clearance needs

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate and patiromer are commonly prescribed to chronic kidney disease patients because of their property of binding to which one of the following electrolytes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Potassium

Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) and patiromer are potassium-binding resins used to treat hyperkalemia, which is particularly common in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD).

• Patiromer exchanges calcium for potassium in the gastrointestinal tract → binds K⁺ → increases fecal potassium excretion.
• Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate selectively traps potassium ions in the gastrointestinal tract in exchange for sodium and hydrogen ions → increases fecal K⁺ elimination.

Both therefore lower serum potassium without directly increasing urinary potassium excretion.

Why not the other options?

• A. Calcium: Patiromer uses calcium as an exchange ion but does not primarily bind calcium therapeutically.
• B. Sodium: SZC exchanges sodium/H⁺ for potassium; sodium is not the target electrolyte.
• D. Phosphate: These are not phosphate binders. Drugs such as sevelamer, calcium acetate, and lanthanum are used for hyperphosphatemia in CKD.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is a patient's urine analysis most likely to show if they have hematuria and hypercalciuria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Isomorphic RBCs

Hematuria with hypercalciuria typically suggests a non-glomerular (urologic) source, such as nephrolithiasis or tubular irritation from calcium crystals. In non-glomerular hematuria, urine microscopy shows isomorphic (normal-shaped) RBCs because the bleeding occurs distal to the glomerulus, so RBCs are not distorted during passage.

In contrast:

• RBC casts indicate glomerular bleeding
• Nephrotic-range proteinuria suggests nephrotic syndrome
• Eosinophiluria suggests acute interstitial nephritis

Thus, hypercalciuria-associated hematuria shows isomorphic RBCs.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is the most appropriate indication for erythropoietin therapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anemia with kidney disease

Erythropoietin (EPO)

• Hormone produced by peritubular interstitial cells in the kidney
• Stimulates erythropoiesis in bone marrow

Anemia in chronic kidney disease is due to deficient erythropoietin production by damaged renal peritubular cells.

Exogenous erythropoietin therapy directly corrects the underlying cause, improving hemoglobin levels.

| Condition | Problem | EPO Role | Verdict

| --------- | ------- | -------- | -------

| Aplastic anemia | Marrow failure | Ineffective | ❌

| Nutritional anemia | Deficiency | Ineffective | ❌

| CKD anemia | ↓ EPO | Highly effective | ✅

| MDS | Marrow dysplasia | Limited | ❌

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following findings in a patient are suggestive of acute nephritis? I. Hematuria II. Oliguria III. Reduced size of both kidneys IV. Edema Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, II and IV

Acute nephritic syndrome is a clinical syndrome caused by acute glomerular inflammation, resulting in reduced glomerular filtration and leakage of red blood cells into the urine. The classical features include:

• Hematuria (often cola- or smoky-colored urine)
• Oliguria
• Edema (especially periorbital edema)
• Hypertension
• Mild to moderate proteinuria
• Azotemia

The patient has the classic features of acute nephritis:

• I. Hematuria: Hallmark feature due to glomerular inflammation causing RBC leakage.
• II. Oliguria: Occurs due to decreased GFR from inflamed glomeruli.
• IV. Edema: Results from sodium and water retention secondary to reduced GFR.

Why is III incorrect?

• III. Reduced size of both kidneys: This is a feature of chronic kidney disease (CKD) due to longstanding nephron loss and fibrosis.
• In acute nephritis, kidneys are usually normal-sized or mildly enlarged because of acute inflammation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct range of Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) for Stage 2 chronic kidney disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 60–89 mL/min/1.73 m²

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is classified according to the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and the degree of albuminuria (KDIGO classification). Stage G2 CKD is defined by an eGFR of 60–89 mL/min/1.73 m², provided there is evidence of kidney damage (e.g., albuminuria, hematuria of renal origin, structural abnormalities, or abnormal renal biopsy). An eGFR of 60–89 mL/min/1.73 m² alone does not diagnose CKD.

KDIGO GFR Classification

| CKD Stage | eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²)

| --------- | ---------------------

| G1 | ≥90 (with evidence of kidney damage)

| G2 | 60–89 (with evidence of kidney damage)

| G3a | 45–59

| G3b | 30–44

| G4 | 15–29

| G5 | <15 (Kidney failure)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following medications is incorrect about microalbuminuria?
options: Urine protein levels range from 30 mg/d to 300 mg/d
It is an independent risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity in diabetic patients
It is the earliest marker of diabetic nephropathy
It is detected by routine dipstick method
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It is detected by routine dipstick method

Microalbuminuria (30–300 mg/day) is the earliest marker of diabetic nephropathy and an independent risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.

It cannot be detected by routine urine dipstick testing because dipsticks detect only overt proteinuria (>300 mg/day).

Detection requires special tests such as urine albumin–creatinine ratio (ACR).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following drugs is associated with calciphylaxis in chronic kidney disease patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Warfarin

Calciphylaxis (calcific uremic arteriolopathy) is a rare but life-threatening complication seen mainly in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD). It is characterized by calcification of small and medium-sized arterioles, leading to painful skin necrosis. Warfarin is a well-recognized risk factor because it inhibits vitamin K-dependent matrix Gla protein, a natural inhibitor of vascular calcification.

Why not the other options?

• A. Calcium channel blocker: Not associated with calciphylaxis.
• C. Non-calcium-based phosphate binder: These (e.g., sevelamer, lanthanum) reduce phosphate burden and may help lower the risk of vascular calcification.
• D. Thiazide diuretic: Not a recognized cause of calciphylaxis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following stages of chronic kidney disease corresponds to a glomerular filtration rate of 55 mL/min/1.73 m²?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3A

An eGFR of 55 mL/min/1.73 m² falls within CKD G3a, which is defined as an eGFR of 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m².

| Stage | eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²)

| ----- | ---------------------

| G1 | ≥90

| G2 | 60–89

| G3a | 45–59

| G3b | 30–44

| G4 | 15–29

| G5 | <15

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 45-year-old man with a 2-year history of prediabetes presents for routine evaluation. He has gained weight over the past year and has a strong family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. His BMI is 32 kg/m², and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Laboratory evaluation shows fasting plasma glucose of 157 mg/dL and HbA1c of 7.4%. Serum creatinine is normal, and urine testing shows no detectable albuminuria. Which of the following renal changes is most likely present at this stage of disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased glomerular filtration rate

The earliest functional change in diabetic nephropathy is glomerular hyperfiltration, characterized by an increased GFR despite normal serum creatinine and absence of albuminuria. This occurs due to afferent arteriolar dilation mediated by altered tubuloglomerular feedback: increased proximal glucose and sodium reabsorption reduces sodium delivery to the macula densa, leading to decreased afferent arteriolar resistance and increased intraglomerular capillary pressure.

This phase precedes structural damage and is potentially reversible. Persistent hyperfiltration, however, leads to glomerular injury, basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, and eventual microalbuminuria, marking progression of disease.

Why not other options?

A. Decreased intraglomerular capillary pressure → Incorrect; early diabetic nephropathy involves increased, not decreased pressure

B. Decreased peritubular capillary oncotic pressure → Not a defining feature of early diabetic kidney disease

C. Glomerular atrophy → Occurs in late-stage CKD, not early disease

D. Increased oncotic pressure in Bowman space → Seen when significant protein leaks into filtrate (i.e., later stages with proteinuria)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 54-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to several hours of severe epigastric abdominal pain radiating to her back. She has also had nausea and several episodes of vomiting. The patient has a history of occasional upper abdominal pain after eating but has never had such severe symptoms. She has no other medical issues and takes no medications. Temperature is 37.6⁰C (99.6⁰F), blood pressure is 110/66 mm Hg, pulse is 118/min, and respirations are 24/min. The patient appears to be in moderate distress. Mucous membranes are dry. The abdomen is distended with marked epigastric tenderness. Bowel sounds are decreased. Laboratory results are as follows: Hematocrit: 48% Leukocytes: 18,800/mm³ Total bilirubin: 2.2 mg/dL Alkaline phosphatase: 370 U/L Lipase: 2,192 U/L Which of the following sets of renal findings are most expected in this patient?
options: Renin secretion high, Efferent arteriolar resistance high, Tubular sodium resporption high
Renin secretion high, Efferent arteriolar resistance low, Tubular sodium resporption high
Renin secretion low, Efferent arteriolar resistance low, Tubular sodium resporption low
Renin secretion low, Efferent arteriolar resistance high, Tubular sodium resporption low
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Renin secretion high, Efferent arteriolar resistance high, Tubular sodium resporption high

Acute pancreatitis with vomiting and third-spacing leads to hypovolemia and decreased renal perfusion, causing prerenal azotemia.

Prerenal state activates RAAS, resulting in:

• ↑ Renin secretion
• ↑ Angiotensin II → ↑ efferent arteriolar resistance (to maintain GFR)
• ↑ Aldosterone → ↑ tubular sodium and water reabsorption

Thus, expected renal findings are high renin, high efferent arteriolar resistance, and high tubular sodium reabsorption.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 71-year-old man has had decreased urine output <500 mL per day for the past 3 days. Physical examination shows vital signs with temperature 37°C, pulse 88/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and blood pressure 85/60 mmHg. Urinalysis shows specific gravity 1.019 and no protein, blood, glucose, ketones, WBCs, RBCs, or casts. His serum creatinine is 3 mg/dL, and urea nitrogen is 62 mg/dL. The fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) is <1%. Which of the following underlying conditions is he most likely to have?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Congestive heart failure

Low urine output with hypotension, bland urine sediment, high BUN:creatinine ratio, and FENa <1% indicates prerenal acute kidney injury due to decreased renal perfusion. In an elderly patient, this is most commonly from reduced effective circulating volume, as seen in congestive heart failure.

B. Membranous nephropathy – Causes proteinuria; urine here is bland.

C. Contrast-induced nephropathy – Causes intrinsic AKI with FENa >1–2%.

D. Urothelial carcinoma – Causes hematuria/obstruction, not prerenal AKI pattern.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 22-year-old HIV/AIDS positive male has been on long term Amphotericin B therapy for mucormycosis. Laboratory studies reveal hypokalemia, and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Which of the following structure/function combinations is most likely defective in this patient?
options: Distal convoluted tubule - Secretion of hydrogen ions
Distal convoluted tubule - Reabsorption of bicarbonate
Collecting duct - Secretion of hydrogen ions
Proximal convoluted tubule - Reabsorption of bicarbonate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Collecting duct - Secretion of hydrogen ions

Amphotericin B can cause type 1 (distal) renal tubular acidosis by damaging the alpha-intercalated cells of the collecting duct, leading to impaired H⁺ secretion.

This results in:

• Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
• Hypokalemia
• Inability to acidify urine

Thus, the primary defect is in the collecting duct – impaired hydrogen ion secretion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 25 year old patient of bipolar disorder on lithium therapy presented with polydipsia and polyuria. Investigations revealed increased low urinary osmolality. Which of the following channels are involved here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. AQP-2

Lithium therapy can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by impairing ADH action in the collecting duct. Lithium reduces insertion and expression of Aquaporin-2 (AQP-2) channels on the luminal membrane of principal cells, leading to decreased water reabsorption.

This results in polyuria, polydipsia, and low urine osmolality due to inability to concentrate urine.

Why not other options:

A. AQP-1: PCT water channel, not ADH-dependent.

C. AQP-3 & D. AQP-4: Basolateral channels.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with hemoptysis and rapidly progressive renal failure. Kidney biopsy shows crescentic glomerulonephritis, and immunofluorescence demonstrates linear IgG deposition along the GBM. Which antigen is targeted by the autoantibodies in this disease?
options: α4 chain of type IV collagen
α3 chain of type IV collagen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. α3 chain of type IV collagen

Goodpasture syndrome is an autoimmune disease characterized by:

• Antibodies against α3 chain of type IV collagen in GBM and lung basement membrane
• Leads to rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage (hemoptysis)
• Immunofluorescence shows linear IgG deposition along GBM
• Classified as type II hypersensitivity reaction

Image is showing linear immuno-fluorescence

Why not other options:

A) α4 chain of type IV collagen:

• Not the antigen involved in anti-GBM disease
• Goodpasture specifically targets the α3 chain

C) Laminin in basement membrane:

• Structural component of basement membrane but not the target of antibodies in this condition
• Not associated with linear IgG deposition pattern

D) Fibronectin in mesangium:

• Located in mesangial matrix, not GBM
• Not implicated in anti-GBM disease

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with progressive muscle weakness and recurrent headaches for the past 2 months. He has no history of palpitations, tremors, or excessive sweating. On examination, his blood pressure is 190/120 mm Hg and pulse rate is 68/min. Laboratory investigations reveal a serum potassium level of 2.8 mEq/L. Plasma renin activity is elevated, and serum aldosterone levels are also increased. A 24-hour urine collection shows increased potassium excretion. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renin-secreting juxtaglomerular cell tumor

This patient has secondary hyperaldosteronism:

• Severe hypertension
• Hypokalemia
• ↑ Renin + ↑ Aldosterone
• ↑ Urinary potassium loss

Pathophysiology:

• Juxtaglomerular (JG) cell tumor → excess renin secretion
• Activates RAAS → ↑ Angiotensin II → ↑ Aldosterone
• Leads to:

• Sodium retention → hypertension
• Potassium loss → hypokalemia

Why not other options?

A. Adrenal cortical adenoma (Conn syndrome) → ↑ Aldosterone, ↓ Renin (primary hyperaldosteronism)

B. Pheochromocytoma → Episodic hypertension + palpitations, sweating

D. Pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) → Hypercortisolism features, not isolated RAAS activation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old man is stranded without water for 36 hours. His urine osmolality is 1100 mOsm/L. Vasopressin plays a major role in concentrating urine. Which part of the nephron responds to vasopressin by absorbing solutes crucial for medullary hypertonicity?
options: Thin ascending limb of loop of Henle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Medullary collecting duct

Vasopressin (ADH) concentrates urine not only by increasing water permeability in the collecting ducts but also by enhancing urea reabsorption in the inner medullary collecting duct (IMCD). Reabsorbed urea accumulates in the renal medulla, contributing significantly to medullary hypertonicity, which is essential for producing maximally concentrated urine during dehydration.

• During water deprivation, ADH levels rise markedly.
• ADH increases the expression of urea transporters (UT-A1 and UT-A3) in the medullary collecting duct.
• Urea is reabsorbed into the medullary interstitium, strengthening the corticomedullary osmotic gradient.
• This hyperosmotic medulla promotes water reabsorption and allows urine osmolality to reach 1000–1200 mOsm/kg.

Why not the others?

• A. Thin ascending limb → Involved in passive NaCl handling but not the principal ADH-responsive site for urea reabsorption.
• B. Cortical collecting duct → ADH increases water permeability here, but it does not significantly contribute to medullary hypertonicity via urea transport.
• C. Proximal tubule → Reabsorbs water and solutes isosmotically; largely independent of ADH.
• E. Early distal tubule → Diluting segment; relatively impermeable to water and not involved in ADH-mediated urea recycling.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 37-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to worsening leg swelling for the past 2 months. She has also felt excessively tired and has had achy pain in her hands. Serum creatinine level is 1.8 mg/dL. Urinalysis is positive for proteinuria and hematuria. Light microscopy of samples from a kidney biopsy shows diffuse, global endocapillary hypercellularity. Direct immunofluorescence demonstrates staining with diffuse, global, granular staining of glomerular capillary walls by IgG, IgM, IgA, C1q, and C3. Electron microscopy will demonstrate which of the following changes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Subendothelial deposits

Diffuse endocapillary hypercellularity with “full house” immunofluorescence (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q) is characteristic of lupus nephritis, especially class III/IV.

In proliferative lupus nephritis, immune complexes deposit mainly in the subendothelial region, producing a “wire-loop” appearance on light microscopy and causing hematuria and proteinuria. Thus, subendothelial immune complex deposits are the key electron microscopy finding.

Why not other options:

B. Mesangial deposits: Seen in IgA nephropathy or class II lupus, not diffuse proliferative lupus.

C. Subepithelial deposits: Seen in membranous nephropathy (“spike and dome”).

D. Intramembranous deposits: Seen in dense deposit disease/MPGN type II.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 44-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of lower extremity swelling and frothy urine. He has a history of chronic hepatitis C infection. Physical examination shows 3+ pitting edema of the lower legs and ankles. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased lipoproteins

Chronic hepatitis C can cause membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, leading to nephrotic syndrome (edema, proteinuria, frothy urine). Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by:

• Heavy proteinuria
• Hypoalbuminemia
• Edema
• Hyperlipidemia with increased lipoproteins (compensatory hepatic synthesis)
• Lipiduria

There is also loss of antithrombin III and immunoglobulins in urine, causing hypercoagulability and increased infection risk.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 47-year-old male presents with 400 ml urine output in 24 hours. On biopsy he had crescents with pauci immune glomerulonephritis. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ANCA

Pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis is most commonly associated with ANCA-associated vasculitis (e.g., granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis). Biopsy shows crescents with minimal or no immune deposits on immunofluorescence (“pauci-immune”).

The next diagnostic step is testing for ANCA (c-ANCA/PR3 or p-ANCA/MPO) to confirm ANCA-associated vasculitis causing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

Why not other options:

A. Anti-GBM: Linear IgG deposits (Goodpasture), not pauci-immune.

C. Anti-PLA2R: Membranous nephropathy (nephrotic).

D. ANA: Lupus nephritis with immune deposits.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of gradually worsening facial and lower extremity swelling. She has had a 4-kg weight gain during this time. Her blood pressure is 150/88 mmHg. Examination shows periorbital edema and 2+ pretibial edema bilaterally. A 24-hour collection of urine shows 4.0 g of proteinuria. Microscopic examination of a kidney biopsy specimen shows thickening of the glomerular basement membrane. Electron microscopy shows dense subepithelial deposits. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anti-phospholipse A2 receptor antibodies

Nephrotic-range proteinuria (4 g/day), edema, and biopsy showing thickened glomerular basement membrane with subepithelial immune complex deposits are characteristic of membranous nephropathy.

Primary membranous nephropathy is strongly associated with anti–phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) antibodies, directed against podocyte antigens. Thus, detection of anti-PLA2R antibodies supports the diagnosis of primary membranous nephropathy.

Why not other options:

B. Anti-myeloperoxidase (MPO) antibodies: Seen in p-ANCA–associated vasculitis → pauci-immune crescentic GN, not membranous nephropathy.

C. Anti-streptolysin O (ASO) antibodies: Seen in post-streptococcal GN → subepithelial “hump” deposits with nephritic syndrome.

D. Anti-proteinase 3 (PR3) antibodies: Seen in c-ANCA vasculitis (GPA) → pauci-immune crescentic GN.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 52-year-old male with Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) was started on tolvaptan therapy. A few weeks later, he presents with symptoms of dry mouth and increased thirst. What is the likely mechanism behind these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased free water clearance

Tolvaptan is a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist used in ADPKD to slow cyst growth. Blocking V2 receptors in the collecting duct decreases aquaporin-2 insertion → reduces water reabsorption → increases free water clearance. This causes aquaresis (excretion of free water), leading to polyuria, thirst, and dry mouth.

Why not other options:

B. V2 receptor agonism: Tolvaptan is a V2 antagonist, not agonist.

C. Increased renal cAMP levels: Tolvaptan decreases cAMP, slowing cyst growth in ADPKD.

D. Increase in urine osmolality: Causes dilute urine → decreased urine osmolality.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 56-year-old man has resistant hypertension despite adherence to four antihypertensive drugs, including a diuretic and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. Secondary causes have been excluded. He is being evaluated for novel non-pharmacological interventional therapies which is?
options: Radiofrequency ablation of renal parasympathetic nerves
Endovascular radiofrequency ablation of renal sympathetic nerves
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Endovascular radiofrequency ablation of renal sympathetic nerves

•

Endovascular radiofrequency ablation of renal sympathetic nerves (renal denervation) is a novel interventional therapy for resistant hypertension.

•

It works by disrupting renal sympathetic nerve activity, which reduces renin release, decreases sodium retention, and lowers systemic vascular resistance, ultimately reducing blood pressure.

•

Renal sympathetic overactivity plays a key role in resistant hypertension; therefore, catheter-based renal denervation is considered in patients with persistent hypertension despite optimal multidrug therapy and exclusion of secondary causes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 56-year-old man with newly diagnosed essential hypertension is started on hydrochlorothiazide as first-line therapy. After 4–6 weeks, his blood pressure is well controlled, but he complains of difficulty in achieving and maintaining an erection, which was not present earlier. He has no history of diabetes or vascular disease. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his new symptom?
options: Decreased testosterone levels due to aldosterone antagonism
Reduced intravascular volume and altered vascular response caused by thiazide therapy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reduced intravascular volume and altered vascular response caused by thiazide therapy

• Thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide) can cause erectile dysfunction as a side effect due to reduced intravascular volume and decreased penile blood flow, leading to altered vascular response.
• They may also reduce zinc levels, indirectly affecting testosterone and sexual function.
• Thus, erectile dysfunction is a recognized adverse effect of thiazide therapy and may require dose adjustment or change of antihypertensive drug.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 6-year-old child with cystic fibrosis presents with recurrent pulmonary infections and thick, tenacious sputum. Genetic testing confirms a CFTR mutation. The pathophysiology involves increased sodium absorption across the airway epithelium, leading to dehydration of airway surface liquid. Which drug, when administered by inhalation, would most directly counteract this abnormal ion transport?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Amiloride

•

In cystic fibrosis, defective CFTR channels lead to increased epithelial sodium (Na⁺) absorption via ENaC and decreased chloride secretion, causing dehydration of airway surface liquid and thick mucus.

•

Inhaled amiloride, an epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) blocker, directly counteracts this abnormal ion transport by reducing sodium and water reabsorption from airway surfaces, thereby improving airway hydration and mucus clearance.

Why not others:

A. Acetazolamide: Acts in kidney (PCT); no airway ENaC effect.

B. Furosemide: Acts in loop of Henle; renal action only.

D. Spironolactone: Blocks aldosterone in kidney; not airway sodium channels.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with chronic congestive cardiac failure (CCF) presents with jugular venous distention, ascites, and bilateral pedal edema. Laboratory evaluation reveals elevated atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) levels. ANP promotes natriuresis by decreasing sodium reabsorption predominantly at which of the following nephron segments?
options: Thick ascending limb of loop of Henle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Medullary collecting duct

Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) promotes natriuresis primarily by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the medullary collecting duct.

Why Medullary Collecting Duct Specifically?

The medullary collecting duct (MCD) is the primary site of ANP action because:

| Feature | Detail

| ------- | ------

| Receptor density | Highest concentration of NPR-A receptors in the entire nephron

| Transport target | Inhibits ENaC (Epithelial Sodium Channels) on luminal side

| Net effect | ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption → Na⁺ stays in tubule → osmotic water retention in lumen → natriuresis + diuresis

| Aldosterone antagonism | ANP opposes aldosterone action at this same segment

ANP Actions Across the Nephron

| Site | Action | Significance

| ---- | ------ | ------------

| Medullary Collecting Duct ⭐ | ↓ ENaC → ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption | Primary natriuretic effect

| Glomerulus | ↑ GFR (dilates afferent, constricts efferent arteriole) | ↑ filtered Na⁺ load

| Proximal tubule | Mild ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption | Minor contribution

| Inner medullary CD | ↓ Urea transporters | Reduces medullary tonicity → impairs concentrating ability

| Adrenal gland | ↓ Aldosterone secretion | Indirect natriuresis

| Vasculature | Vasodilation | ↓ BP, ↓ venous return

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with sudden-onset severe headache and progressive drowsiness for 1 hour. He has a history of long-standing hypertension. On examination, he responds only to painful stimuli and has left-sided weakness. The right pupil is dilated and sluggishly reactive to light. CT scan of the head reveals a right basal ganglia hemorrhage with midline shift. The patient is intubated, and intravenous mannitol is administered to reduce intracranial pressure. Which of the following acute renal effects is most likely to occur following administration of this medication?
options: Decreased serum sodium, increased tubular flow, increased tubular fluid osmolality
No change in serum sodium, decreased tubular flow, increased tubular fluid osmolality
Increased serum sodium, no change in tubular flow, increased tubular fluid osmolality
Decreased serum sodium, no change in tubular flow, decreased tubular fluid osmolality
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased serum sodium, increased tubular flow, increased tubular fluid osmolality

Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that is freely filtered at the glomerulus but not reabsorbed, leading to an increase in tubular fluid osmolality. This prevents water reabsorption in the proximal tubule and descending limb of the loop of Henle, resulting in osmotic diuresis with increased tubular flow.

In the acute setting, mannitol increases plasma osmolality, drawing water from intracellular to extracellular compartments, including from brain parenchyma—thereby reducing intracranial pressure. This initial water shift into the intravascular space causes dilutional hyponatremia, even before diuresis becomes prominent.

Thus, the key acute renal effects are:

• Increased tubular flow due to osmotic diuresis
• Increased tubular fluid osmolality
• Decreased serum sodium (dilutional hyponatremia initially)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with dehydration following acute gastroenteritis. Laboratory investigations reveal increased plasma osmolality. The body responds by activating mechanisms to restore osmotic balance. Which of the following has the most powerful and immediate effect in regulating plasma osmolality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Antidiuretic hormone

The osmoreceptor-ADH axis is the fastest-responding system because:

• Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus (OVLT/organum vasculosum) detect even tiny changes in plasma osmolality (as little as 1–2%) — far more sensitive than baroreceptors detecting volume changes (which typically need a 5–10% change to trigger a response)
• ADH release begins within minutes of an osmolality rise, and its effect on collecting duct aquaporin-2 insertion is rapid
• This makes ADH both the most sensitive (low threshold) and functionally fastest-acting hormonal regulator of osmolality specifically

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 68-year-old man undergoes evaluation of renal function using an exogenous filtration marker (inulin). Laboratory analysis of a timed urine collection shows the following: • Urine concentration (U): 15 mg/dL • Plasma concentration (P): 3 mg/dL • Urine flow rate (V): 16 mL/min What is the renal clearance of this substance, and what does it represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 80 mL/min; represents GFR

Renal clearance is calculated as:

Substituting values:

Since inulin is freely filtered at the glomerulus and neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the renal tubules, its clearance equals the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) — making it the gold-standard exogenous marker for GFR measurement.

High-yield pearl:

| Clearance vs GFR | Interpretation

| ---------------- | --------------

| Clearance = GFR | Marker is filtered only (e.g., inulin)

| Clearance < GFR | Marker is net reabsorbed

| Clearance > GFR | Marker is net secreted (e.g., PAH, used to estimate renal plasma flow)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 70-year-old man comes to the OPD due to increasing headaches, nausea, and vomiting. Medical history is significant for a transient ischemic attack that led to a right carotid endarterectomy 5 years ago. Blood pressure is 220/120 mm Hg and pulse is 70/min. Bilateral abdominal bruits are present. Blood testing in this patient would most likely show which of the following?
options: Low renin, low aldosterone, high angiotensin II, low potassium
High renin, high aldosterone, high angiotensin II, low potassium
Low renin, high aldosterone, high angiotensin II, low potassium
Low renin, low aldosterone, low angiotensin II, high potassium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High renin, high aldosterone, high angiotensin II, low potassium

Severe hypertension with bilateral abdominal bruits suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis, causing renovascular hypertension.

Renal hypoperfusion stimulates renin release, activating RAAS:

• ↑ Renin
• ↑ Angiotensin II
• ↑ Aldosterone → Na⁺ retention & K⁺ loss (hypokalemia)

Thus, renovascular hypertension is characterized by high renin, high angiotensin II, high aldosterone, and low potassium.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 70-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by staff of the group home where he resides because of worsening confusion for the past week. He has a history of major depressive disorder and had an ischemic stroke 4 months ago. Current medications are aspirin and sertraline. His pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 135/88 mmHg. Physical examination shows moist oral mucosa, normal skin turgor, and no peripheral edema. While in the waiting room, he has a generalized, tonic-clonic seizure. Laboratory studies show a serum sodium of 119 mEq/L and an elevated serum antidiuretic hormone concentration. Which of the following sets of additional laboratory is likely in the patient?
options: Serum osmolarity increased, Urine sodium increased, Serum aldosterone increased
Serum osmolarity decreased, Urine sodium increased, Serum aldosterone decreased
Serum osmolarity increased, Urine sodium decreased, Serum aldosterone increased
Serum osmolarity decreased, Urine sodium increased, Serum aldosterone increased
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serum osmolarity decreased, Urine sodium increased, Serum aldosterone decreased

This patient has SIADH (likely due to SSRI use or CNS disease), characterized by excess ADH causing water retention and dilutional hyponatremia.

Typical findings:

• ↓ Serum osmolality (dilutional)
• ↑ Urine sodium (euvolemic state with continued natriuresis)
• ↓ Aldosterone (suppressed due to mild volume expansion)
• Concentrated urine despite hyponatremia

Thus, SIADH presents with low serum osmolality, high urine sodium, and low aldosterone.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A decrease in GFR is associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decreased Bowman's oncotic pressure

Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) depends on Starling forces across the glomerular membrane.

Oncotic pressure in Bowman’s space normally opposes filtration (though usually negligible). A decrease in Bowman’s space oncotic pressure reduces the driving force for filtration when proteins are present in Bowman’s space and then fall, leading to reduced effective filtration pressure and decreased GFR.

Thus, changes in hydrostatic and oncotic pressures across the glomerulus directly influence GFR.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A newborn presents with proteinuria, low–molecular-weight proteins in urine, and vitamin D deficiency despite normal intake. Genetic analysis reveals a mutation in the LRP2 gene. Which of the following proteins is most likely dysfunctional in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Megalin

The LRP2 gene encodes megalin, a multiligand endocytic receptor located on the apical membrane of proximal convoluted tubule (PCT).

Megalin is responsible for reabsorption of:

• Low–molecular-weight proteins
• Vitamin D–binding protein (25-OH vitamin D complex)
• Other filtered proteins
• Retinol-binding protein

Mutation leads to impaired proximal tubular protein reabsorption → low–molecular-weight proteinuria and vitamin D deficiency despite adequate intake.

Why not other options:

A. Cubilin: Different gene (CUBN), not LRP2.

B. Aquaporin-2: Water channel defect → DI, not proteinuria.

D. Na⁺-K⁺-ATPase: General ion pump, not specific for protein reabsorption.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient on chronic furosemide therapy for heart failure develops volume depletion. Laboratory studies show elevated serum bicarbonate. What is the primary mechanism underlying this acid-base disturbance?
options: Direct inhibition of carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
Aldosterone-mediated H⁺ secretion in the distal nephron secondary to volume contraction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aldosterone-mediated H⁺ secretion in the distal nephron secondary to volume contraction

Furosemide-induced volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. The resulting aldosterone excess increases H⁺ secretion (in exchange for Na⁺/K⁺ reabsorption) at the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, generating "contraction metabolic alkalosis." Option A describes the mechanism of acetazolamide, which causes metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis; C and D are unrelated mechanisms not implicated in loop diuretic-induced alkalosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient presents to the OPD with complaints of breathlessness on lying down and chest pain. He was diagnosed to have congestive cardiac failure and was administered torsemide. This drug inhibits which of the following type of transport mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Secondary active Cotransport

Torsemide is a loop diuretic that inhibits the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

This transporter functions via secondary active cotransport, using the sodium gradient generated by Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase to reabsorb Na⁺, K⁺, and Cl⁻ together.

Inhibition leads to marked natriuresis and diuresis, reducing preload and relieving symptoms of congestive heart failure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with type 2 diabetes is started on an SGLT2 inhibitor, which blocks the sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT2) in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT). Following initiation of therapy, which of the following physiological changes is most likely to occur?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decreased renin secretion

SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) inhibit sodium and glucose reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule.

As a result:

• More NaCl reaches the macula densa
• The macula densa interprets this as increased tubular flow
• Tubuloglomerular feedback is activated
• Afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction occurs
• Renin release from juxtaglomerular cells decreases
• Intraglomerular pressure falls, contributing to the renoprotective effects of SGLT2 inhibitors

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Increased aldosterone secretion: Renin suppression leads to reduced RAAS activation, so aldosterone secretion tends to decrease rather than increase.
• B. Decreased vasopressin secretion: SGLT2 inhibition does not directly suppress ADH release.
• D. Decreased urinary sodium excretion: SGLT2 inhibitors produce natriuresis, resulting in increased, not decreased, sodium excretion.

High-yield pearl:

SGLT2 inhibitors:

• ↓ Proximal Na⁺ and glucose reabsorption
• ↑ NaCl delivery to the macula densa
• ↓ Renin secretion
• ↓ Intraglomerular pressure (via tubuloglomerular feedback)
• Renoprotective and cardioprotective effects in patients with diabetes and chronic kidney disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following conditions are known to be associated with chronic Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gianotti-Crosti syndrome

Chronic hepatitis C infection is associated with multiple immune-complex mediated extrahepatic manifestations, including:

• Mixed cryoglobulinemia
• Leukocytoclastic vasculitis
• Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)

These occur due to circulating immune complex deposition.

Gianotti–Crosti syndrome is classically associated with hepatitis B infection (and some viral infections in children like EBV), not chronic hepatitis C.

A self-limiting, childhood exanthem characterized by a symmetric papular or papulovesicular eruption on the face, buttocks, and extremities, typically following a viral infection. Also called: Papular Acrodermatitis of Childhood (PAC)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following statements regarding urea handling and function in the kidney are true, except:
options: Urea contributes significantly to the corticomedullary osmotic gradient
Urea permeability of the inner medullary collecting duct increases in the presence of ADH
Urea recycling helps in maximal concentration of urine
Urea is actively secreted in the proximal convoluted tubule
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urea is actively secreted in the proximal convoluted tubule

Urea plays a key role in urine concentration by contributing to the medullary osmotic gradient.

• It is passively reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.
• ADH increases urea permeability of the inner medullary collecting duct.
• Urea recycling between the collecting duct and loop of Henle helps maintain high medullary osmolality for maximal urine concentration.

Urea is not actively secreted in the proximal convoluted tubule; its movement is mainly passive.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Goldblatt hypertension is best explained by which of the following mechanisms?
options: Increased sodium retention due to primary hyperaldosteronism
Renal artery stenosis causing increased renin release and activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system
Decreased renal perfusion causing pressure natriuresis
Increased sympathetic discharge due to baroreceptor dysfunction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Renal artery stenosis causing increased renin release and activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system

• Goldblatt hypertension results from renal artery stenosis, which decreases renal perfusion pressure.
• This stimulates juxtaglomerular cells to release renin → activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) → causes vasoconstriction, sodium and water retention → systemic hypertension.
• Thus, Goldblatt hypertension is a classic model of secondary hypertension due to renovascular activation of RAAS.

questions.subject: Medicine
