questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Lorundrostat lowers blood pressure primarily by inhibiting which of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2)

• Lorundrostat is a selective aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) inhibitor that lowers blood pressure by reducing aldosterone production in the adrenal zona glomerulosa.
• Decreased aldosterone leads to reduced sodium and water reabsorption and increased potassium retention, thereby lowering intravascular volume and blood pressure.
• It represents a newer targeted therapy for resistant hypertension by directly blocking aldosterone synthesis rather than blocking its receptor or upstream RAAS components.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Renal physiologists are studying tubular fluid osmolality at different segments of the nephron in a healthy individual after 12 hours of water deprivation. A tubular fluid sample is found to have an osmolality of approximately 110 mOsm/kg. Which of the following nephron segments is the most likely site from which this sample was obtained?
options: Descending limb of loop of Henle
Collecting duct (in the presence of ADH)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Distal convoluted tubule

An osmolality of \~100–120 mOsm/kg represents maximally dilute tubular fluid.

This occurs because:

• The thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻
• It is impermeable to water → dilution begins here
• The early distal convoluted tubule continues salt reabsorption without water → most dilute segment

Segment-wise concept:

• PCT → isotonic (\~300 mOsm)
• Descending limb → hypertonic (water leaves)
• Ascending limb → dilution begins
• Early DCT → maximal dilution (\~100 mOsm)
• Collecting duct (with ADH) → concentrated urine

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Scientists studying the kidney's response to hypoperfusion apply a clip to a pig's right renal artery that reduces blood flow to the kidney by about 7 %. After 6 months, they perform a right nephrectomy and examine the glomeruli and tubules microscopically. Which of the following cell types would be most likely to undergo hyperplasia as a result of the clip placement?
options: Cuboidal epithelial cells of the proximal tubules
Endothelial cells of the efferent arteriole
Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole

Chronic renal hypoperfusion (as in renal artery stenosis/Goldblatt model) stimulates increased renin secretion.

Renin is produced by juxtaglomerular (JG) cells, which are modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole. Persistent decreased renal blood flow leads to hyperplasia and hypertrophy of JG cells due to sustained RAAS activation.

Thus, chronic hypoperfusion causes proliferation of modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: What differentiates the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) from the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)?
options: Presence of carbonic anhydrase in luminal membrane
Lack of Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase in the basolateral membrane
Possession of brush border on luminal membrane
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Presence of ‘tight’ tight junctions

The distal convoluted tubule (DCT) has tight tight junctions between epithelial cells, making it relatively impermeable to water and allowing fine regulation of electrolyte transport.

In contrast, the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) has leaky tight junctions and a prominent brush border for bulk reabsorption.

Thus, the presence of tight junctions is a key feature distinguishing the DCT from the PCT.

| Feature | PCT | DCT

| ------- | --- | ---

| Tight junction type | LEAKY
Brush border present | TIGHT

| Paracellular transport | Extensive | Minimal

| Ion/water permeability | High | Low

| Transepithelial gradient | Cannot maintain steep gradient | Can maintain steep gradient

| Fine-tuning ability | Poor | Excellent

| Functional significance | Bulk reabsorption | Precise regulation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: What is the effect of sympathetic nervous system stimulation on glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?
options: Increased GFR due to afferent arteriolar dilation
Increased GFR due to efferent arteriolar dilation
Decreased GFR due to afferent arteriolar constriction
Decreased GFR due to efferent arteriolar constriction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decreased GFR due to afferent arteriolar constriction

• Sympathetic stimulation (e.g., during hemorrhage, severe stress, or exercise) predominantly causes constriction of the afferent arteriole, which reduces glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure and consequently decreases GFR.
• At the same time, sympathetic activation also constricts the efferent arteriole to a degree, along with systemic vasoconstriction — but the net effect at high sympathetic tone is a reduction in renal blood flow and GFR, since afferent constriction dominates the response and reduces overall perfusion to the glomerulus.
• This is a protective mechanism to shunt blood away from the kidneys toward vital organs (heart, brain) during conditions like severe hypotension or shock.
• Options involving dilation (A, B) are incorrect, since sympathetic stimulation causes vasoconstriction, not dilation, in the renal vasculature.

| Substance | Primary Site | Effect on GFR

| --------- | ------------ | -------------

| Sympathetic stimulation (NE) | Afferent >> Efferent constriction | ↓ GFR

| Angiotensin II | Efferent constriction (predominant) | Maintains/↑ GFR (at low doses)

| Prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) | Afferent dilation | Maintains GFR (protective)

| ACE inhibitors/ARBs | Efferent dilation (block AT-II) | ↓ GFR (intended in proteinuric disease)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following are considered poor prognostic factors in PSGN? A. Younger age at presentation B. Nephrotic syndrome at presentation C. Presence of crescent formation on renal biopsy D. Early penicillin therapy for streptococcal infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. B,C

Poor prognostic factors in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) include features indicating severe glomerular injury.

These are:

• Nephrotic syndrome at presentation → suggests severe glomerular damage
• Crescent formation on renal biopsy → indicates rapidly progressive GN and worse renal outcome

Younger age generally has an excellent prognosis, and early penicillin therapy prevents spread of infection but does not worsen prognosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following changes are most likely to occur in this patient’s kidney function after starting therapy with NSAID?
options: Decreased renal perfusion, decreased intraglomerular pressure, and constant filtration fraction
Increased renal perfusion, decreased intraglomerular pressure, and decreased filtration fraction
Decreased renal perfusion, increased intraglomerular pressure, and decreased filtration fraction
Decreased renal perfusion, decreased intraglomerular pressure, and increased filtration fraction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased renal perfusion, decreased intraglomerular pressure, and constant filtration fraction

NSAIDs inhibit renal prostaglandin synthesis (PGE₂, PGI₂), which normally dilate the afferent arteriole.

Blocking prostaglandins causes afferent arteriolar constriction, leading to:

• ↓ Renal perfusion (RPF)
• ↓ Intraglomerular pressure
• ↓ GFR

Since both RPF and GFR fall proportionally, the filtration fraction remains relatively constant.

Thus, NSAIDs can precipitate AKI, especially in patients with CHF, CKD, or volume depletion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following channels is not typically present on the luminal membrane of principal cells of the glomerular/renal collecting system?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Na-K +ATPase

In principal cells of the collecting duct:

• Luminal (apical) membrane: ENaC (Na⁺ reabsorption), ROMK (K⁺ secretion), Aquaporin-2 (ADH-regulated water reabsorption)
• Basolateral membrane: Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase pump

The Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase is located on the basolateral surface, where it maintains the sodium gradient driving luminal sodium reabsorption; therefore, it is not present on the luminal membrane.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the nerve supply of the urinary bladder?
options: Sympathetic fibers (T11–L2) cause detrusor contraction and internal sphincter relaxation
Parasympathetic fibers (S2–S4) cause detrusor contraction and internal sphincter relaxation
Pudendal nerve (S2–S4) supplies the detrusor muscle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parasympathetic fibers (S2–S4) cause detrusor contraction and internal sphincter relaxation

Normal micturition is mediated primarily by parasympathetic fibers (S2–S4) via pelvic splanchnic nerves. These fibers:

• Contract detrusor muscle
• Relax internal urethral sphincter
• Facilitating bladder emptying.

Sympathetic fibers (T11–L2) promote urine storage by relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter, while the pudendal nerve (S2–S4) provides voluntary control of the external urethral sphincter.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding Bartter's syndrome?
options: Indomethacin may be used for treatment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Autosomal dominant disorder

Bartter syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder due to defective Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ transport in the thick ascending limb, mimicking chronic loop diuretic use.

Key features include:

• Hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis
• Normal/low BP with ↑ renin and aldosterone
• ↑ Prostaglandins → treated with indomethacin
• Some variants associated with sensorineural deafness

Thus, it is not autosomal dominant, making that statement false.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is most likely based on the lab values given? Blood pH: 7.3 Na+: 134 mEq/L K+: 2.8 mEq/L Cl: 113 mEq/L HCO3-: 12 mEq/L BUN: 3 mg/dL Creatinine: 0.6 mg/dL Urinary pH: 4.4
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type 2 RTA

• Low pH (7.3) with low HCO₃⁻ (12) indicates metabolic acidosis.
• Normal anion gap with hyperchloremia (Cl⁻ 113) → normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (RTA).
• Presence of hypokalemia (K⁺ 2.8) and acidic urine pH <5.5 (4.4) indicates intact distal acidification but impaired proximal bicarbonate reabsorption → Type 2 (proximal) renal tubular acidosis.
• Thus, Type 2 RTA is characterized by proximal HCO₃⁻ wasting, hypokalemia, and urine that can be acidified (pH <5.5) once plasma bicarbonate falls.

Why not other options:

A. Type 4 RTA: Hyperkalemia present → not here.

B. Type 1 RTA: Urine pH >5.5; here urine is acidic (4.4).

D. HAGMA: Anion gap normal.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding clear cell carcinoma of the kidney? 1. It is the most common sporadic renal tumor 2. Associated with loss of long arm of chromosome 3 3. Arises from distal convoluted tubule 4. Cells show intracellular accumulation of PAS + Diastase sensitive substance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 4

Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common sporadic renal tumor. It typically arises from the proximal convoluted tubule, not the distal tubule. Tumor cells appear “clear” due to intracellular accumulation of glycogen and lipids, which are PAS-positive and diastase-sensitive (glycogen).

Although ccRCC is classically associated with chromosome 3p deletion (VHL gene mutation), the key diagnostic features are:

• Most common RCC subtype
• Clear cytoplasm due to glycogen/lipid accumulation

Thus, statements 1 and 4 are correct.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following substances will have the highest concentration at the end of the proximal tubule compared to the beginning of the proximal tubule?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Creatinine

• Substances that are freely filtered but neither reabsorbed nor significantly secreted become more concentrated in tubular fluid along the proximal tubule because water is reabsorbed (\~65%).
• Creatinine is minimally reabsorbed (and slightly secreted), so as water is reabsorbed, its tubular concentration increases.
• Thus, creatinine concentration is highest at the end of the proximal tubule compared to the beginning.

In contrast:

• A. Bicarbonate → largely reabsorbed
• C. Glucose → almost completely reabsorbed in PCT
• D. Sodium → reabsorbed proportionally with water (remains relatively unchanged in concentration)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which transport mechanism is primarily responsible for bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sodium–hydrogen antiporter

In the proximal convoluted tubule, bicarbonate reabsorption occurs indirectly via the Na⁺–H⁺ antiporter (NHE).

• H⁺ is secreted into the tubular lumen in exchange for Na⁺.
• Secreted H⁺ combines with filtered HCO₃⁻ → forms CO₂ and H₂O (via carbonic anhydrase).
• CO₂ diffuses into tubular cells and is converted back to HCO₃⁻, which enters blood.

Thus, Na⁺–H⁺ antiporter is the primary mechanism driving bicarbonate reabsorption in PCT.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old female with nephritic range proteinuria is found to have low serum complement levels. Which of the following can be the likely etiology? 1. Systemic lupus erythematosus 2. Post-infectious glomerulonephritis 3. Infective endocarditis 4. Mesangio-capillary glomerulonephritis Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Low serum complement (C3 and/or C4) in a patient with nephritic syndrome suggests immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis, where complement is consumed during activation of the classical or alternative pathway. It helps narrow the differential diagnosis of glomerulonephritis.

• Glomerulonephritis associated with low complement:

• Systemic lupus erythematosus (Lupus nephritis)
• Post-infectious glomerulonephritis (PIGN)
• Infective endocarditis-associated GN
• Membranoproliferative (Mesangiocapillary) glomerulonephritis (MPGN)

• Glomerulonephritis with normal complement:

• IgA nephropathy
• Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis)
• Minimal change disease
• Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
• Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome)
• ANCA-associated vasculitis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 5-year-old child with 4+ proteinuria is unresponsive to corticosteroid therapy. There is no history of hematuria and hypertension. Renal biopsy shows segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis, predominantly involving the juxtamedullary glomeruli. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)

Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in a child with segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis on biopsy is characteristic of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS).

Predominant involvement of juxtamedullary glomeruli is a classic histologic clue for FSGS.

| Clue | Interpretation

| ---- | --------------

| 5-year-old child | Suggests MCD or FSGS

| 4+ proteinuria | Nephrotic syndrome

| No hematuria, no HTN | Pure nephrotic picture

| Steroid unresponsive | NOT MCD → think FSGS

| Segmental sclerosis + hyalinosis | Histopath hallmark of FSGS

| Juxtamedullary glomeruli | Typical early involvement in FSGS

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)

| Option | Verdict | Why? | Key Differentiator

| ------ | ------- | ---- | ------------------

| A) IgA nephropathy | ❌ | Nephritic picture (hematuria) | Episodic hematuria post infection

| B) FSGS | ✅ | Steroid-resistant + segmental sclerosis | Correct

| C) Membranous nephropathy | ❌ | Adults, subepithelial deposits | Spike & dome pattern

| D) Minimal change disease | ❌ | Steroid responsive | EM: foot process effacement only

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient has malaise for 2 weeks. His investigations revealed an elevated creatinine of 4.5mg/dl. His blood tests also showed the presence of HBs antigen. A renal biopsy was performed which demonstrated spike and dome on special staining. Which of the following conditions is the patient likely to be suffering from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Membranous glomerulopathy

Hepatitis B infection

↓

Immune complex formation

↓

Deposition in subepithelial region (GBM)

↓

Complement activation (C5b-9)

↓

Podocyte injury

↓

Proteinuria (nephrotic syndrome)

Membranous glomerulopathy shows characteristic “spike and dome” appearance on silver stain due to subepithelial immune complex deposition.

It is classically associated with HBsAg positivity in secondary membranous nephropathy.

Patients present with nephrotic syndrome and elevated creatinine in adults.

Minimal change lacks spikes, FSGS shows segmental sclerosis, and amyloidosis shows Congo red positivity.

| Disease | Key Feature | IF Pattern | Association

| ------- | ----------- | ---------- | -----------

| Membranous | Spike & dome | Granular | HBV, malignancy

| Minimal change | Podocyte effacement | Negative | Children

| FSGS | Segmental sclerosis | IgM/C3 | HIV

| Amyloidosis | Congo red + | Amorphous deposits | Chronic disease

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is on antidiabetic medications and telmisartan. Her HbA1c is 8.5%. Her blood pressure is well controlled, eGFR is 50 mL/min/1.73 m², serum potassium is normal, and she is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate intervention to reduce the risk of further decline in eGFR?
options: Increase the dose of anti-diabetic drug
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase the dose of telmisartan

Maximizing renin–angiotensin system (RAS) blockade with an ACE inhibitor or ARB is the cornerstone of slowing the progression of diabetic kidney disease (DKD). In patients with hypertension, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease, the ARB dose should be titrated to the maximum tolerated dose to reduce intraglomerular pressure, proteinuria, and the rate of eGFR decline, provided serum creatinine and potassium remain acceptable.

Why not the other options?

• B. Shift to ramipril: ACE inhibitors and ARBs provide comparable renal protection. Switching from a well-tolerated ARB to an ACE inhibitor offers no additional benefit.
• C. Increase the dose of anti-diabetic drug: Better glycemic control is important, but optimizing RAS blockade has a more direct renoprotective effect in diabetic kidney disease.
• D. Start carvedilol: Useful for hypertension or heart failure but does not specifically reduce the progression of diabetic kidney disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A child presents with periorbital oedema and pedal oedema. The laboratory investigations reveal serum creatinine = 2.1 mg/dL, urinary protein: 5.2 g/day, and Cholesterol: 310 mg/dL. Which of the following are included in the criteria of diagnosis of Nephrotic syndrome? 1. Proteinuria >3.5 g/day 2. Hyperlipidemia 3. Creatinine more than 1.5mg/dl 4. Hypoalbuminaemia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Core Diagnostic Criteria of Nephrotic Syndrome

| Criterion | Mechanism

| --------- | ---------

| Proteinuria >3.5 g/day | Increased glomerular permeability

| Hypoalbuminemia | Loss of albumin in urine

| Hyperlipidemia | Liver compensatory synthesis

| Edema | ↓ oncotic pressure + Na retention

Nephrotic syndrome is defined by massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) leading to hypoalbuminemia, which in turn causes edema and secondary hyperlipidemia.

Serum creatinine is not part of the diagnostic criteria and may be normal or elevated depending on renal function.

| Statement | Included in Criteria? | Explanation

| --------- | --------------------- | -----------

| 1. Proteinuria >3.5 g/day | ✅ | Hallmark feature

| 2. Hyperlipidemia | ✅ | Liver compensation

| 3. Creatinine | ❌ | Reflects renal function, not definition

| 4. Hypoalbuminemia | ✅ | Due to urinary loss

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly man presents with progressive swelling of the legs and frothy urine. Physical examination reveals bilateral pitting pedal edema. Urinalysis shows 4+ proteinuria and fatty casts. A renal biopsy is performed, and Congo red staining reveals apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of his renal disease?
options: Immune complex deposition due to membranous glomerulopathy
Mesangial proliferation due to IgA deposition
Extracellular deposition of misfolded proteins in amyloidosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Extracellular deposition of misfolded proteins in amyloidosis

Apple-green birefringence on Congo red staining is diagnostic of amyloidosis.

Renal amyloidosis causes nephrotic syndrome with heavy proteinuria, fatty casts, and edema. The underlying mechanism is extracellular deposition of misfolded amyloid proteins in the glomeruli.

Misfolded proteins (β-pleated sheets)

↓

Resistant to degradation

↓

Extracellular deposition in glomeruli

↓

Disrupts filtration barrier

↓

Massive proteinuria (nephrotic syndrome)

| Type | Protein | Cause

| ---- | ------- | -----

| AL | Light chains | Multiple myeloma

| AA | Serum amyloid A | Chronic inflammation

Immune complex, IgA deposition, and podocyte injury describe other glomerulopathies, not amyloidosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Anti-PLA2R antibodies, which are directed against the ‘M-type phospholipase A2 receptor’, are a key biomarker for which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary membranous nephropathy

Anti-PLA2R antibodies are directed against the M-type phospholipase A₂ receptor (PLA2R) on podocytes and are a highly specific biomarker for primary membranous nephropathy. They are present in a large proportion of patients with primary membranous nephropathy and can also be useful for monitoring disease activity and response to treatment.

Why not the other options?

• B. IgA nephropathy: Characterized by mesangial deposition of IgA, often presenting with recurrent hematuria.
• C. Crescentic glomerulonephritis: Associated with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, with causes including anti-GBM antibodies and ANCA-associated vasculitis.
• D. Mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis: A histological pattern seen in several diseases; anti-PLA2R is not its characteristic biomarker.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Urinary dipstick analysis in a child reveals: • Urine pH 5.0 • Specific gravity 1.025 • Blood negative • Protein 3+ • Glucose negative • Ketones negative • Nitrite negative • Leukocyte esterase negative The child most likely has:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nephrotic syndrome

Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by heavy proteinuria (≥3+ on urine dipstick) with no hematuria and no evidence of urinary tract infection. The dipstick findings of 3+ protein, negative blood, negative leukocyte esterase, and negative nitrite strongly suggest nephrotic syndrome.

Why not the other options?

• A. Nephrotic syndrome ✔️: Heavy isolated proteinuria is the hallmark.
• B. Acute glomerulonephritis ❌: Typically shows hematuria (blood positive/RBCs or RBC casts) with mild-to-moderate proteinuria.
• C. Urinary tract infection ❌: Usually leukocyte esterase and/or nitrite positive, often with pyuria.
• D. Diabetes mellitus ❌: Characterized by glycosuria (± ketonuria in DKA), not isolated heavy proteinuria.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are indications for a renal biopsy? 1. Chronic kidney disease of uncertain etiology 2. Nephritic syndrome 3. Uncontrolled severe hypertension 4. Renal transplant dysfunction Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Renal biopsy is an important diagnostic tool that provides histopathological confirmation of renal disease, helps determine prognosis, and guides appropriate therapy.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Chronic kidney disease of uncertain etiology: Correct. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) of uncertain etiology is an indication for renal biopsy when the diagnosis cannot be established clinically and biopsy findings are likely to influence management.
• Statement 2. Nephritic syndrome: Correct. Nephritic syndrome (hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, and reduced renal function) is a common indication to identify the underlying glomerular pathology.
• Statement 3. Uncontrolled severe hypertension: Incorrect. Uncontrolled severe hypertension is not an indication for renal biopsy; rather, it is a relative contraindication because of the increased risk of bleeding.
• Statement 4. Renal transplant dysfunction: Correct. Renal transplant dysfunction is an important indication for allograft biopsy to evaluate causes such as acute rejection, drug toxicity, recurrent disease, or infection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are poor prognostic indicators in glomerular disease? 1. Female sex 2. Hypertension 3. Persistent and severe proteinuria 4. Elevated creatinine levels at presentation Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2, 3 and 4 only

The prognosis of glomerular diseases depends on the severity of renal injury and the extent of irreversible nephron damage. Certain clinical features at presentation are associated with a higher risk of progression to chronic kidney disease (CKD) and end-stage kidney disease (ESKD).

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Female sex: Incorrect. Female sex is not a poor prognostic factor in glomerular disease. In some glomerular diseases, male sex is associated with a less favorable outcome.
• Statement 2. Hypertension: Correct. Hypertension accelerates glomerular injury and is an important predictor of progressive renal dysfunction.
• Statement 3. Persistent and severe proteinuria: Correct. Persistent, severe proteinuria reflects ongoing glomerular damage and is one of the strongest predictors of CKD progression.
• Statement 4. Elevated creatinine levels at presentation: Correct. Elevated serum creatinine at presentation indicates impaired renal function and is associated with a poorer renal prognosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following bands will increase in serum electrophoresis in Nephrotic syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alpha 2 globulin

• Massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day)
• Preferential loss of small proteins:

• Albumin
• Some immunoglobulins

Liver response:

• Compensatory ↑ synthesis of larger proteins:

• α₂-macroglobulin (very large → not filtered)
• Lipoproteins

Result: α₂ band increases

In nephrotic syndrome, there is urinary loss of low–molecular weight proteins like albumin and gamma globulins.

The liver compensatorily increases synthesis of α₂-macroglobulin, a large protein that is not lost in urine.

Hence, α₂-globulin band is increased on serum protein electrophoresis.

| Fraction | Change | Reason

| -------- | ------ | ------

| Albumin | ↓↓↓ | Urinary loss

| Alpha-1 | ↓ / normal | Mild loss

| Alpha-2 | ↑↑↑ | Large proteins retained + ↑ synthesis

| Beta | ↑ (mild) | Lipoproteins

| Gamma | ↓ | Ig loss

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following findings are typically associated with glomerular hematuria? A. Dysmorphic RBCs B. Dysuria absent C. Crystals in urine D. Edema is rare
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A, B

• Glomerular bleeding = microscopic, filtered, non-irritative
• Non-glomerular bleeding = irritative, painful

Glomerular hematuria typically presents with brown or cola-colored urine due to oxidized hemoglobin.

It is painless, so dysuria is absent, reflecting a non-lower urinary tract source.

Crystals suggest metabolic causes, and edema is common, not rare, due to associated glomerular disease.

| Feature | Glomerular Hematuria | Explanation

| ------- | -------------------- | -----------

| Dysmorphic RBC, RBC cast | ✔ | Glomerular distortion

| Dysuria | ❌ | No irritation

| Crystals | ❌ | Stone disease

| Edema | ✔ (common) | Renal involvement

| Feature | Glomerular Hematuria | Non-glomerular Hematuria

| ------- | -------------------- | ------------------------

| Color | Brown/cola | Bright red

| RBC morphology | Dysmorphic | Normal

| Casts | RBC casts present | Absent

| Pain | Absent | Present

| Dysuria | Absent | Present

| Clots | Absent | Present

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following renal histological features is characteristically seen in diabetic nephropathy but not typically seen in other glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kimmelstiel-Wilson

The “signature lesion”: Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules

• Nodular, PAS-positive mesangial expansion
• Located in glomerular tuft
• Strongly associated with long-standing diabetes mellitus

These are pathognomonic of diabetic nephropathy, representing nodular mesangial expansion.

Mesangial sclerosis and GBM thickening can be seen in other chronic glomerulopathies, and foot process effacement is nonspecific.

Thus, nodular glomerulosclerosis uniquely points to diabetic nephropathy.

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| GBM thickening | Early change

| Mesangial expansion | Diffuse

| K-W nodules | Nodular, pathognomonic

| Hyaline arteriolosclerosis | Both afferent & efferent (important!)

| Proteinuria | Nephrotic range

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding anti-glomerular basement membrane disease? 1. It is a rare autoimmune disease which presents as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. 2. Antibodies are formed against α3 chain of type IV collagen GBM. 3. The α3 chain is expressed in basement membrane of glomerulus and the retina. 4. The disease may be associated with retinal hemorrhage when it is known as Goodpasture syndrome. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 2 only

Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease is a rare autoimmune disorder characterized by the formation of autoantibodies against the α3 chain of type IV collagen in the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), leading to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN).

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. It is a rare autoimmune disease which presents as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis: Correct. Anti-GBM disease is a rare autoimmune cause of crescentic (Type I) rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
• Statement 2. Antibodies are formed against α3 chain of type IV collagen GBM: Correct. The pathogenic antibodies are directed against the non-collagenous (NC1) domain of the α3 chain of type IV collagen.
• Statement 3. The α3 chain is expressed in basement membrane of glomerulus and the retina:  Incorrect. The α3 chain is expressed in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, not the retina.
• Statement 4. The disease may be associated with retinal hemorrhage when it is known as Goodpasture syndrome: Incorrect. Goodpasture syndrome refers to anti-GBM disease with pulmonary involvement (diffuse alveolar hemorrhage/hemoptysis), not retinal hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following hereditary tubulo-interstitial kidney diseases has an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nephronophthisis

Nephronophthisis (NPHP) is the most common genetic cause of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) in children and adolescents. It is an autosomal recessive tubulointerstitial kidney disease caused by mutations in genes encoding nephrocystin proteins (NPHP genes), which are involved in primary cilia function (ciliopathy).

The disease is characterized by progressive tubulointerstitial fibrosis, corticomedullary cyst formation, and gradual loss of renal function.

• Polyuria and polydipsia due to impaired urinary concentrating ability
• Progressive CKD leading to ESKD in childhood or adolescence

Why not the other options?

• A. Medullary cystic kidney disease type 1: Autosomal dominant (now classified under Autosomal Dominant Tubulointerstitial Kidney Disease [ADTKD]).
• B. Medullary cystic kidney disease type 2: Also autosomal dominant, commonly associated with UMOD gene mutations.
• D. Juvenile hyperuricemic nephropathy: Autosomal dominant, characterized by hyperuricemia, gout, and progressive CKD due to UMOD mutations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is a contraindication of Renal Biopsy?
options: Acute renal injury of uncertain etiology
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Uncontrolled hypertension

Uncontrolled hypertension is a contraindication to percutaneous renal biopsy because markedly elevated blood pressure significantly increases the risk of severe bleeding and perirenal hematoma following the procedure. Blood pressure should be adequately controlled before performing the biopsy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Nephritic syndrome: Often an indication for renal biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain or histological classification will guide treatment.
• B. Acute renal injury of uncertain etiology: Renal biopsy may be indicated when the cause remains unclear after initial evaluation.
• D. Renal transplant dysfunction: Allograft biopsy is commonly performed to evaluate causes such as acute rejection, drug toxicity, recurrent disease, or infection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which statement about Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) in children is accurate?
options: Second most common cause of Nephrotic Syndrome in children
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Second most common cause of Nephrotic Syndrome in children

Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is the second most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, after Minimal Change Disease (MCD). It is also one of the most important causes of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) in childhood.

Pathological Features:

• Light microscopy: Focal and segmental sclerosis of glomeruli.
• Electron microscopy: Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes.
• Immunofluorescence: Usually negative, though IgM and C3 trapping may be seen.

Minimal Change Disease is the most common cause, while FSGS ranks second and accounts for a significant proportion of children who do not respond to steroid therapy.

Why are the Other Options Incorrect?

B. Good response to steroids

• FSGS characteristically shows a poor response to corticosteroids.
• Many patients are steroid-resistant.

C. Relapses are rare

• Relapses are common, and the disease often follows a chronic course.

D. Renal biopsy is not required

• Renal biopsy is essential for diagnosis, especially in steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome.
• Biopsy shows sclerosis involving some (focal) glomeruli and only part (segmental) of the affected glomerulus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presented to the emergency department with head trauma due to a road traffic accident. In the hospital, the patient developed seizures. An emergency CT scan revealed widespread cerebral edema. Which of the following is the diuretic of choice for cerebral edema in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mannitol

Mannitol is the diuretic of choice for acute cerebral edema as it acts as an osmotic agent, drawing water out of brain parenchyma into the intravascular space.

IV Mannitol

↓

↑ Plasma osmolality

↓

Water shifts from brain → blood

↓

↓ Brain volume

↓

↓ Intracranial pressure (ICP)

This rapidly reduces intracranial pressure and cerebral swelling in head injury.

Other diuretics do not provide rapid osmotic dehydration of brain tissue.

| Drug | Mechanism | Role in Cerebral Edema

| ---- | --------- | ----------------------

| Mannitol | Osmotic | ✅ Drug of choice

| Furosemide | Loop | Adjunct only

| Spironolactone | Aldosterone antagonist | ❌ No role

| Thiazide | DCT | ❌ No role

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old sexually active woman presented with dysuria, lower abdominal pain, and increased urinary frequency. Urine culture was done and it grew Staphylococcus saprophyticus with a colony count of 10⁴ CFU/mL. What is the management?
options: It is a diagnosis of UTI
Sample contaminated. Take 2/3 more spontaneous fresh samples
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is a diagnosis of UTI

In symptomatic women, a colony count of ≥10³–10⁴ CFU/mL is sufficient to diagnose urinary tract infection.

Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of UTI in sexually active young women.

Thus, this represents a true UTI requiring treatment, not contamination.

| Situation | Significant bacteriuria

| --------- | -----------------------

| Symptomatic woman | ≥10³–10⁴ CFU/mL ✔️

| Asymptomatic | ≥10⁵ CFU/mL

| Catheterized sample | ≥10² CFU/mL

Mixed culture of fermenting (yellow colonies) and non-fermenting (blue colonies) bacteria on CLED agar.

| Organism | Scenario

| -------- | --------

| E. coli | Most common overall

| Staph. saprophyticus | Young sexually active women

| Klebsiella | Hospital / catheter

| Proteus | Stones, alkaline urine

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with flank pain, and imaging confirms the presence of a renal calculus. He was recently started on hydrochlorothiazide. What is the likely mechanism by which thiazides can cause this adverse effect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreased excretion of citrate

Citrate is a natural stone inhibitor—↓ urinary citrate = stones (especially Ca stones), and thiazide-induced alkalosis promotes citrate reabsorption.

| Role of Citrate | Effect

| --------------- | ------

| Binds Ca²⁺ | Prevents Ca stone formation

| Inhibits crystallization | Stops nucleation/aggregation

Thiazide diuretics can cause hypocitraturia by increasing proximal tubular citrate reabsorption. Citrate normally inhibits calcium stone formation by binding calcium in urine.

Reduced urinary citrate therefore predisposes to renal calculi, explaining this adverse effect.

| Effect | Direction | Impact on Stones

| ------ | --------- | ----------------

| Ca²⁺ excretion | ↓ | Protective

| Citrate excretion | ↓ | Promotes stones

| Volume | ↓ | Concentrates urine

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus is being evaluated for medications to manage their condition and prevent renal complications. Which of the following drugs will not delay progression of renal disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hydrochlorothiazide

| Drug | Mechanism | Renal Protection

| ---- | --------- | ----------------

| SGLT2 inhibitors | ↓ hyperfiltration | ✔ Strong

| Finerenone | ↓ fibrosis/inflammation | ✔ Strong

| Hydrochlorothiazide | ↓ BP only | ❌ None

| ARBs | ↓ RAAS activity | ✔ Strong

Hydrochlorothiazide is an antihypertensive diuretic but has no proven renoprotective effect in diabetic kidney disease.

SGLT2 inhibitors, finerenone, and ARBs reduce intraglomerular pressure and albuminuria, thereby slowing CKD progression.

Hence, hydrochlorothiazide does not delay progression of renal disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 58-year-old male presents with complaints of burning micturition and increased frequency. Prostatic examination is normal. Urinalysis shows >50 pus cells per high power field, but urine culture shows no growth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic prostatitis

Chronic prostatitis presents with irritative urinary symptoms and persistent pyuria, often with negative routine urine cultures due to low bacterial load or sequestration in prostatic tissue.

Prostate examination may be normal between episodes.

Acute prostatitis has systemic toxicity, granulomatous prostatitis is usually post-BCG, and sterile pyuria is a descriptive finding, not a diagnosis.

Expected MCQ:

Stamey–Meares 4-Glass Test (Prostatitis Localization Test)

Four Samples Collected

1. VB1 (First void urine)

• Initial 10 mL urine
• Represents urethral flora/infection

2. VB2 (Midstream urine)

• Clean-catch sample
• Represents bladder urine

3. EPS (Expressed Prostatic Secretion)

• Obtained after prostatic massage
• Represents prostate secretions

4. VB3 (Post-massage urine)

• First urine after massage
• Flushes out prostatic contents

INTERPRETATION:

• VB1 ↑ bacteria/WBC → Urethritis

• VB2 ↑ bacteria/WBC → Cystitis

• EPS/VB3 ↑ bacteria + WBC → Chronic bacterial prostatitis

• EPS/VB3 WBC ↑ but no bacteria → Chronic pelvic pain syndrome

KEY PEARL:

EPS (or VB3) = most important for diagnosing prostatitis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus is started on chlorthalidone. At his follow-up visit, his blood glucose levels are found to be significantly elevated despite adherence to antidiabetic therapy. Which of the following best explains the mechanism responsible for this adverse effect?
options: Chlorthalidone causes hypokalemia, which reduces insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells
Chlorthalidone directly stimulates hepatic gluconeogenesis by activating glucagon receptors
Chlorthalidone increases insulin secretion, leading to receptor downregulation and hyperglycemia
Chlorthalidone inhibits GLUT-4 translocation in skeletal muscle, causing insulin resistance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chlorthalidone causes hypokalemia, which reduces insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells

Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics (e.g., chlorthalidone, hydrochlorothiazide) can cause hyperglycemia by inducing hypokalemia, which impairs insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells. Potassium is essential for normal β-cell depolarization and insulin release; therefore, hypokalemia decreases insulin secretion, leading to worsening glycemic control, particularly in patients with diabetes mellitus.

Why not the other options?

• B. Chlorthalidone directly stimulates hepatic gluconeogenesis by activating glucagon receptors: Thiazides do not activate glucagon receptors.
• C. Chlorthalidone increases insulin secretion, leading to receptor downregulation and hyperglycemia: Incorrect; thiazides decrease, rather than increase, insulin secretion.
• D. Chlorthalidone inhibits GLUT-4 translocation in skeletal muscle, causing insulin resistance: This is not the primary mechanism of thiazide-induced hyperglycemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient has the following Starling forces at a capillary bed: • Capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc): 18 mmHg • Capillary oncotic pressure (πc): 27 mmHg • Interstitial oncotic pressure (πi): 7 mmHg If there is no net filtration across the capillary, what is the value of the interstitial hydrostatic pressure (Pi)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. -2 mmHg

The Starling equation for net filtration pressure (NFP) is: NFP = (Pc - Pi) - (πc - πi)

Where:

• Pc = capillary hydrostatic pressure (pushes fluid OUT)
• Pi = interstitial hydrostatic pressure (pushes fluid IN)
• πc = capillary oncotic pressure (pulls fluid IN)
• πi = interstitial oncotic pressure (pulls fluid OUT)
•

| Force | Direction | Function

| ----- | --------- | --------

| Pc | Outward | Filtration

| Pi | Inward (if positive) | Opposes filtration

| πc | Inward | Reabsorption

| πi | Outward | Filtration

Net filtration pressure (NFP) = (Pc − Pi) − (πc − πi).

Given no net filtration, NFP = 0 ⇒ (18 − Pi) − (27 − 7) = 0.

So, 18 − Pi − 20 = 0 ⇒ Pi = −2 mmHg, making option D correct.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with a renal stone after a Proteus infection. What is the likely composition of the stone in him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Magnesium ammonium phosphate

Urea

↓ (urease)

Ammonia (NH₃) + CO₂

↓

NH₃ + H₂O → NH₄⁺ + OH⁻

↓

Urine becomes ALKALINE (↑ pH)

Proteus species are urease-producing bacteria that alkalinize urine by splitting urea into ammonia.

Alkaline urine favors formation of struvite stones, composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate.

| Stone Type | Composition | Urine pH | Cause

| ---------- | ----------- | -------- | -----

| Struvite | MgNH₄PO₄ | Alkaline | Proteus, Klebsiella

| Calcium oxalate | CaC₂O₄ | Acidic/neutral | Most common

| Calcium phosphate | CaPO₄ | Alkaline | RTA type 1

| Uric acid | Uric acid | Acidic | Gout

| Cystine | Cystine | Acidic | Genetic defect

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with hypertension. He has a history of renal stones and has experienced a few episodes of renal colic. Which diuretic is the most appropriate to use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydrochlorothiazide

Hydrochlorothiazide reduces urinary calcium excretion by increasing distal tubular calcium reabsorption. This helps prevent recurrent calcium renal stones while effectively treating hypertension.

Thiazide

↓

↓ NaCl reabsorption (DCT)

↓

↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption (via Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger)

↓

↓ Urinary Ca²⁺ (hypocalciuria)

↓

↓ Calcium stone formation

Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion, and spironolactone has no role in stone prevention.

| Diuretic | Site | Effect on Ca²⁺ | Stone Risk

| -------- | ---- | -------------- | ----------

| Thiazide | DCT | ↓ urinary Ca²⁺ | ✅ Prevents stones

| Loop (Furosemide) | TAL | ↑ urinary Ca²⁺ | ❌ Promotes stones

| K⁺-sparing | Collecting duct | Neutral | No effect

| Problem | Drug Benefit

| ------- | ------------

| Hypertension | Thiazide lowers BP

| Recurrent Ca stones | ↓ urinary Ca²⁺

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with diabetes insipidus is treated with hydrochlorothiazide and, paradoxically, his urine output decreases instead of increasing. This unexpected effect occurs due to which of the following mechanisms?
options: Direct stimulation of V2 receptors in the collecting duct
Inhibition of Na⁺ reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule leading to mild volume depletion and increased proximal water reabsorption
Blocking aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct
Down regulation of V2 receptors of vasopressin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inhibition of Na⁺ reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule leading to mild volume depletion and increased proximal water reabsorption

Thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide) paradoxically reduce urine output in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. By inhibiting Na⁺ reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, they produce mild extracellular volume depletion, which activates compensatory increased sodium and water reabsorption in the proximal tubule. As a result, less fluid reaches the collecting duct, leading to a decrease in urine volume despite the kidney’s inability to respond to ADH.

Why not the other options?

• A. Direct stimulation of V₂ receptors in the collecting duct: Thiazides do not act on vasopressin receptors.
• C. Blocking aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct: This would increase, not decrease, urine output.
• D. Down regulation of V₂ receptors of vasopressin: Not the mechanism of thiazides and would worsen diabetes insipidus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All of the following Decreases GFR except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased Bowman Oncotic Pressure

GFR decreases with reduced Kf, increased glomerular oncotic pressure, and reduced glomerular hydrostatic pressure.

Bowman’s space normally has negligible oncotic pressure because proteins do not filter across the glomerulus.

Therefore, increased Bowman oncotic pressure does not occur physiologically and does not decrease GFR.

| Option | Effect on GFR | Mechanism | Verdict

| ------ | ------------- | --------- | -------

| A | ↓ | ↓ filtration capacity | ❌

| B | ↓ | Opposes filtration | ❌

| C | ↓ | ↓ driving pressure | ❌

| D | ↑ | Pulls fluid into Bowman space | ✅

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Choose the incorrect statement about Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA):
options: Bicarbonaturia is a feature of RTA 2
RTA 4 is due to aldosterone resistance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. RTA 4 is associated with hypokalemia

| RTA Type | Site | Key defect | Potassium

| -------- | ---- | ---------- | ---------

| Type 1 (Distal) | Distal tubule | ↓ H⁺ secretion | ↓ K⁺

| Type 2 (Proximal) | PCT | ↓ HCO₃⁻ reabsorption | ↓ K⁺

| Type 4 | Collecting duct | ↓ Aldosterone effect | ↑ K⁺

RTA type 4 is due to aldosterone deficiency or resistance and is characteristically associated with hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia.

Fanconi syndrome causes proximal (type 2) RTA with bicarbonaturia.

Hence, the statement that RTA 4 is associated with hypokalemia is incorrect.

| Feature | Type 1 (Distal) | Type 2 (Proximal) | Type 4

| ------- | --------------- | ----------------- | ------

| Defect | ↓ H⁺ secretion | ↓ HCO₃⁻ reabsorption | ↓ Aldosterone

| K⁺ | ↓ | ↓ | ↑

| Urine pH | >5.5 | Variable | <5.5

| Stones | ✔ Common |  Rare | ❌

| Cause | Autoimmune | Fanconi | Diabetes

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: First part of PCT has which of the following transport proteins? 1. Sodium potassium pump 2. Na- glucose co-transporter 3. Sodium hydrogen antiport 4. Na+ Bicarbonate cotransporter
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3

The early (first) part of the proximal convoluted tubule contains transporters involved in bulk reabsorption.

It has the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase on the basolateral membrane, Na⁺–glucose cotransporter (SGLT), and Na⁺/H⁺ antiporter (NHE3) on the luminal side.

The Na⁺–bicarbonate cotransporter is predominantly involved in later bicarbonate handling, not a defining feature of the first part.

| Transporter | Location | Role | Early PCT Presence

| ----------- | -------- | ---- | ------------------

| Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase | Basolateral | Maintains gradient | ✅

| Na⁺–glucose cotransporter | Luminal | Glucose reabsorption | ✅

| Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger | Luminal | Acid-base balance | ✅

| Na⁺–HCO₃⁻ cotransporter | Basolateral | HCO₃⁻ exit | ❌ (not counted here)

| Feature | Early PCT | Late PCT

| ------- | --------- | --------

| Main transport | Na⁺ + glucose | Na⁺ + Cl⁻

| SGLT | ✔ Present | ❌ Absent

| NHE3 | ✔ Active | ✔

| Cl⁻ transport | Low | High

| Function | Bulk reabsorption | Fine tuning

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the correct match out of the following diuretics and the respective site of action:
options: Carbonic Anhydrase inhibitors → Proximal convoluted tubule
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Carbonic Anhydrase inhibitors → Proximal convoluted tubule

| Class of Diuretic | Site of Action

| ----------------- | --------------

| Osmotic diuretics | Proximal convoluted tubule & Descending limb of loop of Henle

| Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors | Proximal convoluted tubule

| Thiazides | Distal convoluted tubule

| Aldosterone antagonists | Collecting duct

• PCT → bicarbonate handling
• Loop (TAL) → Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ (NKCC2)
• DCT → Na⁺–Cl⁻ (NCC)
• Collecting duct → ENaC, aldosterone, water (ADH)

| Class | Example | Site | Target

| ----- | ------- | ---- | ------

| Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors | Acetazolamide | PCT | ↓ HCO₃⁻ reabsorption

| Osmotic diuretics | Mannitol | PCT, descending limb | ↑ tubular osmolarity

| Loop diuretics | Furosemide | TAL | NKCC2

| Thiazides | HCTZ | DCT | NCC

| K⁺-sparing (ENaC blockers) | Amiloride | Collecting duct | ENaC

| Aldosterone antagonists | Spironolactone | Collecting duct | MR receptor

CA inhibitors act in PCT-

• PCT reabsorbs \~80–90% of filtered HCO₃⁻
• Blocking CA → bicarbonaturia → mild diuresis

Why loop diuretics are strongest-

• TAL handles \~25% Na⁺ reabsorption
• Blocking NKCC2 collapses medullary gradient

Thiazide pearl

• Increase Ca²⁺ reabsorption in DCT

Useful in calcium stones

Aldosterone antagonists

• Act on principal cells
• Reduce Na⁺ reabsorption, spare K⁺
• Risk: hyperkalemia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Increase in glomerular capillary permeability leads to which substance appearing in urine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Protein

The glomerular filtration barrier normally prevents filtration of large, negatively charged plasma proteins, especially albumin, through its three layers:

• Fenestrated endothelium
• Glomerular basement membrane (GBM) (size- and charge-selective)
• Podocyte slit diaphragm

When this barrier becomes more permeable (e.g., glomerular disease), proteins leak into the urine, resulting in proteinuria (albuminuria).

• Protein is normally retained in the circulation. Increased permeability of the glomerular filtration barrier allows its passage into the urine.

Why not the other options?

• A. Glucose: Freely filtered and normally completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule; glucosuria results from hyperglycemia or tubular dysfunction, not increased glomerular permeability.
• B. Ketone bodies: Freely filtered; ketonuria occurs in starvation or diabetic ketoacidosis.
• D. Uric acid: Freely filtered and undergoes filtration, reabsorption, and secretion; its urinary excretion is unrelated to glomerular barrier permeability.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Multiple myeloma can cause proximal tubular injury due to light chain deposition in the tubular epithelium causing acquired Fanconi Syndrome. Which of the following are characteristic findings in this condition? 1. Little/no proteinuria 2. Aminoaciduria 3. Phosphaturia 4. Glycosuria Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Acquired Fanconi syndrome in multiple myeloma occurs due to proximal tubular injury from monoclonal light-chain accumulation, particularly in the tubular epithelial cells. This causes generalized dysfunction of proximal tubular reabsorption.

• 1. Little/no proteinuria: Incorrect

• Fanconi syndrome causes low-molecular-weight proteinuria, so proteinuria is typically present.
• Therefore, “little/no proteinuria” is not characteristic.

• 2. Aminoaciduria: Correct

• Impaired proximal tubular amino acid reabsorption → aminoaciduria.

• 3. Phosphaturia: Correct

• Defective phosphate reabsorption → phosphaturia → hypophosphatemia and potentially osteomalacia.

• 4. Glycosuria: Correct

• Impaired proximal tubular glucose reabsorption → glycosuria despite normal blood glucose.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are adverse effects of loop-acting and thiazide diuretics? 1. Metabolic acidosis 2. Hypovolemia 3. Hyponatremia 4. Hypokalemia Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) and thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide) commonly cause volume depletion (hypovolemia), hyponatremia, and hypokalemia due to increased renal loss of sodium and potassium. They also produce metabolic alkalosis (not acidosis) because of increased hydrogen ion loss.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Metabolic acidosis ❌: They cause metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis.
• 2. Hypovolemia ✔️: Due to excessive diuresis.
• 3. Hyponatremia ✔️: Common, especially with thiazides.
• 4. Hypokalemia ✔️: Due to increased distal potassium excretion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following best explains the development of hyponatremia in a hypovolemic patient presenting with diarrhea?
options: Decreased reabsorption of sodium from kidney
Decreased sodium absorption from the intestine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Non-osmotic release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH)

• Diarrhea → hypovolemia
• Loss of:

• Na⁺
• Water

Effective circulating volume (ECV) > Osmolality

Even if plasma osmolality is low or normal:

ADH is released via non-osmotic stimulus

• Triggered by:

• ↓ blood volume
• ↓ blood pressure

ADH:

• ↑ Water reabsorption (collecting duct)
• No proportional Na⁺ retention

Result:

• Dilutional hyponatremia

Hormonal response in hypovolemia:

| System | Effect

| ------ | ------

| ADH | ↑ Water reabsorption

| RAAS | ↑ Na⁺ reabsorption

| Sympathetic | ↑ Renal vasoconstriction

| Type | Volume Status | Mechanism

| ---- | ------------- | ---------

| Hypovolemic | ↓ volume | ADH due to volume loss

| Euvolemic (SIADH) | Normal | ADH excess

| Hypervolemic | ↑ volume | CHF, cirrhosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following causes an increase in renin secretion?
options: Increased sodium delivery to macula densa
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreased renal perfusion

Renin is secreted by the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells of the afferent arteriole in response to decreased renal perfusion pressure, initiating the renin– angiotensin– aldosterone system (RAAS) to restore blood pressure and extracellular fluid volume.

Major stimuli for renin release:

• ↓ Renal perfusion pressure (afferent arteriole stretch)
• ↓ NaCl delivery to the macula densa
• ↑ Sympathetic stimulation (β₁-adrenergic receptors)

Why is D correct?

• Decreased renal perfusion directly stimulates JG cells to release renin.

Why not the other options?

• A. Increased sodium delivery to the macula densa: Inhibits renin secretion.
• B. Increased renal perfusion: Suppresses renin release.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is correct about Finerenone? 1. It causes less hyperkalemia than spironolactone 2. It has a cardioprotective effect 3. It gets accumulated in the kidneys 4. It causes a significant reduction in blood pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 2

Solution – Finerenone:

• It is a non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA)
• Used mainly in:

• Chronic kidney disease (CKD) with diabetes
• Cardiovascular protection

Statement 3: Gets accumulated in kidneys

• Opposite is true
• Finerenone has Even distribution (heart + kidney)

• Unlike eplerenone/spironolactone→ kidney accumulation

Statement 4: Significant BP reduction

• Only mild antihypertensive effect
• Not used as a primary antihypertensive

Steroidal MRAs (spironolactone, eplerenone) → kidney-predominant distribution → more BP reduction + more hyperkalemia

Finerenone (non-steroidal) → equal heart:kidney distribution → cardioprotective + less hyperkalemia + minimal BP effect

| Feature | Finerenone | Spironolactone

| ------- | ---------- | --------------

| Type | Non-steroidal MRA | Steroidal MRA

| Tissue distribution | Balanced (heart + kidney) | Kidney predominant

| Hyperkalemia | Less | More

| Anti-androgen effects | None | Gynecomastia

| Cardioprotection | Strong | Moderate

| BP reduction | Mild | Moderate

| CKD use | Preferred | Limited

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a mechanism by which antidiuretic hormone (ADH) facilitates the excretion of concentrated urine?
options: Increase absorption of urea in the medullary collecting duct
Increase absorption of urea in the descending loop of Henle
Decrease absorption of NaCl in the ascending loop of Henle
Increase water permeability in the collecting ducts
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increase absorption of urea in the descending loop of Henle

Hypovolemia from diarrhea triggers non-osmotic ADH release via baroreceptor stimulation. ADH causes free water retention, diluting serum sodium and leading to hyponatremia. ADH acts mainly at:

• Collecting duct
• Indirectly enhances medullary osmotic gradient

ADH release: V2 receptor activation (Collecting duct)

↑ Aquaporin-2 insertion

↑ Water reabsorption

Concentrated urine

↑ Urea reabsorption (IMCD)

↑ Medullary osmolarity

Further water reabsorption

| Option | Mechanism | Role in Urine Concentration | Verdict

| ------ | --------- | --------------------------- | -------

| A | Urea reabsorption (IMCD) | ↑ Medullary gradient | ✅

| B | Urea in descending limb | Not ADH-mediated | ❌

| C | NaCl handling | Supports gradient | ✅

| D | Water permeability | Direct effect | ✅

Urea Recycling = Hidden Hero

• Urea contributes \~40–50% of medullary osmolarity
• ADH enhances:

• Urea trapping in medulla

Boosts water reabsorption efficiency

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is true about creatinine clearance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Overestimates GFR

Creatinine clearance (CrCl) is a commonly used clinical estimate of the glomerular filtration rate (GFR). However, it slightly overestimates the true GFR because, in addition to being freely filtered by the glomerulus, creatinine is also secreted in small amounts by the proximal renal tubules. In contrast, inulin clearance is the gold standard for measuring GFR because inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed, secreted, synthesized, nor metabolized by the kidneys.

Why not the other options?

• A. Underestimates GFR: Incorrect. Creatinine clearance overestimates, rather than underestimates, GFR due to tubular secretion.
• C. Gold standard for GFR measurement: Incorrect. The gold standard is inulin clearance, not creatinine clearance.
• D. Equal to inulin clearance: Incorrect. Creatinine clearance is slightly higher than inulin clearance because of tubular secretion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following conditions is caused by mutations in the gene that encodes the sodium-potassium-2-chloride cotransporter (NKCC2), and presents with sodium wasting, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypercalciuria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bartter syndrome

Bartter syndrome is an autosomal recessive renal tubular disorder caused by mutations affecting the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb (TAL) of the loop of Henle. Defective sodium chloride reabsorption results in renal salt wasting, activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), and characteristic electrolyte abnormalities.

The patient has features typical of Bartter syndrome:

• Mutation of NKCC2 transporter ⭐
• Sodium wasting
• Hypokalemia
• Metabolic alkalosis
• Hypomagnesemia
• Hypercalciuria ⭐
• Increased renin and aldosterone with normal or low blood pressure

Why not the other options?

• A. Alport syndrome: Mutation in Type IV collagen, causing hereditary nephritis, sensorineural hearing loss, and ocular abnormalities.
• C. Fanconi syndrome: Generalized proximal tubular dysfunction causing glucosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria, bicarbonate wasting, and proximal renal tubular acidosis.
• D. Gitelman syndrome: Mutation of the Na⁺-Cl⁻ cotransporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule, characterized by hypocalciuria (not hypercalciuria) and hypomagnesemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following hereditary tubulo-interstitial kidney diseases shows Autosomal Recessive pattern of inheritance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nephronophthisis

Nephronophthisis is an autosomal recessive hereditary tubulointerstitial kidney disease. It is the most common genetic cause of end-stage kidney disease in children and young adults and is characterized by progressive tubulointerstitial fibrosis and corticomedullary cyst formation.

Why not the other options?

• B. Juvenile hyperuricemic nephropathy: Classically autosomal dominant, now included within the autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (ADTKD) spectrum.
• C. Medullary cystic kidney disease type 1: Autosomal dominant.
• D. Medullary cystic kidney disease type 2: Autosomal dominant.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 55-year-old woman with a history of Crohn disease is admitted to the hospital due to perforated appendicitis. The patient quickly develops respiratory difficulty, and acute respiratory distress syndrome is diagnosed. She is intubated and mechanically ventilated with positive pressure ventilation. She is intermittently placed in the prone position while mechanically ventilated. Which of the following is most likely to occur due to this position change?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreased physiological shunting

In acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), many dependent (posterior) lung regions collapse, leading to ventilation–perfusion mismatch and physiological shunting.

Prone positioning during mechanical ventilation:

• Improves ventilation of posterior lung regions
• Redistributes perfusion and ventilation more evenly
• Recruits collapsed alveoli
• Improves oxygenation

As a result, physiological shunting decreases because more alveoli become ventilated and able to participate in gas exchange.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 1-hour-old boy born at 29 weeks gestation via cesarean delivery due to maternal preeclampsia with severe features, is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit for respiratory failure. Which of the following best describes the condition of this patient's lungs compared to a normal neonate?
options: Compliance low, FRC high, Airway resistance high
Compliance low, FRC low, Airway resistance high
Compliance high, FRC high, Airway resistance high
Compliance high, FRC high, Airway resistance low
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Compliance low, FRC low, Airway resistance high

A preterm neonate (29 weeks) is at high risk for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS) due to surfactant deficiency from immature type II pneumocytes.

Physiologic consequences:

• ↓ Lung compliance → stiff lungs that are difficult to expand
• ↓ Functional residual capacity (FRC) → alveolar collapse (atelectasis)
• ↑ Airway resistance due to poorly expanded lungs

Pathology:

• Formation of hyaline membranes in alveoli
• Diffuse atelectasis

Management:

• Exogenous surfactant therapy
• Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
• Antenatal corticosteroids to accelerate lung maturation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department for follow-up after experiencing a near-drowning incident that led to ARDS. He was mechanically ventilated for 2 weeks and subsequently discharged. The patient now reports persistent exertional dyspnea and mild fatigue. Which of the following parameters is most likely increased compared to a child with normal cardiopulmonary function?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alveolar-arterial oxygen difference

Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) causes diffuse alveolar damage and thickening of the alveolar–capillary membrane, impairing gas exchange.

• Impaired oxygen diffusion and V/Q mismatch
• Leads to an increased alveolar–arterial (A–a) oxygen gradient

Other expected findings after ARDS:

• Reduced diffusion capacity (DLCO)
• Restrictive lung pattern on pulmonary function tests

Important point:

An increased A–a gradient indicates impaired oxygen transfer from alveoli to blood, seen in conditions like ARDS, pneumonia, pulmonary fibrosis, and V/Q mismatch.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl with a head injury from a car accident was brought to the emergency department by ambulance. On exam, she had a respiratory rate of 8 breaths per minute, and a prolonged duration of inhalation was noted. Damage to which of the following groups of neurons in the brainstem is most likely responsible for this abnormal respiration?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pneumotaxic center

The pneumotaxic center (located in the upper pons) regulates the duration of inspiration by sending inhibitory signals to the inspiratory neurons.

• Terminates inspiration
• Limits inspiratory time
• Helps regulate respiratory rate and pattern

Damage to the pneumotaxic center:

• Causes prolonged inspiration (apneustic breathing)
• Results in slow respiratory rate with deep, prolonged inhalation

Related centers:

• Dorsal respiratory group: controls basic inspiratory rhythm
• Vasomotor center: regulates blood pressure, not respiration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 19-year-old male soccer player undergoes an exercise tolerance test to measure his maximal Oxygen uptake during exercise. Which of the following changes are most likely to occur during exercise?
options: Increased arterial partial pressure of oxygen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decreased physiologic dead space

During exercise, pulmonary blood flow increases due to increased cardiac output. This leads to recruitment and distension of pulmonary capillaries, improving ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) matching.

Effects on dead space:

• More pulmonary capillaries are perfused
• Previously underperfused alveoli participate in gas exchange
• Physiologic dead space decreases

Other changes during exercise:

• Pulmonary vascular resistance decreases
• Minute ventilation increases
• PaO₂ remains relatively constant

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 24-year-old male presents with a history of recurrent sinus infections since childhood and chronic productive cough. On examination, heart sounds are best heard on the right side of the chest. He also reports inability to conceive despite normal libido and erectile function. High-resolution CT of the chest is most likely to show which of the following findings?
options: Dilatation of lower lobe bronchi with thickened bronchial walls
Uniform enlargement of acini predominantly involving lower lobes
Patchy destruction of alveolar septa predominantly in upper lobes
Hyperplasia of mucous glands with Reid index > 50%
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dilatation of lower lobe bronchi with thickened bronchial walls

The triad of chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and situs inversus with male infertility suggests Kartagener syndrome, a form of primary ciliary dyskinesia.

• Defective dynein arms in cilia → impaired mucociliary clearance
• Leads to recurrent respiratory infections and bronchiectasis
• Defective flagella in sperm → infertility

Imaging finding (HRCT): Bronchiectasis characterized by dilatation of bronchi with thickened bronchial walls, commonly affecting the lower lobes.

Why other options are incorrect:

• B. Uniform enlargement of acini in lower lobes: Seen in panacinar emphysema (classically due to α₁-antitrypsin deficiency), not Kartagener syndrome.
• C. Patchy destruction of alveolar septa in upper lobes: Seen in centriacinar emphysema, typically associated with smoking.
• D. Hyperplasia of mucous glands with Reid index >50%: Characteristic of chronic bronchitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy is brought with intermittent fever for 3 weeks. He initially had symptoms of an upper respiratory infection that resolved, but the fever recurred and persists despite symptomatic treatment. On examination, he has multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes. The child is otherwise active with no significant weight loss. Which of the following lymph node locations is most concerning for underlying malignancy rather than a benign infectious cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Supraclavicular

Supraclavicular lymphadenopathy is highly suspicious for malignancy because these nodes drain the thoracic and abdominal cavities, making them common sites for metastatic disease and lymphoma involvement.

• Benign/reactive nodes (common in children):

• Anterior cervical
• Submandibular
• Often tender, mobile

• Red flag nodes:

• Supraclavicular → malignancy until proven otherwise
• Hard, fixed, non-tender

Clinical Correlation:

• Left supraclavicular node (Virchow’s node) → abdominal malignancies (e.g., gastric cancer)
• Right supraclavicular node → mediastinal/thoracic malignancies

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman with bronchial asthma, currently using a SABA/ipratropium combination inhaler as needed, reports nocturnal symptoms waking her 3–4 nights a week along with daytime wheeze on most days. Spirometry shows reversible airflow obstruction. What is the most appropriate next step in her stepwise management?
options: Add a leukotriene receptor antagonist alone
Switch to oral corticosteroids as maintenance therapy
Add a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) plus inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)
Increase the frequency of short-acting beta-agonist nebulization
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Add a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) plus inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)

This patient has persistent uncontrolled asthma, evidenced by frequent daytime symptoms and nocturnal awakenings 3–4 times per week despite use of a rescue inhaler. Step-up therapy should include an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) with a long-acting β₂-agonist (LABA), which provides both anti-inflammatory control and sustained bronchodilation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Leukotriene receptor antagonist alone – less effective than ICS-based therapy for persistent asthma.
• B. Oral corticosteroids as maintenance – reserved for severe refractory asthma due to significant adverse effects.
• D. Increasing SABA use – treats symptoms but does not control underlying airway inflammation and may indicate poor asthma control.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman comes to the office for evaluation of recurrent transient pulmonary infiltrates. The patient has a history of bronchial asthma and has had several exacerbations over the past few years, particularly during the winter months. Her medications include albuterol as needed and medium-dose inhaled glucocorticoids. Complete blood count shows eosinophilia. A chest CT scan reveals proximal bronchiectasis. This patient's condition is most likely related to colonization with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aspergillus fumigatus

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) occurs due to hypersensitivity to colonization of the airways by Aspergillus fumigatus, commonly in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis.

• Recurrent transient pulmonary infiltrates
• Eosinophilia
• Elevated IgE levels
• Central (proximal) bronchiectasis on CT
• Worsening asthma symptoms

Pathophysiology:

• Type I (IgE-mediated) and Type III hypersensitivity reactions to Aspergillus antigens in the bronchi.

Treatment:

• Oral corticosteroids
• Sometimes antifungal therapy (e.g., itraconazole).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension undergoes right heart catheterization. During the procedure, an acute vasoreactivity test is performed using inhaled nitric oxide. Her mean pulmonary artery pressure falls from 55 mmHg to 32 mmHg, with a corresponding fall or stable cardiac output, and she is classified as a "responder." What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic management for this patient?
options: High-dose oral calcium channel blocker (e.g., nifedipine or diltiazem)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. High-dose oral calcium channel blocker (e.g., nifedipine or diltiazem)

Rationale: A positive acute vasoreactivity test — defined as a fall in mean pulmonary artery pressure of ≥10 mmHg to an absolute value ≤40 mmHg, with maintained or increased cardiac output — identifies a small subset (\~10%) of idiopathic PAH patients who respond favorably to long-term high-dose oral calcium channel blockers (typically nifedipine, diltiazem, or amlodipine), which can produce sustained hemodynamic and symptomatic improvement in true responders. This makes vasoreactivity testing essential before committing a patient to CCB therapy, since non-responders treated with CCBs can develop worsening hypotension and right heart failure. Endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors, and prostacyclin analogs (B, C, D) are PAH-specific therapies used in vasoreactivity-negative patients (the majority), targeting the endothelin, nitric oxide, and prostacyclin pathways respectively — they are not the first-line choice in a confirmed acute responder.

Quick reference — Vasoreactivity Testing in PAH:

| Parameter | Detail

| --------- | ------

| Agents used for testing | Inhaled nitric oxide (preferred), IV epoprostenol, IV adenosine

| Positive response criteria | ↓mPAP ≥10 mmHg to an absolute value ≤40 mmHg, with unchanged/increased cardiac output

| Responders (\~10% of idiopathic PAH) | Trial of high-dose oral CCB; reassess response at 3–6 months

| Non-responders (\~90%) | PAH-specific therapy: ERA, PDE-5 inhibitor/sGC stimulator, prostacyclin pathway agents (often combination therapy)

| Caution | CCBs should NOT be given empirically without testing — risk of hypotension/right heart decompensation in non-responders

| Long-term CCB success | Even among initial responders, only about half maintain sustained benefit long-term — requires reassessment

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 37-year-old man with asthma is evaluated for frequent episodes of wheezing and dyspnea that are unrelieved by short-acting β-agonist therapy. He uses his controller medications regularly, including an inhaled long-acting β-agonist and high-dose inhaled corticosteroids. Spirometry shows an FEV₁ of 65% of predicted. After supervised use of a bronchodilator in the office, there is some relief of symptoms, and repeat spirometry 10 minutes after administration of SABA shows FEV₁ increased to 85% of predicted. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in this patient’s management?
options: Have the patient demonstrate his inhaler technique
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Have the patient demonstrate his inhaler technique

In patients with poorly controlled asthma despite appropriate medications, the first step is to assess inhaler technique and medication adherence before escalating therapy.

• Incorrect inhaler use is a common cause of inadequate symptom control.
