• This patient shows significant bronchodilator reversibility (FEV₁ improved from 65% → 85% predicted), suggesting the medications are effective when delivered properly.

Clinical approach in uncontrolled asthma:

1. Check inhaler technique
2. Assess medication adherence
3. Identify triggers/comorbidities
4. Then consider step-up therapy if needed.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 38-year-old man comes to the OPD with reports of dyspnea on exertion and decreased exercise tolerance. His medical history is unremarkable, and he has no history of childhood asthma or cough. The patient has gained almost 30kg over the past 4 years due to a sedentary lifestyle. He currently has a BMI of 41 kg/m2. His respiratory rate is 22/min and pulse oximetry is 93% on room air at rest. Physical examination is notable for central obesity. Lungs are clear on auscultation bilaterally. Which of the following changes are most likely to be seen on pulmonary function testing in this patient?
options: FEV1 low, FVC low, RV normal, TLC low
FEV1 low, FVC low, RV high, TLC high
FEV1 high, FVC low, RV normal, TLC low
FEV1 low, FVC low, RV high, TLC low
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. FEV1 low, FVC low, RV normal, TLC low

Severe obesity (BMI ≥40) can cause a restrictive ventilatory defect due to reduced chest wall compliance and diaphragmatic limitation.

Pulmonary function test findings in obesity-related restriction:

• ↓ FEV₁
• ↓ FVC
• Normal or mildly reduced RV
• ↓ Total lung capacity (TLC)

Reason:

Excess abdominal and thoracic fat limits lung expansion, reducing lung volumes but preserving the FEV₁/FVC ratio (restrictive pattern).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department for difficulty breathing and a productive cough. He has a past medical history of recurrent episodes of sinusitis and otitis media. The respiratory infections typically have a protracted course but respond to high-dose antibiotic therapy. Pulmonary auscultation shows crackles and wheezing. Cardiovascular examination shows a cardiac point of maximal impulse that is palpated at the right 5th intercostal space. Which of the following is most likely to be dysfunctional in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dynein arms

Kartagener syndrome is a subtype of primary ciliary dyskinesia caused by defective dynein arms in motile cilia.

• Dynein arm defect → impaired ciliary motility
• Leads to poor mucociliary clearance and recurrent respiratory infections.

Classic triad:

• Chronic sinusitis
• Bronchiectasis
• Situs inversus (e.g., cardiac apex on the right side)

Other features:

• Recurrent otitis media
• Infertility due to defective sperm flagella.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 42-year-old man presents with intermittent episodes of breathlessness, predominantly occurring at night and occasionally waking him from sleep over the past 10 months. These symptoms began following a severe upper respiratory tract infection. He also reports a persistent dry cough but denies wheezing, chest pain, or hemoptysis. He has no significant past medical history and is not on any medications. He is a non-smoker and denies alcohol or illicit drug use. Family history is significant for atopic dermatitis in a first-degree relative. On examination, vital signs are within normal limits. Chest auscultation reveals normal vesicular breath sounds without added sounds. Cardiovascular examination is unremarkable, and there is no peripheral edema. Pulmonary function testing shows: • FEV₁: 90% of predicted • FEV₁/FVC ratio: 82% • DLCO: 96% of predicted Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
options: High-resolution CT scan of the chest
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Methacholine challenge test

Patients with suspected asthma may have normal baseline spirometry, especially in early or mild disease. In such cases, bronchial hyperresponsiveness can be demonstrated using a methacholine challenge test, which provokes bronchoconstriction and confirms airway hyperreactivity.

Normal DLCO and absence of obstruction on spirometry help exclude alternative diagnoses like COPD or interstitial lung disease.

Other options:

• β1-agonist trial (A): B2 agonist is needed for testing, not B1-That's a silly mistake!
• HRCT (B): Not indicated without structural suspicion
• Serum IgE (D): Supports atopy but not diagnostic

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 44-year-old man presents with high-grade fever, productive cough with greenish sputum, and dyspnea for 3 days. He has a history of chronic smoking. On examination, there is bronchial breath sound, crackles, and egophony over the right lower lung field. Chest X-ray reveals lobar consolidation of the right lower lobe. Which of the following is primarily responsible for the greenish coloration of this patient’s sputum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Release of neutrophil-derived myeloperoxidase

Greenish sputum in bacterial pneumonia is due to myeloperoxidase released from neutrophils, reflecting intense neutrophilic inflammation.

• Acute bacterial pneumonia → neutrophil-rich exudate
• Neutrophils release: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) → green pigment
• Indicates active purulent inflammation

Why Other Options are Incorrect:

A. Epithelial necrosis → does not impart green color

B. Hemoglobin breakdown → causes rusty sputum (e.g., pneumococcal pneumonia)

C. Bacterial load → not responsible for color

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old female patient with class II pulmonary hypertension presents with a positive vasoreactivity test. Which of the following is used in the next step of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nifedipine

In pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), a vasoreactivity test is performed during right heart catheterization using agents such as inhaled nitric oxide, epoprostenol, or adenosine.

• If the vasoreactivity test is positive, the next step is treatment with high-dose calcium channel blockers (CCBs) such as nifedipine, diltiazem, or amlodipine.
• These drugs cause pulmonary vasodilation and reduce pulmonary arterial pressure.

Other drugs (e.g., endothelin receptor antagonists, prostacyclin analogs) are used when vasoreactivity testing is negative or when patients do not respond to CCBs.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive shortness of breath over the past few years. He has no history of smoking and works as an accountant. Physical examination reveals diminished breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion. A chest X-ray shows basilar emphysema. His liver function tests are mildly elevated. Which of the following properties correlate with the histopathology staining in this condition?
options: Periodic Acid Schiff - Positive, Diastase - Sensitive
Periodic Acid Schiff - Positive, Diastase - Resistant
Periodic Acid Schiff - Negative, Diastase - Sensitive
Periodic Acid Schiff - Negative, Diastase - Resistant
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Periodic Acid Schiff - Positive, Diastase - Resistant

Alpha-1 antitrypsin (A1AT) deficiency causes early-onset basilar emphysema and liver disease due to accumulation of abnormal A1AT protein in hepatocytes.

• Hepatocytes contain misfolded A1AT protein aggregates
• These inclusions are Periodic Acid–Schiff (PAS) positive and diastase resistant

Reason:

• PAS stains glycoproteins such as A1AT.
• Diastase removes glycogen, but the protein inclusions remain, so staining persists.

Clinical clue:

• Non-smoker with basilar emphysema + abnormal liver tests → think A1AT deficiency.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient came with hypoxemia and a normal alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient. What can be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypoventilation

The alveolar–arterial (A–a) oxygen gradient helps determine the cause of hypoxemia.

Normal A–a gradient with hypoxemia suggests alveolar hypoventilation, where:

• Ventilation is reduced
• Both alveolar and arterial PO₂ decrease proportionally
• Therefore, the A–a gradient remains normal

Causes of hypoventilation:

• CNS depression (sedatives, opioids)
• Neuromuscular disorders
• Chest wall disorders
• Severe obesity (obesity hypoventilation syndrome)

Contrast:

• Right-to-left shunt, V/Q mismatch, and diffusion impairment → increase the A–a gradient.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 46-year-old woman is evaluated for progressive daytime somnolence, impaired concentration, and poor memory over the past year. She reports loud snoring and unrefreshing sleep. On examination, her BMI is 43 kg/m², and her blood pressure is 170/98 mmHg. An arterial blood gas obtained while she is awake shows: • PaO₂: 70 mmHg • PaCO₂: 53 mmHg • HCO₃⁻: 33 mEq/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome

This patient has Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS), also known as Pickwickian syndrome.

The diagnosis is based on the triad of:

• Obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²)
• Awake daytime hypercapnia (PaCO₂ >45 mmHg)
• Chronic hypoxemia without another cause of hypoventilation

The elevated HCO₃⁻ (33 mEq/L) indicates renal compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis, confirming long-standing hypoventilation rather than an acute event.

Patients commonly present with:

• Excessive daytime sleepiness
• Cognitive impairment
• Loud snoring
• Systemic hypertension
• Morning headaches
• Signs of chronic hypoventilation

Why the other options are incorrect?

• B. Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) – OSA causes recurrent nocturnal airway obstruction but awake ABG is usually normal. Persistent daytime hypercapnia suggests OHS rather than isolated OSA.
• C. Central sleep apnea – Characterized by reduced respiratory drive during sleep and is commonly associated with heart failure, stroke, or opioid use. Severe obesity with chronic daytime hypercapnia favors OHS.
• D. Narcolepsy – Causes excessive daytime sleepiness but does not produce hypoxemia, hypercapnia, or elevated bicarbonate.

High-yield pearl

Differentiate OHS from OSA:

| Feature | OSA | OHS

| ------- | --- | ---

| Obesity | Common | Almost always present

| Daytime PaCO₂ | Usually normal | >45 mmHg ✅

| Serum HCO₃⁻ | Normal | Elevated (chronic compensation)

| Daytime hypoxemia | Uncommon | Common

| Treatment | CPAP | Weight loss + CPAP/BiPAP (BiPAP often required if hypercapnia persists)

Key exam clue:

• An obese patient with daytime hypercapnia (PaCO₂ >45 mmHg) and elevated bicarbonate should be diagnosed with Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome, even if obstructive sleep apnea is also present.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 46-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden onset dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and syncope. She has tachycardia, hypotension, and raised JVP. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with T-wave inversions in V1–V4. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography reveals akinesia of the mid–free wall of the right ventricle with preserved apical contractility. This echocardiographic finding is most classically associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute pulmonary embolism

McConnell sign is an echocardiographic finding characterized by akinesia of the mid–free wall of the right ventricle with preserved apical contractility.

It is classically associated with acute pulmonary embolism (PE).

• Acute PE causes sudden increase in pulmonary vascular resistance
• Leads to acute right ventricular pressure overload
• Results in regional RV wall motion abnormality (McConnell sign)

Clinical clues suggesting PE:

• Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, syncope
• Tachycardia, hypotension, elevated JVP
• ECG may show sinus tachycardia and right heart strain (T-wave inversion V1–V4).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 50-year-old chronic smoker presented with mild recurrent hemoptysis without fever or weight loss. The chest X-ray appears normal and the sputum is negative for AFB. Which of the following is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HRCT thorax

In a chronic smoker with recurrent hemoptysis and a normal chest X-ray, the next best investigation is HRCT of the thorax.

• HRCT is more sensitive than chest X-ray for detecting small lung tumors, bronchiectasis, vascular lesions, or early malignancy.
• It helps localize the source of bleeding and guides further procedures such as bronchoscopy.

Clinical approach to hemoptysis with normal CXR:

1. HRCT thorax to identify occult lung pathology
2. Bronchoscopy if imaging suggests an endobronchial lesion or bleeding source

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 53-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after she collapsed suddenly while standing. She also reports left-sided chest pain. The patient was recently diagnosed with colon cancer on a routine colonoscopy and has been on bed rest since then. Her blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg and pulse is 120/min and regular. Pulse oximetry shows 80% on room air. She is diaphoretic and tachypneic. Jugular venous pressure is 13 cm H2O. Further workup in this patient would most likely show which of the following?
options: Filling defect in PA on CTPA
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Filling defect in PA on CTPA

Pulmonary embolism (PE) commonly presents with sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, syncope, hypotension, tachycardia, and hypoxemia, especially in patients with risk factors for venous thromboembolism such as malignancy, prolonged immobilization, or recent surgery.

• Causes acute increase in pulmonary vascular resistance
• Leads to right ventricular strain and elevated JVP

Diagnostic test of choice in hemodynamically stable patients: CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA), which shows a filling defect in the pulmonary artery due to an intraluminal thrombus.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Cannon a waves on JVP: Seen in AV dissociation (e.g., complete heart block, ventricular tachycardia), not pulmonary embolism.

B. Raised troponin levels: May occur with myocardial infarction; mild elevation can occur in PE due to RV strain but it is not the key diagnostic finding.

C. Mediastinal widening: Suggests aortic dissection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 54-year-old man comes to the OPD due to daytime sleepiness and lack of energy. The symptoms began 6 months ago and have progressively worsened so that he feels "completely drained" by the end of the day. The patient's wife mentions that he snores loudly. The patient does not use tobacco or alcohol, and he works in the warehouse of an agricultural supply company. BMI is 34 kg/m2. Physical examination shows a narrow oropharynx and a large neck circumference. The patient is at increased risk of developing which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pulmonary hypertension

This patient has features of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA): obesity, loud snoring, daytime sleepiness, large neck circumference, and narrow oropharynx.

• Repeated upper airway obstruction during sleep
• Causes intermittent hypoxia and hypercapnia
• Leads to hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction

Long-term consequence:

• Pulmonary hypertension
• May progress to cor pulmonale (right heart failure).

Other complications of OSA:

• Systemic hypertension
• Arrhythmias
• Stroke
• Insulin resistance.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 57-year-old obese man presents with daytime sleepiness, unrefreshing sleep, and loud snoring. His spouse reports recurrent episodes of apnea with gasping during sleep. He has a history of hypertension. Examination reveals a bulky tongue and a crowded oropharynx. Which of the following interventions targets the underlying pathophysiology by improving upper airway patency during sleep?
options: Electrical stimulation of the hypoglossal nerve to activate genioglossus muscle
Blockade of the lingual nerve to reduce tongue sensation
Stimulation of the phrenic nerve to enhance diaphragmatic contraction
Stimulation of the recurrent laryngeal nerve to abduct vocal cords
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Electrical stimulation of the hypoglossal nerve to activate genioglossus muscle

Obstructive sleep apnea is caused by collapse of the upper airway during sleep due to decreased tone of pharyngeal dilator muscles; hypoglossal nerve stimulation improves airway patency by activating the genioglossus muscle.

• Key problem in OSA → posterior displacement of tongue → airway obstruction
• Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies: Genioglossus muscle → protrudes tongue → prevents airway collapse
• Therapy:

• CPAP (first line)
• Hypoglossal nerve stimulation (in selected patients)

Why Other Options are Incorrect:

B. Lingual nerve → sensory only

C. Phrenic nerve → diaphragm, not upper airway obstruction

D. Recurrent laryngeal nerve → vocal cords, not main issue in OSA

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old man develops unilateral calf swelling and tenderness 8 days after knee replacement surgery. His heart rate is 78/min, he has no hemoptysis, no active malignancy, and no prior history of DVT/PE, and an alternative diagnosis is not considered more likely than PE. Based on the modified Wells' criteria, what is his clinical pretest probability category for pulmonary embolism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High probability

The modified Wells score for pulmonary embolism (PE) is used to estimate the pretest probability of PE before diagnostic testing.

In this patient:

• Clinical signs of DVT (leg swelling and tenderness) = 3 points
• Recent surgery/immobilization within 4 weeks = 1.5 points
• Alternative diagnosis less likely than PE = 3 points

Total = 7.5 points

According to the modified Wells criteria:

• Low probability: <2 points
• Moderate probability: 2–6 points
• High probability: >6 points

Therefore, this patient has a high pretest probability of PE.

| Criteria | Points*

| -------- | -------

| Previous PE or DVT | + 1.5

| Heart rate > 100 beats per minute | + 1.5

| Recent surgery or immobilization | + 1.5

| Clinical signs of DVT | + 3.0

| An alternative diagnosis less likely than PE | + 3.0

| Haemoptysis | + 1.0

| Cancer | + 1.0

| DVT: deep vein thrombosis, PE: pulmonary embolism
* Patients with a score of 0-1 are low risk; 2-6 are intermediate risk; and > 7 high risk

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history presents with progressive dyspnea and weight loss. Examination reveals a barrel-shaped chest and decreased breath sounds bilaterally. Pulmonary function testing is performed. Which of the following spirometry and lung volume findings are most consistent with emphysema?
options: ↓ FEV₁, ↑ FEV₁/FVC, normal TLC, normal RV
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ↓ FEV₁, ↓ FEV₁/FVC, ↑ TLC, ↑ RV

Emphysema is an obstructive lung disease characterized by destruction of alveolar walls and loss of elastic recoil, leading to air trapping and lung hyperinflation.

Pulmonary function test findings:

• ↓ FEV₁ due to airway obstruction
• ↓ FEV₁/FVC ratio (<70%) indicating obstructive pattern
• ↑ Total lung capacity (TLC) from hyperinflation
• ↑ Residual volume (RV) due to air trapping

Patients often have progressive dyspnea, barrel-shaped chest, and decreased breath sounds, especially with a long smoking history.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old obese gentleman presents to the emergency department with acute onset of breathlessness. He is a known case of type 2 diabetes mellitus for 10–12 years with poor drug compliance. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history. He was diagnosed with a chronic respiratory illness and started on bronchodilator inhalation 10 years ago but has had no regular follow-up. He gives a history of progressively worsening exertional dyspnea for the past 6 months. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (Pro-BNP)

In patients with acute dyspnea, especially with risk factors for heart failure (obesity, diabetes, smoking), measuring B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) or NT-proBNP helps differentiate cardiac from pulmonary causes of breathlessness.

• BNP is released from ventricular myocardium in response to increased wall stretch and pressure overload.

Clinical utility:

• High BNP/NT-proBNP → suggests heart failure
• Low BNP → makes heart failure unlikely

BNP testing is often used as an initial screening test in the emergency department before further imaging like echocardiography.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 63-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of severe epigastric pain and nausea. She has a 20-year history of alcohol use disorder. Nine hours after admission, she becomes increasingly dyspneic and tachypneic. Pulse oximetry on supplemental oxygen shows an oxygen saturation of 81%. Physical examination shows diffuse lung crackles, marked epigastric tenderness, and a periumbilical hematoma. Laboratory studies show normal brain natriuretic peptide. An x-ray of the chest shows bilateral opacities in the lower lung fields. Which of the following pathomechanisms best explains this patient's pulmonary findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alveolocapillary membrane leakage

This patient with severe epigastric pain, alcohol use, and periumbilical ecchymosis (Cullen sign) likely has acute pancreatitis complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

Pathophysiology of ARDS:

• Systemic inflammation → damage to the alveolar–capillary membrane
• Leads to increased permeability and leakage of protein-rich fluid into alveoli
• Causes noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, diffuse crackles, and bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray.

Key features:

• Severe hypoxemia refractory to oxygen
• Normal BNP (distinguishes from cardiogenic pulmonary edema)
• Diffuse bilateral lung opacities

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 64-year-old man comes to the OPD due to worsening dyspnea on exertion for the past 3 months. The patient has had a nonproductive cough but no chest pain, fever, or chills. He was diagnosed with hypertension several years ago but takes no medications. Physical examination shows bilateral inspiratory crackles as well as dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds at the right lung base. Chest x-ray reveals a right-sided pleural effusion. Which of the following pleuropulmonary changes are most likely present in this patient?
options: Vascular hydrostatic pressure increased, Oncotic pressure increased, lymphatic flow normal
Vascular hydrostatic pressure normal, Oncotic pressure normal, lymphatic flow decreased
Vascular hydrostatic pressure increased, Oncotic pressure normal, lymphatic flow increased
Vascular hydrostatic pressure normal, Oncotic pressure decreased, lymphatic flow increased
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vascular hydrostatic pressure increased, Oncotic pressure normal, lymphatic flow increased

Pleural effusion due to congestive heart failure occurs from increased pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure.

• Elevated hydrostatic pressure in pulmonary capillaries → transudation of fluid into the pleural space
• Oncotic pressure remains normal
• Lymphatic drainage increases initially to compensate but may eventually be overwhelmed.

Characteristics:

• Produces a transudative pleural effusion
• Commonly seen in heart failure

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 64-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea for 3 months and a history of untreated hypertension. Examination reveals bilateral basal crackles and dullness to percussion with decreased breath sounds over the right lung base. Chest X-ray shows a right-sided pleural effusion. The underlying mechanism is suspected to be cardiac dysfunction leading to fluid accumulation in the lungs and pleural space. Which of the following combinations of pleuropulmonary changes is most consistent with this condition?
options: Increased Vascular Permeability; Normal Hydrostatic Pressure; Normal Oncotic Pressure; Decreased Lymphatic Flow
Increased Vascular Permeability; Increased Hydrostatic Pressure; Decreased Oncotic Pressure; Decreased Lymphatic Flow
Normal Vascular Permeability; Normal Hydrostatic Pressure; Decreased Oncotic Pressure; Increased Lymphatic Flow
Normal Vascular Permeability; Increased Hydrostatic Pressure; Normal Oncotic Pressure; Increased Lymphatic Flow
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Normal Vascular Permeability; Increased Hydrostatic Pressure; Normal Oncotic Pressure; Increased Lymphatic Flow

Pleural effusion due to congestive heart failure (CHF) is a transudate caused by increased hydrostatic pressure, with normal vascular permeability and compensatory increase in lymphatic drainage.

• Hypertension → left ventricular dysfunction → ↑ pulmonary venous pressure
• Leads to:

• ↑ Hydrostatic pressure → fluid transudation
• Normal permeability (no inflammation)
• Normal oncotic pressure
• ↑ Lymphatic flow (compensatory)

Why Other Options are Incorrect:

• A & B → suggest inflammation/exudate (↑ permeability)
• C → decreased oncotic pressure (e.g., nephrotic syndrome)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 66-year-old man with a 45-pack-year smoking history presents with chronic cough, weight loss, and intermittent hemoptysis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest reveals a right upper lobe mass highly suggestive of bronchogenic carcinoma. As part of staging, imaging is planned to evaluate common sites of distant metastasis. Which of the following organs should be specifically assessed because it is one of the most frequent sites of metastasis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adrenal glands

The adrenal glands are among the most common sites of distant metastasis from lung carcinoma.

Common metastatic sites of bronchogenic carcinoma

• ✔ Adrenal glands
• ✔ Brain
• ✔ Bone
• ✔ Liver
• ✔ Contralateral lung

Adrenal metastases are often clinically silent and are frequently detected during staging CT or PET-CT.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 67-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history is noted on examination to have paradoxical inward movement of the lower lateral rib cage during inspiration, along with a prolonged expiratory phase and use of accessory muscles. What is this sign called, and what does it indicate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hoover's sign

Hoover’s sign is the paradoxical inward movement of the lower lateral rib cage during inspiration, classically seen in patients with severe COPD and advanced emphysema. It results from hyperinflation of the lungs, which flattens the diaphragm and alters its normal mechanics.

• In emphysema, chronic hyperinflation causes the diaphragm to become flattened.
• During inspiration, the flattened diaphragm pulls the lower ribs inward rather than outward.
• The presence of Hoover’s sign correlates with severe airflow obstruction and increased work of breathing.
•

| Sign | Associated Condition

| ---- | --------------------

| Hoover’s sign | Severe COPD/emphysema

| Hamman’s sign | Mediastinal emphysema/pneumomediastinum

| Carvallo’s sign | Tricuspid regurgitation (murmur increases with inspiration)

| Kussmaul’s sign | Constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, RV failure

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 68-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to cough, fever, breathlessness, and chest pain. The patient has a medical history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He is a former smoker with a 20-pack- year history. The trachea is central in position. There is dullness to percussion over the lower right lung area compared to the resonance on the left. Auscultation of the right lower lobe reveals breath sounds that are loud, hollow, and high-pitched. When the patient recites the word "ninety-nine" in a normal voice, the sound has higher clarity and intensity over the right base compared to other lung areas. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
options: Accumulation of fluid in pleural space
Embolic occlusion of a pulmonary segmental artery
Exudation of neutrophil-rich fluid in the lung parenchyma
Leakage of air from spontaneous rupture of visceral pleura
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Exudation of neutrophil-rich fluid in the lung parenchyma

Lobar pneumonia causes alveolar consolidation due to exudation of neutrophil-rich inflammatory fluid into the lung parenchyma.

Effects on physical examination:

• Dullness to percussion (alveoli filled with fluid)
• Bronchial breath sounds (sound transmission enhanced through consolidated lung)
• Increased tactile fremitus and egophony (“ninety-nine” heard clearly)

Pathophysiology:

• Infection → inflammatory exudate fills alveoli
• Consolidated lung conducts sound better than air-filled lung

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 68-year-old man with severe COPD (FEV₁ < 50% predicted) presents for follow-up. He is an ex-smoker and is on maximal inhaled therapy including a long-acting β₂-agonist, long-acting muscarinic antagonist, and inhaled corticosteroids. Despite good adherence, he has had three acute exacerbations requiring oral steroids and antibiotics in the past year. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce the frequency of future exacerbations?
options: Increase the dose of inhaled corticosteroids further
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Add long-term low-dose azithromycin therapy

In severe COPD with frequent exacerbations despite maximal inhaled therapy (LABA + LAMA + ICS), long-term low-dose macrolide therapy (e.g., azithromycin) can reduce the frequency of exacerbations.

• Macrolides have anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects in addition to antibacterial activity.
• They help reduce airway inflammation and exacerbation risk.

Clinical indication:

• Severe COPD
• ≥2 exacerbations per year despite optimal inhaled therapy
• Particularly useful in former smokers.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy with known bronchial asthma presents to the emergency department with severe breathlessness. His SpO₂ is 89% on room air. He receives three salbutamol nebulizations during the first hour and oral prednisolone. One hour later, he continues to have marked respiratory distress with persistent wheeze and SpO₂ of 91%. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Increase inhaled corticosteroid dose and observe
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Add nebulized ipratropium bromide

Management of acute asthma exacerbation is stepwise:

1. Oxygen supplementation (target SpO₂ >92%)
2. Salbutamol nebulization
3. If inadequate response → add ipratropium nebulization
4. Systemic corticosteroids
5. If still refractory → second-line agents (MgSO₄, terbutaline, theophylline)

The child has persistent symptoms despite initial salbutamol therapy, making ipratropium bromide the next recommended addition before escalation to second-line therapies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fever, cough, and dyspnea for 3 days. On examination, he is confused about time and place (new onset), respiratory rate is 32/min, and blood pressure is 88/56 mmHg. Blood urea is 9 mmol/L. Based on his CURB-65 score, what is the most appropriate management?
options: CURB-65 score = 2; manage as outpatient with oral antibiotics
CURB-65 score = 3; consider hospital admission with close monitoring
CURB-65 score = 5; urgent inpatient management, consider ICU assessment
CURB-65 score = 4; manage in general ward without ICU consideration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CURB-65 score = 5; urgent inpatient management, consider ICU assessment

Rationale: CURB-65 assigns 1 point each for: Confusion (new onset, present here), Urea >7 mmol/L (9 mmol/L, present), Respiratory rate ≥30/min (32/min, present), Blood pressure <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic (88/56, present), and age ≥65 years (70 years, present). All five criteria are met, giving a score of 5/5 — the maximum.

A score of 3–5 falls into the high-risk category (mortality usually >15%), where urgent inpatient management is generally appropriate, and severe cases (especially scores of 4–5) warrant assessment for ICU-level care given the high short-term mortality risk. Option A and B understate the score by missing one or more criteria; D underestimates severity by failing to flag the need for ICU evaluation, which is standard practice at this score level.

CURB-65 scoring & management:

| Component | Criterion | Points

| --------- | --------- | ------

| Confusion | New-onset disorientation (AMTS ≤8) | 1

| Urea | >7 mmol/L (\~19 mg/dL) | 1

| Respiratory rate | ≥30 breaths/min | 1

| Blood pressure | SBP <90 mmHg or DBP ≤60 mmHg | 1

| Age ≥65 | Age 65 years or older | 1

| Score | Risk | Disposition

| ----- | ---- | -----------

| 0–1 | Low (mortality <3%) | Outpatient treatment often appropriate

| 2 | Intermediate (\~3–15%) | Hospital assessment or supervised management

| 3–5 | High (mortality >15%) | Urgent inpatient management; consider ICU for scores 4–5

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 70-year-old woman has been enrolled in a longitudinal research study on aging for the last 30 years. Medical history is significant for osteoporosis; she has developed moderate kyphosis due to gradual loss of vertebral body height. She is otherwise active and healthy with no additional medical issues. She has never smoked. Compared to her physiology testing done years ago, which of the following changes is most consistent with normal aging in 1) lung compliance, 2) total respiratory system compliance and 3) physiologic dead space respectively?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase, decrease, increase

Normal aging causes several changes in respiratory mechanics due to loss of elastic recoil of the lungs and stiffening of the chest wall.

Key changes with aging:

1. Lung compliance → Increased

o    Loss of elastic fibers makes lungs more distensible.

2. Total respiratory system compliance → Decreased

o    Although lung compliance increases, chest wall compliance decreases due to calcification of costal cartilages, kyphosis, and osteoporosis, reducing overall compliance.

3. Physiologic dead space → Increased

o    Due to ventilation–perfusion mismatch and decreased pulmonary capillary perfusion

questions.subject: Medicine

questions.text: A healthy adult reaches a steady state while exercising on a treadmill. His oxygen consumption during exercise is measured as 1500 mL/min, while his resting oxygen consumption is 250 mL/min. What is the metabolic equivalent (MET) level of this activity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 6

A Metabolic Equivalent (MET) represents the energy expenditure of an activity relative to resting metabolic rate.

• 1 MET = oxygen consumption at rest ≈ 3.5 mL O₂/kg/min
• It is commonly approximated as \~250 mL O₂/min in an average adult.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient is started on a short-acting inhaled β2-agonist for COPD. Which of the following effects would be expected with this class of drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypokalemia

Short-acting β₂-agonists (SABAs) such as salbutamol (albuterol) produce bronchodilation by stimulating β₂-adrenergic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle. β₂ receptor activation also enhances Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, driving potassium into cells and causing hypokalemia, especially at higher doses.

Why not the other options?

• A. Hyperkalemia – β₂ agonists lower, rather than raise, serum potassium levels.
• B. Bronchoconstriction – β₂ stimulation causes bronchodilation.
• D. Pulmonary vasoconstriction– β₂ agonists generally promote smooth muscle relaxation, not vasoconstriction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with acute severe asthma shows poor response to nebulized salbutamol alone. After adding IV corticosteroids, bronchodilator responsiveness improves significantly within hours — too quickly to be explained by anti-inflammatory effects alone. What is the most likely mechanism for this rapid synergy?
options: Corticosteroids directly stimulate β-2 receptors as partial agonists
Corticosteroids increase transcription of β-2 receptor genes and prevent receptor desensitization
Corticosteroids inhibit phosphodiesterase, mimicking theophylline's action
Corticosteroids block muscarinic receptors, synergizing with β-2 agonists
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Corticosteroids increase transcription of β-2 receptor genes and prevent receptor desensitization

Corticosteroids enhance bronchial responsiveness to β-2 agonists like salbutamol by increasing transcription of β-2 receptor genes, stabilizing their mRNA, and preventing receptor desensitization (tachyphylaxis) — a genomic effect that can manifest relatively quickly in the context of ongoing receptor turnover. This is distinct from their slower anti-inflammatory actions (reducing mucous secretion and inflammatory cell response). Steroids do not directly activate β-2 receptors (A), do not act through phosphodiesterase inhibition like theophylline (C), and have no direct antimuscarinic action (D).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with COPD reports that she can walk on level ground without difficulty but has to slow down compared to people her age, or stop to catch her breath when walking at her own pace on flat ground. According to the Modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) Dyspnea Scale, what grade best describes her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Grade 2

The Modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) Dyspnea Scale is a simple, validated tool used to quantify the severity of breathlessness in patients with COPD. It is incorporated into GOLD assessment to guide symptom classification and treatment decisions.

This patient’s symptoms are consistent with mMRC Grade 2 because she walks slower than people of the same age on level ground due to breathlessness or has to stop for breath when walking at her own pace on level ground.

mMRC Dyspnea Scale

| Grade | Description

| ----- | -----------

| 0 | Breathless only with strenuous exercise

| 1 | Short of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill

| 2 | Walks slower than people of the same age on level ground or stops for breath while walking at own pace

| 3 | Stops for breath after walking about 100 meters or after a few minutes on level ground

| 4 | Too breathless to leave the house or breathless while dressing/undressing

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with pulmonary edema suddenly develops rapid shallow breathing and dyspnea due to stimulation of receptors located in alveolar walls near pulmonary capillaries. These receptors are:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Juxtacapillary receptors

Juxtacapillary (J) receptors are sensory nerve endings located in the alveolar walls close to pulmonary capillaries. They are stimulated by conditions that increase pulmonary interstitial fluid, such as pulmonary edema, left ventricular failure, pneumonia, and pulmonary congestion. Activation of J receptors produces rapid, shallow breathing (tachypnea), dyspnea, and a sensation of air hunger.

Why not the other options?

• A. Irritant receptors – respond to inhaled irritants, smoke, dust, and noxious gases, causing cough and bronchoconstriction.
• B. Pulmonary stretch receptors – mediate the Hering–Breuer inflation reflex and are activated by lung inflation.
• D. Central chemoreceptors – respond to changes in CSF pH and PaCO₂, regulating ventilation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A preterm neonate on mechanical ventilation develops termination of inspiration when the lungs are inflated beyond a certain volume. The response is mediated via the vagus nerve and is abolished after bilateral vagotomy. Which of the following receptors is primarily responsible for this response?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Slowly adapting pulmonary stretch receptors

The Hering–Breuer inflation reflex prevents overdistension of the lungs during inspiration.

• Lung inflation activates slowly adapting pulmonary stretch receptors located in the bronchial smooth muscle.
• These receptors send signals through the vagus nerve to the medullary respiratory centers.
• This terminates inspiration and prolongs expiration, protecting the lungs from overinflation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A pulmonary function test shows a Tiffeneau–Pinelli index of less than 0.70. This finding is diagnostic of which of the following lung diseases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Obstructive lung disease

The Tiffeneau–Pinelli index is the ratio FEV₁ / FVC used to assess airflow limitation.

• Normal: ≥ 0.70–0.80
• < 0.70: Indicates airflow obstruction

Seen in obstructive lung diseases:

• COPD
• Asthma
• Bronchiectasis
• Emphysema

In obstruction, FEV₁ decreases more than FVC due to difficulty expelling air rapidly.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A researcher is studying pulmonary gas exchange. In a subject breathing room air, the following values are obtained from a lung segment: • Inspired PO₂: 150 mm Hg • Alveolar PO₂: 104 mm Hg • Pulmonary venous PO₂: 70 mm Hg • Pulmonary venous PCO₂: 40 mm Hg Which of the following best explains these findings?
options: Ventilation–perfusion mismatch with low V/Q ratio
Diffusion limitation across the alveolar-capillary membrane
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diffusion limitation across the alveolar-capillary membrane

A large A–a gradient (Alveolar–arterial oxygen difference) with normal CO₂ levels indicates diffusion impairment, where oxygen transfer is affected but carbon dioxide diffusion remains relatively preserved.

• Normal alveolar PO₂ ≈ 100–104 mmHg
• Arterial/venous PO₂ significantly lower (70 mmHg) → Indicates impaired oxygen diffusion
• PCO₂ normal (40 mmHg) → CO₂ diffuses easily → not affected early

Why Other Options are Incorrect:

A. V/Q mismatch → usually affects both O₂ and CO₂ (early compensation)

C. Shunt → severe hypoxemia, less responsive to oxygen

D. Hypoventilation → ↑ CO₂

Dead space → ventilation without perfusion

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A sugarcane farmer presents with dyspnea and cough for the last 3 weeks. HRCT shows bilateral ground glass opacities and centrilobular nodules. Lung biopsy shows poorly formed noncaseating granulomas. BAL CD4: CD8 ratio is 2:1. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) is an immune-mediated interstitial lung disease caused by repeated inhalation of organic antigens such as moldy hay, sugarcane dust, bird proteins, or agricultural dust.

• Type III and Type IV hypersensitivity reactions
• Poorly formed noncaseating granulomas
• Interstitial lymphocytic inflammation

HRCT findings: Ground-glass opacities, Centrilobular nodules and Mosaic attenuation or air trapping.

BAL findings: Typically, lymphocytosis with decreased CD4:CD8 ratio (<1).

Why not other options:

A. Sarcoidosis: Has well-formed noncaseating granulomas and typically bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy; BAL CD4:CD8 ratio is high (>3.5).

B. NSIP: Shows uniform interstitial inflammation/fibrosis, no granulomas.

D. Tuberculosis: Shows caseating granulomas and AFB positivity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following parameters are included in the calculation of the BODE index for COPD except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Blood eosinophil count

The BODE index is a multidimensional grading system used to predict mortality and outcomes in COPD patients, incorporating four parameters: Body mass index, Obstruction (FEV1% predicted), Dyspnea (graded using the mMRC dyspnea scale), and Exercise capacity (6-minute walk distance). Blood eosinophil count is not a component of the BODE index — it is instead used clinically to help predict responsiveness to inhaled corticosteroids and risk of exacerbations in COPD, but plays no role in this particular prognostic scoring system.

Quick reference — BODE Index Components:

| Letter | Parameter | Measure

| ------ | --------- | -------

| B | Body mass index | BMI (kg/m²)

| O | Obstruction | FEV1 % predicted

| D | Dyspnea | mMRC dyspnea scale (0–4)

| E | Exercise capacity | 6-minute walk distance (meters)

Each component is scored 0–3 (BMI scored 0–1), giving a total score of 0–10, with higher scores correlating with increased mortality risk — making BODE a more comprehensive prognostic tool than FEV1 alone.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Arrange the following in ascending order of their normal values: 1. Vital capacity 2. FRC 3. Inspiratory capacity 4. Tidal Volume
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4-2-3-1

Normal lung volumes and capacities can be arranged based on their approximate values in adults:

| Parameter | Approximate Value

| --------- | -----------------

| Tidal volume (TV) | \~500 mL

| Functional residual capacity (FRC) | \~2300 mL

| Inspiratory capacity (IC) | \~3500 mL

| Vital capacity (VC) | \~4500–4800 mL

Thus, in ascending order:

Tidal volume < Functional residual capacity < Inspiratory capacity < Vital capacity

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Atypical pneumonia can be caused by all of the following organisms except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Klebsiella pneumoniae

Atypical pneumonia is caused by pathogens that do not produce classic lobar consolidation and often present with gradual onset of dry cough, low-grade fever, and diffuse interstitial infiltrates.

Common causes:

• Mycoplasma pneumoniae
• Legionella pneumophila
• Viruses (e.g., influenza, human coronavirus)
• Chlamydophila pneumoniae

Klebsiella pneumoniae is a typical bacterial cause of pneumonia, producing lobar consolidation with thick “currant jelly” sputum, often in alcoholics or debilitated patients.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: During strenuous exercise, ventilation remains elevated for a short period even after cessation of exercise. This persistence of increased ventilation is best explained by the overdrive mechanism mediated primarily by which of the following?
options: Dorsal respiratory group activation by peripheral chemoreceptors
Ventral respiratory group–mediated recruitment of expiratory muscles
Pneumotaxic center–mediated shortening of inspiratory time
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ventral respiratory group–mediated recruitment of expiratory muscles

During strenuous exercise, ventilation increases due to activation of the ventral respiratory group (VRG) in the medulla.

Mechanism:

• The VRG becomes active during forced breathing.
• It recruits accessory inspiratory muscles and expiratory muscles (e.g., abdominal muscles, internal intercostals).
• This produces active expiration and increased ventilation.

Even after exercise stops, the central respiratory drive (overdrive) may persist briefly, maintaining elevated ventilation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Find out the true and false statements regarding paradoxical bronchoconstriction with ipratropium bromide: A. It particularly occurred when given by nebulizer B. It is due to antibacterial additives added with ipratropium C. This will not be seen when given by MDI D. This problem primarily is due to blockade of prejunctional M2 receptors E. This problem is not seen with tiotropium bromide
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A-T, B-T, C-F, D-T, E-T

Paradoxical bronchoconstriction can rarely occur with ipratropium bromide, especially when given via nebulization.

• Nebulized preparations may contain antibacterial preservatives (e.g., benzalkonium chloride) that can trigger bronchospasm.
• Blockade of prejunctional M₂ muscarinic receptors may increase acetylcholine release, causing bronchoconstriction.

Important points:

• This reaction is more common with nebulized ipratropium than with MDI formulations.
• Tiotropium is more selective for M₁ and M₃ receptors and spares M₂ receptors, so paradoxical bronchoconstriction is not typically seen.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Hemoglobin is expected to become 100% saturated with oxygen when the partial pressure of oxygen (PO₂) reaches which of the following values?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 100 mm Hg

Hemoglobin oxygen saturation depends on the partial pressure of oxygen (PO₂) and follows a sigmoidal oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve.

• At PO₂ ≈ 100 mm Hg (normal alveolar/arterial oxygen tension), hemoglobin is essentially fully saturated (\~97–100%).
• This plateau region ensures adequate oxygen loading in the lungs even with mild decreases in PO₂.

Key reference points:

• PO₂ ≈ 100 mm Hg → \~100% saturation
• PO₂ ≈ 60 mm Hg → \~90% saturation (start of steep portion)
• PO₂ ≈ 40 mm Hg → \~75% saturation (typical venous blood)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Hypoxia causes vasodilatation in systemic arteries, unlike vasoconstriction in pulmonary arteries, because:
options: Systemic arteries have O₂-sensitive K⁺ channels
Systemic arteries have ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels
Systemic arteries have free pore K⁺ channels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Systemic arteries have ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels

Hypoxia causes vasodilation in systemic circulation because systemic vascular smooth muscle contains ATP-sensitive K⁺ (K_ATP) channels.

• Hypoxia → ↓ intracellular ATP
• Opens ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels
• K⁺ efflux → membrane hyperpolarization
• Closure of voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels
• ↓ Ca²⁺ influx → vascular smooth muscle relaxation → vasodilation

Contrast:

In the pulmonary circulation, hypoxia causes vasoconstriction (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction) to redirect blood toward better-ventilated lung regions.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Indications of chest drain in a parapneumonic effusion are all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pleural fluid LDH > 1000

In parapneumonic effusion, a chest tube (tube thoracostomy) is indicated when the effusion is complicated or progressing toward empyema.

Indications for chest drain include:

• Loculated pleural fluid
• Pleural fluid pH < 7.2
• Pleural fluid glucose < 60 mg/dL
• Positive Gram stain or culture
• Frank pus in pleural space

Although pleural fluid LDH may be elevated, LDH >1000 alone is not an indication for chest tube drainage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Pseudonormalization of the Tiffeneau–Pinelli index on spirometry is most suggestive of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Advanced obstructive lung disease

• The Tiffeneau–Pinelli index (FEV₁/FVC) normally decreases in obstructive lung disease because FEV₁ falls more than FVC.
• In advanced obstructive disease, severe air trapping and hyperinflation reduce FVC disproportionately, causing the FEV₁/FVC ratio to appear normal or near normal (pseudonormalization).
• Example: Severe COPD/emphysema.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Regarding oat cell carcinoma of the lung, which of the following statement is/are correct? 1. It is strongly associated with cigarette smoking 2. It commonly presents as a peripheral lung mass 3. It shows early hematogenous metastasis 4. Paraneoplastic syndromes such as SIADH is most common 5. Surgical resection is the primary treatment modality
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, 4

Small cell (oat cell) carcinoma of the lung is a highly aggressive neuroendocrine tumor strongly associated with cigarette smoking.

• Usually arises centrally near the hilum, not peripherally.
• Shows early hematogenous metastasis.
• Frequently causes paraneoplastic syndromes, especially SIADH (ectopic ADH) and ectopic ACTH.
• Surgery is rarely used because the tumor is usually metastatic at diagnosis; treatment is mainly chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: The non-adrenergic, non-cholinergic (NANC) excitatory innervation of the tracheobronchial tree mediating bronchoconstriction is primarily due to the release of which neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Substance P

The non-adrenergic, non-cholinergic (NANC) excitatory system in the airways mediates bronchoconstriction and increased mucus secretion.

Key neurotransmitter: Substance P

Actions of Substance P:

• Bronchoconstriction
• Increased mucus secretion
• Airway inflammation and vascular permeability

Contrast:

• Inhibitory NANC system releases nitric oxide (NO) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) → bronchodilation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Two alveoli are connected by a common airway: Alveolus X has a radius of 50 μm and Alveolus Y has a radius of 25 μm, both with identical surface tension. According to the Law of Laplace, what would happen in the absence of surfactant?
options: Alveolus X would collapse into Alveolus Y because larger alveoli always have higher collapsing pressure
Alveolus Y would empty its air into Alveolus X because it has the higher collapsing pressure
Both alveoli would remain stable since surface tension is identical
Alveolus X would empty into Alveolus Y due to lower resistance in larger airways
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alveolus Y would empty its air into Alveolus X because it has the higher collapsing pressure

According to the Law of Laplace for alveoli (P = 2T/r), the collapsing pressure (P) is directly proportional to surface tension (T) and inversely proportional to the radius (r). When two alveoli have the same surface tension, the smaller alveolus generates a higher collapsing pressure.

In this case, Alveolus Y (radius 25 μm) has a higher collapsing pressure than Alveolus X (radius 50 μm), causing air to flow from the smaller alveolus into the larger one. As a result, the smaller alveolus tends to collapse (atelectasis) in the absence of surfactant.

Why not the other options?

• A. Alveolus X would collapse into Alveolus Y because larger alveoli always have higher collapsing pressure: Larger alveoli have lower, not higher, collapsing pressure.
• C. Both alveoli would remain stable since surface tension is identical: Equal surface tension does not ensure stability when alveolar radii differ.
• D. Alveolus X would empty into Alveolus Y due to lower resistance in larger airways: Air movement is determined by pressure gradients, not airway resistance in this scenario.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: When considering a patient with lung cancer, the imaging studies have measured the tumor size at 2.5 cm not invading in to the main bronchus. According to the TMN staging system, which stage would be appropriate for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T1

The T component of the TNM staging system for lung cancer is determined mainly by:

1. Tumor size

2. Extent of local invasion (eg\, main bronchus\, pleura\, chest wall)

3. Associated features (atelectasis\, nodules\, etc.)

In this case:

• Tumor size = 2.5 cm
• No invasion into the main bronchus

According to TNM rules, tumors ≤3 cm, surrounded by lung/visceral pleura, without main bronchus invasion, are classified as T1 (specifically T1c if 2–3 cm, but option given is T1).

Key size cutoffs (high yield):

• T1: ≤3 cm (no main bronchus involvement)
• T2: >3 cm to ≤5 cm OR invasion of main bronchus (not carina) / visceral pleura / atelectasis
• T3: >5 cm to ≤7 cm OR chest wall/pericardium/phrenic nerve invasion\, etc.
• T4: >7 cm OR mediastinum/heart/trachea/carina invasion

Therefore, a 2.5 cm tumor not involving main bronchus = T1 (Option B).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following diseases/pathogens are associated with pulmonary renal syndromes? 1. Goodpasture syndrome 2. Leptospirosis 3. Wegener’s granulomatosis 4. Hanta virus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4

Pulmonary–renal syndrome refers to the combination of diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

Common causes include:

• Goodpasture syndrome → anti–GBM antibodies affecting lungs and kidneys
• Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener’s) → ANCA-associated vasculitis
• Leptospirosis → severe infection (Weil disease) causing pulmonary hemorrhage and renal failure
• Hantavirus infection → can cause pulmonary hemorrhage with renal involvement

Clinical manifestations:

• Hemoptysis
• Dyspnea due to alveolar hemorrhage
• Hematuria and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following remains an accepted therapeutic indication for methylxanthines?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Apnea of prematurity

Methylxanthines such as caffeine and theophylline stimulate the respiratory center and improve diaphragmatic contractility, making them useful in apnea of prematurity. They are no longer recommended for acute severe asthma due to poor efficacy and toxicity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old obese bank accountant presents with complaints of excessive daytime sleepiness and fatigue. His spouse reports that he has loud snoring and early morning tiredness. Which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. The patient is most likely suffering from obstructive sleep apnea. 2. The diagnosis requires CT/MRI of the neck. 3. Treatment of choice is Zolpidem. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 only

• 1. Most likely obstructive sleep apnea: Correct.

• The combination of obesity, loud snoring, excessive daytime sleepiness, and unrefreshing sleep is highly suggestive of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).

• 2. Diagnosis requires CT/MRI of the neck: Incorrect.

• OSA is diagnosed primarily by polysomnography (sleep study) or an appropriate home sleep apnea test.
• CT/MRI is not routinely required for diagnosis.

• 3. Treatment of choice is zolpidem: Incorrect.

• Zolpidem and other sedative-hypnotics are not treatment for OSA and may worsen upper-airway obstruction.
• CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) is the standard first-line therapy for moderate-to-severe OSA, along with weight loss and appropriate lifestyle measures.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 56-year-old man was diagnosed with COVID-19 and was put on mechanical ventilation. He passed away after a week. What is the likely post-mortem change seen in the lungs?
options: Thick layer of fibrin lining the alveoli
Pulmonary artery hypertrophy with increased resistance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thick layer of fibrin lining the alveoli

Severe COVID-19 causing respiratory failure leads to diffuse alveolar damage (DAD), the pathological correlate of ARDS.

DAD is characterized by hyaline membranes, formed by fibrin-rich exudate lining the alveoli.

Micrograph showing hyaline membranes, the key histologic feature of diffuse alveolar damage.

Severe infection (COVID-19)

↓

Cytokine storm + endothelial injury

↓

↑ Capillary permeability

↓

Protein-rich fluid leaks into alveoli

↓

Fibrin deposition + epithelial necrosis

↓

Hyaline membrane formation

↓

Impaired gas exchange → hypoxia

Alveolar hemorrhage, perivascular cuffing, and pulmonary artery hypertrophy are not defining features of acute COVID-related lung injury.

| Option | Feature | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | ------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Thick fibrin lining alveoli ✅ | Hyaline membranes | ✔ ARDS/DAD | ✔ Correct | Hallmark of ARDS

| B. Alveolar hemorrhage | RBCs in alveoli | Vasculitis, trauma | ❌ Not classic ARDS finding | Seen in Goodpasture

| C. Perivascular cuffing | Lymphocytes around vessels | Viral infections | ❌ Not defining feature | Seen in bronchiolitis

| D. Pulmonary artery hypertrophy | Vascular remodeling | Chronic pulmonary HTN | ❌ Chronic, not acute | Long-standing disease

| Phase | Key Feature

| ----- | -----------

| Exudative (early) | Hyaline membranes

| Proliferative | Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia

| Fibrotic | Lung fibrosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): 1. Exudative phase lasts from day 7 to day 21 after exposure to a precipitating risk factor. 2. Proliferative phase is characterised by proliferation of type II pneumocytes. 3. Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg body weight) has significantly lower mortality compared to high tidal volume ventilation (12 mL/kg body weight). 4. PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤100 mm Hg is classified as severe ARDS. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3 and 4

• Statement 1. Exudative phase lasts from day 7 to day 21 after exposure to a precipitating risk factor: Incorrect. The exudative phase actually lasts from day 1 to day 7 after the precipitating insult (characterized by diffuse alveolar damage, hyaline membrane formation, and neutrophil-rich edema). The timeframe of day 7–21 actually corresponds to the proliferative phase, not the exudative phase.
• Statement 2. Proliferative phase is characterised by proliferation of type II pneumocytes: Correct. The proliferative phase (roughly days 7–21) is marked by proliferation of type II pneumocytes (which attempt to repair the damaged alveolar epithelium), fibroblast proliferation, and organization of the exudate.
• Statement 3. Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg body weight) has significantly lower mortality compared to high tidal volume ventilation (12 mL/kg body weight): Correct. This is based on the landmark ARDSNet (ARMA) trial, which showed that a lung-protective ventilation strategy using low tidal volumes (6 mL/kg predicted body weight) significantly reduced mortality compared to traditional higher tidal volumes (12 mL/kg), along with plateau pressure limitation (<30 cm H₂O).
• Statement 4. PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤100 mm Hg is classified as severe ARDS: Correct. As per the Berlin Definition of ARDS (2012), severity is graded by the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio (with PEEP ≥5 cm H₂O):

• Mild: 200–300 mm Hg
• Moderate: 100–200 mm Hg
• Severe: ≤100 mm Hg

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Peri-operative respiratory failure is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type III respiratory failure

Type III respiratory failure, also known as peri-operative respiratory failure, occurs due to reduced functional residual capacity (FRC) leading to alveolar collapse (atelectasis). It is commonly seen after major surgery, especially upper abdominal and thoracic procedures, because of anesthesia, pain, diaphragmatic dysfunction, and prolonged recumbency.

Why not the other options?

• A. Type I respiratory failure: Hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO₂ <60 mmHg with normal/low PaCO₂), seen in pneumonia, ARDS, pulmonary edema, and pulmonary embolism.
• B. Type II respiratory failure: Hypercapnic respiratory failure (PaCO₂ >50 mmHg), caused by alveolar hypoventilation (e.g., COPD, neuromuscular disorders, CNS depression).
• D. Type IV respiratory failure: Occurs in shock, where respiratory muscle hypoperfusion leads to ventilatory failure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old female with a history of severe persistent asthma is currently on inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) and long-acting beta-agonists (LABA). Despite adherence to therapy, she continues to have seasonal exacerbations. Her FEV1 is within normal limits. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated serum IgE levels. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subcutaneous omalizumab

Severe persistent asthma with elevated IgE and ongoing exacerbations despite ICS + LABA indicates allergic asthma.

Omalizumab is an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody used as add-on therapy in such patients with normal baseline lung function.

Systemic steroids or IV bronchodilators are reserved for acute severe exacerbations, not long-term control.

| Option | Strategy | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | -------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Antibiotics + SABA | Infection treatment | Bacterial exacerbation | ❌ No infection | Avoid unnecessary antibiotics

| B. IV terbutaline | Acute bronchodilation | Severe acute attack | ❌ Not acute emergency | ICU drug

| C. Omalizumab ✅ | Anti-IgE biologic | ✔ Severe allergic asthma | ✔ Correct | IgE-targeted therapy

| D. IV corticosteroids | Acute inflammation control | Severe exacerbation | ❌ Chronic control needed | Short-term use only

| Drug | Target | Use

| ---- | ------ | ---

| Omalizumab |  IgE | Allergic asthma

| Mepolizumab | IL-5 | Eosinophilic asthma

| Benralizumab | IL-5 receptor | Eosinophilic asthma

| Dupilumab | IL-4/IL-13 | Allergic asthma

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old male who is a known case of bronchial asthma presented for a routine follow-up. PFT was done earlier—his FEV1 was 70%, which improved to 83% after bronchodilator nebulization. He was already on MDI Albuterol daily. On questioning, it seems like he is being symptomatic for at least 2 times per week and is waking up in the nights due to symptoms at least once per week. On examination, there are scattered rhonchi. What should be done?
options: Add Fluticasone MDI two times a day
Shift to MDI Salmeterol two times a day
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Add Fluticasone MDI two times a day

Symptoms ≥2 times/week with nighttime awakening indicate persistent asthma, despite SABA use.

PFT shows reversibility, confirming asthma with inadequate anti-inflammatory control.

The correct step-up is adding an inhaled corticosteroid (fluticasone) to treat airway inflammation.

| Severity | Symptoms | Treatment

| -------- | -------- | ---------

| Intermittent | <2/week | SABA

| Mild persistent | ≥2/week | Low-dose ICS

| Moderate persistent | Daily symptoms | ICS + LABA

| Severe | Continuous | High-dose ICS + LABA

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 62-year-old male chronic smoker has been diagnosed with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). On pulmonary function testing, the ratio of Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second (FEV1) to Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) was 0.6 and FEV1 was 70% of predicted. What is the severity of airflow obstruction in this patient as per GOLD criteria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stage II – Moderate

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is diagnosed when post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.70, indicating persistent airflow limitation. The severity of airflow obstruction is then graded according to the post-bronchodilator FEV₁ (% predicted) as per the GOLD classification.

This patient has:

• FEV₁/FVC = 0.6 (<0.70) → Confirms COPD.
• FEV₁ = 70% predicted → Falls in the 50–79% predicted range, corresponding to GOLD Stage II (Moderate COPD).

Why not the other options?

• A. Stage I (Mild): Requires FEV₁ ≥80% predicted.
• C. Stage III (Severe): Requires FEV₁ 30–49% predicted.
• D. Stage IV (Very severe): Requires FEV₁ <30% predicted (or <50% with chronic respiratory failure).

| GOLD Stage | FEV₁ (% Predicted)

| ---------- | ------------------

| Stage I (Mild) | ≥80%

| Stage II (Moderate) | 50–79%

| Stage III (Severe) | 30–49%

| Stage IV (Very Severe) | <30% (or <50% with chronic respiratory failure)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old man with a history of smoking presents with chronic cough and shortness of breath. Bronchoscopy reveals increased neutrophils and macrophages within the airways. Which of the following enzymes released by these inflammatory cells is primarily responsible for the tissue destruction seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Elastase

Cigarette smoking recruits neutrophils and macrophages into the lungs, where they release elastase, a proteolytic enzyme that degrades alveolar elastic fibers. In smokers, oxidative stress also inactivates α₁-antitrypsin, the major inhibitor of elastase, resulting in unopposed elastase activity and progressive destruction of alveolar walls, leading to emphysema (COPD).

• AAT deficiency: Causes panacinar emphysema (predominantly lower lobes) and may be associated with liver disease.
• Smoking-related emphysema: Centrilobular (centriacinar) emphysema, predominantly affecting the upper lobes.

Why not the other options?

• A. Elastin: A structural protein of the extracellular matrix, not an enzyme.
• B. Peroxidase: Enzyme involved in microbial killing by neutrophils; it does not cause alveolar destruction.
• D. Collagenase: Degrades collagen and contributes to tissue remodeling, but elastase is the principal enzyme responsible for emphysematous destruction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A female patient with a known case of bronchial asthma is on levosalbutamol and Ipratropium bromide metered-dose inhalers. She now reports frequent nocturnal symptoms, including wheezing and breathlessness that wake her up several times a week. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Add LABA and inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)

Frequent nocturnal symptoms indicate poorly controlled persistent asthma despite short-acting bronchodilators.

The appropriate step-up therapy is adding inhaled corticosteroid with a LABA, which addresses airway inflammation and provides sustained bronchodilation.

Increasing SABA or adding oral steroids is inappropriate for long-term control, and montelukast is less effective as monotherapy at this stage.

Intermittent asthma

↓

SABA as needed

↓ (symptoms worsen)

Mild persistent

↓

Low-dose ICS

↓ (nocturnal symptoms / frequent symptoms)

Moderate persistent

↓

ICS + LABA

↓

Severe asthma

↓

High-dose ICS + LABA ± oral steroids

Mechanism synergy:

• ICS → reduces airway inflammation
• LABA → bronchodilation (long acting)

Together → better symptom control + fewer exacerbations

| Severity | Symptoms | Treatment

| -------- | -------- | ---------

| Intermittent | <2/week | SABA

| Mild persistent | >2/week | Low-dose ICS

| Moderate persistent | Nocturnal symptoms |  ICS + LABA

| Severe | Continuous | High-dose ICS + LABA ± OCS

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A man with a history of COPD presents with an acute exacerbation. His vitals are given below. According to GOLD criteria, which of the following is/are used in the management of this case? RR - 30/min, Pulse - 112/min, SpO2 - 87% under RA, pCO2 - 60 mmHg 1. Antibiotics 2. Steroids 3. Antivirals 4. Nebulised bronchodilators
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

• RR: 30/min → Tachypnea
• Pulse: 112/min → Distress
• SpO₂: 87% (room air) → Hypoxemia
• pCO₂: 60 mmHg → Hypercapnia

This is acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD) with Type II respiratory failure.

Rz: Bronchodilators Steroids Antibiotics (if infection)

Oxygen (target SpO2 88–92%)

If CO2 retention → NIV (BiPAP)

| Treatment | Role | Indication

| --------- | ---- | ----------

| Nebulised bronchodilators | Relieve bronchospasm | ALL patients

| Systemic steroids | Reduce inflammation | Moderate–severe

| Antibiotics | If infection suspected | Purulent sputum / severe

| Oxygen | Correct hypoxemia | Target 88–92%

| NIV (BiPAP) | ↓ CO₂ | Hypercapnia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with bronchial asthma is prescribed a salbutamol metered-dose inhaler (MDI) but has difficulty coordinating actuation with inspiration. His physician recommends using a spacer device with the MDI. Which of the following statements is true regarding the use of a spacer with an MDI?
options: It increases systemic absorption of the drug
It decreases drug wastage and oropharyngeal deposition
It makes the inhalation technique more complicated and less effective
It has no effect on drug delivery to the lungs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It decreases drug wastage and oropharyngeal deposition

A spacer (valved holding chamber) improves the effectiveness of a metered-dose inhaler (MDI) by reducing the need for precise coordination between actuation and inhalation. It slows the aerosol particles, allowing more drug to reach the lower airways while reducing drug deposition in the oropharynx and minimizing wastage, thereby improving both efficacy and safety.

• Particularly useful with inhaled corticosteroids (ICS): Reduces the risk of oral candidiasis and dysphonia.
• Technique: Actuate one puff at a time into the spacer, followed by slow deep inhalation (or tidal breathing in young children).

Why not the other options?

• A. It increases systemic absorption of the drug: Incorrect. Spacers reduce oropharyngeal deposition and systemic absorption of the swallowed drug, thereby decreasing systemic adverse effects.
• C. It makes the inhalation technique more complicated and less effective: Incorrect. Spacers simplify inhaler use, especially in children, elderly patients, and those with poor hand-breath coordination.
• D. It has no effect on drug delivery to the lungs: Incorrect. Spacers increase pulmonary drug deposition and improve drug delivery.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with chronic productive cough and progressive breathlessness is diagnosed with COPD. He develops type II respiratory failure. Which of the following statements regarding his condition is not true?
options: Bronchial wall inflammation is a characteristic finding
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lung compliance is decreased

COPD is a spectrum:

• Chronic bronchitis → airway disease
• Emphysema → parenchymal destruction

Both lead to airflow obstruction, but their mechanics differ beautifully (and examiners love this contrast).

Chronic smoking / irritants

Airway inflammation + mucus hypersecretion

Airflow obstruction (↓ FEV1)

Air trapping + hyperinflation

↑ CO2 retention (hypercapnia)

Type II respiratory failure

| Feature | Emphysema (“Pink puffer”) | Chronic Bronchitis (“Blue bloater”)

| ------- | ------------------------- | -----------------------------------

| Main issue | Alveolar destruction | Airway obstruction

| Compliance | ↑ | Normal/slightly ↑

| CO₂ retention | Late | Early

| Cyanosis | Minimal | Prominent

| Body type | Thin | Obese

| Feature | COPD (Emphysema) | Restrictive Lung Disease (ILD)

| ------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------

| Lung compliance |  Increased |  Decreased

| Elastic recoil | Decreased | Increased

| Lung volumes | Increased (hyperinflation) | Decreased

| FEV₁/FVC | ↓ (<70%) | Normal/↑

| TLC | Increased | Decreased

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with dyspnea, respiratory distress due to pan-acinar emphysema, and liver dysfunction is due to a likely defect in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Alpha 1 anti-trypsin deficiency

Pan-acinar emphysema with early-onset dyspnea and liver dysfunction is classic for α₁-antitrypsin deficiency.

Loss of α₁-antitrypsin leads to unopposed neutrophil elastase activity, causing diffuse alveolar destruction, predominantly in lower lobes.

Misfolded protein accumulation in hepatocytes explains the associated liver disease.

Normal:

Neutrophils → Elastase (destroys elastin)

↓ Alpha-1 antitrypsin

↓

Unopposed elastase activity

↓

Alveolar wall destruction

↓

Pan-acinar emphysema

| Type | Cause | Location

| ---- | ----- | --------

| Pan-acinar | A1AT deficiency |  Lower lobes

| Centriacinar | Smoking | Upper lobes

| Paraseptal | Subpleural | Risk of pneumothorax

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Benralizumab acts by targeting which of the following immune mediators or receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anti–IL-5 receptor

Benralizumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets the IL-5 receptor α on eosinophils.

It causes antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity, leading to near-complete eosinophil depletion.

It is used in severe eosinophilic asthma unresponsive to standard therapy.

Contrast:

• Anti-IgE: Omalizumab
