• Anti–IL-4 receptor: Dupilumab
• Anti–IL-6 receptor: Tocilizumab

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following steps for using a metered dose inhaler (MDI): I. Incline the head backward to minimize oropharyngeal deposition II. Remove the cap and shake the inhaler III. Breathe out gently and place the mouthpiece into the mouth IV. Hold the breath for 10 seconds V. Simultaneously, begin a slow deep inspiration, depress the canister and continue to inhale Which one of the following is the correct sequence of using MDI?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. II, III, I, V, IV

Correct metered-dose inhaler (MDI) technique is essential for optimal drug delivery to the lungs. Improper technique results in increased oropharyngeal deposition, reduced pulmonary drug delivery, and poor asthma control.

The correct sequence is:

1. Remove the cap and shake the inhaler.
2. Breathe out gently and place the mouthpiece into the mouth.
3. Slightly tilt the head backward to straighten the upper airway.
4. Begin a slow, deep inspiration while simultaneously pressing the canister, and continue inhaling slowly.
5. Hold the breath for about 10 seconds before exhaling.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a COPD patient what is the critical value of FEV1 for patients to develop resting hypoxemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 30%

COPD + FEV₁ < 30% predicted → resting hypoxemia begins to appear.

• FEV₁ (Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second)

→ Measures severity of airflow obstruction

In COPD, as FEV₁ falls:

• Air trapping ↑
• V/Q mismatch ↑
• Gas exchange ↓

Eventually → hypoxemia at rest

| GOLD Stage | FEV₁ (% predicted) | Severity | Clinical Impact

| ---------- | ------------------ | -------- | ---------------

| GOLD 1 | ≥80% | Mild | Minimal symptoms

| GOLD 2 | 50–79% | Moderate | Dyspnea on exertion

| GOLD 3 | 30–49% | Severe | Marked limitation

| GOLD 4 | <30% | Very severe | Resting hypoxemia

Mechanisms:

1. V/Q mismatch (MOST IMPORTANT)

• Some areas ventilated but not perfused properly

2. Alveolar hypoventilation

• Leads to CO₂ retention (Type II RF)

3.

Loss of alveolar surface area (emphysema)

4.

FEV₁ <30% = critical threshold

5. First: exertional hypoxemia
6. Later: resting hypoxemia
7. COPD death often due to:

• Respiratory failure
• Cor pulmonale

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Omalizumab is helpful in which of the following diseases? 1. Asthma 2. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis 3. Nasal polyposis Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 3 only

Omalizumab is a recombinant monoclonal antibody directed against IgE. By binding free IgE, it prevents IgE from attaching to FcεRI receptors on mast cells and basophils, thereby reducing allergic inflammation.

• 1. Asthma: Correct

• Used as an add-on therapy for moderate-to-severe persistent allergic asthma that remains uncontrolled despite standard treatment.
• Particularly useful in patients with elevated IgE and evidence of perennial allergen sensitization.

• 2. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: Incorrect

• Omalizumab has no established role in the treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
• Antifibrotic drugs such as pirfenidone and nintedanib are used.

• 3. Nasal polyposis: Correct

• Omalizumab is approved as an add-on treatment for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps in appropriate patients.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The distance walked in 6 minutes is an indirect measure of which of the following variables of the BODE Index which is used to assess the prognosis in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Exercise capacity

The BODE Index is a multidimensional prognostic scoring system used to predict mortality, hospitalization, and disease severity in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It is a better predictor of prognosis than FEV₁ alone.

Components of the BODE Index

| Component | Assessment

| --------- | ----------

| B – Body Mass Index (BMI) | Nutritional status

| O – Airflow Obstruction | Post-bronchodilator FEV₁ (% predicted)

| D – Dyspnoea | Modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) dyspnoea scale

| E – Exercise Capacity | 6-minute walk distance (6MWD)

The 6-minute walk test (6MWT) measures the distance a patient can walk in 6 minutes, which is an indirect measure of exercise capacity and functional status.

• Lower 6-minute walk distance is associated with:

• Increased mortality
• More frequent COPD exacerbations
• Poorer quality of life

• A higher BODE score indicates worse prognosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Theophylline was prescribed to a male patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The next day, he noticed that his urine output had increased. Which of the following receptors is responsible for the drug's action?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Adenosine A

Theophylline is a non-selective adenosine receptor antagonist, and blockade of adenosine A₁ receptors in the kidney reduces tubular sodium and water reabsorption.

This leads to increased urine output (diuresis), explaining the patient’s observation.

Bronchodilation is via PDE inhibition, but the diuretic effect is mediated by A₁ receptor antagonism, not β₂ receptors.

Theophylline

↓

1. Inhibits phosphodiesterase (PDE)

↓

↑ cAMP → bronchodilation

AND

2. Blocks Adenosine A1 receptors

↓

↓ Adenosine-mediated effects:

- Bronchoconstriction ↓

- Diuresis ↑

↓

↑ Urine output

| Option | Mechanism | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | --------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Interleukin-10 | Anti-inflammatory cytokine | Immune modulation | ❌ Not drug target here | Seen in immune regulation

| B. Histone deacetylase | Epigenetic control | Anti-inflammatory (steroids synergy) | ❌ Not cause of diuresis | Theophylline may enhance HDAC

| C. Adenosine A1 receptor ✅ | Renal & bronchial effects | ✔ Diuresis + bronchodilation | ✔ Correct | Blockade → ↑ urine

| D. Beta-2 receptors | Bronchodilation | Agonists like salbutamol | ❌ Theophylline does NOT act here | SABA/LABA mechanism

| Action | Mechanism

| ------ | ---------

| Bronchodilation | ↑ cAMP (PDE inhibition)

| CNS stimulation | Adenosine blockade

| Diuresis | A1 receptor blockade

| Anti-inflammatory | HDAC activation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Under the Stepwise Approach to the management of Bronchial Asthma, which one of the following is the correct initial treatment at Step 1 for a patient diagnosed with Asthma?
options: Low dose inhaled corticosteroid plus oral corticosteroid
Low dose inhaled corticosteroid plus long acting anti-muscarinic agents
Low dose inhaled corticosteroid plus leukotriene antagonist
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Low dose inhaled corticosteroid only

Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are the cornerstone of asthma management because asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways. Even patients with mild asthma have underlying airway inflammation, and early initiation of low-dose ICS reduces symptoms, improves lung function, decreases airway hyperresponsiveness, and significantly lowers the risk of severe exacerbations.

At Step 1, the recommended controller treatment is low-dose inhaled corticosteroids, which target the underlying airway inflammation and provide effective long-term disease control.

Why not the other options?

• B. Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus oral corticosteroid: Oral corticosteroids are reserved for acute severe exacerbations or difficult-to-control asthma, not initial therapy.
• C. Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus long-acting antimuscarinic agent (LAMA): LAMA (e.g., tiotropium) is an add-on therapy in severe asthma, not first-line treatment.
• D. Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus leukotriene antagonist: Leukotriene receptor antagonists (e.g., montelukast) are alternative or add-on therapies, not routine initial treatment.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not seen with the use of inhaled β₂-adrenergic agonists?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyperkalemia

Drugs like Salbutamol and Formoterol are bronchodilators acting via:

Mechanism

• Stimulate β₂ receptors (Gs protein)
• ↑ Adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cAMP
• Smooth muscle relaxation → bronchodilation

1) Bronchial smooth muscle relaxation → Bronchodilation

2) Skeletal muscle stimulation → Tremors

3) Cardiac β₁ spillover → Palpitations

4) ↑ Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase activity

K⁺ shifts into cells

Hypokalemia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements about Ciclesonide is incorrect?
options: Oral candidiasis is common with its use
It has fewer side effects than other inhalational corticosteroids.
It is a prodrug activated by bronchial esterase.
It has comparable efficacy to other inhalational corticosteroids.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oral candidiasis is common with its use

Ciclesonide

A clever inhaled corticosteroid that behaves like a “stealth prodrug”→ Active only in the lungs

Ciclesonide is an inhaled corticosteroid prodrug activated in the lungs by bronchial esterases. Because activation occurs locally, oropharyngeal deposition is minimal and oral candidiasis is uncommon. It has fewer systemic and local side effects while maintaining efficacy comparable to other inhaled steroids. Hence stating candidiasis is common is incorrect.

| Feature | Ciclesonide | Other ICS

| ------- | ----------- | ---------

| Prodrug | ✔ Yes | ❌ No

| Activation | Lung only | Everywhere

| Oral candidiasis | ↓ Low | ↑ Higher

| Systemic effects | ↓ Minimal | ↑ More

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: While taking the history of a patient, certain words can hint towards the etiology. Which of the following is suggestive of congestive heart failure rather than obstructive lung pathology?
options: Not able to take a deep breath
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Air hunger

The description of dyspnea provided by the patient can offer valuable clues to the underlying cause. The term “air hunger” is classically associated with congestive heart failure (CHF) due to pulmonary congestion and impaired oxygenation, whereas symptoms such as chest tightness, wheezing, or inability to take a deep breath are more suggestive of obstructive airway diseases like asthma or COPD.

It is commonly seen in:

• Congestive heart failure
• Pulmonary edema
• Severe hypoxemia
• Metabolic acidosis

Why not the other options?

• B. Chest tightness: Typical of asthma due to bronchospasm.
• C. Intermittent wheezing: Characteristic of asthma or COPD, reflecting airflow obstruction.
• D. Not able to take a deep breath: More commonly reported in obstructive airway disease, anxiety, or pleuritic disorders rather than CHF.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with gradually worsening difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs. His muscle strength transiently improves with repeated activity but later deteriorates, causing frequent falls. A chest scan shows a hilar mass. Which type of lung cancer is most likely associated with this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Small cell carcinoma

The patient most likely has Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), a paraneoplastic syndrome strongly associated with small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC). LEMS is caused by autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) at the neuromuscular junction, resulting in decreased acetylcholine release. A characteristic feature is proximal muscle weakness that temporarily improves with repeated muscle use (facilitation), distinguishing it from myasthenia gravis. The patient has:

• Proximal muscle weakness (difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs)
• Transient improvement with repeated activity
• Hilar lung mass
• Frequent falls

These findings are classic for Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome, which is most commonly associated with small cell lung carcinoma.

Why not the other options?

• A. Squamous cell carcinoma: Commonly associated with PTHrP secretion, causing hypercalcemia, not Lambert–Eaton syndrome.
• B. Large cell carcinoma: May produce β-hCG, causing gynecomastia, but is not typically associated with LEMS.
• D. Adenocarcinoma: The most common lung cancer overall, especially in nonsmokers, but has no strong association with Lambert–Eaton syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A biopsy from a bronchial mass in a 55-year-old shows a neuroendocrine tumor. Which of the following statements regarding neuroendocrine tumors is incorrect?
options: Tumor cells show salt and pepper chromatin
Neuroendocrine tumors arising from different organs have identical microscopic features
Electron microscopy shows dense-core neurosecretory granules
Tumor cells may appear as small round blue cells forming rosettes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neuroendocrine tumors arising from different organs have identical microscopic features

Neuroendocrine tumors share common features like salt-and-pepper chromatin and neurosecretory granules, but their microscopic architecture varies by organ (e.g., lung, pancreas, GI tract).

They can show different patterns such as trabecular, insular, or rosette formation.

Hence, they are not identical across organs, making option B incorrect.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A chronic smoker presents with cough and weight loss. Chest X-ray reveals a lung mass, and biopsy demonstrates chromogranin and synaptophysin positivity. Which of the following paraneoplastic syndromes is most likely associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. SIADH

Chromogranin and synaptophysin positivity indicate a neuroendocrine tumor, most commonly small cell carcinoma of the lung in chronic smokers.

Small cell carcinoma classically causes SIADH due to ectopic ADH secretion.

Hypercalcemia is linked to squamous cell carcinoma, gynecomastia to β-hCG–secreting tumors, and clubbing is a nonspecific finding.

| Option | Associated Condition | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | -------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Hypercalcemia | Squamous cell carcinoma | PTHrP secretion | ❌ Not neuroendocrine tumor | Squamous hallmark

| B. SIADH ✅ | Small cell carcinoma | ✔ ADH secretion | ✔ Correct | Most common SCLC syndrome

| C. Gynecomastia | hCG-producing tumors | Germ cell tumors | ❌ Not lung NE tumor | Seen in testicular cancer

| D. Clubbing | Chronic lung disease | ILD, lung cancer | ❌ Not specific paraneoplastic | Non-specific finding

| Cancer Type | Syndrome

| ----------- | --------

| Small cell carcinoma | SIADH, Cushing (ACTH)

| Squamous cell carcinoma | Hypercalcemia (PTHrP)

| Adenocarcinoma | Clubbing (rarely)

| Large cell | Variable

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is an intranuclear immuno-histochemistry marker for neuroendocrine tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. INSM

Most neuroendocrine markers are:

• Cytoplasmic (Chromogranin, Synaptophysin)
• Membranous (NCAM/CD56)

Only one stands out as NUCLEAR: INSM1 (Insulinoma-associated protein 1)

INSM (Insulinoma-associated protein 1) is a nuclear transcription factor and serves as an intranuclear immunohistochemistry marker for neuroendocrine tumors. Seen in:

• Small cell lung carcinoma
• Carcinoid tumors
• Neuroendocrine tumors (GI, pancreas, lung)

| Option | Marker Type | Staining Pattern | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | ----------- | ---------------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Chromogranin | Secretory granule protein | Cytoplasmic (granular) | Classic NET marker | ❌ Not nuclear | More specific but less sensitive than synaptophysin

| B. NCAM (CD56) | Cell adhesion molecule | Membranous | Neuroendocrine tumors, NK cells | ❌ Not nuclear | Very sensitive but NOT specific

| C. Synaptophysin | Synaptic vesicle protein | Cytoplasmic (diffuse) | Most sensitive NET marker | ❌ Not nuclear | First marker to turn positive in NET

| D. INSM1 ✅ | Transcription factor | NUCLEAR | Neuroendocrine differentiation | ✔️ Matches question |

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct with regard to clubbing? 1. It usually affects the fingers symmetrically. 2. It does not involve the toes. 3. It may be associated with malignant lung conditions. 4. It may recede following lung transplantation in cystic fibrosis. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3 and 4

Clubbing is a bulbous enlargement of the distal phalanges caused by proliferation of connective tissue beneath the nail bed. It is commonly associated with chronic pulmonary, cardiac, gastrointestinal, and hepatobiliary diseases.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. It usually affects the fingers symmetrically: Correct. Clubbing usually affects the fingers symmetrically and often involves both hands.
• Statement 2. It does not involve the toes: Incorrect. Clubbing commonly involves both the fingers and toes, not just the fingers.
• Statement 3. It may be associated with malignant lung conditions: Correct. Clubbing is associated with malignant lung diseases, especially bronchogenic carcinoma, as well as chronic suppurative lung diseases.
• Statement 4. It may recede following lung transplantation in cystic fibrosis: Correct. Clubbing may regress after successful treatment of the underlying disease, including lung transplantation in patients with cystic fibrosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient presents with fever, cough, and tenacious white sputum. Which of the following should be used for treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Syrup Bromhexine

Respiratory infection

↑ Viscosity (thick, sticky sputum)

Impaired ciliary clearance

Persistent cough

Need:

→ Mucolytic (break mucus)

→ NOT antitussive (suppression)

The patient has a productive cough with thick, tenacious sputum, indicating retained secretions.

Bromhexine is a mucolytic that reduces sputum viscosity and facilitates expectoration.

Antitussives like codeine or dextromethorphan suppress cough and are contraindicated in productive cough.

| Option | Drug Type | Mechanism | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | --------- | --------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Dextromethorphan + Bromhexine | Antitussive + mucolytic | Suppresses cough + thins mucus | Rare mixed cases | ❌ Suppressing cough is harmful in productive cough | Avoid combo in productive cough

| B. Codeine | Opioid antitussive | Suppresses cough center | Dry, irritating cough | ❌ Will retain sputum → worsens infection | Can cause respiratory depression

| C. Dextromethorphan | Non-opioid antitussive | Central cough suppression | Dry cough | ❌ Productive cough present → contraindicated | No analgesia, unlike codeine

| D. Bromhexine ✅ | Mucolytic | ↓ mucus viscosity | ✔ Productive cough with thick sputum | ✔ Correct | Also increases antibiotic penetration

| Type of Cough | Treatment

| ------------- | ---------

| Dry cough | Antitussives (Dextromethorphan, Codeine)

| Productive cough | Mucolytics (Bromhexine, Ambroxol)

| Thick sputum | Mucolytics + hydration

| Severe irritation | Antitussive (short-term only)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with weight loss, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and pleural effusion. Her HRCT shows a "tree-in-bud" pattern, indicating lung consolidation and effusion. Analysis of pleural fluid reveals high adenosine deaminase (ADA) levels with a predominance of lymphocytes. What is the most likely finding on lymph node biopsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Necrotizing epithelioid granuloma

Solution

| Clue | Interpretation

| ---- | --------------

| Weight loss | Chronic infection (→ TB, malignancy)

| Mediastinal lymphadenopathy | TB / lymphoma

| Pleural effusion + lymphocytes | TB until proven otherwise

| High ADA in pleural fluid | Strong marker for TB

| HRCT “tree-in-bud” | Endobronchial spread of infection → classic for TB

So lymph node biopsy will show:

➡️ Caseating (necrotizing) epithelioid granulomas

➡️ Hallmark of Mycobacterium tuberculosis

| Feature | TB Effusion

| ------- | -----------

| Type | Exudative

| Cells | Lymphocyte predominant

| ADA | ↑↑ (>40 IU/L highly suggestive)

| Protein | High

| Glucose | Low-normal

| Mechanism | Delayed hypersensitivity

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old known case of Parkinson's disease presents with severe oropharyngeal dysphagia and recurrent episodes of aspiration pneumonitis. CXR reveals bilateral bronchiectasis. What is the most appropriate long-term management plan for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. PEG tube

This patient has:

• Parkinson's disease → impaired swallowing
• Oropharyngeal dysphagia → aspiration risk
• Recurrent aspiration pneumonitis
• Result: Bronchiectasis

The root cause is aspiration, not just secretion retention.

Severe oropharyngeal dysphagia in Parkinson’s disease causes recurrent aspiration, leading to aspiration pneumonitis and secondary bronchiectasis.

The most effective long-term strategy is prevention of further aspiration, achieved by PEG tube feeding.

| Benefit | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Prevents aspiration | Bypasses oropharynx

| Ensures nutrition | Long-term feeding

| Reduces lung injury | Stops recurrent pneumonitis

Airway clearance methods or antibiotics do not address the primary problem of unsafe swallowing.

| Approach | Example | Role

| -------- | ------- | ----

| Cause control |  PEG in aspiration | MOST IMPORTANT

| Airway clearance | Physiotherapy | Supportive

| Mucolytics | NAC | Symptomatic

| Antibiotics | Macrolides | Exacerbations

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following has the highest risk of causing invasive pulmonary aspergillosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Febrile neutropenia

Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) is a highly aggressive, angioinvasive fungal infection caused by Aspergillus fumigatus (most common).

Key Pathophysiology

• Neutrophils = primary defense against Aspergillus

• In neutropenia (<500/µL):

• No phagocytosis of hyphae
• Unchecked fungal proliferation
• Angioinvasion → thrombosis → hemorrhagic infarction

Pulmonary infarction → cavitation

Halo sign/ Air crescent sign

Key Findings:

• Halo sign (early) → Ground-glass opacity around nodule (hemorrhage)
• Air crescent sign (late) → Cavitation with air pocket

| Risk Factor | Mechanism | Risk Level

| ----------- | --------- | ----------

| Febrile neutropenia | Loss of neutrophil defense | Highest

| Hematologic malignancy | Immunosuppression | +++

| Bone marrow transplant | Severe immune compromise | +++

| Prolonged steroids | Impaired macrophage function | ++

| Advanced AIDS | T-cell deficiency (less role here) | +

| COPD (severe) | Structural lung disease | +

| Feature | ABPA | Invasive Aspergillosis

| ------- | ---- | ----------------------

| Host | Asthma / CF | Immunocompromised

| Mechanism | Hypersensitivity | Tissue invasion

| Eosinophilia | Present | Absent

| IgE | ↑↑ | Normal

| Hyphae | In mucus | In tissue + vessels

| Severity | Chronic | Life-threatening

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is considered ineffective in the prevention of COVID-19?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ivermectin

COVID-19:

Prevention works by:

• Blocking transmission
• Building immunity
• Reducing viral spread

| Level | Method

| ----- | ------

| Primary prevention | Vaccination

| Barrier protection | Mask

| Behavioral | Cough etiquette

|  Not effective | Ivermectin

| Effective | Not Effective

| --------- | -------------

| Mask |  Ivermectin

| Vaccination |  Hydroxychloroquine (prophylaxis – outdated)

| Hand hygiene |

| Cough etiquette |

• In vitro antiviral activity ≠ clinical benefit

• Required doses in lab:

• Much higher than safe human dose

No real-world effectiveness

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: ‘Masson Bodies’ formed due to proliferation of immature collagen are a characteristic histopathological finding seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia

Masson bodies are the histopathological hallmark of Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP) (formerly called Bronchiolitis Obliterans Organizing Pneumonia [BOOP]). They consist of plugs of loose fibroblastic tissue composed of immature collagen and fibroblasts filling the alveolar ducts, alveoli, and bronchioles, while the underlying lung architecture is preserved.

COP represents an organizing response to lung injury rather than irreversible fibrosis and usually responds dramatically to corticosteroid therapy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Lymphocytic Interstitial Pneumonia (LIP): Characterized by diffuse interstitial lymphocytic infiltration, commonly associated with Sjögren syndrome and HIV, not Masson bodies.
• C. Desquamative Interstitial Pneumonia (DIP): Characterized by accumulation of pigmented macrophages in alveoli, strongly associated with smoking.
• D. Respiratory Bronchiolitis: Also a smoking-related disease, characterized by pigmented macrophages in respiratory bronchioles, not fibroblastic plugs.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 42-year-old male industrial worker presented to a health centre with complaints of diminished working capacity and debilitating respiratory complaints including chronic irritant cough, severe dyspnea on exertion and occasional pain in chest. He gave an occupational history of working in the same industry since the onset of adulthood till date. An X-ray of the chest showed “snowstorm” appearance in the lung fields. High-resolution radiographic imaging showed dense nodular fibrosis in the lungs. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Silicosis

The most likely diagnosis is silicosis, an occupational pneumoconiosis caused by prolonged inhalation of crystalline silica dust.

• Long-standing industrial exposure
• Chronic cough and progressive dyspnea
• Snowstorm appearance on chest X-ray due to multiple small nodular opacities
• HRCT showing nodular pulmonary fibrosis
• Classically involves the upper lobes
• May show eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes

Why not the other options?

• A. Asbestosis: Characteristically causes lower-lobe interstitial fibrosis with pleural plaques.
• B. Bagassosis: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by inhalation of moldy sugarcane bagasse.
• C. Byssinosis: Caused by cotton, flax or hemp dust; classically causes Monday chest tightness.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old male working in a stone industry presents with breathlessness and cough. CT Chest shows calcified mediastinal lymph nodes and pulmonary nodules. He is diagnosed with silicosis. Which of the following statements are correct? 1. Silicosis typically involves lower lobes of the lung. 2. The patient is at a higher risk of developing pulmonary tuberculosis. 3. Pulmonary fibrosis after occupational exposure to silica is dose-dependent. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 and 3 only

• 1. Silicosis typically involves lower lobes: Incorrect

• Silicosis classically produces small rounded opacities predominantly in the upper lobes.
• Hilar and mediastinal lymph-node calcification may produce the characteristic “eggshell” calcification.

• 2. Increased risk of pulmonary tuberculosis: Correct

• Silicosis significantly increases susceptibility to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
• The combination is called silicotuberculosis.

• 3. Pulmonary fibrosis is dose-dependent: Correct

• The risk and severity of silicosis correlate with the cumulative dose and duration of silica exposure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old female, a stone-cutter by occupation, had multiple well-circumscribed nodular opacities in upper and middle zones of a chest X-ray along with mediastinal lymph nodes showing egg-shell calcification. Which one of the following is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Silicosis

Silicosis is a pneumoconiosis caused by chronic inhalation of crystalline silica dust, commonly affecting stone-cutters, miners, sandblasters, quarry workers, and ceramic workers.

• Occupational history: Stone-cutting with prolonged silica exposure.
• Chest X-ray:

• Multiple small, well-circumscribed nodular opacities predominantly in the upper and middle lung zones.
• “Egg-shell” calcification of hilar/mediastinal lymph nodes is a classic radiological feature.

• Progressive disease may lead to progressive massive fibrosis (PMF).

Complications:

• Increased risk of tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis)
• COPD
• Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale
• Lung cancer
• Increased risk of autoimmune diseases (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis)

Why not the other options?

• A. Byssinosis: Due to cotton dust exposure; causes chest tightness and obstructive airway disease, not nodular upper lobe fibrosis with egg-shell calcification.
• C. Berylliosis: Due to beryllium exposure (aerospace/electronics); causes granulomatous lung disease resembling sarcoidosis.
• D. Siderosis: Due to iron dust exposure (welders); usually a benign pneumoconiosis without egg-shell lymph node calcification.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A middle aged cement factory worker has developed mesothelioma. This is likely to be associated with
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Asbestosis

Mesothelioma is classically associated with asbestos exposure, leading to asbestosis. Asbestos fibers cause chronic pleural inflammation and malignant transformation of mesothelial cells.

Inhalation of asbestos fibers

↓

Fibers lodge in pleura

↓

Chronic inflammation + ROS damage

↓

DNA damage

Malignant transformation

↓

Mesothelioma (pleural cancer)

| Option | Exposure | Disease | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | -------- | ------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Silicosis | Silica dust | Fibrotic lung disease | Mining, sandblasting | ❌ No mesothelioma link | ↑ TB risk

| B. Asbestosis ✅ | Asbestos fibers | Mesothelioma + fibrosis | ✔ Classic association | ✔ Correct | Pleural plaques

| C. Anthracosis | Coal dust | Carbon deposition | Mild disease | ❌ No malignancy link | “Black lung”

| D. Byssinosis | Cotton dust | Occupational asthma | Textile workers | ❌ Not malignancy | “Monday disease”

Silicosis, anthracosis, and byssinosis are not linked to mesothelioma.

| Exposure | Disease

| -------- | -------

| Asbestos | Mesothelioma + Lung cancer

| Silica | Silicosis + TB

| Coal | Anthracosis

| Cotton | Byssinosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to you with fever, night sweats, ptosis, and bilateral facial nerve palsy. Investigations showed leukocytosis and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sarcoidosis

Fever, night sweats with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and cranial nerve involvement (ptosis, bilateral facial nerve palsy) are classic for neurosarcoidosis.

Sarcoidosis causes non-caseating granulomas and commonly presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

| Option | Key Feature | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | ----------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Sarcoidosis ✅ | BHL + CN VII palsy | ✔ Classic presentation | ✔ Correct | Non-caseating granulomas

| B. Tuberculosis | Caseating granulomas | Fever, weight loss | ❌ Usually unilateral LN + no facial palsy | ADA ↑

| C. Lymphoma | Malignancy | B symptoms + lymphadenopathy | ❌ No cranial nerve palsy | Reed-Sternberg cells

| D. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis | Immune reaction | Exposure history | ❌ No lymphadenopathy + no neuro signs | Bird fancier’s lung

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An industrial worker was brought to a medical facility due to health problems. On his workup including laboratory tests, a finding of basophilic stippling of red blood cells (RBC) was observed. Which among the following is he/she likely to be having?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lead poisoning

Lead poisoning (Plumbism) is an important occupational disease seen in workers involved in battery manufacturing, painting, smelting, ceramics, printing, soldering, and recycling industries.

• Lead inhibits the enzymes δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) dehydratase and ferrochelatase, resulting in defective heme synthesis.
• This leads to:

• Microcytic hypochromic anemia
• Basophilic stippling of RBCs (coarse blue granules due to retained ribosomal RNA)

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Asbestosis: Causes interstitial pulmonary fibrosis, pleural plaques, and mesothelioma; does not cause basophilic stippling.
• B. Farmer’s lung: A hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by inhalation of moldy hay (Micropolyspora faeni); unrelated to RBC changes.
• D. Brucellosis: A zoonotic bacterial infection causing undulant fever; basophilic stippling is not a feature.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: On a chest radiograph, which of the following occupational diseases is most likely to be mistaken as a case of tuberculosis of lungs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Silicosis

• Silicosis is the occupational lung disease most commonly mistaken for pulmonary tuberculosis on chest X-ray.
• Causative agent: Free crystalline silica dust.
• High-risk occupations: Mining, quarrying, sandblasting, stone cutting, foundry work, ceramics, and glass industries.
• Chest X-ray findings:

• Multiple small rounded upper lobe nodules
• Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF)
• “Eggshell” calcification of hilar lymph nodes (classic finding).

• Major complication: Silicotuberculosis due to impaired macrophage function.
• Silicosis also increases the risk of lung cancer, COPD, and cor pulmonale.

Other Important Pneumoconioses

• Anthracosis (Coal workers’ pneumoconiosis): Coal dust exposure.
• Asbestosis: Lower lobe interstitial fibrosis, pleural plaques; associated with bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma.
• Siderosis: Iron dust exposure; benign pneumoconiosis with little or no fibrosis.
• Byssinosis: Cotton dust exposure; presents with chest tightness and occupational asthma (“Monday chest tightness”).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Patient presents with cough, stridor, and dyspnea. On examination, there was lymphadenopathy. Histopathological examination of the lymph node shows granulomas with giant cells and stellate concretions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sarcoidosis

Non-caseating granulomas with giant cells containing stellate concretions (asteroid bodies) are characteristic of sarcoidosis.

Sarcoidosis commonly presents with lymphadenopathy and airway involvement causing cough, stridor, and dyspnea.

• Non-caseating granulomas
• Epithelioid histiocytes
• Inclusion bodies:

• ⭐ Asteroid bodies (stellate)
• Schaumann bodies (calcified)

Schaumann body

Asteroid bodies (stellate)

Tuberculosis shows caseating granulomas, while hypersensitivity pneumonitis and Churg–Strauss lack asteroid bodies.

| Option | Disease Type | Histopathology | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | ------------ | -------------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| Hypersensitivity pneumonitis | Immune-mediated ILD | Poorly formed granulomas | Exposure to organic dust | ❌ No asteroid bodies | Associated with bird exposure

| Churg-Strauss syndrome (EGPA) | Vasculitis | Eosinophils + necrotizing granulomas | Asthma + eosinophilia | ❌ No stellate inclusions | p-ANCA positive

| Tuberculosis | Infectious granuloma | Caseating granuloma | Chronic infection | ❌ Caseation present, no asteroid bodies | ADA ↑ in pleural fluid

| Sarcoidosis ✅ | Non-caseating granuloma | Giant cells + ⭐ asteroid bodies | ✔ Classic finding | ✔ Correct | Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Raju is 30 years of age. He has been working in the ceramic and pottery industry for the last 10 years. Which one of the following conditions should he be screened for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Silicosis

Silicosis is a chronic fibrosing occupational lung disease caused by prolonged inhalation of crystalline silica dust. Workers in ceramic, pottery, mining, quarrying, sandblasting, stone cutting, and foundry industries are at high risk and should undergo regular screening.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Anthracosis:

• Caused by coal dust exposure.
• Seen in coal miners (Coal Workers’ Pneumoconiosis).

• C. Byssinosis:

• Caused by cotton, flax, or hemp dust.
• Seen in textile workers.

• D. Asbestosis:

• Caused by asbestos fibers.
• Seen in shipbuilding, insulation, roofing, and construction workers.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common cause of death in patients with Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Respiratory Failure

Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic progressive interstitial lung disease characterized by:

• Diffuse pulmonary fibrosis
• Progressive stiffening of lung tissue
• Impaired gas exchange

The pathology pattern is called: Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP).

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis causes progressive restrictive lung disease with worsening hypoxemia.

The most common terminal event is respiratory failure due to extensive fibrotic destruction of lung parenchyma.

Pulmonary hypertension and lung cancer may occur but are less common immediate causes of death.

Aspiration pneumonia is not the typical terminal event in IPF.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: With which variety of asbestos, Mesothelioma has been shown to have a strong association?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Crocidolite

Mesothelioma is a highly aggressive malignancy arising from the pleura or peritoneum and is strongly associated with occupational asbestos exposure. Among the different types of asbestos, crocidolite (blue asbestos) has the strongest association with malignant mesothelioma because of its thin, straight fibers, which penetrate deep into the lungs and pleura.

High-Yield Pearls

• Crocidolite (blue asbestos) has the strongest association with mesothelioma. ⭐
• Chrysotile (white asbestos) is the most commonly used form of asbestos but is less strongly associated with mesothelioma than crocidolite. ⭐
• Amosite (brown asbestos) also increases the risk of mesothelioma but less than crocidolite.
• Anthophyllite is the least commonly used and least strongly associated with asbestos-related malignancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A 34-year-old medical student has fever, chest pain, severe breathlessness, and dry cough. Chest X-ray shows right homogeneous opacity. Ultrasound lung confirms massive pleural effusion on the right side. Which of the following statements are correct? 1. A therapeutic pleural tap should be done to relieve dyspnoea and sent for analysis. 2. If pleural fluid analysis is inconclusive, a thoracoscopy may be done. 3. Thoracoscopy should be done under general anesthesia. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 2 only

• 1. Therapeutic pleural tap should be done: Correct

• A massive pleural effusion causing severe breathlessness is an indication for therapeutic thoracentesis to relieve dyspnea.
• The aspirated fluid should also be sent for diagnostic analysis, including protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cell count, Gram stain/culture, and cytology as appropriate.

• 2. Thoracoscopy if pleural fluid analysis is inconclusive: Correct

• If the cause remains undiagnosed after pleural fluid analysis, thoracoscopy (medical thoracoscopy/VATS) can be performed for direct visualization and pleural biopsy.
• It is particularly useful when malignancy or tuberculosis is suspected.

• 3. Thoracoscopy should be done under general anesthesia: Incorrect

• Medical thoracoscopy is generally performed under local anesthesia with conscious sedation.
• VATS (video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery) is performed under general anesthesia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman is diagnosed with pulmonary arterial hypertension. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for reducing pulmonary arterial pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bosentan

Bosentan is an endothelin receptor antagonist (ETA and ETB blocker) used in the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor and smooth muscle mitogen. By blocking endothelin receptors, bosentan reduces pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary arterial pressure, improves exercise capacity, and delays disease progression.

Why not the other options?

• A. Furosemide: Used to relieve fluid overload and right heart failure symptoms, but does not directly reduce pulmonary arterial pressure.
• B. Amlodipine: A calcium channel blocker that is beneficial only in the small subset of PAH patients with a positive vasoreactivity test; it is not the standard treatment for most patients.
• D. Enalapril: An ACE inhibitor used for systemic hypertension and heart failure, but it has no established role in treating PAH.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A 43-year-old male presented with right-sided rib pain and shortness of breath. A chest X-ray showed a significant right-sided pneumothorax with cardio-mediastinal shift to the left. Which of the following changes will be seen?
options: Increased lung volume, Increased thoracic volume
Decreased lung volume, Increased thoracic volume
Decreased lung volume, thoracic volume remains unaffected
Lung volume remains unaffected, Decreased thoracic volume
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decreased lung volume, Increased thoracic volume

A large pneumothorax with mediastinal shift indicates a tension pneumothorax.

Air accumulation in the pleural space causes collapse of the affected lung (decreased lung volume) and expansion of the hemithorax (increased thoracic volume).

The raised intrathoracic pressure leads to mediastinal displacement to the opposite side.

Air enters pleural space (one-way valve)

↑ Intrapleural pressure

Lung collapses → ↓ lung volume

Thoracic cavity expands outward → ↑ thoracic volume

Mediastinum shifts to opposite side

↓ Venous return → shock risk

| Parameter | Change | Why

| --------- | ------ | ---

| Lung volume | ↓ Decreased | Lung collapses due to pressure

| Thoracic volume | ↑ Increased | Chest wall expands outward due to trapped air

| Option | Lung Volume | Thoracic Volume | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | ----------- | --------------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Increased lung + thoracic volume | ↑ | ↑ | Hyperinflation (emphysema) | ❌ Lung actually collapses here | Seen in COPD

| B. Decreased lung, Increased thoracic volume ✅ | ↓ | ↑ | ✔ Tension pneumothorax | ✔ Correct |  Classic combo

| C. Decreased lung, thoracic same | ↓ | No change | Simple collapse (atelectasis) | ❌ Thorax expands in pneumothorax | No mediastinal shift

| D. Lung same, thoracic decreased | Same | ↓ | Restrictive disorders | ❌ Opposite of pneumothorax | Seen in fibrosis

| Type | Key Feature

| ---- | -----------

| Simple pneumothorax | No mediastinal shift

| Tension pneumothorax |  Mediastinal shift + hemodynamic compromise

| Traumatic | Due to injury

| Spontaneous | Young tall males

questions.text: A 44-year-old female who is a known case of scleroderma presented with shortness of breath, especially during exercise. She underwent right heart catheterization, and her mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) was 35 mm Hg. Which of the following is true regarding her condition?
options: CCBs are the first line in all patients
Lung transplant is the best treatment if identified early
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endothelin antagonists improve symptoms

Scleroderma with mPAP ≥25 mmHg indicates pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).

Endothelin receptor antagonists (e.g., bosentan, ambrisentan) reduce pulmonary vascular resistance and improve symptoms and exercise capacity.

| Option | Statement | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | --------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. CCBs are first line in all patients | Vasodilators | Only in vasoreactive patients | ❌ Not for all PAH patients | Do vasoreactivity testing first

| B. Endothelin antagonists improve symptoms ✅ | Block vasoconstriction | ✔ PAH (especially CTD-related) | ✔ Correct |  First-line targeted therapy

| C. Lung transplant is best early | Surgical option | End-stage disease | ❌ Not first-line | Reserved for refractory cases

| D. Lifestyle modification | Supportive care | Mild disease adjunct | ❌ Not definitive therapy | Only supportive

questions.text: A 44-year-old male presented with cough. Chest X-ray revealed pleural effusion. Thoracentesis was done, and the following was observed. Pleural fluid protein to serum protein ratio was 0.6. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pleural TB

A pleural fluid protein-to-serum protein ratio of 0.6 fulfills Light’s criteria for an exudative effusion.

Tuberculous pleural effusion is classically exudative, with high protein content due to increased capillary permeability.

Cirrhosis, CHF, and nephrotic syndrome cause transudative effusions with low protein ratios.

| Feature | Exudate | Transudate

| ------- | ------- | ----------

| Protein ratio | >0.5 | <0.5

| LDH | High | Low

| Cause | Inflammation | Pressure imbalance

| Example | TB, malignancy | CHF, cirrhosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A 53-year-old male patient who is a known case of COPD developed breathlessness and is on mechanical ventilation. He suddenly developed hypoxia, and on examination, he has reduced/absent breath sounds on the left hemithorax with increased peak inspiratory pressure. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pneumothorax

Sudden hypoxia in a ventilated COPD patient with absent breath sounds on one side and increased peak inspiratory pressures is classic for acute pneumothorax, often tension pneumothorax.

COPD patients have fragile bullae that can rupture, especially under positive pressure ventilation.

Mechanical ventilation (positive pressure)

↓

Alveolar overdistension

↓

Alveolar rupture

↓

Air leaks into pleural space

↓

Lung collapse

↓

↓ Breath sounds + ↑ airway pressure

↓

Sudden hypoxia

Pulmonary embolism does not cause unilateral absent breath sounds or raised airway pressures.

| Finding | Likely Diagnosis

| ------- | ----------------

| ↑ Peak pressure + absent breath sounds |  Pneumothorax

| ↑ Peak pressure + wheeze | Bronchospasm

| Normal breath sounds + hypoxia | Pulmonary embolism

| Fever + crackles | Pneumonia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Which of the following drugs used in this condition act as prostacyclin receptor agonists? 1. Epoprostenol 2. Iloprost 3. Ambrisentan 4. Selexipag
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, and 4

Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a story of:

• Vasoconstriction
• Endothelial dysfunction
• Vascular remodeling

The imbalance:

| Vasodilators ↓ | Vasoconstrictors ↑

| -------------- | ------------------

| Prostacyclin (PGI₂) ↓ | Endothelin-1 ↑

| Nitric oxide ↓ | Thromboxane ↑

Treatment targets these pathways like a three-pronged attack.

| Class | Drugs | Mechanism

| ----- | ----- | ---------

| Prostacyclin analogs / agonists | Epoprostenol, Iloprost, Selexipag | Vasodilation, ↓ proliferation

| Endothelin receptor antagonists | Ambrisentan, Bosentan | Block vasoconstriction

| PDE-5 inhibitors | Sildenafil, Tadalafil | ↑ NO → vasodilation

| Pathway | Drug Example | Mnemonic

| Prostacyclin | Epoprostenol | “PROS-tacyclin = PROS vasodilation”

| Endothelin | Ambrisentan | “Endothelin = enemy constrictor”

| NO pathway | Sildenafil | “Sildenafil = smooth flow”

• Prostacyclin drugs = Epoprostenol, Iloprost, Selexipag
• Ambrisentan = NOT prostacyclin (endothelin blocker)
• PAH = 3 major pathways targeted
• Severe PAH → IV prostacyclin (life-saving)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A patient presented with pain on the left side of the chest. On examination, there was dullness on percussion on left infra-axillary area. X-ray Chest showed left opaque hemithorax. Which one of the following is an indication for tube thoracentesis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pleural fluid glucose < 60 mg/dL

• The patient has a left-sided pleural effusion causing dullness to percussion and an opaque hemithorax. Tube thoracostomy (intercostal chest tube drainage) is indicated when the pleural fluid suggests a complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema, particularly when the pleural fluid glucose is <60 mg/dL.
• A low pleural fluid glucose indicates high metabolic activity of bacteria and inflammatory cells and impaired glucose transport across the inflamed pleura.

Why not the other options?

• A. Straw-coloured fluid: Common in uncomplicated pleural effusions and does not itself indicate chest-tube drainage.
• B. Pleural fluid pH >7.2: A pH >7.20 generally argues against a complicated parapneumonic effusion requiring drainage. pH <7.20 is the important threshold.
• D. Pleural fluid LDH <600 IU/L: A low LDH does not indicate complicated infection. Markedly elevated LDH supports an inflammatory/exudative process.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A patient who had undergone knee replacement surgery 7 days back, now presents with complaints of sudden shortness of breath and tachycardia. What is the next appropriate diagnostic test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CT pulmonary angiography

| Clue | What it screams

| ---- | ---------------

| Recent surgery (knee replacement) | Major risk for DVT

| 7 days later | Peak risk window

| Sudden dyspnea | Acute event

| Tachycardia | Physiologic stress

Recent major orthopedic surgery with sudden dyspnea and tachycardia indicates high clinical probability of pulmonary embolism.

In high-risk patients, CT pulmonary angiography is the first-line diagnostic test to directly visualize pulmonary arterial thrombi.

CT pulmonary angiography image showing filling defects in the pulmonary vasculature.

D-dimer is unreliable post-surgery, and V/Q scan is reserved when CTPA is contraindicated.

| Clinical Suspicion | Next Step

| ------------------ | ---------

| Low probability | D-dimer

| High probability | CTPA directly

| Renal failure / pregnancy | V/Q scan

questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: Consider the following criteria: 1. Pleural fluid protein:Serum protein ratio > 0.5 2. Pleural fluid LDH:Serum LDH ratio > 0.6 3. Pleural fluid LDH > Two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH Which of the above criteria, if present in pleural fluid, will indicate an exudate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

The Light’s criteria are the most widely used criteria to differentiate exudative from transudative pleural effusions. A pleural effusion is classified as an exudate if any one of the following criteria is present:

1. Pleural fluid protein / Serum protein ratio > 0.5
2. Pleural fluid LDH / Serum LDH ratio > 0.6
3. Pleural fluid LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH

Common causes:

• Exudative effusions: Pneumonia (parapneumonic effusion), tuberculosis, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, pancreatitis, connective tissue diseases.
• Transudative effusions: Congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminemia.

Limitations:

• Light’s criteria are highly sensitive for detecting exudates but may misclassify some transudates (especially in patients with heart failure receiving diuretics) as exudates. In such cases, the serum–pleural fluid albumin gradient (>1.2 g/dL) or protein gradient (>3.1 g/dL) can help identify a true transudate.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: Consider the following pleural fluid analysis: • pH: 7.6 • Pleural fluid protein: 0.5 g/dL • Serum total protein: 6.5 g/dL • Pleural fluid LDH: 100 U/L • Serum LDH: 300 U/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Myxedema

The pleural fluid analysis is consistent with a transudative pleural effusion according to Light’s criteria:

• Pleural fluid protein/Serum protein = 0.5/6.5 = 0.08 (<0.5)
• Pleural fluid LDH/Serum LDH = 100/300 = 0.33 (<0.6)
• Pleural fluid LDH is not greater than two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

These findings indicate a transudative effusion. Myxedema (severe hypothyroidism) is a recognized cause of transudative pleural effusion due to increased capillary permeability and impaired lymphatic drainage.

Why not the other options?

• A. Pancreatitis: Produces an exudative pleural effusion with very high amylase levels.
• C. Sarcoidosis: Rarely causes pleural effusion, but when present it is exudative.
• D. Rheumatoid arthritis: Causes a characteristic exudative effusion with low pH (<7.2), low glucose, and high LDH.

| Transudative Effusion | Exudative Effusion

| --------------------- | ------------------

| Heart failure | Pneumonia (parapneumonic)

| Cirrhosis | Tuberculosis

| Nephrotic syndrome | Malignancy

| Myxedema (hypothyroidism) | Pancreatitis

| Hypoalbuminemia | Rheumatoid arthritis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to pulmonary embolism: 1. Unexplained breathlessness is the most common symptom. 2. When congestive heart failure or pneumonia fail to improve despite standard medical treatment, occult pulmonary embolism should be considered. 3. Patients with high clinical likelihood of venous thromboembolism should first undergo D-dimer testing alone without obligatory imaging tests. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 2 only

Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a potentially life-threatening condition caused by obstruction of the pulmonary arteries, most commonly by thrombi originating from the deep veins of the lower limbs.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Unexplained breathlessness is the most common symptom: Correct. Unexplained dyspnoea (breathlessness) is the most common presenting symptom of pulmonary embolism.
• Statement 2. When congestive heart failure or pneumonia fail to improve despite standard medical treatment, occult pulmonary embolism should be considered: Correct. If congestive heart failure or pneumonia fails to improve despite appropriate treatment, occult pulmonary embolism should be suspected, especially in patients with risk factors for venous thromboembolism.
• Statement 3. Patients with high clinical likelihood of venous thromboembolism should first undergo D-dimer testing alone without obligatory imaging tests: Incorrect. In patients with a high clinical probability of PE, imaging (usually CT pulmonary angiography) should be performed promptly. D-dimer testing alone is not recommended, as a negative D-dimer cannot reliably exclude PE in high-risk patients.

questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: Inhaled NO is used in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary Pulmonary Artery Hypertension

-It selectively dilates pulmonary vessels only

-Improves ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) matching

-Reduces pulmonary artery pressure

Hence used in:

• Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH)
• Especially:

• Acute vasoreactivity testing
• ICU settings
•

Inhaled nitric oxide causes selective pulmonary vasodilation by increasing cGMP in pulmonary vascular smooth muscle.

It reduces pulmonary artery pressure without causing systemic hypotension, making it useful in primary pulmonary arterial hypertension.

It is not indicated for OSA, unstable angina, or erectile dysfunction.

| Option | Condition | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | --------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Primary Pulmonary Artery Hypertension ✅ | ↑ Pulmonary vascular resistance | ✔ Used for selective pulmonary vasodilation | ✔ Correct | Used for vasoreactivity testing in PAH

| B. Obstructive Sleep Apnea | Upper airway obstruction | CPAP is treatment | ❌ Problem is airway collapse, not vascular tone | Treat with CPAP, not NO

| C. Unstable Angina | Coronary ischemia | Systemic nitrates (GTN) used | ❌ Inhaled NO acts only in lungs | NO inhalation does NOT affect coronary arteries significantly

| D. Erectile Dysfunction | Vascular relaxation needed | PDE-5 inhibitors (Sildenafil) used | ❌ Inhaled NO not practical/systemic | Sildenafil works via NO pathway, not inhaled NO

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: 2, 3 BPG binds with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Globin part of hemoglobin

2,3-BPG binds to the globin chains of deoxyhemoglobin in the central cavity between the β-chains.

This stabilizes the T (tense) state, reducing hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen and facilitating tissue oxygen delivery.

2,3-BPG produced in RBC glycolysis

↓

Binds to deoxyhemoglobin (β-globin chains)

↓

Stabilizes T (tense) state of Hb

↓

↓ Affinity of Hb for O₂

↓

↑ Oxygen release to tissues

↓

Right shift of O₂ dissociation curve

It does not bind to the heme moiety or to myoglobin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old male rapidly ascends from sea level to an altitude of 4000 meters and, within 24 hours, develops headache, dizziness, ataxia, confusion, and shortness of breath. On examination, he is tachycardic and tachypneic, with low oxygen saturation and signs of pulmonary edema. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediate descent to a lower altitude
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immediate descent to a lower altitude

Severe acute mountain sickness (AMS) with features of high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE) (ataxia, confusion) and high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) (dyspnea, hypoxemia, pulmonary edema) is a life-threatening medical emergency. The definitive treatment is immediate descent to a lower altitude, which rapidly improves hypoxia and prevents progression to respiratory failure or death. Supplemental oxygen should be administered whenever available.

Why not the other options?

• A. Acetazolamide: Used for prevention and treatment of mild AMS by inducing a mild metabolic acidosis that stimulates ventilation; not sufficient for HACE or HAPE.
• C. Dexamethasone: Effective for HACE and can be used as an adjunct or when descent is delayed, but it does not replace immediate descent.
• D. Intravenous furosemide: Not recommended for HAPE because pulmonary edema is non-cardiogenic and diuresis may worsen dehydration and hypovolemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old male presented to OPD with complaints of excessive daytime sleepiness, and his wife also complains that he snores a lot at night during sleep. Which of the following is incorrect regarding his condition?
options: Increased tone of the pharyngeal muscles worsens obstruction
Fall of oxygen saturation triggers waking episodes at night
Episodes of apnea increase stress on the heart
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased tone of the pharyngeal muscles worsens obstruction

Clues:

• Excessive daytime sleepiness
• Loud snoring

Classic for Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)

Sleep

↓

↓ Pharyngeal muscle tone

↓

Airway collapse

↓

Apnea (no airflow)

↓

↓ Oxygen saturation

↓

Arousal from sleep

↓

Cycle repeats

| Feature | OSA Mechanism

| ------- | -------------

| Muscle tone | ↓ (causes obstruction)

| Oxygen level | ↓ (hypoxemia)

| Arousal | Triggered by hypoxia

| Cardiac effect | ↑ Stress (HTN, arrhythmia)

| Respiratory drive | ↑ due to hypoxemia

OSA Risk Factors

| Factor | Effect

| ------ | ------

| Obesity | ↑ airway narrowing

| Large neck circumference | ↑ obstruction

| Alcohol | ↓ muscle tone

| Sedatives | ↓ muscle tone

| Treatment | Role

| --------- | ----

| CPAP | First-line

| Weight loss | Essential

| Surgery | Selected cases

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 42-year-old patient’s pulmonary function test shows FEV1/FVC = 0.62 FVC = 60% RV/TLC = 142% Which of the following best explains these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Air trapping

| Parameter | Value | Interpretation

| --------- | ----- | --------------

| FEV₁/FVC | 0.62 (<0.7) |  Obstructive pattern

| FVC | 60% predicted | Reduced (due to air trapping)

| RV/TLC | 142% ↑ |  Air trapping (key finding)

Air enters lungs but cannot fully exit due to:

• Airway narrowing
• Loss of elastic recoil

Leads to:

• ↑ Residual Volume (RV)
• ↑ RV/TLC ratio
• Hyperinflation

Air Trapping-

Air enters lungs but cannot fully exit due to:

• Airway narrowing
• Loss of elastic recoil

Leads to:

• ↑ Residual Volume (RV)
• ↑ RV/TLC ratio
• Hyperinflation

| Feature | Obstructive (COPD) | Restrictive (ILD)

| ------- | ------------------ | -----------------

| FEV₁/FVC | 🔻 Decreased | Normal/↑

| FVC | Normal/↓ | 🔻 ↓

| RV |  ↑ | ↓

| RV/TLC |  ↑ | Normal/↓

| TLC | ↑ | ↓

| Feature | True Restriction | Pseudo Restriction (Obstruction)

| ------- | ---------------- | --------------------------------

| TLC | ↓ | Normal/↑

| RV | ↓ |  ↑

| RV/TLC | Normal |  ↑

| Cause | ILD | COPD

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old male, with a history of smoking presents with progressive dyspnea and dry cough. Examination reveals clubbing and fine basal crackles. Spirometry shows low forced vital capacity (FVC) and low diffusion capacity (DLCO). CT Chest shows extensive bilateral reticular shadows and subpleural honeycombing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

The combination of elderly age, progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, clubbing, fine “Velcro” basal crackles, restrictive PFTs (↓FVC), ↓DLCO, and CT showing bilateral subpleural reticular opacities with honeycombing is classic for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern.

Why not the other options?

• B. Sarcoidosis: Typically shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, perilymphatic nodules, and upper/mid-zone predominance.
• C. COPD: Shows an obstructive pattern with ↓FEV₁/FVC; emphysema may show hyperinflation rather than restrictive physiology and classic basal honeycombing.
• D. Bronchiectasis: Characterized by permanent bronchial dilation, recurrent productive cough, and CT findings such as signet-ring sign, not subpleural honeycombing.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old patient with bronchogenic carcinoma undergoes a pneumonectomy one side. Which of the following parameter should be measured to accurately assess the elasticity of the remaining lung, independent of changes in lung volume?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Specific lung compliance

Specific lung compliance is the lung compliance normalized for lung volume (usually functional residual capacity, FRC). It reflects the intrinsic elastic properties of the lung tissue, independent of lung size. After pneumonectomy, total lung volume is reduced, making specific compliance the most accurate parameter for assessing the elasticity of the remaining lung.

Why not the other options?

• A. Total lung compliance: Depends on lung size and volume; it decreases after pneumonectomy even if the intrinsic elasticity of the remaining lung is normal.
• C. Static lung compliance: Measured in the absence of airflow and reflects lung distensibility, but it is still affected by lung volume.
• D. Chest wall compliance: Assesses the elasticity of the thoracic cage, not the lung parenchyma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A decline in total lung capacity to less than 80% of the patient’s predicted value is an indication of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Restrictive lung disease

A reduction in total lung capacity (TLC) to <80% of the predicted value is the hallmark of restrictive lung disease. Restrictive disorders reduce lung expansion, leading to decreased TLC, FRC, and residual volume (RV). Spirometry typically shows reduced FVC with a normal or increased FEV₁/FVC ratio.

Why not the other options?

• B. Obstructive lung disease: Characterized by airflow limitation with reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio; TLC is often normal or increased due to air trapping.
• C. Pulmonary arterial hypertension: Does not typically cause a reduced TLC; pulmonary function tests may be normal or show only mild abnormalities.
• D. Pulmonary embolism: Usually does not produce a restrictive pattern with reduced TLC.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A man is flying at an altitude of 3,400 meters and develops confusion, headache, and signs of cerebral edema. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the pathophysiology of high-altitude cerebral edema?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypoxia causing cerebral vasodilation

High altitude (↓ atmospheric pressure)

↓

↓ Inspired PO₂ → Hypoxemia

↓

Cerebral hypoxia

↓

Cerebral vasodilation (to increase O₂ delivery)

↓

↑ Cerebral blood flow + ↑ capillary hydrostatic pressure

↓

Capillary leak + BBB disruption

↓

Cerebral edema → ↑ ICP

↓

Confusion, headache, coma (HACE)

High-altitude cerebral edema results from hypoxia-induced cerebral vasodilation that increases cerebral blood flow and capillary pressure. This disrupts the blood–brain barrier and causes vasogenic edema. Hypoxia does not cause vasoconstriction in the brain. CO₂ retention is not the primary driver at altitude. The key mechanism is hypoxia-mediated cerebral vasodilation.

| Option | Mechanism | Correct/Incorrect | Explanation

| ------ | --------- | ----------------- | -----------

| A | Hypoxia → vasodilation | ✅ CORRECT | Primary mechanism → ↑ CBF → edema

| B | Metabolic acidosis | ❌ Incorrect | High altitude causes respiratory alkalosis, not metabolic acidosis

| C | Hypoxia → vasoconstriction | ❌ Incorrect | Brain responds with vasodilation, not constriction

| D | High PCO₂ → vasoconstriction | ❌ Incorrect | CO₂ actually causes vasodilation, not constriction

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient expired as he has accidentally suffered from an unknown gas poisoning. He had cherry red appearance of his blood at the post-mortem finding. Which of the following is the likely cause of his death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anemic hypoxia

Cherry red coloration of blood is characteristic of carbon monoxide poisoning, where CO binds hemoglobin with high affinity forming carboxyhemoglobin.

This reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood, despite normal PaO₂, producing anemic hypoxia.

| Option | Type of Hypoxia | Mechanism | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | --------------- | --------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Hypoxic hypoxia | ↓ PaO₂ | High altitude, lung disease | Low oxygen in blood | ❌ PaO₂ may be normal in CO poisoning | Cyanosis present

| B. Histotoxic hypoxia | Cells can’t use O₂ | Cyanide poisoning | Mitochondrial poisoning | ❌ Blood O₂ normal, no cherry red | Venous O₂ high

| C. Anemic hypoxia ✅ | ↓ O₂-carrying capacity | CO poisoning, anemia | ✔ Hb ineffective | ✔ Correct | Cherry-red hallmark

| D. Ischemic hypoxia | ↓ blood flow | Shock, heart failure | Perfusion problem | ❌ Not Hb issue | Local hypoxia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a history of chronic smoking presented with breathlessness for the last one year. On examination, there were bilateral rhonchi in the chest. The Chest X-ray was suggestive of hyper-inflated lung field. Which of the following parameters of the pulmonary function test are consistent with the diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in this case? 1. Decreased FEV₁ 2. Increased diffusion capacity 3. Increased residual volume 4. Decreased peak expiratory flow rate Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3 and 4

COPD is an obstructive airway disease characterized by reduced expiratory airflow and air trapping. The PFT findings in this patient are:

• 1. Decreased FEV₁: Correct.

• Airflow obstruction causes a marked reduction in FEV₁.
• FEV₁/FVC < 0.70 is characteristic of persistent airflow obstruction.

• 2. Increased diffusion capacity: Incorrect.

• In emphysema, destruction of alveolar walls reduces the surface area for gas exchange → ↓ DLCO.
• In chronic bronchitis, DLCO is usually normal.

• 3. Increased residual volume: Correct.

• Air trapping due to expiratory airway collapse → ↑ RV and often ↑ RV/TLC.

• 4. Decreased peak expiratory flow rate: Correct.

• Airway obstruction reduces maximal expiratory flow → ↓ PEFR.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A preterm baby who was delivered at 28 weeks developed respiratory distress syndrome. Which of the following is true about surface tension and compliance in this baby?
options: Both surface tension and compliance decreased
Both surface tension and compliance increased
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Surface tension - increased; Compliance - decreased

Preterm infants lack adequate surfactant, leading to increased alveolar surface tension.

High surface tension causes alveolar collapse, resulting in decreased lung compliance and increased work of breathing.

This pathophysiology underlies neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

Prematurity (Type II pneumocytes immature)

↑ Surface tension in alveoli

Alveolar collapse (atelectasis)

↓ Lung compliance (stiff lungs)

Respiratory distress

| Option | Surface Tension | Compliance | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | --------------- | ---------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A | ↓ | ↑ | Surfactant excess | ❌ Opposite of RDS | Seen in therapy

| B ✅ | ↑ | ↓ | ✔ Surfactant deficiency | ✔ Correct | Classic NRDS

| C | ↓ | ↓ | Mixed pattern | ❌ Surface tension actually ↑ | Illogical combo

| D | ↑ | ↑ | Not physiologically valid | ❌ Compliance always ↓ with ↑ tension | Trap option

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding respiratory function in old age: I. There is increasing ventilation-perfusion mismatch II. There is increased ventilatory response to hypoxia and hypercapnia III. There is a decline in maximum oxygen uptake leading to reduction in cardiorespiratory reserve IV. There is decline in the Forced Expiratory Volume to Forced Vital Capacity ratio (FEV1/FVC) by around 0.2% per year after the forties Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, III and IV

Normal aging is associated with several physiological changes in the respiratory system that reduce pulmonary reserve and gas exchange efficiency. These changes increase the susceptibility of older adults to respiratory failure, pneumonia, and hypoxemia.

The following statements are true:

• I. There is increasing ventilation-perfusion mismatch: Age-related loss of alveolar surface area and uneven ventilation/perfusion lead to progressive V/Q mismatch, causing a gradual decline in PaO₂.
• III. There is a decline in maximum oxygen uptake leading to reduction in cardiorespiratory reserve: There is a reduction in VO₂ max due to decreased cardiac output, muscle mass, and pulmonary reserve, resulting in reduced cardiorespiratory reserve.
• IV. There is decline in the Forced Expiratory Volume to Forced Vital Capacity ratio (FEV1/FVC) by around 0.2% per year after the forties: Aging causes loss of elastic recoil and increased chest wall stiffness, leading to a gradual decline in FEV₁ that exceeds the decline in FVC, resulting in a small annual reduction in the FEV₁/FVC ratio.

Why is Statement II incorrect?

• II. There is increased ventilatory response to hypoxia and hypercapnia: This is incorrect because aging decreases the ventilatory response to both hypoxia and hypercapnia due to reduced chemoreceptor sensitivity. Consequently, elderly individuals are more prone to respiratory failure and drug-induced hypoventilation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: During which phase is the surface tension in the alveoli at its highest?
options: Goes from standing to supine position
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inspiration

Alveoli are lined by fluid → this creates surface tension, which:

• Tends to collapse alveoli
• Is counteracted by surfactant

Laplace Law

Where:

• P = collapsing pressure
• T = surface tension
• r = radius of alveolus

Alveolus size changes during breathing

↓

Inspiration → alveolus expands (↑ radius)

↓

Surfactant spreads → ↓ surfactant concentration leading to increased surface tension

| Feature | Inspiration | Expiration

| ------- | ----------- | ----------

| Alveolar size | ↑ | ↓

| Radius (r) | ↑ | ↓

| Surfactant spread | Diluted | Concentrated

| Surface tension | ↑ | ↓

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a case of myasthenia gravis, repetitive nerve stimulation shows a decremental response. What is the rationale explaining this?
options: Reduced ACh receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
Depletion of ACh in the presynaptic vesicles
Autoantibodies blocking Calcium entry in the presynaptic terminal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reduced ACh receptors on the postsynaptic membrane

Myasthenia gravis is a postsynaptic disorder:

• Autoantibodies against:

• Nicotinic ACh receptors (Nm type)

• Result:

• ↓ number of functional receptors
• ↓ end-plate potential

Muscle fiber fails to reach threshold with repeated stimulation.

| Feature | Myasthenia Gravis | Lambert-Eaton Syndrome

| ------- | ----------------- | ----------------------

| Site | Postsynaptic | Presynaptic

| Antibody | ACh receptor | Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channel

| EMG response | 🔻 Decremental | 🔺 Incremental

| Muscle strength | Worsens with use | Improves with use

| Reflexes | Normal | Reduced

| Association | Thymoma | Small cell lung cancer

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In Decompression sickness, which one of the following is not seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemodilution

Decompression sickness results from nitrogen bubble formation causing vascular obstruction and endothelial injury.

High pressure underwater

↓

↑ Nitrogen dissolved in tissues

↓

Rapid ascent

↓

↓ Pressure

↓

Nitrogen bubbles form

↓

Vascular obstruction + inflammation

↓

Ischemia + organ dysfunction

It produces neurologic deficits, hearing and visual disturbances, and can trigger thrombosis/coagulopathy due to intravascular bubble-induced activation.

Types of Decompression Sickness:

| Type | Feature

| ---- | -------

| Type I | Mild (joint pain, skin)

| Type II | Severe (CNS, lungs, vestibular)

Hemoconcentration, not hemodilution, is typically seen due to plasma leakage. Hence hemodilution is not a feature.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Peripheral chemoreceptors are most sensitive to which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypoxia

Located in:

• Carotid body (most important)
• Aortic body

They respond to:

• ↓ PaO₂ (primary stimulus)
• ↑ PaCO₂
• ↓ pH (acidosis)

Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies are most sensitive to arterial hypoxemia (↓PaO₂), especially when PaO₂ falls below \~60 mmHg.

They respond rapidly to hypoxia and provide the primary ventilatory drive in low-oxygen states.

CO₂ and pH are mainly sensed by central chemoreceptors.

| Feature | Peripheral | Central

| ------- | ---------- | -------

| Location | Carotid & aortic bodies | Medulla

| Primary stimulus |  ↓ O₂ | ↑ CO₂ (via pH)

| Speed | Rapid | Slower

| Role in COPD | Important | Blunted

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The respiratory motor neuron associated with origin of respiratory cycle is located in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior medulla oblongata

The dorsal respiratory group (DRG), located in the posterior (dorsal) medulla oblongata within the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), is classically regarded as the inspiratory centre responsible for initiating the normal respiratory cycle. It generates the inspiratory drive during quiet breathing and receives afferent input from peripheral chemoreceptors and pulmonary stretch receptors via the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal expiration is called:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Functional residual capacity

Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal (tidal) expiration. It represents the sum of:

• Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV)
• Residual Volume (RV)

FRC = ERV + RV

Why not the other options?

• A. Expiratory residual volume: Not a standard lung volume term.
• C. Residual volume: Air remaining after maximal forced expiration.
• D. Vital capacity: Maximum volume exhaled after a maximal inspiration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What physiological change causes the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to shift to the left?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreased CO₂

A left shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve occurs with decreased CO₂, reflecting reduced hydrogen ion concentration (alkalosis).

This increases hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen, favoring oxygen loading in the lungs. In contrast, increased temperature, increased 2,3-BPG, and decreased pH cause a right shift.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following occur during the beginning cough reflex?
options: Forced expiration against a closed glottis
Forced expiration against an open glottis
Forced inspiration against a closed glottis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Forced expiration against a closed glottis

| Phase | Event

| ----- | -----
