| Inspiratory phase | Deep inspiration

| Compression phase | Forced expiration against closed glottis

| Expulsive phase | Sudden opening of glottis → explosive airflow

The cough reflex begins with deep inspiration followed by closure of the glottis.

This is followed by forced expiration against a closed glottis, generating high intrathoracic pressure.

Sudden opening of the glottis then expels air explosively to clear irritants.

Hence, forced expiration against a closed glottis marks the beginning of the cough reflex.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is correct about physiological dead space?
options: It is less than anatomical dead space
It can be measured by spirometry
It is because of inadequate perfusion
It is because of inadequate ventilation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is because of inadequate perfusion

| Type | Definition

| ---- | ----------

| Anatomical dead space | Conducting airways (no alveoli)

| Alveolar dead space | Ventilated alveoli but no perfusion

|  Physiological dead space | Anatomical + alveolar dead space

Physiological dead space includes alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused, due to inadequate pulmonary blood flow.

It equals anatomical dead space plus alveolar dead space and therefore is greater than or equal to anatomical dead space.

Spirometry measures volumes, not dead space, and inadequate ventilation cause shunt, not dead space.

| Feature | Dead Space | Shunt

| ------- | ---------- | -----

| Ventilation | ✔️ Present | ❌ Absent

| Perfusion | ❌ Absent | ✔️ Present

| V/Q ratio | ∞ | 0

| Example | PE | Pneumonia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 27-year-old man presents with acute onset severe pain, swelling, and redness of the left knee for 2 days. He reports associated fever and inability to bear weight. There is no history of trauma. He consumes alcohol regularly. On examination, temperature is 38.3°C. The left knee is erythematous, warm, markedly tender, and has severely restricted active and passive range of motion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Start NSAIDs and review after 48 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Synovial fluid analysis

This patient presents with acute monoarthritis with systemic features (fever)—a clinical scenario that must be assumed to be septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Key red flags:

• Acute monoarticular arthritis
• Fever
• Severe pain with restriction of both active and passive movement

The most important next step is urgent arthrocentesis to analyze synovial fluid for:

• Gram stain and culture
• Cell count (typically >50,000 WBCs in septic arthritis)
• Crystals (to rule out gout/pseudogout)

Why not other options?

A. NSAIDs → Delays diagnosis of a potentially joint-destructive emergency

B. Serum uric acid → Can be normal during acute gout; does not rule out septic arthritis

C. Rheumatoid factor → Chronic disease; not relevant in acute monoarthritis

MRI → Not first-line; diagnosis is clinical + synovial fluid

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 72-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to persistent headaches, fatigue, and muscle pain. She has a history of hypertension and osteoarthritis. Her father had a subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm. She is treated with prednisone, leading to marked and rapid improvement in her symptoms. Which of the following pathologic processes is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?
options: Homogenous acellular thickening of arteriolar walls
Onion-like concentric thickening of arteriolar walls
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Granulomatous inflammation of the media

An elderly patient with headache, fatigue, muscle pain (polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms) and rapid response to prednisone --> suggests Giant cell (temporal) arteritis.

Pathology of giant cell arteritis:

• Granulomatous inflammation of large and medium arteries
• Predominantly involves branches of carotid artery (temporal artery)
• Granulomatous inflammation of tunica media
• Multinucleated giant cells and fragmentation of internal elastic lamina
• Leads to luminal narrowing → ischemic symptoms (headache, jaw claudication, vision loss)

Key association:

• Strong association with polymyalgia rheumatica
• Elevated ESR/CRP
• Dramatic response to corticosteroids

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 20-year-old man presents with severe abdominal pain, numbness of both lower limbs and the right upper limb, and generalized malaise. On examination, his pulse is 88/min and blood pressure is 160/110 mmHg. All peripheral pulses are palpable. Laboratory evaluation shows: Normal renal function Urinalysis: proteinuria with RBCs but no casts Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Classical polyarteritis nodosa

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that causes multisystem ischemia without glomerulonephritis.

• Severe abdominal pain (mesenteric ischemia)
• Mononeuritis multiplex → limb numbness/neuropathy
• Hypertension due to renal artery involvement
• Constitutional symptoms (fever, malaise)

Renal findings:

• Renal ischemia → hypertension
• Proteinuria and hematuria without RBC casts
• No glomerulonephritis (distinguishes from microscopic polyangiitis and GPA)

Thus, systemic symptoms + neuropathy + abdominal pain + hypertension with preserved renal function strongly suggest classical PAN.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 24-year-old man presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales over the extensor surfaces for 6 months. He later develops pain and swelling of DIP joints with morning stiffness. His father has a similar skin disease. Which HLA type is most strongly associated with this patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HLA-Cw6

•

The patient has psoriasis with psoriatic arthritis (extensor erythematous plaques with silvery scales + DIP joint involvement + family history).

•

The HLA type most strongly associated with psoriasis (especially early-onset and familial psoriasis) is HLA-Cw6.

Key associations:

• HLA-Cw6 → Psoriasis
• HLA-B27 → Ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis
• HLA-DR4 → Rheumatoid arthritis
• HLA-B51 → Behçet’s disease

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and non-erosive arthritis. Urinalysis reveals proteinuria and hematuria. Renal biopsy is performed, and immunofluorescence shows deposition of multiple immunoglobulins and complement components in the glomeruli. Which of the following immunofluorescence findings is most characteristic of lupus nephritis?
options: IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q deposition
IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C2 deposition
IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and properdin deposition
IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1 inhibitor deposition
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q deposition

This patient has systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with lupus nephritis. The characteristic immunofluorescence finding is the “full-house” pattern, reflecting deposition of multiple immunoglobulins and complement components due to immune complex-mediated glomerular injury.

The classic full-house immunofluorescence pattern consists of:

• IgG
• IgA
• IgM
• C3
• C1q

Presence of C1q indicates activation of the classical complement pathway, a hallmark of lupus nephritis.

Why not the others?

• B. IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C2 deposition → C2 participates in complement activation but is not part of the classic diagnostic immunofluorescence pattern.
• C. IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and properdin deposition → Properdin is associated with the alternative complement pathway, not the characteristic lupus pattern.
• D. IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1 inhibitor deposition → Not a recognized feature of lupus nephritis immunofluorescence.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents with chronic inflammatory low back pain, marked morning stiffness lasting >1 hour, and improvement with physical activity. Imaging shows bilateral sacroiliitis. He has no peripheral arthritis or extra-articular organ involvement. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)

This patient has ankylosing spondylitis (axial spondyloarthritis), characterized by inflammatory back pain, prolonged morning stiffness, improvement with exercise, and bilateral sacroiliitis. In patients with predominantly axial disease and no significant peripheral manifestations, NSAIDs are the recommended first-line treatment because they reduce pain, stiffness, and inflammation and may slow radiographic progression.

Why not the other options?

• A. Methotrexate – ineffective for isolated axial disease; mainly used for peripheral arthritis.
• B. Sulfasalazine – may benefit peripheral joint involvement but has limited efficacy in axial symptoms.
• D. Anti-TNF-α therapy – reserved for patients with active disease despite an adequate trial of NSAIDs.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents with recurrent painless oral ulcers that have not responded to vitamin B12 injections. She also complains of easy fatigability and low-grade fever for the past 2 months. There is no significant past medical history. Which of the following laboratory findings is not expected in this patient?
options: All of the above can occur
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased serum complement levels

Recurrent painless oral ulcers with constitutional symptoms may suggest systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

Typical laboratory findings in SLE:

• Positive ANA (usually ≥1:160)
• Positive direct Coombs test due to autoimmune hemolysis
• Low complement levels (C3, C4) due to immune-complex consumption

Complement levels are typically decreased, not increased, especially during active disease.

Thus, increased serum complement levels are not expected in active SLE.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) after presenting with photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and inflammatory polyarthritis. Her renal and CNS evaluation is currently normal. Which of the following drugs is recommended for long-term use in all patients with SLE, unless contraindicated, due to its disease-modifying and survival benefits?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydroxychloroquine

Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is recommended for all patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) unless contraindicated because it provides significant disease-modifying and survival benefits.

• Reduces disease flares
• Improves skin and joint symptoms
• Decreases thrombosis risk
• Protects against organ damage
• Improves overall survival

It is considered baseline long-term therapy even in mild SLE without major organ involvement.

Other drugs:

B. Anesthetic agents → no role in SLE treatment

C. Corticosteroids → for acute flares, not ideal long-term due to toxicity

D. Methotrexate → used for arthritis/skin disease in selected patients

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department due to progressive lethargy, fatigue, and nausea over the past month. She has also experienced constipation, muscle weakness, increased thirst, and frequent urination. She reports taking high doses of calcium and vitamin D supplements after reading they could improve bone health. On examination, she is stuporous and has dry mucous membranes. The metabolic abnormality most likely responsible for this patient’s clinical findings can also occur in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sarcoidosis

Excess intake of calcium and vitamin D can lead to hypercalcemia, which presents with:

• Lethargy, confusion, stupor
• Constipation
• Polyuria and polydipsia
• Muscle weakness
• Dehydration

This patient’s symptoms are classic for hypercalcemia. Hypercalcemia can also occur in sarcoidosis because activated macrophages in granulomas express 1-α hydroxylase, which converts vitamin D to its active form (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D).

This leads to increased intestinal calcium absorption → hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to a 3-month history of painful, swollen wrists and knees. She also has joint stiffness, which is worse upon wakening and limits her daily activities. The patient's only other medical condition is hypothyroidism for which she takes levothyroxine. Plain radiographs of the joints show joint space narrowing and marginal erosions. Which of the following cytokines are primarily involved in the pathogenesis of this patient's joint destruction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IL-1 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is driven by pro-inflammatory cytokines that promote synovial inflammation and joint destruction. The key cytokines involved are:

• Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α)
• Interleukin-1 (IL-1)
• Also IL-6 contributes significantly

These cytokines cause:

• Synovial proliferation (pannus formation)
• Cartilage degradation
• Osteoclast activation → bone erosion
• Systemic inflammation

This understanding forms the basis for biologic therapy:

• Anti-TNF drugs (etanercept, infliximab)
• IL-1 inhibitors
• IL-6 inhibitors (tocilizumab)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician due to painful urination. Physical examination shows a watery penile discharge. Urethral swabs obtained from the patient are negative for gonococcal infection. He is treated appropriately and his symptoms resolve. Two weeks later, he develops acute conjunctivitis, right knee pain, and vesicular rash on his palms and soles. This patient's condition is most likely associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sacroilitis

This patient has reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome) following a nongonococcal urethritis (commonly due to Chlamydia).

Classic triad:

• Urethritis
• Conjunctivitis
• Arthritis

Additional features:

• Asymmetric oligoarthritis (often knee)
• Vesicular rash on palms/soles (keratoderma blennorrhagicum)
• Strong association with HLA-B27
• May develop sacroiliitis and axial involvement

Thus, reactive arthritis is commonly associated with sacroiliitis, a feature of seronegative spondyloarthropathies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 35-year-old man comes to the clinic with acute right knee pain and swelling. His symptoms have been present for a week and have moderately worsened over this period. The patient is able to bear weight but has significant pain when climbing stairs or walking for extended distances. Past medical history is unremarkable, though the patient was seen by his primary care provider for a diarrheal illness 2 weeks before onset of the current symptoms. Examination shows a moderate-sized effusion at the right knee. Cultures of a joint aspirate reveal no bacteria. Which of the following is most likely associated with this patient's joint symptoms?
options: High titors of antistreptolysin O antibodies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Histocompatibility antigen HLA-B27

This patient has reactive arthritis, suggested by:

• Acute monoarthritis (knee effusion)
• Sterile joint aspirate
• Recent diarrheal illness (post-infectious trigger)

Reactive arthritis is:

• A seronegative spondyloarthropathy
• Triggered by GI infections (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter) or GU infections (Chlamydia)
• Strongly associated with HLA-B27

Clinical features may include:

• Asymmetric oligoarthritis (lower limbs)
• Conjunctivitis or uveitis
• Urethritis
• Sacroiliitis
• Enthesitis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 36-year-old woman is referred for evaluation because of hematuria and haemoptysis since 2 weeks. DLCO is 120% of normal with normal lung volumes. What is the likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Microscopic polyangiitis

An increased DLCO with normal lung volumes in a patient with hemoptysis and hematuria suggests diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) due to pulmonary capillaritis.

• DLCO increases because intra-alveolar hemoglobin binds carbon monoxide, enhancing diffusion.
• DAH commonly occurs in small-vessel vasculitis presenting with pulmonary-renal syndrome.
• Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) classically causes:

o    Hemoptysis (alveolar hemorrhage)

o    Hematuria (rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis)

o    ↑ DLCO with normal lung volumes

Why MPA most likely:

• Causes pulmonary capillaritis without granulomas
• Associated with p-ANCA (MPO)
• Pulmonary hemorrhage → ↑ DLCO

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 38-year-old man comes to the OPD due to pain in multiple joints. He has a 5-year history of lumbar pain and a 2-year history of bilateral knee pain. The patient works in construction and his pain is worst after a long day on his feet. He has taken ibuprofen intermittently, but the pain is no longer tolerable. The patient has a paternal aunt with osteoarthritis. Physical examination shows blue-black spots on his sclerae and diffuse darkening of the auricular helices. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's arthritis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Homogentisic acid dioxygenase deficiency

Ochronosis (alkaptonuria) is caused by homogentisic acid dioxygenase deficiency, leading to accumulation of homogentisic acid in connective tissues.

• Blue-black pigmentation of sclera and ear cartilage
• Darkening of urine on standing
• Early-onset degenerative arthritis of spine and large joints
• Calcification of intervertebral discs

Pathophysiology:

• Defect in tyrosine metabolism → homogentisic acid deposition in cartilage and connective tissue → ochronotic arthropathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 42-year-old man with a long history of bronchial asthma and allergic rhinitis presents with fever, weight loss, and progressive mononeuritis multiplex. Examination reveals palpable purpura over the lower limbs. Laboratory investigations show marked eosinophilia and elevated ESR. Renal biopsy demonstrates necrotizing vasculitis with extravascular granulomas. Which of the following autoantibodies is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. p-ANCA (MPO-ANCA)

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA/Churg–Strauss syndrome) is a small- to medium-vessel necrotizing vasculitis characterized by:

• Long-standing asthma and allergic rhinitis
• Eosinophilia
• Palpable purpura
• Mononeuritis multiplex
• Necrotizing vasculitis with extravascular granulomas

The autoantibody most commonly associated is p-ANCA (myeloperoxidase/MPO-ANCA).

Differentiation from other vasculitis:

• A. Anti-dsDNA: Systemic lupus erythematosus
• B. c-ANCA (PR3): Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener)
• D. Anti-GBM: Goodpasture syndrome

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 43-year-old man presents with gradually progressive exertional dyspnea and occasional nocturnal breathlessness over the past 3 months. Examination reveals perioral skin tightening, smooth shiny skin with patchy depigmentation over the hands, a prominent lower sternal heave, and an S3 gallop. His lungs are clear on auscultation. Which of the following autoantibodies is most strongly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) antibodies

The patient has diffuse systemic sclerosis (diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis).

Clinical clues include:

• Skin tightening and shiny skin
• Vitiligo-like depigmentation
• Progressive cardiopulmonary involvement
• Signs of pulmonary hypertension/right ventricular strain

Diffuse systemic sclerosis is strongly associated with anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) antibodies and carries an increased risk of interstitial lung disease.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Anticentromere antibodies: Associated with limited systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome).
• B. Antimitochondrial antibodies: Primary biliary cholangitis.
• C. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies: Autoimmune thyroid disease.
• E. Anti-Smith antibodies: Highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 43-year-old man presents with progressive difficulty climbing stairs and lifting objects overhead for 6 weeks. He reports increasing fatigue and has recently started using his hands to push himself up from a chair. There is no history of trauma, sensory loss, diplopia, or fluctuation in symptoms throughout the day. On examination, there is symmetric proximal muscle weakness involving the shoulder and hip girdles. Deep tendon reflexes are normal. No cutaneous findings. Muscle biopsy demonstrates endomysial inflammatory infiltrates predominantly composed of cytotoxic lymphocytes invading non-necrotic muscle fibers. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Polymyositis

Polymyositis:

• Symmetric proximal muscle weakness (hips, shoulders)
• No skin manifestations
• Normal reflexes, no sensory loss
• Biopsy hallmark:

• Endomysial inflammation with CD8+ cytotoxic T cells invading non-necrotic muscle fibers
• Associated with MHC class I overexpression

Mechanism: Cell-mediated immunity (CD8+ T cells) → direct muscle fiber injury

Differentials:

• Dermatomyositis:

• Rash (heliotrope, Gottron papules)
• Perifascicular atrophy + complement-mediated microangiopathy

• Lambert-Eaton syndrome:

• Proximal weakness but improves with use
• Autonomic symptoms, ↓ reflexes
• Presynaptic Ca²⁺ channel antibodies

• Polymyalgia rheumatica:

• Pain and stiffness > weakness
• Normal CK

• Systemic sclerosis: Skin tightening, Raynaud’s → not primary myopathy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 44-year-old man with a long history of asthma and allergic rhinitis develops new-onset palpable purpura on his lower legs along with pain, tingling, and weakness in the distribution of the right peroneal and left ulnar nerves. Blood counts reveal marked eosinophilia, and p-ANCA is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss syndrome)

The triad of asthma, peripheral eosinophilia, and mononeuritis multiplex (asymmetric peripheral neuropathy affecting multiple individual nerves, as seen here with two separate nerve territories) in a patient with skin lesions like palpable purpura is classic for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss syndrome) — a necrotizing vasculitis of small-to-medium vessels often p-ANCA positive. Polyarteritis nodosa typically lacks asthma/eosinophilia and is usually ANCA-negative; granulomatosis with polyangiitis is c-ANCA-associated and classically involves the upper/lower respiratory tract and kidneys without the prominent eosinophilia; Henoch-Schönlein purpura is IgA-mediated and lacks this asthma-eosinophilia-neuropathy triad.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with a known autoimmune rheumatological disorder presents with ocular symptoms. Different rheumatological diseases are associated with characteristic eye manifestations, which are often helpful in diagnosis and management. Which of the following disease–ocular manifestation pairs is not correctly matched, with respect to the most common ocular involvement?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Systemic lupus erythematosus — Cataract

Many rheumatologic diseases have characteristic ocular manifestations:

Correct associations:

• Ankylosing spondylitis → Acute anterior uveitis (most common extra-articular feature)
• Behçet’s disease → Panuveitis (can cause severe vision loss)
• Rheumatoid arthritis → Sicca syndrome (secondary Sjögren) and episcleritis/scleritis

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) most commonly causes retinal vasculitis and keratoconjunctivitis sicca, not cataract. Cataracts in SLE patients are usually secondary to long-term corticosteroid therapy, not a primary ocular manifestation of the disease itself.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with long-standing Rheumatoid arthritis continues to have active synovitis despite treatment with methotrexate. She is started on Abatacept. The drug acts by preventing activation of T lymphocytes. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of abatacept?
options: Blockade of CD80/CD86 preventing T-cell co-stimulation
Depletion of B lymphocytes by CD20 targeting
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Blockade of CD80/CD86 preventing T-cell co-stimulation

Abatacept is a biologic DMARD used in rheumatoid arthritis that inhibits T-cell activation by blocking the essential co-stimulatory signal required for full T-cell activation.

• Abatacept is a CTLA-4–Ig fusion protein.
• It binds to CD80 (B7-1) and CD86 (B7-2) on antigen-presenting cells.
• This prevents interaction with CD28 on T lymphocytes, thereby blocking the second (co-stimulatory) signal required for T-cell activation.
• Result: Reduced T-cell proliferation, cytokine production, and downstream inflammation.

| Signal | Interaction

| ------ | -----------

| Signal 1 | TCR ↔ MHC-antigen complex

| Signal 2 (Co-stimulation) | CD28 (T cell) ↔ CD80/CD86 (APC)

Why not the others?

• A. Inhibition of TNF-α release → Mechanism of TNF inhibitors such as etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab.
• C. Inhibition of IL-6 receptor signaling → Mechanism of tocilizumab.
• D. Depletion of B lymphocytes by CD20 targeting → Mechanism of rituximab.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 46-year-old woman presents with acute swelling and pain in her right knee. Synovial fluid analysis reveals rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals. Laboratory tests show mild leukocytosis and normal serum uric acid. Which of the following investigations is most appropriate to evaluate an underlying metabolic cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thyroid-stimulating hormone

Rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals on synovial fluid analysis indicate calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystal deposition disease (pseudogout). Pseudogout commonly presents as an acute monoarthritis in large joints (classically the knee) and can occur idiopathically in older adults, but in relatively younger patients or recurrent disease, clinicians must evaluate for associated metabolic/endocrine disorders. Important underlying causes include hypothyroidism, hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, and hypomagnesemia. Therefore, the most appropriate investigation among the options to evaluate a metabolic association is thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) to assess for hypothyroidism. ANA and rheumatoid factor assess autoimmune inflammatory arthritis, and CPK is used for muscle injury/myositis, none of which explain CPPD.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 46-year-old woman presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness, difficulty climbing stairs, and a violaceous rash over the eyelids. Examination reveals erythematous papules over the knuckles and periungual telangiectasia. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated creatine kinase levels, and muscle biopsy demonstrates perifascicular atrophy. Further evaluation is most likely to reveal an underlying malignancy of which of the following organs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ovary

• Dermatomyositis is an autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and characteristic skin findings, including heliotrope rash (violaceous rash on eyelids) and Gottron papules (erythematous papules over knuckles).
• Muscle biopsy classically shows perifascicular atrophy.
• In adults, dermatomyositis may occur as a paraneoplastic syndrome, so patients should be screened for an underlying malignancy.
• In women, dermatomyositis is most commonly associated with ovarian carcinoma. Therefore, the malignancy most likely to be detected is ovarian cancer.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 48-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has persistent high disease activity despite adequate trials of methotrexate and a TNF-α inhibitor. Laboratory tests show markedly elevated CRP and ESR, disproportionate to clinical synovitis. A biologic agent is planned that is particularly effective in suppressing acute-phase reactant production. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tocilizumab

Tocilizumab is a monoclonal antibody against the IL-6 receptor and is particularly effective in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) who have markedly elevated acute-phase reactants (CRP, ESR).

• IL-6 is a major stimulator of hepatic acute-phase protein production
• Blocking IL-6 → rapid and profound reduction in CRP and ESR
• Used in RA patients with inadequate response to methotrexate and/or TNF-α inhibitors

Why others are less specific:

A. Etanercept: TNF-α inhibitor

B. Abatacept: Inhibits T-cell costimulation (CTLA-4 analog)

D. Rituximab: Anti-CD20 (B-cell depletion)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 5-month-old infant is brought with 9 days of high-grade fever, irritability, bilateral nonpurulent conjunctival injection, a polymorphous erythematous rash, and swelling of both feet. Laboratory investigations demonstrate: • Anemia • Leukocytosis • Platelet count: 720,000/mm³ • Elevated CRP • Mild transaminitis • Hypoalbuminemia Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Kawasaki disease

The child fulfills the diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki disease:

• Fever ≥5 days
• Bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis
• Polymorphous rash
• Extremity edema/erythema
• Laboratory evidence of inflammation

Supportive laboratory findings include:

• Thrombocytosis
• Elevated CRP/ESR
• Mild elevation of liver enzymes
• Hypoalbuminemia

Untreated disease can lead to coronary artery aneurysms.

Why the other options are incorrect

• A. EBV: Usually causes lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and atypical lymphocytosis.
• B. Hematologic malignancy: Does not produce the classic mucocutaneous features.
• C. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis: Rash is evanescent and conjunctivitis is uncommon.
• E. Measles: Characterized by cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and Koplik spots.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 51-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of severe pain in her left knee. To lose weight, she recently started jogging for 30 minutes a few times per week. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension treated with metformin and chlorothiazide. On examination, her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 138/87 mm Hg. The left knee is swollen and tender to palpation with a significantly impaired range of motion. A 1.5 cm painless ulcer is seen on the plantar surface of the left foot. Which of the following is most likely to help establish the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Perform arthrocentesis

An acutely swollen, painful joint with fever should be considered septic arthritis until proven otherwise, especially in a patient with:

• Diabetes mellitus
• Foot ulcer (possible source of bacteremia)
• Monoarticular involvement
• Marked limitation of range of motion

The most important step to establish the diagnosis is: Urgent arthrocentesis

• Synovial fluid analysis (cell count, Gram stain, culture)
• Helps differentiate septic arthritis from gout or inflammatory arthritis

Serum uric acid and rheumatoid factor are not diagnostic in acute monoarthritis.

HLA-B27 testing is irrelevant in this acute febrile presentation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 52-year-old man with long-standing gout continues to have recurrent acute attacks despite achieving partial control with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor. His serum uric acid remains above target. Renal function is normal. An additional oral drug is added that enhances renal excretion of uric acid and is approved only as add-on therapy, not for monotherapy. Which of the following drugs was most likely added?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lesinurad

Lesinurad is a selective URAT1 inhibitor that increases renal excretion of uric acid and is used in patients with gout who have inadequate response to xanthine oxidase inhibitors (eg, allopurinol, febuxostat).

• Used only as add-on therapy with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor
• Not used as monotherapy due to risk of acute renal failure
• Lowers serum uric acid by blocking renal tubular reabsorption

Other drugs:

A. Probenecid: Uricosuric that can be used as monotherapy

B. Febuxostat: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor

C. Pegloticase: IV uricase for severe refractory gout

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has been receiving hydroxychloroquine therapy for the past 8 years. She presents for routine follow-up and asks about the long-term safety of her medication, particularly concerning ocular toxicity. Fundus examination is currently normal, and she undergoes regular ophthalmologic screening. To minimize the risk of developing bull’s-eye maculopathy, what is the maximum recommended safe daily dose of hydroxychloroquine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5 mg/kg/day

Hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity (bull’s-eye maculopathy) is a serious long-term adverse effect related to cumulative dose and daily dosing.

To minimize risk:

• Maximum safe dose: ≤5 mg/kg/day (based on actual body weight)
• Risk increases with therapy >5 years, high cumulative dose, renal disease, or concomitant tamoxifen use
• Regular ophthalmologic screening (fundus exam, OCT, visual fields) is essential

Maintaining hydroxychloroquine dose at ≤5 mg/kg/day significantly reduces the risk of irreversible retinal toxicity while preserving its disease-modifying benefits in SLE and rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with fever, weight loss, and generalized myalgias for 3 weeks. He has a history of smoking and remote intravenous drug use. A few weeks earlier, he had an episode of melena with abdominal discomfort; upper gastrointestinal endoscopy at that time was normal. On current evaluation, a muscle biopsy reveals transmural inflammation of medium-sized arteries with fibrinoid necrosis and disruption of the internal elastic lamina. Which of the following is the most likely predisposing factor for this patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chronic hepatitis B infection

This is a classic presentation of Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN):

• Systemic symptoms: fever, weight loss, myalgias
• GI involvement (abdominal pain, melena due to mesenteric ischemia)
• Medium vessel vasculitis
• Biopsy: transmural inflammation + fibrinoid necrosis + disrupted internal elastic lamina

Association:

• Strongly associated with hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection
• Mechanism: immune complex deposition (HBsAg–anti-HBs) in vessel walls

Why not other options?

A. Antibiotic use → Can cause hypersensitivity vasculitis (small vessel, not PAN)

B. Asthma → Associated with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA)

C. Hypertriglyceridemia → No association with vasculitis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman comes for evaluation of persistent morning stiffness. She was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis 4 months ago and was prescribed methotrexate. The patient currently takes the maximum tolerated dose, along with folic acid and as-needed naproxen. On examination, swelling, tenderness, and pain on range of motion are found at the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints and wrists bilaterally. Treatment with etanercept is considered. Which of the following tests should be performed before beginning treatment with this agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Interferon gamma release assay

All patients must be screened for latent tuberculosis before starting TNF-α inhibitors (e.g., etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab).

• TNF-α is essential for granuloma maintenance and containment of latent TB
• TNF-α inhibitors can cause reactivation of latent tuberculosis
• Screening is mandatory before therapy using:

o    Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) or

o    Tuberculin skin test (TST)

o    ± Chest X-ray if needed

If latent TB is detected → treat TB first before starting biologic.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 57-year-old man comes to the physician because of sudden-onset fever, malaise, pain and swelling of his wrists and ankles that began a week ago. One month ago, he was started on hydralazine for adjunctive treatment of hypertension. His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F). Examination shows swelling, tenderness, warmth, and erythema of both wrists and ankles; range of motion is limited. Further evaluation is most likely to show an increased level of which of the following autoantibodies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anti-histone

Drug-induced lupus commonly occurs after exposure to drugs such as:

• Hydralazine
• Procainamide
• Isoniazid
• Minocycline
• Anti-TNF agents

Key features:

• Fever, malaise, arthritis/arthralgia
• Serositis common
• Renal and CNS involvement uncommon (unlike SLE)

Characteristic antibody: Anti-histone antibodies present in \~90% cases → most sensitive marker

Other antibodies:

• Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith → typical of SLE, not DIL
• Symptoms usually resolve after stopping offending drug

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 65-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to a 3-day history of headaches localized to the right temporal region. The headaches are accompanied by intermittent blurring of vision in both eyes. The patient has also felt fatigued for the past week, with stiffness in the shoulders and hips. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 115 mm/hr. Which of the following is the most important mediator of this patient's current condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. IL-6

This patient has giant cell (temporal) arteritis, suggested by:

• Age >50 years
• Temporal headache with visual symptoms
• Polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms (shoulder/hip stiffness)
• Very high ESR

Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is the key inflammatory mediator driving:

• Systemic inflammation and constitutional symptoms
• Elevated ESR and CRP
• Vascular inflammation and intimal proliferation
• IL-6 inhibitors (eg, tocilizumab) are effective treatments in giant cell arteritis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 68-year-old man presents with acute onset pain and swelling of the knee joint. Synovial fluid analysis reveals rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals. X-ray of the knee shows chondrocalcinosis. Which of the following underlying conditions is most commonly associated with this disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All of the above

This patient has calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD, pseudogout), characterized by:

• Acute monoarthritis
• Rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals
• Chondrocalcinosis on X-ray

CPPD is associated with several metabolic disorders, classically remembered as:

“Pseudo-Gout = 5 H’s”

• Hemochromatosis
• Hyperparathyroidism
• Hypomagnesemia
• Hypothyroidism
• Hypophosphatasia

Therefore, all of the listed conditions are recognized associations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 68-year-old woman presents with a transient episode of painless vision loss in her left eye that lasted 20 minutes and resolved spontaneously. Over the past 2 months, she reports fatigue, proximal muscle aches involving the hips and shoulders, and pain in the left jaw while chewing that improves with rest. On examination, vital signs are stable. Neurological examination and fundoscopic findings are normal. She also has a history of hypertension and hypothyroidism. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation to support the suspected diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate

This patient has classic features of giant cell arteritis (GCA)—a large vessel vasculitis seen in elderly individuals. Key clues include:

• Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular vision loss)
• Jaw claudication (highly specific)
• Polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms (proximal muscle pain and stiffness)
• Systemic features (fatigue, malaise)

The best initial investigation is an inflammatory marker such as ESR (and CRP), which is typically markedly elevated and helps support the diagnosis quickly.

• Temporal artery biopsy is the gold standard, but it is not the initial test and should not delay treatment.
• Carotid Doppler evaluates embolic causes (atherosclerosis), but jaw claudication + systemic symptoms strongly favor GCA.
• MRI brain is not indicated as there are no persistent neurological deficits.
• Rheumatoid factor is unrelated to this presentation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 72-year-old woman presents with bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain, profound early-morning stiffness, and difficulty rising from a chair for the past 3 months. She has marked elevation of ESR and CRP and shows a dramatic response to low-dose corticosteroids. During follow-up, which of the following vasculitic conditions should be actively screened for, as it is most commonly associated with this patient’s diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Giant cell arteritis

This patient has polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR), characterized by bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain, prolonged morning stiffness, elevated ESR/CRP, and a dramatic response to low-dose corticosteroids. PMR is strongly associated with giant cell arteritis (GCA), a granulomatous vasculitis of large and medium-sized arteries.

Patients with PMR should be actively screened for symptoms of GCA because untreated disease can lead to irreversible vision loss. Features suggesting Giant Cell Arteritis:

• New-onset headache
• Scalp tenderness
• Jaw claudication
• Visual disturbances (amaurosis fugax, diplopia, vision loss)
• Temporal artery tenderness

Why not the other options?

• A. Takayasu arteritis – affects younger women (<40 years) and is not commonly associated with PMR.
• B. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) – medium-vessel vasculitis with no established association with PMR.
• C. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) – ANCA-associated vasculitis affecting the respiratory tract and kidneys.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following can be given to a pregnant woman with SLE except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mycophenolate mofetil

Management of SLE in pregnancy requires use of drugs that are safe for the fetus while maintaining disease control.

Drugs considered safe in pregnancy:

• Hydroxychloroquine → continue in all patients (reduces flares, improves outcomes)
• Azathioprine → safe immunosuppressant (≤2 mg/kg/day)
• Sulfasalazine → safe with folic acid supplementation
• Low-dose steroids if required

Contraindicated in pregnancy:

• Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF)

o    Highly teratogenic

o    Causes congenital malformations (ear, facial, cardiac defects) and miscarriage

o    Must be stopped before conception

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following conditions are associated with granulomatous pathology, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)

Granulomatous inflammation is characterized by collections of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), often with multinucleated giant cells.

Conditions associated with granulomatous pathology:

• EGPA=Churg-Strauss disease
• Wegener's granulomatosis
• Takayasu arteritis → granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), however, is a necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis without granuloma formation. It shows transmural inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis but no granulomatous inflammation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following findings may be seen in long-standing chronic seropositive arthritis, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hepatic dysfunction

Long-standing chronic seropositive rheumatoid arthritis (RA) can have several extra-articular manifestations due to persistent systemic inflammation. Common findings:

• Anemia of chronic disease
• Neutropenia (eg, Felty syndrome: RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia)
• Peripheral neuropathy (due to vasculitis or nerve entrapment)

However, hepatic dysfunction is not a direct manifestation of RA. Abnormal liver function tests in RA patients are more commonly due to:

• Drug toxicity (eg, methotrexate)
• Coexisting conditions

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following statements are true regarding overlap syndrome / mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) except:
options: Patients have overlapping clinical features of systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis
Both antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and rheumatoid factor (RF) are commonly positive
Presence of anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) antibodies is specific for MCTD
Prognosis is worse compared to individual connective tissue disorders
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prognosis is worse compared to individual connective tissue disorders

Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) is an overlap autoimmune disorder with features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis, and is strongly associated with anti-U1 RNP antibodies.

• Overlapping manifestations: Raynaud phenomenon, myositis, arthritis, sclerodactyly
• Anti-U1 RNP antibody: highly specific diagnostic marker
• ANA and RF are often positive
• Typically responds well to therapy

Prognosis of MCTD is generally better than many individual connective tissue diseases (especially systemic sclerosis and SLE), unless severe pulmonary hypertension develops. Thus, the statement that prognosis is worse is incorrect.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following statements regarding drug-induced lupus (DIL) are correct except:
options: Drug-induced lupus occurs equally in both males and females
Anti-histone antibodies are present in about 80–90% of cases
Anti–TNF-α agents are known to cause severe disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nephritis is commonly present

Drug-induced lupus (DIL) is an autoimmune syndrome triggered by certain medications (eg, hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, anti-TNF agents).

• Occurs equally in males and females (unlike SLE which is female predominant)
• Anti-histone antibodies present in \~80–90% cases
• Usually mild with arthralgia, fever, serositis
• Renal and CNS involvement are rare (unlike SLE)
• Resolves after stopping the offending drug
• Anti-TNF drugs can cause more severe lupus-like disease

Thus, nephritis is not commonly present in drug-induced lupus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All the following conditions are manifestations of IgG4RD except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Crescentic glomerulonephritis

IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is a chronic fibroinflammatory disorder characterized by:

• Dense IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltration
• Storiform fibrosis
• Obliterative phlebitis
• Often elevated serum IgG4 levels
• Commonly affects multiple organs and produces tumefactive (mass-like) lesions.

Common manifestations of IgG4-RD:

• Autoimmune pancreatitis (most classic)
• IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis
• Orbital pseudotumor / dacryoadenitis
• Retroperitoneal fibrosis
• Lymphoplasmacytic aortitis
• Salivary & lacrimal gland enlargement (Mikulicz disease)
• Tubulointerstitial nephritis (most common renal involvement)

Why crescentic glomerulonephritis is NOT seen:

• IgG4-RD typically causes tubulointerstitial nephritis, not primary glomerular disease
• Crescentic GN is characteristic of:

o    ANCA-associated vasculitis

o    Anti-GBM disease

o    Immune complex GN

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: An 18-year-old woman presents with a rapidly progressive purpuric rash over both lower limbs. Two days earlier, she developed mild pain in her knees and ankles. The lesions initially appeared around one knee and subsequently spread symmetrically over both legs. She has no fever, constitutional symptoms, gastrointestinal complaints, or recent sore throat. Laboratory investigations show: • Hemoglobin: 14 g/dL • Platelet count: 260,000/mm³ • Leukocyte count: 9,000/mm³ Which of the following histopathologic findings is most likely in a biopsy of the skin lesion?
options: Extensive intravascular fibrin deposition without inflammatory infiltrate
Obliterative endarteritis with lymphocytes and plasma cells
Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with eosinophils around vessels
Small-vessel wall damage with perivascular neutrophilic infiltration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Small-vessel wall damage with perivascular neutrophilic infiltration

This patient most likely has cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis, presenting with:

• Palpable purpura over dependent areas, especially the lower limbs
• Arthralgia
• Normal platelet count
• Absence of systemic toxicity

The characteristic histology is small-vessel vasculitis with neutrophilic infiltration, vessel-wall necrosis, and fragmented neutrophil nuclei known as leukocytoclasia.

Typical biopsy findings include:

• Perivascular neutrophils
• Fibrinoid necrosis of small vessels
• Nuclear debris from fragmented neutrophils
• Extravasation of red blood cells

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Extensive intravascular fibrin deposition without inflammatory infiltrate: More consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation.
• B. Obliterative endarteritis with lymphocytes and plasma cells: Classically seen in syphilis.
• C. Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with eosinophils around vessels: Suggests eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, usually associated with asthma and eosinophilia.

High-yield pearl:

• Leukocytoclastic vasculitis = palpable purpura + normal platelets + neutrophilic small-vessel inflammation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: False-positive rheumatoid factor (RF) is seen in all of the following conditions except:
options: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection early stage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection early stage

Rheumatoid factor (RF) is an IgM antibody directed against the Fc portion of IgG and is not specific for rheumatoid arthritis. It can be falsely positive in several chronic inflammatory and infectious conditions due to polyclonal B-cell activation.

Common causes of false-positive RF:

• Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
• Infectious mononucleosis (EBV infection)
• Chronic infections such as tuberculosis
• Chronic liver disease and other autoimmune disorders

Early HIV infection is not typically associated with false-positive RF (although advanced HIV may cause nonspecific autoantibody production).

Thus, RF positivity must always be interpreted in the appropriate clinical context.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Match the following infectious organisms with the autoimmune disease: List I (Organism) A. Epstein–Barr virus B. Mycoplasma pneumoniae C. Chlamydia D. Parvovirus B19 List II (Disease) 1. Systemic lupus erythematosus 2. Reactive arthritis 3. Rheumatoid arthritis 4. Systemic sclerosis 5. Ankylosing spondylosis 6. Psoaritic arthropathy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4

Certain infections are associated with triggering or mimicking autoimmune diseases through molecular mimicry or immune dysregulation:

A. Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) → 1. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

• EBV infects B cells and promotes autoantibody production.

B. Mycoplasma pneumoniae → 3. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)

• Can trigger autoimmune arthritis through immune cross-reactivity.

C. Chlamydia → 2. Reactive arthritis

• Classic cause of post-infectious reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome).

D. Parvovirus B19 → 4. Systemic sclerosis–like autoimmune phenomena

• Associated with autoimmune connective tissue disorders.

Thus, correct pairing is: A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Patients with Sjögren’s syndrome have an increased risk of developing which of the following lymphomas?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Marginal zone B-cell lymphoma

Sjögren’s syndrome is associated with a markedly increased risk of non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphomas, most commonly marginal zone B-cell lymphoma (MALT lymphoma) arising in salivary glands.

• Chronic autoimmune stimulation of B cells → lymphoid proliferation
• Persistent parotid enlargement, lymphadenopathy, or cryoglobulinemia increases suspicion
• Can transform into diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in advanced cases

Thus, the most characteristic lymphoma associated with Sjögren’s syndrome is marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Two weeks after being treated for nongonococcal urethritis, a 34-year-old man develops acute conjunctivitis, right-knee pain, and vesicular lesions on his palms and soles. This syndrome is most strongly associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sacroiliitis

This patient has Reactive Arthritis (Reiter syndrome), a seronegative spondyloarthropathy that typically develops 1–4 weeks after a genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection, most commonly due to Chlamydia trachomatis. The classic triad includes:

• Urethritis
• Conjunctivitis
• Arthritis

The presence of vesicular/hyperkeratotic lesions on the palms and soles (keratoderma blennorrhagica) further supports the diagnosis.

Reactive arthritis belongs to the seronegative spondyloarthropathies, which are strongly associated with:

• HLA-B27
• Sacroiliitis
• Inflammatory back pain
• Enthesitis

Therefore, sacroiliitis is a well-recognized associated feature.

Why not the others?

• B. Polymyositis → Associated with inflammatory myopathies, not reactive arthritis.
• C. Esophageal dysmotility → Seen in systemic sclerosis.
• D. Hyperparathyroidism → Unrelated to reactive arthritis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Upper-lobe–predominant lung involvement is classically seen in many interstitial lung diseases and connective tissue–related disorders. All of the following conditions commonly involve the upper lobes of the lung, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rheumatoid arthritis

Certain lung diseases show upper-lobe–predominant involvement on imaging:

Common upper-lobe–predominant conditions:

• Coal worker pneumoconiosis
• Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) – strongly upper-lobe predominant, seen in smokers
• Ankylosing spondylitis – causes apical fibrobullous disease

Rheumatoid arthritis–related interstitial lung disease most commonly shows a lower-lobe predominant pattern (usual interstitial pneumonia or NSIP).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following anti rheumatoid drug increases extracellular adenosine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methotrexate

Methotrexate works primarily by inhibiting AICAR transformylase and thymidylate synthetase.

AICAR accumulates intracellularly and competes with AMP deaminase, resulting in AMP accumulation. AMP is released and converted extracellularly to adenosine, which is acts as the powerful anti-inflammatory agent. As a result, neutrophils, macrophages, dendritic cells, and lymphocytes' inflammatory functions are suppressed.

Other Options:

Option B. Leflunomide: Leflunomide inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, which is involved in the de novo synthesis of pyrimidines, thereby suppressing the proliferation of activated lymphocytes. It does not increase extracellular adenosine.

Option C. Sulphasalazine: Sulphasalazine is a prodrug that is metabolized into sulfapyridine and 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA). Its anti-inflammatory effects are primarily due to the action of 5-ASA. It does not increase extracellular adenosine.

Option D. Hydroxychloroquine: Hydroxychloroquine is thought to exert its anti-inflammatory effects by interfering with lysosomal activity and autophagy in immune cells, and by modulating the activity of toll-like receptors (TLRs). It does not increase extracellular adenosine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with chronic low back pain and morning stiffness that improves with activity. He also reports pain and redness in one eye associated with photophobia. On examination, there is restricted lumbar spine mobility and tenderness over the sacroiliac joints. Which of the following is most likely associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HLA B27

| Clue | What it points to

| ---- | -----------------

| Uveitis | Extra-articular inflammatory feature

| Sacroiliitis | Axial skeleton involvement

Uveitis with sacroiliitis is characteristic of seronegative spondyloarthropathies, especially ankylosing spondylitis. These conditions show a strong association with HLA-B27, particularly with acute anterior uveitis.

HLA-B51 is linked to Behçet’s disease.

ankylosing spondylitis

| HLA Type | Disease Association

| -------- | -------------------

| HLA-B27 | Ankylosing spondylitis, Reactive arthritis, Psoriatic arthritis

| HLA-B8 | Autoimmune diseases (e.g., myasthenia gravis, SLE)

| HLA-B5 / B51 | Behçet’s disease

| Disease | Key Feature

| ------- | -----------

| Ankylosing spondylitis | Bamboo spine

| Reactive arthritis | “Can’t see, can’t pee, can’t climb a tree”

| Psoriatic arthritis | Nail pitting + DIP

| Enteropathic arthritis | IBD-associated

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old lady complains of progressive deformities of her hands and fingers associated with stiffness which is present in both the hands and improves as the day progresses. On examination, there is symmetrical involvement of hands and fingers of both the upper limbs with flexion and ulnar deviation at the metacarpophalangeal joints. What is the most likely diagnosis in this lady?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rheumatoid arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis:

• The patient has the classical features of RA:

• Symmetrical involvement of small joints of the hands
• Morning stiffness improving with activity
• Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint involvement
• Ulnar deviation and flexion deformities, which are characteristic of long-standing RA.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Osteoarthritis: Typically affects the DIP and PIP joints (Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes), has brief morning stiffness (<30 minutes), and pain worsens with activity.
• B. Ankylosing spondylitis: Primarily affects the axial skeleton and sacroiliac joints, not the small joints of the hands.
• D. Tenosynovitis: Causes localized tendon sheath inflammation but does not produce symmetrical polyarthritis or ulnar deviation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with pain, swelling, stiffness, and tenderness involving multiple joints, particularly in the morning or after prolonged periods of inactivity. She also reports fatigue and fever. She has been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is involved in rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Type 4

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is primarily a T-cell–mediated autoimmune disease (Type IV hypersensitivity) in which CD4⁺ T cells, macrophages, and pro-inflammatory cytokines (especially TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6) drive chronic synovial inflammation, pannus formation, and progressive destruction of cartilage and bone. Although immune complexes (Type III mechanism) contribute to disease progression, the predominant hypersensitivity reaction tested in exams is Type IV.

Why not the other options?

• A. Type 1: IgE-mediated immediate reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis, allergic rhinitis, bronchial asthma).
• B. Type 2: Antibody-mediated cytotoxicity (e.g., autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Goodpasture syndrome, Graves disease, myasthenia gravis).
• C. Type 3: Immune complex-mediated disease (e.g., SLE, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, serum sickness); although rheumatoid factor forms immune complexes in RA, it is not the predominant mechanism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 48-year-old smoker presents to the OPD with complaints of cramping pain in both the calves on walking to about 100–150 metres. The pain is relieved on taking rest for about 2–3 minutes and the patient is able to walk for some more distance again before the pain appears. This presentation is suggestive of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intermittent claudication

Intermittent claudication is the classical symptom of peripheral arterial disease (PAD) caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries supplying the lower limbs. It is characterized by exercise-induced ischemic muscle pain that is reproducible, relieved by rest, and recurs after walking a predictable distance. The patient has cramping calf pain after walking 100–150 meters, which is relieved within a few minutes of rest and recurs with exertion—this is the classic presentation of peripheral arterial disease (PAD).

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Muscular fatigue: Causes generalized tiredness rather than reproducible ischemic calf pain related to walking distance.
• B. Osteoarthritis of the knee: Pain is localized to the joint, worsens with movement, and is not consistently relieved within minutes of rest.
• D. Neurogenic claudication: Seen in lumbar spinal canal stenosis. Pain is relieved by sitting or spinal flexion (shopping cart sign) rather than simply stopping walking. Walking uphill is often easier than downhill.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 52-year-old female complains of increasing pain in the right shoulder. She is also finding it increasingly difficult to do overhead abduction of the affected joint. She had been diagnosed as a diabetic 20 years back and is on treatment since then. What is the most likely cause of her clinical condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Frozen shoulder

Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) is a condition characterized by progressive pain and restriction of both active and passive movements of the shoulder, especially abduction and external rotation. It is strongly associated with diabetes mellitus, occurring more frequently and often more severely in diabetic patients.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Rotator cuff tear:

• Causes painful weakness of active abduction, but passive range of motion is relatively preserved.
• Often follows trauma or chronic degeneration.

• C. Bacterial arthritis: Presents with acute severe pain, fever, warmth, swelling, and marked tenderness, not a chronic progressive course.
• D. Osteoarthritis: Primary osteoarthritis of the shoulder is relatively uncommon and usually causes pain with movement rather than marked global restriction of motion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman with breast cancer is receiving combination chemotherapy that includes methotrexate. Leucovorin is administered to reduce methotrexate toxicity. Leucovorin rescue bypasses inhibition of which enzyme during methotrexate therapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dihydrofolate reductase

Methotrexate is a folate antagonist that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), preventing the formation of tetrahydrofolate (THF). This blocks the synthesis of thymidylate (dTMP) and purines, thereby inhibiting DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells. Leucovorin (folinic acid) is a reduced form of folic acid that bypasses DHFR inhibition and replenishes intracellular THF, rescuing normal cells from methotrexate toxicity without significantly reducing its antitumor effect.

Why not the other options?

• A. Thymidylate synthase: Inhibited by 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), not methotrexate.
• C. Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD): Enzyme responsible for the metabolism of 5-FU; DPD deficiency increases 5-FU toxicity.
• D. Methionine synthase: Vitamin B₁₂-dependent enzyme involved in homocysteine metabolism; not the target of methotrexate.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A middle-aged female patient with RA for 5 years also has a family history of RA. She's on treatment with methotrexate with worsening symptoms. She was enrolled in a trial of a new epigenome-modifying drug. After 8 weeks, her symptoms improved. All of the following regarding this drug is true except:
options: It directly binds to cytokine receptors to block inflammatory signalling
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It directly binds to cytokine receptors to block inflammatory signalling

The stem gives:

• RA patient (chronic autoimmune arthritis)
• Methotrexate failure → escalation therapy
• “Epigenome-modifying drug” → think upstream gene regulation

Epigenetic drugs regulate gene expression upstream; they do NOT directly block cytokine receptors (that’s biologics like tocilizumab). Epigenetics = changing gene expression WITHOUT altering DNA sequence

Mechanisms include:

• Histone modification (acetylation/deacetylation)
• DNA methylation
• microRNA regulation

These affect inflammatory gene transcription.

| Feature | Epigenetic Drugs | Biologics

| ------- | ---------------- | ---------

| Level of action | Gene expression | Protein/cytokine

| Target | DNA/chromatin | Cytokines/receptors

| Example | HDAC inhibitors | Tocilizumab, Etanercept

| IL-6/TNF effect | ↓ production | Block action

| Specificity | Broad | Targeted

D) It directly binds to cytokine receptors to block inflammatory signalling

• This is the mechanism of biologics, not epigenetic drugs

| Drug | Target

| ---- | ------

| Tocilizumab | IL-6 receptor

| Etanercept | TNF-α

| Infliximab | TNF-α

These are receptor-level blockers, not gene modulators.

• RA synovium shows abnormal DNA methylation patterns
• Epigenetic therapy aims to “reset” this inflammatory memory

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with morning stiffness and tests positive for anti-CCP antibodies. Which of the following histological features is most characteristic of the underlying disease?
options: Basophilic deposition in the synovial cavity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pannus formation with synovial hypertrophy

Rheumatoid Arthritis ( RA):

• Morning stiffness (>1 hour)
• Anti-CCP positive (highly specific)
• Symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis

Pannus is not just “thick synovium” — it’s a hyper-aggressive, tumor-like granulation tissue that:

• Arises from inflamed synovium
• Invades cartilage and bone
• Causes irreversible joint destruction

Anti-CCP positivity with morning stiffness is characteristic of rheumatoid arthritis.

The hallmark histology is pannus formation—hyperplastic inflamed synovium invading and eroding cartilage and bone.

Osteophytes suggest osteoarthritis, tophi indicate gout, and basophilic deposition is not a feature of RA.

The boutonniere and swan neck deformity, ulnar deviation of the metacarpophalangeal joints and Z-thumb along with rheumatoid nodules on the joints of hands (Panel A,C); hallux valgus deformity and rheumatoid nodules in feet (Panel B).

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| Synovial hypertrophy | Thickened synovium (villous projections)

| Pannus formation | Invasive granulation tissue

| Inflammatory infiltrate | T cells, B cells, plasma cells

| Neovascularization | Increased vascularity

| Cartilage erosion | Due to enzymes (MMPs)

| Bone destruction | Osteoclast activation

| Feature | RA | OA | Gout | Pseudogout

| ------- | --- | --- | ---- | ----------

| Type | Inflammatory | Degenerative | Crystal | Crystal

| Stiffness | >1 hr | <30 min | Acute | Acute

| Antibody | Anti-CCP, RF | None | None | None

| Histology | Pannus | Cartilage loss | Tophi | CPPD crystals

| Joints | Symmetrical | Weight-bearing | 1st MTP | Knee

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with chronic gout presents with an acute flare characterized by severe pain, swelling, and tenderness of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. His serum uric acid level is elevated. Following resolution of the acute attack, which is the best drug for long-term use in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Allopurinol

Allopurinol is the first-line urate-lowering therapy for the long-term management of chronic gout. It is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that decreases the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid, thereby reducing serum urate levels and preventing recurrent gout attacks, tophi formation, and uric acid nephrolithiasis. Urate-lowering therapy should be initiated only after the acute gout attack has resolved, as starting it during an acute flare may worsen or prolong symptoms.

Why not the other options?

• B. Colchicine: Used for acute gout attacks and as prophylaxis when initiating urate-lowering therapy, but it does not reduce serum uric acid and is not the primary long-term urate-lowering drug.
• C. Rasburicase: Converts uric acid to allantoin and is mainly used for tumor lysis syndrome, not chronic gout.
• D. Indomethacin: An NSAID used for symptomatic treatment of acute gout, but it has no role in long-term urate reduction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with recurrent attacks of gout was started on a therapy that inhibits the synthesis of uric acid. His symptoms were relieved after therapy. Identify the drug he was prescribed.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Allopurinol

Recurrent gout requiring long-term control is treated by reducing uric acid synthesis.

Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, decreasing conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid.

Probenecid increases uric acid excretion, while colchicine and NSAIDs only treat acute inflammation.

| Category | Drug | Mechanism

| -------- | ---- | ---------

| ↓ Synthesis | Allopurinol | XO inhibition

| | Febuxostat | XO inhibition

| ↑ Excretion | Probenecid | URAT1 inhibition

| Breakdown urate | Pegloticase | Uric acid oxidation

| Anti-inflammatory | Colchicine | Microtubule inhibition

| | NSAIDs (Diclofenac) | COX inhibition

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All of the following are causes of secondary osteoarthritis of the hip, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diabetes

Secondary osteoarthritis (OA) of the hip occurs due to an identifiable underlying condition that damages the hip joint.

• (a) Trauma — Correct: Previous hip trauma or fracture can lead to secondary OA.
• (b) Diabetes — Incorrect → Diabetes is not a classical direct cause of secondary hip OA.
• (c) Perthes’ disease — Correct: Childhood avascular necrosis of the femoral head can cause deformity and subsequent secondary OA.
• (d) Avascular necrosis — Correct: Collapse and deformity of the femoral head can result in secondary OA.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly patient presents with knee pain, and X-ray findings reveal arthritic changes. Synovial fluid analysis shows rhomboid-shaped crystals that are positively birefringent under polarized light. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pseudo gout

Rhomboid-shaped crystals with positive birefringence on polarized microscopy are diagnostic of pseudogout, caused by calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) deposition. It commonly affects elderly patients, especially the knee, and may mimic osteoarthritis or acute gout flares.

X-ray may show chondrocalcinosis, a hallmark of CPPD crystal deposition.

| Feature | Gout | Pseudogout

| ------- | ---- | ----------

| Crystal | Monosodium urate | Calcium pyrophosphate

| Shape | Needle-shaped | Rhomboid-shaped

| Birefringence | Negative | Positive

| Color under polarized light | Yellow when parallel | Blue when parallel

| Common joint | 1st MTP (podagra) | Knee

Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals in cartilage

Leads to:

• Cartilage calcification → chondrocalcinosis
• Inflammatory response → acute arthritis

| Feature | Pseudogout | Gout | Septic Arthritis | RA

| ------- | ---------- | ---- | ---------------- | ---

| Age | Elderly | Middle-aged | Any | Middle-aged

| Joint | Knee | 1st MTP | Any | Small joints

| Crystals | CPPD | Urate | None | None

| Shape | Rhomboid | Needle | — | —

| Birefringence | Positive | Negative | — | —

| X-ray | Chondrocalcinosis | Erosions | Joint destruction | Joint space narrowing

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Anti-citrullinated peptide antibody is useful in diagnosis of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rheumatoid arthritis

Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (Anti-CCP or ACPA) antibodies are highly specific serological markers for Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). They may be detected years before the onset of symptoms and are associated with more aggressive, erosive disease and a poorer prognosis.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Sjögren’s syndrome: Characteristically associated with Anti-Ro (SSA) and Anti-La (SSB) antibodies.
• C. Scleroderma: Associated with Anti-centromere antibodies (limited cutaneous disease) and Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) antibodies (diffuse disease).
• D. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): Characteristically associated with ANA, Anti-dsDNA, and Anti-Smith (Sm) antibodies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Heberden’s nodes are present mainly in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Osteoarthritis

Heberden’s nodes are bony enlargements of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints and are a classical feature of osteoarthritis (OA). They result from osteophyte (bony spur) formation due to degeneration of the articular cartilage and are commonly seen in elderly women.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Rheumatoid arthritis: Typically involves the MCP and PIP joints, while the DIP joints are usually spared. Rheumatoid nodules are found over pressure points, not at the DIP joints.
• C. Psoriatic arthritis: Can involve the DIP joints, but is associated with dactylitis, nail pitting, and pencil-in-cup deformity, not Heberden’s nodes.
• D. Gouty arthritis: Characterized by tophi and recurrent episodes of acute monoarthritis, most commonly involving the first MTP joint (podagra).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Treatment of first choice in acute Gout is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Oral Colchicine

Acute gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by the deposition of monosodium urate crystals in the joints. The primary goal of treatment is to rapidly suppress inflammation and relieve pain.

Colchicine, NSAIDs, and corticosteroids are first-line options for an acute gout attack. In this question, oral colchicine is the correct answer.

• Colchicine inhibits microtubule polymerization, preventing neutrophil chemotaxis, activation, and phagocytosis of urate crystals, thereby reducing inflammation.
• It is most effective when started within the first 24–36 hours of symptom onset.

Why not the other options?

• A. Oral Methotrexate: Used for rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases; it has no role in acute gout.
• C. Allopurinol: A xanthine oxidase inhibitor used for long-term urate-lowering therapy, not for treating an acute attack. It should not be initiated during an acute attack unless the patient is already taking it.
• D. Sulfasalazine: A disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) used in rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease; not indicated for gout.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Urate crystals are described as having the following shape:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Long and needle-like

Monosodium urate (MSU) crystals are the diagnostic hallmark of gout. On polarized light microscopy, they appear as long, slender, needle-shaped crystals showing strong negative birefringence. In contrast, calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals seen in pseudogout are rhomboid-shaped and exhibit weak positive birefringence.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Short and stout: Not the characteristic morphology of urate crystals.
• C. Small and triangular: Not seen in crystal-induced arthropathies.
