• D. Large and rhomboid: Rhomboid crystals are characteristic of CPPD deposition disease (pseudogout), not gout.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of pegloticase?
options: Inhibition of URAT1 in renal tubules
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oxidation of uric acid

Humans lack the enzyme uricase, so:

• Uric acid accumulates → gout
• Poor solubility → crystal deposition (MSU crystals)

Pegloticase

• A pegylated recombinant uricase enzyme
• Given IV for refractory chronic gout

It oxidizes uric acid → allantoin, which is:

• Highly soluble
• Easily excreted in urine

Pegloticase is a recombinant pegylated uricase that catalyzes oxidation of uric acid to allantoin, which is highly water-soluble and easily excreted.

Humans lack endogenous uricase, making this mechanism unique and effective in refractory gout.

| Drug | Mechanism | Example

| ---- | --------- | -------

| Xanthine oxidase inhibitors | ↓ uric acid synthesis | Allopurinol, Febuxostat

| Uricosuric drugs | ↑ uric acid excretion (URAT1 inhibition) | Probenecid

| Uricase analog | Oxidation of uric acid → allantoin | Pegloticase

| Anti-inflammatory | Reduce inflammation | NSAIDs, Colchicine

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are correct regarding acetaminophen? 1. It does not interfere with platelet function. 2. It is toxic to the liver in high doses. 3. It is a non-narcotic analgesic. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Acetaminophen (Paracetamol) is a non-opioid (non-narcotic) analgesic and antipyretic with minimal anti-inflammatory activity. Unlike NSAIDs, it does not inhibit platelet function or prolong bleeding time, making it the preferred analgesic in patients at risk of bleeding. However, overdose can cause severe hepatotoxicity due to accumulation of the toxic metabolite NAPQI.

Why is D correct?

• 1. It does not interfere with platelet function: Acetaminophen has minimal effect on COX-1 in platelets and therefore does not impair platelet aggregation.
• 2. It is toxic to the liver in high doses: Overdose leads to hepatic necrosis due to accumulation of NAPQI, especially when glutathione stores are depleted.
• 3. It is a non-narcotic analgesic: Acetaminophen is a non-opioid analgesic used for mild to moderate pain and fever.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of colchicine in the acute treatment of gout?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inhibition of chemotaxis

Colchicine relieves an acute gout attack by inhibiting microtubule polymerization through binding to tubulin, thereby preventing neutrophil chemotaxis, adhesion, phagocytosis, and degranulation. This suppresses the inflammatory response to monosodium urate crystals without affecting serum uric acid levels.

Why not the other options?

• A. Inhibition of xanthine oxidase: Mechanism of allopurinol and febuxostat, which reduce uric acid production for long-term gout management.
• B. Inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase (COX): Mechanism of NSAIDs (e.g., indomethacin, naproxen), which reduce prostaglandin-mediated inflammation.
• D. Blockade of IL-1 receptors: Mechanism of anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist), used in selected refractory cases of acute gout.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following cannot be used to differentiate psoriatic arthritis from other conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Presence of diarrhea

• A seronegative inflammatory arthritis
• Associated with psoriasis
• Falls under spondyloarthropathies

Key hallmarks:

• Enthesitis
• Dactylitis
• Nail changes
• Asymmetric oligoarthritis

Genetic predisposition (HLA-B27)

↓

Immune activation (IL-17, TNF-α)

↓

Inflammation at enthesis (tendon insertion)

↓

Enthesitis + synovitis

↓

Dactylitis + joint damage

| Feature | Psoriatic Arthritis | Enteropathic Arthritis

| ------- | ------------------- | ----------------------

| Skin | Psoriasis | IBD (Crohn’s/UC)

| Nail pitting | ✔️ | ❌

| Dactylitis | ✔️ | Rare

| Enthesitis | ✔️ | ✔️

| Diarrhea | ❌ | ✔️ hallmark

| Feature | Think

| ------- | -----

| Diarrhea + arthritis | Enteropathic arthritis

| Urethritis + arthritis | Reactive arthritis

| Nail pitting + DIP | Psoriatic arthritis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following classical disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs is/are considered safe for use during pregnancy? 1. Methotrexate 2. Sulfasalazine 3. Hydroxychloroquine 4. Leflunomide Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 and 3

1. Methotrexate: Incorrect

• Contraindicated in pregnancy because it is teratogenic and can cause fetal loss and congenital abnormalities.

2. Sulfasalazine: Correct

• Considered safe during pregnancy.
• Folic acid supplementation is recommended because sulfasalazine can interfere with folate metabolism.

3. Hydroxychloroquine: Correct

• Considered safe and is commonly continued during pregnancy, particularly in rheumatoid arthritis and SLE.

4. Leflunomide: Incorrect

• Contraindicated in pregnancy due to teratogenic potential.
• It has a long half-life; cholestyramine washout is used when pregnancy is planned or occurs.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following joints are commonly affected in osteoarthritis? I. First metatarsophalangeal joint II. Proximal interphalangeal joint III. Ankle joint IV. 5th and 6th cervical vertebrae joint Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, II and IV only

Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common degenerative joint disease, characterized by progressive loss of articular cartilage, subchondral bone remodeling, osteophyte formation, and varying degrees of synovial inflammation. It primarily affects weight-bearing joints and joints subjected to repetitive mechanical stress.

• I. First metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint ✅

• Commonly involved, especially in hallux rigidus, a form of OA affecting the great toe. This causes pain and stiffness during walking.

• II. Proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint ✅

• OA commonly affects the PIP joints, producing Bouchard’s nodes.
• Distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints are also commonly involved, producing Heberden’s nodes.

• III. Ankle joint ❌

• The ankle is uncommonly affected in primary OA because of its highly congruent articular surfaces.
• OA of the ankle is usually secondary to trauma, inflammatory arthritis, or congenital deformity.

• IV. 5th and 6th cervical vertebral joints ✅

• Cervical spondylosis, particularly involving C5–C6 and C6–C7, is a common manifestation of osteoarthritis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old female presents with generalized swelling, facial puffiness, hypertension, and frothy urine. She also reports a history of recurrent oral ulcers, photosensitivity, and intermittent joint pain. Investigations reveal positive ANA and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, decreased serum C3 and C4 levels, and proteinuria of 4.2 g/day. What is the most likely underlying mechanism responsible for her renal injury?
options: ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis causing glomerular damage
Formation and deposition of immune complexes in the glomeruli with subsequent complement activation
Autoantibodies directed against the glomerular basement membrane
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Formation and deposition of immune complexes in the glomeruli with subsequent complement activation

The patient has systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with lupus nephritis, characterized by proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), edema, hypertension, positive ANA, anti-dsDNA antibodies, and low C3/C4 levels, photosensitivity, oral ulcers and arthritis. The renal injury in lupus nephritis is caused by Type III hypersensitivity, in which circulating antigen-antibody immune complexes deposit in the glomeruli, activate the classical complement pathway, and trigger inflammation, leading to glomerular damage.

Why not the other options?

• A. ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis causing glomerular damage: Seen in granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; typically ANCA-positive and complement levels are normal.
• B. T-lymphocyte-mediated cytotoxic injury (Type IV hypersensitivity): Characteristic of diseases such as contact dermatitis and type 1 diabetes mellitus, not lupus nephritis.
• D. Autoantibodies directed against the glomerular basement membrane: Seen in Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease), which presents with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old female patient presents with dry mouth and a gritty sensation in the eyes. She has normal anion gap metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia. She also has enlarged salivary glands. What is the best investigation to arrive at a diagnosis?
options: Serum ACE levels and Chest X-ray
Schirmer test and auto antibodies measurement
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Schirmer test and auto antibodies measurement

This question is packed with classic clues:

| Feature | Significance

| ------- | ------------

| Dry mouth (xerostomia) | Salivary gland involvement

| Gritty eyes | Keratoconjunctivitis sicca

| Enlarged salivary glands | Lymphocytic infiltration

| Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis + hypokalemia | Distal renal tubular acidosis (Type 1 RTA)

Put together → Primary Sjögren Syndrome with renal involvement

Sjögren is an autoimmune disease where:

• CD4+ T cells + B cells infiltrate exocrine glands
• Leads to:

• ↓ saliva → xerostomia
• ↓ tears → dry eyes

• Systemic involvement:

• Kidney → distal RTA → hypokalemia
• Lungs, nerves, joints

• Strong B-cell activation → ↑ risk of lymphoma

1. Schirmer Test

Measures tear production

• <5 mm wetting in 5 min → diagnostic

2. Autoantibodies

| Antibody | Significance

| -------- | ------------

| Anti-Ro (SSA) | Most sensitive

| Anti-La (SSB) | More specific

| ANA, RF | Often positive

A) Serum ACE levels and Chest X-ray

• Used for → Sarcoidosis
• Sarcoid can cause:

• Parotid enlargement
• Dryness (mimics Sjögren)

B) Improvement on trial with methylprednisolone

• Steroid response is NOT diagnostic
• Many autoimmune diseases respond to steroids

D) Salivary gland scintigraphy

• Assesses gland function
• Used as supportive evidence

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with dry eyes, dry mouth, and dry cough. She requires frequent sips of water while eating. Schirmer test was positive. Laboratory investigations revealed ANA, anti-Ro/SSA, and anti-La/SSB antibodies. What are the characteristic features seen in this condition?
options: Destruction of salivary glands due to neutrophilic infiltration
Destruction of salivary glands and lacrimal glands due to lymphocytic infiltration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Destruction of salivary glands and lacrimal glands due to lymphocytic infiltration

This vignette sketches Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune exocrinopathy:

• Xerophthalmia (dry eyes)
• Xerostomia (dry mouth)
• Needs water while eating (saliva is missing)
• Schirmer test positive (↓ tear production)

Serology seals it:

• ANA
• Anti-Ro/SSA
• Anti-La/SSB

A slow, targeted siege:

• CD4+ T cells and B cells infiltrate salivary & lacrimal glands
• Acinar cells are destroyed
• Ducts get replaced by lymphoid tissue
• Over time → glands shrink, dry, and fail

The presentation is classic for Sjögren syndrome, confirmed by positive Schirmer test and anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies.

The characteristic pathology is chronic lymphocytic infiltration of salivary and lacrimal glands causing glandular destruction and sicca symptoms.

Neutrophilic destruction, amyloid deposition, or malar rash are not defining features of Sjögren syndrome.

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| Lymphocytic infiltration | Mainly CD4+ T cells

| Acinar destruction | Loss of secretory units

| Epimyoepithelial islands | Ductal epithelial hyperplasia

| Glandular atrophy | Chronic stage

| Fibrosis | Late feature

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with dryness of the eyes requiring frequent use of artificial tears and dryness of the mouth requiring frequent sipping of water. She also reports pain and stiffness involving multiple joints of the hands. There is no history of skin tightening, Raynaud phenomenon, oral ulcers, or photosensitive rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sjögren syndrome

Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune exocrinopathy characterized by lymphocytic destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands, leading to keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) and xerostomia (dry mouth). It may occur as a primary disorder or secondary to another autoimmune disease, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis.

• Autoantibodies: Anti-SSA (Ro) and Anti-SSB (La) are highly characteristic; ANA and RF are frequently positive.
• Diagnosis: Positive Schirmer test (↓ tear production), ocular surface staining, and minor salivary gland (lip) biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis.
• Complications: Dental caries, oral candidiasis, parotid gland enlargement, corneal damage, and a markedly increased risk of MALT (marginal zone B-cell) lymphoma.
• Treatment: Artificial tears, saliva substitutes, muscarinic agonists (pilocarpine, cevimeline), and immunomodulatory therapy for systemic disease.

Why not the other options?

• A. SLE: Typically presents with photosensitive rash, oral ulcers, nephritis, serositis, and hematologic abnormalities; sicca symptoms may occur but are not the predominant feature.
• B. Systemic sclerosis: Characterized by skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and internal organ fibrosis rather than isolated sicca symptoms.
• C. Rheumatoid arthritis: Causes symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis but does not cause prominent dry eyes and dry mouth unless associated with secondary Sjögren syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with skin tightening and arthralgia. Raynaud's phenomenon was positive. Lab investigations showed ANA positive and Anti-Scl-70 antibody. The presence of which of the following conditions is associated with this antibody?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Interstitial Lung Disease

Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies are characteristic of diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

They are strongly associated with interstitial lung disease, which is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in these patients.

| Antibody | Disease Type | Key Association

| -------- | ------------ | ---------------

| Anti-Scl-70 | Diffuse SSc | Interstitial lung disease (ILD)

| Anti-centromere | Limited SSc (CREST) | Pulmonary hypertension

| Anti-RNA polymerase III | Diffuse SSc | Renal crisis

A) Calcinosis cutis

• Seen in CREST syndrome (limited SSc)
• Associated with Anti-centromere antibody, NOT Scl-70

B) Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE)

• “Watermelon stomach”
• Seen in systemic sclerosis but:

• More linked with limited SSc / anti-centromere

• Not specifically tied to Scl-70

Calcinosis and GAVE are linked to limited cutaneous disease, while myositis is not a typical association.

| Feature | Diffuse SSc | Limited SSc (CREST)

| ------- | ----------- | -------------------

| Skin involvement | Widespread | Distal only

| Antibody | Anti-Scl-70 | Anti-centromere

| Lung | Interstitial fibrosis (ILD) | Pulmonary HTN

| Renal crisis | Common | Rare

| Progression | Rapid | Slow

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Löfgren syndrome: 1. It is an acute illness and is more commonly seen in females. 2. It is a clinically distinct phenotype of sarcoidosis characterized by peripheral arthropathy and uveitis. 3. Clinical features include fever, erythema nodosum and bilateral lymphadenopathy. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1 and 3 only

Löfgren syndrome is an acute, self-limiting presentation of sarcoidosis with an excellent prognosis. It is considered a distinct clinical phenotype of sarcoidosis and is seen more commonly in young females.

Löfgren syndrome (acute sarcoidosis, good prognosis):

• Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy
• Erythema nodosum
• Migratory polyarthralgia (ankles especially)
• ± Fever
• No uveitis or neuropathy in this triad — that's the trap

Heerfordt syndrome (uveoparotid fever) — this is the one with uveitis

• Anterior uveitis
• Parotid gland enlargement
• Facial nerve palsy (cranial neuropathy, not peripheral)
• Fever

Neurosarcoidosis (general):

• Cranial neuropathies (CN VII most common)
• Can also cause peripheral neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex or symmetric polyneuropathy) — less classic than the cranial nerve involvement, but tested
• CNS involvement (mass lesions, meningitis, hypothalamic-pituitary axis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Drug of choice for long-term management of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) to reduce disease activity and flares is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydroxychloroquine

Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is the cornerstone of long-term treatment for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and is recommended for nearly all patients unless contraindicated. Hydroxychloroquine exerts its effect by inhibiting lysosomal antigen processing and Toll-like receptor (TLR-7 and TLR-9) signaling, thereby decreasing autoantigen presentation and cytokine production.

• Hydroxychloroquine is the drug of choice for long-term maintenance therapy in SLE because it:

• Reduces disease flares
• Improves skin and joint manifestations
• Prevents disease progression
• Improves long-term survival
• Lowers thrombotic risk, especially in patients with antiphospholipid antibodies

Why not the other options?

• B. Methotrexate: Used as a steroid-sparing agent for lupus arthritis or skin disease but is not the first-line maintenance drug for all SLE patients.
• C. Cyclophosphamide: Reserved for severe organ-threatening lupus (e.g., lupus nephritis, neuropsychiatric lupus) because of significant toxicity.
• D. Ibuprofen: Provides symptomatic relief of pain and arthritis but does not modify disease activity or prevent flares.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The best drug for maintenance therapy of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) during pregnancy is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydroxychloroquine

Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is the drug of choice for maintenance therapy in pregnant women with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). It is considered safe throughout pregnancy and should be continued because it reduces disease flares, improves maternal outcomes, and decreases the risk of adverse fetal outcomes.

Discontinuing hydroxychloroquine during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of lupus flares. May reduce the risk of congenital heart block in anti-Ro/SSA-positive mothers

Why not the other options?

• B. Sulfasalazine: Used mainly for rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease, not as maintenance therapy for SLE.
• C. Tacrolimus: May be used in selected cases (e.g., lupus nephritis), but it is not the first-line maintenance drug.
• D. Progestins: Used for contraception or prevention of preterm birth in selected situations, not for treating SLE.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following autoantibodies is most commonly associated with fetal heart block?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anti-Ro antibody

Anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies are the autoantibodies most strongly associated with congenital heart block (CHB) in the fetus. These maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and can damage the fetal atrioventricular (AV) node, leading to irreversible congenital complete heart block. They are classically seen in mothers with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) or Sjögren syndrome, although they may also be present in asymptomatic women.

• Anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies are the most common cause of immune-mediated congenital heart block.
• Fetal manifestations include:

• Congenital complete heart block
• Fetal bradycardia
• Neonatal lupus syndrome

Why not the other options?

• A. Anti-dsDNA antibody: Highly specific for SLE and correlates with disease activity, especially lupus nephritis, but is not associated with fetal heart block.
• C. Anti-Smith antibody: Highly specific for SLE, but has no association with congenital heart block.
• D. Anti-Jo antibody: Associated with polymyositis/dermatomyositis (antisynthetase syndrome), not neonatal lupus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common clinical feature of systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arthralgia & Myalgia

• Immune complex deposition (Type III hypersensitivity)
• Autoantibodies (anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm)
• Cytokine-mediated inflammation

Synovial tissue is highly vascular → prone to immune complex deposition therefore commonly involved-

• Leads to:

• Non-erosive arthritis
• Arthralgia (most common)
• Myalgia

Clinical Manifestations of SLE and Prevalence over the Entire Course of Disease

| Feature | SLE | RA

| ------- | --- | ---

| Arthritis | Non-erosive | Erosive

| Deformity | Rare | Common

| Pain | Mild-moderate | Severe

| Antibodies | ANA, anti-dsDNA | RF, anti-CCP

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following antibodies is commonly associated with Drug-induced Lupus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anti-histone antibody

Drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DIL) is an autoimmune syndrome triggered by certain medications and resembles systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The hallmark serological finding is the presence of anti-histone antibodies, which are positive in >95% of cases. Symptoms usually resolve after discontinuation of the offending drug.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Anti-centromere antibody: Associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome).
• B. Anti-Jo-1 antibody: Associated with polymyositis/dermatomyositis, particularly antisynthetase syndrome.
• D. Anti-RNP antibody: Characteristic of Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD); may also be seen in SLE.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct in respect of pulmonary involvement in rheumatoid disease?
options: Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules are usually asymptomatic and detected incidentally on imaging
Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules are often solitary and located near hilum
Pleural effusion in these patients is transudative and usually bilateral
Combination of pleural effusion and pneumoconiosis in these patients is known as Caplan syndrome
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules are usually asymptomatic and detected incidentally on imaging

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune disease with several extra-articular pulmonary manifestations, including interstitial lung disease (ILD), pleural disease, pulmonary nodules, airway disease, and pulmonary hypertension. Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules are usually:

• Asymptomatic
• Multiple
• Peripheral and subpleural
• Incidentally detected on chest X-ray or CT scan
• More common in seropositive RA, males, smokers, and patients with rheumatoid nodules elsewhere.

Why not the other options?

• B. Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules are often solitary and located near hilum: Incorrect. They are typically multiple, peripheral, and subpleural, not hilar.
• C. Pleural effusion is transudative and usually bilateral: Incorrect. Rheumatoid pleural effusions are exudative, usually unilateral, with low glucose, low pH, and high LDH. ⭐
• D. Combination of pleural effusion and pneumoconiosis is known as Caplan syndrome: Incorrect. Caplan syndrome is the combination of rheumatoid arthritis and pneumoconiosis (especially coal workers’ pneumoconiosis or silicosis) with multiple pulmonary nodules—not pleural effusion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following terms denotes the extensive sclerosis of the skin of the chest wall which restricts chest wall movement and is seen as a rare complication of systemic sclerosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hidebound Chest

Hidebound chest refers to extensive fibrosis and sclerosis of the skin and subcutaneous tissues of the chest wall seen in systemic sclerosis (scleroderma). The skin becomes thick, tight, and adherent, restricting chest wall expansion and leading to reduced respiratory movements and a restrictive ventilatory defect.

In addition to skin fibrosis, interstitial lung disease (ILD) is a common pulmonary manifestation of systemic sclerosis and further contributes to restrictive lung disease.

Why not the other options?

• A. Flail chest: Caused by multiple consecutive rib fractures resulting in paradoxical chest wall movement after trauma.
• C. Barrel chest: Increased anteroposterior diameter of the chest, classically seen in emphysema/COPD.
• D. Pigeon chest (Pectus carinatum): Congenital protrusion of the sternum and anterior chest wall.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient developed difficulty in standing from a seated position, walking up steps, squatting and lifting arms overhead. Chronic therapy with which of the following drugs is likely to result in such presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glucocorticoids

Glucocorticoid-induced myopathy is a common complication of chronic corticosteroid therapy. It presents with painless, symmetric proximal muscle weakness, causing difficulty in rising from a chair, climbing stairs, squatting, and lifting the arms overhead. It results from muscle protein catabolism, predominantly affecting type II (fast-twitch) muscle fibers.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Acetaminophen❌: Does not cause myopathy; toxicity primarily affects the liver.
• B. Fexofenadine❌: A second-generation antihistamine that is not associated with proximal muscle weakness.
• D. Metformin ❌

• May rarely cause vitamin B12 deficiency or lactic acidosis, but does not cause steroid-like proximal myopathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the major contributor to frailty?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sarcopenia

Frailty is a geriatric syndrome characterized by reduced physiological reserve and increased vulnerability to stressors. Sarcopenia (age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and function) is the major biological contributor to frailty and is central to its pathogenesis.

Why is A correct?

• Sarcopenia leads to:

• Decreased muscle strength
• Reduced physical performance
• Increased risk of falls
• Functional dependence

• It is the primary contributor to the development and progression of frailty.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with fatigue and intermittent low-grade fever. She reports dizziness and weakness of her left upper limb during physical activity. On examination, the pulse in the left radial artery is diminished compared with the right, and there is a marked difference in blood pressure between the two arms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Takayasu arteritis

Takayasu arteritis is a chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis that primarily affects the aorta and its major branches, especially in young women (<40 years). Inflammation causes arterial wall thickening, stenosis, and occlusion, leading to diminished or absent peripheral pulses, blood pressure discrepancy between the arms, upper limb claudication, diminished left radial pulse and vascular bruits. Because of these characteristic findings, it is known as the “pulseless disease.”

These findings result from stenosis of the subclavian artery or aortic arch branches.

Why not the other options?

• A. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis): A small-vessel ANCA-associated vasculitis presenting with upper airway disease, pulmonary nodules, and glomerulonephritis, not absent pulses.
• C. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN): A medium-vessel vasculitis affecting kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, skin, and peripheral nerves; classically associated with hepatitis B, but does not cause pulse deficits or inter-arm BP differences.
• D. Giant cell (temporal) arteritis: A large-vessel vasculitis affecting patients >50 years, presenting with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and vision loss, often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 42-year-old man presented with recurrent oral ulcers since one year, episodes of redness of eye and genital ulcers. Which one of the following tests is of diagnostic value?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pathergy test

Behçet’s disease is a chronic multisystem inflammatory vasculitis characterized by the classic triad of:

• Recurrent oral aphthous ulcers
• Genital ulcers
• Ocular involvement (uveitis)

The Pathergy test is a useful bedside diagnostic test that demonstrates cutaneous hyperreactivity. A sterile papule or pustule develops 24–48 hours after a needle prick, reflecting an exaggerated inflammatory response.

Why not the other options?

• A. Mantoux test: Used to detect tuberculosis infection, not Behçet’s disease.
• B. Drug-sensitivity test: Used to determine antimicrobial susceptibility and has no role in diagnosing Behçet’s disease.
• D. Patch test: Used to diagnose allergic contact dermatitis (Type IV hypersensitivity).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 75-year-old man presented with temporal headache, jaw pain, exacerbated by chewing and talking. Which one of the following investigations will most likely help in diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Temporal artery biopsy

Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis) is a granulomatous vasculitis of medium- and large-sized arteries, classically affecting individuals >50 years of age. It presents with new-onset temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and visual symptoms. Temporal artery biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis and should be performed promptly, although high-dose corticosteroids must be started immediately if the diagnosis is suspected to prevent irreversible blindness.

• A. Temporal artery biopsy:

• Gold standard investigation for Giant Cell Arteritis.
• Shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells, disruption of the internal elastic lamina, and intimal thickening.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Electromyography: Used to evaluate neuromuscular disorders, not vasculitis.
• C. MRI of the brain: May exclude intracranial pathology but does not diagnose Giant Cell Arteritis.
• D. Carotid colour Doppler: Evaluates carotid artery disease and stroke risk, but is not the diagnostic test for temporal arteritis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with chronic sinusitis, nasal crusting, and a saddle nose deformity. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener granulomatosis) is an ANCA-associated necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that classically involves the upper respiratory tract, lungs, and kidneys. Chronic sinusitis, persistent nasal crusting, recurrent epistaxis, and saddle nose deformity due to destruction of the nasal septum are characteristic ENT manifestations and should strongly suggest the diagnosis.

Why not the other options?

• B. Allergic rhinitis: Causes sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal itching, and pale boggy mucosa; does not cause septal destruction or saddle nose deformity.
• C. Nasal polyposis: Presents with nasal obstruction, hyposmia, and multiple pale polyps; crusting and saddle nose are not typical features.
• D. Rhinoscleroma: A chronic Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis infection causing granulomatous nodules and nasal obstruction, but saddle nose deformity is not a classic presentation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis, palpable purpura, myalgia, and pulmonary hemorrhage was found to have p-ANCA positivity. Which of the following is the likely vasculitis in him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Microscopic polyangiitis

p-ANCA–positive pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with palpable purpura and pulmonary hemorrhage is characteristic of microscopic polyangiitis.

It is a non-granulomatous small-vessel vasculitis involving capillaries, venules, and arterioles.

Organ damage:

- Kidney → RPGN (crescentic GN)

- Lung → Pulmonary hemorrhage

- Skin → Purpura

| ANCA Type | Antigen | Disease Association

| --------- | ------- | -------------------

| p-ANCA /Microscopic polyangiitis | MPO (myeloperoxidase) | MPA, EGPA

| c-ANCA /Granulomatosis with polyangiitis | PR3 (proteinase-3) | GPA (Wegener)

| Feature | MPA | GPA | PAN

| ------- | --- | --- | ---

| Vessel size | Small | Small | Medium

| ANCA | p-ANCA (MPO) | c-ANCA (PR3) | Negative

| Granulomas | ❌ | ✔ | ❌

| Lung involvement | Hemorrhage | Nodules + cavitation | ❌

| Kidney | RPGN | RPGN | Mild

GPA is usually c-ANCA with granulomas, PAN spares lungs, and Behçet’s is not ANCA-associated.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Vibration white finger refers to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Raynaud’s syndrome

Vibration white finger (VWF) is an occupational form of secondary Raynaud’s phenomenon caused by prolonged exposure to hand-transmitted vibration, such as from jackhammers, chain saws, grinders, or pneumatic drills. Repeated vibration causes vasospasm of the digital arteries, leading to episodic finger blanching and ischemia.

Why not the other options?

• A. Buerger’s disease (Thromboangiitis obliterans): An inflammatory occlusive vascular disease affecting young smokers, causing distal ischemia, ulcers, and gangrene rather than vibration-induced vasospasm.
• C. Acrocyanosis: Persistent, painless bluish discoloration of the hands and feet due to vasomotor instability; not episodic and does not show the classic triphasic color change.
• D. Takayasu disease: Large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis involving the aorta and its branches, presenting with absent pulses (“pulseless disease”), not digital vasospasm.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following in IgA vasculitis warrants the use of corticosteroids?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. GI bleeding

IgA vasculitis is a small vessel vasculitis with IgA immune complex deposition.

Classic tetrad:

• Palpable purpura (skin)
• Arthralgia/arthritis
• Abdominal pain
• Renal involvement

Usually self-limiting, especially in children

Corticosteroids in IgA vasculitis are indicated for severe gastrointestinal involvement, especially GI bleeding, due to risk of complications like intussusception and perforation.

Skin rash, arthritis, and mild abdominal pain are usually self-limiting and managed with supportive care.

Steroids are reserved for organ-threatening disease, not routine symptoms.

| Feature | Management

| ------- | ----------

| Skin rash only | Supportive

| Arthritis | NSAIDs

| Mild abdominal pain | Supportive

| GI bleeding | Steroids

| Renal involvement | Steroids ± immunosuppressants

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not correct regarding Behçet's disease?
options: Pathergy test is a criterion as per the ISG diagnostic criteria
Ulcers are common on the dorsum of the penis
Aphthous ulcers occur similar to Crohn’s disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ulcers are common on the dorsum of the penis

Behçet’s disease is like a restless storm that targets vessels of all sizes, leaving behind a trail of ulcers, eye inflammation, and systemic mischief.

• Immune-mediated vasculitis (both arteries & veins)
• Strong association with HLA-B51
• Neutrophil hyperactivity → endothelial damage

| System | Manifestation

| ------ | -------------

| Oral | Recurrent aphthous ulcers (most common)

| Genital | Painful ulcers (scrotum in males)

| Eye | Bilateral uveitis, hypopyon

| Skin | Erythema nodosum, acneiform lesions

| Vessels | Thrombosis, aneurysms

| Test | Pathergy test positive

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following vasculitis does not involve medium-sized arteries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis

Vasculitides are classified according to the predominant size of the blood vessels involved. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis, whereas Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) and Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) primarily involve medium-sized arteries, and Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) predominantly affects small vessels but may occasionally involve medium-sized arteries.

• Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is an immune complex– mediated small-vessel vasculitis involving postcapillary venules, characterized histologically by neutrophilic infiltration with leukocytoclasia (nuclear debris) and palpable purpura.

Key vessel involvement:

• PAN → Medium-sized muscular arteries (spares pulmonary arteries)
• Buerger disease → Small- and medium-sized arteries and veins of the extremities
• GPA → Predominantly small vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles), but medium arteries may also be involved
• Leukocytoclastic vasculitis → Small vessels only

| Vessel size | Entities

| ----------- | --------

| Large | Takayasu, GCA

| Medium | PAN, Kawasaki

| Small — ANCA-associated | GPA, MPA, EGPA

| Small — immune complex | Cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis, IgA vasculitis (HSP), cryoglobulinaemic, anti-GBM, hypocomplementaemic urticarial

| Variable vessel | Behçet, Cogan

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following diseases affects predominantly large arteries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Giant cell arteritis

Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) is a large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, especially the extracranial branches of the carotid artery (e.g., temporal artery). It commonly occurs in patients >50 years and presents with headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, and is often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica.

Why not the other options?

• A. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA): Small-vessel vasculitis involving the upper/lower respiratory tract and kidneys.
• B. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN): Medium-vessel vasculitis affecting renal, mesenteric, and other medium-sized arteries.
• D. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA): Small-vessel vasculitis associated with asthma and eosinophilia.
